Let $y\in X(k)$, and suppose that $c_1^{-1}(y)$ is a single reduced point
$z$, with $c_2(z)=y$. Suppose that $F_0=\{z\}$ is an isolated reduced
component of $\Fix(c)$, open and closed, and that on a neighbourhood of $F_0$
the ideal $I_y$ satisfies

$$
c_2^{-1}(I_y)\mathcal O_C\subset c_1^{-1}(I_y)\mathcal O_C,
\qquad
\bigl(c_2^{-1}(I_y)\mathcal O_C\bigr)^n
\subset\bigl(c_1^{-1}(I_y)\mathcal O_C\bigr)^{n+1}
\quad\text{for some }n\geq1.
$$

Then for every $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ and every morphism
$u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$, the local term at $F_0$ is the categorical
trace of the restriction $u_Z$ to $Z=\{y\}$ of $u$ restricted to
that neighbourhood, defined in (E.21). In particular, for
$c=(\operatorname{id}_X,h)$,

$$
\operatorname{LT}_y(u)
=\operatorname{tr}_A(u_{\bar y}\mid K_{\bar y}).
$$

Let $X/k$ be smooth, proper and connected of pure dimension $d$, with
$k$ algebraically closed, and let $\Lambda$ be a field. For every $i$
the pairing

$$
\langle a,b\rangle=\operatorname{tr}_X(a\cup b),\qquad
H^i(X,\Lambda)\times H^{2d-i}(X,\Lambda)\longrightarrow\Lambda(-d),
$$

is perfect, and $\langle b,a\rangle=(-1)^i\langle a,b\rangle$. In
particular, if $d$ is odd and $\Lambda$ has characteristic zero, the
pairing on $H^d(X,\Lambda)$ is alternating, as for a compact complex
manifold of odd dimension.

Let $\mathcal V$ be a nonzero lisse Weil sheaf of rank $r$ on a smooth
geometrically connected curve.  Its determinant has finite geometric
monodromy and is punctually pure of weight
$r\operatorname{dw}_\iota(\mathcal V)$. The number
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(\mathcal V)$ does not depend on the choice of
$s$ or of a finite coefficient field over which $\mathcal V$ is defined.

Let $U_0/k_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected curve, with the
coefficients and Weil group of Convention [sec-Weil-sheaves-and-weights]. Let $\rho$ be a lisse
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-representation of $W(U_0)$ on a
finite-dimensional space $V$, put $r=\dim V$, and let $s$ be the chosen
degree-one lift.

The set $\det\rho(\pi_1(U))$ is finite. Moreover, for every closed point
$x$ of $U_0$,

$$
\frac{2\log|\iota(\det\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_x))|}{\log q_x}
=\lambda_\iota(\det\rho(s)).
$$

When $r=0$, $\det\rho$ is the trivial character and both sides vanish. For
$r>0$, since $\operatorname{dw}_\iota(\mathcal V)=\lambda_\iota(\det\rho(s))/r$
(Definition [definition-determinant-weight]), the formula says that the
determinant line is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight
$r\operatorname{dw}_\iota(\mathcal V)$, where $\mathcal V$ is the sheaf
corresponding to $\rho$.

Let $W$ be a weakly contractible object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, for instance
$W=\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ with $D$ w-contractible.

1. The functor $F\mapsto F(W)$ from abelian sheaves on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ to
   abelian groups is exact. Hence $H^q(W,F)=0$ for $q>0$, and
   $R\Gamma(W,K)\simeq K(W)$ for every complex $K$, with the right side
   computed term by term.
2. If $W$ is affine, evaluation at $W$ preserves all limits and all
   colimits of $\mathcal R$-modules.
3. Exactness of complexes and isomorphisms of $\mathcal R$-module
   sheaves can be tested by evaluation on all affine weakly contractible
   objects of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.
Evaluation $F\mapsto F(W)$ from abelian sheaves to abelian groups is exact.
For an abelian sheaf $F$, one has $H^q(W,F)=0$ for $q>0$.
For every complex $K$, $R\Gamma(W,K)\simeq K(W)$, with the right side computed term by term.

If $W$ is affine, evaluation $M\mapsto M(W)$ from sheaves of
$\mathcal R$-modules to $\mathcal R(W)$-modules preserves all existing
limits, whatever the size of the indexing category.

If $W$ is affine, evaluation $M\mapsto M(W)$ from sheaves of
$\mathcal R$-modules to $\mathcal R(W)$-modules preserves all existing
colimits, whatever the size of the indexing category.

Let $A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C$ be a sequence of
$\mathcal R$-module sheaves with $g\circ f=0$. It is exact at $B$ if and
only if

$$
A(W)\xrightarrow{f(W)}B(W)\xrightarrow{g(W)}C(W)
$$

is exact for every affine weakly contractible $W$.

Consequently a complex $K$ of $\mathcal R$-module sheaves is acyclic if
and only if $K(W)$ is acyclic for every such $W$. No boundedness
assumption is needed.

A morphism $f\colon A\to B$ of $\mathcal R$-module sheaves is an
isomorphism if and only if $f(W)\colon A(W)\to B(W)$ is bijective for
every affine weakly contractible $W$.

Likewise, a morphism $v\colon K\to L$ of complexes of
$\mathcal R$-module sheaves is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if
$v(W)\colon K(W)\to L(W)$ is a quasi-isomorphism for every such $W$.
No boundedness assumption is needed.

*Shared context.* Let $W$ be weakly contractible in
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, for example $\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ with $D$
w-contractible. Let $\mathcal R$ be a sheaf of rings, not necessarily
commutative. Complexes are cochain complexes indexed by $\mathbf Z$,
with no boundedness assumption.

For every $n\geq1$ there is a canonical exact sequence on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{E,X}
\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}\mathcal O_{E,X}
\longrightarrow(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X\longrightarrow0.
$$

Thus the quotient is represented by the two-term complex
$[\mathcal O_{E,X}\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}\mathcal O_{E,X}]$ in degrees
$-1,0$. Under this representation, reduction from level $n+1$ to level
$n$ is the chain map $(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$. These resolutions and maps
commute with inverse image along every morphism of schemes.

attrs.title: Finite quotients and their transition maps

objects.body:
For every $n\geq1$ there is a canonical exact sequence on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{E,X}
\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}\mathcal O_{E,X}
\longrightarrow(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X\longrightarrow0.
$$

Here the coefficient sheaves are obtained by pulling back the continuous
condensed coefficients from the point, and the quotient carries its
restricted $\mathcal O_{E,X}$-action. The arrows are the pullbacks of
multiplication by the chosen uniformizer power and the quotient map.
There is no assumption that $\ell$ is invertible on $X$.

attrs.title: Finite quotients and their transition maps (1)

objects.body:
Put $R=\mathcal O_{E,X}$ and $B_n=(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X$. For $n\geq1$, the
augmentation

$$
[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}R]\longrightarrow B_n[0],
$$

with the two terms in degrees $-1,0$ and given in degree $0$ by the quotient
map of clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--1], is a quasi-isomorphism. Reduction from level
$n+1$ to level $n$ is represented by the chain map $(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$ from
$[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^{n+1}}R]$ to $[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}R]$: it is compatible
with the two augmentations and the reduction map $B_{n+1}\to B_n$, so under
these quasi-isomorphisms it is that map in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$.

attrs.title: Two-term resolutions of the finite quotients

objects.body:
For every morphism of schemes $f:X\to Y$, there is a canonical monoidal
natural isomorphism

$$
f^{-1}\circ p_Y^*\xrightarrow{\sim}p_X^*
$$

on condensed abelian groups. Its naturality applies to multiplication
by $\pi_E^n$, to reduction modulo $\pi_E^n$, and to the quotient
transition maps. Thus it identifies the inverse images of the coefficient
exact sequences, two-term resolutions and their transition maps on $Y$
with the corresponding sequences, resolutions and maps on $X$.

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated and let $\Lambda$ be a discrete
Noetherian ring. The equivalence
$\nu_X^*:D^b_c(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ of
Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves] restricts to an equivalence

$$
D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\simeq D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda).
$$

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated and let $\Lambda$ be a discrete
commutative Noetherian ring. There is a derived comparison functor

$$
\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\longrightarrow
D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)
$$

with a natural isomorphism
$\nu_X^*Q_{\acute{e}t}(P)\simeq Q_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}(\nu_X^*P)$
for every complex $P$, where $Q$ denotes localization at quasi-isomorphisms
and the inverse image on the right is applied termwise.
For every $K\in D^b_c(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and integers $a\leq b$,

$$
K\text{ has Tor amplitude in }[a,b]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\nu_X^*K\text{ has Tor amplitude in }[a,b].
$$

Here Tor amplitude is tested against every sheaf of modules on the
respective site, placed in degree zero, as in
[definition-constructible-sheaves]. Consequently, the bounded constructible
equivalence of [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves] restricts to an
equivalence

$$
D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\simeq D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda).
$$

These are full subcategories of the ambient derived categories, and the
forward equivalence, followed by inclusion, is naturally isomorphic to
$\nu_X^*$ restricted to $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

Let $X_0/\mathbf F_q$ be smooth and proper of pure dimension $d$, and let
$\ell\nmid q$. Put $H^i=H^i(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf Q_\ell)$, let $F_i$ be the Frobenius operator $F$ on $H^i$
(Section [sec-Weil-complexes]), and put

$$
b_i=\dim_{\mathbf Q_\ell}H^i,\qquad \chi=\sum_i(-1)^ib_i,\qquad
D=\prod_i\det(F_i)^{(-1)^i}.
$$

Then $b_{2d-i}=b_i$, $d\chi$ is even, $D^2=q^{d\chi}$, and in $\mathbf Q_\ell(T)$

$$
Z\!\left(X_0,\frac1{q^dT}\right)=(-1)^{\chi}D\,T^{\chi}\,Z(X_0,T)
=\varepsilon q^{d\chi/2}T^{\chi}Z(X_0,T),
\qquad \varepsilon=(-1)^\chi Dq^{-d\chi/2}\in\{1,-1\}.
$$
Put $b_i=\dim_{\mathbf Q_\ell}H^i$.

In $\mathbf Q_\ell(T)$,

$$
Z\!\left(X_0,\frac1{q^dT}\right)=\varepsilon q^{d\chi/2}T^\chi Z(X_0,T).
$$
Put $\chi=\sum_i(-1)^ib_i$.
Put $D=\prod_i\det(F_i)^{(-1)^i}$.
One has $b_{2d-i}=b_i$.
The integer $d\chi$ is even.
One has $D^2=q^{d\chi}$.

In $\mathbf Q_\ell(T)$,

$$
Z\!\left(X_0,\frac1{q^dT}\right)=(-1)^\chi D\,T^\chi Z(X_0,T).
$$
Put $\varepsilon=(-1)^\chi Dq^{-d\chi/2}$.
The sign $\varepsilon$ lies in $\{1,-1\}$.

We have $H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)=0$, and there is a Frobenius-equivariant
isomorphism $H_c^1(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)\simeq(j'_*M')_{0'}$ with the stalk
at the origin $0'$ of the dual line. In particular $H_c^1(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$

objects.body:
Let $k_0=\Fq$, let $\ell$ be a prime different from
$\operatorname{char}(k_0)$, and let
$\psi:k_0\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$ be an additive character.
Let $M$ and $M'$ be lisse Weil $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaves on
dense opens $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ and
$j':U'_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^{1\vee}_{k_0}$, and suppose that

$$
\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\simeq(j'_*M')[1].
$$

Then $H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)=0$.

objects.body:
Let $k_0=\Fq$, let $\ell$ be a prime different from
$\operatorname{char}(k_0)$, and let
$\psi:k_0\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$ be an additive character.
Let $M$ and $M'$ be lisse Weil $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaves on
dense opens $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ and
$j':U'_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^{1\vee}_{k_0}$, and suppose that

$$
\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\simeq(j'_*M')[1].
$$

There is a Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism

$$
H_c^1(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)\simeq(j'_*M')_{0'},
$$

where $0'$ is the rational origin of the dual line. Geometric Frobenius
on the cohomology corresponds to local Frobenius at $0'$.

Give $\Lambda_X$ the Weil structure of constant sheaves defined after
Definition [definition-weil-structure]. For every coefficient
ring $\Lambda$ of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula] and every $m\geq1$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tr}_{\Lambda}
(\operatorname{Frob}_{X,\Lambda_X}^m\mid R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X))
=\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\cdot1_{\Lambda}.
\tag{12.9}
$$

For $\Lambda=\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, this gives

$$
\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})
=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}
(\operatorname{Frob}_{X,\Lambda_X}^m\mid H_c^i(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X)),
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z(X_0,T)
&:=\exp\left(\sum_{m\geq1}
\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\frac{T^m}{m}\right)\\
&=\prod_{x\in|X_0|}(1-T^{\deg(x)})^{-1}
=\prod_i\det(1-T\operatorname{Frob}_{X,\Lambda_X}\mid H_c^i(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X))^{(-1)^{i+1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first two series lie in $1+T\mathbf Z[[T]]$, and the last equality
holds in $\Lambda[[T]]$. Moreover, $Z(X_0,T)$ belongs to
$\mathbf Q(T)$.

attrs.title: Alternating point-counting trace over a field

objects.body:
Define

$$
Z(X_0,T):=\exp\left(\sum_{m\geq1}\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\frac{T^m}{m}\right).
$$

Let $X_0$ be any scheme of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$. Then, in
$\mathbf Q[[T]]$,

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\prod_{x\in|X_0|}(1-T^{\deg(x)})^{-1},
\qquad \deg(x)=[\kappa(x):\mathbf F_q].
$$

The product is over closed points and converges coefficient by coefficient:
the coefficient of $T^n$ is already determined by the finitely many points
of degree at most $n$.

For $\Lambda=\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, in $\Lambda[[T]]$,

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\prod_i\det(1-T\operatorname{Frob}_{X,\Lambda_X}\mid H_c^i(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X))^{(-1)^{i+1}}.
$$

Let $X_0$ be any scheme of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$. There is a
series $Z_{\mathbf Z}(T)\in\mathbf Z[[T]]$ whose image in
$\mathbf Q[[T]]$ is $Z(X_0,T)$, and $Z(X_0,0)=1$. Consequently
$Z_{\mathbf Z}(0)=1$, and the exponential series and Euler product of
[corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--4] lie in
$1+T\mathbf Z[[T]]$.

Let $X_0$ be any scheme of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$. There are
polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbf Q[T]$ with $Q(0)=1$ such that

$$
Z(X_0,T)Q(T)=P(T)\quad\text{in }\mathbf Q[[T]].
$$

In particular, $Z(X_0,T)$ belongs to $\mathbf Q(T)$.
*Shared context.* Use the separated finite-type $X_0/\mathbf F_q$ of the preceding trace formula and its constant sheaf with the prescribed Weil structure. The integer $m$ is positive.

Every rank-one lisse Weil sheaf on a smooth geometrically connected
curve is punctually $\iota$-pure.  For $c=\chi(s)$ its weight is
$\lambda_\iota(c)=2\log_q|\iota(c)|$.

Let $U_0/\Fq$ be a smooth geometrically connected curve, put
$U=U_0\times_{\Fq}\Fbar$, and fix a prime $\ell\nmid q$ and an embedding
$\iota:\Qbarl\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$ as in [sec-Weil-sheaves-and-weights]. Let $W(U_0)$
be its Weil group, with geometric subgroup $\ker(\deg)=\pi_1(U)$ and chosen
degree-one lift $s$.

Let $\chi:W(U_0)\to\Qbarl^\times$ be a character whose restriction to
$\pi_1(U)$ is continuous, and put $c=\chi(s)$. For every closed point
$x$ of $U_0$, the local weight is

$$
\frac{2\log|\iota(\chi(\operatorname{Frob}_x))|}{\log q_x}
=\frac{2\log|\iota(c)|}{\log q}
=\lambda_\iota(c).
$$

In particular, every rank-one lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$ is punctually
$\iota$-pure of weight $\lambda_\iota(c)$, where $\chi$ is its character.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C/k$ be a smooth proper
connected curve of genus $g$, and let $n>0$ be invertible in $k$.
Then there is a noncanonical isomorphism

$$
J(C)[n](k)\simeq(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2g}.
$$

For every algebraically closed
extension $k'/k$, the natural map

$$
J(C)[n](k)\longrightarrow J(C_{k'})[n](k')
$$

is an isomorphism. Multiplication by $n$ on $J(C)(k)$ is
surjective, and consequently

$$
\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]=J(C)[n](k),
\qquad
\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)
\xrightarrow[\deg]{\ \sim\ }\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z.
$$

objects.body:
Let $A/k$ be an abelian variety of dimension $d$. There is a
noncanonical isomorphism of abelian groups

$$
A(k)[n]\simeq(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2d}.
$$

In particular, taking $A=J(C)$ and $d=g$ gives
$J(C)[n](k)\simeq(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^{2g}$.
For every algebraically closed $k'/k$, the natural map $J(C)[n](k)\to J(C_{k'})[n](k')$ is an isomorphism.

For every abelian variety $A/k$ and every integer $m>0$,
multiplication by $m$ on $A(k)$ is surjective. No invertibility
assumption on $m$ is needed.

In particular, $J(C)(k)$ is divisible. Under its identification
with $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)=\ker(\deg)$, this says that

$$
\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}^0(C),
\qquad \cL\longmapsto\cL^{\otimes m}
$$

is surjective for every $m>0$.
One has $\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]=J(C)[n](k)$.

There is an isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n\operatorname{Pic}(C)
\simeq\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z.
$$

The kernel statement identifying this quotient by degree holds
without an invertibility assumption: for every integer $m>0$,

$$
\ker\bigl(\deg\bmod m:\operatorname{Pic}(C)
\longrightarrow\mathbf Z/m\mathbf Z\bigr)
=m\operatorname{Pic}(C).
$$

Together with the surjectivity of degree, this identifies the
quotient isomorphism with the one induced by degree.
*Shared context.* Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $C/k$ a smooth proper connected curve of genus $g$, and $n>0$ invertible in $k$.

For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ there are natural isomorphisms of functors on
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$, respectively $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb D_YRf_!&\simeq Rf_*\mathbb D_X,&
\mathbb D_YRf_*&\simeq Rf_!\mathbb D_X,\\
\mathbb D_Xf^*&\simeq f^!\mathbb D_Y,&
\mathbb D_Xf^!&\simeq f^*\mathbb D_Y.
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, for an open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and a closed
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$,

$$
\mathbb D_Xj_!\simeq Rj_*\mathbb D_U,\qquad
\mathbb D_XRj_*\simeq j_!\mathbb D_U,\qquad
i^*\mathbb D_X\simeq\mathbb D_Zi^!.
$$

The isomorphisms in the left column are (10.3)
and (10.4); those in the right column are
obtained from them by biduality, as displayed in the proof.

On $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ there is the natural isomorphism

$$
\mathbb D_YRf_{!,\Lambda}\simeq Rf_{*,\Lambda}\mathbb D_X.
$$

On $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ there is the natural isomorphism

$$
\mathbb D_YRf_{*,\Lambda}\simeq Rf_{!,\Lambda}\mathbb D_X.

On $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ there is the natural isomorphism

$$
\mathbb D_Xf^*_\Lambda\simeq f^!_\Lambda\mathbb D_Y.

On $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ there is the natural isomorphism

$$
\mathbb D_Xf^!_\Lambda\simeq f^*_\Lambda\mathbb D_Y.

For an open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and a closed $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$, the indicated specialization is

$$
\mathbb D_Xj_{!,\Lambda}\simeq Rj_{*,\Lambda}\mathbb D_U.

For an open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and a closed $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$, the indicated specialization is

$$

For an open $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ and a closed $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$, the indicated specialization is

$$

A ring map $R\to B$ is *ind-étale* if
$B=\varinjlim_\alpha B_\alpha$ for a filtered system of étale
$R$-algebras $B_\alpha$. A *pro-étale affine over $X$* is a scheme
$U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ that is the limit of a cofiltered system of affine
schemes $U_i$ étale over $X$. If $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is affine,
the pro-étale affines over $X$ are the schemes

$$
\operatorname{Spec}(B)=\varprojlim_\alpha
\operatorname{Spec}(B_\alpha)\longrightarrow X
$$

with $R\to B$ ind-étale.

A scheme morphism $u:U\to X$ is *weakly étale* if $u$ and its
diagonal $\Delta_u:U\to U\times_XU$ are flat.

$$
Rf_{1*}M_1\boxtimes Rf_{2*}M_2

h^*(Rf_{1*}M_1\boxtimes Rf_{2*}M_2)

M_1\boxtimes M_2,

where $\varepsilon_{f_i}$ is the counit of $f_i^*\dashv Rf_{i*}$ and the first
isomorphism comes from $h^*p_i^*\simeq p_i^*f_i^*$.

$\iota\det(1-T\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid\mathcal G_{\bar x})$ has real coefficients for

eigenvalues at each point is stable under complex conjugation.  In
particular, the traces of all positive powers of local Frobenius are
real.

Let $T$ be a scheme and let $F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$T_{\acute{e}t}$. The following conditions are equivalent:

1. The canonical map
   $$
   \varinjlim_{n\geq1}F[n]\longrightarrow F

   is an isomorphism, where positive integers are ordered by divisibility
   and $F[n]$ is as in [definition-torsion-sheaves--2].
2. Every section of $F$ is locally killed by a positive integer on an
   étale covering; the integer may vary between members of the covering.
3. For every algebraically closed field $\Omega$ and every geometric
   point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$, the stalk of $F$ is a torsion
   abelian group.

Condition 2 is also equivalent to torsion in the sense of
[definition-torsion-sheaves--1], using all separably closed geometric
points.

A topological space is *extremally disconnected* if the closure of
every open subset is open. A spectral space $T$ is *w-local* if its set $T^c$ of closed
points is closed and every point specializes to exactly one closed
point. A ring $R$ is w-local if $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is w-local.
It is *w-strictly local* if it is w-local and
$R_{\mathfrak m}$ is strictly henselian for every maximal ideal
$\mathfrak m$. It is *w-contractible* if it is w-strictly local
and the profinite space $\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}(R))$ is
extremally disconnected.

For $U=\mathbf A^1_k$ in characteristic $p$ we get

$$
H^1(U,\mathbf F_p)=k[t]/\{h^p-h:h\in k[t]\}.
$$

Every class has a unique representative with zero constant term
and all positive exponents prime to $p$.  Indeed, we can remove
exponents divisible by $p$ using $p$th roots in the perfect field, and
we can remove the constant term since $a\mapsto a^p-a$ is surjective on $k$.
For uniqueness, note that a nonconstant polynomial $h^p-h$ has
degree divisible by $p$.  In particular the quotient is infinite, because the
classes of $t^m$ for positive $m$ prime to $p$ are $\mathbf F_p$-linearly
independent.  For an algebraically closed extension $k\subsetneq k'$
and $a\in k'\setminus k$, the class of $at$ is not in the image of the
quotient over $k$. Indeed, the reduction of a polynomial in $k[t]$ uses only
$p$th roots and roots of $x^p-x=c$ in $k$, so its reduced representative
lies in $k[t]$, whereas $at$ is already reduced. Thus finiteness and
invariance under field extension in degree one fail for $p$-torsion
coefficients on an affine curve.

For $U=\mathbf A^1_k$ in characteristic $p$ we get

$$
H^1(U,\mathbf F_p)=k[t]/\{h^p-h:h\in k[t]\}.
$$

Every class has a unique representative with zero constant term
and all positive exponents prime to $p$.  Indeed, we can remove
exponents divisible by $p$ using $p$th roots in the perfect field, and
we can remove the constant term since $a\mapsto a^p-a$ is surjective on $k$.
For uniqueness, note that a nonconstant polynomial $h^p-h$ has
degree divisible by $p$.

In particular the quotient is infinite, because the
classes of $t^m$ for positive $m$ prime to $p$ are $\mathbf F_p$-linearly
independent.  For an algebraically closed extension $k\subsetneq k'$
and $a\in k'\setminus k$, the class of $at$ is not in the image of the
quotient over $k$. Indeed, the reduction of a polynomial in $k[t]$ uses only
$p$th roots and roots of $x^p-x=c$ in $k$, so its reduced representative
lies in $k[t]$, whereas $at$ is already reduced.

Thus finiteness and
invariance under field extension in degree one fail for $p$-torsion
coefficients on an affine curve.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $X=\mathbf A^1_k$, $i:0\to X$ the origin and
$j:U=\mathbf G_{m,k}\to X$ its complement, and take $\Lambda$ finite. The
sheaf $j_!\Lambda_U$ has stalk zero at $0$, but its dual does not. By
(10.3) for $j$ and $\omega_U=\Lambda_U(1)[2]$,

$$
\mathbb D_X(j_!\Lambda_U)\simeq Rj_*\mathbb D_U\Lambda_U
=Rj_*\Lambda_U(1)[2],
$$

and by Example [example-closed-support] its stalk at $0$ is $\Lambda(1)$
in degree $-2$ and $\Lambda$ in degree $-1$. The term in degree $-1$ comes from
$R^1j_*\Lambda_U=i_*\Lambda(-1)$. The same answer comes out of the triangle
$j_!\Lambda_U\to\Lambda_X\to i_*\Lambda\to$. Dualizing it, with
$\mathbb D_X\Lambda_X=\Lambda_X(1)[2]$ and
$\mathbb D_X(i_*\Lambda)=i_*\mathbb D_0\Lambda=i_*\Lambda$, gives a triangle

$$
i_*\Lambda\longrightarrow\Lambda_X(1)[2]\longrightarrow
\mathbb D_X(j_!\Lambda_U)\longrightarrow.
$$

On stalks at $0$ the first map, from degree $0$ to degree $-2$, is zero.
Hence the cone has $\Lambda(1)$ in degree $-2$ and $\Lambda$ in degree $-1$.

Dualizing once more, biduality predicts $\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_X(j_!\Lambda_U)
\simeq j_!\Lambda_U$, with zero stalk at $0$. In other words, the second dual
cancels the stalk that the first created. Here this follows from the two easy
cases. The map $\delta$ is a morphism of triangles, and it is an isomorphism on $\Lambda_X$ and on $i_*\Lambda$, so by the five lemma it is an isomorphism on
$j_!\Lambda_U$. The argument used, however, that $\Lambda_U$ extends to the locally constant sheaf $\Lambda_X$. A locally constant $L$ on $U$ with nontrivial monodromy around $0$ has no such extension, and that is the case which needs the henselian
disc.

Let $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R=k[x,y]/(xy,y^2)$, the line $y=0$
with an embedded point at the origin, and let $U=D(x)$. On $U$ the
element $y$ is zero, since $xy=0$ and $x$ is invertible, so
$U$ is not schematically dense in $T$. On the other hand, the ideal $I=(x)$ is the unit
ideal on $U$, so its blow-up is $U$-admissible. Since the ideal is principal,
the chart formula above gives $R[I/x]=R/\{b:x^nb=0\text{ for some }n\}$.
Now every element of $R$ is uniquely $f(x)+cy$ with $c\in k$, and
$x^n(f+cy)=x^nf$, so the $x$-power torsion is $ky$ and the blow-up is
$\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$. Thus the embedded point is gone, $U$ is dense, and
the boundary is the Cartier divisor $x=0$, as in
Lemma [lemma-making-open-schematically-dense].

objects.body:
Let $X$ be a geometric point and let $S=\mathbf Z_\ell$ be regarded as
a profinite object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. The completed coefficient sheaf
$\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$ has sections
$\operatorname{Cont}(S,\mathbf Z_\ell)$ on $S$, among them the
identity function. The pullback $\nu_X^*$ from $X_{\acute{e}t}$ of the
constant sheaf with value the *discrete* abelian group
$\mathbf Z_\ell$ has only locally
constant functions as sections, and these have finite image on the
compact space $S$. Hence the identity function does not come from any
finite stage of the profinite presentation of $S$, and
$\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$ is not classical. Its reductions
$\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, on the other hand, are classical. So étale arguments
apply at each finite level, while the coefficient sheaf itself is defined
once on the pro-étale site.

We use the open immersion $j_\infty:\mathbf A^1\to\mathbf P^1$ of
Example [example-running-example], base changed to $\bar k$, and we let
$i_\infty:\{\infty\}\to\mathbf P^1_{\bar k}$ be the inclusion of
the complementary point.

By definition, $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,A)=R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1,j_{\infty!}A)$. The
localization triangle
$j_{\infty!}A\to A_{\mathbf P^1}\to i_{\infty*}A$ and (6.4)
show that

$$
R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1_{\bar k},A)
\simeq\fib\bigl(A\oplus A(-1)[-2]\to A\bigr)
\simeq A(-1)[-2],
$$

since restriction to $\infty$ is an isomorphism on $H^0$. In other words,
$H^2_c(\mathbf A^1)=A(-1)$ is the only nonzero compactly supported
cohomology group. The trace on it is the same $\operatorname{Tr}_p$.

Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ and $\Lambda=E$. Then
$\Ext^n(E,E)=H^n(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)$ is $E$ for $n=0,1$ and vanishes for
$n\geq2$. To see the vanishing, consider first $\mathbf Z_\ell$ and the Milnor sequence
(2.11) with $F_m=(\mathbf Z/\ell^m)_X$. Since
the field $\mathbf F_q$ has $\ell$-cohomological dimension one, we have
$H^n(X,\mathbf Z/\ell^m)=0$ for $n\ge2$ and all $m$, while the finite
groups $H^1(X,\mathbf Z/\ell^m)$ have vanishing $\varprojlim^1$. The
Milnor sequence therefore gives $H^n(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf Z_{\ell,X})=0$ for
$n\geq2$. From here, inverting $\ell$ and using
Example [example-first-cohomology-finite-field] for $n=1$ gives the
claim for $\mathbf Q_\ell$; for $E\neq\mathbf Q_\ell$ we tensor with $E$ over $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

As in the example over $\mathbf R$, products are exact
(Proposition [proposition-exact-products]) and the complexes $E[n]$
live in distinct degrees. Hence $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}E[n]=\prod_{n\ge0}E[n]$, and

$$
\Hom\Bigl(E,\bigoplus_{n\ge0}E[n]\Bigr)
=\prod_{n\ge0}\Ext^n(E,E)
=E\oplus E
=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\Hom(E,E[n]).
$$

The product equals the sum because only two factors are nonzero. Over
$\mathbf R$ every factor is nonzero, and the product is larger.

Let $X=C=\mathbf A^1=\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$, let $Z$ be the origin,
with $I=(x)$, and let $c_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $c_2(x)=x^2$, so that
$c_2^*x=x^2$. Then $I_1=(x)$ and $I_2=(x^2)=I_1^2$, so $c$ contracts
towards $Z$ with $n=1$. The fixed scheme is $V(x^2-x)$. It consists of
the two reduced points $0$ and $1$, and only the first meets $Z$.

The deformation to the normal cone is
$\operatorname{Spec}k[t]_{(t)}[x,x/t]$. This is the constant family
$\mathbf A^1_T$ in the coordinate $x'=x/t$. In this coordinate the first
leg is the identity and the second is $x'\mapsto x^2/t=tx'^2$. Hence, on the
special fibre $t=0$, the second leg is the constant map to $0$, as (2) of
the lemma predicts, and the deformed fixed scheme there is the point
$x'=0$. On the generic fibre, by contrast, there are two fixed points: one is $x'=0$,
the constant family of the origin, and the other is $x'=1/t$, the point
$x=1$. This second point leaves every bounded region of the $x'$-line as $t\to0$, and
so it does not reach the special fibre.

Corollary [corollary-contracting-local-terms-point] below therefore
gives $\operatorname{LT}_0(u)=\operatorname{tr}_A(u_{\bar 0}\mid K_{\bar
0})$ for every $K$ and $u$. For instance, the local term is zero if
$K=j_!A$ with $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$, as
$K_{\bar 0}=0$. The condition fails for the identity correspondence.
There $I_2=I_1$, the inclusion $I_1^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$ is false for
every $n$, and the fixed scheme is all of $X$.

Let $X=s$, let $C=\coprod_{i=1}^ns$ be $n$ points, with $c_1=c_2$ the
structure map, and let $u:c_2^*A=A_C\to c_1^!A=A_C$ be the identity, using

$\operatorname{tr}_A(1\mid A)=1$ by Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point].
The right side of the theorem is therefore $n$ as well. Note that the local terms are indexed by the points of $C$, not of $X$: here $X$ has one point and the fixed locus has
$n$.

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field, with
origin $O$, and let $\Delta\subset E\times E$ be the diagonal. On
$E\times E$ put

$$
\mathcal L=\mathcal O_{E\times E}\bigl(\Delta-E\times\{O\}-\{O\}\times E\bigr).
$$

Consider the slice $E\times\{t\}$. It meets the diagonal in the point
$t$, and the divisor $\{O\}\times E$ meets it in the point $O$. The divisor $E\times\{O\}$, on the other hand, is pulled back from the second factor, so it
contributes the trivial sheaf for every $t$. Hence the restriction is
$\mathcal O_E(t-O)$. By symmetry the restriction to $\{t\}\times E$ is
also $\mathcal O_E(t-O)$. In particular $\mathcal L$ is trivial on both
slices through $(O,O)$.

However, $\mathcal L$ is not trivial, because for $t\neq O$ the sheaf
$\mathcal O_E(t-O)$ is nontrivial. Indeed, a rational function with
divisor $t-O$ would be a map $E\to\mathbf P^1$ of degree one, which is
impossible in genus one. The set of $t$ over which the fibre is trivial
is the point $O$. It is closed, as Lemma [lemma-triviality-fibres]
below predicts, but not open.

Over $k$, let $C\subset\mathbf P^2$ be the cuspidal cubic $zy^2=x^3$,
with cusp $c=(0:0:1)$. Its normalization is the map $h:\mathbf P^1\to C$,
$(s:u)\mapsto(su^2:u^3:s^3)$. It sends $u=0$ to the
cusp and the affine line $u\neq0$ isomorphically onto $C\setminus\{c\}$.
So $X=\mathbf A^1$ has the two compactifications $\mathbf P^1$ and $C$.
Since $h^{-1}(C\setminus\{c\})=\mathbf A^1$, the map $h$ is a refinement. The refinement map $j_!\Lambda\to Rh_*j'_!\Lambda$ is the identity on $X$, and at the cusp both stalks vanish: for the right side, proper base change
shows that the stalk of
$Rh_*j'_!\Lambda$ at $c$ is the cohomology of $j'_!\Lambda$ on the single
point $h^{-1}(c)=\{\infty\}$, where $j'_!\Lambda$ is zero. So the
singularity of $C$ does not affect $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda)$.

Over $k$, let $C\subset\mathbf P^2$ be the cuspidal cubic $zy^2=x^3$,
with cusp $c=(0:0:1)$. The map $h:\mathbf P^1\to C$,
$(s:u)\mapsto(su^2:u^3:s^3)$, is the normalization. It sends $u=0$ to the
cusp and the affine line $u\neq0$ isomorphically onto $C\setminus\{c\}$.
So $X=\mathbf A^1$ has the two compactifications $\mathbf P^1$ and $C$.
Since $h^{-1}(C\setminus\{c\})=\mathbf A^1$, the map $h$ is a refinement.
The refinement map $j_!\Lambda\to Rh_*j'_!\Lambda$ is the identity on $X$.
At the cusp both stalks vanish. For the right side, proper base change
shows that the stalk of
$Rh_*j'_!\Lambda$ at $c$ is the cohomology of $j'_!\Lambda$ on the single
point $h^{-1}(c)=\{\infty\}$, where $j'_!\Lambda$ is zero. So the
singularity of $C$ does not affect $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda)$.

attrs.title: A singular compactification of the line (1)

objects.body:
Let $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$, $V=\mathbf A^1_k$ with coordinate $x$, and let
$s$ be the origin. The blowup of $V\times\mathbf A^1=\mathbf A^2$, with
coordinates $(x,t)$, at the origin is covered by two charts. On the chart with
coordinates $(u,t)$ and $x=tu$ the exceptional divisor is $t=0$; on the chart
with coordinates $(x,v)$ and $t=xv$ it is $x=0$, and the strict transform of
the line $V\times\{0\}=\{t=0\}$ is $v=0$. Since a point of the second chart with
$v\neq0$ lies on the first chart, with $u=1/v$, removing the strict
transform leaves exactly the first chart:

$$
\mathcal D_{s(S)}V=\operatorname{Spec}k[u,t]\longrightarrow
V\times\mathbf A^1,\qquad (u,t)\longmapsto(tu,t),
$$

with $\widetilde g$ the projection to $t$ and $\widetilde s$ the line $u=0$.
For $t=c\neq0$ the fibre is the line $V$ itself, with coordinate $u=x/c$ and
the origin as section. For $t=0$ the fibre is the $u$-line, mapped to the
origin of $V$; it is the tangent line $N_s=T_0\mathbf A^1$, and $u$ is the
linear coordinate given by the class of $x$ in $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$.
So the family rescales the line by $1/t$ and in the limit keeps only the
first-order information at the section. Here the family is the product
$\mathbf A^1_u\times\mathbf A^1_t$, so $\widetilde s^*\omega_{\widetilde g}$
is visibly constant along $t$. In general this holds only étale locally,
after a choice of coordinates, and the point of
Lemma [lemma-section-normal-bundle] is that the comparison normalized at
$t=1$ does not depend on that choice.

attrs.title: The origin in the affine line (1)

objects.body:
On $C=\mathbf P^1_k$ a divisor $\sum_in_ia_i+n_\infty\infty$ of degree
zero, with $a_i\in k$, is the divisor of the rational function
$\prod_i(x-a_i)^{n_i}$, whose order at $\infty$ is
$-\sum_in_i=n_\infty$. So
$\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathbf P^1)=0$, and the degree is an isomorphism
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1)\simeq\mathbf Z$. This agrees with
$J(\mathbf P^1)=0$ for $g=0$.

On an elliptic curve $E$ with origin $O$ the kernel is as large as the
curve. Let $\mathcal L$ have degree zero. Then $\mathcal L(O)$ has degree
one, and by Riemann–Roch with $g=1$ it has a one-dimensional space of
sections. Hence $\mathcal L(O)\simeq\mathcal O_E(P)$ for a unique point
$P$, and $P\mapsto\mathcal O_E(P-O)$ is a bijection
$E(k)\to\operatorname{Pic}^0(E)$. In particular $\mathcal O_E(P-Q)$ is
nontrivial for $P\neq Q$. One can also see this directly: a rational
function with divisor $P-Q$ would be a map $E\to\mathbf P^1$ of degree
one, that is, an isomorphism.

Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ and consider $\mathbf Z/\ell^2\to\mathbf F_\ell$.
Let $K$ be the lisse sheaf $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ on which Frobenius, the
topological generator of $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbf F}_q/\mathbf F_q)
\simeq\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, acts by multiplication by the unit $1+\ell$.
Recall that for a finite module $M$ with a continuous action of $\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, cohomology is computed by the complex $M\xrightarrow{F-1}M$ in degrees $0$
and $1$, where $F$ is the action of the generator. For $K$ this differential is multiplication by $\ell$. Hence $H^0(X,K)=\ell\mathbf Z/\ell^2$
and $H^1(X,K)=(\mathbf Z/\ell^2)/\ell$, both of order $\ell$. On the other
hand, $K_{\mathbf F_\ell}=K/\ell K$ is $\mathbf F_\ell$ with trivial action,
and $H^0(X,K/\ell K)=\mathbf F_\ell$. The map $H^0(X,K)\otimes\mathbf F_\ell\to H^0(X,K/\ell K)$ is zero, since the
generator $\ell$ of $H^0(X,K)$ reduces to $0$.

The derived comparison is nevertheless an isomorphism. The terms of the
complex are free over $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$. Therefore
$R\Gamma(X,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbf F_\ell$ is
$\mathbf F_\ell\xrightarrow{0}\mathbf F_\ell$, which is
$R\Gamma(X,K/\ell K)$. The class $1\in H^0(X,K/\ell K)$ comes from the
element $1$ of the degree-zero term, which is not a cocycle before
reduction.

For $K$, this differential is multiplication by $\ell$. Both terms are free over $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$.
One has $H^0(X,K)=\ell\mathbf Z/\ell^2$, of order $\ell$.
One has $H^1(X,K)=(\mathbf Z/\ell^2)/\ell$, of order $\ell$.

The map $H^0(X,K)\otimes\mathbf F_\ell\to H^0(X,K/\ell K)$ is zero, since the generator $\ell$ reduces to $0$.
The derived comparison $R\Gamma(X,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^2}\mathbf F_\ell\to R\Gamma(X,K/\ell K)$ is an isomorphism.
The complex $R\Gamma(X,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^2}\mathbf F_\ell$ is $\mathbf F_\ell\xrightarrow{0}\mathbf F_\ell$ in degrees $0$ and $1$, the complex computing $R\Gamma(X,K/\ell K)$.

*Shared context.* Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, with coefficient map $\mathbf Z/\ell^2\to\mathbf F_\ell$. Let $K$ be the lisse sheaf $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ on which Frobenius, the topological generator of $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbf F}_q/\mathbf F_q)\simeq\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, acts as multiplication by $1+\ell$.

Let $X_0=\mathbf G_{m,\mathbf F_q}$, with coordinate $t$, let $X$ be its base
change to $k$, and let $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, with the constant Weil sheaf. Since
$\operatorname{Pic}(X)=0$ and the units of $k[t,t^{-1}]$ are the $ct^m$, the
Kummer sequence gives $H^0(X,\Lambda)=\Lambda$ and
$H^1(X,\Lambda(1))=\Lambda$, generated by the Kummer class of $t$
(Proposition [proposition-cohomology-smooth-affine-curve], with $g=0$ and
two punctures). Thus
$H^1(X,\Lambda)=\Lambda(-1)$, and the other groups vanish. For compact support, on the other hand, we write $X=\mathbf P^1\setminus\{0,\infty\}$. The long exact sequence of
$j_!\Lambda_X\to\Lambda_{\mathbf P^1}\to\Lambda_{\{0,\infty\}}\to$ reads

$$
0\to H^0_c(X)\to\Lambda\xrightarrow{\ \text{diag}\ }\Lambda^2\to H^1_c(X)
\to H^1(\mathbf P^1)=0\to0\to H^2_c(X)\to H^2(\mathbf P^1)\to0,
$$

so $H^0_c=0$, $H^1_c=\Lambda^2/\Lambda\simeq\Lambda$ and
$H^2_c=H^2(\mathbf P^1,\Lambda)=\Lambda(-1)$. Poincaré duality with $d=1$
pairs $H^1_c$ with $H^1$ and $H^2_c$ with $H^0$, and the dimensions match.

The Frobenius eigenvalues show the twist at work. On $H^1_c$, which comes from
the two rational points $0$ and $\infty$, Frobenius acts by $1$, whereas on $H^1=\Lambda(-1)$ it acts by $q$. Their product is $1\cdot q=q^d$, as
Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius] requires. Without the twist,
duality would predict the eigenvalue $1/1=1$ on $H^1$ instead of $q$.
Likewise $H^0$ and $H^2_c$ have eigenvalues $1$ and $q$.

Let $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ and $i:0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$
be the inclusions over $k$, and put $\delta_0=i_*E$. The sheaf $j_!E$ has no punctual subsheaf, as
its stalk at the origin is zero, so $j_!E[1]$ is perverse. It is not
simple. Rotating the triangle of the exact sequence
$0\to j_!E\to E\to\delta_0\to0$ gives the triangle
$\delta_0\to j_!E[1]\to E[1]\to$. Its three terms are perverse, and
so

$$
0\longrightarrow\delta_0\longrightarrow j_!E[1]
\longrightarrow E[1]\longrightarrow0
$$

is exact in the perverse heart. Thus, while among sheaves the skyscraper is a
quotient of $E$, in the perverse heart it becomes a subobject of
$j_!E[1]$. By contrast, the middle extension of $E|_{\mathbf G_m}$ is $E$ itself
(Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk]), and $E[1]$ is simple. On the other
hand $(E\oplus\delta_0)[1]$ is not perverse, because $\mathcal H^{-1}$
has the punctual subsheaf $\delta_0$, which is the subsheaf $F_{\rm p}$
of Lemma [lemma-largest-punctual-subsheaf], the kernel of
$E\oplus\delta_0\to j_*j^*(E\oplus\delta_0)=E$.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $\neq2$, let
$u:\mathbf A^1_k\to\mathbf A^1_k$ be $x\mapsto x^2$, and let $A$ be a finite
ring. Over a point $t\neq0$ the fibre consists of the two points
$\pm\sqrt t$, whereas over $t=0$ it is the single point $x=0$, with a nonreduced
structure that the étale topology does not see. By the lemma, therefore,

$$
(u_*A)_{\bar t}=A\oplus A\quad(t\neq0),\qquad (u_*A)_{\bar0}=A,
$$

and the rank of the stalks jumps at the origin, so $u_*A$ is not lisse. It is,
however, constructible for the stratification $\mathbf G_m\sqcup\{0\}$. Base
change to the origin gives the stalk $A$, the cohomology of the fibre, as
the lemma predicts. For the open immersion $j:\mathbf G_m\to\mathbf A^1$,
by contrast, the stalk of $j_*A$ at $0$ is $A$ while the fibre is empty.

For $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ and $\ell\nmid q$,

$$
H^1(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf Z_{\ell,X})\simeq\mathbf Z_\ell,
\qquad H^1(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf Q_{\ell,X})\simeq\mathbf Q_\ell.
$$

At each finite level the first cohomology is
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(\widehat{\mathbf Z},
\mathbf Z/\ell^n)=\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, and the groups in degree zero are
finite, so that their $\varprojlim^1$ vanishes. Hence the sequence
(2.11) for $F_n=(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_X$
proves the integral statement. Since $X$ is qcqs, its
pro-étale cohomology commutes with filtered colimits [Stacks, [09A3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A3)], in
particular with inverting $\ell$, and the rational statement follows. For
the constant étale sheaf with value the discrete group $\mathbf Q_\ell$,
on the other hand, the first cohomology is
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(\widehat{\mathbf Z},\mathbf Q_\ell)=0$,
because a continuous homomorphism from a profinite group to a discrete
torsion-free group has finite, hence zero, image.

Let $X=\mathbf P^1_k$, $K=A_X$, and let $\psi$ be the constant Frobenius
correspondence, so that $\psi_m$ is the identity on every stalk. Both sides of
the Lefschetz–Verdier formula for the graph $c_m$ can be computed explicitly. The
fixed points of $\Phi_X^m$ are the $q^m+1$ points of
$\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_{q^m})$. By the proposition each has local term
$\operatorname{tr}_A(1\mid A)=1$, so the local side is $q^m+1$. On the global
side, $R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1,A)=A\oplus A(-1)[-2]$. By
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] the operator
$T_{c_m}(\psi_m)$ is the $m$-th power of geometric Frobenius. It acts by $1$
on $H^0$ and by $q^m$ on $H^2=A(-1)$, and both degrees are even, so its trace
is $1+q^m$ with no signs. Compare the identity correspondence at the start
of Section [sec-Trace-classes-and-local-terms]. There the fixed locus is all of $\mathbf P^1$
and the answer $2$ is a self-intersection. Here the fixed locus is finite
and each point counts once.

For $X_0=\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf F_q}$ we have $d=1$, $b_0=b_2=1$, $b_1=0$, so
$\chi=2$, and $D=\det(F_0)\det(F_2)=1\cdot q=q$, so that $\varepsilon=1$. The
corollary predicts $Z(\mathbf P^1,1/(qT))=qT^2Z(\mathbf P^1,T)$. Directly,

$$
\frac1{(1-(qT)^{-1})(1-T^{-1})}
=\frac{qT^2}{(qT-1)(T-1)}
=\frac{qT^2}{(1-T)(1-qT)}.
$$

Here the factor $T^{\chi}$ is not trivial, unlike for the elliptic curve, and
the constant $q^{d\chi/2}=q$ comes from the twist $(-1)$ on $H^2$.

corollary predicts $Z(\mathbf P^1,1/(qT))=qT^2Z(\mathbf P^1,T)$. Directly,

$$
\frac1{(1-(qT)^{-1})(1-T^{-1})}=\frac{qT^2}{(qT-1)(T-1)}.
$$

objects.body:
Take $q=3$, a primitive cube root of unity $\omega\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ and
$\psi(x)=\omega^x$ on $\mathbf F_3$. Pull $\mathcal L_\psi$ back along
$h:\mathbf A^1\to\mathbf A^1$, $x\mapsto x^2$. By the lemma, the trace
of Frobenius on the stalk of $h^*\mathcal L_\psi$ at $x\in\mathbf F_3$ is
$\psi(x^2)$, so the trace formula gives

$$
\sum_r(-1)^r\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F\mid H^r_c(\mathbf A^1_k,h^*\mathcal L_\psi)\bigr)
=\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_3}\omega^{x^2}=1+2\omega ,
$$

and $(1+2\omega)^2=-3$.
The sheaf $h^*\mathcal L_\psi$ is lisse of rank one. It is geometrically
nontrivial, since the cover $u^3-u=x^2$ is geometrically irreducible.
Hence its geometric coinvariants vanish, and $H^0_c=H^2_c=0$
(Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve]). The sum is therefore
$-\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid H^1_c)$.

To see that $H^1_c$ is a line, we use the running example. The cover
$u^3-u=x^2$ is the affine part $Y_0$ of the elliptic curve
$C_0\colon y^2=x^3-x$ of the introduction, with the coordinates renamed
($x^2=u^3-u$). It lies over $\mathbf A^1$ by $\pi(u,x)=x$. Since $\pi$ is
the pullback along $h$ of the Artin–Schreier cover, $\pi_*E$ is the direct sum
of $h^*\mathcal L_{\psi'}$ over the three characters $\psi'$ of $\mathbf F_3$.
Over $k=\overline{\mathbf F}_3$ we obtain

$$
H^1_c(Y,E)=H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,E)\oplus H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,h^*\mathcal L_\psi)
\oplus H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,h^*\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}).
$$

The left side is $H^1(C,E)$, because $C$ minus $Y$ is the single point
at infinity, and it has dimension $2$. Since the first summand on the right is
zero, it remains to see that the last two summands have the same
dimension. For this, note that the automorphism $(u,x)\mapsto(-u,ix)$ of $Y$, with $i^2=-1$ in
$\mathbf F_9$, conjugates the translation by $c$ into the translation by
$-c$. It therefore exchanges the last two summands, and each of them is a
line. This automorphism is defined only over $\mathbf F_9$, but we use it
only to count dimensions. The decomposition itself is stable under
Frobenius, because the translations are defined over $\mathbf F_3$.

Thus Frobenius acts on the line $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,h^*\mathcal L_\psi)$
by $-(1+2\omega)$. This is a square root of $-3$, and it is one of the two
reciprocal roots $\pm i\sqrt3$ of $P_1(T)=1+3T^2$ found in the
introduction. Moreover, the number $1+2\omega=\omega-\omega^2$ is the Gauss sum $g$
of the quadratic character of $\mathbf F_3$. The classical fact $|g|=\sqrt q$ is
thus the statement that this $H^1_c$ is pure of weight one.
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] proves the analogue for every such
sheaf.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $\neq2$ and let
$R=k[t]_{(t)}$, the local ring of $\mathbf A^1_k$ at the origin, with
maximal ideal $J=(t)$. The finite $R$-algebra $B=R[x]/(x^2-1-t)$ is a domain,
because $1+t$ is not a square in $k(t)$. Hence $Z=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is
connected and $\Gamma(Z,\mathbf Z/2)=\mathbf Z/2$. The closed fibre, on the other hand, is
$\operatorname{Spec}k[x]/(x^2-1)$, which consists of the two points
$x=\pm1$, and so $\Gamma(Z_0,\mathbf Z/2)=(\mathbf Z/2)^2$. Thus the
conclusion of the theorem fails for $(R,J)$. The reason is that
$(R,J)$ is not henselian: the factorization $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ modulo $t$
does not lift. In the henselization, by contrast, and in $k[[t]]$, the element $1+t$
has the square root $1+t/2-t^2/8+\cdots$. There the factorization lifts,
and $Z$ splits into two copies of the base, so both sides become
$(\mathbf Z/2)^2$.

On the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, take for $K$ the sheaf
attached to an $\mathcal O_E$-module. The computation is then one with
modules, and it shows where the uniform rate comes from. Resolving
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^e$ by $[\mathcal O_E\xrightarrow{\pi_E^e}\mathcal O_E]$ in
degrees $-1,0$ and reducing modulo $\pi_E$, we find

$$
\mathcal O_E\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}\mathbf F_E=\mathbf F_E,
\qquad
\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^e\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}\mathbf F_E
=\bigl[\mathbf F_E\xrightarrow{\,0\,}\mathbf F_E\bigr]
=\mathbf F_E\oplus\mathbf F_E[1]\quad(e\geq1),
$$

since $\pi_E^e$ becomes zero modulo $\pi_E$. For
$P=\mathcal O_E^r\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^s\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{e_i}$ the
reduction $K_1$ has $H^0=\mathbf F_E^{r+s}$ and $H^{-1}=\mathbf F_E^s$. Thus
$H^{-1}(K_1)$ counts the cyclic torsion summands. For
$K=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ we get
$K_1=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}(\mathbf F_E\oplus\mathbf F_E[1])$. This is not
constructible, because its cohomology is an infinite-dimensional vector space in
degrees $0$ and $-1$. In other words, a constructible $K_1$ allows only finitely
many torsion summands. For $P$ the single power $\pi_E^{\max e_i}$ then kills all
the torsion, and this is the uniform rate.

The completeness hypothesis cannot be dropped either. The module $E$ is
$\pi_E$-divisible, so $E\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n=0$ for all
$n$. Hence $K_1=0$ is constructible, yet $E$ is not a finitely generated
$\mathcal O_E$-module. The criterion does not apply because $E$ is not derived
complete: its derived
completion $R\varprojlim_n(E\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$ is zero.

Over an algebraically closed $k$, let $j:U=\mathbf G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow
X=\mathbf A^1_k$ and let $i$ be the inclusion of the origin. The
localization sequence $0\to j_!\Lambda_U\to\Lambda_X\to i_*\Lambda\to0$
shows that $\Lambda_X$ is built from $j_!\Lambda_U$ and $i_*\Lambda$, and the
formula above computes $\cHom$ out of each piece. By
Example [example-closed-support],

$$
\cHom(j_!\Lambda_U,\Lambda_X)=Rj_*\Lambda_U,
\qquad
\cHom(i_*\Lambda,\Lambda_X)=i_*i^!\Lambda_X\simeq i_*\Lambda(-1)[-2].
$$

The first has $\mathcal H^0=\Lambda_X$ and $\mathcal H^1=i_*\Lambda(-1)$. In
the second, the local Ext sheaves from the skyscraper sheaf $i_*\Lambda$ to
the constant sheaf vanish except in degree two. Both results are
constructible but not lisse. The first is computed by a nonproper direct
image, and the second by $i^!$.

On $\mathbf G_{m,k_0}$ with coordinate $t$, the $\mu_{\ell^n}$-torsors
$u^{\ell^n}=t$ give the Kummer cocycle $\kappa$, a continuous map from
$\pi_1(\mathbf G_{m,k_0})$ to $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$. Let $\chi$ be the cyclotomic character,
by which $\pi_1$ acts on $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$. The matrices

$$
\sigma\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}\chi(\sigma)&\kappa(\sigma)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
$$

define a lisse sheaf $\mathcal E$ on $\mathbf G_{m,k_0}$, an extension
$0\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)\to\mathcal E\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to0$. Geometric Frobenius acts
on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ by $q_x^{-1}$. Hence at a closed point $x$ the eigenvalues of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$ are $q_x^{-1}$ and $1$, of weights $-2$ and $0$, and
$\mathcal E$ is mixed of weights at most $0$ and not pure. The filtration does not
split. Indeed, on $\pi_1(\mathbf G_{m,k})$ the character $\chi$ is trivial, and
$\kappa$ is a homomorphism onto $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$ because the covers
$u^{\ell^n}=t$ of $\mathbf G_{m,k}$ are connected. So the line $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ is the only stable line. At each
closed point, by contrast, the two eigenvalues are distinct and the stalk
is the direct sum of its eigenlines.

$u^{\ell^n}=t$ give the Kummer cocycle $\kappa$, a continuous map from

Let $M$ be the Kummer sheaf of a nontrivial character $\chi$ on
$U_0=\mathbf G_m$. It is irreducible and pure of weight $0$. Since it is tame
at infinity, it has no geometric constituent $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$,
and so it satisfies the hypotheses of this section. Inertia at the
origin acts on $M$ through $\chi$, nontrivially, and hence
$(j_*M)_{\bar0}=0$ by Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk]. This means that
$j_!M=j_*M$ and $B=0$, and the lemma gives $G\simeq j'_*M'$. On
$\mathbf F_q$-points this is visible: by (16.3) the trace
of $G$ at $y\ne0$ is $-\sum_x\chi(x)\psi(xy)=-\overline\chi(y)g$, with
$g=\sum_x\chi(x)\psi(x)$, and for the quadratic character this is the trace
of $M'$ computed at the start of Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves].
At $y=0$, on the other hand, the trace of $G$ is $-\sum_x\chi(x)=0$, in agreement with
$H^1_c(\mathbf G_m,M)=0$.

objects.body:
Let $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ and let $L$ be the sheaf on the nodal curve $X$ from the start of
this chapter, obtained from $E_Y$ on the chain of lines $Y\to X$ by letting
the generator of $\mathbf Z$ act by $\ell$. Over $Y$ the lattices in
$L|_Y=E_Y$ are the constant lattices $\ell^m\mathbf Z_\ell$, so over $Y$ the scheme of
lattices is $\coprod_{m\in\mathbf Z}Y$. The generator of $\mathbf Z$ moves the
copy indexed by $m$ to the copy indexed by $m+1$ while translating $Y$. Hence the
scheme of lattices over $X$, which is the quotient by $\mathbf Z$, is a single
copy of $Y$. It is surjective and étale over $X$, as the lemma says, but it
has no section. Indeed, a section would trivialize the $\mathbf Z$-torsor $Y\to X$,
whereas $Y$ is connected and $\coprod_{\mathbf Z}X$ is not. This is
the absence of a global lattice seen geometrically, and the universal
lattice lives on $Y$, where $L$ becomes constant.

Let $Y_0=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}=\operatorname{Spec}k_0[y]$, and suppose that $G$
is lisse on the relative line $\mathbf A^1_{Y_0}=\operatorname{Spec}k_0[y,T]$
off the curve $Z=V(yT-1)$. This curve is not finite over the base. Indeed, over a point $y\ne0$ the fibre of $Z$ is the
single point $T=1/y$, and over $y=0$ it is empty, since the equation
becomes $-1=0$. So $Z\to Y_0$ is quasi-finite, but its image
is $D(y)$, which is not closed, whereas a finite map is closed; geometrically, as $y$
tends to $0$ the point $1/y$ runs off to infinity. To repair this, the construction in
the proof takes $g=yT-1$ with leading coefficient $b=y$. Over $D(y)$ the
polynomial $T-y^{-1}$ is monic, and indeed $k_0[y,y^{-1},T]/(yT-1)=k_0[y,y^{-1}]$
is finite over the base. The closed stratum $y=0$, which has smaller
dimension, is treated by induction, and on it the complement of the
lisse locus happens to be empty.

attrs.title: Why the leading coefficient is inverted

objects.body:
Let $Y_0=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}=\operatorname{Spec}k_0[y]$, and suppose that $G$
is lisse on the relative line $\mathbf A^1_{Y_0}=\operatorname{Spec}k_0[y,T]$
off the curve $Z=V(yT-1)$. Over a point $y\ne0$ the fibre of $Z$ is the
single point $T=1/y$, and over $y=0$ it is empty, since the equation
becomes $-1=0$. So $Z\to Y_0$ is quasi-finite but not finite. Its image
is $D(y)$, which is not closed, whereas a finite map is closed. As $y$
tends to $0$ the point $1/y$ runs off to infinity. The construction in
the proof takes $g=yT-1$ with leading coefficient $b=y$. Over $D(y)$ the
polynomial $T-y^{-1}$ is monic, and $k_0[y,y^{-1},T]/(yT-1)=k_0[y,y^{-1}]$
is finite over the base. The closed stratum $y=0$ has smaller
dimension and is treated by induction. On it the complement of the
lisse locus happens to be empty.

objects.body:
Let $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ over $k_0$, let $F=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$,
which is pure of weight $0$, and let $s=0$. Since inertia at the origin acts
trivially on the constant sheaf,
$(j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)_{\bar 0}=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ by Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk], with
Frobenius acting by $1$, of weight $0$. On the other side, the Kummer covers
$t\mapsto t^{\ell^n}$ of a punctured neighbourhood of the origin give
$(R^1j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)_{\bar 0}=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$
(Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f]), on which geometric
Frobenius acts by $q$, of weight $2$. The pairing of
Lemma [lemma-local-duality-point-c-u] is the multiplication

coefficients $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)\otimes\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ Frobenius acts
by $q$.

attrs.title: Local duality at the origin of the line

objects.body:
Let $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ over $k_0$, let $F=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$,
which is pure of weight $0$, and let $s=0$. Inertia at the origin acts
trivially on the constant sheaf, so
$(j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)_{\bar 0}=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ by Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk], with
Frobenius acting by $1$, of weight $0$. The Kummer covers
$t\mapsto t^{\ell^n}$ of a punctured neighbourhood of the origin give
$(R^1j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)_{\bar 0}=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$
(Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f]), on which geometric
Frobenius acts by $q$, of weight $2$. The pairing of
Lemma [lemma-local-duality-point-c-u] is the multiplication
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\otimes\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$. So in this case the two stalks have
weights $0$ and $2$. The gap of two comes entirely from the Tate
twist. With coefficients $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$, $H^1$ of a punctured disc is spanned

coefficients $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)\otimes\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$, Frobenius therefore acts
by $q$.

Let $k'$ be a separably closed field, let $S=\varprojlim_iS_i$ be a
profinite set written as a limit of finite sets, and let $R=LC(S,k')$ be
the ring of locally constant functions $S\to k'$. Then
$R=\varinjlim_ik'^{\,S_i}$, and $\operatorname{Spec}(k'^{\,S_i})$ is the
finite discrete set $S_i$, so $\operatorname{Spec}(R)=\varprojlim_iS_i=S$:
the point $s\in S$ is the maximal ideal of functions vanishing at $s$.
Every point is closed and is its own component, so $R$ is w-local with
$\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}(R))=S$. The local ring at $s$ is the colimit
of the local rings $k'$ of the $k'^{\,S_i}$ at the image of $s$, that is,
$k'$, which is strictly henselian. Thus $R$ is w-strictly local: it is the
family of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k'$ indexed by $S$. It is
w-contractible exactly when $S$ is extremally disconnected. In this example
the definitions are statements about $S$ alone. Over $\operatorname{Spec}k'$
every pro-étale affine is of this form
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed] below).

Let $A$ be a commutative ring and let $S$ be a compact topological
space. The finite discrete quotients $Q$ of $S$, ordered by refinement,
give a filtered colimit of $A$-algebras

$$
LC(S,A)=\varinjlim_Q A^Q,
$$

whose structure maps are pullback along $S\to Q$.

If $S$ is profinite, evaluation gives a homeomorphism

$$
S\times\operatorname{Spec}(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\operatorname{Spec}(LC(S,A)),\qquad
(s,\mathfrak p)\longmapsto\{f\mid f(s)\in\mathfrak p\}.
$$

In particular, for any field $k'$ the spectrum of $LC(S,k')$ is $S$,
and $s$ corresponds to the maximal ideal of functions vanishing at $s$.

*Proof.* On a discrete quotient $Q$, locally constant functions are all functions
$Q\to A$. Every locally constant function on $S$ factors through the
quotient by its fibres, which is finite by compactness. Pullback from
any quotient is injective because $S\to Q$ is surjective. These two
facts verify the filtered colimit property on underlying sets, hence
on $A$-algebras.

Write $\Phi(s,\mathfrak p)=\{f\mid f(s)\in\mathfrak p\}$. This is a
prime ideal, and $\Phi$ is continuous: near $(s,\mathfrak p)$ the
condition $f(s)\notin\mathfrak p$ is constant in the $S$-coordinate
and is a basic open condition in $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$.

For a prime ideal $P$ of $LC(S,A)$, consider the clopen subsets $U$ of
$S$ whose characteristic functions $\chi_U$ do not belong to $P$.
They form a family of nonempty closed sets stable under finite
intersections. Compactness gives a point $s$ in their intersection.
The identities $\chi_U\chi_{U^c}=0$ and $\chi_U+\chi_{U^c}=1$ imply
that $\chi_U\notin P$ whenever $s\in U$, and then that every function
vanishing at $s$ lies in $P$. Subtracting the constant function with
value $f(s)$ shows that $P=\Phi(s,\mathfrak p)$, where $\mathfrak p$
is the contraction of $P$ to $A$. Thus $\Phi$ is surjective.

Contraction recovers $\mathfrak p$, and clopen subsets separate distinct
points of the profinite set $S$, so $\Phi$ is injective. Finally, for
$U$ clopen and $a\in A$, the image of $U\times D(a)$ is
$D(\chi_Ua)$. These sets form bases, so $\Phi$ is open and hence a
homeomorphism. For a field, its spectrum consists of the zero ideal,
giving the last assertion.

Now let $k'$ be a separably closed field, let $S=\varprojlim_iS_i$ be a
profinite set written as a limit of finite sets, and let $R=LC(S,k')$.
Then $R=\varinjlim_ik'^{\,S_i}$ and $\operatorname{Spec}(R)=S$, the point
$s\in S$ being the maximal ideal of functions vanishing at $s$. Every point
is closed and is its own component, so $R$ is w-local with
$\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}(R))=S$. The local ring at $s$ is the colimit
of the local rings $k'$ of the $k'^{\,S_i}$ at the image of $s$, that is,
$k'$, which is strictly henselian.

Thus $R$ is w-strictly local: it is the
family of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k'$ indexed by $S$. It is
w-contractible exactly when $S$ is extremally disconnected. In this example
the definitions are statements about $S$ alone. Over $\operatorname{Spec}k'$
every pro-étale affine is of this form
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed] below).

Nearby cycles see more than the special fibre when the family
degenerates. For example, for $\mathcal Y=V(xy-t)\subset\mathbf A^2_S$ the special
fibre is the pair of axes $xy=0$, while the generic fibre is smooth.
To see what to expect, note that over $\mathbf C$ the part of the fibre $xy=\varepsilon$ near the origin
is an annulus $\{(x,\varepsilon/x)\}$, which retracts onto a circle
that vanishes as $\varepsilon\to0$. Correspondingly, in our setting the stalk of
$R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}(A)$ at the node is $A$ in degree zero and $A(-1)$
in degree one; the twist is that of $H^1(\mathbf G_m)$
(see [sga7-2, Exposé XV]). At every other point of the
special fibre, by contrast, the family is smooth over $S$, and there the nearby cycles are
$A$ in degree zero, by smooth base change and the first calculation below.

Without surjective transition maps the derived limit can be nonzero in
degree one. To see this, work over a geometric point and evaluate on the final object, which is weakly
contractible, so that we may compute with abelian groups. Let $M_n=\mathbf Z$
for all $n$, with transition maps multiplication by $\ell$. Then the maps
$M_n\to\mathbf Z$, $m\mapsto\ell^nm$, form a map to the constant tower
$\mathbf Z$ whose cokernel is the tower $(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)$. The constant
tower has limit $\mathbf Z$ and no $R^1\varprojlim$, and $\varprojlim_nM_n=0$,
because an element of $M_0$ in the image of every $M_n$ is divisible by every
power of $\ell$. The long exact sequence of $R\varprojlim$ therefore reads

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathbf Z\longrightarrow\mathbf Z_\ell\longrightarrow R^1\varprojlim_nM_n\longrightarrow0,
$$

so the sections of $R^1\varprojlim_nM_n$ over the point form $\mathbf Z_\ell/\mathbf Z$, an
uncountable group. If the $M_n$
are the groups $H^{q-1}$ of a tower of complexes, this group appears in
$H^q$ of the derived limit by (2.2).

If $X$ is smooth at a point $Z=\{y\}$, then
$\bigoplus_rI^r/I^{r+1}$ is the symmetric algebra of $I/I^2$ and
$N_ZX$ is the tangent space at $y$. At a singular point, however, the normal cone
is the tangent cone, and it need not be reduced. For example, for the cusp
$X=V(y^2-x^3)\subset\mathbf A^2$ and $Z$ the origin, with $I=(x,y)$, the
graded algebra is $k[\xi,\eta]/(\eta^2)$, where $\xi,\eta$ are the
classes of $x,y$ in $I/I^2$ and $\eta^2$ is the lowest-degree part of
$y^2-x^3$; so $N_ZX$ is a double line. Similarly, for a nonreduced point
$Z=V(x^m)\subset\mathbf A^1$, each $I^r/I^{r+1}=(x^{mr})/(x^{m(r+1)})$ is
free of rank one over $\mathcal O_Z=k[x]/(x^m)$, and
$N_ZX=Z\times\mathbf A^1$ is a line thickened along $Z$; this is the case
treated in Lemma [lemma-case-z-v-x-m].

Let $R$ be a strictly henselian discrete valuation
ring with uniformizer $t$ and algebraically closed residue field of
characteristic $\neq2$, and let $X\subset\mathbf P^2_R$ be the closure of
the affine curve $y^2=x^3-x^2+t$. Then $X$ is regular (at the origin of
the closed fibre the equation has the linear term $t$), while its closed
fibre $X_s$ is the nodal cubic $y^2=x^2(x-1)$. Let
$f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be the structure map. Since $R$ is strictly
henselian, the stalk of $R^1f_*\mathbf Z$ at the closed point is
$H^1(X,\mathbf Z)$.

This group is zero. Indeed, $X$ is normal and connected, so
$\mathbf Z$-torsors on $X$ correspond to continuous homomorphisms
$\pi_1(X)\to\mathbf Z$, and the image of such a homomorphism is a compact
subgroup of $\mathbf Z$, hence zero. On the closed fibre, however,
$H^1(X_s,\mathbf Z)=\mathbf Z$, generated by the loop through the node.
This means that the base change map from the stalk of $R^1f_*\mathbf Z$
at the closed point to $H^1(X_s,\mathbf Z)$ is not surjective.

With $\mathbf Z/n$ in place of $\mathbf Z$, the class of the loop is
realized by the cyclic étale cover of $X_s$ of degree $n$ obtained by
unwinding the node, and because $R$ is henselian, this cover lifts to $X$.
This is the phenomenon the torsion hypothesis captures.

The square of the lemma is itself an instance of smooth base change, and
the simplest case shows what remains to be proved. Let $Y=S=\operatorname{Spec}L$
with $L$ algebraically closed, let $g:Y'=C=\mathbf A^1_L\to Y$ be the
structure map, and take direct image along
$f:X=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to Y$ for an algebraically closed extension
$\Omega$ of $L$, so that $X'=\mathbf A^1_\Omega$ and $f'=h$. The sheaf
$R^qf_*\mathbf Z/m$ on $\operatorname{Spec}L$ is
$H^q(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega,\mathbf Z/m)$, which vanishes for $q\geq1$.
So smooth base change for this square says exactly that
$R^qh_*\mathbf Z/m=0$ for $q\geq1$. For $m$ invertible in $L$ this is the
content of
Proposition [proposition-base-change-larger-algebraically-closed] below.

Let $q=1$ and $m$ invertible in $L$. The sections over $C$ itself are no
problem: choosing $\mu_m\simeq\mathbf Z/m$, the Kummer sequence gives
$H^1(\mathbf A^1_\Omega,\mathbf Z/m)=\Omega^*/(\Omega^*)^m=0$, since
$\Gamma(\mathbf A^1_\Omega,\mathcal O)^*=\Omega^*$ is divisible and
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf A^1_\Omega)=0$. However, the presheaf whose
sheafification is $R^1h_*\mathbf Z/m$ has other sections. For example, on
the open $U=\mathbf G_{m,L}$ of $C$ the group
$H^1(\mathbf G_{m,\Omega},\mathbf Z/m)$ is cyclic of order $m$, and such a
class has to be killed by an étale
covering of $U$, as we shall see after the statement of the proposition.

For $m=p$ in characteristic $p$ the argument breaks down already over $C$
itself. Indeed, the group $H^1(\mathbf A^1_\Omega,\mathbf F_p)$ is the
cokernel of $u\mapsto u^p-u$ on $\Omega[x]$, and for $\omega\in\Omega$ transcendental over
$L$ it contains the class of $\omega x$, which does not come from $C$
(compare the class of $tx$ at the beginning of the chapter).

$$
\{0\}\xrightarrow{\ i\ }\mathbf A^1_k\xleftarrow{\ j\ }\mathbf G_{m,k},
\qquad \mathbf A^1_k\xrightarrow{\ j_\infty\ }\mathbf P^1_k .
$$

The sheaf $j_!\Lambda_{\mathbf G_m}$ is constructible for the

Let $C_0\colon y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ be the elliptic curve of
the introduction, and $C=C_0\times_{\mathbf F_3}k$. Since $C$ has genus
one, $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ is a plane. Indeed, by the Kummer sequence it is the dual of
the rational Tate module $V_\ell J$ of the Jacobian, a $\mathbf Q_\ell$-vector space of
dimension $2g=2$
(Corollary [corollary-torsion-jacobian-field-extension] and Proposition [proposition-kummer-duality-integral-tate-module]).
For $d=1$ the middle pairing on $H^1$ is alternating and perfect, with values
in $\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$ (Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing]). By
Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius] it satisfies
$\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=3\langle x,y\rangle$. On a plane an alternating
form is unique up to a scalar, so $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=\det(F)\langle
x,y\rangle$. Hence $\det(F\mid H^1)=3$. If $\alpha,\beta$ are the
eigenvalues, then $\alpha\beta=3$, and
$\det(1-TF\mid H^1)=1-(\alpha+\beta)T+3T^2$. This is the functional
equation of a curve of genus one: replacing $T$ by $1/(3T)$ multiplies
the polynomial by $(3T^2)^{-1}$.

Duality alone does not give $|\alpha|=3^{1/2}$. For example, the pair $\alpha=3$, $\beta=1$, with $\det(1-TF)=1-4T+3T^2$, consists of algebraic integers and
satisfies $\alpha\beta=3$. Here the count $N_1=4$ gives $\alpha+\beta=0$ and excludes it; in general only purity does.

(Example [example-running-example-duality]) turns it into the lower bound.

For the elliptic curve $C_0\colon y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$,
geometric Frobenius acts on $H^0(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)=\mathbf Q_\ell$ by $1$ and on
$H^2(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)=\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$ by $3$, and $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ is a plane
(Example [example-running-example-duality]). The point-counting formula reads

$$
N_m=1-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F^m\mid H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)\bigr)+3^m .
$$

From $N_1=4$ we get $\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid H^1)=0$. Duality gives
$\det(F\mid H^1)=3$, so $\det(1-TF\mid H^1)=1+3T^2$. Hence

$$
Z(C_0,T)=\frac{1+3T^2}{(1-T)(1-3T)}.
$$

The formula predicts $N_2=1+9+6=16$ and $N_3=1+27-0=28$, and direct
counts over $\mathbf F_9$ and $\mathbf F_{27}$ confirm this. In general, for a

For the elliptic curve $C_0\colon y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$,
geometric Frobenius acts on $H^0(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)=\mathbf Q_\ell$ by $1$ and on
$H^2(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)=\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$ by $3$, and $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ is a plane
(Example [example-running-example-duality]). The point-counting formula reads

$$
N_m=1-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F^m\mid H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)\bigr)+3^m .
$$

From $N_1=4$ we get $\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid H^1)=0$. Duality gives
$\det(F\mid H^1)=3$, so $\det(1-TF\mid H^1)=1+3T^2$.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $S=\mathbf A^1$ with coordinate $t$, and
let $X\subset\mathbf A^1_S$ be the complement of the two sections $x=0$
and $x=t$, with $f:X\to S$ the projection and $L=\Fell$. The morphism $f$ is smooth. For $t\neq0$ its fibre is $\mathbf A^1$ minus two points, that
is, a projective line minus three points. Its $H^1$ is
$\Fell(-1)^{\oplus2}$. The fibre over $t=0$, however, is $\mathbf G_m$, with $H^1=\Fell(-1)$. On $S_0=\mathbf G_m$ the lemma applies, but no open containing the origin works. Suppose $R^1f_*L$ were locally constant near
$0$ and commuted with base change to the points of $S$. Then its stalks at
$0$ and at nearby $t$ would be the $H^1$ of the fibres, which have
different ranks. What happens is that the two missing points collide at $t=0$, and $Rf_*$ cannot see this from the generic
fibre.

Let $q$ be odd, let $f_0:\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_q}\to\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_q}$
be $x\mapsto x^2$, and let $K=\Lambda_X$ with its constant Weil structure, so
that $t_{K,m}=1$. The fibre of $f_0$ over $y\in\mathbf F_{q^m}$ has
$1+\chi_m(y)$ rational points, where $\chi_m$ is the quadratic character of
$\mathbf F_{q^m}^*$, extended by $\chi_m(0)=0$. Hence

$$
t_{Rf_!\Lambda,m}(y)=1+\chi_m(y).
$$

The trace function of $Rf_!\Lambda$ is not constant, although the sheaf we pushed forward is: over $\mathbf G_m$ the map is a finite étale double cover,
and $\chi_m(y)$ records whether the fibre over $y$ splits into two
rational points or is a single point of degree $2$. Summing over $y$ recovers the
trace formula on the source. Since $\chi_m$ takes the values $\pm1$ equally
often on $\mathbf F_{q^m}^*$, the sum is $q^m=\#\mathbf A^1(\mathbf F_{q^m})$.

Let $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ and let $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$, with the
terms in degrees $0$ and $1$. This is the perfect complex from
Section [sec-Constructibility] whose cohomology modules
$H^0(P)=\ell A$ and $H^1(P)=A/\ell A$ are not perfect. The chain maps
$1_P=(1,1)$ and $v=(1+\ell,1)$ commute with the differential, since
$\ell(1+\ell)=\ell$ in $A$, and both induce the identity on $H^0(P)$
and on $H^1(P)$. By the chain formula of
Proposition [proposition-properties-trace],

$$
\operatorname{tr}_A(1_P\mid P)=1-1=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}_A(v\mid P)=(1+\ell)-1=\ell\neq0.
$$

Thus, over a finite ring, the trace of an endomorphism of a perfect
complex is not determined by the maps it induces on cohomology. The trace
formula has to be stated for the operator on the complex.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic different from two
and let $E\colon y^2=(x-e_1)(x-e_2)(x-e_3)$ with distinct $e_i\in k$,
with origin $O$ at infinity and $P_i=(e_i,0)$. The function $x-e_i$
has a double zero at $P_i$, because $y$ is a local parameter there. It
has a double pole at $O$. Hence $\operatorname{div}(x-e_i)=2P_i-2O$, and
the classes $\mathcal O_E(P_i-O)$ are killed by $2$. They are nonzero and
pairwise distinct, since $\mathcal O_E(P_i-P_j)$ is trivial only for $i=j$
(Example [example-degree-sequence-genus-zero-one]). The divisor
$\operatorname{div}(y)=P_1+P_2+P_3-3O$ shows that the three classes add up
to zero. So $0$ and the classes of $P_i-O$ form a subgroup
$\{0,P_1-O,P_2-O,P_3-O\}\simeq(\mathbf Z/2)^2$ of
$\operatorname{Pic}(E)[2]$. By
Corollary [corollary-torsion-jacobian-field-extension] below,
$\operatorname{Pic}(E)[2]$ has order $2^{2g}=4$, so this subgroup is all of it.

Under the Kummer sequence, the class $P_i-O$, with the trivialization of
its square given by $x-e_i$, is the $\mu_2$-torsor obtained by adjoining a
square root of $x-e_i$. This torsor is unramified everywhere because the
divisor of $x-e_i$ is even. For the running example $y^2=x^3-x$ over
$\overline{\mathbf F}_3$ the $e_i$ are $0,1,-1\in\mathbf F_3$. Hence the
three torsors are defined over $\mathbf F_3$, and Frobenius fixes all of
$E[2]$, as noted in Section [sec-Tate-modules].

Let $X$ be a geometric point, so that the affine objects of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$
are the profinite sets
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed] below). A
continuous surjection $S\to T$ of profinite sets is a covering, so $h_S\to h_T$
is an epimorphism, and by the Yoneda lemma a section of it is a continuous
map $T\to S$ that is a section of the surjection. If $T$ is finite, such a
section exists: choose a preimage of each point; it is continuous because
$T$ is discrete. If $T=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ is a convergent
sequence, it need not exist. Let $S=T_0\amalg T_1$, where $T_0$ is the
convergent sequence $\{2,4,6,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty_0\}$ and $T_1$ is
$\{1,3,5,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty_1\}$, and map $S\to T$ by the identity on
integers and $\infty_0,\infty_1\mapsto\infty$. A section must send each
integer $n$ to its only preimage $n$, and then the even integers converge to
$\infty_0$ while the odd ones converge to $\infty_1$, so no value at $\infty$
makes the section continuous. Hence $T$ is not weakly contractible. In
agreement with Gleason's theorem, $T$ is not extremally disconnected: the
set of odd integers is open, and its closure, which contains $\infty$, is
not open, because every neighbourhood of $\infty$ contains even integers.

We have $\#\mathbf P^d(\mathbf F_{q^m})=1+q^m+\cdots+q^{dm}$, so
that $Z(\mathbf P^d_{\mathbf F_q},T)=\prod_{i=0}^d(1-q^iT)^{-1}$.
Grouping the reciprocal roots by absolute value as in (2), we find
$P_{2i}=1-q^iT$ for $0\le i\le d$ and $P_i=1$ for odd $i$. For an
elliptic curve $C_0$, we have $P_0=1-T$ and $P_2=1-qT$ by (3).
Since $b_1=2$ (Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves]), the polynomial $P_1$ has two
reciprocal roots $\alpha,\beta$. Poincaré duality matches them as
$\beta=q/\alpha$, so $P_1=1-aT+qT^2$ with $a=\alpha+\beta$. The
point-counting formula for $m=1$ gives $\#C_0(\mathbf F_q)=1-a+q$, that
is, $a=1+q-\#C_0(\mathbf F_q)\in\mathbf Z$. By (2) both $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ have absolute value $q^{1/2}$, and we get Hasse's theorem
$|a|\le2q^{1/2}$.

For a $k_0$-scheme $X$ and $f\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$, put
$\mathcal L_{\psi,f}=f^*\mathcal L_\psi$. For any two global functions
$f,g$ there is an isomorphism of Weil sheaves

$$
\mathcal L_{\psi,f}\otimes_E\mathcal L_{\psi,g}
\simeq\mathcal L_{\psi,f+g}.
$$

Taking $X=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}\times_{k_0}\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ and $f,g$
to be its two coordinates gives

$$
m^*\mathcal L_\psi\simeq
\operatorname{pr}_1^*\mathcal L_\psi\otimes_E
\operatorname{pr}_2^*\mathcal L_\psi.
$$

The assertion is existence of an isomorphism, with no normalization
at zero imposed.

For $a\in k_0$ write $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}=\mathcal L_{\psi,ax}$ for the
pullback of $\mathcal L_\psi$ along $x\mapsto ax$, in the notation of
[lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--2], and define
$\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}(ax)}$ in the same way from the sheaf
$\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}$ of the nontrivial character $\psi^{-1}$. For every
$a\in k_0$ there is an isomorphism of Weil sheaves

$$
\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}^\vee\simeq\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}(ax)}.
$$

Here the dual is the internal hom into the constant Weil sheaf.
The case $a=1$ gives $\mathcal L_\psi^\vee\simeq\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}$.
No compatibility with a chosen trivialization at zero is asserted.
The multiplication isomorphism respects the specified trivializations at zero.
The dual-character isomorphism respects the specified trivializations at zero.

For every $a\in k_0$, every $n\geq1$, and every $x\in\Fqn$, the trace of
local geometric Frobenius on the sheaf $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ of
[lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--3] is

$$
t_{\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)},n}(x)
=\psi\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{\Fqn/k_0}(ax)\bigr).
$$

In particular, $a=1$ gives the asserted trace function of $\mathcal L_\psi$.

For every $a\in k_0$ and every closed point $x$ of $\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$,
there is $c\in k_0$, depending only on $a$ and $x$ and not on $\psi$, such that

$$
\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid(\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)})_{\bar x}
=\psi(c)\,\operatorname{id},
$$

with $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ as in [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--3].

More generally, if $K$ is a finite field, $R$ is a commutative ring,
$\chi:K\to R$ is an additive character, and $\iota:R\to\C$ is a ring
homomorphism, then $|\iota(\chi(c))|=1$ for every $c\in K$.
Applied to $R=\Qbarl\supset E$, this shows that the Frobenius eigenvalues above
have absolute value one under every embedding $\iota:\Qbarl\hookrightarrow\C$.
Thus $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ is pure of weight zero in the sense of
[definition-weights].

Let $f:X'\to X$ be a morphism of separated $k$-schemes of finite type,
let $Z'=f^{-1}Z$ schematically, and let $f_Z:Z'\to Z$ be the
restriction of $f$.  There are isomorphisms

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{X,Z}(Rf_*L')&\simeq Rf_{Z*}C_{X',Z'}(L')
&&(f\text{ proper}),\\
C_{X',Z'}(f^*L)&\simeq f_Z^*C_{X,Z}(L)
&&(f\text{ smooth}).
\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover, $C_{X,Z}(i_*M)=0$ for every $M\in D^b_c(Z_{\acute et},A)$.
Consequently, writing $j:X\setminus Z\hookrightarrow X$, we have

$$
C_{X,Z}(j_!j^*L)\xrightarrow{\sim}C_{X,Z}(L).
$$

over a point $z$ of $X_0-U_0$, and let $I_z$ be the inertia group at

canonical Frobenius-equivariant identification

$$

$$

If $\mathcal F$ extends to a lisse sheaf on $X_0$, the adjunction map
from that extension to $j_*\mathcal F$ is an isomorphism.
