All three parts follow from the fact that every epimorphism onto a
sheaf is surjective on sections over $W$, together with the fact that
such $W$ cover every object. Exactness and conservativity
follow directly, and for colimits we need in addition that $W$ is
quasi-compact.

(1) Taking sections is left exact for any object of a site, since it
preserves kernels. By weak contractibility every epimorphism of sheaves
is surjective on sections over $W$, so the sections functor is also right
exact. An exact functor carries acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes,
and so it agrees with its derived functor, also for unbounded complexes.
In particular $H^q(W,F)=0$ for $q>0$.

(2) Limits of sheaves are computed on sections, so only colimits need an
argument. We first consider a direct sum $\bigoplus_iM_i$. The direct sum
sheaf is the sheafification of the presheaf direct sum, so a section over
$W$ is, locally on $W$, a finite sum of sections of the $M_i$. Since $W$
is affine, hence quasi-compact as an object of the site, a finite
covering suffices, and a single finite set of indices $i$ serves for all
members of this covering. By the sheaf condition, the section is then a
section of the corresponding finite subsum, and finite sums commute with
evaluation. It follows that evaluation preserves arbitrary direct sums
[Stacks, [0935](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0935)]. An arbitrary colimit of modules is the cokernel of a map
between direct sums, and evaluation preserves cokernels by (1). Hence it
preserves all colimits.

(3) Suppose that a sequence $F'\to F\to F''$ with composite zero becomes
exact on all affine weakly contractible $W$. A local section of the
kernel of $F\to F''$ is, after restriction to a covering by such $W$,
the image of a section of $F'$, because these objects cover every object.
Hence it lies in the image sheaf, and the sequence is exact. Applied to
kernels and cokernels of a map, this criterion shows that a map which is
an isomorphism on all such $W$ is an isomorphism, and applied in each
degree it gives the statement for complexes; see [Stacks, [0945](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0945)].

Sections preserve kernels, so evaluation is left exact. Weak contractibility makes every epimorphism of sheaves surjective on sections over $W$. Thus evaluation is also right exact, and hence exact.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects].

Apply the exact functor of clause [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects--1] to an injective resolution of $F$. The resulting complex is exact in positive degrees. Its cohomology is $H^q(W,F)$, which therefore vanishes for $q>0$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects].

By clause [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects--1], termwise evaluation takes acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes and quasi-isomorphisms to quasi-isomorphisms. For any complex $K$, an injective replacement evaluates to a complex quasi-isomorphic to $K(W)$, giving the asserted identification without a boundedness restriction.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects].

Limits of sheaves are computed sectionwise. The induced module operations are also computed sectionwise, so evaluation at $W$ preserves the limit of every diagram of $\mathcal R$-modules.

If $f$ is an isomorphism, so is every $f(W)$. Conversely, suppose that every
$f(W)$ is bijective. Apply clause [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects--6] to the sequence
$0\to A\xrightarrow{f}B$. On every affine weakly contractible $W$ the sequence
$0\to A(W)\to B(W)$ is exact because $f(W)$ is injective, so the sequence is
exact at $A$, that is, $f$ is a monomorphism. Apply clause [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects--6]
to $A\xrightarrow{f}B\to0$. On every such $W$ it is exact at $B(W)$ because
$f(W)$ is surjective, so $f$ is an epimorphism. In the abelian category of
$\mathcal R$-module sheaves a monomorphism that is an epimorphism is an
isomorphism.

For complexes, let $C=\Cone(v)$, with $C^q=K^{q+1}\oplus L^q$ and the usual
differential. The termwise split exact sequence $0\to L\to C\to K[1]\to0$
gives a long exact cohomology sequence whose connecting maps are, up to sign,
the maps $H^q(v)$. Hence $v$ is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if $C$ is
acyclic. Evaluation at $W$ is additive and commutes with the differentials,
so $C(W)$ is the cone of $v(W)$, and in the same way $v(W)$ is a
quasi-isomorphism if and only if $C(W)$ is acyclic. By the second assertion
of clause [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects--6], $C$ is acyclic if and only if $C(W)$ is acyclic
for every affine weakly contractible $W$. This proves the assertion for
complexes, again without any boundedness assumption.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects].

A map $U\to Y$ is the same as a section over $U$ of the projection
$Y\times_SX\to X$. The theorem extends this section to an open of a
blow-up, and properness of $Y$ forces this open to be everything.

Apply Theorem [theorem-extension-partial-section], with $T=X$ and $V=U$, to the section
$(f,\mathrm{id}):U\to Y\times_SX$ of the proper projection to $X$.
This gives an extension on an open $W\subseteq X'$ whose graph is
closed in $Y\times_SX'$. The open $W$ is dense, because it contains the
inverse image of $U$, which is dense in $X'$. Since $Y\to S$ is
proper, the observation after
Definition [definition-quasi-domination] shows that $W=X'$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-extension-proper-target], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

It suffices to prove exactness on the point, since $p_X^*$ is exact and
inverse image along $f:X\to Y$ satisfies $p_Y\circ f=p_X$. Now, on a profinite
set $S$, multiplication by $\pi_E^n$ is injective on continuous functions
$S\to\mathcal O_E$, and its image is the kernel of reduction. Moreover, reduction is
surjective because a continuous function $S\to\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ takes
finitely many values, and choosing a representative of each gives a
continuous lift. Finally, the chain map $(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$ commutes with the
differentials because $\pi_E^{n}\pi_E=\pi_E^{n+1}$, and its degree-zero
component is the identity, so it induces the quotient projection.

It suffices to work over the point, since $p_X^*$ is exact. On a profinite set $S$, multiplication by $\pi_E^n$ on continuous maps to $\mathcal O_E$ is injective and its image is the kernel of reduction. A continuous map to $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ has finite image. Lift its finitely many values on their clopen inverse images to obtain a continuous lift to $\mathcal O_E$. This proves surjectivity.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps].

Write $q_n:R\to B_n$ for the quotient map of clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--1]. Since
$q_n\circ\pi_E^n=0$ by exactness of that sequence in the middle, the zero map
in degree $-1$ and $q_n$ in degree $0$ form a chain map
$[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}R]\to B_n[0]$. The cohomology of the two-term complex
is $\ker(\pi_E^n)$ in degree $-1$ and $\coker(\pi_E^n)$ in degree $0$. By
clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--1] the kernel is zero and $q_n$ induces an isomorphism
$\coker(\pi_E^n)\simeq B_n$. Hence the augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism.

The pair $(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$ is a chain map from
$[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^{n+1}}R]$ to $[R\xrightarrow{\pi_E^n}R]$, because
$\pi_E^n\circ\pi_E=\pi_E^{n+1}=\mathrm{id}\circ\pi_E^{n+1}$. In degree $0$
it is the identity of $R$, and the reduction map $r:B_{n+1}\to B_n$ satisfies
$r\circ q_{n+1}=q_n$. So the square formed by the two augmentations,
$(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$ and $r[0]$ commutes already on the level of complexes.
Since the augmentations are quasi-isomorphisms, $(\pi_E,\mathrm{id})$
represents $r$ in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps].

For $f:X\to Y$, the equality $p_Yf=p_X$ identifies inverse image of the coefficient sheaves and of multiplication by $\pi_E$. For one direction we represent an étale complex by a bounded flat
complex and pull it back, and for the other we use the fact that $\nu_X^*$ detects
vanishing.

The functor $\nu_X^*$ is exact (Proposition [proposition-comparison-morphism-inverse-image]),
and since $\nu_X^*\Lambda=\Lambda_X$ it is symmetric monoidal on sheaves
of modules. The pullback of a flat sheaf of modules is flat
[Stacks, [05VD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05VD)]. An étale complex of Tor amplitude in $[a,b]$ is
represented by a complex of flat sheaves in degrees $[a,b]$, so its
pullback is a complex of flat pro-étale sheaves in the same degrees
and has Tor amplitude in $[a,b]$ against every pro-étale module,
not only against pulled-back ones. Conversely, let $K$ be an étale complex. Its
Tor amplitude can be read off from $K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_\Lambda M$ for
arbitrary étale sheaves of modules $M$. The inverse image of this complex is
$\nu_X^*K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda_X}\nu_X^*M$, and since $\nu_X^*$
is exact and fully faithful, it detects vanishing of cohomology. Hence a
Tor bound on $\nu_X^*K$ implies the same bound on $K$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Duality gives the relations $b_{2d-i}=b_i$ and $D^2=q^{d\chi}$. If we substitute
$1/(q^dT)$ into each factor of the cohomological expression for
$Z(X_0,T)$, duality turns the factor in degree $i$ into
the factor in degree $2d-i$ times an explicit scalar.

We apply Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius] with $K=\mathbf Q_\ell$ and $X$ proper.
It gives $b_{2d-i}=b_i$, and it shows that the eigenvalues of $F_{2d-i}$ are the $q^d/\alpha$ for
the eigenvalues $\alpha$ of $F_i$, with multiplicities. Hence
$\det F_i\cdot\det F_{2d-i}=q^{db_i}$. Since $(-1)^i=(-1)^{2d-i}$, we get

$$
D^2=\prod_i\bigl(\det F_i\cdot\det F_{2d-i}\bigr)^{(-1)^i}
=q^{d\chi}.
$$

Since $b_{2d-i}=b_i$, the terms of $\chi$ for $i$ and $2d-i$ are equal
and cancel modulo $2$, so $\chi\equiv b_d\pmod 2$. If $d$ is even,
$d\chi$ is even anyway. If $d$ is odd,
the pairing on $H^d$ of each connected component of $X$ is perfect and
alternating (Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing]), so $b_d$ is even. In
both cases $d\chi$ is even. Then $\varepsilon^2=1$ because $D^2=q^{d\chi}$.

Now consider a single factor. Since $F_i$ is invertible, its
eigenvalues $\alpha$ are nonzero. Pulling $-\alpha/(q^dT)$ out of
each linear factor gives

$$
\det\bigl(1-q^{-d}T^{-1}F_i\bigr)
=\prod_\alpha\Bigl(-\frac{\alpha}{q^dT}\Bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac{q^d}{\alpha}T\Bigr)
=(-1)^{b_i}\frac{\det F_i}{(q^dT)^{b_i}}\det\bigl(1-TF_{2d-i}\bigr).
$$

By Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function], and since $H^i_c=H^i$ as $X_0$ is
proper, $Z(X_0,T)$ is the product of the
$\det(1-TF_i)^{(-1)^{i+1}}$. We substitute $1/(q^dT)$ for $T$ and apply
the last display to each factor. Since $(-1)^i=(-1)^{2d-i}$, the factors
$\det(1-TF_{2d-i})^{(-1)^{i+1}}$ multiply to $Z(X_0,T)$, and the scalar
factors multiply to

$$
(-1)^{\chi}D^{-1}(q^dT)^{\chi}=(-1)^{\chi}D\,T^{\chi},
$$

by $D^2=q^{d\chi}$. The second form of the equation is the definition
of $\varepsilon$.

Substitute the definition of $\varepsilon$ from clause [corollary-functional-equation--8] into the scalar factor $(-1)^\chi D T^\chi$ in clause [corollary-functional-equation--7]. This rewrites that factor as $\varepsilon q^{d\chi/2}T^\chi$, proving the claimed form of the same functional equation.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

Because $X_0$ is proper, compactly supported and ordinary cohomology agree. Apply the perfect duality and dimension equality of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--7] to the constant sheaf $\mathbf Q_\ell$ on every connected component. Taking the sum of dimensions gives $b_{2d-i}=b_i$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

By clause [corollary-functional-equation--4], the terms of $\chi$ outside the middle degree pair up modulo $2$, giving $\chi\equiv b_d\pmod2$. If $d$ is even then $d\chi$ is even. If $d$ is odd, Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing] gives a perfect alternating pairing on middle cohomology on each connected component, so $b_d$ is even. This again makes $d\chi$ even.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

The determinant identity of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--9] gives $\det F_i\det F_{2d-i}=q^{db_i}$. Multiply these identities with exponents $(-1)^i$. Since $(-1)^{2d-i}=(-1)^i$, the left side is $D^2$ and the right side is $q^{d\sum_i(-1)^i b_i}=q^{d\chi}$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

Now consider a single factor. Since $F_i$ is invertible, its

By Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function], and since $H^i_c=H^i$ as $X_0$ is

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

The integer $d\chi$ is even by clause [corollary-functional-equation--5], so the power occurring in the definition of $\varepsilon$ is defined over $\mathbf Q$. Squaring that definition and applying $D^2=q^{d\chi}$ from clause [corollary-functional-equation--6] gives $\varepsilon^2=1$. In the characteristic-zero coefficient field this implies $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-functional-equation].

We compute the stalk at $0'$ of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])$ in
two ways: by the stalk formula, which gives the cohomology of $j_*M$,
and through the isomorphism with $(j'_*M')[1]$, which gives a stalk of
a middle extension.

At the rational origin $0'$ of the dual line, the kernel
$\mathcal K_\psi$ restricts to the pullback of $\mathcal L_\psi$ along
the constant map to $0$, which is canonically trivial (on traces this
is $\psi(0)=1$). The stalk formula of
Proposition [proposition-base-change-fourier-inversion], which is
compatible with Frobenius, therefore gives

$$
\bigl(\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\bigr)_{0'}
=R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)[2].
$$

We compare this with the stalk of $(j'_*M')[1]$, which is concentrated
in degree $-1$. In degree $0$ we therefore see that
$H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)=0$, and in degree $-1$ we obtain

$$
H_c^1(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)
\simeq(j'_*M')_{0'}
=(M'_{\bar\eta})^{I_{0'}},
$$

where $I_{0'}$ is the inertia group at the origin $0'$ of the dual line
acting on the generic fibre of $M'$, and the last equality is the formula
of Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk] for the stalk of a middle extension.
By Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]
the weights of this stalk are at most the weight of $M'$, which is
$w+1$ by Theorem [theorem-weight-fourier-transform].
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-h-1-c-stalk-fourier], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We argue on the étale site. The theorem gives the case of
$\Fell$-sheaves, and we pass to $\mathbf Z/\ell^r$-sheaves by
filtrations, to $A$-sheaves by forgetting the $A$-structure,
and to complexes by truncation.

For a constructible $\Fell$-sheaf this is
Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj] with $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$. A
constructible sheaf $F$ killed by $\ell^r$ has the finite filtration
$F\supset\ell F\supset\cdots\supset\ell^rF=0$. Its successive quotients
$\ell^iF/\ell^{i+1}F$ are constructible and killed by $\ell$, that is,
constructible $\Fell$-sheaves. Each short exact sequence in the filtration
is a triangle in the derived category, and $Rj_*$ carries it to a
triangle. By induction on $r$, the long exact cohomology sequences of
these triangles give (6.22). The base change maps form
morphisms between the resulting triangles, and they are isomorphisms by
the five lemma.

For a finite $\ell$-primary ring $A$, we apply this to the
underlying $\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$-sheaf and carry the
$A$-action along all maps. This is possible for two reasons. First,
$Rj_*:D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},A)\to D^+(Y_{\acute{e}t},A)$ commutes with the
forgetful functors to $D^+(-_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z)$
[Stacks, [0D6J](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D6J)]. Second, an $A$-sheaf is constructible if and only if
its underlying sheaf is. To see this, consider a stratum where the
underlying sheaf is finite locally constant. There the action of each of
the finitely many elements of $A$ is a section of the finite locally
constant sheaf of endomorphisms, hence constant étale locally. Therefore
the $A$-module is locally constant on that stratum. Truncation triangles extend both
conclusions from sheaves to bounded constructible complexes.

Let $n$ be a positive integer killing $A$ and invertible in $k$. The
finite ring $A$ is the product of its $\ell$-primary parts $A_\ell$ for the
primes $\ell$ dividing $n$, cut out by orthogonal idempotents, and each
$\ell$ is invertible in $k$. Every étale sheaf of $A$-modules, and every
complex of such sheaves, is the direct sum of its parts on which $A$ acts
through $A_\ell$. Since $Rj_*$ is additive and a sheaf is constructible if
and only if each of its finitely many parts is, we may assume that $A$ is
killed by a power of a single prime $\ell$ invertible in $k$. The scheme
$X$ is of finite type over $k$, being open in $Y$. For such $A$ the
argument of the proof of Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field] applies: the case
of constructible $\Fell$-sheaves is
Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj] with
$S=\operatorname{Spec}k$, whose only nonempty open is $S$ itself, and one
passes to $\mathbf Z/\ell^r$-sheaves by the filtration by the
$\ell^iF$, to $A$-sheaves by forgetting the $A$-structure [Stacks, [0D6J](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D6J)],
and to bounded complexes by truncation triangles.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

As for the classical transform, the proof is by orthogonality of
characters. We expand the square of the sum in (16.3),
using that the complex conjugate of a character value is its inverse.
This writes the left side as a double sum over $x,z\in\mathbf F_{q^n}^r$
of $\iota t_{K,n}(x)\overline{\iota t_{K,n}(z)}$ times a character sum
over $y$, which we now compute.
For $x,z\in\mathbf F_{q^n}^r$, the orthogonality of characters gives

$$
\sum_y\iota\psi\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}\langle x-z,y\rangle\bigr)
=\begin{cases}q^{nr},&x=z,\\0,&x\ne z.\end{cases}
$$

Indeed, for $x\ne z$ the linear form
$y\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/k_0}\langle x-z,y\rangle$ is
nonzero, since the trace pairing is nondegenerate, and hence
surjective onto $k_0$. As $\psi$ is nontrivial, there is $y_0$ with
$c=\psi(\operatorname{Tr}\langle x-z,y_0\rangle)\ne1$, and
substituting $y+y_0$ for $y$ multiplies the sum by $\iota(c)$, so the sum is zero.
Therefore only the diagonal terms remain, and they
give the asserted identity. On a line, finally, the factor $q^n$ raises
$\nu$ by one.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-plancherel], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Since $X_0$ is proper, the point-counting formula of
Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function] reads

$$
\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})
=\sum_{i=0}^{2d}(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}(F^m\mid H^i_\ell).
$$

The terms in degrees $0$ and $2d$ are $1$ and $q^{dm}$ by
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes](3). The
left side of the estimate is therefore the absolute value of the sum of
the remaining terms. In degree $i$, the trace is a sum of $b_i$
eigenvalues of $F^m$, each of complex modulus $q^{mi/2}$ by
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes](2). Its
absolute value is thus at most $b_iq^{mi/2}$, and the triangle
inequality proves the first bound. For a curve, $b_1=2g$ by the
cohomology calculation of Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves].
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-count-estimates], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The identities over $\Lambda$ are the trace formula and the Euler
product for the constant sheaf. What needs an argument is that
$Z(X_0,T)$ has rational coefficients, which we deduce at the end from
the rationality over $\mathbf Q_\ell$ by linear algebra.

For $K=\Lambda_X$, every stalk is $\Lambda$, and every stalk Frobenius
$\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}$ is its identity, with categorical trace $1_\Lambda$. Thus
(12.9) follows from Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula],
and the formula over the fields follows from its cohomological form
(12.4). By the orbit count in the proof of
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product], we have
$\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})=\sum_{\deg(x)\mid m}\deg(x)$. Expanding each
$(1-T^{\deg(x)})^{-1}$ as a geometric series shows that the product over
closed points has integer coefficients. By the orbit count, its
logarithm is the series defining $Z(X_0,T)$. The last equality is
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product] for $K=\Lambda_X$.

Rationality descends from $\mathbf Q_\ell$ to $\mathbf Q$ for the following reason. A power series is rational exactly when its coefficients eventually satisfy a
linear recurrence with constant coefficients. The existence of such
a recurrence is a system of linear equations, and a system with rational
coefficients has a rational solution as soon as it has any solution.
More precisely, write $Z(X_0,T)=\sum_{n\geq0}z_nT^n$, with $z_n\in\mathbf Z$.
Rationality over $\mathbf Q_\ell$ means that there are integers $d,N$ and
$b_1,\ldots,b_d\in\mathbf Q_\ell$ such that
$z_n+b_1z_{n-1}+\cdots+b_dz_{n-d}=0$ for all $n>N$.
These are linear equations with rational coefficients in the $d$
unknowns $b_i$. Their coefficient rows span a finite-dimensional
subspace of $\mathbf Q^{d+1}$, and hence finitely many of the equations imply
all the others. This finite rational linear system has a solution over
$\mathbf Q_\ell$, and hence one over $\mathbf Q$ by Gaussian elimination. With these
rational $b_i$, the product of $1+b_1T+\cdots+b_dT^d\in\mathbf Q[T]$
and $Z(X_0,T)$ is a polynomial. Therefore $Z(X_0,T)\in\mathbf Q(T)$.

Apply Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula] to the constant Weil sheaf $\Lambda_X$. Each rational-point stalk is $\Lambda$ in degree zero, with identity Frobenius and categorical trace $1_\Lambda$. Summing these identical stalk contributions gives the number of $\mathbf F_{q^m}$-points times $1_\Lambda$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

Apply the field-valued cohomological trace formula of Proposition [proposition-properties-trace--6] to the global perfect complex in clause [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--1]. This replaces its categorical trace by the alternating sum in the assertion.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

A closed point of degree $e$ contributes exactly $e$ points over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$ when $e\mid m$, and none otherwise. Thus $\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})=\sum_{e\mid m}eN_e$, where $N_e$ counts degree-$e$ closed points. Substitute this into the defining exponential for $Z$ and use $-\log(1-T^e)=\sum_{r\ge1}T^{er}/r$. Exponentiation gives the Euler product; every coefficient involves only finitely many closed points.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

For a finite-dimensional endomorphism $F$, the formal identity $-\log\det(1-TF)=\sum_{m\ge1}\operatorname{Tr}(F^m)T^m/m$ follows after scalar extension by multiplying the linear eigenvalue factors. Insert clause [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--2] into the exponential defining $Z$ and apply this identity in every cohomological degree. The alternating signs give precisely the determinant product.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

Each factor $(1-T^{\deg(x)})^{-1}$ of clause [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--4] has integral coefficients and constant term $1$. There are only finitely many closed points of bounded degree on a scheme of finite type over a finite field, so each coefficient of the product is a finite sum of integers. Thus $Z$ belongs to $1+T\mathbf Z[[T]]$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

Clause [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--5] gives rationality over $\mathbf Q_\ell$, while clause [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function--6] gives rational Taylor coefficients.

On unbounded étale derived categories, proper direct image preserves
arbitrary direct sums by [Stacks, [0F0D](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0D)]. Forgetting coefficients gives
the $A$-linear statement, and
Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category] transports it to
the pro-étale localizing categories.

Since $Rp_*$ maps $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ into $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,A)$ by
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients], the objects
$K\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$ whose direct image belongs to
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,A))$ form a triangulated subcategory closed under direct
sums and containing $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$, that is, all of $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients-localizing], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The constant sheaf has weight zero, since its local Frobenius is the
identity. So Theorem [theorem-purity-higher-direct-images-under]
applies to the structure map $f_0:X_0\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$
with $w=0$. The base has a single closed point, with $q_y=q$. The
stalk of $R^if_{0*}\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ there is $H^i(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ with its geometric
Frobenius, and its eigenvalues therefore satisfy
$|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{i/2}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We separate from $\chi$ the part that depends only on the degree. Put
$\varepsilon(w)=\chi(w)c^{-\deg w}$, a character of $W(U_0)$ that is
trivial on $s$.  Every element of $W(U_0)$ can be written as $w=gs^d$
with $g\in\pi_1(U)$ and $d=\deg w$, and then
$\varepsilon(w)=\chi(g)\chi(s)^dc^{-d}=\chi(g)$. So $\varepsilon$
has the same image as $\chi|_{\pi_1(U)}$, which is finite
by Theorem [theorem-rank-one-sheaves-have-finite].  At a closed point $x$ the
eigenvalue is $\varepsilon(\operatorname{Frob}_x)c^{\deg(x)}$, where the first factor
has finite order, hence complex absolute value one. Therefore the eigenvalue
has absolute value $q_x^{\lambda_\iota(c)/2}$.  This number does not depend
on $s$, because changing $s$ multiplies $c$ by a value of $\chi$ on
$\pi_1(U)$, which has finite order.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-rank-one-weights], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We factor the duality on $C$ through a finite map to $\mathbf P^1_k$,
where the trace is an explicit residue, and check that each step is
compatible with extension of scalars.

A nonconstant rational function on $C$ extends to a finite map
$\phi:C\to\mathbf P^1_k$, which is flat because $\phi_*\mathcal O_C$ is
torsion free over the discrete valuation rings of $\mathbf P^1_k$. We
may construct the duality on $C$ as duality for $\phi$, given by the
dual of the finite locally free module $\phi_*\mathcal L$, followed by
duality on $\mathbf P^1_k$, whose trace $H^1(\mathbf P^1_k,\omega)\to k$
takes the coefficient of $t^{-1}dt$ in a Čech cocycle for the
standard cover. Both steps commute with extension of scalars, hence so
does the resulting pairing. Flat base change shows that
$g=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ is unchanged by field extension.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-serre-duality-field-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-serre-duality-field-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

By naturality it suffices to show that
$\theta_Y\sigma_Y(\omega_Y)$ is the identity of $\omega_Y$. For proper
$Y$ this follows from the adjunction defining $\theta_Y$. We deduce the
case of general $Y$ by a compactification, and the case of nonreduced
$F$ by invariance under nilpotent thickenings.

*Proper $Y$ and $F=Y\times S$.* Here
$\theta_Y\sigma_Y(\omega_Y)=\operatorname{id}_{\omega_Y}$. The unit
$\sigma_Y(\omega_Y):\omega_Y\to \Psi_Y\omega_{Y_\eta}$ is an isomorphism by
Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family]. For the proper
structure map $a$ of $Y$, the base change isomorphism for proper maps and
its compatibility with $\sigma$ give

$$
\nu_a\,Ra_!\sigma_Y(\omega_Y)
=\sigma_{\operatorname{Spec}k}(Ra_!\omega_Y)
=\operatorname{id}_{Ra_!\omega_Y}.
$$

By the defining adjunction (E.6),
$\theta_Y\sigma_Y(\omega_Y)$ is therefore the adjoint of the counit
$Ra_!\omega_Y\to A$, which is $\operatorname{id}_{\omega_Y}$. Naturality of $\sigma$ then gives
$\theta_Y\Psi_Y(z)\sigma_Y(A)=z$ for every section $z$ of the
dualizing complex.

*General $Y$.* Choose a proper compactification
$j:Y\hookrightarrow\overline Y$, so that
$\omega_Y=j^*\omega_{\overline Y}$. We compare the two sides of the identity under
restriction along $j$. The units for the
constant families correspond by base change along the open immersion, and the map $\theta_Y$ corresponds to $j^*\theta_{\overline Y}$ by the composition
rule (E.9) together with
$\beta_j=\alpha_j^{-1}$ for the open immersion. Restricting the identity
$\theta_{\overline Y}\sigma_{\overline Y}(\omega_{\overline Y})=1$
therefore gives $\theta_Y\sigma_Y(\omega_Y)=1$, and by naturality the
assertion follows again for all sections of the dualizing complex.

*Nonreduced $F$.* If only $F_{\mathrm{red}}=Y\times S$, we replace $F$
by its reduction. This does not change $\operatorname{sp}_F$, because
invariance under nilpotent thickenings of the total family
and of its fibres shows that the six operations, their units and counits,
and nearby cycles agree with those of the reduction.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For $j_!$ the trace function is that of $\mathcal G$ extended by zero,
and for $j_*$ it differs from this at finitely many points of small
weight, which Lemma [lemma-growth-finite-corrections] allows us to
ignore.

The open curve $U_0$ is again smooth, geometrically connected and
affine, and Theorem [theorem-weights-sums-squared-traces] on $U_0$ gives
$\nu(\mathcal G)=w$. Extension by zero only adds zero traces, so
$\nu(j_!\mathcal G)=w$. The trace functions of $j_*$
and of the extension by zero differ only at the points of
$X_0-U_0$, by the trace function of the boundary stalks. These stalks
have weights at most $w$ by
Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points], so if $i$
denotes the inclusion of $X_0-U_0$, then
Lemma [lemma-bounds-squared-traces](2), applied to the sheaf
$i_*i^*j_*\mathcal G$, bounds the squared sum of the difference by
$Cq^{nw}$. Since $\nu(j_!\mathcal G)=w>w-1$,
Lemma [lemma-growth-finite-corrections] shows that
$\nu(j_*\mathcal G)$ is still $w$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-sums-squared-traces-j-shriek], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The assertions about $J(C)$ are those of Appendix [chap-Abelian-varieties]
for this abelian variety, and the degree sequence carries them over to
$\operatorname{Pic}(C)$.

By Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n], the kernel $J(C)[n]$
is finite étale of rank $n^{2g}$. A finite étale scheme of rank $r$
over the algebraically closed field $k$ is a disjoint union of $r$
copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, a description stable under base
extension. By Theorem [theorem-picard-scheme-jacobian-over-separably]
the formation of the Jacobian and of $[n]$ commutes with base change, so
the natural map $J(C)[n](k)\to J(C_{k'})[n](k')$ is a bijection.

If $\ell^m$ is the exact power of a prime $\ell$ dividing $n$, then
$J(C)[\ell^m](k)\simeq(\mathbf Z/\ell^m)^{2g}$ by
Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module] applied to $J(C)$. Combining the
parts for the primes dividing $n$, we get the stated
$\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$-module structure.

By Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n], the group
$J(C)(k)$ is divisible. In the exact sequence of
Corollary [corollary-degree-jacobian], the group $\mathbf Z$ has no
$n$-torsion and $J(C)(k)/n=0$. This proves the two assertions for
$\operatorname{Pic}(C)$.

The left side is a trace on a stalk of $Rf_!K$. By base change that
stalk is the compactly supported cohomology of a fibre. Hence the corollary
is the trace formula for the fibre, once we check that the Frobenius
operators correspond.

Fix $y$ and let $X_{0,y}$ be the fibre of $f_0$ over $y$. It is a separated
scheme of finite type over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, and its rational points are
the $x\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ with $f_0(x)=y$. Restrict $K$ to its
geometric fibre $X_{\bar y}$ and give the restriction the Weil
structure over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$ obtained from the $m$-th iterate of
$\phi$. By base change for compact supports, $(Rf_!K)_{\bar y}$ is
$R\Gamma_c(X_{\bar y},K|_{X_{\bar y}})$, and
$\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}$ is the geometric Frobenius operator of
this Weil complex. For finite $A$ this is part (4) of
Lemma [lemma-comparison-via-relative-frobenius], applied to the Frobenius
correspondence $\phi\kappa_1$ and translated by
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius]. By the comparisons of
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients] it extends to the other
coefficient rings. Since the Frobenius acting on the stalk of the
Weil complex on the fibre at a rational point $x$ of $X_{0,y}$ is
$\operatorname{Frob}_{x,m}$, the stated identity is
Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula] for
$X_{0,y}$ over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, with exponent $1$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-trace-functions-direct-image-compact], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both assertions are local on $T$, so we may replace $T$ by one of the
$U_\alpha$ and assume that $\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal O_{P\times T}$.
Since $H^0(P,\mathcal O_P)=k$ [Stacks, [0BUG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BUG)], and $T$ is flat over $k$,
flat base change gives $f_*\mathcal O_{P\times T}=\mathcal O_T$. Hence
the chosen trivialization identifies $f_*\mathcal L$ with the
invertible sheaf $\mathcal O_T$. Under the same identification the
evaluation map $f^*f_*\mathcal L\to\mathcal L$ becomes the identity of
$\mathcal O_{P\times T}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-triviality-over-open-cover-base], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Purity follows from the upper bounds for the sheaf and for its dual,
provided the stalk of the dual is the dual of the stalk, and trivial
inertia guarantees this. So we apply
Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points] to the sheaf and to its
dual, which is pure of weight $-a$.  Since the inertia acts trivially,
the stalk of the extended dual is the dual of the stalk of the
extension, and so every eigenvalue $\alpha$ satisfies
$|\iota\alpha|^2\le q_z^a$ and $|\iota\alpha^{-1}|^2\le q_z^{-a}$, and
equality holds.

For a sheaf that is already lisse on the curve, the inertia is trivial, and
Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk] identifies the stalk of $j_*$ with the
original stalk. The first assertion, applied at each of the finitely many
points outside the dense open, then gives the second.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-unramified-boundary-point], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Corollary [corollary-unramified-boundary-point], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Two of the formulas are Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas], and we obtain the other two by applying these to the Verdier dual of the argument and
using biduality on both schemes. Explicitly, for $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ and
$L\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$ this reads

$$
\mathbb D_YRf_*K\simeq\mathbb D_YRf_*\mathbb D_X(\mathbb D_XK)
\simeq\mathbb D_Y\mathbb D_YRf_!\mathbb D_XK\simeq Rf_!\mathbb D_XK,
$$

$$
\mathbb D_Xf^!L\simeq\mathbb D_Xf^!\mathbb D_Y(\mathbb D_YL)
\simeq\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_Xf^*\mathbb D_YL\simeq f^*\mathbb D_YL.
$$

The formulas for $j$ and $i$ are the special cases $f=j$ and $f=i$.

By Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas], internal adjunction identifies $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda_Y}(Rf_{!,\Lambda}K,a_Y^!\Lambda)$ with $Rf_{*,\Lambda}R\!\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda_X}(K,f_\Lambda^!a_Y^!\Lambda)$. The composition comparison identifies $f_\Lambda^!a_Y^!\Lambda$ with $a_X^!\Lambda$. These are precisely the two sides of the assertion, with its natural comparison.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

Apply clause [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--1] to $\mathbb D_XK$ and then apply $\mathbb D_Y$. Biduality on $X$ and $Y$ (Theorem [theorem-verdier-biduality--1] and its coefficient extensions) cancels both double duals and gives the asserted comparison. The preservation assertions of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf--1]–[proposition-six-operations-dctf--15] ensure that biduality applies to every object involved.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

The inverse-image formula in Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas], with the dualizing objects $a_Y^!\Lambda$ and $a_X^!\Lambda\simeq f_\Lambda^!a_Y^!\Lambda$, is precisely the specified natural isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

Apply clause [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--3] to $\mathbb D_YL$ and dualize on $X$. Biduality on $X$ and $Y$ cancels both double duals and gives $\mathbb D_Xf_\Lambda^!L\simeq f_\Lambda^*\mathbb D_YL$. The preservation results of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf--1]–[proposition-six-operations-dctf--15] ensure that these biduality maps are isomorphisms.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

In clause [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--1] put $f=j$. The construction of compact direct image for an open immersion identifies $Rj_{!,\Lambda}$ with extension by zero $j_{!,\Lambda}$, giving the displayed comparison.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

In clause [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--2] put $f=j$ and use $Rj_{!,\Lambda}=j_{!,\Lambda}$.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

In clause [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--4] put $f=i$ and invert the resulting natural isomorphism. Its source and target are $i_\Lambda^*\mathbb D_X$ and $\mathbb D_Zi_\Lambda^!$ as asserted.

*Source:* the proof of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas].

On an affine chart of $X_0$, a finitely generated $\mathbf F_q$-algebra is finite over its subring of $q$th powers: monomials in a finite set of generators with exponents less than $q$ generate it as a module over that subring. Thus the $q$-power Frobenius is finite. It is integral, surjective and radicial, hence a universal homeomorphism. Both properties survive base change to $k$. By its construction as that base change, $\Phi_X$ is a morphism over $k$.

At a closed point let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ be the eigenvalues after applying $\iota$, counted with multiplicity. Their multiset is stable under complex conjugation. For every positive integer $m$, conjugation therefore fixes $\sum_j\alpha_j^m$. This sum is the trace of the $m$th power of local Frobenius, so that trace is real.

Associativity of derived tensor gives

$$
(K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_T}B_T)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{B_T}C_T
\simeq K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_T}(B_T\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{B_T}C_T)
\simeq K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_T}C_T.
$$

The first and last terms are $(K_B)_C$ and $K_C$ by definition. The associativity maps are natural in $K$, so this is the canonical comparison.

The finite twists are rank one locally by clause [definition-tate-twists--2] and scalar extension. A compatible system of roots trivializes the inverse-limit twist on a pro-étale cover, and therefore trivializes $\mathcal O_{E,X}(1)$. Inverting $\ell$ and extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ preserve a rank-one free module. Thus every admissible coefficient twist is locally free of rank one.

Since $\ell$ is invertible on $X$, adjoining a primitive $\ell^n$th root of unity gives an étale covering on which $\mu_{\ell^n,X}$ is cyclic of order $\ell^n$. Sending $1$ to that root identifies it with the constant sheaf $(\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z)_X$. Pulling the covering to $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ gives the stated local identification.

For $s\geq r$, the power map $\mu_{\ell^s,X}\to\mu_{\ell^r,X}$ sends a primitive root to a primitive root. After the étale trivializations of clause [definition-tate-twists--2], it is the reduction map $\mathbf Z/\ell^s\to\mathbf Z/\ell^r$. Tensoring with $A$, which is killed by $\ell^r$, makes this an isomorphism. The power maps compose, so these identifications satisfy transitivity and identify all admissible choices of the exponent.

On a pro-étale covering choose a compatible system of primitive $\ell^n$th roots of unity. It identifies $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}(1)$ with $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$ and, compatibly, the integral and field twists with their coefficient sheaves. On that covering the asserted map is the associativity isomorphism for scalar extension. These maps are independent of the chosen generator, since a change of generator multiplies both sides by the same unit of $\mathbf Z_\ell$. They descend and give the required identification after the filtered colimit over finite $E$.

Geometric stalks commute with filtered colimits and finite limits. Thus the stalk of $\varinjlim_nF[n]\to F$ is the inclusion of the union of the subgroups killed by positive integers into the stalk of $F$. For an abelian group this inclusion is an equality precisely when every element is torsion. Geometric stalks detect isomorphisms in the setting of this definition, so the sheaf equality is equivalent to the stated torsion condition.

Choose a K-injective complex representing $\omega_X$. Derived internal Hom into this complex carries a mapping-cone triangle in the first variable to the corresponding contravariant mapping-cone triangle, with the usual shift and sign. Every distinguished triangle is isomorphic to a cone triangle. Hence $\cHom_{\Lambda_X}(-,\omega_X)$ sends distinguished triangles in the opposite category to distinguished triangles and has the required shift identification. It is therefore exact.

An abelian variety is geometrically reduced because it is smooth, and
geometrically irreducible because the identity component of a group
scheme over a field is geometrically irreducible [Stacks, [0B7R](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B7R)] and $A$
is connected.

For commutativity, consider $h:A\times A\to A$,
$h(x,y)=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$. It maps $A\times\{e\}$ to $e$. By
Lemma [lemma-rigidity], applied with the first factor as the
proper one, there are an open $V\ni e$ and $g:V\to A$ with
$h|_{A\times V}=g\circ\operatorname{pr}_2$. Composing with
$(e,\operatorname{id}):V\to A\times V$ gives $g=h(e,-)=e$, so $h=e$ on
$A\times V$. To pass from $A\times V$ to $A\times A$, we compare $h$
with the constant map $e$. Since $A\times A$ is smooth, hence reduced,
and irreducible, the nonempty open $A\times V$ is scheme-theoretically
dense. Two maps to a separated scheme that agree on a

This is Leray's acyclicity lemma [Stacks, [015E](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/015E)], and the first assertion
is the case of a resolution of $F$. We recall the argument, which compares
$M^\bullet$ with an injective replacement through the cone.

In a bounded below exact complex of $v$-acyclic
objects the cycles are again $v$-acyclic, by induction along the short
exact sequences of cycles, so the complex stays exact after applying
$v$. We apply this to the cone of a quasi-isomorphism
$M^\bullet\to J^\bullet$ into a bounded below complex of injectives.
This cone is bounded below and exact, and its terms are $v$-acyclic,
being finite direct sums of terms of $M^\bullet$ and of $J^\bullet$.
It follows that $vM^\bullet\to vJ^\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and
the target computes $Rv(M^\bullet)$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-acyclic-resolutions], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We prove vanishing on affine charts by Gabber's theorem, deduce the case
$q\geq2$ by Mayer–Vietoris, and treat $q=1$ by lifting classes to finite
torsors over $\mathbf P^1_R$, where injectivity of $I$ kills them.

*Step 1: affine opens.* Let $W=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be an affine open of
$\mathbf P^1_R$ and set $J=\mathfrak mB$. We show that $I_0|_{W_0}$ has no
cohomology in positive degrees. Since the pair $(B,J)$ need not be henselian, we pass
to its henselization $(B^h,JB^h)$, for which $B^h/JB^h=B/J$. Moreover, $B^h$ is the
filtered colimit of the étale $B$-algebras $B'$ equipped with
$B'/JB'\simeq B/J$. Gabber's theorem (Theorem [theorem-gabber-affine-proper-base-change]) and continuity of étale
cohomology give

$$
H^q(W_0,I_0|_{W_0})
\simeq H^q(\operatorname{Spec}B^h,I|)
\simeq\varinjlim_{B'}H^q(\operatorname{Spec}B',I|).
\tag{4.11}
$$

Every group on the right vanishes for $q>0$, because the restriction of an
injective sheaf to an étale object is injective: the restriction functor
has an exact left adjoint, namely extension by zero in the localized site.

*Step 2: degrees $q\geq2$.* The two standard affine charts
$U,V\subset \mathbf P^1_R$ have affine intersection, so
(4.11) shows that the restriction of $I$
to each of $U_0$, $V_0$ and $(U\cap V)_0$ has no cohomology in positive
degrees. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence on $\mathbf P^1_\kappa$ therefore gives
$H^q(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0)=0$ for $q\geq2$ (this is the case of two
charts in [Stacks, [0A51](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A51)]). In degree one the same sequence only identifies
$H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0)$ with the cokernel of
$\Gamma(U_0,I_0)\oplus\Gamma(V_0,I_0)\to\Gamma((U\cap V)_0,I_0)$, and
nothing said so far shows that this cokernel vanishes.

*Step 3: degree one.* Let $\xi\in H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0)$. Following
[Stacks, [0A5H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A5H)], we show that $\xi=0$. First write $I$ as a filtered
colimit of constructible $\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaves. Since pullback and $H^1$ on
$\mathbf P^1_\kappa$ commute with this colimit, $\xi$ is the image of a
class $\zeta\in H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,G_0)$ for some constructible $G$ with a map
$G\to I$. Next choose (4.9) and put
$P=\bigoplus_a(h_a)_*\underline{M_a}$. Since $I$ is injective, the map
$G\to I$ extends to $P\to I$. Let $\zeta'$ be the image of $\zeta$ in
$H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,P_0)$.

The class $\zeta'$ lifts to $H^1(\mathbf P^1_R,P)$. Indeed,
(4.10) and the Leray spectral sequence give

$$
H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,P_0)
\simeq\bigoplus_a H^1((Y_a)_0,\underline{M_a}),\qquad
H^1(\mathbf P^1_R,P)\simeq\bigoplus_a H^1(Y_a,\underline{M_a}).
$$

Each $Y_a$ is finite over $\mathbf P^1_R$, hence proper over $R$, so the
comparison (4.8) for finite torsors
(Theorem [theorem-finite-etale-covers-proper-henselian])
lifts $\zeta'$. This lift maps to zero in $H^1(\mathbf P^1_R,I)$ because
$I$ is injective. Now the commutative square of restriction maps

$$
\begin{CD}
H^1(\mathbf P^1_R,P) @>>> H^1(\mathbf P^1_R,I)\\
@VVV @VVV\\
H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,P_0) @>>> H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0)
\end{CD}
$$

shows that the image of $\zeta'$ in $H^1(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0)$ is zero, and this image is $\xi$, because $G\to P\to I$ is the given map $G\to I$.
Hence $\xi=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-closed-fibre], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The sheaf $R^q\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*I$ is associated to
$V\mapsto H^q(V_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\nu_X^*I)$, so it suffices to show that
positive cohomology vanishes on affine étale objects $V$. The
restriction of $I$ to $V_{\acute{e}t}$ is injective, since restriction has an
exact left adjoint, namely extension by zero. Hence we may assume $X$ affine.
By Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale], every pro-étale covering of
an affine object is refined by a finite covering by affines that are
ind-étale over it. By the Čech acyclicity criterion for a basis,
it therefore suffices to show that the Čech complexes of $\nu_X^*I$
for such coverings have no positive cohomology.

As in [Stacks, [099U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099U)], we claim that the Čech complex of such a covering is a
filtered colimit of Čech complexes of étale coverings. Write each
covering map as an inverse limit of affine étale maps
over the object being covered. By (2.6), the
Čech complex of the covering is the filtered colimit of the
Čech complexes of these étale approximations. Each finitely
presented approximation descends to a common étale stage over the
base, becomes a covering after increasing that stage, and its nerve
descends by taking fibre products. Each augmented Čech complex at
a finite stage is obtained by applying $\Hom(-,I)$ to the exact augmented
complex of free sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules on the nerve, so it has no
positive cohomology because $I$ is injective. Filtered colimits are exact, so the same holds for the
pro-étale covering, and the criterion implies the required vanishing.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-pulled-back-injectives], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The four induced correspondences come from base change, and $R\Gamma_c$
of the localization triangle is a two-step filtered object with an

square with $j$ is cartesian, and by base change we get the correspondences on

correspondences on $i^*K$ and $Ri_*i^*K$ from

to the Frobenius correspondence and take direct images with
compact support. Since the triangle is functorial, the Frobenius
correspondence becomes an endomorphism of a two-step filtered object, and hence
the traces add by Proposition [proposition-properties-trace].
Finally, Lemma [lemma-comparison-via-relative-frobenius](3) for $j$ and $i$ identifies the
endomorphisms $T_{c_m}$ of the cohomology of $j_!j^*K$ and $Ri_*i^*K$ with those on $U$ and
$Z$.

Both parts follow formally from uniqueness of right adjoints. Part (1)
comes from (6.9) and $j_!\dashv j^*$ for $\mathbf A^1\subset\mathbf P^1$, and
part (2) from $u_!\dashv u^*$ for étale $u$.

(1) Let $j:\mathbf A^1_S\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^1_S$ be the open
immersion, so that $Rp_{1!}=Rp_*j_!$ for $d=1$.
Since $j_!\dashv j^*$ and $Rp_*\dashv p^*(1)[2]$ by (6.9),
composing right adjoints gives $p_1^!=j^*p^*(1)[2]$. This equals
$p_1^*(1)[2]$ because $p\circ j=p_1$. For general $d$, write $p_d$ as a
composite of $d$ projections $r_1,\dots,r_d$ of affine lines. By the composition isomorphism for $Rf_!$ (Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](1)) we have
$Rp_{d!}\simeq Rr_{1!}\circ\dots\circ Rr_{d!}$.
Hence $p_d^!$ is the composite of the right adjoints of the $Rr_{i!}$,
which is $p_d^*(d)[2d]$ by the case $d=1$. Under this isomorphism, the
counit of $Rp_{d!}\dashv p_d^*(d)[2d]$ is the composite of the $d$ counits
for the affine lines. Each of these is a trace (6.5)
composed with the counit of $j_!\dashv j^*$. By the associativity in Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](1), the composite does not depend
on how the $d$ factors are grouped. Each factor and the composition
isomorphism commute with base change (Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](2)), and therefore so does the counit. The unit is determined
by the counit through the triangle identities, and it commutes with base
change as well.

(2) For an étale $u$, the functor $Ru_!$ is extension by zero. By its
elementary construction [Stacks, [03S2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03S2)], it is an exact functor
$u_!:\operatorname{Mod}(U_{\acute{e}t},A)\to\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ left adjoint to $u^*$.
As both functors are exact, they need not be derived, and the adjunction
extends to derived categories. For every $M\in D(U_{\acute{e}t},A)$,

$$
\Hom(M,u^*f^!N)
=\Hom(u_!M,f^!N)
=\Hom(Rf_!u_!M,N)
=\Hom(R(fu)_!M,N),
$$

where the last step is the composition isomorphism of
Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](1). The Yoneda lemma therefore gives (6.12). Taking $M=u^*f^!N$ and the
identity on the left, we see that the counit of $R(fu)_!\dashv(fu)^!$ is the composite of the counits as stated. For the cocycle condition, the isomorphism for $uu'$ and the
composite of those for $u$ and $u'$ both correspond under the Yoneda lemma
to the bijections obtained from the composition isomorphism for
$f\circ u\circ u'$. These bijections agree by associativity of the
composition isomorphisms (Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](1)).

We define $\mathcal L_\psi$ as an eigensheaf in the direct image of the
constant sheaf under an Artin–Schreier cover, and read off its
properties from the corresponding properties of the cover: addition of
roots for the first isomorphism, a fibrewise pairing for the second,
and the action of Frobenius on roots for the trace.

Fix a nontrivial character $\psi_0:\mathbf F_p\to E^\times$. Since the
trace pairing on $k_0$ is nondegenerate, there is $a\in k_0^\times$
such that $\psi(z)=\psi_0(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_0/\mathbf F_p}(az))$.
The cover $u^p-u=ax$ of the affine line is finite étale, with group
of translations $\mathbf F_p$. Let $\mathcal L_\psi$ be the image of

$$
e_{\psi_0}=\frac1p\sum_{c\in\mathbf F_p}\psi_0(c)^{-1}\tau_c^*
$$

on the direct image of the constant sheaf $E$ under this cover. It is
lisse of rank one, since its stalk is the $\psi_0$-eigenspace in the
regular representation, and the root $u=0$ over $x=0$ specifies the
trivialization at zero. For the first isomorphism, adding roots of two
Artin–Schreier equations identifies the contracted product of the two
torsors with the torsor for the sum, and passing to the character
eigenspaces we obtain the isomorphism. For the second, the pairing on the direct image given by
summing products over the fibres is perfect and invariant under the
translations. Since, for an invariant pairing, the $\chi$- and
$\chi'$-eigenspaces of two characters are orthogonal unless
$\chi\chi'=1$, our pairing pairs the $\psi_0$-eigenspace perfectly
with the $\psi_0^{-1}$-eigenspace. Since
$\psi^{-1}(z)=\psi_0^{-1}(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_0/\mathbf F_p}(az))$, the
$\psi_0^{-1}$-eigenspace of the same cover is $\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}$,
and we obtain $\mathcal L_\psi^\vee\simeq\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}$.

For a root $u$ above $x\in\mathbf F_{q^n}$ we have

$$
u^{q^n}=u+
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/\mathbf F_p}(ax).
$$

Geometric Frobenius acts on functions on the torsor by pullback along
this map, and hence on the chosen eigenspace by
$\psi_0(\operatorname{Tr}(ax))$. By transitivity of field traces, this is
the asserted trace. Since these scalars are roots of unity, their images
under any field embedding have absolute value one.

Fix a nontrivial character $\psi_0:\mathbf F_p\to E^\times$. Since the
trace pairing on $k_0$ is nondegenerate, there is $a\in k_0^\times$
such that $\psi(z)=\psi_0(\operatorname{Tr}_{k_0/\mathbf F_p}(az))$.
The cover $u^p-u=ax$ of the affine line is finite étale, with group
of translations $\mathbf F_p$. Let $\mathcal L_\psi$ be the image of

$$
e_{\psi_0}=\frac1p\sum_{c\in\mathbf F_p}\psi_0(c)^{-1}\tau_c^*
$$

on the direct image of the constant sheaf $E$ under this cover. It is
lisse of rank one, since its stalk is the $\psi_0$-eigenspace in the
regular representation. The root $u=0$ over $x=0$ specifies the
trivialization at zero.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

Adding two roots of $u^p-u=ax$ and $v^p-v=ay$ gives a root of $(u+v)^p-(u+v)=a(x+y)$. This identifies the contracted product of the two $\mathbf F_p$-torsors with the torsor for $x+y$. Passing to their $\psi_0$-eigenspaces sends the tensor of the two character lines to the character line of the sum, giving the asserted multiplication isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

On a fibre of the cover in clause [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--1], use the translation-invariant pairing $(f,g)\mapsto p^{-1}\sum_u f(u)g(u)$; $p$ is invertible in $E$. Distinct character spaces are orthogonal unless their characters multiply to $1$, and the pairing between the $\psi_0$ and $\psi_0^{-1}$ lines is perfect. The inverse-character line is exactly $\mathcal L_{\psi^{-1}}$, so this pairing induces the stated duality isomorphism. The factor $p^{-1}$ fixes its normalization at zero.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

The chosen trivializations in clause [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--1] use the root $0$ in the fibre over zero. Under the torsor addition in clause [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--2], the pair $(0,0)$ maps to $0$. Thus the tensor of the two chosen basis vectors maps to the chosen basis vector, which is the required normalization.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

In the fibre over zero, the character eigenfunction taking value $1$ at the root $0$ takes values $\psi_0(c)$ at the other roots, and the inverse-character eigenfunction takes $\psi_0(c)^{-1}$. Their pointwise products are all $1$. The normalized pairing in clause [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--3] therefore evaluates to $p^{-1}\sum_{c\in\mathbf F_p}1=1$. This identifies the chosen inverse-character basis with the dual chosen basis, as required.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

For a root $u$ above $x\in\mathbf F_{q^n}$ we have

$$
u^{q^n}=u+
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/\mathbf F_p}(ax).
$$

Geometric Frobenius acts on functions on the torsor by pullback along
this map, and hence on the chosen eigenspace by
$\psi_0(\operatorname{Tr}(ax))$. By transitivity of field traces, this is
the asserted trace.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

The Frobenius scalars computed in clause [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf--6] are values of the finite additive character, hence roots of unity. Every embedding sends a root of unity to a complex number of absolute value one. Since the sheaf has rank one, this is exactly punctual purity of weight zero.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf].

The idea is to compactify $f$, so that only an open immersion remains,
and for an open immersion base change along a product projection holds even
when $T$ is singular. We argue on the étale site, where $M$ is a bounded
complex with torsion coefficients, and transport the result to the
pro-étale site by Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images].

Choose a compactification $f=\bar f j$, with $j:X\hookrightarrow\bar X$
open and $\bar f:\bar X\to Y$ proper (Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem]).
Since base change maps compose, it suffices to prove the lemma for $j$ and
for $\bar f$ separately.
For the open immersion $j$, the base change map
$p_{\bar X}^*Rj_*M\to R(j\times\operatorname{id}_T)_*p_X^*M$ is an
isomorphism by [Stacks, [0F1H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1H)], applied to the cohomology sheaves of $M$
and combined with the bounded-below spectral sequence. For $\bar f$, proper
base change, applied to $Rj_*M$, shows that

$$
p_Y^*R\bar f_*Rj_*M\longrightarrow
R(\bar f\times\operatorname{id}_T)_*p_{\bar X}^*Rj_*M
$$

is an isomorphism. By Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting] the composite of
the two base change maps is the base change map for $f$.

The step for $j$ does not depend on
Proposition [proposition-ordinary-external-kunneth] below, so there is no
circularity. Indeed, the proof of [Stacks, [0F1H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1H)] has two inputs. The first is
base change under extension of the ground field [Stacks, [0F1C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1C)], which by
[Stacks, [0F09](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F09)] follows from smooth base change
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-classical-torsion-2]), because
after passing to perfect closures the larger field is a filtered union of
smooth algebras over the smaller one. The second input, [Stacks, [0F1G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F1G)], is a
Künneth formula with one proper factor, which comes from proper base
change and the projection formula.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-base-change-along-product-projection], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both the source and the target of $\tau$ are compatible with proper
direct image and smooth pullback, so the cone is as well. To prove the
vanishing on $i_*M$, we reduce to the pair $(Z,Z)$, where the

By Lemma [lemma-functoriality-deformation], $f$ induces a morphism
$\widetilde f$ of deformations, which is proper if $f$ is proper and
smooth if $f$ is smooth. To this morphism we apply the base change maps of
nearby cycles, together with proper or smooth base change for the
restriction to the zero section.  The resulting squares for
$\tau$ then commute because the base change map for pullback is compatible
with composition, and their cofibres give the two isomorphisms.
In the special case $f=i$, the source pair is $(Z,Z)$ and
$\mathcal D_ZZ=Z\times S$, so $\tau_{Z,Z}$ is the
inverse of the isomorphism of Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family].
Hence $C_{Z,Z}=0$, and since $i$ is proper, the first isomorphism gives
$C_{X,Z}(i_*M)=0$.
The last assertion then follows by applying the exact functor $C_{X,Z}$
to $j_!j^*L\to L\to i_*i^*L$.

Since
$\kappa_M=t_{p_1}(\xi\otimes1)$, the main point is
the case of the constant complex,

$$
\beta_{p_1}\Psi(\xi)\alpha_{p_2}
=p_{1s}^!\sigma_X\,\xi_s\,p_{2s}^*\theta_X,
\tag{C}
$$

and the general case follows from (C) by
Lemma [lemma-compatibilities-base-change-maps]. Since the proof uses
proper base change, we prove (C) for a proper
family and then extend it by compactification.

Suppose first that $a=a_X:X\to S$ is proper. On the fibre over $\eta$,
let

$$
Q_\eta(L):a_\eta^*Ra_{\eta*}L\xrightarrow{\sim}Rp_{1\eta*}p_{2\eta}^*L
$$

be the proper base change isomorphism, and define $Q_s$ in the same way.
On each fibre, the $Rp_{1!}$-adjoint of $\xi$ is $Q(\omega_X)^{-1}$
followed by $a^*\varepsilon_a$. We compare these adjoints using the
identity

$$
\nu_{p_1}Rp_{1s*}(\alpha_{p_2})Q_s(\Psi_XL)
=\Psi_X(Q_\eta(L))\alpha_a(Ra_{\eta*}L)\,a_s^*\nu_a(L).
$$

To prove it, we take adjoints for $p_{1s}^*\dashv Rp_{1s*}$. By the
composition rule for $\alpha$ and $ap_1=ap_2$, both adjoints are the composite of $a_s^*\nu_a$, the base change map
$\alpha_{ap_1}=\alpha_{ap_2}$, and the pullback by $p_{2\eta}$ of the
counit $a_\eta^*Ra_{\eta*}L\to L$. Substituting this identity into the
$Rp_{1s!}$-adjoint of the left side of
(C), and using naturality of $\alpha_a$ with
respect to $\varepsilon_{a_\eta}$ and $\alpha_a(A)=\sigma_X$, we find that this
adjoint is the composite

$$
a_s^*Ra_{s!}\Psi_X\omega_{X_\eta}
\xrightarrow{a_s^*\nu_a}
a_s^*Ra_{\eta!}\omega_{X_\eta}
\xrightarrow{a_s^*\varepsilon_{a_\eta}}A_{X_s}
\xrightarrow{\sigma_X}\Psi_XA_{X_\eta}.
$$

By (E.6) for $a$, this composite equals
$\sigma_X a_s^*(\varepsilon_{a_s}Ra_{s!}\theta_X)$, which is the
$Rp_{1s!}$-adjoint of the right side. This proves
(C) for proper $X$.

If $X$ is not proper over $S$, we choose an open immersion
$j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$ into a proper $S$-scheme and restrict
both factors of the product from $\overline X$ to $X$. Both sides of
(C) are compatible with this restriction.
For the maps $\xi$ this follows from the composition rule for
exceptional inverse images. For the base change maps it holds because
$j^!=j^*$, the map $\alpha_j$ is invertible by smooth base change, and
$\beta_j=\alpha_j^{-1}$. So
(C) on $\overline X$ implies it on $X$.
Applying Lemma [lemma-compatibilities-base-change-maps] to $p_1$ and using
$\mu(\sigma\otimes1)=1$, we deduce
(E.10).

We prove the formula for finite coefficients, where it is Galois
theory of the punctured henselian neighbourhood, and pass to the limit.

The stalk of $j_*\mathcal F$ at $\bar z$ is the colimit of the sections
of $\mathcal F$ over the inverse images of $U$ in étale neighbourhoods
of $\bar z$, that is, the group of sections over the
punctured spectrum of the strict henselization at $\bar z$. This
punctured spectrum is the spectrum of a field, whose absolute Galois
group is the inertia group $I_z$, so finite
locally constant sheaves there correspond to finite continuous
representations of the inertia group, and their sections are the
invariant vectors. Applying this to the finite reductions of a stable
lattice and passing to the inverse limit, we obtain the formula with
integral coefficients.

Two compatibilities take us to rational coefficients and to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.
Rationalization commutes with taking invariants, since a power of the
uniformizer carries an invariant rational vector into the lattice.  A finite
extension of scalars also commutes with invariants. Indeed, it is exact, hence
commutes with finite intersections of kernels, and in a finite-dimensional space
the intersection of the kernels of all $g-1$ is the intersection of
finitely many of them.
This gives the formula with rational coefficients, after finite
extension of scalars, and hence also over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Since all these maps
commute with the action of the decomposition group, the identification is
Frobenius equivariant. Finally, if $\mathcal F$ extends to a lisse sheaf on
$X_0$, the local inertia acts trivially, and so the adjunction map is
an isomorphism on every geometric stalk.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

At every closed point $x$ the eigenvalues of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on the stalk of a mixed sheaf are those on the
stalks of the quotients of its filtration. If the quotients have weights
at most $w$, the sheaf is therefore punctually of weights $\le w$.
Conversely, each nonzero
quotient has a nonzero stalk at some closed point $x$, and the
eigenvalues of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ there are eigenvalues on the
stalk of the sheaf. So if the sheaf is punctually of weights $\le w$,
the weight of the quotient is at most $w$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Everything about $K_n$ is obtained from $K_1$ by induction on $n$, using
that $K_n$ is an extension of $K_{n-1}$ by $K_1$. The Tor bound needs an
extra argument with minimal resolutions, and the bound on $K$ itself then
follows from the Milnor sequence.

The filtration of $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ by the powers of $\pi_E$ has
graded pieces $\mathbf F_E$. Tensoring its short exact sequences with
$K$ over $\mathcal O_{E,X}$, we get triangles
$K_1\to K_{n}\to K_{n-1}$, up to the identification
$\pi_E^{n-1}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n\simeq\mathbf F_E$. Moreover, complexes with
constructible cohomology in $[a,b]$ are closed under extensions in
triangles, by the long exact cohomology sequence and the fact
that constructible sheaves form a weak Serre subcategory. Induction on $n$ now shows
that $K_n$ is bounded in $[a,b]$ with constructible cohomology. Since locally constant
finite sheaves of modules also form a weak Serre subcategory, the same
induction works on a fixed stratum, and a single stratification works for
all $n$. By the comparison theorem for constructible sheaves
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]), these finite sheaves and
complexes are classical, that is, pulled back from the étale site.

For the Tor bound we use
$K_n\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n}\mathbf F_E\simeq K_1$.
At an étale geometric point $\bar x$, take a bounded above resolution of the
stalk of $K_n$ by finite free modules over the Artinian local ring
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$. Cancelling a two-term identity summand whenever
a differential matrix has a unit entry, we obtain a minimal resolution, whose
differentials have entries in $(\pi_E)$, so they vanish after
tensoring with $\mathbf F_E$. Since stalks commute with derived tensor
products, the minimal resolution tensored with $\mathbf F_E$ computes the
stalk of $K_1$ at $\bar x$, with zero differential. Its rank
in degree $q$ is therefore $\dim_{\mathbf F_E}H^q(K_1)_{\bar x}$. This vanishes
outside $[a,b]$, and we conclude that the stalk has a bounded finite free
resolution in $[a,b]$. Such a bound on stalks gives the same Tor bound on the
étale site, and Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison] carries
it to the pro-étale site, for Tor against arbitrary sheaves of modules there.

By completeness $K=R\varprojlim K_n$, so the Milnor sequence
(2.2) gives the lower bound and the vanishing above
$b+1$. For $H^{b+1}(K)$ we use the top degree, where
$H^b(K_n)=H^b(K_{n+1})\otimes_{\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n+1}}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$,
so the transition maps are epimorphisms. Their $R^1\varprojlim$ vanishes by the
last assertion of Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence], and this means
that $H^{b+1}(K)=0$.

The filtration of $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ by the powers of $\pi_E$ has

For (1), the trace at
each point of $X_0(k_n)$ has absolute value at most
$rq^{na/2}$, and Lemma [lemma-point-count-bound] gives
$S_n\le Dr^2q^{n(a+1)}$. For (2),
Lemma [lemma-point-count-bound] bounds the number of points of
the support with values in $k_n$ independently of $n$, so it suffices
to bound the trace at each of them. Since the support consists of
finitely many points with finite-dimensional stalks, the sum $c$ of the
ranks of the stalks of the $\mathcal H^i(K)$ is finite, and at each such
point the trace has absolute value at most $cq^{na/2}$. For (3),
the trace of $\mathcal B_b$ at a $k_n$-point is $b^n$, so tensoring by
$\mathcal B_b$ multiplies $S_n$ by $|\iota(b)|^{2n}=q^{n\lambda_\iota(b)}$.

At each point of $X_0(k_n)$, at most $r$ eigenvalues contribute and each has absolute value at most $q^{na/2}$. The trace has absolute value at most $rq^{na/2}$, so its squared absolute value is at most $r^2q^{na}$. Lemma [lemma-point-count-bound] bounds the number of points by $Dq^n$. Summing yields $S_n(F)\le Dr^2q^{n(a+1)}$.

Apply the linear form of Cartan's solvability criterion [humphreys72, §4.3], explicitly quoted in the reference. It applies over the characteristic-zero field of this appendix to the finite-dimensional representation $\mathfrak a\subseteq\operatorname{End}(M)$. Its trace hypothesis is exactly $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=0$ for $X\in[\mathfrak a,\mathfrak a]$ and $Y\in\mathfrak a$. The conclusion is that $\mathfrak a$ is solvable.

We give a homotopy argument. The contraction $x\mapsto ax$ joins the identity
($a=1$) to a map that factors through $Z$ ($a=0$), and the endomorphisms of
$z^*\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(M_X)$ that these maps induce form a family
over $\mathbf A^1$. Since $\mathbf A^1$ has the
cohomology of a point, the family is constant, and comparing its two
ends shows that $\tau_{X,Z}(M_X)$ has an inverse.

Consider the contraction $h:X\times\mathbf A^1\to X$, $h(x,a)=ax$,
and write $h_a=h(-,a):X\to X$ for $a\in k$.  It maps
$Z\times\mathbf A^1$ schematically into $Z$, since
$h^*(x^m)=a^m x^m\in(x^m)$, and by Lemma [lemma-functoriality-deformation],
whose hypothesis is this inclusion of ideals, all $h_a$ lift to the
deformations.  Moreover, $h_1=\operatorname{id}$, and $h_0$ factors
through $Z$ and restricts to the identity on $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$.  Set $N=z^*\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(M_X)$.
The base change maps for pullback along these lifts induce endomorphisms
$\phi_a:N\to N$, with $\phi_1=\operatorname{id}_N$.

There is one endomorphism $\phi$ of the pullback of $N$ to
$Z\times\mathbf A^1$ whose fibre at $a$ is $\phi_a$.  To construct it,
we apply the base change map for pullback along $h:X\times\mathbf A^1\to X$
and then invert the base change map for the projection to $X$, which is
smooth; by flat base change, the deformation of
$X\times\mathbf A^1$ is $\mathcal D_ZX\times\mathbf A^1$.  The restrictions of $h$ and
of the projection to $Z\times\mathbf A^1$ induce the same map to $Z$ on
reduced schemes, so invariance under nilpotent thickenings identifies
$h_Z^*N$ with $\operatorname{pr}_Z^*N$, naturally in $N$, and we may
view the family as an endomorphism of a
single pullback.  By compatibility with composition, its fibres are the
endomorphisms $\phi_a$ constructed above.

The family $\phi$ is constant; this is the
algebraic form of homotopy invariance.
Since $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a point, invariance under nilpotent
thickenings identifies $D^b_c(Z_{\acute et},A)$ with the bounded derived
category of finite $A$-modules.  Pullback along the projection
$p:Z\times\mathbf A^1\to Z$ is fully faithful on this category.
Indeed, the calculation for the affine line and the hypercohomology
spectral sequence show that $R\Gamma(\mathbf A^1,p^*B)=B$ for every such
bounded complex $B$, and full faithfulness follows by adjunction.
Thus $\phi$ is the pullback of a single endomorphism of $N$. Its two
restrictions $\phi_0$ and $\phi_1$ therefore coincide, and
$\phi_0=\operatorname{id}_N$.

Because $h_0$ factors through $Z$, we can also express $\phi_0$ in
terms of $\tau_{X,Z}(M_X)$.  Let
$\alpha:M_Z\to N$ be the restriction of the unit of nearby cycles for
the constant sheaf on $\mathcal D_ZX$.  By naturality, and since $h_0$
factors as $X\to Z\hookrightarrow X$, we get

$$
\phi_0=\alpha\tau_{X,Z}(M_X),\qquad
\tau_{X,Z}(M_X)\alpha=\operatorname{id}_{M_Z}.
$$

The second equality holds because the composite is the specialization
map for the constant family $Z\times S$, followed by its fixed inverse.  Since
$\phi_0=\phi_1=\operatorname{id}_N$, the maps $\alpha$ and
$\tau_{X,Z}(M_X)$ are inverse isomorphisms.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-case-z-v-x-m], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The argument depends on the kind of map $\Lambda\to\Lambda'$. For maps of finite rings we use a projection formula, whereas in the other cases extension of
scalars is either a finite construction (finite sums and a cone), with
which every exact functor commutes, or a filtered colimit, with which
$Rf_*$ commutes on uniformly bounded below systems.

*Maps $A\to B$ of finite rings.* We compute on the étale site using
Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category], which
identifies the pro-étale and étale categories in this case, and we test
the comparison on derived sections over quasi-compact étale objects. For a
quasi-compact étale $V\to Y$, we apply the projection formula for constant
coefficients [Stacks, [0F12](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F12)] on both $V$ and $X_V=X\times_YV$ and obtain

$$
R\Gamma(V,(Rf_*K)_B)
\simeq R\Gamma(X_V,K)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}B
\simeq R\Gamma(X_V,K_B).
$$

Here the first identification uses the projection formula on $V$ and
then $R\Gamma(V,Rf_*K)=R\Gamma(X_V,K)$, and the second is the projection
formula on $X_V$. This projection formula needs only cohomological bounds
for $\ell$-primary coefficients, which hold for schemes of finite type over
$k$, and so it applies to every finite $A$-algebra $B$. Since
these isomorphisms commute with restriction in $V$, the comparison map is
an isomorphism in $D(Y_{\acute{e}t},B)$, and hence, by
Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category], in
$D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},B)$.

*Maps $\mathcal O_E\to A$ with $A$ finite.* Since $\mathcal O_E$ is a
discrete valuation ring, $A$ has a finite free $\mathcal O_E$-resolution of
length at most one. Its condensed version is again exact. Indeed, a
continuous map from a profinite set to the finite quotient $A$ is constant
on the pieces of a finite clopen partition, and hence lifts to a continuous
map to the free module. The pullback of this resolution to $X$ is a finite free resolution of $A_X$ over
$\mathcal O_{E,X}$. Consequently, tensoring with $A_X$ is computed by finite
sums and a cone, and these commute with the exact functor $Rf_*$.

*Finite extensions.* For $\mathcal O_E\to\mathcal O_F$ and $E\to F$,
the ring $\mathcal O_F$ is free of rank $[F:E]$ over $\mathcal O_E$. Hence
$K_{\mathcal O_F}$ is, as an $\mathcal O_E$-complex, a finite direct sum of
copies of $K$. The assertion follows because $Rf_*$ commutes with finite
sums.

*The maps $\mathcal O_E\to E$ and $E\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.* These are not finite,
and we use continuity. For $\mathcal O_E\to E$, the complex $K_E$ is the
colimit of $K\xrightarrow{\ell}K\xrightarrow{\ell}\cdots$, and for

over finite extensions $F/E$ in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Since $K$ is bounded, all terms of
these systems are bounded below by a common integer. Hence the colimits
commute with $Rf_*$ by Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology].
