Since $f^!$ is only known through its adjunction, there is no formula into
which we could substitute $K_{\Lambda'}$ directly. Instead we show that
$\beta_{f,K}$ is an isomorphism in two cases where $f^!$ has been computed:
closed immersions and the projection $\mathbf P^1_Y\to Y$. We then factor
a general $f$ locally into such maps, using that $\beta$ is compatible
with composition and with restriction to opens.

*Closed immersions.* For a closed immersion $i$ with open complement
$j$, the functor $i^!$ is determined by the localization triangle

$$
i_*i^!K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K.
$$

It expresses $i_*i^!K$ as the fibre of a map between objects whose
behaviour under extension of scalars we already know. Extension of scalars
commutes with $i_*$, $j^*$ and, by
Lemma [lemma-change-coefficients-direct-image], $Rj_*$. Hence the
extension of scalars of this triangle is the triangle for $K_{\Lambda'}$
over $\Lambda'$. Since the first map is the counit, the comparison on
fibres is $i_*\beta_{i,K}$. The comparisons on the other two terms are
isomorphisms, and therefore $i_*\beta_{i,K}$ is one as well. Since $i_*$
is fully faithful, $\beta_{i,K}$ is an isomorphism.

*The projective line.* Let $q:\mathbf P^1_Y\to Y$. Recall that the adjunction $Rq_*\dashv q^*(1)[2]$ between $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\mathbf P^1_Y,\Lambda)$ and
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$ is defined by the diagonal class and the trace. Through these two maps, $q^!$ is identified with $q^*(1)[2]$. It therefore
suffices to know that the two maps commute with all the maps of
coefficient rings listed above.
This holds by construction
(Propositions [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]
and [proposition-ell-adic-cycle-class-diagonal]). Indeed, the classes with finite coefficients are constructed from the Kummer sequence and derived
extension of scalars, while the integral classes are their compatible limits, and
the classes over fields are obtained from these by extension of scalars.
Only one map in the list needs a further remark. For $\mathcal O_E\to A$,
the proof of Lemma [lemma-change-coefficients-direct-image] shows that
$A_X$ is perfect. Hence the derived tensor product with $A_X$ commutes with
the inverse limits defining the integral classes, and so the resulting classes are exactly the classes with finite coefficients. Consequently the identification $q^!\simeq q^*(1)[2]$ is
compatible with extension of scalars. Under this identification, finally, $\beta_{q,K}$ becomes the isomorphism of
Definition [definition-change-of-coefficients-maps](1) for $q^*$,
twisted by $(1)[2]$.

*General $f$.* The open immersion
$\mathbf A^1_Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^1_Y$ is a case of restriction to
opens, and so $\beta$ is an isomorphism for $\mathbf A^1_Y\to Y$. Since the projection $\mathbf A^d_Y\to Y$ is a composite of $d$ projections of this kind, the compatibility of $\beta$ with composition gives the case of affine space. In general, whether $\beta_{f,K}$ is an isomorphism may be
checked locally on $X$. Using a finite affine cover, we may therefore
assume that $f$ factors as a closed immersion into an affine space over
$Y$ followed by the projection. Then the two cases already treated and
compatibility with composition give the claim.

$$

Let $x_0,x_1$ and $y_0,y_1$ be the pullbacks along $p_1$
and $p_2$ of the homogeneous coordinates of $\mathbf P^1_S$. Then
$\Delta$ is the zero locus of the section $x_0y_1-x_1y_0$ of
$p_1^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes p_2^*\mathcal O(1)$. On the open where
$x_0$ and $y_0$ are invertible, in the affine coordinates
$x=x_1/x_0$ and $y=y_1/y_0$, this equation becomes $y-x$. It is a
nonzerodivisor, and the quotient
$\mathcal O_S[x,y]/(y-x)\simeq\mathcal O_S[x]$ is flat over $S$. The open
where $x_1$ and $y_1$ are invertible is treated in the same way, and these
two opens cover $\Delta$. Hence $\Delta$ is a relative effective Cartier
divisor, and it remains one after every base change.

To show $s_i=1$, note that both sides are endomorphisms of a sheaf
placed in degree zero. We have

$$
\Hom_{D((\mathbf P^1_S)_{\acute{e}t},A)}
(A_{\mathbf P^1_S},A_{\mathbf P^1_S})
=\Hom_{\operatorname{Mod}((\mathbf P^1_S)_{\acute{e}t},A)}
(A_{\mathbf P^1_S},A_{\mathbf P^1_S}),
$$

so $s_i$ is a morphism of sheaves and is determined by its geometric
stalks. By proper base change and the compatibility of $\delta$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}_{p_i}$ with base change, the stalk of (6.6) at a
geometric point $\bar x$ of $\mathbf P^1_S$ is computed on the fibre
$p_i^{-1}(\bar x)\simeq\mathbf P^1_{\bar x}$. On this fibre the equation $x_0y_1-x_1y_0$ restricts to a nonzero linear form, so the diagonal cuts out a single reduced point, whose line bundle is $\mathcal O(1)$.
By Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor], the class of this point
composed with the unit is $c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. In turn, the trace $\operatorname{Tr}_p$ sends $c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ to $1$, since by
definition (6.5) it is the projection onto the summand of
(6.4) spanned by this class. Thus the stalk of $s_i$ at every
geometric point $\bar x$ sends $1$ to $1$, and so $s_i=1$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-class-diagonal-projective-line], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

$$

This is base change for coherent cohomology along a proper morphism,
applied to a flat finitely presented module, together with the openness
criterion for a perfect complex (see [Stacks, [0B91](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B91), [0B9S](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9S)]).
To construct the complex, one may use a projective embedding,
sufficiently large twists and a finite affine Čech complex; by Serre
vanishing we then obtain models that are finite locally free.
Given such a model, openness follows from a calculation with matrices. Indeed, near a point $t$
where the derived fibre of the complex has cohomology only in degree
$0$, of dimension $1$, we may cancel the differentials that are
invertible at $t$, and what remains is an invertible module in
degree $0$.

Choose a dense open $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ on which $F$ is lisse,
and let $i$ be the inclusion of the finite complement. The sequence
$0\to j_!j^*F\to F\to i_*i^*F\to0$ gives a long exact sequence in
which $H^r_c(C,i_*i^*F)$ vanishes for $r\ne0$, because the support is
finite. It therefore suffices to show $H^r_c(U,j^*F)=0$ for
$r\notin\{0,1,2\}$. For $r<0$ there is nothing to prove, and for $r>2$,
degreewise Poincaré duality
(Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields], with $d=1$) shows
that $H^r_c(U,j^*F)$ is dual to $H^{2-r}(U,(j^*F)^\vee(1))$, which is
zero because $(j^*F)^\vee$ is a sheaf and $2-r<0$.

An injective sheaf of modules is acyclic for the section functor on every
object of the site, although it need not be injective as an abelian sheaf
[Stacks, [03FD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03FD)]. Hence an injective resolution of modules computes the
cohomology of the underlying abelian sheaf, on every object. Applying this
to the objects over the target gives the statement for $R^qu_*$, and
bounded below resolutions give it for $Ru_*$.

We compute on $C_{\acute{e}t}$. In degree one, descent for invertible modules
identifies $\mathbf G_m$-torsors with line bundles. In degrees at least two, by contrast, the vanishing comes from Tsen's theorem, which we prove first (see
also [Stacks, [03RM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RM)]). There are three steps: Tsen's theorem,
proved by counting dimensions with Riemann–Roch; the vanishing of the
Brauer group and of the Galois cohomology of $k(C)$; and the passage from
the generic point to $C$ by the divisor sequence.

Tsen's theorem says that $k(C)$ is $C_1$, that is, a homogeneous form
of degree $d$ in $m>d$ variables with coefficients in $k(C)$ has a
nonzero zero.  To see this, let $\overline C$ be the smooth proper model
of $k(C)$, of genus $g$, choose an effective divisor $D$ on
$\overline C$ bounding the poles of all coefficients, and let the
unknowns range over $H^0(\overline C,\mathcal O(NH))$ for an effective divisor
$H$ of positive degree.  The value of the form then lies in
$H^0(\overline C,\mathcal O(dNH+D))$.  Once $N\deg H>2g-2$, we know both
dimensions by Theorem [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality].  In
terms of bases, the $m$ unknowns amount to $m(N\deg H+1-g)$ unknowns in
$k$. Each coordinate of the value, in a basis of the target space, is a
homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ in these unknowns, so the vanishing
of the value amounts to $dN\deg H+\deg D+1-g$
homogeneous polynomial equations in them.  The number of unknowns minus the number of equations is
$(m-d)N\deg H+(m-1)(1-g)-\deg D$, which is positive for large $N$
because $m>d$.  Since $k$ is algebraically closed, homogeneous equations
in more unknowns than equations have a nonzero solution [Stacks, [03RD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RD)].

The reduced norm form of a division algebra of degree $d>1$ over $k(C)$
has degree $d$ in $d^2>d$ variables and does not vanish on a nonzero
element.  Therefore Tsen's theorem implies that $\operatorname{Br}(k(C))=0$
[Stacks, [03RF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RF)].  The same holds for every finite extension of $k(C)$,
since it is again the function field of a curve over $k$. This is enough for Galois cohomology, because a field all of
whose finite extensions have trivial Brauer group has
$H^q(K,(K^{\mathrm{sep}})^\times)=0$ for all $q\geq1$ [Stacks, [03R8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03R8)]; hence
this holds for $K=k(C)$. To pass from $k(C)$ to $C$ we use the divisor
sequence, which relates $\mathbf G_m$ on $C_{\acute{e}t}$ to the pushforward of the
multiplicative group at the generic point and to skyscraper sheaves
$\mathbf Z$ at the closed points. Of these, the former has no higher cohomology by
this Galois vanishing, and the latter have none because the residue
fields are algebraically closed. Therefore, from the long exact cohomology sequence,
we conclude that $H^q(C_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf G_m)=0$ for $q\geq2$.

Choose a nonempty affine open $U\subseteq C$. Its ring of functions is a
finitely generated $k$-domain of dimension at most one, and its fraction
field is $k(C)$. Noether normalization identifies the transcendence
degree with the dimension, giving $\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(C)\leq1$.
In transcendence degree zero the field is $k$, which is algebraically
closed. Otherwise it is algebraic over a rational function field
$k(t)$. The latter is $C_1$ by a count of the coefficients of
polynomial unknowns, and the $C_1$ property passes to algebraic
extensions.

It remains to see that a $C_1$ field $K$ has
$H^2(\operatorname{Spec}(K)_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf G_m)=0$. Compute
degree-two cohomology on finite Galois covers by Čech cohomology.
Hilbert 90 supplies the required exactness on sections, and the
crossed-product argument for a $C_1$ field kills the second Galois
Čech cohomology.

The divisor sequence is a short exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathbf G_m\longrightarrow i_*i^*\mathbf G_m
\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{x\in X^{(1)}}i_{x,*}\mathbf Z\longrightarrow0,
$$

where $X^{(1)}$ denotes the points of codimension one and
$i_x:\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(x))\to X$.
Each point sheaf $i_{x,*}\mathbf Z$ has vanishing $H^1$, by the
injective degree-one Leray edge map and the vanishing of
$H^1(\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(x)),\mathbf Z)$. The same vanishing holds
for their direct sum: by quasi-compactness, the differences of local
lifts involve only finitely many of the point sheaves. Hence the long
exact sequence makes
$H^2(X,\mathbf G_m)\to H^2(X,i_*i^*\mathbf G_m)$ injective.

The degree-two Leray edge map from the latter group to
$H^2(\operatorname{Spec}(k(X)),i^*\mathbf G_m)$ is injective as well.
Indeed, embed $i^*\mathbf G_m$ in an injective sheaf. On the generic
fibres of affine étale $X$-schemes, Hilbert 90 lifts sections of its
cokernel to the injective sheaf. Thus $i_*$ takes the cokernel map to
an epimorphism. The composite of the two injections is the asserted
pullback map.

The idea is that, since the monodromy is an $\ell$-group, we may filter
the coefficients until they become the constant sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$.
For constant coefficients, $M_z=0$ is a statement on the strict localization
of $X$ at $z$: restriction from the complement of $D_2$ to the punctured
curve $D_1-z$ is an isomorphism on cohomology. This holds because a
local equation of $D_2$ gives the generator of $H^1$ on both sides. Once we
know that $M$ is locally constant along $D_2-z$, the vanishing of the
restriction map follows from $M_z=0$ by specialization along $D_2$.

For the assertion at $z$, pass to the strict localization $S$ of
$X$ at $z$ and write $D_{1,S},D_{2,S}$ for the two transverse divisors.
By the formula for stalks of a direct image along an open immersion
[Stacks, [03Q7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q7)] and localization we have

$$
M_z=R\Gamma(S-D_{2,S},j'_!N).
$$

To prove that this object is zero we may forget the $A$-action,
since the exact forgetful functor is conservative and the cohomology of
sheaves of modules agrees with the cohomology of the underlying abelian sheaves
[Stacks, [03FD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03FD)]. A finite abelian $\ell$-group with an action of a
finite $\ell$-group has a finite filtration whose quotients are
$\mathbf F_\ell$ with trivial action. To see this, filter by powers of
$\ell$ and use the nilpotence of the augmentation ideal of the group algebra over
$\mathbf F_\ell$. Since $j'_!$ and $R\Gamma(S-D_{2,S},-)$ are exact, the
class of $N$ for which $R\Gamma(S-D_{2,S},j'_!N)=0$ is closed under
extensions. Using truncations and these composition series we reduce
the assertion to $N=\mathbf F_\ell$ on $S-(D_{1,S}\cup D_{2,S})$.

By Lemma [lemma-punctured-surface-punctured-curve], applied to $S$ with the
divisors $D_{1,S},D_{2,S}$, the restriction map
$R\Gamma(S-D_{2,S},\mathbf F_\ell)\to R\Gamma(D_{1,S}-z,\mathbf F_\ell)$ is an
isomorphism. The localization sequence for $D_{1,S}-z$ and its complement
in $S-D_{2,S}$ identifies $R\Gamma(S-D_{2,S},j'_!\mathbf F_\ell)$ with the cone
of this map, shifted by $-1$. Hence this complex is zero, and $M_z=0$ in $D(A)$ by
conservativity.

We turn to the local constancy of $M$ along $D_2-z$, where only the
divisor $D_2$ remains. Since $D_1$ meets $D_2$ only at
$z$, we have $j'_!N=N$ near $D_2-z$, so $M=Rj_*N$ there. To compute $Rj_*N$ we use Abhyankar's lemma along the regular divisor $D_2$ [Stacks, [0EYG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYG)]: étale locally on $D_2$, a finite
tame local system is trivialized by a Kummer cover of a local
parameter of $D_2$ and an unramified cover. The lemma applies here because our finite $\ell$-group monodromy is tame, wild inertia being pro-$p$. Consequently, the
stalks of $Rj_*N$ are the continuous cohomology of the same
representation of tame inertia, and their specialization maps along $D_2-z$
are isomorphisms. Explicitly, the pro-$\ell$ part of tame inertia is
$\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$. Its cohomology with coefficients in a finite $\ell$-primary
module is computed by the two-term complex given by a topological
generator minus one. On the other hand, the finite quotients of the remaining factors of tame inertia have order prime to $\ell$, so taking invariants under them is exact
on these coefficients. Finally, we may choose the parameter and the unramified cover on an étale neighbourhood. Hence this
description, including the specialization maps, is locally constant.
Applying the argument to the cohomology sheaves of $N$ and using the
bounded spectral sequence proves the assertion for $N$.

The last assertion combines the two facts just proved. A global
section of $M|_{D_2}$ specializes to every stalk. Its image at $z$ is zero,
and along $D_2-z$ specialization is an isomorphism on stalks. To make
this precise, choose a geometric generic point $\bar\eta$
of the connected regular curve $D_2$, together with specialization maps
from $\bar\eta$ to $z$ and to $w$. By naturality of restriction we get a
commutative square

$$
\begin{CD}
R\Gamma(D_2,M|_{D_2}) @>>> M_w\\
@VVV @VV{\sim}V\\
M_z=0 @>>> M_{\bar\eta}.
\end{CD}
$$

The right arrow is an isomorphism by the local constancy just
proved, so the upper arrow is zero.

By the comparison theorems for the cohomology and the proper direct image
of bounded below complexes
(Theorems [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison] and
[theorem-comparison-direct-images]), it suffices to
prove the assertions on $\sigma_S$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_p$ in $D^+(S_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$

Both components of $\sigma_S$ are globally defined. The second
comes from Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor] applied to the
section at infinity, whose line bundle is $\mathcal O(1)$. Geometric stalks
detect isomorphisms, and by proper base change the stalk of $Rp_*\Lambda$
at a geometric point $\bar s$ is $R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_{\bar s},\Lambda)$.
It therefore suffices to check that $\sigma_S$ is an isomorphism on a geometric fibre,
first for $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$. By the genus zero case of
Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime], the
cohomology lives only in degrees $0$ and $2$, with
$H^0=\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$ and $H^2=(\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z)(-1)$.
The Kummer description sends a line bundle to its degree modulo $\ell^r$.
As $\mathcal O(1)$ has degree one, its class generates $H^2$, and
$\sigma_S$ is an isomorphism. The unit and the class of
$\mathcal O(1)$ commute with base change. Therefore so do
$\sigma_S$, its inverse, and $\operatorname{Tr}_p$.

For a finite $\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$-algebra $\Lambda$, the projection
formula [Stacks, [0GL5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL5)] gives $Rp_*\Lambda=Rp_*(\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z)
\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^r}\Lambda$. Under this identification,
$\sigma_S$ for $\Lambda$ is $\sigma_S$ for $\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$
tensored with $\Lambda$. It is therefore again
an isomorphism compatible with base change.

The functor $p_X^*$ commutes with colimits, so the second and third
isomorphisms reduce to identities on the point. The first is an inverse
limit, and since $p_X^*$ need not commute with inverse limits, we use

On the point, $\underline{\mathcal O_E}$ is represented by the profinite
set $\mathcal O_E=\varprojlim_n\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$, so its pullback to
$X$ is represented by the pro-étale $X$-scheme
$\varprojlim_n\coprod_{\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n}X$. By the Yoneda lemma the
sheaf this scheme represents is $\varprojlim_n(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X$,
and the ring structures match.

A continuous map from a profinite set to $E$ has compact image, and hence
lands in $\ell^{-m}\mathcal O_E$ for some $m$. Thus
$\underline E=\underline{\mathcal O_E}[1/\ell]$ on the point. Since
inverting $\ell$ is a filtered colimit and $p_X^*$ commutes with colimits,
we obtain the second isomorphism. In the same way the third follows from
$\underline{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}=\varinjlim_E\underline E$. All three isomorphisms are
obtained by applying $p_X^*$, and $p_Y\circ f=p_X$ for every morphism
$f:X\to Y$, so they are compatible with pullback.

The only geometric fact we use is that, since $r_m$ is a universal
homeomorphism, pullback along it is an equivalence and its unit is an
isomorphism. The rest is base change and composition of units, and each
part uses the previous ones.

*Proof of (1).* The identities $p_mr_m=\Phi_X^m$ and $f'_mr_m=f$
hold by the definition of $r_m=(f,\Phi_X^m)$, since $f\Phi_X^m=\Phi_Y^mf$.
The map $r_m$ is the geometric base change of the
relative $q^m$-power Frobenius of $X_0/Y_0$. It is integral, radicial
and surjective [Stacks, [0CCB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CCB)], and finite because it is integral and of
finite type. For affine $Y_0=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and
$X_0=\operatorname{Spec}S$, with $F$ the $q$-power Frobenius of $R$,
it is given on coordinate rings by

$$
R\otimes_{F^m,R}S\longrightarrow S,
\qquad b\otimes a\longmapsto f^\#(b)a^{q^m}.
$$

By topological invariance for classical objects of finite Tor amplitude, $r_m^*$
is an equivalence, so the unit $\eta_{r_m}$ in the construction is
an isomorphism. In the construction, the first arrow is base change for compact supports, and
the last comes from the composition of direct images with compact support, since $r_m$ is
proper.
Moreover, pasting the cartesian squares defining $X'_m$ and $X'_n$, we get the
comparison for $m+n$, because the relative Frobenii compose and the unit of
their composite is the composite of the units. Thus

$$
\theta_{f,m+n,K}=
\theta_{f,m,(\Phi_X^n)^*K}\circ
(\Phi_Y^m)^*\theta_{f,n,K},
$$

which is the compatibility with iteration.

is the pullback along $p_m$, and the
next arrow in $\theta_{f,m}$ becomes $r_m^*$. Their composite is

Theorem [theorem-pbc-injective-acyclicity] reduces both parts to the
condition $\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda$ of injective acyclicity, and we read off
this vanishing from the Leray spectral sequence of the base-changed
composite. For (ii) the hypotheses do not apply directly to an injective
sheaf on $Y$, so we first realize it as a direct summand of $u_*J$ with
$J$ injective on $X$.

To set up the spectral sequence, fix an
arbitrary base change $Z'\to Z$. Write $g_X:X'\to X$ and $g_Y:Y'\to Y$
for the projections, and $u':X'\to Y'$, $v':Y'\to Z'$ for the induced
maps. The direct image $u'_*$ preserves injectives, because its left
adjoint $u'^*$ on sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules is exact. Hence for every
sheaf $J$ of $\Lambda$-modules on $X$ we have the
Grothendieck spectral sequence for the composite direct image
[Stacks, [0734](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0734)]:

$$
R^pv'_*R^qu'_*g_X^*J
\ \Longrightarrow\ R^{p+q}(v'u')_*g_X^*J.
\tag{4.13}
$$

*Part (i).* Let $J$ be an injective sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules on
$X$. We show $R^m(v'u')_*g_X^*J=0$ for $m>0$, which is
$\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(vu)$. For this it suffices that the $E_2$-terms of
(4.13) vanish except for $p=q=0$, and they do. Indeed,
$R^qu'_*g_X^*J=0$ for $q>0$ by $\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(u)$. For $q=0$, proper
base change in degree zero
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-degree-zero]) gives

$$
u'_*g_X^*J\simeq g_Y^*u_*J,
$$

and the sheaf $u_*J$ is injective, so $R^pv'_*g_Y^*u_*J=0$ for $p>0$ by
$\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(v)$. The abutment therefore vanishes in positive
degrees.

*Part (ii), the splitting.* Let $I$ be an injective sheaf of
$\Lambda$-modules on $Y$. Choose a monomorphism of sheaves

$$
u^*I\hookrightarrow J
$$

with $J$ injective on $X$, and let $\iota:I\to u_*J$ be its adjoint.
The map $\iota$ is a monomorphism. To see this, given a geometric point
$\bar y$, choose a geometric point $\bar x$ above it, which exists because
$u$ is surjective. Then the composite

$$
I_{\bar y}\xrightarrow{\iota_{\bar y}}(u_*J)_{\bar y}
\longrightarrow J_{\bar x}
$$

is the stalk of the chosen monomorphism, under
$(u^*I)_{\bar x}=I_{\bar y}$, so it is injective.
As $I$ is an injective sheaf, there is then a map of sheaves
$s:u_*J\to I$ with $s\iota=\mathrm{id}_I$. In other words, $I$ is a direct
summand of $u_*J$.

*Part (ii), the vanishing.* We first show
$R^pv'_*g_Y^*u_*J=0$ for $p>0$. The hypotheses $\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(u)$
and $\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(vu)$ give

$$
R^qu'_*g_X^*J=0\quad(q>0),\qquad
R^m(v'u')_*g_X^*J=0\quad(m>0),
$$

so the spectral sequence (4.13)
collapses to its row $q=0$. This means that
$R^pv'_*u'_*g_X^*J\simeq R^p(v'u')_*g_X^*J=0$ for $p>0$. Since
$u'_*g_X^*J\simeq g_Y^*u_*J$ by proper base change in degree zero, we
obtain

$$
R^pv'_*g_Y^*u_*J
\simeq R^pv'_*u'_*g_X^*J=0\qquad(p>0).
$$

Now $g_Y^*I$ is a direct summand of $g_Y^*u_*J$, by applying $g_Y^*$ to the
splitting $s\iota=\mathrm{id}_I$, and as $R^pv'_*$ is additive,
$R^pv'_*g_Y^*I$ is a direct summand of $R^pv'_*g_Y^*u_*J$. Hence
$R^pv'_*g_Y^*I=0$ for $p>0$, which is $\mathrm{IA}_\Lambda(v)$.

For (1) we use smoothness to see that irreducible and connected components
coincide; for (2), Chevalley's theorem gives an open subset of the closure
inside the image, and translations spread it over the closure; (3) is a
dimension count.

*Components.* The irreducible components of $G$ are finite in number,
as $G$ is Noetherian, and they are exactly the connected components. Indeed,
$G$ is smooth by Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem], and a
regular local ring is a domain. So distinct irreducible components of
$G$ do not meet, and they are open and closed. Let $G^\circ$ be the
component containing $1$. It is a subgroup. To see this, note that
$G^\circ\times G^\circ$ is irreducible, $\Omega$ being algebraically
closed. Hence the image of the morphism $G^\circ\times G^\circ\to G$,
$(x,y)\mapsto xy^{-1}$, is irreducible. It contains $1$, so it lies in
$G^\circ$. For the same reason the image of $G^\circ$ under conjugation
by a point of $G$ is irreducible and contains $1$, so $G^\circ$ is
normal. Translating $G^\circ$ by points of
$G$, we see that the other components are its cosets. Since $G^\circ$ is
open in $G$ and contains $1$, both have the same local ring at $1$, so
$\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$.

For example, the homomorphism $\mathbf G_m\to\mathbf G_m$, $x\mapsto x^2$, has image all
of $\mathbf G_m$ and kernel $\mu_2$, a closed subgroup with two
components.

*Images.* Let $f:G\to G'$ be a homomorphism. We show that its image
equals the closure $J$ of the image, which is a subgroup by continuity of
multiplication and inversion. First, the subgroup $f(G(\Omega))$ of
$J(\Omega)$ contains the $\Omega$-points of a nonempty open
$U\subseteq J$. Indeed, $f(G)$ is constructible by Chevalley's theorem
[Stacks, [054K](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054K)], a dense constructible subset contains a nonempty open
subset of its closure, and $\Omega$ is algebraically closed. Translating
$U$ by the inverse of one of its points in the image, we obtain an open
neighbourhood of $1$ contained in the image. Translating further by
points of the image, we see that the image is open in $J$. It is then
also closed, since its complement is a union of cosets of this open
subgroup. As it is dense in $J$, it is equal to $J$.

*Lie algebras.* Let $K$ be as in (3). Cartier's theorem gives
$\dim K=\dim\operatorname{Lie}(K)=\dim G$, so $K$ and $G$ have the same
underlying closed subset, as a proper closed subset of the irreducible
variety $G$ has smaller dimension. They are equal as schemes, since both
are reduced by Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem].

Part (1) is the substantial one. All three closure properties are local on a common
stratification, so it suffices to treat lisse sheaves on a single stratum,
and there the only difficulty is the kernel of a morphism. Parts (2) and
(3), by contrast, are formal.

(1) Given finitely many constructible sheaves, we refine their
stratifications to a common one. Then all three closure properties can
be checked on a single stratum $S$.

*Extensions.* Let $0\to F'\to F\to F''\to0$ be exact with $F'$ and
$F''$ lisse on $S$. After passing to a cover, $F'$ and $F''$ are free.
Since $F\to F''$ is surjective, after a further cover a basis of $F''$
lifts to sections of $F$. Hence the sequence splits locally, and
$F$ is locally free of finite rank.

*Kernels and cokernels.*
Locally, a morphism of lisse sheaves is a matrix of continuous
functions to $E$, and a priori its kernel need not be locally free. Once
we choose lattices, however, the morphism becomes a constant matrix on
a suitable pro-étale cover, because its reductions are maps of finite
locally constant sheaves. The kernel and cokernel of a constant matrix
over $E$ are constant of finite rank, and since being lisse is a local
property for the pro-étale topology, this suffices.

First let $\Lambda=E$ and let $f:L\to L'$ be a morphism of lisse
sheaves on $S$. By Lemma [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves] we may replace $S$
by a connected quasi-compact affine étale neighbourhood $V$ on which
$L$ and $L'$ contain lattices $M$ and $N$. On a finite
quasi-compact pro-étale covering trivializing both lattices, the matrix
entries of $f$ have a common denominator, so $h=\pi_E^mf$ maps $M$ into
$N$ for some $m\ge0$.

The reductions $M_n=M/\pi_E^nM$ and $N_n=N/\pi_E^nN$ are finite locally
constant étale sheaves, and $M=\varprojlim M_n$, $N=\varprojlim N_n$ by
Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients], checked where $M$ and $N$ are
free. Fix a geometric point $\bar v$ of $V$. Then the completed fibres
$M_{\bar v}=\varprojlim(M_n)_{\bar v}$ and
$N_{\bar v}=\varprojlim(N_n)_{\bar v}$ are finite free
$\mathcal O_E$-modules with continuous $\pi_1(V,\bar v)$-actions, and
the reductions of $h$ give an equivariant map $h_{\bar v}$ between them.
To make $h$ constant, note that each $M_n$ and $N_n$ becomes constant on a connected finite étale
cover of the connected scheme $V$, and we may choose these covers to form
a tower. Their inverse limit $V'\to V$ is a connected pro-étale
covering, so maps between constant sheaves on $V'$ are constant.
On $V'$ the lattices $M$ and $N$ are identified
with the constant sheaves attached to $M_{\bar v}$ and $N_{\bar v}$, and
$h$ with the constant matrix $h_{\bar v}$. Hence on $V'$ the kernel and
the cokernel of $f=\pi_E^{-m}h$ are the constant sheaves attached to the
kernel and the cokernel of $h_{\bar v}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}E$. In particular
they are lisse.

For $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, we descend $L$, $L'$ and $f$ to a finite extension
$E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ by Lemma [lemma-descent-lisse-qbar-sheaves-finite]. Since the
functor $\QbarX\otimes_{E_X}-$ is exact, it takes the kernel and cokernel
over $E$ to those of $f$. Finally, restriction to strata is exact, so the
kernel and cokernel of a morphism of constructible sheaves on $X$ are
constructible.

(2) We choose the sites in a fixed universe. Up to isomorphism, a
constructible sheaf is then determined by a finite stratification and, on
each stratum, descent data of finite rank on a covering, and these data form a
set.

(3) By Noetherian induction we refine the stratification of $F$ so that
there is an open stratum $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with closed complement
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ that is again a union of strata. The exact sequence
$0\to j_!j^*F\to F\to i_*i^*F\to0$ separates the stratum $U$ from the rest,
and here $j^*F$ is lisse. Applying the same step to $i^*F$ on $Z$ and iterating,
we obtain a finite filtration of $F$ whose subquotients are $a_!(F|_S)$ for
the strata $a:S\hookrightarrow X$, and each $F|_S$ is lisse.

For $\Lambda=E$, realize a local presentation matrix as a matrix of
continuous $E$-valued functions. Its cokernel has fibre dimension equal
to the number of rows minus the pointwise rank. Geometric fibres show
that this dimension agrees on overlaps of presentation covers. Flatness
of the covering maps lifts generalizations, and continuous functions to
the Hausdorff field $E$ agree at comparable points. The fibre dimension
therefore descends to a function constant on specializations. The
finitely many irreducible components and their generic points make its
level sets open and closed.

On each rank level, cover by the nonvanishing loci of maximal minors.
Invert a chosen minor and apply row and column operations to reduce the
matrix to an identity block and its Schur complement. Constant
pointwise rank forces the Schur complement to vanish, so the cokernel
is finite free. Rank zero is treated by the zero matrix, and composing
the covers proves the assertion.

For $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, first refine the presentation
covers so that the finitely many matrix entries are continuous functions
with values in a common finite extension $E$. Fibre dimensions are
unchanged by extending $E$ to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. The same rank
and minor argument gives finite free modules over the actual
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ coefficient sheaf. Compose these refinements
with the original presentation cover.

We reduce to a single generator $a_!L$ and then use
(3.1) to turn Hom into cohomology on the stratum $S$,
where Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology] applies. The common lower bound
is used at the end, to compare the abutments of two spectral sequences.

In both cases $M$ is obtained by finitely many extensions and shifts from
sheaves $a_!L$, with $a:S\hookrightarrow X$ a locally closed immersion and
$L$ a finite locally free $\Lambda_S$-module: in case (1) by
Corollary [corollary-coefficient-heart-b], and in case (2) by assumption.
Both sides are cohomological functors of $M$. By the five lemma, the class
of objects $M$ for which the claim holds is therefore closed under
extensions and shifts, so it suffices to treat $M=a_!L$, with $a=i\circ
u:S\hookrightarrow Z\hookrightarrow X$ as in
Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme]. The only property of $L$ used
below is that $L^\vee\otimes-$ is exact.

By (3.1), we must show that the cohomology of
$R\Gamma(S,L^\vee\otimes u^*R\underline\Gamma_ZK)$ commutes with the
colimit, where $K=\varinjlim_\alpha K_\alpha^\bullet$. To this end we apply the exact
functor
$L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*(-):D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$
to the triangle $i_*R\underline\Gamma_ZK\to K\to Rj_*j^*K\to$ and to the
corresponding triangles for the $K_\alpha^\bullet$. By the
long exact sequence and the five lemma, it suffices to treat the two
terms

$$
R\Gamma\bigl(S,L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*K\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
R\Gamma\bigl(S,L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*Rj_*j^*K\bigr).
$$

For the first term, Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology] on $S$
applies, because the functor $L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*(-)$ is exact, commutes
with colimits and preserves the lower bound. For the second term, consider the
hypercohomology spectral sequence

$$
E_2^{p,r}=H^p\bigl(S,L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*R^rj_*(j^*K)\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
H^{p+r}\bigl(S,L^\vee\otimes u^*i^*Rj_*j^*K\bigr)
$$

which is functorial in $K$. The sheaves $R^rj_*(j^*K_\alpha)$ commute with the
colimit by the second part of Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], and
$H^p(S,-)$ does by its first part. Hence, after passing to the
colimit, the map of spectral sequences is an isomorphism on $E_2$. The
abutments agree as well, since by the common lower bound only finitely
many $E_2^{p,r}$ contribute to a given total degree.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Part (1) is a transcendence degree count. For part (2), note that a point
of $Z$ has all its coordinates in the finite sets of excluded values.
After shrinking $S$, these sets are cut out by monic polynomials, and
monic equations in every coordinate force finiteness.

(1) We use that the dimension of an integral scheme of finite type over a
field is the transcendence degree of its function field. Consider an
irreducible component of $X_{k(S)}\cap Y_\alpha$ with function field $L$.
If $t_{\alpha r}$ is algebraic over $k(S)$ on it, the component does
not meet the generic fibre of $t_{\alpha r}$, as it does not dominate
$\mathbf A^1_{k(S)}$. Otherwise $t_{\alpha r}$ is transcendental, and

$$
\operatorname{trdeg}_{k(S)(t_{\alpha r})}L
=\operatorname{trdeg}_{k(S)} L-1\leq n-1.
$$

The left-hand side is the dimension of the corresponding component of the
generic fibre of $t_{\alpha r}$, and every component of that generic
fibre arises in this way.

(2) Let $t$ be the coordinate of $\mathbf A^1_S$. The ideal of the
complement of $V_{\alpha r}$ contains a nonzero polynomial
$P_{\alpha r}\in\mathcal O(S)[t]$. Indeed, since $V_{\alpha r}$ is dense,
its complement is a proper closed subset of the integral scheme
$\mathbf A^1_S$, and its ideal is nonzero. After
inverting the leading coefficients of these finitely many polynomials, we
may assume that all of them are monic. The function
$P_{\alpha r}(t_{\alpha r})$ is zero in the coordinate ring of the reduced
affine scheme $Z\cap Y_\alpha$, because it vanishes at every point, $t_{\alpha r}$
mapping $Z\cap Y_\alpha$ into the complement of $V_{\alpha r}$. This ring is
therefore a quotient of

$$
\mathcal O(S)[t_{\alpha1},\ldots,t_{\alpha m_\alpha}]/
(P_{\alpha1}(t_{\alpha1}),\ldots,
P_{\alpha m_\alpha}(t_{\alpha m_\alpha})),
$$

which is generated as an $\mathcal O(S)$-module by the monomials whose
exponent in each variable is less than the degree of the corresponding
polynomial. Each $Z\cap Y_\alpha$ is thus finite over $S$, and
$Z\to S$ has finite fibres. As $Z$ is closed in the projective scheme $Y$,
the morphism $Z\to S$ is also proper, and a proper morphism with finite
fibres is finite [Stacks, [02LS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02LS)].

We take the fixed field of an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup of the monodromy, adjust
the degree by an Eisenstein extension, and descend to curves.

Let $F$ be the fraction field of the discrete valuation ring of $S$.
Then the punctured trait $S-s$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(F)$, so the
$\mathcal F_i$ are finite sets with a continuous action of
$\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F)$. We choose a finite Galois extension $L/F$ over which all of them become constant, let $P$ be an $\ell$-Sylow
subgroup of $G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)$, and put $F_1=L^P$ and
$d_1=[F_1:F]=[G:P]$, which is prime to $\ell$.

Let $d=d_1e$ be a
multiple of $d_1$ prime to $\ell$. The normalization $S_1$ of $S$ in the
separable extension $F_1$ is finite over $S$, and it is local because it
is a domain finite over a henselian local ring. Hence $S_1$ is a strictly
henselian discrete valuation ring with residue field $k$, and it has
degree $d_1$ over $S$. If $e>1$, let $t$ be a uniformizer of $S_1$. The
Eisenstein polynomial $z^e+tz-t$ is irreducible, and its derivative
$ez^{e-1}+t$ is nonzero, also when $p\mid e$, so it is separable. Hence
$S'=S_1[z]/(z^e+tz-t)$ is a discrete valuation ring, totally ramified of
degree $e$ over $S_1$, with separable fraction field $F'$ over $F$. If
$e=1$ we put $S'=S_1$. Then $S'\to S$ is finite flat of degree $d$, with
a single point $s'$ over $s$, and $S'-s'=\operatorname{Spec}(F')\to
\operatorname{Spec}(F)$ is finite étale. The group
$\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F')$ acts on the stalks of the
$\mathcal F_i$ through its image in $G$, which lies in
$\operatorname{Gal}(L/F_1)=P$ since $F_1\subset F'$.

Finally, by a limit
argument $S'\to S$ descends to a finite flat morphism $C'\to C$ onto an
étale neighbourhood $C$ of $s$, which we may take with normal source. Since $k$ is perfect, the normal curve $C'$ is smooth. Moreover, the morphism $C'\to C$ is étale over a dense open of $C$, and after shrinking $C$ around $s$
it is étale away from $s$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed,
$C'\times_CS$ is the product of the strict localizations of $C'$ at the
points over $s$. As it equals the local scheme $S'$, there is a single
point over $s$, and $S'$ is the strict localization of $C'$ there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-covers-degree-prime-to-ell], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We cut $X$ by a general hypersurface through $S$, show that it is
smooth and that both it and its inverse image in $T$ are connected,
and then repeat.

*The linear system.* Embed $X$ in a projective closure $\overline X$.
For large $n$, the sections of $\mathcal O_{\overline X}(n)$ vanishing on
$S$ have base locus exactly $S$ on $X$ and define an immersion off $S$
([Stacks, [0FD5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FD5)]). They also surject onto the first-order jets
$\bigoplus_{s\in S}\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2\otimes
\mathcal O_{\overline X}(n)$ at $S$. Indeed, if $\mathcal I$ is the
ideal sheaf of $S$, then $H^1(\overline X,\mathcal I^2(n))=0$ for large
$n$ by Serre vanishing ([Stacks, [0B5U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5U)]), and the cohomology sequence of
$0\to\mathcal I^2(n)\to\mathcal I(n)\to(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)(n)\to0$
shows that $H^0(\overline X,\mathcal I(n))$ surjects onto the jets.

*Smoothness.* A general divisor of these sections is smooth on $X$.
The immersion off $S$ says nothing about the points of $S$ themselves,
and there smoothness is controlled by the jets. A divisor through $s$ is
smooth at $s$ exactly when its equation has nonzero image in
$\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2$. Since the sections surject onto the
jets, the condition that a section have nonzero derivative at each $s$
is nonempty and open. On $X\setminus S$ the divisors are the pullbacks
of hyperplanes under the immersion of $X\setminus S$ into a projective
space that these sections define. By Bertini's theorem ([Stacks, [0FD6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0FD6)]) a
general one is smooth there.

*Connectedness.* A general divisor and its inverse image in $T$ are
irreducible. We use Bertini's irreducibility theorem
[Stacks, [0G4F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0G4F)]: if $Z$ is an irreducible scheme of finite type over an
algebraically closed field and $Z\to\mathbf P^N$ is a morphism whose
image has closure of dimension at least two, then the inverse image of
a general hyperplane is irreducible. We apply it to the immersion of
$X\setminus S$ above and to its composition with the restriction of
$T\to X$ over $X\setminus S$. In both cases the hyperplanes correspond
to the sections vanishing on $S$ and their pullbacks to $T$. Both
sources are smooth and connected, hence irreducible. Both images have
closure of dimension $\dim X\ge2$, because $T\to X$ is finite and
surjective. So for a general divisor $D$, both $D\cap(X\setminus S)$
and its inverse image in $T$ are irreducible. The finitely many points
over $S$ cannot be components, since every component of a divisor has
dimension $\dim X-1\ge1$, and the claim follows.

*Induction.* Intersecting these nonempty open conditions in the space
of sections, we obtain a smooth connected affine hypersurface $H$
containing $S$ whose inverse image in $T$ is connected. It is smooth,
connected and affine of dimension $\dim X-1$, it contains $S$, and
$T\times_XH\to H$ is a connected finite étale cover. Thus $H$ again
satisfies the hypotheses of the lemma, and we repeat the construction
until the dimension is one.
The curve is defined over a finite field, because it has finitely many

This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-curve-preserving-finite-cover], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The map $c_D$ will be the boundary map of the extension of
$i_*\mathbf Z_D$ by $\mathbf G_m$ formed by meromorphic functions
with poles along $D$, reduced modulo $\ell^r$; this extension is the étale
version of the divisor sequence $0\to\mathcal O_Z\to\mathcal O_Z(D)\to
\mathcal O_Z(D)|_D\to0$.

We construct $c_D$ in $D(Z_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. The functor $\nu_Z^*$, which
commutes with inverse images and with change of coefficients, then
transports it and its compatibilities to $Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.

Let $j:Z\setminus D\hookrightarrow Z$ be the open complement. Let
$\mathcal M_D\subset j_*\mathbf G_m$ be the subsheaf which, on an open
where $D$ has a regular equation $t$, consists of the products
$ut^{-m}$ with $u$ a unit and $m$ a locally constant integer on
$D$; equivalently, it is generated by $\mathbf G_m$ and $t^{-1}$.
Since replacing $t$ by a unit multiple gives the same subsheaf,
$\mathcal M_D$ is globally defined. Sending $t^{-1}$ to $1$, we obtain
a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on $Z_{\acute{e}t}$

$$
\Sigma_D:\ 0\longrightarrow\mathbf G_m\longrightarrow \mathcal M_D
\longrightarrow i_*\mathbf Z_D\longrightarrow0,
\tag{6.3}
$$

whose exactness can be checked on geometric stalks. Away from $D$, the function $t$ is a unit, so there $\mathcal M_D=\mathbf G_m$, and both the
quotient and the stalk of $i_*\mathbf Z_D$ are zero. At a point of $D$, on the other hand, no
nonzero power of a regular nonunit $t$ is a unit, and therefore the
exponent $m$ in $ut^{-m}$ is well defined. The kernel of the map $ut^{-m}\mapsto m$ is then $\mathbf G_m$, and the map is surjective because exponents lift locally to
powers of $t^{-1}$. For example, for
$D=\{0\}\subset Z=\mathbf A^1=\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$, the sections of
$\mathcal M_D$ near the origin are the functions $ut^{-m}$, that is, the
rational functions whose only zero or pole is at $0$, and the map
records the order of the pole, $m=-\operatorname{ord}_0$.

The boundary of $\Sigma_D$ is a morphism $i_*\mathbf Z_D\to\mathbf G_m[1]$
in $D(Z_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf Z)$, to which
we apply $-\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$. The
source becomes $i_*\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$. For the target, the
Kummer sequence [Stacks, [03PL](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03PL)] shows that the cone of multiplication by
$\ell^r$ on $\mathbf G_m$ has the single cohomology sheaf
$\mu_{\ell^r}$ in degree $-1$, and hence the target becomes
$\mu_{\ell^r}[2]$. This is $c_D$ for $\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$.
For a finite $\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$-algebra $\Lambda$, we apply
$-\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^r}\Lambda$. Since
$\mu_{\ell^r}$ is locally free of rank one over
$\mathbf Z/\ell^r\mathbf Z$, the target becomes $\Lambda_Z(1)[2]$.

To identify the composite with $c_1$, we cover $Z$ by opens with local
equations $t_\alpha$. The local lifts of the section $1$ of
$i_*\mathbf Z_D$ through $\Sigma_D$ are the $t_\alpha^{-1}$. Their
ratios are the transition functions of $\mathcal O_Z(D)$; this fixes the
sign convention. Hence the boundary of $\Sigma_D$ followed by the
Kummer boundary is the class of $\mathcal O_Z(D)$. Changing a local equation
multiplies a lift by a unit, and this changes the cocycle by a coboundary.

Naturality holds because the local equations, the units and the
sequence $\Sigma_D$ pull back, compatibly with the boundary maps. On the
source we use the identity $g^*i_*=i'_*g_D^*$ for a base change
$g:Z'\to Z$ with $i':D'\hookrightarrow Z'$ and $g_D:D'\to D$;
it can be checked on geometric stalks.

Both sides are sheaves on $Y'_{\acute{e}t}$, so it is enough to compare their
sections on a family of étale objects $U\to Y'$ that cover $Y'$. We
choose these objects so that both sections can be computed from sections of
$F_{\acute{e}t}$ over a single scheme $V\times_YX$.

Such objects exist locally on every étale $U\to Y'$: by
[Stacks, [0EY5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EY5)], locally on $U$ there is a factorization $U\to V\to Y$ in
which $V\to Y$ is étale and $U\to V$ is flat and qcqs with geometrically
connected fibres. Pullback along such a map does not change the sections
of the pullback of an étale sheaf [Stacks, [0A3H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3H), [0EZX](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZX)], and we use this
twice. Applying it to
$U\to V$, we compute the left side from $(f_*F_{\acute{e}t})(V)$; applying it to
the base change $U\times_YX\to V\times_YX$, which again has geometrically
connected fibres, we compute the right side. On these objects we
therefore have

$$
(g^{-1}f_*F_{\acute{e}t})(U)
=F_{\acute{e}t}(V\times_Y X)
=(f'_*g'^{-1}F_{\acute{e}t})(U),
$$

and the base change map is bijective on sections over every such $U$,
because these equalities are induced by it. As these $U$ cover $Y'$, the
lemma follows by descent, as in the argument in degree zero of
[Stacks, [0EYS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYS)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-calculation], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We deduce both formulas from the description of a lisse sheaf by its
representation, using Poincaré duality to reduce $H^2_c$ to $H^0$, and
then we read off the weights from the stalks.

A global section of a local system is determined by its value at
$\bar\eta$, and a vector of the fibre extends to a global section
exactly when it is fixed by the monodromy. This is the first
formula.  For the second, by degreewise Poincaré
duality (Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields]) we have

$$
H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)^\vee
=H^0(U,\mathcal F^\vee(1))=(V^\vee)^{\pi_1(U)}(1).
$$

Since the dual of $(V^\vee)^{\pi_1(U)}$ is $V_{\pi_1(U)}$, this gives the second
formula, with its twist. Moreover, the identification is induced by the
canonical duality pairing and is therefore Frobenius equivariant.

Duality also gives the vanishing outside degrees $0,1,2$. Indeed, for
$i<0$ there is nothing to prove, and for $i>2$ the space
$H_c^i(U,\mathcal F)$ is dual to $H^{2-i}(U,\mathcal F^\vee(1))$,
which is zero because $2-i<0$. For torsion coefficients the vanishing comes instead from the bound on cohomological dimension of
Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves].

Suppose that $U_0$ is affine, and choose a smooth proper completion of
$U$. Its boundary is nonempty, because a connected proper curve has
only constant global functions and hence is not affine. A compactly
supported section extends by zero to the completion, so it vanishes
on a neighbourhood of the boundary. Since a section of a lisse sheaf
on a connected curve is determined by its generic value, the section
is zero, and $H_c^0(U,\mathcal F)=0$.

For the weights we compare the global Frobenius on these two spaces
with the local Frobenius at a closed point. Since $\pi_1(U)$ acts
trivially on $V^{\pi_1(U)}$ and on $V_{\pi_1(U)}$, the action of $W(U_0)$
on them factors through the degree quotient.  If $\beta$ is an eigenvalue of the operator of degree one,
then $\beta^{\deg(x)}$ is an eigenvalue of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on
$\mathcal F_{\bar x}$ for every closed point $x$. Indeed, $V^{\pi_1(U)}$
is a subspace and $V_{\pi_1(U)}$ a quotient of $V\simeq\mathcal F_{\bar x}$,
both stable under $\operatorname{Frob}_x\in\pi_1(U)s^{\deg(x)}$, which
acts on them as $s^{\deg(x)}$.  If $\mathcal F$ is punctually of
weights $\le a$, it follows that $|\iota(\beta)|\le q^{a/2}$, and if $\mathcal F$
is pure of weight $a$, equality holds.
Finally, the twist $(-1)$ multiplies each global eigenvalue by $q$,
which gives the stated weights for $H_c^2$.

Morphisms descend because $\QbarX$ is the filtered colimit of the $E'_X$
and Hom out of a constructible complex commutes with this colimit
(Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex]). Objects are built from
lisse sheaves by finitely many extensions, each classified by a
morphism, and so they descend as well.

(1) Extension of scalars $E'_X\otimes_{E_X}-$ is left adjoint to
restriction of scalars $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E')\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)$. Hence
$\Hom_{D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E')}(C_{E'},D_{E'}[r])=\Hom_{D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)}(C,D_{E'}[r])$,
and similarly for $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Represent $D$ by a bounded complex $D^\bullet$.
Then the complexes $D^\bullet\otimes_{E_X}E'_X$ form a filtered system of
complexes of $E_X$-modules, all vanishing below the lower bound of
$D^\bullet$, and their colimit is $D^\bullet\otimes_{E_X}\QbarX$, which
represents $D_{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}$. Applying Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex]
to $C\in\Dbc(X,E)$, we get

$$
\varinjlim_{E'}\Hom_{D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)}(C,D_{E'}[r])
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Hom_{D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)}(C,D_{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}[r]),
$$

which is the claim after the adjunction.

(2) First let $K$ be a constructible $\QbarX$-module, with filtration
$N_1\subset\cdots\subset N_m=K$ as in
Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](3). We descend $N_k$ by induction on
$k$. The subquotient $N_k/N_{k-1}=a_!L$ descends, because $L$ does by
Lemma [lemma-descent-lisse-qbar-sheaves-finite] and $a_!$ commutes with
extension of scalars. Suppose $N_{k-1}$ and
$N_k/N_{k-1}$ descend to $E$. Then the extension
$0\to N_{k-1}\to N_k\to N_k/N_{k-1}\to0$ gives a distinguished triangle,
classified by a morphism $N_k/N_{k-1}\to N_{k-1}[1]$. By (1) this
morphism descends after a finite extension of $E$. The fibre of the
descended morphism, that is, its cone shifted by $[-1]$, is a model of
$N_k$.

For a bounded complex $K$, we argue in the same way by induction on the
number of nonzero cohomology sheaves. Let $i$ be the largest degree with
$\mathcal H^i(K)\neq0$, and consider the truncation triangle
$\tau_{<i}K\to K\to\mathcal H^i(K)[-i]\to$. Once
$\tau_{<i}K$ and $\mathcal H^i(K)$ have models over a finite $E$, the
connecting morphism $\mathcal H^i(K)[-i-1]\to\tau_{<i}K$ descends after a
finite extension by (1), and the cone of the descended morphism is a
model of $K$. Each step replaces $E$ by a finite extension, so after finitely many steps $K$ is defined over a single finite $E$.

The data are described by finitely many matrices with entries in
$\QbarX$ over finitely many quasi-compact objects, and each entry already
lies in some $E_X$. We make this precise.

Since $X$ is quasi-compact, we may choose a finite covering by
quasi-compact pro-étale affines on which all the modules are
free; such refinements exist by [Stacks, [0988](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0988)]. Their pairwise
intersections $U_i\times_XU_j$ are quasi-compact since $X$ is quasi-separated,
and quasi-separated since they are subschemes of the affine schemes
$U_i\times U_j$. On a quasi-compact quasi-separated object, taking sections
commutes with filtered colimits, because coverings admit finite
quasi-compact refinements and the sheaf condition involves only finite
limits [Stacks, [0739](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0739)]. By Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients] we have
$\QbarX=\varinjlim_EE_X$. Hence the finitely many transition matrices,
their inverses, and the matrices of the given morphisms have entries
in $E_X$ for a single finite $E$. Moreover, their cocycle and compatibility
identities already hold over $E_X$, since $E_X\to\QbarX$ is injective.
Descent of sheaves of modules now gives the required lisse modules and
morphisms.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-descent-lisse-qbar-sheaves-finite], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Since $f$ is finite étale, $f_*=f_!$ is exact, and the trace map
$f_*f^{-1}\mathcal F\to\mathcal F$ composed with the adjunction unit
$\mathcal F\to f_*f^{-1}\mathcal F$ is multiplication by $n$ for every
sheaf of $A$-modules $\mathcal F$ [Stacks, [03SH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SH)]. Since both maps are natural and
the functors are exact, applying them termwise to a complex
representing $L$ gives maps $L\to f_*f^{-1}L\to L$ in $D(W_{\acute{e}t},A)$ whose
composite is $n$. Applying $R\Gamma(W,-)$ and using
$R\Gamma(W,f_*f^{-1}L)=R\Gamma(W',f^{-1}L)$, we see that $n^{-1}$ times the
map induced by the trace is a left inverse of the pullback.
