Recall Burnside's theorem: an algebra of endomorphisms of a
finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field that
acts irreducibly is the full endomorphism algebra. Absolute
irreducibility thus means that the group spans the full matrix algebra. We
detect spanning by a nonzero determinant of $n^2$ group elements. Such
a determinant stays nonzero when we change the elements by a congruence
modulo a high power of $\pi_E$.

The compact group $\rho(\Pi)$ stabilizes a lattice $L$. Indeed, the
stabilizer of any lattice $L_0$ is open, hence of finite index in
$\rho(\Pi)$. So $L_0$ has only finitely many translates, and their sum
is a $\rho(\Pi)$-stable lattice. By absolute irreducibility and
Burnside's theorem, there are elements $g_1,\ldots,g_{n^2}$ whose
matrices span $\operatorname{End}_E(V)$. In a basis of $L$, the
determinant $\Delta$ of their matrices, written as column vectors, is
nonzero and integral. Choose $N>v_{\pi_E}(\Delta)$. Suppose that
$g'_1,\ldots,g'_{n^2}$ have matrices congruent to those of the $g_i$
modulo $\pi_E^N$. Since the determinant is a polynomial with integer
coefficients in the entries, their determinant $\Delta'$ satisfies
$\Delta'\equiv\Delta\pmod{\pi_E^N}$. Hence
$v_{\pi_E}(\Delta')=v_{\pi_E}(\Delta)$, and in particular
$\Delta'\ne0$. A subgroup as in the statement contains such elements.
Its matrices therefore span the whole matrix algebra, also after any
field extension, and by Burnside's theorem it acts absolutely
irreducibly. Finally, the image of $\Pi$ in $\GL(L/\pi_E^NL)$ is a
finite quotient of $\Pi$, since by continuity the kernel is open.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-detecting-irreducibility-finite-quotient], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Using the localization triangle we split $K$ into a part on $U$, which is
known, and a part on $Z$. Since $Z$ is finite over $S$, the part on $Z$ is
detected by its direct image to $S$. We compute this direct image from
$Rb_*K$ and the known part.

We work on the étale sites, in $D^+(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$ and
$\operatorname{Mod}(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$.

*Finite direct images.* Let $h:Z\to S$ be finite. Then $h_*$ is
exact and conservative, and $Rh_*M\in\Dbc$ implies $M\in\Dbc$. The first
two properties hold because, for a sheaf $F$ of $\Fell$-modules on $Z$,
$h_*F$ has stalks

$$
(h_*F)_{\bar s}
=\prod_{\bar z\in |Z_{\bar s}|}F_{\bar z}
\tag{6.17}
$$

by [Stacks, [03QP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03QP)]. Suppose $h_*F$ is constructible. The counit
$h^*h_*F\to F$ is surjective, since on stalks it is a projection from the
finite product (6.17). Its source is constructible, and a
quotient of a constructible sheaf is constructible [Stacks, [09BH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BH)]. Hence $F$
is constructible. For a complex $M$ we have $H^n(Rh_*M)=h_*H^n(M)$ because $h_*$ is exact, so the statement for complexes follows from
conservativity and the sheaf case in each degree.

*The localization triangle.* The exact sequence for an open and its
closed complement [Stacks, [095L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095L)], applied termwise to $K$, gives a triangle

$$
j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K
\longrightarrow j_!j^*K[1].
\tag{6.18}
$$

*Part (1).* The first term $j_!j^*K$ is bounded constructible, because
$j^*K$ is and extension by zero preserves constructibility. Its direct
image $Rb_*j_!j^*K$ is bounded constructible by the finiteness theorem
[Stacks, [0GL0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL0), [0G2A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0G2A)], which applies since $Rb_*=Rb_!$ for proper $b$.
Applying $Rb_*$ to (6.18), we obtain a triangle whose first
two terms, $Rb_*j_!j^*K$ and $Rb_*K$, are bounded constructible. Hence the
third term $Rb_*i_*i^*K=R(bi)_*i^*K$ is bounded constructible too. The
first step, applied to $h=bi$, now gives $i^*K\in\Dbc(Z,\Fell)$. As $i_*$
is exact and preserves constructibility, (6.18) shows that
$K\in\Dbc(Y,\Fell)$.

*Part (2).* Let $M$ be a cone of $\varphi$; we must show $M=0$. We
have $j^*M=0$ because $j^*\varphi$ is an isomorphism. By
(6.18), this means $M=i_*i^*M$. Because $Rb_*\varphi$ is an
isomorphism, we also have $0=Rb_*M=R(bi)_*i^*M$. Since $(bi)_*$ is exact,
the cohomology sheaves of $R(bi)_*i^*M$ are the sheaves
$(bi)_*H^n(i^*M)$. Conservativity of $(bi)_*$ then shows that every
$H^n(i^*M)$ vanishes, and so $M=i_*i^*M=0$.

Using the localization triangle we split $K$ into a part on $U$, which is
known, and a part on $Z$. Since $Z$ is finite over $S$, the part on $Z$ is
detected by its direct image to $S$. We compute this direct image from
$Rb_*K$ and the known part.

We work on the étale sites, in $D^+(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$ and
$\operatorname{Mod}(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$.

*Finite direct images.* Let $h:Z\to S$ be finite. Then $h_*$ is
exact and conservative, and $Rh_*M\in\Dbc$ implies $M\in\Dbc$. The first
two properties hold because, for a sheaf $F$ of $\Fell$-modules on $Z$,
$h_*F$ has stalks

$$
(h_*F)_{\bar s}
=\prod_{\bar z\in |Z_{\bar s}|}F_{\bar z}
$$

by [Stacks, [03QP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03QP)]. Suppose $h_*F$ is constructible. The counit
$h^*h_*F\to F$ is surjective, since on stalks it is a projection from the
finite product (6.17). Its source is constructible, and a
quotient of a constructible sheaf is constructible [Stacks, [09BH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BH)]. Hence $F$
is constructible. For a complex $M$ we have $H^n(Rh_*M)=h_*H^n(M)$ because
$h_*$ is exact. The statement for complexes then follows from
conservativity and the sheaf case in each degree.

*The localization triangle.* The exact sequence for an open and its
closed complement [Stacks, [095L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095L)], applied termwise to $K$, gives a triangle

$$
j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K
\longrightarrow j_!j^*K[1].
$$

*Part (1).* The first term $j_!j^*K$ is bounded constructible, because
$j^*K$ is and extension by zero preserves constructibility. Its direct
image $Rb_*j_!j^*K$ is bounded constructible by the finiteness theorem
[Stacks, [0GL0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL0), [0G2A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0G2A)], which applies since $Rb_*=Rb_!$ for proper $b$.
Applying $Rb_*$ to (6.18), we obtain a triangle whose first
two terms, $Rb_*j_!j^*K$ and $Rb_*K$, are bounded constructible. Hence the
third term $Rb_*i_*i^*K=R(bi)_*i^*K$ is bounded constructible too. The
first step, applied to $h=bi$, now gives $i^*K\in\Dbc(Z,\Fell)$. As $i_*$
is exact and preserves constructibility, (6.18) shows that
$K\in\Dbc(Y,\Fell)$.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image].

Using the localization triangle we split $K$ into a part on $U$, which is
known, and a part on $Z$. Since $Z$ is finite over $S$, the part on $Z$ is
detected by its direct image to $S$. We compute this direct image from
$Rb_*K$ and the known part.

We work on the étale sites, in $D^+(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$ and
$\operatorname{Mod}(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$.

*Finite direct images.* Let $h:Z\to S$ be finite. Then $h_*$ is
exact and conservative, and $Rh_*M\in\Dbc$ implies $M\in\Dbc$. The first
two properties hold because, for a sheaf $F$ of $\Fell$-modules on $Z$,
$h_*F$ has stalks

$$
(h_*F)_{\bar s}
=\prod_{\bar z\in |Z_{\bar s}|}F_{\bar z}
$$

by [Stacks, [03QP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03QP)]. Suppose $h_*F$ is constructible. The counit
$h^*h_*F\to F$ is surjective, since on stalks it is a projection from the
finite product (6.17). Its source is constructible, and a
quotient of a constructible sheaf is constructible [Stacks, [09BH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BH)]. Hence $F$
is constructible. For a complex $M$ we have $H^n(Rh_*M)=h_*H^n(M)$ because
$h_*$ is exact. The statement for complexes then follows from
conservativity and the sheaf case in each degree.

*The localization triangle.* The exact sequence for an open and its
closed complement [Stacks, [095L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095L)], applied termwise to $K$, gives a triangle

$$
j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K
\longrightarrow j_!j^*K[1].
$$

*Part (2).* Let $M$ be a cone of $\varphi$; we must show $M=0$. We
have $j^*M=0$ because $j^*\varphi$ is an isomorphism. By
(6.18), this means $M=i_*i^*M$. Because $Rb_*\varphi$ is an
isomorphism, we also have $0=Rb_*M=R(bi)_*i^*M$. Since $(bi)_*$ is exact,
the cohomology sheaves of $R(bi)_*i^*M$ are the sheaves
$(bi)_*H^n(i^*M)$. Conservativity of $(bi)_*$ then shows that every
$H^n(i^*M)$ vanishes, and so $M=i_*i^*M=0$.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image].

The determinant of $Q$ is an algebraic character of $H$, and its image on
the dense subgroup $\rho(\pi_1(U))$ is finite, and hence its image on all of
$H$ lies in the same finite group of roots of unity. Taking
determinants in $z=h\rho(s)^N$, we find

$$
c_Q^{\dim Q}=\det(h\mid Q)\det(s\mid Q)^N.
$$

Now apply $\lambda_\iota$, which vanishes on the first factor, and
divide by $N\dim Q$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-determinant-weight-from-central-scalar], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Replacing $X$ by an affine open we may assume $X$ affine. The twist $(1)[2]$ appears because $X$ has one more dimension than its
generic fibre, and we see it by embedding both in affine spaces whose
dimensions differ by one. To do this, choose a closed immersion $i$ over $\mathbf A^1_k$ of $X$ into $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1_k}$.
Since $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1_k}$ is smooth of dimension $r+1$ over
$k$, by composition of exceptional inverse images and Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] we get
$\omega_X\simeq i^!A(r+1)[2r+2]$. In the same way, the geometric
generic fibre is a closed subscheme of $\mathbf A^r_{\bar\eta}$, so
$\omega_{X_{\bar\eta}}\simeq i_{\bar\eta}^!A(r)[2r]$. By the second
comparison,
$g_X^*i^!A(r+1)[2r+2]\simeq i_{\bar\eta}^!A(r+1)[2r+2]$, which is
$\omega_{X_{\bar\eta}}(1)[2]$.

For the double-dual maps, note that the comparison for internal
Hom is adjoint to the pullback of the evaluation
$K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\cHom_X(K,M)\to M$, so it carries evaluation to
evaluation. Together with the twist it gives
$g_X^*\mathbb D_XK\simeq\mathbb D_{X_{\bar\eta}}(g_X^*K)(1)[2]$. This twist does no harm, because the double-dual map does not change if the dualizing
complex is replaced by an isomorphic object $\omega'$: an isomorphism
$\omega\simeq\omega'$ is used once in each of the two duals, and the two
uses cancel in $\delta$. We apply this to
$\omega'=\omega_{X_{\bar\eta}}(1)[2]$, using that
$\cHom(\cHom(N,\omega(1)[2]),\omega(1)[2])\simeq\cHom(\cHom(N,\omega),\omega)$
compatibly with evaluation. It follows that the isomorphism
$g_X^*\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK\simeq\mathbb D_{X_{\bar\eta}}
\mathbb D_{X_{\bar\eta}}g_X^*K$ obtained by applying the comparison twice
carries $g_X^*\delta_K$ to $\delta_{g_X^*K}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-double-dual-geometric-generic-fibre], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Let $G$ be a finite quotient of $P$. Since $G$ is a $p$-group, the
order $|G|$ is invertible in $A$, and the invariants are the image of
the idempotent $e=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}g$.  Verdier duality sends this
idempotent to the same averaging idempotent for the contragredient
action, since inversion permutes the summands. Hence the image of
$\mathbb D(e)$ is the dual of $\operatorname{im}e$, and the evaluation
pairing restricts as stated.  As invariants are exact, continuity gives
the assertion for the pro-$p$ group $P$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-duality-invariants-pro-p], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Apply the matrix form of Engel's theorem [humphreys72, §3.3], which is the external input explicitly quoted in the reference. Its hypothesis is that every element of the Lie subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(M)$ acts nilpotently. For $M\ne0$ it gives a nonzero vector annihilated by all these operators, that is, a nonzero common kernel.

Induct on $\dim M$. The zero-dimensional case has the empty basis. Otherwise clause [lemma-engel-s-theorem--1] gives a nonzero common kernel vector $v$. The induced operators on $M/\Omega v$ remain nilpotent, so their Lie algebra has a strictly triangular basis by induction. Lift that basis and place $v$ first. All operators are then strictly upper triangular in the resulting basis of $M$.

In the basis of clause [lemma-engel-s-theorem--2], the Lie algebra lies in the strictly upper triangular matrices. Let $N_r$ consist of matrices supported at least $r$ places above the diagonal. Matrix multiplication gives $[N_r,N_s]\subseteq N_{r+s}$. The $r$th term of the lower central series lies in $N_r$, and $N_{\dim M}=0$. Thus the lower central series terminates and $\mathfrak n$ is nilpotent.

By clause [lemma-engel-s-theorem--3], the lower central series of $\mathfrak n$ terminates. Each successive derived commutator lies in a later term of that lower central series (or use $[N_r,N_s]\subseteq N_{r+s}$ from its proof). Hence the derived series also terminates, and $\mathfrak n$ is solvable.

We first bound the complex in (3.1) for the torsion
reductions of $b_!M_0$ by cohomological dimensions, and then pass to the
derived limit, which costs one degree. Both cohomological dimensions are
finite by [Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)] and
Lemma [lemma-cohomological-dimension-base-field].

By Lemma [lemma-integral-models](3) and (4), $b_!M_0$ lies in
$\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$, so it is derived complete. Since $b_!$ is exact
and $M_0$ is $\pi_E$-torsion free, its reductions are

$$
b_!M_0\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,X}}\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E^n
=b_!(M_0/\pi_E^n).
$$

These are constructible torsion sheaves. They are pulled back from
$X_{\acute{e}t}$, because extension by zero and closed direct image commute with
this pullback [Stacks, [09AF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AF), [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)].

*Torsion targets.* We bound the complex that appears in
(3.1) when the target is one of the torsion sheaves
$b_!(M_0/\pi_E^n)$. By [Stacks, [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)], $Rj_*$ in
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$ of a sheaf pulled back from the
étale site is the pullback of its direct image in
$D(X_{\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$. On the étale site the degrees are
controlled by the cohomological dimension, and hence
$Rj_*j^*b_!(M_0/\pi_E^n)$ has cohomology in degrees
$[0,\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)]$. The fibre of the map from a sheaf to
this complex lives in degrees $[0,\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+1]$, so the
fibre formula of Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme](1) shows that

$$
R\underline\Gamma_Z\,b_!(M_0/\pi_E^n)\in D^{[0,\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+1]}(Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n),
$$

and its cohomology sheaves are torsion sheaves pulled back from the
étale site, though not necessarily constructible. Restricting to $S$
and tensoring with the locally free lisse sheaf $L_0^\vee/\pi_E^n$
does not change this range of degrees. Since the cohomology of $S$ with
coefficients in a torsion sheaf vanishes above $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(S)$,
the hypercohomology spectral sequence on $S$ gives

$$
H^q R\Gamma\bigl(S,(L_0^\vee/\pi_E^n)\otimes u^*R\underline\Gamma_Z\,b_!(M_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)=0
\quad(q>\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+\operatorname{cd}_\ell(S)+1),
\tag{5.2}
$$

for every $n$, $b$ and $M_0$.

*Integral targets.* For the lattice $b_!M_0$ itself we write the
relevant complex as a derived limit of its reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$. Consider the complex
$L_0^\vee\otimes u^*R\underline\Gamma_Z\,b_!M_0$.
By Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support], the functors that form it
commute with derived inverse limits of sequences. They also commute with
reduction modulo $\pi_E^n$, which is the cone of multiplication by
$\pi_E^n$. Since $b_!M_0$ is derived complete, so is this complex, and
its reductions are the complexes in (5.2).
In other words, the complex is the derived limit of its reductions, and
we may compute its cohomology on $S$ from theirs.
Derived global sections preserve products and cones, and hence derived
inverse limits. Using (3.1) with $\mathcal O_E$
coefficients, that is, for $R\!\operatorname{Hom}$ in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$, we get

$$
R\!\operatorname{Hom}_X(a_!L_0,b_!M_0)
=R\Gamma\bigl(S,L_0^\vee\otimes u^*R\underline\Gamma_Z\,b_!M_0\bigr)
=R\varprojlim_n R\Gamma\bigl(S,(L_0^\vee\otimes u^*R\underline\Gamma_Z\,b_!M_0)\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n\bigr).
$$

A derived inverse limit of a sequence raises an upper bound on cohomology
by at most one. Indeed, it is the fibre of the difference of the identity and the
transition maps on the product, and
products of abelian groups are exact. This is the Milnor sequence
[Stacks, [08TB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08TB)]. Applied to the bound (5.2)
for the reductions, it gives (5.1).
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-ext-bound-lattices], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The map $\psi$ is the projection to $M$ of the closure of the graph of
$V\to M$. By elimination of indeterminacy this closure becomes an open
of a blow-up of $Y$, and $\psi$ is proper because the graph is closed.

Let $G$ be the schematic closure of the graph of $V\to M$ in
$Y\times_SM$. Its projection to $Y$ is separated of finite type,
and it is an isomorphism over $V$. By
Theorem [theorem-elimination-indeterminacy], after a $V$-admissible blow-up
$Y'\to Y$ its strict transform $G'$ is an open $V'\subseteq Y'$.
This strict transform is the closure of the graph of $V\to M$ in
$Y'\times_SM$, since both are the closure of the same graph outside
the exceptional divisor [Stacks, [0F3Y](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3Y)]. So $G'$ is closed in
$Y'\times_SM$, and since the projection of $Y'\times_SM$ to $M$ is proper,
the map $V'\simeq G'\to M$ is proper. It remains to identify the inverse image of $V$. For this, note that over $V\subseteq M$ the graph
of the inclusion $V\to Y'$ is already closed in $Y'\times_SV$, because
$Y'$ is separated over $S$. The inverse image of $V$ under $\psi$ is
therefore this graph, that is, $V$ itself. See also [Stacks, [0F3Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3Z)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-extending-graph-from-compactification], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We separate the closure of $F$ from the closure of the locus where $q$
fails to be an isomorphism, and then apply elimination of
indeterminacy on the complement of the second closure.

Inside $V$, the set $F$ is disjoint from the closed complement of the
largest open over which $q$ is an isomorphism. Since $V$ is spectral, both
closed subsets can be enlarged to disjoint constructible closed subsets. To these we apply Lemma [lemma-separation-closures] so that their closures
in $T$ become disjoint. Then, on the complement $T_0$ of the second closure,
the restriction of $q$ is an isomorphism over an open $V_0$ containing
$F$. After making this open schematically dense, we apply
Theorem [theorem-elimination-indeterminacy] on $T_0$. The resulting strict transform is both open and proper over the
modification, and hence it is an isomorphism there.
By the extension part of Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow],
this blow-up of $T_0$ extends to a $V$-admissible blow-up of $T$,
which is an isomorphism over an open containing the closure of $F$. We have only sketched the argument; the precise version, including the choice of constructible enlargements, is [Stacks, [0F3W](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3W)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-extending-isomorphism-over-closure-closed], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Lemma [lemma-smooth-morphisms-locally-constant-sheaves] controls the
direct image $R(bj)_*F$ of $Rj_*F$ to $S$.
Then Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image] turns this, together with the hypothesis on $G$, into control of $Rj_*F$ along $Z$. Throughout, we work on the étale sites.

For constructibility we check the hypotheses of part (1) of
Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image] for $K=Rj_*F$ and
$U=G$. The complex $Rj_*F$ lies in $D^+(Y_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$ because $F$ is a
sheaf. Its restriction to $G$ is in $\Dbc$ by assumption, and
$Z=Y\setminus G$ is finite over $S$. It remains to treat the direct image.
Since $bj:X\to S$ is smooth and $F$ is locally constant, we may apply
Lemma [lemma-smooth-morphisms-locally-constant-sheaves]. After
shrinking $S$ to a nonempty open $S_0$, the complex $Rb_*Rj_*F=R(bj)_*F$
lies in $\Dbc(S_0,\Fell)$, and its formation commutes with base change
along every $T\to S_0$ of finite type over $k$. Part (1) of
Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image] then gives
$Rj_*F\in\Dbc(Y_{S_0},\Fell)$.

For base change we use part (2) of the lemma instead. Let $T\to S_0$ be a
$k$-scheme of finite type, and let $\varphi$ be the base change map
$g_Y^*Rj_*F\to Rj_{T,*}g_X^*F$. By assumption it is an isomorphism on
$G_T$. Proper base change for $b$ and the compatibility of base change maps
with composition [Stacks, [0E46](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0E46)] identify $Rb_{T,*}\varphi$ with the base
change map for $R(bj)_*F$, which is an isomorphism. Since $b_T$ is proper
and $b_Ti_T$ is finite, part (2) of
Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image] applies over $T$. It shows
that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-extension-across-finite-subset], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

An object that is locally $\Lambda_S\otimes P$ on a stratum $S$, with $P$
perfect, remains of this form after derived extension of scalars, since
$P\otimes^{\mathbf L}_\Lambda\Lambda'$ is a perfect $\Lambda'$-complex.
Moreover, extension of scalars commutes with extension by zero and with
finite cones. Every object of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is built from such objects
by extension by zero from strata and finite cones, and so its extension of
scalars lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda')$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-extension-scalars-preserves-dctf], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

A purely inseparable extension does not change the étale topos, which
allows us to replace $k$ and $k'$ by their algebraic closures and then
apply $(C_7)$.

By the classical
comparison we may compute on the étale site. Choose compatible
algebraic closures $\bar k\subseteq\bar k'$. Since $\bar k/k$ and
$\bar k'/k'$ are purely inseparable, $C_{\bar k}\to C$ and
$C_{\bar k'}\to C_{k'}$ are universal homeomorphisms, and hence they induce
equivalences of small étale topoi [Stacks, [03SI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SI)]. This reduces the
claim to the pullback from $C_{\bar k}$ to $C_{\bar k'}$, which is an
isomorphism by $(C_7)$ of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves]. Since all these maps are
pullback maps, the comparison square commutes [Stacks, [0A5E](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A5E)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-extension-separably-closed-ground-field], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The exceptional Künneth formula
(Proposition [proposition-exceptional-external-kunneth]) and the ordinary one
give Künneth formulas for internal Hom and for Verdier
duals, and these give the two displayed isomorphisms.

*Internal Hom and Verdier duals.*
On the point this is the identity
$\Hom(V_1,W_1)\otimes\Hom(V_2,W_2)=\Hom(V_1\otimes V_2,W_1\otimes W_2)$
for finite free modules.
For $E_i,L_i\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_i,A)$ the external comparison
$\cHom_A(E_1,L_1)\boxtimes\cHom_A(E_2,L_2)\to
\cHom_A(E_1\boxtimes E_2,L_1\boxtimes L_2)$ is an isomorphism. By
dévissage it suffices to check this on generators $E_i=Rh_{i!}F_i$, with $h_i$ the
inclusion of a stratum and $F_i$ a lisse sheaf with finite projective stalks
(Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators]), for
which

$$
\cHom_A(Rh_{i!}F_i,L_i)
\simeq Rh_{i*}(F_i^\vee\otimes^{\mathbf L} h_i^!L_i).
$$

By the ordinary Künneth formula and $\alpha$, the exterior product of
these expressions is identified with internal Hom on the product. Taking
$L_i=\omega_{X_i}$ and using $\alpha$ for the structure maps, we get,
for $M_i\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_i,A)$,

$$
\mathbb D_{X_1\times X_2}(M_1\boxtimes M_2)
\simeq \mathbb D_{X_1}M_1\boxtimes \mathbb D_{X_2}M_2.
$$

*The two isomorphisms.*
The first isomorphism is the sheaf version of
$\Hom(V,W)\simeq W\otimes V^\vee$, and we obtain it by writing
internal Hom as a dual of a tensor product. Indeed, for $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(U,A)$, $N\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(V,A)$ and the projections
$p_U,p_V$ of $V\times U$, Verdier exchange and biduality let us rewrite
$\cHom_A(p_U^*M,p_V^!N)$ as
$\mathbb D_{V\times U}(\mathbb D_VN\boxtimes M)$. By the formula for
duals of exterior products this is
$N\boxtimes \mathbb D_UM$. Taking $M=N=K$, with the
factors of the product ordered as above, we obtain the first isomorphism.
The second isomorphism follows from the canonical exchange of exceptional inverse
image with Hom, for $P,Q\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X\times X,A)$,

$$
c^!\cHom_A(P,Q)\simeq\cHom_A(c^*P,c^!Q),
$$

applied to $P=p_2^*K$ and $Q=p_1^!K$. To prove the exchange, we
use Yoneda inside $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(C,A))$, the category on which
$c_!\dashv c^!$ is defined
(Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image]). Test objects in all
of $D(C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$ would not do, since $c^!$ is not defined there. Both
sides of the exchange lie in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(C,A)$ by
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], so these test objects
suffice. By Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category]
the localizing categories are $D(C_{\acute{e}t},A)$ and $D((X\times X)_{\acute{e}t},A)$,
where the projection formula for $c_!$ holds for all objects
[Stacks, [0GL5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL5)], and tensoring with $c^*P$ preserves $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(C,A))$.
For $M$ in $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(C,A))$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Hom\bigl(M,c^!\cHom_A(P,Q)\bigr)
&\simeq\Hom\bigl(c_!M\otimes^{\mathbf L}P,Q\bigr)
\simeq\Hom\bigl(c_!(M\otimes^{\mathbf L}c^*P),Q\bigr)\\
&\simeq\Hom\bigl(M\otimes^{\mathbf L}c^*P,c^!Q\bigr)
\simeq\Hom\bigl(M,\cHom_A(c^*P,c^!Q)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$

by $c_!\dashv c^!$ and the tensor–Hom adjunction, the projection formula,
$c_!\dashv c^!$ again, and the tensor–Hom adjunction.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Write $T^{\delta}$ for the underlying set of $T$ with the discrete
topology and take $S=\beta(T^{\delta})$, its Stone–Čech
compactification. The Stone–Čech compactification of a discrete
space is extremally disconnected, and the identity $T^{\delta}\to T$
extends uniquely to a continuous surjection $\beta(T^{\delta})\to T$; see
[Stacks, [090D](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/090D)]. An extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is
totally disconnected, since the closure of an open set is clopen, and
hence it is profinite.

Give the underlying set $T^\delta$ the discrete topology and take $S=\beta(T^\delta)$. By [Stacks, [090D](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/090D)], this Stone–Čech compactification is extremally disconnected. The identity map $T^\delta\to T$ extends continuously to $S\to T$ because $T$ is compact Hausdorff. Its image contains every point of $T$, so it is surjective.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-extremally-disconnected-covers].

A profinite space is compact Hausdorff, so clause [lemma-extremally-disconnected-covers--1] gives a
continuous surjection $S\to T$ with $S$ compact Hausdorff and extremally
disconnected, for instance $S=\beta(T^\delta)$. It remains to see that $S$ is
profinite. By the definition of extremal disconnectedness
(clause [definition-w-local-w-strictly-local--1]), the closure of every open subset of $S$ is open,
hence clopen. Let $s\neq s'$ be points of $S$. Since $S$ is Hausdorff, there
are disjoint open sets $U\ni s$ and $V\ni s'$. The closure $\overline U$ is
clopen and contains $s$. It does not contain $s'$, because $V$ is an open
neighbourhood of $s'$ that does not meet $U$. Thus clopen subsets separate
the points of $S$. A compact Hausdorff space in which clopen subsets separate points is profinite: the map to the inverse limit of its finite quotients by finite partitions into clopen subsets is continuous, injective because clopen subsets separate points, and surjective by compactness, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. Hence $S$ is profinite.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-extremally-disconnected-covers].

Let $S$ be extremally disconnected and Hausdorff. By
clause [definition-w-local-w-strictly-local--1], the closure of every open subset of $S$ is open,
hence clopen. Let $s\neq s'$ be points of $S$, and choose disjoint open sets
$U\ni s$ and $V\ni s'$, which exist because $S$ is Hausdorff. The closure
$\overline U$ is clopen and contains $s$. It does not contain $s'$, since $V$
is an open neighbourhood of $s'$ that does not meet $U$. Hence $\overline U$
separates $s$ from $s'$. Neither compactness nor regularity is used.

If $S$ is moreover compact, then it is a compact Hausdorff space in which
clopen subsets separate points. A compact Hausdorff space in which clopen subsets separate points is profinite: the map to the inverse limit of its finite quotients by finite partitions into clopen subsets is continuous, injective because clopen subsets separate points, and surjective by compactness, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

The trace morphism is the composite of four steps: the exceptional
tensor–Hom adjunction, external duality, the adjoint of evaluation
along the diagonal, and exceptional proper base change for the closed
diagonal. Since each is defined by units, counits and tensor evaluation,
the composite has a filtered version

$$
\cHom_F(c_2^*\mathcal K,c_1^!\mathcal K)
\simeq c^!(\mathcal K\boxtimes_F\mathbb D_F\mathcal K)
\longrightarrow Ri_{c*}\omega_{\Fix(c)}
$$

whose graded pieces, computed by
Lemma [lemma-graded-pieces-filtered-operations], are the unfiltered
versions. In particular the filtered comparison for external duality is
an isomorphism, because each of its graded maps is a finite sum of the
isomorphisms in Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], and
graded pieces detect isomorphisms of finitely filtered complexes.
Forgetting the filtration we recover the trace morphism for $K$.

The target is pure of weight zero, so $\operatorname{tr}_F$ vanishes on
$F^1$, and its restriction to $F^0$ factors through $\operatorname{gr}^0$.
This factorization holds on filtered dg models, hence also in the
filtered derived category. By Lemma [lemma-graded-pieces-filtered-operations],
$\operatorname{gr}^0$ of the source is $\bigoplus_a\cHom(c_2^*K_a,c_1^!K_a)$.
Now the steps for internal Hom and external duality preserve the two indices, and on a pair of equal indices evaluation along the diagonal is the
evaluation of $K_a$. Hence the map on the summand $a$ is the trace
morphism for $K_a$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-filtered-trace-morphism], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Recall that $\mathbf P^n$ parametrizes binary forms of degree $n$
up to scalars, and the map $\sigma_n$ multiplies $n$ linear forms; over a field
it is the quotient of $(\mathbf P^1)^n$ by the symmetric group. Explicitly, we use the coefficients of a product of binary linear forms:

$$
\prod_{i=1}^n(x_iT+y_iU)
=\sum_{j=0}^nF_jT^{n-j}U^j,\qquad
\sigma_n\bigl(([x_i:y_i])_i\bigr)=[F_0:\cdots:F_n].
$$

Every $F_j$ is homogeneous of degree one in each pair $(x_i,y_i)$, and
the corresponding sections of $\mathcal O(1,\ldots,1)$ have no common
zero. Indeed, at a geometric point every linear factor is nonzero, and
hence so is their product. Therefore the sections define the stated morphism over any
$S$, and the construction commutes with base change.

For example, on the chart $F_0\ne0$ of the target, whose preimage is the
chart where every $x_i$ is invertible, the coordinates $c_j=F_j/F_0$ pull
back to the elementary symmetric polynomials in the $w_i=y_i/x_i$, as in
the classical description of $\mathbf A^n$ as the quotient of
$\mathbf A^n$ by the symmetric group.

Finiteness of $\sigma_n$ follows from properness and finiteness of
the fibres. Since the source is proper over $S$ and the target is separated over
$S$, the morphism $\sigma_n$ is proper. For the fibres, recall that over an algebraically closed
field, a nonzero binary form of degree $n$ is a product of $n$ linear
forms $x_iT+y_iU$, and these are unique up to order and up to
multiplying each by a nonzero constant. Here a factor with $x_i=0$ is a
multiple of $U$ and corresponds to the point $[0:1]$. In other words, the form determines the multiset of
points $[x_i:y_i]\in\mathbf P^1$. Hence every geometric fibre of
$\sigma_n$ is nonempty, and $\sigma_n$ is surjective. Moreover, each geometric
fibre has at most $n!$ geometric points, namely the orderings of this
multiset. Since a scheme of finite type over a field with finitely many
geometric points is zero dimensional, $\sigma_n$ is quasi-finite, and a
proper quasi-finite morphism is finite [Stacks, [02LS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02LS)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-finite-cover-projective-space], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We delete a rational point where $F$ is lisse, which replaces $H^1_c$
by a group surjecting onto it, and move that point to infinity by an
automorphism of $\mathbf P^1$. First choose a closed point of $W_0$ and a finite
extension $k_m$ of the constant field over which it has a rational
point $s$.
The restriction of $F$ to $W_0\otimes_{k_0}k_m$ is again pure of
weight $w$, because a residue extension raises an eigenvalue and the
residue cardinality to the same power.
Next, some element of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(k_m)$ sends $s$ to infinity, and we
transport $F|_{W\setminus\{s\}}$ by this automorphism. As $F$ is
lisse at $s$, its local inertia there is trivial, so the
transported sheaf $G$ extends to a lisse sheaf across the new infinity.
It is defined on the image $V_0$ of
$W_0\setminus\{s\}$, a dense open of the affine line, and
$H^1_c(V,G)=H^1_c(W\setminus\{s\},F)$ because the automorphism
identifies the two pairs. The surjection follows from the localization
sequence

$$
H_c^1(W\setminus\{s\},F)\to H_c^1(W,F)\to H_c^1(\{s\},F_{\bar s})=0,
$$

in which the last group vanishes because a point has no cohomology in
positive degrees. Since every construction is defined over $k_m$, the
map commutes with the Frobenius of $k_m$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-finite-extension-base-field-moving], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The map is given by a function with a single pole, at a point at
infinity, and we choose the order of this pole prime to $p$ so that
the map is generically étale. We find the function by Riemann–Roch,
we show by a local computation at the pole that its differential is
nonzero, and we check the assertions about $K$ stalk by stalk.

Let $\overline C_0$ be the smooth projective completion, choose a
closed point $s$ of $\overline C_0$ outside $C_0$, and choose $m$
prime to $p$ with $(m-1)\deg(s)>2g(\overline C_0)-2$. Both divisors
$ms$ and $(m-1)s$ then have degree $>2g-2$, so Riemann–Roch
(Theorem [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality]) gives
$h^0(\mathcal O(ns))=n\deg(s)+1-g$ for $n=m,m-1$, and hence

$$
h^0(\mathcal O(ms))-h^0(\mathcal O((m-1)s))=\deg(s)>0.
$$

Therefore there is a function $f$ whose only pole is at $s$, of exact
order $m$. The sections $1,f$ define a nonconstant map
$\overline C_0\to\mathbf P^1$ whose inverse image of infinity
is $\{s\}$, and this map is proper with finite fibres, hence finite.
To see that it is generically étale, choose a uniformizer $t$ at $s$
and write $f=t^{-m}u$ with $u$ a unit. Since $\kappa(s)/k_0$ is
separable and the curve is smooth, $dt$ generates the module of
differentials near $s$. Writing $du=u'\,dt$, we get

$$
df=t^{-m-1}(-mu+tu')\,dt\ne0,
$$

since $-mu+tu'$ is congruent to the unit $-mu$ modulo $t$, and $mu$ is
a unit because $p\nmid m$. The differential of this finite map between
smooth curves is therefore invertible at the generic point, and the map is
generically étale. We set $C'_0=\overline C_0\setminus\{s\}$ and
let $\pi$ be the restriction of the map to $C'_0$.

Over the open in the statement, $\pi$ is
finite étale and its inverse image lies in $C_0$, where $j_!F=F$.
Moreover, the direct image of a lisse sheaf under a finite étale map is lisse,
because étale locally the map is a disjoint union of copies of the
base. Hence $K$ is lisse there. For purity, note that at a closed point $y$ of this open,
the stalk of $K$ is a sum over the geometric points of the fibre, which
Frobenius permutes.
Consider such a cycle of length $e$, corresponding to a point over $y$ with
residue extension of degree $e$. On it the $e$th power of the operator is
the local Frobenius upstairs, so an eigenvalue $\beta$ satisfies
$|\iota\beta|^e=q_y^{ew/2}$, and the weight is still $w$. Since
$R\pi_!=\pi_*$ for the finite map $\pi$, the identification of cohomology
follows by composing direct images with compact support. It
commutes with Frobenius because the construction is defined over $k_0$.

Everything follows from the stalk formula. To prove it, note that over a
strict localization the source splits into strictly henselian local
pieces, and on such a piece taking sections is the same as taking a stalk.

After base change to the strict henselization of $W$ at $\bar w$, the finite
scheme $V$ becomes a finite disjoint union of strictly henselian local schemes.
On each such local scheme, the sections of an étale sheaf are its stalk at
the closed geometric point. Indeed, every étale neighbourhood of that
point admits a section, so a germ extends to a global section, and two
sections with the same germ agree after pulling back along such a section. In
particular, taking sections is exact on abelian sheaves. Combining this with
the description of stalks of direct images via strict localizations
[Stacks, [03QP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03QP)], we obtain the displayed formula.
Since geometric stalks are conservative and finite products of abelian groups
are exact, $u_*$ is exact.

In a cartesian square over $W'\to W$, a geometric point of $W'$ and
its image in $W$ have the same geometric fibre. Therefore the underived
base change map is the identity on the corresponding factors of the displayed
formula, hence an isomorphism. Since both
direct images in the square are exact, their derived functors and
the base change map are computed term by term. Finally, the same argument applies to
sheaves of modules.

We first treat a finite map and then reduce to it by Zariski's main
theorem, which writes a quasi-finite map as an open immersion followed
by a finite map. All the computation is in the finite case, since
extension by zero does not change any nonzero stalk.

For a finite map, exactness follows from
Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms] and the comparison of coefficients. The same
lemma shows that the stalk at a geometric point $\bar y$ over a closed point $y$
is the direct sum of the stalks at the geometric points of $Z_0$ over
$\bar y$, and the local Frobenius at $y$ permutes these summands. Let
$z$ be a point of residue degree $e=[\kappa(z):\kappa(y)]$. Frobenius
cycles through the $e$ summands over $z$, and its $e$th power on each
of them is conjugate to the local Frobenius at $z$. Each eigenvalue
$\beta$ on this cycle therefore satisfies $\beta^e=\alpha$ for an
eigenvalue $\alpha$ at $z$. If the input has weight $w$, then

$$
|\iota(\beta)|^e=|\iota(\alpha)|=q_z^{w/2}=q_y^{ew/2},
$$

and we find $|\iota(\beta)|=q_y^{w/2}$. This proves that finite direct
image preserves purity. For example, for the constant sheaf on
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^2}$ over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$,
the direct image has rank two and Frobenius swaps the two summands.
Its eigenvalues $\pm1$ have weight $0$, as the constant sheaf does.

In general, $Y_0$ is Noetherian, hence quasi-compact and
quasi-separated, and Zariski's main theorem in the form
[Stacks, [05K0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05K0)] applies. It factors $g$ as an open immersion
$j:Z_0\hookrightarrow\overline Z_0$ followed by a finite map
$\bar g:\overline Z_0\to Y_0$. By
Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek] we have
$Rg_!=\bar g_*j_!$, and both functors are exact. Extension by zero
preserves purity, since its other stalks are zero. Now take a mixed
sheaf of weights at most $w$ on $Z_0$, with a finite filtration by
Weil subsheaves whose quotients are pure of weights at most $w$. Since
$j$ and $\bar g$ are defined over $k_0$, the functors $j_!$ and
$\bar g_*$ take Weil subsheaves to Weil subsheaves. Being exact, they
take the filtration to a finite filtration of the direct image whose
quotients are the direct images of the pure quotients. By the first
part these are pure of the same weights, which proves the assertion on
sheaves. Since $Rg_!$ is exact, it commutes with taking cohomology
sheaves, and the assertion on $D_{\leq w}$ follows.

Restricting $I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$ to $F$, where the two legs agree,
gives $I_F^n\subset I_F^{n+1}$. The reverse inclusion always holds, so
the coherent ideal $M=I_F^n$ satisfies $M=I_FM$. Hence, at a point of
$V(I_F)$, Nakayama's lemma shows that $M=0$ in the local ring, and hence on a
neighbourhood of the point, whereas at a point outside $V(I_F)$ we have
$M=\mathcal O_F$. The closed set $V(I_F)$ is therefore also open. It is
nonempty by assumption, and $F$ is connected, so $V(I_F)=F$ and
$I_F^n=0$. This proves the first assertion.
As $I_F$ is nilpotent, each generator
$h/t$ of $\mathcal O_{F_T}[I_F/t]$ over $\mathcal O_{F_T}$ is nilpotent.
Hence the reduction of $\mathcal D_{d^{-1}(Z)}F$ is
$(F_T)_{\mathrm{red}}$.

It remains to see that $\widetilde F$ has no further points. On the
generic fibre the deformed correspondence is $c$ itself, so the
generic fibre of $\widetilde F$ is that of $F_T$. Let $x$ be a
point of the special fibre of $\widetilde F$. Then $\gamma_2(x)$ lies in
the zero section by Lemma [lemma-normal-cones-contracting-ideals](2),
and so does $\gamma_1(x)=\gamma_2(x)$. By
Lemma [lemma-normal-cones-contracting-ideals](1), the point $x$ lies on the
zero section $Z'\subset N_{Z'}C$. On $Z'$ the two maps are the restrictions
of $c_1$ and $c_2$. Their equalizer is $F\cap Z'$, whose underlying space
is $F$ by the first assertion. Thus every fixed point in the special
fibre lies in the closed subscheme above, and the closed immersion of
reduced schemes is surjective. Its ideal has zero radical and is
therefore zero, so the immersion is an isomorphism.

The flat model exists on the étale site by a classical result, and we
pull it back. The generators then come from two filtrations: the stupid
filtration of the model, and the filtration of each term by strata.

By Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison], $C=\nu_X^*C_{\acute{e}t}$ with
$C_{\acute{e}t}\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$, where
$\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$ is the comparison inverse
image. By [Stacks, [0F4M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F4M)] the complex $C_{\acute{e}t}$ has a bounded flat model, and
since $\nu_X^*$ is exact on sheaves, its pullback is a
bounded flat constructible model on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. We choose a common stratification on
which its finitely many terms are locally constant, and their stalks are then
finite projective, because a finite flat
module over the Noetherian ring $A$ is finite projective. If $F$ is a flat
constructible sheaf, then the exact sequences for the successive open and closed
strata express $F$ as a finite extension of the sheaves $a_!L$ attached to its
strata. Similarly, the stupid filtration of the bounded flat complex expresses
$C$ as a finite extension of shifts of its *terms*, and shifts and finite
extensions preserve finite Tor amplitude. The same argument proves the
corresponding statement on $X_{\acute{e}t}$, which we use in the proof of
Proposition [proposition-compactness-finite-coefficients] before passing to the pro-étale site.

By Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison], write $C=\nu_X^*C_{\acute{e}t}$ with $C_{\acute{e}t}\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$. The bounded flat constructible model exists there by [Stacks, [0F4M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F4M)]. The stupid filtration expresses the complex as finite extensions of shifts of those terms. These operations preserve finite Tor-amplitude; allowing direct summands gives the stated generation.

The three assertions are of different kinds. That the transform
of $j_!M$ is a single sheaf is a vanishing statement for the
cohomology of the twisted sheaves $M\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)}$ on
$U$, whereas the exact sequence comes from transforming the boundary sequence
$0\to j_!M\to j_*M\to B\to0$ term by term. Finally, the
bound on $B'$ comes from the stalks of $B$, which are known from
Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points].

For $G$, the stalk formula
of Proposition [proposition-base-change-fourier-inversion] says that
the stalk of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_!M)$ at $y$ is
$R\Gamma_c(U,M\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)})[1]$, so we must show that
only $H^1_c$ is nonzero. We apply
Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve] to the lisse
sheaf $M\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)}$ on the affine curve $U$, with $j$
the identity. It shows that the group in degree zero vanishes and that
the group in degree two is a twist of
the coinvariants of geometric monodromy on
$M\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)}$. But a nonzero coinvariant would be a
geometric quotient of $M$ isomorphic to $\mathcal L_{\psi(-yx)}$, and
our assumption on $M$ excludes such a constituent, so
the group in degree two vanishes as well. The shift then places the
remaining group $H^1_c$ in degree zero, and the transform is a sheaf
$G$.

The transform of $B$ is computed point by point. After geometric base
change, the punctual sheaf
$B$ is a finite sum of skyscrapers with coefficient modules, and the
transform of each skyscraper is a linear character sheaf tensored with
that module and shifted by one. Since a linear character sheaf is lisse
on the whole dual line, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(B)=B'[1]$ with $B'$ lisse.

Applying the Fourier transform to the triangle obtained from
$0\to j_!M\to j_*M\to B\to0$, and using
Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension] for the
middle term, we obtain a triangle
$G\to j'_*M'\to B'[1]\to$. Here $G$ and $j'_*M'$ are sheaves in degree
zero, and $B'[1]$ is a sheaf in degree $-1$. Hence the long exact
sequence of cohomology sheaves has only three nonzero terms, and it is
the stated exact sequence.

The weights of $B'$ come from those of $B$, because a character sheaf has
weight zero, and the weights of $B$ are at most $w$ by
Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]. Only at boundary
points that are not rational does this need an argument. So let $s$ be a
boundary point of
degree $d$ and $y$ a rational point of the dual line. The geometric
points over $s$ contribute $d$ summands to $B'_{\bar y}$, which
$\operatorname{Frob}_y$ permutes cyclically, and its $d$th power acts
on one summand as $\operatorname{Frob}_s$ on $B_{\bar s}$ times a root
of unity coming from the character sheaf. Every eigenvalue
$\beta$ of $\operatorname{Frob}_y$ on these summands therefore satisfies
$\beta^d=\zeta\alpha$, with $\zeta$ a root of unity and $\alpha$ an
eigenvalue of $\operatorname{Frob}_s$. Since
$|\iota\alpha|\le q^{dw/2}$, we get $|\iota\beta|\le q^{w/2}$.
At a point $y$ of higher degree we replace $q$ by the cardinality of
$\kappa(y)$.

For a filtration of $B'$ with pure quotients, choose for each boundary
point, over its

We reduce to a closed subscheme of affine space, where the equations
$t^{q^m}=t$ have simple roots.

For every open $U_0\subset X_0$ the restriction to
$U=U_0\times_{k_0}k$ of the fixed scheme of $\Phi_X^m$ is the fixed scheme of
$\Phi_U^m$, because $\Phi_X$ is the base change of a morphism of $X_0$ and so
maps $U$ into itself. As $X_0$ is quasi-compact, we may therefore assume that $X_0$
is a closed subscheme of $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf F_q}$, with coordinates
$t_1,\ldots,t_r$.

In this case the fixed scheme is the pullback of the diagonal along the graph.
Since the equations of $X_0$ have coefficients in $\mathbf F_q$, we have
$(\Phi_X^m)^\#t_i=t_i^{q^m}$, and the fixed scheme is cut out by the defining
equations of $X_0$ together with $t_i^{q^m}-t_i=0$. Each polynomial
$t^{q^m}-t$ is separable, so the algebra $k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]/(t_i^{q^m}-t_i)_i$
is a product of copies of $k$ indexed by $\mathbf F_{q^m}^r$. Its quotient by
the defining equations of $X_0$ retains exactly the factors at the rational
solutions of those equations, as asserted. In particular the fixed scheme is
a closed subscheme of a finite étale $k$-scheme, hence étale. The argument
uses only the equations of $X_0$, so $X_0$ need not be reduced.

An irreducible Weil representation is geometrically semisimple. A
power of Frobenius fixes each isotypic component, and on it we can
triangularize this power. The flags obtained in this way are stable
under the Weil group of the constant extension, and by them we refine a
composition series to the required filtration.

In detail, take a composition series for the Weil representation. By
Lemma [lemma-restriction-normal-subgroup], applied to the geometric
fundamental group, which is normal in the Weil group, the geometric
restriction of each irreducible factor is semisimple. Frobenius
permutes the finitely many geometric isotypic components of the
factor, and we choose a lift $s$ of geometric Frobenius to the
Weil group and a power $s^m$ fixing all of them. On a component
$S\otimes M$, geometric monodromy acts irreducibly on $S$ and
trivially on $M$. Since $s^m$ fixes the isomorphism type of $S$, there
is an isomorphism $u$ from $S$ to its conjugate by $s^m$. We claim that
the action of $s^m$ on the component has the form $u\otimes v$ with $v$
invertible on $M$. Indeed, the composite of the
action of $s^m$ with $u^{-1}\otimes1$ commutes with geometric monodromy,
and by Schur's lemma the endomorphisms of $S\otimes M$ commuting with
it are $1\otimes\operatorname{End}(M)$. Triangularizing $v$, we obtain
a stable flag whose geometric factors are $S$.

We take a common $m$ for the finitely many factors. Then the subgroup
generated by geometric monodromy and $s^m$ is the Weil group after the
constant extension of degree $m$. Choose a finite extension $E'$ of
the coefficient field over which these flags are defined. Since a subspace
defined over $E'$ is stable under this group if and only if its
extension to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is, the flags define lisse Weil subsheaves,
and refining the composition series by them gives the required
filtration.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-geometric-constituents-after-constant-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We compare a component $Y_1$ with the normalization $N$ of $X$
in the function field of $Y_1$. By Zariski's main theorem, $Y_1$ is an open
subscheme of $N$, and by the valuative hypothesis this open
subscheme contains every point of $N$.

Since $Y$ is étale over $X$, it is locally noetherian and normal
[Stacks, [033C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/033C)]. Hence its connected components are integral, open
and closed [Stacks, [033N](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/033N)]. Fix a nonempty component $Y_1$. Since a valuative
lift whose generic point lies in $Y_1$ stays in $Y_1$, the
hypothesis also holds for $Y_1\to X$.

The image of $Y_1$ is nonempty and open, hence contains the generic
point $\eta$ of $X$. The generic fibre of $Y_1$ is integral and
étale over $k(X)$, so it is $\operatorname{Spec}k(Y_1)$. Thus the
function field $k(Y_1)$ is a finite separable extension of $k(X)$, and we let $N$
be the normalization of $X$ in $k(Y_1)$. Since $X$ is Nagata, $N$ is finite over $X$ [Stacks, [035B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/035B), [0AVK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AVK)].
We claim that $Y_1\to X$ factors through a map $f:Y_1\to N$. Indeed,
since $Y_1$ is normal, an element of $k(Y_1)$ that is integral over the
coordinate ring of an affine open of $X$ lies in every local ring of
$Y_1$ over that open. These regular functions agree in $k(Y_1)$, and hence
they glue. The map $f$ is separated, locally of finite type and
locally quasi-finite, because its fibres lie in the zero-dimensional
fibres of $Y_1\to X$.

We show that $f$ is an open immersion. Choose affine opens
$W\subseteq Y_1$ and $N_0\subseteq N$ with $f(W)\subseteq N_0$.
By Zariski's main theorem [Stacks, [05K0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05K0)], $W$ is an open subscheme of
a finite $N_0$-scheme, and the reduced closure of $W$ in it is integral,
finite and birational over $N_0$, with function field $k(Y_1)$. Since
$N_0$ is normal, this closure is $N_0$ [Stacks, [0AB1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AB1)], and therefore
$W\to N_0$ is an open immersion. These local inverses glue: on the
intersection of two such open images, the inverse sections agree generically, hence everywhere by
separatedness, and so they glue to an inverse on the union of the
images.

Finally, let $n\in N$ and choose a valuation ring $V\subseteq k(Y_1)$
dominating $\mathcal O_{N,n}$ [Stacks, [00IA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00IA)]. By hypothesis, the
generic map $\operatorname{Spec}k(Y_1)\to Y_1$ extends to a map
$\operatorname{Spec}V\to Y_1$, whose composite with $f$ agrees with the
canonical map $\operatorname{Spec}V\to N$ generically and over $X$.
By separatedness of $N\to X$ the two maps agree, so $n$
lies in the open image of $Y_1$. We conclude that $Y_1=N$ is finite
étale over $X$. In particular its image is open and closed, and being
nonempty, it is all of $X$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-geometric-coverings-normal-scheme], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The scheme of lattices satisfies the valuative condition of
Lemma [lemma-geometric-coverings-normal-scheme], so it has a finite étale
surjective component, and we push the universal lattice of this component down to
$X$ by the trace.

We may assume that $L$ has positive rank $r$. Let
$Y$ be the $X$-scheme representing lattices in $L$
(Lemma [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves]), a separated surjective étale
$X$-scheme with a universal lattice. Pro-étale locally on $X$, the scheme $Y$ is constant: the proof of that lemma shows that, for a
quasi-compact pro-étale covering $U\to X$, with $U$ a pro-étale
affine on which $L$ is free,

$$
Y\times_XU\simeq
\coprod_{\GL_r(E)/\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)} U,
$$

where $\GL_r(E)/\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)$ is the
discrete set of lattices in $E^r$.

We check the valuative property of
Lemma [lemma-geometric-coverings-normal-scheme]. Let $V$ be a valuation ring
with fraction field $K$, and suppose given $\operatorname{Spec}V\to X$
and a lift $\xi:\operatorname{Spec}K\to Y$. Since $U\to X$ is flat
and surjective, there are a local extension of valuation rings
$V\to V'$ and a compatible map $\operatorname{Spec}V'\to U$
[Stacks, [089F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/089F)]. This extension is faithfully flat, because it is local
and $V'$ is torsion-free, hence flat, over $V$ [Stacks, [0539](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0539)]. By the
displayed description of $Y\times_XU$, the
pullback of $\xi$ to the spectrum of the fraction field of $V'$ picks out a
lattice in $E^r$, and the constant
section with this value extends it to a map
$\xi':\operatorname{Spec}V'\to Y$.

We descend $\xi'$ by fpqc descent, which needs its two pullbacks to
$R=V'\otimes_VV'$ to agree. Over the domain $V'\otimes_VK$, the maps $\xi'$
and $\xi$ agree at the generic point, hence everywhere by separatedness,
so the two pullbacks agree after base change to $K$. This suffices: since $R$ is flat
over $V$, the map $R\to R\otimes_VK$ is injective, and therefore
$\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_VK)$ is schematically dense in
$\operatorname{Spec}R$. As the equalizer of the two pullbacks is closed
by separatedness, they agree on $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Descent then gives a lift
$\operatorname{Spec}V\to Y$ restricting to $\xi$, which is unique
by separatedness and the density of $\operatorname{Spec}K$.

By Lemma [lemma-geometric-coverings-normal-scheme], every nonempty component
$p_1:Y_1\to X$ of $Y$ is therefore finite étale and surjective. We fix one, and
let $N\subseteq p_1^*L$ be its universal lattice.
As in Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification], set

$$
M=\operatorname{im}\bigl(
p_{1*}N\longrightarrow p_{1*}p_1^*L
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}}L\bigr).
$$

The sheaf $M$ is lisse with $M[1/\ell]=L$. Indeed, after the cover is
split into $d$ sheets, this image is the sum of $d$ lattices. On a
common pro-étale refinement these become constant lattices in $E^r$, and their sum is a
finite free $\mathcal O_E$-lattice spanning $E^r$.

By Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves] the finite reductions
$M_n=M/\pi_E^nM$ are finite locally constant étale sheaves, and
$M=\varprojlim_nM_n$ by
Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients], which we may check where
$M$ is free.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-global-lattice-normal-scheme], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We glue the $T_i$ along the closure of $U$ in $T_1\times_ST_2$, after
blow-ups that make this closure open in both. The glued scheme is
separated because the closure is closed in the product.

Let $G$ be the schematic closure of $U$ in $T_1\times_ST_2$. Then Theorem [theorem-elimination-indeterminacy], applied to the two projections, makes the strict transforms of $G$ opens in suitable
blow-ups of the two sides. To obtain a single modification, we blow up
$G$ in the product of the two pulled-back centers, which gives a common
refinement. By
Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow], these further
centers extend from the opens to each side, and the resulting scheme
$G'$ is an open in both $T_i'$.

The map $G'\to T_1'\times_ST_2'$ is a closed immersion. It is an
immersion, and it is proper because $G'\to G$ is proper,
$G\subseteq T_1\times_ST_2$ is closed, and the modified product
is separated over the original product. We glue the two $T_i'$ along
$G'$, and the glued scheme $T$ is covered by $T_1'$ and $T_2'$. To see
that $T$ is separated, note that the
diagonal of $T$ restricted to $T_i'\times_ST_j'$ is the diagonal of
$T_i'$ for $i=j$ and the graph $G'$ for $i\neq j$. Both are closed, so
$T$ is separated. It is of finite type because it has a finite
cover by opens of finite type.

Suppose that $U$ is dense in both $T_i$. The complement of the
exceptional divisor of a blow-up is schematically dense, as in the proof
of Lemma [lemma-making-open-schematically-dense], and it contains
the inverse image of $U$ as a dense open. Hence $U$ is dense in each
$T_i'$, and so in $T$. This construction is [Stacks, [0F3X](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3X)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-gluing-after-admissible-blow-ups], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The equivalence of (2) and (3) is linear algebra. For the equivalence
of (1) and (3), note that a denominator $Q$ gives a linear recurrence
among the rows. Conversely, the characteristic polynomial of the
shift on a finite-dimensional row span is a denominator. The descent
statement holds because (2) does not change when we extend the field.

For example, $C=1/(1-T)$ has all $c_n=1$, every row is $(1,1,\ldots)$,
and the row span is a line. For $C=1/(1-T)^2$ we have $c_n=n+1$, and
$R_j=R_0+j(R_1-R_0)$, so the row span is a plane.

For (3)$\Rightarrow$(2), a nonzero $k\times k$ minor of a finite submatrix
gives $k$ linearly independent rows. So every finite submatrix has
rank at most the dimension of the row span. For (2)$\Rightarrow$(3),
let $R_{j_1},\ldots,R_{j_m}$ be linearly independent. On their span
the coordinate functionals have common kernel zero. They therefore span
its dual, and $m$ of them already do. The corresponding $m\times m$
minor is nonzero, and so $m$ is at most the bound in (2).

For (1)$\Rightarrow$(3), suppose that $QC=P$ with $Q(0)=1$. Comparing
coefficients gives a fixed linear recurrence for all sufficiently
large indices, and the same recurrence expresses every sufficiently
late row in terms of a fixed finite list of earlier rows.

For (3)$\Rightarrow$(1), the left shift $S(v)_n=v_{n+1}$ preserves the
finite-dimensional row span $V$, since $S(R_j)=R_{j+1}$. Let $e$ be
evaluation at coordinate zero and $v=R_0$. In any basis of $V$, with
$M$ the matrix of the shift, we have

$$
C(T)=e(I-TM)^{-1}v
=\frac{e\operatorname{adj}(I-TM)v}{\det(I-TM)}.
$$

The first equality holds coefficient by coefficient. Indeed,
$(I-TM)^{-1}=\sum_nT^nM^n$, and $eM^nv$ is the coordinate zero of
$S^n(R_0)=R_n$, that is, $c_n$. As the denominator has constant
coefficient one, this proves (1).

For the descent, note that condition (2) involves only the
coefficients $c_n\in K$, and the rank of a matrix with entries in $K$
does not change when we pass to $K'$. So (2) holds over $K$ if and
only if it holds over $K'$. Applying (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) over $K'$
and (2)$\Rightarrow$(1) over $K$ gives the descent of rationality.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The set-theoretic conditions are general facts about derived categories
of Grothendieck abelian categories. Compactness, on the other hand, was proved separately for each kind of coefficients, and generation follows from the
definition of the localizing category.

As the derived category of a Grothendieck abelian category of module
sheaves, the ambient category is locally small, and so is its
full subcategory $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda))$. Moreover, the latter has direct sums by definition, so its idempotents split [Stacks, [05QW](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05QW)]. Finally, the subcategory $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is thick, since constructibility and finite Tor
amplitude are preserved by shifts, cones and direct summands.

To see that $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is essentially small, note first that the
constructible sheaves in the heart have a set of representatives for each
admissible $\Lambda$. A bounded complex with such cohomology is built from its
cohomology sheaves by finitely many extensions, formed with truncations
in the ambient category. Each extension step is classified by an
element of a Hom set of the ambient category, and these Hom sets are
sets because the ambient category is locally small. Hence these
complexes form an essentially small category, of which
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is a full subcategory.

Compactness for finite $A$ is Proposition [proposition-compactness-finite-coefficients].
For $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ it is
Theorem [theorem-compactness-rational-coefficients], and for $\mathcal O_E$
it is Proposition [proposition-compactness-proper-direct-image]; in the integral and rational cases,
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}=\Dbc$.

For generation, suppose that $K\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ receives no
nonzero maps from shifts of objects of a small skeleton. The objects
$M$ with $\Hom(M[n],K)=0$ for all $n$ form a localizing subcategory
containing $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$. Hence this subcategory contains $K$. Then $\mathrm{id}_K=0$, and so $K=0$.

The category of coefficient-module sheaves is Grothendieck abelian, so its derived category has Hom sets. The localizing category in the statement is a full subcategory of this derived category, and hence has the same Hom sets between its objects.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability].

The localizing subcategory generated by $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ is, by definition, closed under shifts and distinguished triangles in the ambient derived category. It therefore inherits its triangulated structure.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability].

Closure under arbitrary direct sums is part of the definition of the localizing subcategory. Because the subcategory is full, the ambient direct sum has the same universal mapping property within it and is its coproduct.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability].

By clauses [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability--2] and [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability--3], this is a triangulated category with countable coproducts. The idempotent-splitting theorem [Stacks, [05QW](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05QW)] applies to precisely these hypotheses and shows that every idempotent splits.

containing $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$. Hence this subcategory contains $K$. Then $\mathrm{id}_K=0$, and so $K=0$.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability].

A connected algebraic group is determined by its Lie algebra among its
closed connected subgroups, so it suffices to show that the Lie algebras
of $Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ and $H^\circ$ together span that of $G^\circ$. We show
that this Lie algebra is reductive, hence the sum of its center and its
derived algebra, and that the derived algebra lies in the Lie algebra of
$H$ because commutators lie in $H$.

*Reductivity.* Write $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ)$. Then

$$
\mathfrak g=Z(\mathfrak g)+[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g],
$$

by Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation],
once we know that $V$ is a faithful semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module. The
$\rho(W(U_0))$-stable subspaces are precisely the $G$-stable subspaces,
because the stabilizer of a subspace is closed. Hence $V$ is semisimple as a
$G(\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$-module, and by Lemma [lemma-restriction-normal-subgroup]
it is also semisimple as a $G^\circ(\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$-module. Then
Lemma [lemma-stable-subspaces-center] makes it a faithful
semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module.

*The center and the derived algebra.* Put $T=Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ and
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ)$. The comparison between
groups and Lie algebras in Lemma [lemma-stable-subspaces-center] gives
$\operatorname{Lie}(T)=Z(\mathfrak g)$. Moreover
$[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\subseteq\mathfrak h$, because the
commutator morphism $G\times G\to G$ factors through the closed
subgroup $H$: it does so on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-points by
Lemma [lemma-normality-geometric-monodromy], and $G\times G$ is
reduced. To deduce the inclusion, let $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ and put
$R=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell[\varepsilon,\eta]/(\varepsilon^2,\eta^2)$. The commutator of
$1+\varepsilon X$ and $1+\eta Y$ in $G(R)$ is $1+\varepsilon\eta[X,Y]$, and
it lies in $H(R)$. Here the subring $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell[\varepsilon\eta]\subset R$
is a ring of dual numbers, and the equations of $H$ vanish on
$1+\varepsilon\eta[X,Y]$ already over this subring. Hence
$[X,Y]\in\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\mathfrak h$, and

$$
\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(T)+\mathfrak h.
$$

*Back to groups.* The multiplication $T\times H^\circ\to G^\circ$ is a
homomorphism, because $T$ is central. By
Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms] its
image is a closed connected subgroup, whose Lie algebra contains
both summands on the right, hence equals that of $G^\circ$. By the
same lemma the image is therefore $G^\circ$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-identity-component], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Each base change map is a unit followed by a square isomorphism and a
counit. When two squares are pasted, the square isomorphisms compose, and the triangle identities
cancel the inner unit and counit. In the vertical case we also use that direct image
preserves injectives, so that $R(gf)_*\simeq Rg_*Rf_*$ is computed on
the same resolution.

For an identity square, the inverse-image comparison is the identity. In the unit–comparison–counit expression for base change, the remaining unit and counit cancel by the triangle identity. Hence the base-change map is the identity.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].

Expand the two base-change maps as unit, square comparison and counit. In their horizontal composite, naturality moves the middle unit next to its counit, and the triangle identity cancels this pair. The two square comparisons compose to that for the pasted rectangle, leaving its defining base-change map.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].

Compute the composite direct image on a common injective resolution: direct image preserves injectives, so $R(gf)_*\simeq Rg_*Rf_*$ there. Expand the two maps as units, square comparisons and counits. Naturality and the triangle identity cancel the inner unit–counit pair; composition of the square comparisons gives exactly the map for the vertical rectangle.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].

The two-term resolution of $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ gives an exact sequence

$$
0\to H^q(Q^\bullet)/\pi_E^n\to H^q(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^n)
\to H^{q+1}(Q^\bullet)[\pi_E^n]\to0.
$$

For the transition from level $m$ to level $n$,
the induced map on the right-hand terms is multiplication by
$\pi_E^{m-n}$, because the corresponding map of resolutions is the
identity in degree zero and multiplication by $\pi_E^{m-n}$ in degree
$-1$. If $m-n\ge e$, this map is zero, since $H^{q+1}(Q^\bullet)[\pi_E^m]$
consists of torsion elements and $\pi_E^e$ kills them. The image of
$H^q(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^m)$ therefore lies in the left-hand term
$H^q(Q^\bullet)/\pi_E^n$ at level $n$, which is the image of
$H^q(Q^\bullet)$. The reverse inclusion holds because the map from
$H^q(Q^\bullet)$ factors through level $m$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-images-cohomology-finite-levels], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We embed $M$ into an injective sheaf and compare the long exact sequences
of the two sides. The induction hypothesis identifies everything in degree
$q-1$, and since the injective sheaf has no higher direct images upstairs,
a diagram chase shows that $b^q_M$ is injective with cokernel inside
$R^qf'_*g'^{-1}I$.

Choose $0\to M\to I\to Q\to0$ with $I$ as in the statement. By the long
exact sequences, the rows of the following diagram are exact. Here the upper
row ends in $0$ because $R^qf_*I=0$ for the injective sheaf $I$, whereas the
lower row does not, because $g'^{-1}I$ need not be injective.

$$
\begin{CD}
g^{-1}R^{q-1}f_*I @>>> g^{-1}R^{q-1}f_*Q
@>>> g^{-1}R^qf_*M @>>>0\\
@V{\sim}VV @V{\sim}VV @VVV @VVV\\
R^{q-1}f'_*g'^{-1}I @>>> R^{q-1}f'_*g'^{-1}Q
@>>>R^qf'_*g'^{-1}M @>>>R^qf'_*g'^{-1}I.
\end{CD}
$$

The first two vertical arrows are isomorphisms by
$\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q-1)$, applied to $I$ and to $Q$. Exactness of the upper row says that $g^{-1}R^qf_*M$ is the cokernel of the
map $g^{-1}R^{q-1}f_*I\to g^{-1}R^{q-1}f_*Q$, and exactness of the lower row
says that the kernel of $R^qf'_*g'^{-1}M\to R^qf'_*g'^{-1}I$ is the cokernel
of the corresponding map in the lower row. Since the first two vertical
isomorphisms identify these two maps, $b_M^q$ is an isomorphism onto this kernel.
In particular $b^q_M$ is injective, and its cokernel embeds into
$R^qf'_*g'^{-1}I$, which is the last assertion. For $M\subset N$, choose an
injective $I$ containing $N$.
What we have just shown, applied to $M\subset I$ and to $N\subset I$,
embeds the cokernels of $b_M^q$ and $b_N^q$ compatibly into
$R^qf'_*g'^{-1}I$. As in [Stacks, [0F03](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F03)], the map between the cokernels
induced by $M\subset N$ is compatible with these two embeddings and is
therefore injective.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
