Both assertions are [Stacks, [0F04](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F04), [0F05](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F05)]. They use three properties of
direct image along an integral morphism $\pi$: it is exact and
conservative [Stacks, [04C2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04C2)], even if $\pi$ is not surjective, and it
commutes with arbitrary base change [Stacks, [0EYP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYP)]. By exactness, the
Leray spectral sequence for a composite with $\pi$ degenerates, which means
that direct images along the composite are computed by applying $\pi_*$
first.

We use the notation $b^q_{h,N}$ and $C(h,N)=\operatorname{coker}b^q_{h,N}$ of
the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduction-field], for a $Y$-scheme $T$, its base
change $g_T:T'=Y'\times_YT\to T$, a qcqs morphism $h:Z\to T$ and a sheaf $N$
of $\mathbf Z/n$-modules on $Z_{\acute{e}t}$. By
Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree], $b^q_{h,N}$ is
injective, so a failure of base change in degree $q$ means $C(h,N)\neq0$.

For the first assertion, let $f:Z\to T$ and $M$ give a failure, so
$C(f,M)\neq0$, and let $\pi:\widetilde Z\to Z$ be integral and surjective.
We show that $C(f\pi,\pi^{-1}M)\neq0$. Since $\pi$ is surjective, the unit
$M\to\pi_*\pi^{-1}M$ is injective, as one sees on stalks. By the second
assertion of Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree] it induces
an injection $C(f,M)\hookrightarrow C(f,\pi_*\pi^{-1}M)$, and so
$C(f,\pi_*\pi^{-1}M)\neq0$. It remains to identify $C(f,\pi_*\pi^{-1}M)$ with
$C(f\pi,\pi^{-1}M)$. Let $\pi':\widetilde Z_{T'}\to Z_{T'}$ be the base
change of $\pi$, again integral. Upstairs, $\pi_*$ is exact, so the Leray
spectral sequence for $f\circ\pi$ degenerates and gives
$R^qf_*(\pi_*\pi^{-1}M)=R^q(f\pi)_*\pi^{-1}M$. Downstairs, $\pi_*$ commutes
with base change, $g_Z^{-1}\pi_*\pi^{-1}M\simeq\pi'_*g_{\widetilde Z}^{-1}\pi^{-1}M$,
and $\pi'_*$ is exact, so in the same way

$$
R^qf'_*\bigl(g_Z^{-1}\pi_*\pi^{-1}M\bigr)
\simeq R^qf'_*\pi'_*\bigl(g_{\widetilde Z}^{-1}\pi^{-1}M\bigr)
=R^q(f\pi)'_*\bigl(g_{\widetilde Z}^{-1}\pi^{-1}M\bigr).
$$

These identifications are compatible with the base change maps
[Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)], so they carry $b^q_{f,\pi_*\pi^{-1}M}$ to
$b^q_{f\pi,\pi^{-1}M}$. Hence $C(f\pi,\pi^{-1}M)\simeq C(f,\pi_*\pi^{-1}M)\neq0$,
and base change fails for the new source.

For the second assertion, let $f:Z\to T$ factor as $f=\pi\circ f_1$ with
$\pi:T_1\to T$ integral and $f_1:Z\to T_1$, and suppose base change fails
for $f$ and $M$, that is, $C(f,M)\neq0$. We show that it fails for $f_1$ and
$M$ over the new base $T_1$. Put $T'_1=Y'\times_YT_1=T'\times_TT_1$, and let
$\pi':T'_1\to T'$ be the base change of $\pi$, again integral. The base
change map for $f_1$ is

$$
b^q_{f_1,M}:g_{T_1}^{-1}R^qf_{1*}M\longrightarrow R^qf'_{1*}g_Z^{-1}M
\qquad\text{on }T'_{1,\acute{e}t}.
$$

We push it down to $T'$ by $\pi'_*$. Since $\pi'_*$ is exact and
$\pi_*$ commutes with base change,
$\pi'_*g_{T_1}^{-1}R^qf_{1*}M\simeq g_T^{-1}\pi_*R^qf_{1*}M
=g_T^{-1}R^qf_*M$, where the last equality is the degenerate Leray spectral
sequence for $f=\pi f_1$. In the same way
$\pi'_*R^qf'_{1*}g_Z^{-1}M=R^qf'_*g_Z^{-1}M$. Under these identifications
$\pi'_*\bigl(b^q_{f_1,M}\bigr)=b^q_{f,M}$, again because base change maps
compose. Since $\pi'_*$ is exact, it follows that
$\pi'_*C(f_1,M)\simeq C(f,M)\neq0$, so $C(f_1,M)\neq0$, which is the
assertion.

Use the injectivity and cokernel comparison in Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree], together with exactness and integral base change [Stacks, [04C2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04C2), [0EYP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYP), [0F04](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F04)].

For the first assertion, let $\pi$ be the integral surjective change of the
source. Since $\pi$ is surjective, the map $M\to\pi_*\pi^{-1}M$ is
injective. By Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree] the
cokernel for $\pi_*\pi^{-1}M$ is therefore nonzero. Exactness of $\pi_*$
and the Leray spectral sequence identify the base change map for
$\pi_*\pi^{-1}M$ with the one for $\pi^{-1}M$ and the composite morphism.
Hence base change fails for the new source.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-integral-changes-source-base].

Use exactness of integral direct image and its compatibility with base change [Stacks, [04C2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04C2), [0EYP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYP), [0F05](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F05)].

For the second, let $\pi:T'\to T$ be integral, put
$Y'_T=Y'\times_YT$, and let $\pi':Y'_T\times_TT'\to Y'_T$ be the
base change of $\pi$, again an integral morphism. The new base change map
lives on $Y'_T\times_TT'$, and we compare it with the old one by applying
$\pi'_*$. As $\pi'_*$ is exact, it commutes with taking $R^q$. As it
commutes with base change, the pushed-down terms are the inverse images of
the corresponding terms on $T$. Using the Leray spectral sequence, which
degenerates by exactness, we see that $\pi'_*$ of the new map is the old
base change map. Because $\pi'_*$ is exact and conservative, the old map
would be an isomorphism if the new one were.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-integral-changes-source-base].

On the line, from the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1$ and
localization at the point at infinity, we get
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,E)=E(-1)[-2]$, identified by the trace map
(Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves]). Every translation acts trivially on it,
since it preserves the trace and the cohomology is concentrated in
degree two. Now let $\pi:\mathbf A^1\to\mathbf A^1$, $u\mapsto u^p-u$,
be the Artin–Schreier cover, which is finite étale and whose total
space is again an affine line. Let $\mathcal L_{\psi_0}$ be the
$\psi_0$-eigenspace of $\pi_*E$, that is, the sheaf of the proof of
Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf] for $a=1$. The projector $e_{\psi_0}$ of
that proof cuts out
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal L_{\psi_0})$ from
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\pi_*E)=R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,E)$ as the
$\psi_0$-eigenspace of the deck translations. As we have just seen,
these translations act trivially on the cohomology of the upper line,
so, since $\psi_0$ is nontrivial, the eigenspace is zero, that is,
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal L_{\psi_0})=0$. Finally, by its construction,
$\mathcal L_\psi$ is the pullback of $\mathcal L_{\psi_0}$ by the
automorphism $x\mapsto ax$ of the line, and hence
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal L_\psi)=0$ as well.

On $\mathbf A^r$ with $\lambda\ne0$, we choose linear
coordinates in which $\lambda$ is the first coordinate. Then
$\lambda^*\mathcal L_\psi$ is the external product of $\mathcal L_\psi$
on the first factor with the constant sheaf on $\mathbf A^{r-1}$, and
the Künneth isomorphism of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-formula-compact-supports] writes its
cohomology as a tensor product with the first factor
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal L_\psi)=0$. For $\lambda=0$, on the other hand, the sheaf
is constant, so the trace map of Definition [definition-trace-map]
for the projection $\mathbf A^r\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an
isomorphism $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^r,E)(r)[2r]\simeq E$. On constant
coefficients this map is the trace map of affine space
(9.11), obtained by integrating along
one coordinate line at a time. Finally, all these calculations take
place with coefficients in $E$ and commute with extension of scalars.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The hypothesis gives an isomorphism $(P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W\simeq K_n$ at
each level $n$, but these isomorphisms need not be compatible with the
reduction maps, so they do not assemble to a map into
$K=R\varprojlim_nK_n$. What we need is a compatible family of maps, that
is, an element of the inverse limit of the Hom groups between the
reductions. Such an element lifts to a map
$\mathcal O_{E,W}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet\to K$, because $K$ is derived
complete. To find one that is an isomorphism at level $1$, we show that
these Hom groups satisfy the Mittag–Leffler condition with a rate $e$
independent of $n$. Derived Nakayama then shows that the lift is an
isomorphism.

Consider the tower of complexes

$$
\cHom_{(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_W}\bigl((P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W,K_n\bigr)
\in D(W_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n),
$$

with transition maps induced by the reduction maps $K_{n+1}\to K_n$, and
the tower of groups
$\Hom_{D(W_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)}\bigl((P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W,K_n\bigr)$
obtained by applying $H^0R\Gamma(W,-)$. Since $P^\bullet$ is finite
free, the first tower is the tower of reductions of
$(\mathcal O_{E,W}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}(P^\bullet)^\vee)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,W}}K$.

These Hom groups can be infinite, so the Mittag–Leffler condition
has to come from a uniform bound. Let $Q^\bullet=(P^\bullet)^\vee\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$
and choose $e$ such that $\pi_E^e$ kills the torsion of
$H^1(Q^\bullet)$. Let $N\ge m\ge n+e$ and choose one isomorphism
$(P^\bullet/\pi_E^N)_W\simeq K_N$. Its reductions to levels $m$ and
$n$ identify the three internal Hom complexes at levels $N\to m\to n$
with the constant complexes
$Q^\bullet/\pi_E^N\to Q^\bullet/\pi_E^m\to Q^\bullet/\pi_E^n$. Their
zeroth cohomology sheaves are therefore the constant sheaves on the groups
$H^0(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^N)\to H^0(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^m)\to H^0(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^n)$.
By Lemma [lemma-images-cohomology-finite-levels] the images from levels $N$
and $m$ at level $n$ agree, as subsheaves. Since $W$ is weakly
contractible, taking sections over $W$ is exact, and so it commutes with
taking cohomology and images. Hence the images in the Hom group at level $n$
from levels $N$ and $m$ coincide as well. Since $e$ does not depend on
$n$, $m$ or $N$, we obtain the Mittag–Leffler condition: for every $n$ the
images at level $n$ are constant from level $n+e$ on.

To lift, note that each Hom group contains an isomorphism, and its
reduction to level $1$ is again an isomorphism. The stable image at
level $1$ is the image from level $1+e$, so it contains an invertible
class. By the Mittag–Leffler property this class lifts to a compatible
family $(\varphi_n)_n$ in the inverse limit of the Hom groups. The
Milnor sequence gives a surjection

$$
\begin{aligned}
&H^0R\varprojlim_n R\Gamma\bigl(W,\cHom_{(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_W}
((P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W,K_n)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\longrightarrow
\varprojlim_n\Hom_{D(W_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)}
\bigl((P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W,K_n\bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$

whose source is
$\Hom_{D(W_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)}(\mathcal O_{E,W}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet,K)$.
This holds because derived sections commute with inverse limits, $K$ is complete, and
tensoring with the finite free dual of $P^\bullet$ commutes with
inverse limits. The family $(\varphi_n)$ therefore lifts to a morphism
$\mathcal O_{E,W}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet\to K$ whose first reduction is an isomorphism.
Since both objects are complete, derived Nakayama
(Lemma [lemma-reduction-derived-nakayama]) shows that this morphism is an
isomorphism. Here completeness of the source follows termwise from
$\mathcal O_{E,W}=\varprojlim(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_W$. Indeed, the
transition maps are epimorphisms, so this limit agrees with the
derived limit by Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-integral-model-weakly-contractible], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

In (1) and (2) we compare two coefficient sheaves related by a flat map
that is an isomorphism modulo every $\pi_E^n$, so they have the same
derived complete objects. For (3)
we use the two characterizations of integral constructibility, while for (4) we
combine the dévissage of
Corollary [corollary-coefficient-heart-b] with the lattices of
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification].

(1) and (2). The map from the constant sheaf $\mathcal O_E$ to
$\mathcal O_{E,X}$ is flat and induces isomorphisms modulo every
$\pi_E^n$ [Stacks, [099L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099L)]. Hence by [Stacks, [099I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099I)] restriction of scalars
is an equivalence on derived complete objects, which is (1).
By [Stacks, [09C1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C1)], an object of $\Dc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ is a derived complete
complex whose reduction modulo $\pi_E$ is constructible of finite Tor
dimension over $\mathbf F_E$. Since over the field $\mathbf F_E$ every
bounded complex has finite Tor dimension, this
description agrees with the description of $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ in
Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion], and
together with (1) this gives (2).

(3) By Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion], an object of
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$ lies in $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ if and only if
it satisfies condition (2) there: it is derived complete with constructible
reduction modulo $\pi_E$. Equivalently, it satisfies condition (3): there is a
finite stratification such that on each stratum $S$, pro-étale locally,
$K|_S\simeq\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$ for a bounded
complex $P^\bullet$ of finite free $\mathcal O_E$-modules; here the implication
from (2) to (3) is
Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes].
For each of the three operations we therefore check whichever of these two conditions is convenient.

*Inverse image.* By Lemma [lemma-inverse-image-coefficient-sheaves], $f^*$
sends finite free $\mathcal O_{E,Y}$-modules to finite free
$\mathcal O_{E,X}$-modules, so it preserves the local description of
condition (3).

*Extension by zero.* The functor $a_!=i_*j_!$ preserves derived
completeness. Indeed, $j_!$ for a quasi-compact open immersion $j$ preserves
limits by [Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)], and $i_*$ is exact and preserves limits by
[Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)]. Moreover, both functors commute with reduction
modulo $\pi_E$ and preserve constructibility of the reductions, so $a_!$
preserves condition (2).

*Tensor product.* Let $K,M\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$, and choose a
stratification for $K$ as above. Derived completeness and
constructibility of the reduction modulo $\pi_E$ are both preserved by
cones, so $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ is closed under cones. Moreover, the localization
triangles along the strata exhibit $K$ as a finite iterated extension of
the objects $a_!a^*K$, for the strata $a:S\hookrightarrow X$, and the functor
$-\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ preserves these triangles. It therefore suffices to
show that $(a_!a^*K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ lies in $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$.

For this we use the projection formula for a locally closed immersion:
for $L\in D(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$ and $M\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$
the canonical map

$$
(a_!L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M\longrightarrow a_!(L\otimes^{\mathbf L}a^*M)
$$

is an isomorphism. Indeed, write
$a=i\circ j$ with $j$ open and $i$ closed, so that $a_!=i_*j_!$. On $S$
the map restricts to the identity of $L\otimes^{\mathbf L}a^*M$, while on
every complementary stratum both sides restrict to zero. Since restriction to
the strata is exact and jointly conservative
by [Stacks, [09AD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AD)], the map is an isomorphism.

Given the parts on inverse image and extension by zero,
we are reduced to showing that $a^*K\otimes^{\mathbf L}a^*M$ lies in
$\Dbc(S,\mathcal O_E)$. Tensoring with $a^*K$ preserves derived
completeness, because $a^*K$ is pro-étale locally a bounded
complex of finite free modules. Moreover, the reduction modulo $\pi_E$ of the
tensor product is the tensor product of the reductions, and this is constructible.

(4) For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, we first descend to a finite $E$ by
Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field]. By
Corollary [corollary-coefficient-heart-b], every object of $\Dbc(X,E)$ is
obtained by finitely many cones and shifts from sheaves $a_!L$ with $L$
lisse. We refine the stratum $S$ by a finite stratification as in
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification]. This replaces $a_!L$
by finitely many extensions of such sheaves, and on each new stratum $L$

(3) By Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion], an object of
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$ lies in $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ if and only if

reduction modulo $\pi_E$. Equivalently, it satisfies condition (3): there is a
finite stratification such that on each stratum $S$, pro-étale locally,
$K|_S\simeq\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$ for a bounded
complex $P^\bullet$ of finite free $\mathcal O_E$-modules. The implication
from (2) to (3) is
Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes].
For each of the three operations we check one of these two conditions.

*Inverse image.* By Lemma [lemma-inverse-image-coefficient-sheaves], $f^*$
sends finite free $\mathcal O_{E,Y}$-modules to finite free
$\mathcal O_{E,X}$-modules, so it preserves the local description of
condition (3).

*Extension by zero.* The functor $a_!=i_*j_!$ preserves derived
completeness. Indeed, $j_!$ for a quasi-compact open immersion $j$ preserves
limits by [Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)], and $i_*$ is exact and preserves limits by
[Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)]. Both functors commute with reduction
modulo $\pi_E$ and preserve constructibility of the reductions. Hence $a_!$
preserves condition (2).

stratification for $K$ as above. Derived completeness and
constructibility of the reduction modulo $\pi_E$ are both preserved by
cones, so $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ is closed under cones. The localization
triangles along the strata exhibit $K$ as a finite iterated extension of
the objects $a_!a^*K$, for the strata $a:S\hookrightarrow X$. The functor

show that $(a_!a^*K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ lies in $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$.

For this we use the projection formula for a locally closed immersion:

$$
(a_!L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M\longrightarrow a_!(L\otimes^{\mathbf L}a^*M)
$$

tensor product is the tensor product of the reductions, and this is constructible.

We check each isomorphism by Yoneda. After applying

The adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ lives on the localizing
categories $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ and $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$, and the functors in the argument preserve
them. Indeed, pullback is exact, preserves direct sums, and carries the constructible generators to constructible objects by
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], so it maps $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$ into
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$. For the same reasons, tensoring with a fixed constructible complex preserves the localizing category. In particular,
for $N\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$ the objects $f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}K$ and

The second step of the computation below is the projection formula

$$
Rf_!(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}K)\simeq N\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_!K
\qquad(N\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))).
$$

For finite coefficients it follows from
Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category] and [Stacks, [0GL5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL5)], and for
rational coefficients it is Proposition [proposition-projection-formula-rational-coefficients].

immersion and $p$ proper, and combine

$j_!(M\otimes^{\mathbf L}j^*N)

$Rf_*\cHom_X(K,f^!L)$ belong to $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$, so we may test the
comparison map between them by Yoneda inside the full subcategory
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$. For every object $N$ of this category we obtain, by the adjunctions and the
projection formula,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Hom_Y(N,\cHom_Y(Rf_!K,L))
&\simeq\Hom_Y(N\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_!K,L)\\
&\simeq\Hom_Y(Rf_!(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}K),L)\\
&\simeq\Hom_X(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}K,f^!L)\\
&\simeq\Hom_Y(N,Rf_*\cHom_X(K,f^!L)).
\end{aligned}
$$

with the double-dual map of the perfect complex $R\Gamma(X,K)$. Both
maps are determined by pairings, and we compare the pairings.
For proper $f$ we have
$Rf_!=Rf_*$, and the isomorphism (10.3) is adjoint
to the pairing

$$
Rf_*K\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_*\mathbb D_XK
\longrightarrow Rf_*(K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb D_XK)
\longrightarrow Rf_*\omega_X\longrightarrow\omega_Y.
$$

Using (10.3) for $K$ and for $\mathbb D_XK$, we
view both $Rf_*\delta_K$ and $\delta_{Rf_*K}$ as maps
$Rf_*K\to\mathbb D_YRf_*\mathbb D_XK$. Up to the symmetry of the
tensor product, both are adjoint to this pairing. For
$\delta_{Rf_*K}$ this holds because under (10.3) for
$K$ evaluation on $Y$ corresponds to the pairing. For
$Rf_*\delta_K$ it holds because $\delta_K$ is adjoint to evaluation
on $X$ and (10.3) for $\mathbb D_XK$ is adjoint
to the analogous pairing.

After scaling, the coordinates of $a$ reduce modulo $\ell^n$ to a
compatible system of Frobenius-fixed classes in
$H^1(U,\mathbf Z/\ell^n)$, which vanish by
Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]. This needs $H^1$ to be
identified with homomorphisms.

Recall that for a finite abelian
group $G$ the group $H^1(U,G)$ classifies $G$-torsors. By
[Stacks, [0DV5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0DV5)], finite locally constant sheaves on the connected scheme
$U$ correspond to finite continuous $\pi_1(U)$-sets, and under this
correspondence a $G$-torsor becomes a finite $\pi_1(U)$-set with a commuting
simply transitive action of $G$, that is, a continuous homomorphism
$\pi_1(U)\to G$. Hence $H^1(U,G)=\Hom_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1(U),G)$.
In this description Frobenius acts on $H^1(U,G)$ through the action of
$s$ on $\pi_1(U)$ by conjugation. The Frobenius-fixed classes are therefore
the homomorphisms $b$ with $b(s^{-1}gs)=b(g)$.

Choose a $\mathbf Q_\ell$-basis of $E$, with coordinate maps $t_i$.  Since
$\pi_1(U)$ is compact, each $t_i a(\pi_1(U))$ is bounded, and after multiplying all
coordinates by one power of $\ell$ we may assume that they take values
in $\mathbf Z_\ell$.  Each coordinate is then a continuous homomorphism
$\pi_1(U)\to\mathbf Z_\ell$ invariant under conjugation by $s$. Its reductions
modulo $\ell^n$ are compatible classes in $H^1(U,\mathbf Z/\ell^n)$
fixed by Frobenius. By the proposition they vanish, and hence every
coordinate of $a$ is zero.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-invariant-additive-characters], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For the twists, $\ell$ is invertible on $Y$, hence on $X$, as
Definition [definition-tate-twists] requires. The torsion twists
$\mu_{\ell^n}$ are then represented by finite étale group
schemes, and these commute with base change. Their inverse limit is

is represented by the base change [Stacks, [09A5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A5)]. This proves the
assertion for $\mathcal O_E(1)$. For a finite $A$ killed by

scalars from $\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, so inverse image
commutes with it as well. The other twists are obtained by inverting $\ell$,

The preservation statements follow from
Lemma [lemma-integral-models](3), since closed
direct image is exact and preserves limits [Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)]. The
two inverse images agree on objects that are pro-étale locally of the form
$\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes P$ with $P$ finitely generated, and by the local
structure of Lemma [lemma-structure-integral-constructible-complexes](1) and (2) they
therefore agree on $\Dbc$.

The coefficient sheaves are pulled back from the point, and by
clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--3] there is a canonical monoidal isomorphism
$f^{-1}\circ p_Y^*\simeq p_X^*$. Hence $f^{-1}\Lambda_Y\simeq\Lambda_X$ as
sheaves of rings, and the module inverse image
$f^*=\Lambda_X\otimes_{f^{-1}\Lambda_Y}f^{-1}(-)$ is $f^{-1}$, which is exact.
So $\mathbf Lf^*$ is computed termwise by $f^{-1}$, and
$H^q(\mathbf Lf^*K)=f^{-1}H^q(K)$. If $K$ is bounded, so is $\mathbf Lf^*K$,
and it remains to show that $f^{-1}N$ is constructible for every
constructible $\Lambda_Y$-module $N$.

First let $g:V\to W$ be a quasi-compact morphism of qcqs schemes, and let
$N$ be constructible on $W$ in the sense of Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves--2], with
stratification $W=\coprod_aW_a$. The inverse image of a quasi-compact open
under $g$ is quasi-compact, so the inverse images $V_a=g^{-1}(W_a)$ are
constructible. They are locally closed, and with the subscheme structures
$V\times_WW_a$ they form a finite stratification of $V$. Let
$\{U_{a,i}\to W_a\}$ be a pro-étale cover with
$N|_{U_{a,i}}\simeq\Lambda_{U_{a,i}}\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P_{a,i}$ as in
condition (1) of Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves--1]. The base changes
$\{U_{a,i}\times_{W_a}V_a\to V_a\}$ form a pro-étale cover. Inverse image
commutes with restriction and with colimits, hence with
$-\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P_{a,i}$ for the constant sheaf $P_{a,i}$, and it
carries $\Lambda_{U_{a,i}}$ to $\Lambda_{U_{a,i}\times_{W_a}V_a}$ by
clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--3]. So $(g^{-1}N)|_{V_a}$ satisfies condition (1) with the
same finitely presented modules $P_{a,i}$, and $g^{-1}N$ is constructible on
$V$. Applied to a quasi-compact open immersion, this shows that
constructibility on a qcqs scheme passes to quasi-compact opens. Conversely,
if a qcqs scheme $V$ is covered by quasi-compact opens $V_1,\dots,V_m$ on each
of which a module is constructible, then it is constructible on $V$:
intersect the strata on $V_b$ with the constructible locally closed subset
$V_b\setminus(V_1\cup\dots\cup V_{b-1})$; condition (1) persists on the
smaller strata by restricting the covers.

Now let $f:X\to Y$ be arbitrary and $N$ constructible on $Y$. Then $Y$ is
covered by affine opens on which $N$ is constructible: by definition if $Y$
is arbitrary, and by the previous paragraph if $Y$ is qcqs, since an affine
open of $Y$ is then a quasi-compact open. By the previous paragraph, $N$ is
also constructible on every affine open contained in one of them. Let $V\subset X$
be an affine open. Its image is quasi-compact, so $V$ is covered by finitely
many affine opens $V_b$, each mapping into an affine open $W_b\subset Y$ on
which $N$ is constructible. The morphisms $V_b\to W_b$ are morphisms of affine
schemes, hence quasi-compact, so $(f^{-1}N)|_{V_b}$ is constructible, and by
the gluing remark $(f^{-1}N)|_V$ is constructible. Thus $f^{-1}N$ is
constructible on every affine open of $X$. If $X$ is qcqs, the gluing remark
applied to a finite covering of $X$ by affine opens shows that $f^{-1}N$ is
constructible on $X$ in the sense of Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves--2] for qcqs
schemes. Hence $\mathbf Lf^*K\in\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$.

Here $i_*$ sends $\Lambda_Z$-modules to $\Lambda_X$-modules through
$\Lambda_X\to i_*i^{-1}\Lambda_X=i_*\Lambda_Z$, where $i^{-1}\Lambda_X=\Lambda_Z$
because both are pulled back from the point (clause [corollary-finite-quotients-their-transition-maps--3]). On the
pro-étale sites $i_*$ is exact and $i^{-1}i_*=\mathrm{id}$
[Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)]. Hence $\mathbf Ri_*$ is computed termwise,
$H^q(\mathbf Ri_*K)=i_*H^q(K)$, and $\mathbf Ri_*K$ is bounded when $K$ is. It
remains to show that $i_*N$ is constructible for a constructible
$\Lambda_Z$-module $N$.

Since the underlying space of $X$ is Noetherian, $X$ and its closed subscheme
$Z$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and every locally closed subset of
$X$ is constructible (Remark [remark-constructible-sheaves-coefficient-rings--1](1)). Choose a finite
stratification $Z=\coprod_aS_a$ for $N$ as in Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves--2]. The
$S_a$, regarded as locally closed subschemes of $X$ via $i$, together with the
open complement $U$ of $Z$, form a finite stratification of $X$ by
constructible locally closed subschemes. On $S_a$ the restriction of $i_*N$ is
the restriction of $i^{-1}i_*N=N$, which satisfies condition (1) of
Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves--1] by the choice of the stratification. On $U$ the
restriction vanishes: for an object $V$ of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ lying over $U$ one has
$V\times_XZ=\emptyset$, so $(i_*N)(V)=N(\emptyset)=0$. The zero module
satisfies condition (1) with $P=0$. Hence $i_*N$ is constructible, and
$\mathbf Ri_*K\in\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$.

Pullback is exact and commutes with cohomology. If the restrictions have
cohomology in $[a_U,b_U]$ and $[a_Z,b_Z]$, then $K$ has cohomology in
$[\min(a_U,a_Z),\max(b_U,b_Z)]$: outside this interval both restrictions
of each cohomology sheaf vanish, and open and closed restriction jointly
detect zero objects. For each degree, concatenate stratifications of the
two restrictions. The resulting stratification of $X$ shows that the
cohomology sheaf is constructible.

We first use Cartan's criterion to show that the kernel of $B$ is a
solvable ideal, hence zero; nondegeneracy then identifies the orthogonal
of the derived algebra with the center. By invariance of $B$, that is,
$B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$, the kernel $\mathfrak k$ of $B$
is an ideal. For $x\in[\mathfrak k,\mathfrak k]$ and $y\in\mathfrak k$,
the operators $\operatorname{ad}x$ and $\operatorname{ad}y$ map
$\mathfrak l$ into $\mathfrak k$, so the trace of
$\operatorname{ad}x\operatorname{ad}y$ may be computed on $\mathfrak k$.
Since $x\in\mathfrak k$, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak k}
(\operatorname{ad}(x)|_{\mathfrak k}
\operatorname{ad}(y)|_{\mathfrak k})=B(x,y)=0.
$$

By Cartan's criterion (Lemma [lemma-cartan-s-criterion]), the
image of $\mathfrak k$ in $\operatorname{End}(\mathfrak k)$ is
solvable. The kernel of $\mathfrak k\to\operatorname{End}(\mathfrak k)$
is the center of $\mathfrak k$, which is abelian. So $\mathfrak k$
is a solvable ideal of $\mathfrak l$. Since $\operatorname{rad}\mathfrak l=0$,
we get $\mathfrak k=0$, that is, $B$ is nondegenerate. Invariance and nondegeneracy then give

$$
[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak l]^\perp=Z(\mathfrak l).
$$

The center is a solvable ideal, hence zero, and a subspace with zero
orthogonal complement is all of $\mathfrak l$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-killing], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first treat constructible sheaves $M$ and $Q$, by the usual argument for
comparing a $\delta$-functor with an exact functor, and then pass to
complexes by truncation. We may compute with the small étale models of
$M$ and $Q$, since Theorems [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]
and [theorem-comparison-direct-images] identify the operations and the
adjunction maps defining $\kappa_{M,Q}$ on the two sites.

*Sheaves.* Let $M$ and $Q$ be constructible sheaves of $L$-modules.
By [Stacks, [09Z7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09Z7)](3), applied on $T$, there is a short exact sequence of constructible $L$-sheaves

$$
0\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow Q'\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
P=\bigoplus_a\pi_{a*}L_{T_a}^{\oplus n_a},
\quad \pi_a\text{ finite}.
$$

Indeed, every constructible sheaf on a qcqs scheme embeds into a finite sum
of finite direct images of constant sheaves with finite coefficients, and
over $L$ these coefficients are finite sums of $L$. For $r\geq0$ put

$$
F^r(Q)=p_Y^*R^rf_*M\otimes_Lp_T^*Q,
\qquad
G^r(Q)=R^rh_*(p_X^*M\otimes_Lp_T^*Q).
$$

Since tensoring over $L$ is exact, each $F^r$ is exact in $Q$, while the
$G^r$ form a long exact sequence. On cohomology sheaves the Künneth map
induces natural maps $a_Q^r:F^r(Q)\to G^r(Q)$, and $a_P^r$ is an isomorphism
for every $r$ by Lemma [lemma-kunneth-finite-direct-image]. It follows
that each $a_Q^r$ is injective. Indeed, in its naturality square for
$Q\hookrightarrow P$ the map $F^r(Q)\to F^r(P)$ is injective and $a_P^r$ is
an isomorphism. Surjectivity is proved by induction on $r$, simultaneously for all
constructible $Q$.
For $r=0$, the beginning of the long exact sequence of the $G^r$ identifies
$G^0(Q)$ with the kernel of $G^0(P)\to G^0(Q')$, and since $F^0$ is exact,
$F^0(Q)$ is the kernel of $F^0(P)\to F^0(Q')$. As $a_P^0$ is an
isomorphism and $a_{Q'}^0$ is injective, $a^0_Q$ maps the second kernel
onto the first. For $r>0$, the induction hypothesis for $Q'$ and the
surjection $F^{r-1}(P)\to F^{r-1}(Q')$ imply that
$G^{r-1}(P)\to G^{r-1}(Q')$ is surjective. By the long exact
sequence,

$$
G^r(Q)=\ker\bigl(G^r(P)\to G^r(Q')\bigr).
$$

Since $F^r(Q)=\ker(F^r(P)\to F^r(Q'))$ by exactness of $F^r$, the
isomorphism $a_P^r$ and the injectivity of $a_{Q'}^r$ identify this
kernel with $F^r(Q)$. This completes the induction, so
$\kappa_{M,Q}$ is an isomorphism for sheaves.

*Complexes.* The source and target of $\kappa_{M,Q}$ are exact
functors of $M$ and of $Q$, and $\kappa_{M,Q}$ is natural in both. Using the finitely many
truncation triangles of $M$ and of $Q$ and two-out-of-three, we can
therefore extend the case of sheaves to $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,L)$ and
$Q\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(T,L)$. This is possible because over the field $L$ the
truncations stay in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, since constructible cohomology sheaves have
Tor amplitude zero, and all operations are bounded on the schemes under
consideration.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-field-coefficients], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both sides are additive in $Q$, so we may assume $Q=\pi_*A_{T'}$. Set

$$
v=\operatorname{id}_Y\times\pi,\qquad
w=\operatorname{id}_X\times\pi,\qquad
h'=f\times\operatorname{id}_{T'}.
$$

Direct image along a finite morphism is exact and commutes with pullback, and by the
projection formula we have

$$
Rf_*M\boxtimes\pi_*A_{T'}
\simeq v_*p_{Y,T'}^*Rf_*M,
\qquad
M\boxtimes\pi_*A_{T'}\simeq w_*p_{X,T'}^*M.
$$

Since $hw=vh'$, the comparison between these two expressions is
$v_*$ of the base change map of
Lemma [lemma-base-change-along-product-projection] for $h'$, hence it
is an isomorphism.
Moreover, this comparison is $\kappa_{M,Q}$, because under the adjunction
$h^*\dashv Rh_*$ and the adjunctions for the finite maps, both correspond to
the counit $\varepsilon_f\otimes^{\mathbf L}1$ that defines $\kappa_{M,Q}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-finite-direct-image], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We show that the cone $N$ of $\kappa_{M,Q}$ vanishes modulo every maximal
ideal of $A$, and conclude by derived Nakayama on stalks. The source and
target of $\kappa_{M,Q}$ are in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y\times T,A)$ by Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], so every
geometric stalk of $N$ is a perfect $A$-complex. Now let
$\mathfrak m\subset A$ be a maximal ideal and put $k=A/\mathfrak m$. The
change-of-coefficients maps of
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients] for pullback, tensor product and
ordinary direct image respect the counit defining the
Künneth map. Hence they identify the reduction $\kappa_{M,Q}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_A k$
with $\kappa_{M\otimes^{\mathbf L}_Ak,\,Q\otimes^{\mathbf L}_Ak}$, which is
an isomorphism by
Lemma [lemma-kunneth-field-coefficients]. This means that
$N\otimes^{\mathbf L}_A k=0$ for every maximal ideal. Since the
Artinian ring $A$ is a product of local rings, derived Nakayama for the
perfect complex $N_{\bar z}$ at a geometric point $\bar z$ shows that
$N_{\bar z}=0$. Finally, since $N$ lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y\times T,A)$, it comes
from a complex on the small étale site by
Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves], where vanishing is
detected on geometric stalks, so $N=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-one-identity-factor], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Let $L$ be a lisse sheaf. For a geometric point $\bar x$ and a
geometric generic point $\bar\eta$ specializing to it, the
generization map $L_{\bar x}\to L_{\bar\eta}$ is injective. Indeed, for a
sheaf defined over a finite extension $E$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, this holds for the
finite locally constant reductions of the lattice in
Proposition [proposition-lattices-representations-normal-scheme], and we pass to
the inverse limit, invert the uniformizer and extend scalars. Now a
punctual subsheaf $G\subset L$ has $G_{\bar\eta}=0$, and since the
generization maps of $G$ and $L$ are compatible, $G_{\bar x}=0$.

Now let $F$ and $U$ be as in the statement. The sheaf $F_{\rm p}$ is
supported on the finite set $C\setminus U$, hence punctual. Conversely, a
punctual subsheaf $G$ of $F$ restricts to a punctual subsheaf of the
lisse sheaf $j^*F$, hence to zero. Since its map to $j_*j^*F$ is adjoint to
$j^*G\to j^*F$, this map vanishes, and $G\subset F_{\rm p}$. Finally,
$j_*j^*F$ has no nonzero punctual subsheaf. Indeed, if
$H\subset j_*j^*F$ is punctual, then $j^*H=0$, and the inclusion is zero
since $\Hom(H,j_*j^*F)=\Hom(j^*H,j^*F)=0$. As $F/F_{\rm p}$ embeds in
$j_*j^*F$, it has no nonzero punctual subsheaf either.

Let $Y\to X$ be the étale $X$-scheme representing lattices in $L$
(Lemma [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves]), with its universal lattice.

*Pushing down by the trace.* Choose finitely many quasi-compact
affine opens of this scheme whose images cover $X$, and let
$p:V\to X$ be their disjoint union. Then $p$ is quasi-compact, separated,
surjective and étale, and the universal lattice gives a lattice
$M_0\subset p^*L$. By [Stacks, [07RY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07RY), [07RZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07RZ)], $X$ has a finite
stratification by locally closed subschemes over each of which $p$ is
finite étale and surjective. On such a stratum $S$, let
$\operatorname{Tr}:p_*p^*L\to L$ be the trace of the finite étale map $p$
over $S$, and define $L_0\subset L|_S$
as the image of the composite

$$
p_*M_0\longrightarrow p_*p^*L\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}}L.
$$

To see that $L_0$ is a lattice, we split the finite étale cover
locally on $S$ into $d$ copies of $S$. Then $p_*M_0$ is a direct sum of
$d$ lattices $M_1,\dots,M_d$ in $L$, and the trace is their sum, so
$L_0=M_1+\cdots+M_d$. If we further trivialize $L$ pro-étale locally,
each $M_k$ becomes a locally constant function to the discrete set of lattices
in $E^r$, and after a common refinement each $M_k$ is the constant sheaf
attached to a lattice $N_k\subset E^r$. Then $L_0$ is the constant sheaf
attached to $N_1+\cdots+N_d$, which is a finite free $\mathcal O_E$-lattice
spanning $E^r$. Hence $L_0$ is lisse and $L_0[1/\ell]=L|_S$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Where $L$ is free of rank $r$, a lattice is the same as a lattice in $E^r$,
so the sheaf of lattices is locally the constant sheaf on the discrete set
$\GL_r(E)/\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)$. The representing scheme is obtained by
descending the corresponding disjoint unions of copies of the
trivializing objects.

The rank of $L$ is a locally constant function on $|X|$. Indeed, on a
trivializing covering the subsets of constant rank are open, closed
and saturated, and they descend by fpqc descent of open subsets. So
$X$ is the disjoint union of the open and closed subsets on which the rank
is constant. Since the sheaf of lattices restricts to the sheaf of lattices
on each of them, we may assume that $L$ has constant rank $r$.

We now construct the representing scheme.
On a pro-étale affine $V$ where $L$ is free of rank $r$, the
sheaf of lattices is the constant sheaf on the set

$$
\GL_r(E)/\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)
$$

of lattices in $E^r$, which is discrete because $\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)$
is an open subgroup of $\GL_r(E)$. To glue these constant sheaves, recall from
Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients] that on an affine object, sections
of $E_X$ are continuous functions to $E$, with bounded denominators by
quasi-compactness. A change of basis on $V\times_XV$ is therefore a
continuous function to $\GL_r(E)$. Since the stabilizer of a lattice
is open, the image of each fixed lattice under this function is locally
constant on $V\times_XV$. Now consider the disjoint union of
copies of $V\times_XV$ indexed by the lattices in $E^r$. On each component, the
preimages of the target components are then open and closed and form a disjoint open
cover, so the induced map from this disjoint union to itself is a
morphism of schemes. In this way the cocycle of the transition matrices defines a descent datum of
schemes for these disjoint unions of copies of $V$.

For affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$, the disjoint union of copies of $V$
indexed by a set $I$ is ind-quasi-affine, since its finite subunions are
affine open subschemes and together they cover it. Since descent along fpqc coverings is
effective for ind-quasi-affine morphisms [Stacks, [0APK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0APK)], the descent datum above is effective. Taking a finite
affine trivializing covering of each affine open of $X$ and gluing, we
therefore obtain a scheme representing the sheaf of lattices. This scheme is separated and
étale over $X$ by [Stacks, [02KU](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02KU), [02VN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02VN)], and it is surjective because
every free module has a lattice. By descent of sheaves of modules, this
scheme carries a universal lattice.

The rank of $L$ is a locally constant function on $|X|$. Indeed, on a
trivializing covering the subsets of constant rank are open, closed
and saturated, and they descend by fpqc descent of open subsets. So
$X$ is the disjoint union of the open and closed subsets on which the rank
is constant. The sheaf of lattices restricts to the sheaf of lattices
on each of them, and we may therefore assume that $L$ has constant rank $r$.

Consider the
sheaf on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ whose sections over $U$ are the lisse
$\mathcal O_{E,U}$-submodules $M\subset L|_U$ with $M[1/\ell]=L|_U$. We
show that it is represented by a separated surjective étale $X$-scheme.
On a pro-étale affine $V$ where $L$ is free of rank $r$, this
sheaf is the constant sheaf on the set

$$
\GL_r(E)/\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)
$$

of lattices in $E^r$. This set is discrete because $\GL_r(\mathcal O_E)$
is an open subgroup of $\GL_r(E)$. Recall from
Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients] that on an affine object, sections
of $E_X$ are continuous functions to $E$, with bounded denominators by
quasi-compactness. A change of basis on $V\times_XV$ is therefore a
continuous function to $\GL_r(E)$. Since the stabilizer of a lattice
is open, its action on each fixed lattice is locally
constant. Consider the disjoint union of
copies of $V\times_XV$ indexed by the lattices in $E^r$. On each component, the
preimages of the target components are open and closed and form a disjoint open
cover. Hence the induced map from this disjoint union to itself is a
morphism of schemes. In this way the cocycle of the transition matrices defines a descent datum of
schemes for these disjoint unions of copies of $V$.

For affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$, the disjoint union of copies of $V$
indexed by a set $I$ is ind-quasi-affine, since its finite subunions are
affine open subschemes and together they cover it. Descent along fpqc coverings is
effective for ind-quasi-affine morphisms [Stacks, [0APK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0APK)]. Taking a finite
affine trivializing covering of each affine open of $X$ and gluing, we
obtain a scheme representing the sheaf of lattices. It is separated and
étale over $X$ by [Stacks, [02KU](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02KU), [02VN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02VN)], and it is surjective because
every free module has a lattice. By descent of sheaves of modules, this
scheme carries a universal lattice.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves].

By Remark [remark-constructible-sheaves-coefficient-rings--1](3), an $E_X$-module that is locally free of finite
rank is lisse, so clause [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves--1] applies to $L$. Let $Y\to X$ be the
separated surjective étale $X$-scheme representing the sheaf of lattices
in $L$, and let $M_Y\subset L|_Y$ be its universal lattice. Cover $Y$ by
affine open subschemes $Y_i$, $i\in I$, and let $f_i:Y_i\to X$ be the
composite. Each $f_i$ is étale, and together they are surjective because
$Y\to X$ is, so $\{f_i\}$ is an étale covering. Since $Y_i$ is étale
over $X$, it is an object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ and $f_i^{-1}L=L|_{Y_i}$. Put
$M_i=M_Y|_{Y_i}$. Since the lattices form a sheaf, $M_i$ is a lattice in
$L|_{Y_i}$: by Definition [definition-lattice--1] it is a lisse
$\mathcal O_{E,Y_i}$-submodule with $M_i[1/\ell]=L|_{Y_i}$.

The module $M_i$ is locally free of finite rank. Indeed, $\ell$ acts
invertibly on $L|_{Y_i}$, so multiplication by $\ell$ is injective on the
submodule $M_i$. Thus $M_i$ is a torsion free lisse
$\mathcal O_{E,Y_i}$-module, and such a module is locally free of finite rank
by Remark [remark-constructible-sheaves-coefficient-rings--1](6). Finally, $E_{Y_i}=\mathcal O_{E,Y_i}[1/\ell]$ by
clause [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients--2], and localization is a filtered colimit, so
$M_i\otimes_{\mathcal O_{E,Y_i}}E_{Y_i}=M_i[1/\ell]$. Under this
identification the map induced by the inclusion $M_i\subset L|_{Y_i}$ is the
equality $M_i[1/\ell]=L|_{Y_i}$ in the definition of a lattice. This proves
the first assertion.

Now let the underlying space of $X$ be Noetherian, so that $X$ is
quasi-compact. Since étale morphisms are open, the images $f_i(Y_i)$ form
an open covering of $X$, and finitely many of them, say for $i\in I_0$,
already cover $X$. Put $U=\coprod_{i\in I_0}Y_i$, let $p$ be induced by the
$f_i$, and let $M$ be $M_i$ on $Y_i$. A finite disjoint union of affine
schemes is affine, so $U$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The map $p$
is étale and surjective, and $M$ is locally free of finite rank with
$M\otimes_{\mathcal O_{E,U}}E_U\simeq p^{-1}L$, componentwise by the first
part. The argument nowhere uses that the rank is constant, and it applies
verbatim when $L=0$ or $X$ is empty.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-lattices-lisse-e-sheaves].

This is Lie's theorem over the algebraically closed characteristic-zero field $\Omega$ fixed in this appendix, in the form [humphreys72, §4.1] quoted in the reference. The representation is finite dimensional and nonzero, and the Lie algebra is solvable, so that theorem supplies a one-dimensional invariant subspace $\Omega v$. Every $a$ acts on it by a scalar $\lambda(a)$, and linearity of the action makes $\lambda$ a linear functional. This gives $av=\lambda(a)v$ for all $a$.

By the hypothesis $c_1^{-1}(Z)\subset c_2^{-1}(Z)$, base change of
$Rc_{1!}$ along $i$, and the adjunction $i^*\dashv Ri_*$, we have

$$
i^*\Theta K_U=0,\qquad
R\operatorname{Hom}_X(\Theta K_U,K_Z)
\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_Z(i^*\Theta K_U,i^*K)=0.
$$

The second vanishing is that of the whole mapping complex, including
all shifts. Hence the composite $\Theta K_U\to\Theta K\xrightarrow{\widehat u}K$
factors through $K_U\to K$, with a contractible space of choices. The
coherent cofibre of this factorization is a morphism of two-step
filtered objects

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\Theta K_U&\longrightarrow&\Theta K&\longrightarrow&\Theta K_Z\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow \widehat u&&\downarrow\\
K_U&\longrightarrow&K&\longrightarrow&K_Z.
\end{array}
$$

Since this cofibre includes the homotopy, it is a morphism in the filtered derived
category, and its adjoint under the filtered adjunction
$Rc_{1!}\dashv c_1^!$ is the lift $\tilde u$. By base change, composition
and nilpotent invariance (which lets us use the reduced scheme $C_Z$),

$$
\Theta K_U\simeq j_!Rc_{1U!}c_{2U}^*j^*K,
\qquad i^*\Theta K\simeq Rc_{1Z!}c_{2Z}^*i^*K.
$$

Applying $i^*$ to the right-hand square and using $i^*\Theta K_U=0$, so
that $i^*\Theta K\simeq i^*\Theta K_Z$, we obtain the formula for
$\widehat u_Z$ restricted to $Z$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-lift-correspondence-invariant-decomposition], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The functor $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ is left $t$-exact because it is right
adjoint to the exact functor $i_*$. Restricting along the open
immersion $u$ is exact, so $u^*R\underline\Gamma_Z$ is left $t$-exact as
well.

For the limits, recall that the derived inverse limit of a
sequence $(K_n)$ is the fibre of the map
$\prod_nK_n\to\prod_nK_n$ given by the identity minus the transition
maps. It therefore suffices to show
that the functors preserve products and fibres. Restriction to an open
is exact and preserves limits, so this holds for $j^*$ and $u^*$. It
holds for $i^*$ by [Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA)], and for $Rj_*$ because $Rj_*$ is a right
adjoint. It follows for
$R\underline\Gamma_Z=i^*\fib(\mathrm{id}\to Rj_*j^*)$.
Finally, tensoring with a finite locally free sheaf $L$ is exact and is right
adjoint to tensoring with $L^\vee$, so it preserves products as well.

The functor $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ is right adjoint to the exact functor $i_*$. A derived right adjoint to an exact functor preserves $D^{\ge0}$, so it is left $t$-exact.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

Write $R\underline\Gamma_Z=i^*\fib(\mathrm{id}\to Rj_*j^*)$. Open restriction preserves products and is exact; $i^*$ preserves the required products by [Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA)]; $Rj_*$ is a right adjoint and preserves products. All are exact as derived functors. Thus this fibre construction preserves products and fibres, and hence preserves the cone construction of derived inverse limits.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

By clause [lemma-limits-sections-support--1], $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ preserves $D^{\ge0}$. The open restriction $u^*$ is exact, so their composite has the same property.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

Clause [lemma-limits-sections-support--2] gives the assertion before restriction. Open restriction $u^*$ is exact and preserves products; applying it to the product–fibre formula for derived inverse limits preserves that formula. The composite therefore commutes with these limits.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

Tensoring with a finite locally free sheaf is exact on sheaves. Its derived tensor functor is consequently $t$-exact, in particular left $t$-exact, and preserves the left $t$-exactness of the displayed composite.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

Tensoring with $L$ is exact and right adjoint to tensoring with $L^\vee$. It therefore preserves products and fibres, hence derived inverse limits. Combine this with clause [lemma-limits-sections-support--4] for the other factors of the displayed functor.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

We first compute $R\underline\Gamma_Z$. Represent $K$ by a K-injective
complex $J$ with injective terms, so that $Rj_*j^*K$ is represented by
$j_*j^*J$. The unit $J\to j_*j^*J$ is surjective in each degree: for an
injective $\mathcal R$-module $I$ and an object $V$, a section of
$j_*j^*I$ over $V$ is a map $j_!j^*\mathcal R_V\to I$, and it extends along
the monomorphism $j_!j^*\mathcal R_V\to\mathcal R_V$. Hence the kernel of
$J\to j_*j^*J$, taken termwise, represents the fibre of the unit, and
applying the exact functor $i^*$ gives
$R\underline\Gamma_ZK\simeq i^*\fib(K\to Rj_*j^*K)$.

Let $F=\fib(K\to Rj_*j^*K)$. Since $j^*i_*M=0$, we have
$\operatorname{Hom}(i_*M,Rj_*j^*K)=\operatorname{Hom}(j^*i_*M,j^*K)=0$
in all degrees, so maps $i_*M\to K$ are the same as maps $i_*M\to F$.
The restriction $j^*F$ vanishes, because $j^*$ of the unit is an
isomorphism, so the localization sequence gives $F\simeq i_*i^*F$, and
$\operatorname{Hom}(i_*M,i_*i^*F)=\operatorname{Hom}(M,i^*F)$ since
$i_*$ is fully faithful.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-cohomology-right-adjoint], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-cohomology-right-adjoint], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first show that a model of a stalk spreads out to a neighbourhood, and
then use connectedness to see that the model is the same everywhere.

Every stalk $L_{\bar t}$ has finite Tor amplitude and finite cohomology,
hence is perfect over the local ring $A$, that is, represented by a
bounded complex $M_{\bar t}$ of finite free $A$-modules. An isomorphism
$M_{\bar t}\simeq L_{\bar t}$ is then a section at $\bar t$ of the zeroth
cohomology sheaf of $R\cHom(\underline{M_{\bar t}},L)$; here the stalks of this
sheaf are computed stalkwise, since $\underline{M_{\bar t}}$ is a bounded
complex of finite free modules. We extend the section to an étale
neighbourhood of $\bar t$ and lift it there to a morphism
$\underline{M_{\bar t}}\to L$. Its cone has bounded locally constant finite
cohomology and zero stalk at $\bar t$. Hence its finitely many cohomology
sheaves vanish after shrinking the neighbourhood, and $L$ is isomorphic to
$\underline{M_{\bar t}}$ there. In particular, the stalks of $L$
at all geometric points over the image of this neighbourhood are
isomorphic to $M_{\bar t}$ in $D(A)$.

For each isomorphism class $c$ in $D(A)$, let $S_c\subset S$ be the set of
points at whose geometric points the stalk of $L$ lies in $c$. By the
previous paragraph and openness of étale morphisms, each $S_c$ is open.
Moreover, the sets $S_c$ are disjoint and cover $S$. Since $S$ is connected, $S=S_c$
for the class $c$ of $M$. Thus every point has an étale neighbourhood
on which $L\simeq\underline M$; compare [Stacks, [09BI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BI)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-constancy-finite-level], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The two stalks are cohomology sheaves of the complexes $i^*Rj_*F^\vee$
(in degree zero) and $i^*Rj_*F$ (in degree one) on the boundary. We
compute the Verdier dual of the second complex by duality on the curve,
and we find the first one, shifted and twisted.

Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow C$ be the inclusion of the whole finite
complement, and put $K_F=i^*Rj_*F$. For a lisse sheaf $G$ on $U$, the
adjunction $j^*\dashv Rj_*$ shows that $i^!Rj_*G=0$, and applying
$i^!$ to the localization triangle for $Rj_*G$ we obtain
$i^!j_!G\simeq i^*Rj_*G[-1]$. Since duality
exchanges $Rj_*$ with $j_!$ and $i^*$ with $i^!$, this formula lets us
write the result again in the form $i^*Rj_*$. Indeed, by Verdier duality on
the smooth curve, $\mathbb D_UF=F^\vee(1)[2]$ for the lisse sheaf $F$,
and we find

$$
\begin{split}
\mathbb D_Z K_F
&\simeq i^!\mathbb D_C Rj_*F
\simeq i^!j_!\mathbb D_UF\\
&\simeq i^*Rj_*(F^\vee(1)[2])[-1]
=K_{F^\vee}(1)[1].
\end{split}
$$

On the finite geometric scheme $Z$, Verdier duality is the exact
duality of coefficient vector spaces, so taking degree $-1$ at $\bar s$
we get $(R^1j_*F)_{\bar s}^\vee=(j_*F^\vee)_{\bar s}(1)$, which
is the pairing. It is Frobenius-equivariant because the adjunction,
localization and duality maps are natural in $F$ and respect its Weil
structure.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-duality-point-c-u], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We show that the local term and the displayed composite are both
adjoint to one map $R\gamma_*\gamma^!P\to R\delta_*\omega_X$. Once the class
$[\psi]$ and the map $\rho$ are built, the comparison is formal, and
computing on étale models changes nothing.

By external duality, $\gamma^!P$ is identified with
$\cHom((\Phi_X^m)^*K,K)$, so exceptional adjunction identifies $\psi$
with $[\psi]$. The map $\rho$ is constructed from the
two canonical arrows

$$
R\gamma_*\gamma^!P\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow R\delta_*\delta^*P.
$$

After restriction to $\Delta$, the source is supported on
$\Gamma\cap\Delta$. By Lemma [lemma-frobenius-fixed-scheme] the scheme
$\Gamma\cap\Delta$ is reduced, and on $T$ it is the single point
$(y,y)$. Hence the resulting map factors through
$R\Gamma_y(\Delta,\delta^*P)$. Equivalently, it is the ordinary pullback
of the object with supports, followed by the base change map to local
cohomology with support in the intersection.

The adjoint of $\mathrm{ev}_K:\delta^*P\to\omega_X$ is the map
$P\to R\delta_*\omega_X$ used to define the trace morphism in
Definition [definition-trace-morphism]. Hence the displayed composite, before
$\int_y$, is adjoint to the map

$$
R\gamma_*\gamma^!P\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow R\delta_*\omega_X.
$$

The local term is built from the same map. Indeed, by exceptional proper base change
for $\delta$, the adjoint of this map, which is supported on $y$, is the trace
map $\gamma^!P\to Ri_*\omega_y$ of Definition [definition-trace-class-local-terms]. The triangle
identities of the ordinary and exceptional adjunctions then show that the
two constructions give the same element of $A$.

The constructions above also make sense on the constructible étale
models, where restriction to the strict localization is the filtered
limit over étale neighbourhoods. The comparison theorems identify
inverse images, exceptional adjunctions, duality and the support maps
on the two sites, and hence they identify the class obtained on the
étale models with the pro-étale local term of
Definition [definition-trace-class-local-terms].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-term-restriction-map], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

On the point each step of the construction of the trace class is a
step of the categorical trace. Here $\omega_s=A_s$, so $\mathbb D_sP=P^\vee$, and $P_s=P\boxtimes
P^\vee=P\otimes^{\mathbf L}P^\vee$. First, under the first isomorphism of Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], the map $u$ becomes the element of
$P\otimes^{\mathbf L}P^\vee$ obtained by applying $u\otimes1$ to the
coevaluation. Next, the diagonal of $s$ is the identity, so the trace morphism is the evaluation $P\otimes^{\mathbf L}P^\vee\to A$, taken
after the symmetry that puts the factors in the order
$P^\vee\otimes P$. That symmetry is precisely the symmetry in
Definition [definition-categorical-trace], and integration over $s$ is the
identity of $A$. The composite is therefore the categorical trace.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For a single eigenvalue $\alpha$ the identity is
$-\log(1-\alpha T)=\sum_m\alpha^mT^m/m$, and the general case could be
reduced to this by triangularizing $v$ over an algebraic closure. Instead we use logarithmic derivatives, which allows us to stay over $L$.
In $L[[T]]$, the matrix $1-Tv$ is invertible, with inverse
$\sum_{r\geq0}T^rv^r$. Moreover, the logarithmic derivative of the determinant of an invertible matrix $M$ over $L[[T]]$ is
$\operatorname{Tr}(M^{-1}M')$, and hence

$$
\frac{d}{dT}\log\det(1-Tv)
=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(v(1-Tv)^{-1}\bigr)
=-\sum_{m\geq1}\operatorname{Tr}(v^m)T^{m-1}.
$$

Since both logarithms have constant coefficient zero and $L$ has
characteristic zero, we may integrate and exponentiate, and we obtain
(12.5). For a perfect complex, the categorical trace
over a field is the alternating sum of the traces on the finitely many
nonzero cohomology spaces (Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]), and the
assertion follows by multiplying the identities for the $H^i(P)$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-logarithm-determinant], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-logarithm-determinant], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We blow up an ideal that cuts out the complement of $U$. Its pullback
is then locally generated by a nonzerodivisor $a$, and an open whose
complement is cut out by a nonzerodivisor is schematically dense,
because a section killed by a power of $a$ is zero.

Choose a quasi-coherent ideal $\mathcal I$ of finite type with
$V(\mathcal I)=T\setminus U$. Such an ideal exists because $U$ is a
quasi-compact open in a qcqs scheme [Stacks, [01PH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01PH)]. We blow up this
ideal, and the extended ideal defines the exceptional Cartier divisor.
On the affine charts its local equation $a$ is a nonzerodivisor. Hence
each chart ring injects into its localization at $a$. The complement of
the divisor is the inverse image of $U$, and it is therefore
schematically dense.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-making-open-schematically-dense], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Since $g^*G$ is mixed, so is $g_*g^*G$ by
Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images]. The unit
$G\to g_*g^*G$ has the Weil-equivariant retraction

the diagonal and the trace is the sum over the copies. These local
maps glue because the sum is invariant under permutations of the
copies. So $G$ is a Weil subsheaf of $g_*g^*G$. A Weil subobject of a
mixed sheaf is mixed
(Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations]), and
therefore $G$ is mixed.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-mixedness-descends-constant-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Every assertion holds because the base change map is
assembled from units, counits and composition isomorphisms for inverse
images, and each of the operations in the lemma respects these ingredients. Naturality in $K$ is immediate, since the counit
$\varepsilon_f$ is a natural transformation.

By definition, the base change map is the adjoint transpose of a counit preceded
by the composition isomorphism for inverse images. Since the counit for a
composite adjunction is the composite of the two counits, taking
adjoint transposes proves pasting, in either order of composing the
two directions of a rectangle. Similarly, the assertion about identity squares
follows from the triangle identities, as in Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].
Finally, the comparisons of sites of Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images]
identify the composition maps for inverse images and the units and counits
(Lemma [lemma-comparison-direct-images-compatibilities]),
and hence also the base change maps constructed from them.

The geometric identifications follow from the coordinate description of
the deformation space. Every comparison of dualizing complexes is then
the identity at $t=1$, and so the uniqueness in Lemma [lemma-section-normal-bundle]
identifies it with the comparison of that lemma.

*The geometry.* Since $g$ is smooth and $s$ is a section,
$N_s\simeq s^*T_{V/S}$. Since formation of relative differentials for a
smooth map commutes with arbitrary base change, and an étale map
induces an isomorphism on relative tangent bundles, this proves both
assertions about normal bundles.

For deformation spaces, we use the cartesian étale coordinate chart
$U\to\mathbf A^d_S$ of the proof of Lemma [lemma-section-normal-bundle]. There the
deformation is

$$
\mathcal D_{s(S)}U
\simeq U\times_{\mathbf A^d_S}\mathbf A^d_{\mathbf A^1_S},
\qquad x_i=t u_i,
$$

because this is the chart of the blowup along $(t,x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ on
which the pullback of the ideal is generated by $t$, and this description
commutes with every change of base. Away from the centre, the
deformation is $(V\setminus s(S))\times\mathbf G_m$, which also
commutes with base change. After passing to an étale cover of $S$ if
necessary, these opens cover the deformation space, and their identifications
glue to the canonical one. For an étale map of pairs as in (2), we
obtain the étale map of deformation spaces by flat base change for the
blowup and for the removal of the strict transform, and the coordinate
description identifies its special fibre with the map of normal
bundles.

*The comparison of dualizing complexes.* In both parts the strategy
is the same: transport the comparison over $\mathbf A^1_S$ along the
geometric identification, check that the result is still the identity at
$t=1$, and invoke uniqueness. Write

$$
\chi_{g,s}:\widetilde s^*\omega_{\widetilde g}\xrightarrow{\sim}a^*s^*\omega_g
$$

for the isomorphism of Lemma [lemma-section-normal-bundle] that is the identity at
$t=1$, so that $\alpha_{g,s}$ is the inverse of its restriction to
$t=0$. For (1), we apply Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism](3) to $g$,
$\pi$ and $\widetilde g$. These exceptional base change isomorphisms
commute with restriction to $t=1$ and $t=0$, because they are
adjoint transposes of base change for compactly supported direct image
applied to the same counit, and this base change respects composition of
cartesian squares. Transported through these isomorphisms, the pullback of
$\chi_{g,s}$ is therefore a comparison for $(g',s')$ that is the identity at $t=1$,
and by uniqueness it equals $\chi_{g',s'}$. Restricting to $t=0$ and inverting
proves (1).

For (2), composing $Re_!\dashv e^*$ with $Rg_!\dashv g^!$ gives
$e^*\omega_g\simeq\omega_{g'}$, and likewise for the induced étale
map of deformation spaces. On the fibres $t=1$ and $t=0$ these
identifications are the ones for the original pairs and for the normal
bundles, since the counit of a composite adjunction is the composite of
the counits. They transport $\chi_{g,s}$ to a comparison that is the
identity at $t=1$, which is $\chi_{g',s'}$ by uniqueness.

For the coherence assertions we use the same uniqueness once more.
The geometric identifications respect composition, and so do the
identifications obtained from adjunctions, as we see by transposing
composite counits. Therefore each composite in the coherence assertions is
a comparison that is the identity at $t=1$, and by uniqueness any two of
them agree.

The compatibilities (1) and (2) are formal. For the isomorphism we show
that the cone $C_Y(L)$ of $\sigma_Y(L)$ vanishes. To do this we use that, like nearby
cycles, the cone commutes with smooth pullback and proper direct image.
Smooth pullback lets us check vanishing locally, and it also shows that
the cone vanishes generically, by
reduction to constant coefficients and the calculation $R\Psi_S(M_\eta)=M$.
Proper direct image along a compactified linear projection then shows
that the remaining support is empty, by induction on the dimension of
an affine space containing $Y$.

By the comparison for constructible complexes, we may work on the small
étale site. There $\sigma$ is $\bar i^*$ of the unit of
$\bar j^*\dashv R\bar j_*$ and the base change maps are $\bar i^*$ of
mates, so (1), (2) and naturality follow from the triangle identities.

We take cofibres in the stable $\infty$-category underlying the derived
category, where they are functorial, unlike cones in a triangulated
category, and set
$C_Y(L)=\operatorname{cofib}(\sigma_Y(L))$.  This is an exact functor
with bounded constructible values.  By (1) and (2), the base change maps yield

$$
C_Y(Rf_*L')\simeq Rf_*C_{Y'}(L')\quad(f\text{ proper}),\qquad
C_{Y'}(f^*L)\simeq f^*C_Y(L)\quad(f\text{ smooth}).
$$

By the base change isomorphism for étale maps, the question is local on $Y$.  For
a closed immersion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^n$, the base change isomorphism for
proper maps identifies the direct image of $C_Y(L)$ with
$C_{\mathbf A^n}$ of the direct image of $L$, and since direct image along a
closed immersion is conservative, it suffices to treat affine
spaces.

For $Y=\mathbf A^n$, the complex $C_Y(L)$ vanishes on a dense open
subset.  Indeed, by the truncation triangles we may assume that $L$ is
a sheaf. After shrinking, it is locally constant, and after pulling
back to a finite étale cover, it is constant. The pullback does no
harm: $C$ commutes with étale pullback, so vanishing can be checked
after a surjective étale pullback.  For a constant sheaf $M$ on a smooth
$k$-scheme, the base change isomorphism for its smooth structure map identifies $C$
with the pullback of $C_{\operatorname{Spec}k}(M)$, which is zero
because $R\Psi_S(M_\eta)=M$.

We argue by induction on $n$, the case of a point being the calculation
above.  By the preceding paragraph, the closure $T$ of the support of
$C_{\mathbf A^n}(L)$ is a proper closed subset.  By the linear form of Noether
normalization there is a linear projection $q:\mathbf A^n\to\mathbf A^{n-1}$
that is finite on $T$: we choose its kernel line so that it avoids the
intersection of the projective closure of $T$ with the hyperplane at
infinity.  Compactifying that line, we get

$$
\bar q:\bar Y=\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf A^{n-1}
\longrightarrow\mathbf A^{n-1},
\qquad v:\mathbf A^n\hookrightarrow\bar Y,
\qquad \bar L=v_!L.
$$

We compactified the line so that the support becomes finite over
$\mathbf A^{n-1}$ and can be detected by direct image there.
As $C$ commutes with restriction to the open subscheme $\mathbf A^n$
of $\bar Y$, the complex $C_{\bar Y}(\bar L)$ is supported on
$T\cup(\bar Y\setminus\mathbf A^n)$.  This union is closed in
$\bar Y$ and finite over $\mathbf A^{n-1}$. Indeed, $T$ is finite, hence
proper, over $\mathbf A^{n-1}$, and therefore closed in $\bar Y$; the
boundary $\bar Y\setminus\mathbf A^n$ is a section.  By the base change isomorphism
for proper maps and the induction hypothesis,

$$
R\bar q_*C_{\bar Y}(\bar L)
\simeq C_{\mathbf A^{n-1}}(R\bar q_*\bar L)=0.
$$

Direct image is conservative on complexes supported on a closed
subscheme finite over the base, since on a geometric stalk the direct
image of each cohomology sheaf is the finite product of its stalks on
the finite fibre.  Therefore $C_{\bar Y}(\bar L)=0$, and restricting to
$\mathbf A^n$ gives $C_{\mathbf A^n}(L)=0$.

For the first equality, we precompose with $\Pi_{K,\mathbb DK}$ and take
tensor–Hom adjoints. Both maps then have source

$$
(p_{1s}^*K'\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_{2s}^*\Psi_X\mathbb DK)\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_{2s}^*K'
$$

and target $p_{1s}^!K'$. The adjoint defining $\lambda_K$ is

$$
(p_1^*K\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_2^*\mathbb DK)\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_2^*K
\xrightarrow{1\otimes\widetilde{\operatorname{ev}}_K}
p_1^*K\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_2^*\omega_X
\xrightarrow{\sim}p_2^*\omega_X\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_1^*K
\xrightarrow{\kappa_K}p_1^!K,
$$

where $\widetilde{\operatorname{ev}}_K$ is
$\mathbb DK\otimes^{\mathbf L} K\xrightarrow{\sim}K\otimes^{\mathbf L} \mathbb DK
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_K}\omega_X$. In both displays the arrows
marked $\sim$ are the symmetry isomorphisms of the tensor product, and
all Koszul signs come from these symmetries. Since $\alpha$ is
monoidal, we can move the ordinary comparison maps past $\mu$. By
(E.10) we know what $\beta_{p_1}$ does
to the last arrow $\kappa_K$. What remains on the factors $K'$ and
$\Psi_X\mathbb DK$ is the composite
$\theta_X\Psi_X(\operatorname{ev}_K)\mu_X$. This is the pairing
(E.12), that is, evaluation
against $\delta_K$. The result is the adjoint of
$\lambda_{K'}(1\boxtimes\delta_K)$. Since $\Pi$ is invertible, the
first equality follows.

For the second equality, we again precompose with $\Pi_{K,\mathbb DK}$
and take adjoints for $\Delta_s^*\dashv R\Delta_{s*}$. Since $\alpha$
is monoidal and compatible with composition, the map
$\alpha_\Delta\Delta_s^*\Pi_{K,\mathbb DK}$ is
$\mu_X:K'\otimes^{\mathbf L} \Psi_X\mathbb DK\to \Psi_X(K\otimes^{\mathbf L} \mathbb DK)$. Hence both
adjoints are the pairing (E.12) defining $\delta_K$.
Since $\Delta$ is proper, the comparison map for direct image is
$\chi_\Delta$.

Under Verdier duality for the proper map $f_\eta$, evaluation on
$Rf_{\eta*}M$ is the composite of the lax monoidal map of $Rf_{\eta*}$,
the map $Rf_{\eta*}\operatorname{ev}_M$, and the
trace $Rf_{\eta*}\omega_{X_\eta}\to\omega_{Y_\eta}$. Hence,
after taking tensor–Hom adjoints, both sides of
(E.13) are the pairing

$$
\begin{split}
Rf_{s*}\Psi_XM\otimes Rf_{s*}\Psi_X\mathbb D M
&\xrightarrow{\chi_f^{-1}\otimes\chi_f^{-1}}
\Psi_YRf_{\eta*}M\otimes \Psi_YRf_{\eta*}\mathbb DM\xrightarrow{\mu_Y}
\Psi_Y(Rf_{\eta*}M\otimes Rf_{\eta*}\mathbb DM)\\
&\longrightarrow \Psi_YRf_{\eta*}(M\otimes \mathbb DM)
\longrightarrow \Psi_YRf_{\eta*}\omega_{X_\eta}
\longrightarrow \Psi_Y\omega_{Y_\eta}
\xrightarrow{\theta_Y}\omega_{Y_s}.
\end{split}
$$

To identify the pairing obtained from $Rf_{s*}\delta_{X,M}$ with this
one, we move the lax monoidal maps past the base change maps for proper
morphisms, and we use the identity
$\theta_X=f_s^!\theta_Y\circ\beta_f(\omega_{Y_\eta})$ of
(E.9).
The lax monoidal maps are compatible with the base change maps because,
after taking ordinary adjoints, both become the tensor
product of the two counits for the open immersions of the generic
fibres. This proves (E.13).

For an open immersion $j$, the map $\alpha_j$ is an isomorphism,
$j^!=j^*$ and $\beta_j=\alpha_j^{-1}$. The argument above therefore
applies with $\alpha_j$ in place of $\chi_f^{-1}$.

For (E.14) we apply
(E.13) to the structure morphism $a$
of $X$. On the trait, $\Psi_S$ takes the stalk at the geometric generic
point, and the pairing (E.12) is
ordinary evaluation. So $\delta_{S,Ra_{\eta*}M}$ is the identity of
$R\operatorname{Hom}_A(R\Gamma(X_{\bar\eta},M),A)$. Global Verdier
duality on both fibres now gives
(E.14).

For the last arrow $\theta_X$, we claim
that under (E.2) and
(E.16), the map $g_s^*\theta_X$
corresponds to $(\theta_{X'})^P\otimes A(1)[2]$. We check
this on a smooth ambient space, where $\theta$ is the identity by smooth
purity, and descend along the closed immersion
$i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1_S}$ of the statement, which we abbreviate
to $i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^r$. First, on $\mathbf A^r$ and on its slice, smooth
purity and the base change isomorphism of nearby cycles for smooth
pullback identify $\theta$ with the identity of the dualizing complex of
a smooth scheme, and these identifications differ by $A(1)[2]$. To descend to $X$, we use
the identity (E.9) for $i$, which gives
$\theta_X=i_s^!\theta_{\mathbf A^r}\circ\beta_i(\omega_{\mathbf A^r_\eta})$.
By (E.6), $\theta_X$ is then the adjoint,
for $Ri_{s*}\dashv i_s^!$, of $\nu_i$, followed by $\Psi$ of the
exceptional counit $Ri_{\eta*}i_\eta^!\to1$ and by
$\theta_{\mathbf A^r}$. Now the base change map $\nu_i$ for the proper map
$i$ and the factorization used for slicing commute with this counit,
because their ordinary adjoints are the same composite of the counit
for the open immersion of the generic fibre and the counit for $i$.
Since generic restriction is compatible with $i^!$ and with evaluation,
the claim for $\mathbf A^r$ gives it for $X$ before taking invariants.

It remains to pass to $P$-invariants. For a finite quotient $G$ of $P$,
the additive functor $i_{s'}^!$ commutes with the action of $G$, and so
it preserves the image of the averaging idempotent. Thus $i_{s'}^!$
commutes with $(-)^P$, and the same descent works after taking
$P$-invariants. Since the shift $[2]$ is even, no additional Koszul
sign appears.

We read everything off from the graded algebras. The first leg sends
$I$ onto generators of $I_1$, so it identifies the ideals of the zero
sections. The second leg, on the other hand, sends $I$ into $I_2$, and by the hypothesis
$I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$ the images of degree-one classes are
nilpotent in $\operatorname{gr}_{I_1}\mathcal O_C$.

The algebra of the normal cone is
$\operatorname{gr}_I\mathcal O_X=\bigoplus_{r\geq0}I^r/I^{r+1}$,
and the algebra of the deformation is the subalgebra of
$\mathcal O_{X_T}[t^{-1}]$ generated by
$\mathcal O_{X_T}$ and the fractions $a/t$, $a\in I$. Since
$c_i^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_C\subset I_1$ for both legs (for $i=2$ this is the
hypothesis $I_2\subset I_1$), the maps on generic fibres preserve these
subalgebras. This gives the lifts.

The zero section of $N_ZX$ is defined by the ideal of elements of
positive degree of $\operatorname{gr}_I\mathcal O_X$. Since $I_1$ is the
ideal generated by $c_1^{-1}(I)$, the images of elements of degree one
under the first leg generate $I_1/I_1^2$ as an $\mathcal O_{Z'}$-module, and
hence they generate the ideal of elements of positive degree of
$\operatorname{gr}_{I_1}\mathcal O_C$. Therefore the quotient by the
pullback of the ideal of the zero section is
$\mathcal O_C/I_1=\mathcal O_{Z'}$, which proves (1).

Under the second leg, a product of $n$ images of elements of degree
one is the class of an element of $I_2^n$ in $I_1^n/I_1^{n+1}$, and this
class is zero since $I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$. The pullback of the
ideal of the zero section is therefore nilpotent. Its vanishing set is
all of $N_{Z'}C$, which means that $(N_{Z'}C)_{\mathrm{red}}\to N_ZX$
factors through the zero section. This proves (2).

The map is computed on stalks by the formula for stalks of finite direct
images, and the cokernel has finite support because $\pi$ is an
isomorphism away from finitely many points. Compatibility with field
extension holds because normalization commutes with algebraically
closed extension.

Normalization is finite for reduced schemes of finite type over a
field.  On each one-dimensional component, its normal model is regular,
hence smooth over the perfect field, while the isolated components of
dimension zero are reduced points, that is, copies of the spectrum of the
ground field.  Since the normalization is an
isomorphism over a dense open of each component, the locus
where it is not an isomorphism is finite.

By the calculation of stalks in Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms], the
displayed map at a geometric point is the diagonal $M\to M^b$, with
$b\geq1$, so its kernel is zero and its cokernel has the asserted
form.  Where $\pi$ is an isomorphism we have $b=1$ and the cokernel
vanishes; hence the cokernel is supported on the finite locus found above.

After algebraically closed extension, the normalization remains smooth
and is a finite birational normal model of the reduced base change,
so it is the normalization of the base change.  Base change for
finite morphisms identifies the fibres and their sets of branches, and
therefore the diagonal maps and their cokernels are obtained by
extension of scalars.
