Every section $t$ on an étale $X$-scheme $V$ acquires a root of
$y^p-y-t$ on the base change to $V$ of
$\operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)[y]/(y^p-y-t))$.
This cover is étale because the derivative is $-1$, and surjective
because the algebra is faithfully flat, being free of positive rank
$p$. Hence $\varphi-1$ is locally surjective and therefore an
epimorphism of sheaves. Together with its kernel inclusion, this
gives the short exact sequence.

The constants in $\mathbf F_p$ lie in $K$. Distinct constants cannot
agree on a nonempty étale scheme, since their difference is a unit.
Conversely, if $x^p-x=0$, put
$y_r=\prod_{s\in\mathbf F_p,\,s\ne r}(x-s)$. On $D(y_r)$ we have
$x=r$, and these basic opens cover: Lagrange interpolation expresses
$1$ as a linear combination of the $y_r$. Thus the map from the
constant presheaf is locally injective and locally surjective onto
$K$. After sheafification it is an isomorphism.

Every étale covering of an affine étale $X$-scheme $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$
admits a finite affine refinement $V_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$, whose
Čech nerve consists of affine schemes. The map
$A\to\prod_iB_i$ is faithfully flat. The Čech complex of
$\mathbf G_a$ is identified with the corresponding complex of tensor
products of the $B_i$ over $A$; after this faithfully flat base change
the cover has sections and the complex is contractible in positive
degrees. Faithfully flat descent therefore gives exactness of the
original Čech complex.

Cartan's criterion, that exactness of the Čech complexes for such
covering families implies the vanishing of higher sheaf cohomology,
now applies to the final object $X$ of $X_{\acute{e}t}$.

attached to open and closed immersions on the pro-étale site are
exact when the complementary open is quasi-compact. Since
$\overline X$ is Noetherian, the complement of $Z$ is quasi-compact,
so all functors below are exact and may be applied degreewise
to unbounded complexes.
The inverse image of $j_!K$ on $Z$ is $j_{Z,!}K$, so we have the
natural map $j_!K\to i_*i^*j_!K=i_*j_{Z,!}K$. It is the identity on the
open $X$, and both sides restrict to zero on the closed complement of
$X$. By the localization sequence for an open and its closed
complement, this map is therefore an isomorphism. The second identification then follows by
applying $Rp_*$ and using $Rp_*Ri_*\simeq R(p\circ i)_*$.

Once $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ is identified with

By the comparisons of Section [sec-Continuous-cohomology], taking global
sections identifies $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ with the full subcategory of
$D(\Lambda)$ of complexes with bounded finitely generated cohomology and
finite Tor dimension, and we show that these complexes are perfect
separately for the three kinds of coefficients.
A constructible complex with finite coefficients has
bounded finite cohomology and finite Tor amplitude, so it is perfect:
take a bounded-above resolution by finite free modules and
truncate it below the Tor bound. Then the last syzygy that remains is finitely
presented and flat, hence projective, so the truncated resolution is a
bounded complex of finite projective modules. With integral coefficients, by contrast, the
constructible complexes on the point are those with bounded finitely
generated $\mathcal O_E$-cohomology, and since a discrete valuation ring has
global dimension one, these complexes are perfect. Finally, with field
coefficients, bounded complexes with finite-dimensional cohomology are perfect.

By Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], the two
direct images of $a_X$ lie in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ and are
therefore perfect. If we represent such a
complex by a bounded complex of finite projective modules, its termwise
dual is again of this form, and the double evaluation map is termwise
an isomorphism. The stalk $K_{\bar x}$ is the complex of global sections of
$\bar x^*K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ (Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf]), so it
is perfect as well.

The comparisons of Section [sec-Continuous-cohomology] identify the category on the geometric point with the complexes of $A$-modules having bounded finite cohomology and finite Tor amplitude. Resolve such a complex by a bounded-above complex of finite free modules and truncate below its Tor bound. The last syzygy is finitely presented and flat, hence projective. This gives a bounded finite-projective representative. Conversely, every bounded finite-projective complex has the required constructibility and Tor bounds.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point].

On the geometric point, the comparison of Section [sec-Continuous-cohomology] identifies integral constructible complexes with complexes of $\mathcal O_E$-modules having bounded finitely generated cohomology. A DVR has global dimension one, so each such cohomology module has a finite free resolution of length at most one. The truncation triangles build the complex from finitely many of these resolutions, hence make it perfect. Conversely, a perfect complex has bounded finitely generated cohomology and finite Tor amplitude.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point].

Over either field $E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, a complex with bounded finite-dimensional cohomology is quasi-isomorphic to the finite direct sum of those cohomology spaces placed in their degrees. Each space is finite free, so the complex is perfect. Conversely, a bounded complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces has exactly those finiteness properties. Represent $P$ by a bounded complex of finite projective $\Lambda$-modules. Its derived dual is computed by the ordinary termwise dual, whose terms are again finite projective and which is bounded. Hence $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(P,\Lambda)$ is perfect.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point].

Use a bounded finite-projective representative of $P$. For each finite projective module, evaluation into the double dual is an isomorphism. With the standard dual-complex signs these evaluation maps form the double-dual chain map. It is termwise an isomorphism and thus an isomorphism in the derived category, equal to the specified evaluation map.

We use that a minimal complex over the local ring
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ is determined up to isomorphism of complexes, not
only up to homotopy, so that the transition maps can be made into
equalities of matrices and passed to the limit.

Represent each $M_n$ by a minimal finite free complex, obtained by
cancelling unit entries in the differential matrices. Its reduction
modulo $\pi_E$ has zero differential, so its rank in degree $q$ is
$\dim_{\mathbf F_E}H^q(M_1)$, which is independent of $n$ and nonzero only in
finitely many degrees. The given isomorphism
$M_{n+1}/\pi_E^n\simeq M_n$ between minimal complexes is represented
by a chain homotopy equivalence $f$, with homotopy inverse $g$. Since both
complexes have zero differential modulo $\pi_E$, the relations
$gf-1=dh+hd$ and $fg-1=dh'+h'd$ show that $f$ is an isomorphism modulo
$\pi_E$ in each degree. By Nakayama's lemma its matrices are then invertible over
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$. Lifting them to invertible matrices over
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n+1}$ and changing bases, we may assume that the
differential at level $n+1$ reduces exactly to the differential at
level $n$, with the given transition in the derived category.
Induction on $n$ gives compatible matrices, and their limits define
$P^\bullet$. Its differential squares to zero because it does so
modulo every $\pi_E^n$, and the identifications with the $M_n$ are
compatible by construction.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-over-oe], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The truncation triangle of $K$ splits $\mathcal H^0K$ into its largest
punctual subsheaf, which goes into ${}^pD^{\le0}$, and the quotient,
which goes into ${}^pD^{\ge1}$, using
Lemma [lemma-largest-punctual-subsheaf].

The shift axioms are immediate from the definitions. For orthogonality, if
$A\in{}^pD^{\le0}$ and $B\in{}^pD^{\ge1}$, then ordinary truncation
identifies $\Hom(A,B)$ with
$\Hom(\mathcal H^0A,\mathcal H^0B)$, which is zero because the source
is punctual and the target has no punctual subsheaf.
To construct the truncation triangle for $K$, put $K'=\tau^{\le0}K$
and $F=\mathcal H^0K$, and let $A$ be the fibre of
$K'\to F/F_{\rm p}$. Then the cohomology of $A$ is that of $K$ below zero,
and $\mathcal H^0A=F_{\rm p}$, so that $A\in{}^pD^{\le0}$.
By the octahedral axiom, applied to $A\to K'\to K$, we obtain a
triangle $A\to K\to B\to$, in which the cone $B$ is an extension of
$\tau^{\ge1}K$ by $F/F_{\rm p}$ in degree zero, so it
has no negative ordinary cohomology and
$\mathcal H^0B=F/F_{\rm p}$. Since $F/F_{\rm p}$ has no punctual
subsheaf by Lemma [lemma-largest-punctual-subsheaf],
$B\in{}^pD^{\ge1}$. Finally, the t-structure is bounded because the ordinary
one is.

The heart of any t-structure is abelian, with kernels
and cokernels computed from the perverse cohomology of a cone
[bbd82, Théorème 1.3.6]; the proof uses only the octahedral axiom and
orthogonality. Punctual sheaves in degree zero clearly lie in the
heart. So does $(j_*M)[1]$, since $j_*M$ has no punctual subsheaf, as
follows from Lemma [lemma-largest-punctual-subsheaf] applied
to $F=j_*M$, for which $F_{\rm p}=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-perverse-sheaves-curve], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Frobenius pullback is an exact equivalence for the ordinary
t-structure, and it preserves punctual support and the absence of
punctual subsheaves. It is therefore t-exact for the perverse
t-structure, which means that it carries the kernel and cokernel of a
compatible morphism of perverse sheaves to the kernel and cokernel of the
pulled-back morphism. The Weil isomorphisms and their inverses
therefore induce inverse isomorphisms on the kernel and cokernel, and by
naturality the coimage–image map is compatible with them. So
perverse Weil sheaves form an abelian category, with kernels and
cokernels computed in perverse sheaves on $C$, and this is the assertion
about the forgetful functor.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-perverse-weil-sheaves], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We map $U_0$ finitely and flatly onto the affine line, whose
number of $k_n$-points is $q^n$, and bound the size of the fibres.

By Noether normalization [Stacks, [00OY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00OY)] there is a finite map
$U_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$, and the coordinate ring of $U_0$ is a finite
torsion-free module over $k_0[t]$. To see this, let $f\ne0$ in
$k_0[t]$ and $fa=0$. On each irreducible component of $U_0$ the image
of $f$ is nonzero, since otherwise the component would be finite over
$k_0[t]/(f)$ and hence of dimension zero. Since the coordinate ring of
each component is a domain, $fa=0$ forces $a$ to vanish on every
component, and then $a=0$ because $U_0$ is reduced.  As $k_0[t]$ is a
principal ideal domain, it follows that the
coordinate ring of $U_0$ is free of some rank $D$.  Hence, after any
extension of the base field, every fibre has a coordinate ring of
dimension $D$, and by the Chinese remainder theorem it has at most $D$ rational
points.  Summing over $\mathbf A^1(k_n)$, we obtain the
first bound.  The second holds because the number of rational points
of a finite scheme is at most its number of geometric points.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-point-count-bound], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We compare coefficients and then apply Cauchy's estimate. To compare, write
$f_j=\sum_na_{j,n}t^n$ and $L=\sum_nA_nt^n$. Since the product is
coefficientwise locally finite, $A_n$ is already the coefficient of $t^n$ in a
finite subproduct containing $f_j$, which is $f_j$ times
a series $g$ with constant coefficient one and nonnegative coefficients.
The coefficient of $t^n$ in $f_jg$ is $a_{j,n}$ plus a sum of products of
nonnegative numbers, so that $0\le a_{j,n}\le A_n$; positivity enters
only here.  Next, for every $0<r<R$, Cauchy's estimate gives
$|A_n|\le C_rr^{-n}$. Hence the radius of convergence of $f_j$ is at least
$r$ for every such $r$, and so at least $R$.  A zero of $P_j$ in the disc
would be a pole of $f_j=1/P_j$, which is impossible.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We write an inverse characteristic polynomial as the exponential of a
series in the traces of powers, whose coefficients are then visibly
nonnegative. For a square matrix $A$, triangularizing $A$ and expanding
the logarithm of each factor we get the formal identity

$$
\det(1-tA)^{-1}
=\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Tr}(A^n)\frac{t^n}{n}\right).
$$

On an even tensor power, the trace of the $n$th power of Frobenius is
$\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x^n\mid\mathcal G)^{2m}$. Since
$\mathcal G$ is real, this is nonnegative after applying $\iota$.  Every
coefficient of the exponential is then a finite sum of products of nonnegative
numbers. This remains true after replacing $t$ by $t^{\deg(x)}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-positivity-euler-factors], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

All three assertions are statements about ideals, because products of ideals
dominate blow-ups, composites are computed by products of ideals, and
extension from an open amounts to extending a quasi-coherent ideal of
finite type.
Let $\mathcal I,\mathcal J$ be ideals, both equal to $\mathcal O$ on
$U$, so that their product is too. Then the blow-up of their product
factors through both blow-ups. Indeed, on it the product
$\mathcal I\mathcal J$ is invertible, hence so is each factor, and the
universal property of each blow-up then gives the factorization. The
first assertion follows by induction. For the second, blowing up first $\mathcal I$ and
then the pullback of $\mathcal J$ yields the blow-up of
$\mathcal I\mathcal J$ [Stacks, [080A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080A)], which proves the composition
assertion when the second center is pulled back from $T$. In general, however, the second center
lives only on the first blow-up, and the composite is a blow-up of $T$
by the calculation with ideals of finite type in [Stacks, [080B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080B)].
For the extension assertion we extend a quasi-coherent ideal of finite
type from a quasi-compact open, keeping the center outside $U$; such
an extension exists because on a qcqs scheme every quasi-coherent
sheaf is the union of its quasi-coherent subsheaves of finite type, and the
precise result on admissible extensions is
[Stacks, [080M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080M)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For bounded below $K$ everything is read off from the hypercohomology
spectral sequence, which has only $2d+2$ nonzero columns. A general $K$, in turn, is the derived limit of its truncations $\tau_{\geq-n}K$, and the
column bound shows that in each fixed degree the tower of direct images
is eventually constant. The window (5.6) and the
preservation of direct sums follow from this.

*Bounded below $K$.* The hypercohomology spectral sequence

$$
E_2^{u,v}=R^up_*\mathcal H^v(K)\Longrightarrow\mathcal H^{u+v}(Rp_*K)
$$

converges. By Lemma [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image], its only nonzero
columns are $0\leq u\leq2d+1$, and their terms lie in
$\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. So each $\mathcal H^n(Rp_*K)$ has a finite
filtration whose graded pieces are subquotients of objects of
$\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. Since this category is closed under kernels,
cokernels and extensions by Proposition [proposition-ind-constructible-sheaves], we get
$\mathcal H^n(Rp_*K)\in\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. Both amplitude bounds
can be read off from the columns.

*Arbitrary $K$.* By Proposition [proposition-left-completeness], $K\simeq R\varprojlim_n
\tau_{\geq-n}K$. Since $Rp_*$ is a right adjoint, it preserves products and
hence derived inverse limits. Thus
$Rp_*K\simeq R\varprojlim_nRp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K$, and it suffices to see
that in each fixed degree the tower $Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K$ stabilizes. The fibre of
$\tau_{\geq-n-1}K\to\tau_{\geq-n}K$ is $\mathcal H^{-n-1}(K)[n+1]$, a
single ind-constructible sheaf in degree $-n-1$. By the bounded below
case its direct image has cohomology only in degrees
$[-n-1,-n-1+2d+1]=[-n-1,2d-n]$. In particular it has none
in degrees $q-1$, $q$, $q+1$ once $n>2d+1-q$. For fixed $q$, the long exact
sequences then show that the transition maps of the
towers $\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ and
$\mathcal H^{q-1}(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ are isomorphisms for $n$ large.
Since an eventually constant tower has vanishing $\varprojlim^1$, the
Milnor sequence of Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence] gives

$$
\mathcal H^q(Rp_*K)\simeq
\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.
$$

The bounded below case, applied to the right-hand side, shows that
$\mathcal H^q(Rp_*K)\in\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$, with the bound $b+2d+1$ if $K\in
\Dic^{\leq b}(X,\Lambda)$. The lower bound needs no new argument, because
an object of $\Dic^{\geq a}$ is bounded below.

*The isomorphism (5.6).* It comes from the bounds,
applied to the truncation triangles

$$
\tau_{\leq q}K\to K\to\tau_{\geq q+1}K,
\qquad
\tau_{\leq q-2d-2}K\to\tau_{\leq q}K\to\tau_{\geq q-2d-1}\tau_{\leq q}K.
$$

The direct image of $\tau_{\geq q+1}K$ lives in degrees $\geq q+1$, and
that of $\tau_{\leq q-2d-2}K$ in degrees $\leq q-1$. The long exact
cohomology sequences of the two triangles therefore yield isomorphisms
$\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\leq q}K)\simeq\mathcal H^q(Rp_*K)$ and
$\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\leq q}K)\simeq
\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\geq q-2d-1}\tau_{\leq q}K)$.

*Direct sums, assertion (3).* The window (5.6)
reduces us to families with cohomology in a common finite interval, and for such a family $(M_\alpha)$ we show by induction on the length of the interval
that the map
$\bigoplus_\alpha Rp_*M_\alpha\to Rp_*(\bigoplus_\alpha M_\alpha)$ is an
isomorphism. When the length is zero, each $M_\alpha$ is a shifted object of $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$, and the claim is
the assertion about direct sums in Lemma [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image], in
each degree. Then, for the inductive step, we take the direct sum of the truncation
triangles that split off the top cohomology sheaf and apply the five lemma to the long exact cohomology sequences.

Now let $(K_\alpha)$ be arbitrary and fix $q$. Since direct sums of sheaves
are exact, cohomology and truncations commute with direct sums. The
objects $\tau_{\geq q-2d-1}\tau_{\leq q}K_\alpha$ have cohomology in the
common interval $[q-2d-1,q]$. Applying (5.6) to each
$K_\alpha$ and to $\bigoplus_\alpha K_\alpha$, and the first paragraph to
the truncated family, we see that
$\bigoplus_\alpha Rp_*K_\alpha\to Rp_*(\bigoplus_\alpha K_\alpha)$ is an
isomorphism on $\mathcal H^q$. Since $q$ is arbitrary, the map is an isomorphism.

*Bounded below $K$.* The hypercohomology spectral sequence

$$
E_2^{u,v}=R^up_*\mathcal H^v(K)\Longrightarrow\mathcal H^{u+v}(Rp_*K)
$$

converges. By Lemma [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image], its only nonzero
columns are $0\leq u\leq2d+1$, and their terms lie in
$\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. So each $\mathcal H^n(Rp_*K)$ has a finite
filtration whose graded pieces are subquotients of objects of
$\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. Since this category is closed under kernels,
cokernels and extensions by Proposition [proposition-ind-constructible-sheaves], we get
$\mathcal H^n(Rp_*K)\in\IndCons(Y,\Lambda)$. Both amplitude bounds
can be read off from the columns.

*Arbitrary $K$.* By Proposition [proposition-left-completeness], $K\simeq R\varprojlim_n
\tau_{\geq-n}K$. Since $Rp_*$ is a right adjoint, it preserves products and
hence derived inverse limits. Thus
$Rp_*K\simeq R\varprojlim_nRp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K$, and it suffices to see
that in each fixed degree the tower $Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K$ stabilizes. The fibre of
$\tau_{\geq-n-1}K\to\tau_{\geq-n}K$ is $\mathcal H^{-n-1}(K)[n+1]$, a
single ind-constructible sheaf in degree $-n-1$. By the bounded below
case its direct image has cohomology only in degrees
$[-n-1,-n-1+2d+1]=[-n-1,2d-n]$. In particular it has none
in degrees $q-1$, $q$, $q+1$ once $n>2d+1-q$. For fixed $q$, the long exact
sequences then show that the transition maps of the
towers $\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ and
$\mathcal H^{q-1}(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ are isomorphisms for $n$ large.
Since an eventually constant tower has vanishing $\varprojlim^1$, the
Milnor sequence of Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence] gives

$$
\mathcal H^q(Rp_*K)\simeq
\mathcal H^q(Rp_*\tau_{\geq-n}K)\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.

The bounded below case, applied to the right-hand side, shows that

\Dic^{\leq b}(X,\Lambda)$. The lower bound needs no new argument, because

We compactify by Nagata's theorem and then normalize. On a curve,
normality is the same as regularity, and over a perfect field
regularity is smoothness, so the normalization is the model we want.

By Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem], $U_0$ is an open subscheme of a
proper $k_0$-scheme, and we take the reduced closure of $U_0$ in it and
normalize this closure in $k_0(U_0)$.  Since a scheme of finite type
over a field is Nagata, the normalization is finite
[Stacks, [035B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/035B), [035S](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/035S)], and it is an isomorphism over the normal
open $U_0$.  The resulting proper normal curve is regular, because a
one-dimensional noetherian normal local domain is a discrete valuation
ring. Hence it is smooth over the perfect field $k_0$
[Stacks, [0B8Y](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B8Y)].  Its boundary is zero-dimensional and proper over $k_0$,
hence finite. Since $k_0$ is perfect, the reduced boundary is étale.  After base change to $k$, the curve $U$ is dense and
connected, and therefore its closure $C$ is connected.  Finally, a
proper scheme of dimension one over a field is projective
[Stacks, [0A26](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A26)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-proper-smooth-model], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both complexes have cohomology $\mathbf F_\ell$ in degree zero,
$\mathbf F_\ell(-1)$ in degree one, and zero in all other degrees.
For the surface this follows from localization, the acyclicity of the
strictly local schemes $S,D_2$, and the purity identity
$i_{D_2}^!\mathbf F_\ell=\mathbf F_\ell(-1)[-2]$. This identity, in turn, comes by transitivity from the dualizing complexes of the smooth schemes $S$ and $D_2$.

For the punctured trait $D_1-z$, vanishing in degrees $\geq2$ follows from
Proposition [proposition-cohomology-smooth-affine-curve], by passing to the
filtered limit of punctured neighbourhoods that are curves. In degree one the
Kummer sequence gives $H^1(-,\mu_\ell)=k'^*/k'^{*\ell}$, where $k'$ is the
fraction field. Moreover, the units of the strictly henselian trait are $\ell$-divisible.
Hence the valuation induces $k'^*/k'^{*\ell}\simeq\mathbf Z/\ell$, and the
class of a uniformizer is a generator.

To see that the restriction map itself, and not only the two sides, is an
isomorphism, we find a generator of $H^1$ on each side. The restriction is clearly the identity in degree zero. In degree one, let $g$ be a local equation of $D_2$. Since
the regular local ring of $S$ is factorial, $\operatorname{Pic}(S-D_2)=0$
and the units on $S-D_2$ are the units of $S$ times the powers of $g$.
As the units of $S$ are $\ell$-divisible, the Kummer sequence shows that
$H^1(S-D_2,\mu_\ell)\simeq\mathbf Z/\ell$, generated by the class of $g$.
Since $D_1$ and $D_2$ meet transversely, $g$ restricts to a uniformizer
of $D_1$, whose class generates $H^1(D_1-z,\mu_\ell)$. So the
restriction is an isomorphism in degree one as well, and since both
complexes vanish in the other degrees, it is an isomorphism.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-punctured-surface-punctured-curve], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The inequality $q\leq\dim X_{\bar\eta}$ holds by flatness. Choose a system
of parameters $f_1,\ldots,f_q$ of the local ring
$\mathcal O_{X_s,x}$ of the special fibre, defined on an affine
neighbourhood, and lift them to functions on the corresponding affine
open of $X$. The resulting map $b:X\to\mathbf A^q_S$ is quasi-finite at
$x$, because its fibre through $x$ is the fibre of
$b_s=(f_1,\ldots,f_q)$, in which $x$ is isolated. Let $V$ be the
open locus where $b$ is quasi-finite; as $b_\eta$ is quasi-finite on
$V_\eta$, the generic fibre of $V$ has dimension at most $q$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-quasi-finite-coordinates], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The identity (19.2) holds because both sides
are reduced fractions for $Z(X_0,T)$ over $\mathbf Q_\ell$. By
Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety], the
reciprocal roots of $P_{i,\ell}$ have absolute value $q^{i/2}$ under
every embedding $\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$. Since $q>1$,
distinct degrees give distinct absolute values, and so the polynomials
$P_{i,\ell}$ are pairwise coprime. Their products over odd and over
even degrees are therefore coprime, and they have constant coefficients
one. By (19.1) their quotient is
$Z(X_0,T)$. On the other hand, $A$ and $B$ remain coprime in
$\mathbf Q_\ell[T]$, since a Bézout relation over $\mathbf Q$ remains
valid over $\mathbf Q_\ell$. The two reduced fractions agree by the

We repeat the construction in the proof of Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality]
with an integral basis of the row span. This gives an integral
fraction, which we then reduce with Gauss' lemma.

Let $V$ be the rational row span of Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality], and put
$L=V\cap\mathbf Z^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$. Then $L$ contains all rows,
spans $V$, and is preserved by the left shift. Since $V$ is
finite-dimensional, some $r$ of the coordinate functionals span its
dual, as in the proof of (2)$\Rightarrow$(3) in
Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality], and so they are jointly injective on $V$.
These coordinates embed $L$ into $\mathbf Z^r$. Since a subgroup
of $\mathbf Z^r$ is free of finite rank, $L$ is a shift-stable lattice
in $V$, free of rank $\dim V$.

In a basis of $L$, the shift matrix $M$, the row $e$ and the column
$v=R_0$ are integral. The matrix identity in the proof of
Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality] yields integral polynomials

$$
A_0=e\operatorname{adj}(I-TM)v,\qquad B_0=\det(I-TM),
\qquad C=A_0/B_0.
$$

Both constant coefficients are one. Let $G$ be a primitive integral
polynomial that is a greatest common divisor of $A_0$ and $B_0$ in
$\mathbf Q[T]$. By Gauss' lemma the quotients $A_0/G$ and $B_0/G$ are
integral. Since $G(0)$ divides $B_0(0)=1$, we may choose the sign of
$G$ so that $G(0)=1$. Dividing by $G$, we obtain polynomials $A$ and
$B$ that are coprime and have constant coefficients one.

For uniqueness, let $A/B=A'/B'$ be two such fractions, so that
$AB'=A'B$ in $\mathbf Q[T]$. Since $B$ is coprime to $A$, it divides
$B'$, and in the same way $B'$ divides $B$. So $B'=cB$ for a scalar
$c$. Comparing constant coefficients gives $c=1$, and then $AB=A'B$
forces $A=A'$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduced-fractions-integer-coefficients], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first simplify the source of the direct image and the coefficients,
then show that the source of the base change map vanishes, and finally
replace the base by a normal one.

By Lemma [lemma-reduction-field] there is a failure with direct image
from the spectrum of a field $\Omega$. Since the map from the spectrum of an
algebraic closure of $\Omega$ to $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is integral
and surjective, Lemma [lemma-integral-changes-source-base] allows us
to replace $\Omega$ by an algebraic closure. On this geometric point, a
sheaf of $\mathbf Z/n$-modules is a $\mathbf Z/n$-module, hence a direct
sum of cyclic groups $\mathbf Z/m$ with $m\mid n$. As the base change map
commutes with this direct sum by continuity of qcqs direct images,
base change still fails for some summand $\mathbf Z/m$.

The source of the base change map is the pullback of
$R^qf_*\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$ for $f:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$, and
we show that it is zero. The stalk of this sheaf at a geometric point
$\bar t$ of $T$ is the cohomology of
$\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\times_T\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{T,\bar t}$.
This scheme is a limit of étale $\Omega$-schemes, which, since $\Omega$ is
algebraically closed, are disjoint unions of copies of
$\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. By continuity of cohomology the stalk therefore
vanishes for $q\geq1$. As the source of the base change map is zero, the failure
means that the target $R^qh_*\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$ is nonzero.

The extension theorem for covers will require a normal base with
algebraically closed fraction field.
If the base is $\operatorname{Spec}B$, we replace it by
$\operatorname{Spec}R$, where $R$ is the integral closure in $\Omega$ of the
image of $B$. This is allowed, because the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}B$
factors through $\operatorname{Spec}R$, and $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}B$
is integral, so the failure persists by
Lemma [lemma-integral-changes-source-base].
Moreover, the fraction field $L$ of $R$ is the algebraic closure of
$\operatorname{Frac}(\operatorname{im}(B\to \Omega))$ in $\Omega$, hence
algebraically closed, although in general $\Omega/L$ is transcendental. We
are now in the situation of [Stacks, [0F08](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F08)].

The argument does not use that $g$ is affine or smooth. These hypotheses only
serve to make $C$ a smooth affine curve, by base change.

Since $\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q-1)$ holds and $\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q)$ fails,
Lemma [lemma-reduction-field] gives a failure in degree $q$ for an affine
base change $T=\operatorname{Spec}B\to Y$, direct image along a morphism
$f:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega_0\to T$ with $\Omega_0$ a field, and a sheaf $M$
of $\mathbf Z/n$-modules on $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega_0$.

*Algebraic closure.* Let $\Omega$ be an algebraic closure of $\Omega_0$,
and let $\pi:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega_0$ be the
projection, which is integral and surjective. The hypothesis of
clause [lemma-integral-changes-source-base--1], for $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n$ and the base change
$Y'\times_YT\to T$, is degree-$(q-1)$ base change for all qcqs morphisms to
$T$ and all sheaves, which is part of $\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q-1)$. The morphism $f$
is a morphism of affine schemes, hence qcqs. So by
clause [lemma-integral-changes-source-base--1] base change in degree $q$ also fails for $f\circ\pi$
and $\pi^{-1}M$.

*Normal base.* Let $R$ be the integral closure in $\Omega$ of the image
of $B\to\Omega$. It is a domain, integrally closed in $\Omega$ and hence
normal. Its fraction field $L$ is algebraically closed: if $\alpha\in\Omega$
is algebraic over the fraction field of the image of $B$, then $d\alpha$ is
integral over that image for some nonzero $d$ in it, so $\alpha\in L$. Thus
$L$ is the algebraic closure of that fraction field in the algebraically
closed field $\Omega$. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ factors
through $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, and $S\to T$ is integral. By
clause [lemma-integral-changes-source-base--2], base change in degree $q$ fails for the square with
base change $C=Y'\times_YS\to S$ and direct image along
$f_1:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$, with the same sheaf $\pi^{-1}M$.

*Constant coefficients.* A sheaf of $\mathbf Z/n$-modules on
$(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega)_{\acute{e}t}$ is a $\mathbf Z/n$-module $N$. An abelian
group of bounded exponent is a direct sum of cyclic groups, so
$N\simeq\bigoplus_i\mathbf Z/m_i$ with $m_i\mid n$. Inverse images commute
with direct sums, and so do higher direct images along the qcqs morphisms
$f_1$ and $h$, because they commute with filtered colimits [Stacks, [09Z1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09Z1)].
Hence the base change map for $N$ is the direct sum of those for the
$\mathbf Z/m_i$, and it fails for some $m=m_i$.

*The source vanishes.* The source of this base change map is the
pullback to $C$ of $R^qf_{1,*}\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$. Its stalk at a
geometric point $\bar s$ of $S$ is the cohomology of
$\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,\bar s}$.
This scheme is a limit of étale $\Omega$-schemes. Since $\Omega$ is
algebraically closed, these are disjoint unions of copies of
$\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. By continuity of cohomology the stalk vanishes
for $q\geq1$. The target is
$R^qh_*$ of the inverse image of $\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$ to $C_\Omega$,
which is $R^qh_*\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$. As the source is zero, the failure
means that $R^qh_*\underline{\mathbf Z/m}\neq0$, and $m\geq2$.

We shrink the source of the direct image, keeping a fixed
nonzero element of the cokernel, until it becomes the spectrum of a field. A
minimal closed subscheme carrying the failure exists by a limit argument,
and its generic point still carries it. The one nonformal step is the
third property below, which says that a failure on a scheme is seen either
on an open subscheme or on its closed complement, and whose proof uses the
injectivity of the base change map.

We first fix notation for the cokernels. Let $T$ be a $Y$-scheme, put
$T'=Y'\times_YT$, and let $g_T:T'\to T$ be the projection. For a qcqs
morphism $h:Z'\to T$ we write $h':Z'_{T'}=Z'\times_TT'\to T'$ and
$g_{Z'}:Z'_{T'}\to Z'$ for its base changes, and for a sheaf $N$ of
$\mathbf Z/n$-modules on $Z'_{\acute{e}t}$ we put

$$
b^q_{h,N}:g_T^{-1}R^qh_*N\longrightarrow R^qh'_*g_{Z'}^{-1}N,
\qquad
C(h,N)=\operatorname{coker}\bigl(b^q_{h,N}\bigr),
$$

a sheaf on $T'_{\acute{e}t}$. These cokernels are functorial in two ways. A map of
sheaves $N\to N_1$ on $Z'_{\acute{e}t}$ induces $C(h,N)\to C(h,N_1)$, and a morphism
$u:Z''\to Z'$ induces $C(h,N)\to C(hu,u^{-1}N)$, by pulling back along $u$:
upstairs through $N\to u_*u^{-1}N$ and the edge map
$R^qh_*u_*\to R^q(hu)_*$, and downstairs in the same way. These pullback maps
are compatible with the base change maps, and with composition in $u$,
because base change maps compose [Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)].

Since $\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q)$ fails, there are a $Y$-scheme $T$, a qcqs morphism
$f:Z\to T$ and a sheaf $M$ of $\mathbf Z/n$-modules on $Z_{\acute{e}t}$ such that
$b^q_{f,M}$ is not an isomorphism. By
Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree] it is injective, so
$C(f,M)\neq0$, and we fix a geometric point $\bar t'$ of $T'$ and a nonzero
element $\xi\in C(f,M)_{\bar t'}$. For a qcqs morphism $u:Z'\to Z$ let
$P(Z')$ mean that the image $\xi_{Z'}$ of $\xi$ in
$C(fu,u^{-1}M)_{\bar t'}$ is nonzero. The verification in [Stacks, [0F07](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F07)]
shows that $P$ has three properties.

1. thickenings preserve $P$, by topological invariance;
2. limits with affine transition maps preserve $P$, by continuity;
3. if $P(Z')$ holds and $V\subset Z'$ is a quasi-compact open with
   closed complement $W$, then $P(V)$ or $P(W)$ holds.

To prove the third property, write $h=fu:Z'\to T$ and $M'=u^{-1}M$, and let
$j:V\to Z'$ and $i:W\to Z'$ be the inclusions. We split $M'$ into an open
part and a closed part. Choose an injective sheaf $J$ of
$\mathbf Z/n$-modules on $V_{\acute{e}t}$ containing $j^{-1}M'$. Then the map

$$
M'\longrightarrow j_*J\oplus i_*i^{-1}M',
$$

whose components are adjoint to $j^{-1}M'\subset J$ and to the identity of
$i^{-1}M'$, is injective. Indeed, at a geometric point of $V$ its first
component is the inclusion $M'_{\bar v}\subset J_{\bar v}$, and at a
geometric point of $W$ its second component is the identity of
$M'_{\bar w}$. By the second assertion of
Lemma [lemma-injectivity-base-change-map-degree], the induced map

$$
C(h,M')\longrightarrow C(h,j_*J)\oplus C(h,i_*i^{-1}M')
$$

is injective as well. Since $P(Z')$ holds, $\xi_{Z'}\neq0$, and therefore its
image in $C(h,j_*J)_{\bar t'}$ or its image in $C(h,i_*i^{-1}M')_{\bar t'}$
is nonzero. We show that the second case gives $P(W)$ and the first gives
$P(V)$.

The closed summand is formal. The base change $i':W_{T'}\to Z'_{T'}$ of $i$
is again a closed immersion, and closed direct images are exact and commute
with every base change (Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms]). Hence, for a
sheaf $N$ on $W_{\acute{e}t}$,

$$
R^qh_*(i_*N)=R^q(hi)_*N,
\qquad
R^qh'_*\bigl(g_{Z'}^{-1}i_*N\bigr)=R^qh'_*\bigl(i'_*g_W^{-1}N\bigr)
=R^q(hi)'_*g_W^{-1}N,
$$

and these identifications are compatible with the base change maps
[Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)]. Thus
$C(h,i_*N)=C(hi,N)$. For $N=i^{-1}M'$ the image of $\xi_{Z'}$ in
$C(h,i_*i^{-1}M')_{\bar t'}$ becomes $\xi_W$, and so it is nonzero exactly when
$P(W)$ holds.

The open summand needs the induction hypothesis, because $j$ is not finite.
Let $j':V_{T'}\to Z'_{T'}$ and $g_V:V_{T'}\to V$ be the base changes of $j$,
and compare the Leray spectral sequences for $hj=h\circ j$ and
$h'j'=h'\circ j'$. Upstairs, $R^bj_*J=0$ for $b>0$ because $J$ is injective,
so the Leray spectral sequence collapses and gives

$$
R^qh_*(j_*J)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R^q(hj)_*J .
$$

Downstairs we use $\mathrm{BC}(g,n,q-1)$. The scheme $Z'$ is a $Y$-scheme
through $T$, and $Z'_{T'}=Y'\times_YZ'$, so the square formed by $j$, $j'$,
$g_{Z'}$ and $g_V$ is one of the squares in the definition of $\mathrm{BC}$.
Hence

$$
g_{Z'}^{-1}R^bj_*J\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R^bj'_*g_V^{-1}J
\qquad(0\le b\le q-1).
$$

For $b=0$ this identifies $g_{Z'}^{-1}j_*J$ with $j'_*g_V^{-1}J$, and for
$0<b<q$ it shows that $R^bj'_*g_V^{-1}J=0$. Consequently, in the Leray
spectral sequence

$$
E_2^{a,b}=R^ah'_*R^bj'_*g_V^{-1}J\ \Longrightarrow\
R^{a+b}(h'j')_*g_V^{-1}J
$$

the rows $0<b<q$ vanish. No differential can reach $E^{q,0}$: the
differential $d_r$ into $E_r^{q,0}$ starts at $E_r^{q-r,r-1}$, which is zero
for $2\le r\le q$ because then $0<r-1<q$, and for $r>q$ because then
$q-r<0$. So $E_2^{q,0}=E_\infty^{q,0}$, which is the bottom step of the
filtration of the abutment, and the edge map

$$
e:R^qh'_*\bigl(j'_*g_V^{-1}J\bigr)\longrightarrow R^q(h'j')_*g_V^{-1}J
$$

is injective. Since base change maps compose [Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)] and edge
maps are natural, the square

$$
\begin{CD}
g_T^{-1}R^qh_*(j_*J) @>{b^q_{h,j_*J}}>> R^qh'_*\bigl(j'_*g_V^{-1}J\bigr)\\
@V{\wr}VV @VV{e}V\\
g_T^{-1}R^q(hj)_*J @>{b^q_{hj,J}}>> R^q(h'j')_*g_V^{-1}J
\end{CD}
$$

commutes. Its left arrow is an isomorphism and its right arrow is injective,
so it induces an injective map $C(h,j_*J)\to C(hj,J)$. (In the top row we
have identified $g_{Z'}^{-1}j_*J$ with $j'_*g_V^{-1}J$ by the case $b=0$; this
does not change the cokernel.) The vertical arrows are the pullback maps
along $j$, so this map is pullback along $j$ followed by $j^{-1}j_*J=J$.

It remains to pass from $J$ back to $j^{-1}M'$. By naturality, the composite
$C(h,M')\to C(h,j_*J)\to C(hj,J)$ equals the composite
$C(h,M')\to C(hj,j^{-1}M')\to C(hj,J)$ of pullback along $j$ and the map
induced by $j^{-1}M'\subset J$. In the first case the image of $\xi_{Z'}$ in
$C(h,j_*J)_{\bar t'}$ is nonzero, hence so is its image in
$C(hj,J)_{\bar t'}$. This image is the image of $\xi_V$ under the second
composite, and so $\xi_V\neq0$, which is $P(V)$.

The field comes out of the three properties as follows. The intersection
of a decreasing chain of closed subschemes is the limit of the chain, with
affine transition maps. By the second property and Zorn's lemma there is
therefore a minimal closed subscheme with $P$. It is nonempty, since $P$
fails for the empty scheme, and by the first property it is reduced. Let
$\xi$ be the generic point of an irreducible component. We claim that every
affine open neighbourhood of $\xi$ has $P$. Indeed, by the third property,
either the neighbourhood or its closed complement has $P$, and the
complement is a closed subscheme not containing $\xi$, hence strictly
smaller, so by minimality it does not have $P$. Since the minimal closed
subscheme is reduced, the limit of these neighbourhoods is
$\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\xi)$. It has $P$ by the second property
(compare [Stacks, [0F06](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F06)]), and so $\kappa(\xi)$ is the field asserted in the
lemma.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduction-field], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Cutting off the cohomology above degree $m$ is harmless for degree
reasons alone. To remove the cohomology below degree $m-d_C$ we use the
uniform bound: for bounded $K$ it kills the tail layer by layer, and for $K$ unbounded below we
write $K$ as the derived limit of its truncations and control the
resulting $\varprojlim^1$ term.

Replacing $K$ by $K[m]$, we may assume $m=0$. The truncation
$\tau_{>0}K$ lies in $D^{\geq1}$, and $C$ is a sheaf in degree $0$, so
there are no nonzero maps from $C$ to an object of $D^{\geq1}$. Hence
$\Hom(C,\tau_{>0}K[s])=0$ for
$s=0,-1$. In the long exact sequence of $\Hom(C,-)$ for the truncation triangle $\tau_{\leq0}K\to K\to\tau_{>0}K\to$, these are the two groups
adjacent to $\Hom(C,K)$, and so
$\Hom(C,K)=\Hom(C,\tau_{\leq0}K)$. To remove the cohomology
in degrees $\leq-d_C-1$ from $K'=\tau_{\leq0}K$, we use the triangle
$\tau_{\leq-d_C-1}K'\to K'\to\tau_{\geq-d_C}K'\to$. It suffices to show that

$$
\Hom(C,L)=0\qquad
\text{for every }L\in\Dic(X,\Lambda)\text{ with }H^q(L)=0\text{ for }q>-d_C-1,
\tag{5.4}
$$

applied to $L=\tau_{\leq-d_C-1}K'$ and to $L=\tau_{\leq-d_C-1}K'[1]$.

We first prove (5.4) for bounded $L$. Such
an $L$ is a finite extension of its shifted cohomology
sheaves $H^q(L)[-q]$, and by the long exact Hom sequences it suffices
to show that each of them receives no nonzero map from $C$. A layer
$H^q(L)[-q]$ with $q\leq-d_C-1$ contributes
$\Hom(C,H^q(L)[-q])=\Ext^{-q}(C,H^qL)$. Since $-q>d_C$ and $H^q(L)$ is
ind-constructible, this group vanishes by
Corollary [corollary-ind-heart-b]. For $L$ unbounded
below we cannot argue in finitely many steps, and we use instead that
the derived category is left complete.

The pro-étale site has a basis of weakly contractible objects
(Theorem [theorem-enough-affine-weakly-contractible-objects]). For
this reason
Proposition [proposition-exact-products] applies: products of $\Lambda_X$-modules are
exact, products in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ are computed termwise, and

$$
L=R\varprojlim_n\tau_{\geq-n}L
$$

for every $L$. Concretely, if $L^\bullet$ is a complex representing $L$,
the limit is the derived inverse limit of the tower of good truncations
$\tau_{\geq-n}L^\bullet$ with their canonical transition maps. Since $\Hom(C,-)$ takes
products to products, the triangle defining $R\varprojlim$ yields the
Milnor exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n{}^1
\Hom(C,\tau_{\geq-n}L[-1])
\longrightarrow\Hom(C,L)
\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n\Hom(C,\tau_{\geq-n}L)
\longrightarrow0.
$$

Each $\tau_{\geq-n}L$ is bounded with cohomology in degrees $\leq-d_C-1$,
and hence the right-hand term vanishes by the bounded case. For the left-hand
term, the triangle

$$
H^{-n-1}(L)[n+1]\longrightarrow \tau_{\geq-n-1}L
\longrightarrow \tau_{\geq-n}L\longrightarrow H^{-n-1}(L)[n+2]
$$

gives an exact sequence

$$
\Ext^{n}(C,H^{-n-1}L)\to\Hom(C,\tau_{\geq-n-1}L[-1])\to\Hom(C,\tau_{\geq-n}L[-1])
\to\Ext^{n+1}(C,H^{-n-1}L).
$$

The outer terms vanish for $n>d_C$ by Corollary [corollary-ind-heart-b].
The transition maps are therefore isomorphisms for $n>d_C$, so the tower is
eventually constant and its $\varprojlim^1$ vanishes. This proves
(5.4).
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduction-finitely-many-degrees], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The filtration comes from the representation theory of
$\ell$-groups, whose only simple module over $\mathbf F_\ell$ is the
trivial one, and the splitting from the trace, whose composite
with the unit is multiplication by the degree.

By Proposition [proposition-locally-constant-sheaves-finite-presentation], $G$ is the pullback of a
finite étale local system, which corresponds to a finite continuous
representation of the fundamental group.  Let $H$ be the finite image
of this representation, choose an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup $P$, and take the
cover associated to its inverse image in the fundamental group.  Its
degree is $[H:P]$, which is prime to $\ell$, and the restricted action
factors through $P$.  Since the augmentation ideal of $\mathbf F_\ell[P]$ is
nilpotent, the simple modules of the finite $\ell$-group $P$ are
trivial of dimension one, and a composition series yields the required
filtration [Stacks, [0A3R](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3R)].

On a fibre, the unit $G\to v_*v^*G$ is the diagonal and the trace map
$\operatorname{Tr}:v_*v^*G\to G$ adds the $d$ entries.
Their composite is therefore multiplication by $d$, which is invertible on an
$\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaf, so $d^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}$ is a retraction.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduction-unipotent-local-system], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-reduction-unipotent-local-system], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We spread out Noether normalization from the generic points of the
target, and then argue by induction on the dimension of the complement.
Spreading out is possible because a normalization over the fraction
field involves finitely many equations with finitely many denominators.
Recall Noether normalization over a field $k'$ [Stacks, [00OY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00OY)]: a
nonzero finitely generated $k'$-algebra is finite over a polynomial
subalgebra.

Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $k'$, let
$\operatorname{Spec}R$ be an affine open of the target, and let $B$ be
a finitely generated $R$-algebra. If $B\otimes_Rk'=0$, then $B_s=0$ for
some nonzero $s\in R$. Otherwise, Noether normalization over $k'$
provides elements $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ and monic equations for each of a
fixed set of algebra generators of $B$ over $k'[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$.
Choose a nonzero $s\in R$ divisible by all denominators of the $t_i$
and of the coefficients of these equations. Each equation, read in
$B_s$, has a left-hand side that vanishes in $B\otimes_Rk'$ and is
therefore killed by a nonzero element of $R$. Multiplying $s$ by these
finitely many elements, we may assume that the equations hold in
$B_s$. Then bounded powers of the generators span
$B_s$ over $R_s[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$, and the resulting map to
$\mathbf A^d_{R_s}$ is finite.

To obtain the partitions, choose disjoint integral affine opens
containing the generic points of the reduced target. Partition their
inverse images into finitely many reduced affine locally closed pieces
and apply the preceding construction to each piece. On each target
open, a single product of the finitely many denominators then works for all pieces. Since the
complement of the resulting open has smaller dimension, by
induction on this complement we obtain finite partitions of the whole
source and target. Moreover, all choices are made over $k_0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-relative-noether-normalization-over-stratification], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The third term of the exact sequence displayed above is supported on the finite set $Z$, so
by Lemma [lemma-sheaves-finite-support-finite-morphisms] it has finite sections and no
higher cohomology. Comparing the long exact sequences of $F$ and
$j_!j^*F$ then shows that each assertion passes in both directions.

The sheaf $j_!j^*F$ is again killed by $\ell$, so the hypotheses
on the coefficient prime are the same for both sheaves. Since the last
term of the exact sequence has no positive cohomology, the long exact
sequence yields

$$
\begin{split}
0\to H^0(C,j_!j^*F)\to H^0(C,F)\to H^0(Z,i^*F)\to{}\qquad\qquad\\
H^1(C,j_!j^*F)\to H^1(C,F)\to0,
\end{split}
$$

and isomorphisms in degrees at least two. Since the sequence is natural
under field extension and its term supported on $Z$ is unchanged,
the two long exact sequences show that the pullback maps
are isomorphisms for $F$ in all degrees if and only if they are
isomorphisms for $j_!j^*F$ in all degrees. For $(C_8)$, we apply the
degree-two identifications after restriction to every open subset of
$C$. See also [Stacks, [0GJA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GJA)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-removing-finitely-many-points], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The preceding lemmas assume $C$ geometrically integral. To see that this
holds, note that $\bar k/k$ is purely inseparable. Hence $C_{\bar k}\to C$
is a homeomorphism, and $C_{\bar k}$ is connected and smooth, hence
integral. We rigidify using a point $P\in C(k)$. Such a point exists
because $k$ is separably closed and the $k$-points of the smooth curve
$C$ are dense [Stacks, [056U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/056U)].

By Proposition [proposition-divisors-degree-g-open-chart] we have a
representable open subfunctor $F\subset\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$. For a fixed class
$M\in\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)$, the translate
$M^{-1}F$, consisting of the classes $\mathcal L$ with
$\mathcal L\otimes M$ in $F$, is another representable open
subfunctor.

We show that these translates cover $\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$. Let a
class on a $k$-scheme $T$ and a point $t\in T$ be given. We apply
Lemma [lemma-twisting-h-0-1-h] to its fibre over the residue field
$k'=\kappa(t)$. This gives an invertible sheaf $\mathcal M_0$ on $C$,
defined over $k$, such that the twisted fibre has $h^0=1$ and $H^1=0$.
By Lemma [lemma-coherent-base-change-invertible-sheaves], the twisted class then
lies in $F$ over an open neighbourhood of $t$. Letting $t$ vary, we see
that the open loci where the corresponding translated class lies
in $F$ cover $T$. Note that the translates are indexed by classes over
$k$, while the points of $T$ have arbitrary residue fields. This is why
Lemma [lemma-twisting-h-0-1-h] asks for a twist defined over $k$ for
every extension $k'$.

The intersections of the charts are open in either chart, and their
transition isomorphisms satisfy the cocycle condition by functoriality.
An fppf sheaf covered by representable open subfunctors is
representable [Stacks, [0B9Q](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9Q), [0B9Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9Z)]. Hence gluing the charts gives a
scheme representing $\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$. It is locally of finite
type because each chart is an open of $\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-representability-picard-functor], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We prove the comparisons in the order stated, each using the
previous ones: the direct image by continuity along a limit of étale
maps, $i^!$ by the localization triangle, and internal Hom by
dévissage to generators $t_!P$. Throughout, with finite coefficients
Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category] lets us
compute $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ and the direct images by their classical
étale counterparts.

*Direct image.* The geometric generic point is a limit of étale
$B$-schemes. Indeed, a separable closure of $k(B)$ is the inverse limit of
nonempty affine opens in the normalizations of $B$ in its finite separable
extensions, with the branch loci removed, and each stage is étale over
an open of $B$. The functor $Rh_*$ commutes with pullback to each stage,
because pullback to an étale $B$-scheme is restriction to an object of
the small site. It remains to pass to the limit.

Every affine object étale over the limit descends to a stage. Continuity
of cohomology (Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]) therefore shows
that, degree by degree, the derived sections with finite coefficients
commute with this filtered limit along affine transition maps, provided the
complexes vanish below one fixed degree. They do, because $L$ is bounded.
Moreover, all the direct images lie in one fixed range of degrees. The base
changes of $h$ to the stages are of finite type of bounded dimension, and
[Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)] bounds their $\ell$-cohomological dimensions
(Definition [definition-cohomological-dimension]) independently of the
stage. This proves the first comparison over the separable closure. It
also holds over the algebraic closure, since a purely inseparable extension
induces the same classical étale topos.

*Exceptional inverse image.* Let $j$ be the open complement of
$i$ and pull back

$$
i_*i^!M\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*M
\longrightarrow.
$$

We compare the pulled-back triangle with the triangle with closed support
on the generic fibre, whose first term is $i_{\bar\eta,*}i_{\bar\eta}^!g_X^*M$. Their second terms agree. The third terms agree too, because the first
comparison identifies the pullback of $Rj_*j^*M$ with
$Rj_{\bar\eta,*}j_{\bar\eta}^*g_X^*M$, and the map between them is the same.
It follows that the first terms are determined functorially. Indeed, there are no nonzero
maps, in any degree, from a complex supported on $Z_{\bar\eta}$ to one of the form
$Rj_{\bar\eta,*}N$, so the first term of each triangle is the fibre of the second map. Now pullback commutes with direct image along a closed immersion, so
the first term of the pulled-back triangle is $i_{\bar\eta,*}g_Z^*i^!M$. By construction, the induced map $i_{\bar\eta,*}g_Z^*i^!M\to i_{\bar\eta,*}i_{\bar\eta}^!g_X^*M$
is adjoint to the pulled-back counit, that is, it is $i_{\bar\eta,*}$ of our
comparison map, and it is an isomorphism. Since $i_{\bar\eta,*}$ is fully
faithful, the comparison map itself is an isomorphism.

*Internal Hom.* The complexes $K$ for which the comparison is an
isomorphism are closed under cones and shifts, because both sides are exact
functors of $K$. The dévissage of
Lemma [lemma-verdier-duality-preserves-constructibility] therefore
reduces us to $K=t_!P$,
where $t$ is the inclusion of a stratum and $P$ is locally perfect
on it. For these generators, internal adjunction and the dualizability of the locally perfect complex $P$ express internal Hom
through operations we have already compared:

$$
\cHom_X(t_!P,M)
\simeq Rt_*(P^\vee\otimes^{\mathbf L}t^!M).
$$

We check that $g^*$ commutes with each operation on the right. For $t^!$ we factor $t$ as a closed immersion followed by an open immersion: for the open immersion $t^!$ is restriction, which commutes with $g^*$, and for the closed immersion
we use the second comparison. Similarly, pullback commutes with $Rt_*$ by the first
comparison, and it commutes with tensor products and with $P^\vee$. The first two comparisons apply here, because by
Lemma [lemma-verdier-duality-preserves-constructibility]
all complexes used remain bounded constructible. Hence the comparison holds
for $K=t_!P$.

*Direct image.* The geometric generic point is a limit of étale
$B$-schemes. Indeed, a separable closure of $k(B)$ is the inverse limit of
nonempty affine opens in the normalizations of $B$ in its finite separable
extensions, with the branch loci removed, and each stage is étale over
an open of $B$. The functor $Rh_*$ commutes with pullback to each stage,
because pullback to an étale $B$-scheme is restriction to an object of
the small site. It remains to pass to the limit.

Every affine object étale over the limit descends to a stage. Continuity
of cohomology (Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]) therefore shows
that, degree by degree, the derived sections with finite coefficients
commute with this filtered limit along affine transition maps, provided the
complexes vanish below one fixed degree. They do, because $L$ is bounded.
Moreover, all the direct images lie in one fixed range of degrees. The base
changes of $h$ to the stages are of finite type of bounded dimension, and
[Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)] bounds their $\ell$-cohomological dimensions
(Definition [definition-cohomological-dimension]) independently of the
stage. This proves the first comparison over the separable closure. It
also holds over the algebraic closure, since a purely inseparable extension
induces the same classical étale topos.

It suffices to consider a simple $\Gamma$-module $V$. A nonzero
$N$-submodule $A$ of least dimension is simple, and since $N$ is
normal, each translate $gA$ is again a simple $N$-submodule. The sum
of all these translates is a nonzero $\Gamma$-submodule, hence equals
$V$. It remains to see that a finite sum of simple submodules is semisimple. Indeed, the
intersection of a simple submodule with the sum of
those already chosen is either zero or the whole submodule, so we add it
in the first case and omit it in the second, and after finitely many steps we
obtain a direct-sum decomposition.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-restriction-normal-subgroup], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The source is $R\Gamma(X-D_2,j'_!N)=R\Gamma(X,M)$, by the definition
$M=Rj_*j'_!N$. Since $C$ meets $D_2$ only at $w$, the punctured curve
$C_{(w)}-w$ lies over the strict localization of $X$ at $w$ and avoids

restriction to $R\Gamma(D_2,M|_{D_2})$, followed by the
restriction to the stalk $M_w=R\Gamma(X_{(w)}-D_2,j'_!N)$ (by the stalk formula), followed
by the restriction to the displayed target. Since all these maps are restrictions of the same complex, the composite is the given map.
If $w\ne z$, the middle map is zero by Lemma [lemma-cohomology-near-two-transverse-divisors].
If $w=z$, the intermediate object $M_z$ is zero.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-restriction-punctured-curve], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The point is that rigidified pairs have no automorphisms other than the
identity. Because of this they form a sheaf, and the quotient presheaf
maps isomorphically onto this sheaf.

An automorphism of an invertible sheaf is multiplication by a global
unit. By condition $(\ast)$ this unit comes from a unit on $T$, and
compatibility with a rigidification forces it to be $1$. To see that the
rigidified functor is a sheaf, suppose we are given
rigidified classes on an fppf cover that agree on overlaps. We then choose local isomorphisms and rescale them so that they preserve the
rigidifications. Such isomorphisms are unique, since rigidified pairs have
no nontrivial automorphisms. In particular they satisfy the cocycle
condition, and the pairs glue by effective descent for invertible sheaves.

The normalization map identifies the quotient presheaf
$T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)/f_T^*\operatorname{Pic}(T)$ with this
rigidified functor. Since the latter is already a sheaf, the quotient
presheaf needs no sheafification and equals $\operatorname{Pic}_{C/S}$.
The sequence splits since
$\sigma_T^*f_T^*=\mathrm{id}$; for this argument see [Stacks, [0B9N](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9N)].

Near $X\times y_0$ the map $h$ lands in an affine open of $Z$, and a
map to an affine scheme is given by functions. Since $X$ is proper and
geometrically integral, functions on $X\times V$ are functions on $V$.
Hence $h$ factors through $V$.

Let $W\subset Z$ be an affine open containing $h(X\times y_0)$. Since
$X$ is proper, the image in $Y$ of the closed set $h^{-1}(Z\setminus W)$
is closed, and its complement contains $y_0$. Let $V$ be an affine
open neighbourhood of $y_0$ in this complement. Then $h$ maps
$X\times V$ into the affine scheme $W$. It is therefore determined by
the ring map $\mathcal O(W)\to H^0(X\times V,\mathcal O)$ [Stacks, [01I1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I1)].
By flat base change [Stacks, [02KH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02KH)] and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)=k$
[Stacks, [0BUG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BUG)], we have $H^0(X\times V,\mathcal O)=\mathcal O(V)$. The
ring map is thus $\operatorname{pr}_2^*$ composed with a ring map
$\mathcal O(W)\to\mathcal O(V)$, and this ring map defines $g$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-rigidity], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The scheme-theoretic image is the smallest closed subscheme through
which $i$ factors. Its ideal is
$\ker(\mathcal O_T\to i_*\mathcal O_U)$, which is quasi-coherent
because $i$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Its formation
commutes with flat base change $T'\to T$: pushforward along the
quasi-compact quasi-separated $i$ commutes with flat base change, and
pullback along a flat morphism is exact, so the pullback of the ideal is
the ideal of the base change [Stacks, [081I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/081I)]. Restriction to an open of
$T$ is a special case. On an open
where the immersion is closed the image is therefore $U$ itself, and
this shows that $U$ is open in its image. By construction, a section of
$\mathcal O_{\overline U}$ vanishing on $U$ is zero, which is the
definition of schematic density. For these statements see
[Stacks, [01R8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01R8), [01RG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01RG)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The maps $\Phi_X$ and $\operatorname{Fr}_X$ differ by the
absolute Frobenius, and pullback along the absolute Frobenius is
naturally the identity on étale sheaves. This gives $\kappa_m$, and we then compare the two pullback maps on one
compactification.
On coordinate rings the two maps are

$$
\Phi_X^\#(a\otimes b)=a^q\otimes b,
\qquad \operatorname{Fr}_X^\#(a\otimes b)=a\otimes b^{1/q}
$$

so that $\Phi_X=F_X\operatorname{Fr}_X$, where
$F_X$ is the absolute $q$-power Frobenius of $X$. The absolute Frobenius
commutes with every morphism of schemes over $\mathbf F_p$, so also
$\Phi_X^m=\operatorname{Fr}_X^mF_X^m$. On the classical constructible
category, pullback along absolute Frobenius is naturally isomorphic to the
identity, because for an étale object its relative Frobenius is an
isomorphism, functorial in that object. Transporting this natural
isomorphism to $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ by the comparison with the pro-étale site,
we obtain $\theta:F_X^*\simeq\mathrm{id}$. It is compatible with pullback
along every morphism $h$, that is, $h^*\theta=\theta h^*$ under
$h^*F^*=F^*h^*$, since relative Frobenius of étale objects is
compatible with base change. Let $\theta^m:(F_X^m)^*\simeq\mathrm{id}$ be
its $m$-fold composite and put

$$
\kappa_m=\theta^m_{(\operatorname{Fr}_X^m)^*K}:
(\Phi_X^m)^*K=(F_X^m)^*(\operatorname{Fr}_X^m)^*K
\xrightarrow{\sim}(\operatorname{Fr}_X^m)^*K .
$$

Compatibility with iteration means that
$\kappa_{m+1}=\kappa_{m,\operatorname{Fr}_X^*K}\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*\kappa_1$,
and it follows from the compatibility of $\theta$ with pullback along
$\Phi_X^m$. Now $\psi_m=\phi_m\kappa_m$ follows by induction on $m$. If it
holds for $m$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\psi_{m+1}&=\psi_m\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*\psi
=\phi_m\circ\kappa_m\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*\phi\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*\kappa_1\\
&=\phi_m\circ(\operatorname{Fr}_X^m)^*\phi\circ\kappa_{m,\operatorname{Fr}_X^*K}\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*\kappa_1
=\phi_{m+1}\kappa_{m+1},
\end{aligned}
$$

where the third equality is the naturality of $\kappa_m$ in $K$.

For the pullback maps on compact cohomology, let $j:X\hookrightarrow\bar X$
be the base change of a compactification of $X_0$ over $k_0$, and use the
pullback maps $\operatorname{pb}_h$ of Section [sec-Weil-complexes]. The
endomorphisms $\Phi_{\bar X}$, $\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}$ and
$F_{\bar X}$ of the scheme $\bar X$ restrict to $\Phi_X$,
$\operatorname{Fr}_X$ and $F_X$. Each of them has inverse image $X$ of $X$,
so each commutes with $j_!$, and
$\Phi_{\bar X}^m=\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^mF_{\bar X}^m$. Put
$L=j_!K$, so that $R\Gamma_c(X,K)=R\Gamma(\bar X,L)$.

First, the map $(\Phi_X^m)^*$ of
Definition [definition-frobenius-correspondences-their-operators] is
$\operatorname{pb}_{\Phi_{\bar X}^m,L}$. Indeed, $\Phi_X^m$ is finite, so
$R(\Phi_X^m)_!=R(\Phi_X^m)_*$, and the square $j\Phi_X^m=\Phi_{\bar X}^mj$
is cartesian, so $j_!R(\Phi_X^m)_*\simeq R(\Phi_{\bar X}^m)_*j_!$. Under
this isomorphism the identification
$R\Gamma_c(X,R(\Phi_X^m)_*-)=R\Gamma_c(X,-)$ used there is the composition
of direct images $R\Gamma(\bar X,R(\Phi_{\bar X}^m)_*-)=R\Gamma(\bar X,-)$,
and the unit for $\Phi_X^m$ corresponds to the unit for $\Phi_{\bar X}^m$.

Second, by transitivity,
$\operatorname{pb}_{\Phi_{\bar X}^m,L}
 =\operatorname{pb}_{F_{\bar X}^m,(\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^m)^*L}\circ
 \operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^m,L}$. The absolute Frobenius
$F_{\bar X}^m$ satisfies the hypothesis of [Stacks, [03SP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SP)], since its
relative Frobenius over each étale object is an isomorphism, functorial
in that object. Since $A$ is finite, we may compute on the étale site
(Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category]). There
the formal argument of [Stacks, [03SP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SP)] identifies $(F_{\bar X}^m)_*$ and
$(F_{\bar X}^m)^{-1}$ with the identity functors of the topos, compatibly
with the unit, and this identification is $\theta^m$, since both come from
the relative Frobenius isomorphisms of étale objects. Hence for every
$N\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\bar X,A)$ the pullback map
$\operatorname{pb}_{F_{\bar X}^m,N}$ followed by
$R\Gamma(\bar X,\theta^m_N)$ is the identity of $R\Gamma(\bar X,N)$. With $N=(\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^m)^*L$
this gives

$$
R\Gamma_c(X,\kappa_m)\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*=\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_X^m} .
$$

Finally, the naturality of $\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_X}$ moves the maps
$R\Gamma_c(X,(\operatorname{Fr}_X^i)^*\phi)$ past the pullback maps, and
transitivity gives
$\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m=R\Gamma_c(X,\phi_m)\circ\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_X^m}$.
Hence

$$
T_{c_m}(\psi_m)=R\Gamma_c(X,\phi_m)\circ R\Gamma_c(X,\kappa_m)\circ(\Phi_X^m)^*
=R\Gamma_c(X,\phi_m)\circ\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_X^m}
=\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m .
$$

The same computation with an arbitrary morphism
$\chi:(\operatorname{Fr}_X^m)^*K\to K$ in place of $\phi_m$ gives
$T_{c_m}(\chi\kappa_m)=R\Gamma_c(X,\chi)\circ\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_X^m}$.

The fibres of $\widetilde s^{*}\omega_{\widetilde g}$ at $t=1$ and $t=0$
are the two sides of (9.13), so it suffices to show that this
shifted sheaf of rank one is pulled back from $S$, étale locally on $S$.
In positive characteristic a locally constant sheaf on $\mathbf A^1_S$ need
not be pulled back from $S$, so we use coordinates. Étale locally on
$S$, near the section the deformation is étale over
$\mathbf A^d_{\mathbf A^1_S}=\mathbf A^d_S\times\mathbf A^1$, a family
pulled back from $S$, and hence so is
$\widetilde s^{*}\omega_{\widetilde g}[-2d]$. We then normalize the local
comparisons at $t=1$; since the geometric fibres of $\mathbf A^1_S\to S$
are connected, this makes them agree on overlaps. Finally, they glue because all
objects involved are shifted locally constant sheaves.

*Step 1: the objects.* The restrictions of
$\widetilde s^{*}\omega_{\widetilde g}$ to $t=1$ and $t=0$ are
$s^{*}\omega_{g}$ and $z^{*}\omega_{\pi}$, by
Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism](3) applied to the inclusions
of these fibres. Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism](1) shows that both
$\widetilde s^{*}\omega_{\widetilde g}[-2d]$ and
$s^{*}\omega_{g}[-2d]$ are locally constant sheaves, free of rank one
over $\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$. Hence morphisms between two such
complexes are morphisms of sheaves, and they glue.

*Step 2: local construction.* Étale
locally on $S$ we reduce to the zero section of affine space, whose deformation is
pulled back from $S$. After passing to an étale cover
$\{S_\alpha\to S\}_\alpha$ we may choose, for the base change of the section
$s_\alpha:S_\alpha\to V\times_SS_\alpha$, a neighbourhood $U_\alpha$ of $s_\alpha(S_\alpha)$ and an
étale map $e_\alpha:U_\alpha\to\mathbf A^d_{S_\alpha}$ sending $s_\alpha$ to the zero
section. We may assume that the inverse image of the zero section under
$e_\alpha$ is exactly $s_\alpha(S_\alpha)$. Indeed, this inverse image is
separated and étale over $S_\alpha$, so $s_\alpha(S_\alpha)$ is open and
closed in it, and we remove the complement, which is closed in $U_\alpha$.
Then $e_\alpha$ is an étale map of pairs whose square of centers is
cartesian. Since blowing up and removing the strict transform commute with
étale base change, $e_\alpha$ induces an étale map from a
neighbourhood of the deformed section in $\mathcal D_{s(S)}V$ to the
deformation space of the zero section of $\mathbf A^d_{S_\alpha}$. The latter
is $\mathbf A^d_{\mathbf A^1_{S_\alpha}}$, with coordinates $u_1,\ldots,u_d$
and $t$, and its map to $\mathbf A^d_{S_\alpha}\times\mathbf A^1$ sends
$(u,t)$ to $(tu,t)$, that is, $x_i=tu_i$, and the deformed zero section is
$u=0$.

The adjunction for affine space identifies the relative dualizing complex
of the projection
$\mathbf A^d_{\mathbf A^1_{S_\alpha}}\to\mathbf A^1_{S_\alpha}$ with the
constant sheaf $(\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z)(d)[2d]$. Pulling back along the
étale map just constructed, and composing adjunctions for it, gives the
same identification for $\omega_{\widetilde g}$ near the deformed section.
Similarly, the chart $e_\alpha$ gives the analogous identification of
$s^{*}\omega_{g}$ over $S_\alpha$. Composing the two identifications we
obtain an isomorphism over $\mathbf A^1_{S_\alpha}$

$$
\widetilde s^{*}\omega_{\widetilde g}\xrightarrow{\sim}
a^{*}s^{*}\omega_{g}.
$$

At $t=1$ it restricts to an automorphism of $s^{*}\omega_{g}$ over
$S_\alpha$. Composing with the pullback along $a$ of the inverse of this
automorphism, we may assume that the local isomorphism is the identity
at $t=1$.

*Step 3: gluing.* The local isomorphisms from different charts agree on
overlaps, because of the normalization at $t=1$. Over $S_\alpha\times_SS_\beta$ the two local
isomorphisms that are the identity at $t=1$ differ by an automorphism of the locally constant sheaf
$a^{*}s^{*}\omega_g[-2d]$ of rank one, that is, by a section of a locally
constant sheaf of units of $\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$. The locus where
this section equals $1$ is open and closed, and it contains the point $t=1$
of each geometric fibre $\mathbf A^1_{\bar b}$. As these fibres are
connected, the section is $1$ at every geometric point. So the local
isomorphisms glue to a unique isomorphism over $\mathbf A^1_S$ that is the
identity at $t=1$. Restricting it to $t=0$ gives an isomorphism
$z^{*}\omega_{\pi}\simeq s^{*}\omega_g$, whose inverse is
(9.13).

Let $y\in Y$ be the image of $\bar y$, let
$Y_{(\bar y)}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{Y,\bar y}$
and $X_{(\bar y)}=X\times_YY_{(\bar y)}$. In degree zero the stalk is
computed on the strict localization, that is,

$$
(f_*F)_{\bar y}\simeq\Gamma(X_{(\bar y)},F|_{X_{(\bar y)}}).
$$

For quasi-compact quasi-separated $f$ this holds by continuity of étale
sections ([Stacks, [03Q9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q9)], whose proof in degree zero applies to sheaves
of sets). To recall the argument: by definition, the stalk $(f_*F)_{\bar y}$ is the filtered colimit of
$\Gamma(X\times_YV,F|)$ over pointed affine étale neighbourhoods $V$
of $\bar y$, where $F|$ denotes the inverse image of $F$. Since the limit
of these neighbourhoods is $Y_{(\bar y)}$, there is a natural map from
the colimit to the sections over $X_{(\bar y)}$, and we must see that it is
bijective. A section over the limit is represented by finitely many
covering objects and finitely many agreement conditions, because
$X_{(\bar y)}$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Since all these data are of
finite presentation, they descend to one neighbourhood. This proves
surjectivity, and the same descent for two representatives proves
injectivity.

The local ring of $Y_{(\bar y)}$ is strictly henselian, with separably
closed residue field $\kappa(y)^{\mathrm{sep}}\subseteq\Omega$. Thus
$\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{Y,\bar y}$ with its maximal ideal is a henselian
pair, and $X_{(\bar y)}$ is proper over it with closed fibre
$X_{\kappa(y)^{\mathrm{sep}}}$. Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree] therefore identifies the
sections on the right with those
over $X_{\kappa(y)^{\mathrm{sep}}}$. These in turn equal
$\Gamma(X_{\bar y},F|_{X_{\bar y}})$, because extending a separably closed
ground field from $\kappa(y)^{\mathrm{sep}}$ to $\Omega$ does not change
the sections of the pullback of an étale sheaf [Stacks, [0A3I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3I)].

Lemma [lemma-local-cohomology-right-adjoint] gives the adjunction
between $i_*$ and $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ on derived categories. What is new
here is that $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ is the right derived functor of
$\underline\Gamma_Z$, and this upgrades the adjunction to $R\!\operatorname{Hom}$ complexes
and yields formula (3.1). For this we show two things:
$\underline\Gamma_Z$ is right adjoint to the exact functor $i_*$ on
sheaves, and $M\to j_*j^*M$ is surjective for injective $M$. The second means
that on injective sheaves the kernel of this map is also its fibre.

We use that $i^*$ and $i_*$ are exact, that $i^*i_*=\mathrm{id}$, and
that every sheaf $M$ sits in the localization sequence
$0\to j_!j^*M\to M\to i_*i^*M\to0$ [Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)].
The last fact shows that a sheaf whose restriction to $V$ vanishes is of
the form $i_*$ of a sheaf on $Z$. In particular
$\ker(M\to j_*j^*M)=i_*\underline\Gamma_Z(M)$.

*Adjunction on sheaves.* The functor $\underline\Gamma_Z$ is right
adjoint to $i_*:\operatorname{Mod}(Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.
Indeed, a map $i_*N\to M$ composes to zero with $M\to j_*j^*M$, because
$j^*i_*N=0$, so it factors through
$\ker(M\to j_*j^*M)=i_*\underline\Gamma_Z(M)$. Since $i_*$ is fully
faithful, such factorizations are the maps $N\to\underline\Gamma_Z(M)$.
Moreover, as $i_*$ is exact, its right adjoint $\underline\Gamma_Z$ preserves
K-injective complexes.

*Surjectivity on injectives.* For an injective sheaf $I$ the unit
$I\to j_*j^*I$ of the adjunction $j^*\dashv j_*$ on
$\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is surjective, because it has a right inverse.
To construct it, extend the inclusion $j_!j^*I\to I$ along
$j_!j^*I\hookrightarrow j_*j^*I$ to a map $s:j_*j^*I\to I$, which is
possible because $I$ is injective. Then the composite
$j_*j^*I\xrightarrow{s}I\to j_*j^*I$ restricts to the identity on $V$.
Since $j_*$ is fully faithful, an endomorphism of $j_*j^*I$ is determined by
its restriction to $V$, and so this composite is the identity.

*Comparison with the fibre.* The right derived functor of
$\underline\Gamma_Z$ agrees with $i^*\fib(K\to Rj_*j^*K)$. To see this,
represent $K$ by a K-injective complex $I^\bullet$ with injective terms
[Stacks, [079P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079P)]. Then $\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)$ computes the right
derived functor of $\underline\Gamma_Z$ at $K$. On the other side, the complex
$j^*I^\bullet$ is K-injective, because the left adjoint $j_!$ of $j^*$ is
exact. Hence $j_*j^*I^\bullet$ represents $Rj_*j^*K$. By the surjectivity just
proved, the sequences

$$
0\to i_*\underline\Gamma_Z(I^n)\to I^n\to j_*j^*I^n\to0
$$

are exact termwise, and they define a distinguished triangle
$i_*\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)\to K\to Rj_*j^*K\to i_*\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)[1]$.
Applying $i^*$ and using $i^*i_*=\mathrm{id}$ identifies
$\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)$ with $i^*\fib(K\to Rj_*j^*K)$.

*Part (1).* With $I^\bullet$ as above, the complex
$\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)$ is K-injective by the adjunction on

$$
R\!\operatorname{Hom}_X(i_*N,K)=\Hom^\bullet(i_*N,I^\bullet)
=\Hom^\bullet(N,\underline\Gamma_Z(I^\bullet)),
$$

whose right-hand side is $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_Z(N,R\underline\Gamma_ZK)$.

We quote this from [Stacks, [0F3V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3V)] and sketch the argument, which
works with closed subschemes of $T$ rather than closed subsets of $V$. Let
$\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2$ be ideals of finite type on $T$ cutting out
closed subschemes $Z_1,Z_2$ that are disjoint over $V$ and restrict
to $F_1,F_2$ there. Producing such ideals on all of $T$ is where
constructibility and finite presentation are needed. Since
$\mathcal I_1+\mathcal I_2$ is the unit ideal over $V$, its blow-up
is $V$-admissible. On each affine chart the extended ideal is
generated by a single element of $\mathcal I_1$ or of $\mathcal I_2$.
On a chart where it is generated by $f\in\mathcal I_1$, the strict
transform of $Z_1$ is obtained from its inverse image by dividing out
the $f$-power torsion. Since $f$ vanishes on $Z_1$, every element of
the ring of the inverse image is killed by $f$. Hence the strict
transform of $Z_1$ does not meet that chart. The same holds for
$Z_2$ on the other charts, and therefore the strict transforms of $Z_1$
and $Z_2$ are disjoint [Stacks, [080P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080P)].
In the Noetherian applications below, every closed subset is
constructible and its reduced ideal is of finite type.

points. On these points taking sections is exact
because $k$ is algebraically closed, and the sections are the
product, here a finite direct sum, of the stalks, which do not
change under extension of $k$. Finally, Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms-cohomology] carries these assertions over to $C$.
