Since a middle extension has no punctual subobject or
quotient and $M$ is irreducible on the open, the
middle extension is simple. Conversely, ordinary truncation splits an arbitrary perverse
sheaf into a punctual part and a part of the form $F[1]$, and
simplicity forces one of them to vanish.

We first show that $P=(j_*M)[1]$ has no punctual subobject or quotient.
The adjunction calculations below are geometric, so they apply equally
to compatible Weil morphisms. Let $i$ be the inclusion of a finite set
of closed points and $A$ a sheaf on it. A map $P\to i_*A$ is zero, because by
adjunction it corresponds to a map from $i^*P=(i^*j_*M)[1]$ to the
sheaf $A$, that is, to a negative Ext. A map in the other direction is
also zero, and to see this we first enlarge the boundary. Since $M$ is lisse, $j_*M$ does not change when we replace $U$
by a smaller dense open and $M$ by its restriction, so we may assume that the support of $A$ lies in
$Z=C\setminus U$, and we let $i$ now denote the inclusion of $Z$. Then the
adjunction $j^*\dashv Rj_*$ shows that $i^!Rj_*M=0$. In the triangle

$$
j_*M\longrightarrow Rj_*M\longrightarrow
\tau^{\ge1}Rj_*M\longrightarrow
$$

the last term is supported on $Z$, so that $i^!$ agrees with $i^*$ on
it. Applying $i^!$ and using $i^!Rj_*M=0$, we find
$i^!j_*M\simeq(i^*\tau^{\ge1}Rj_*M)[-1]$, which has ordinary
cohomology only in degrees at least two. Hence $i^!P$ has ordinary
cohomology only in degrees at least one.
Therefore $\Hom(i_*A,P)=\Hom(A,i^!P)=0$.

To see that $P$ is simple, note that on a dense open a
perverse subobject of $P$ is a shifted lisse subsheaf of $M$. By
irreducibility it is $0$ or everything there, and the difference is
then punctual. In detail, consider a perverse exact sequence
$0\to Q\to P\to R\to0$, restrict it to a smaller dense open on which
all ordinary cohomology sheaves are lisse. There $P=M[1]$, and the
sequence is a shifted exact sequence of lisse sheaves. Moreover, restriction to
a dense open preserves irreducibility, because the fundamental group
of a dense open of a normal connected curve surjects onto that of the
curve, as in the proof of Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves], and the same
holds for the Weil groups. Hence $Q$ or $R$ has zero generic
restriction. Such a perverse object is
punctual. Indeed, its $\mathcal H^{-1}$ is then supported on a finite
set, and a sheaf without punctual subsheaves with this property is
zero, while its $\mathcal H^0$ is punctual by definition. Thus $Q$ or $R$
is a punctual subobject or quotient of $P$, which by the vanishing just
proved is zero, and so $P$ is simple.

Conversely, let $P$ be simple. We show that $P$ is punctual or a middle
extension of an irreducible lisse sheaf. Ordinary truncation gives a
perverse exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow(\mathcal H^{-1}P)[1]
\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow\mathcal H^0P\longrightarrow0.
$$

Hence a simple $P$ is either punctual or of the form $F[1]$, where $F$
has no punctual subsheaf. In the second case, choose a dense open $U$
on which $F$ is lisse and put $M=F|_U$.
Then the map $F\to j_*M$ is injective, since its kernel is $F_{\rm p}=0$
(Lemma [lemma-largest-punctual-subsheaf]),
and its cokernel $B$ is punctual. Rotating the corresponding triangle of sheaves we obtain the perverse
exact sequence $0\to B\to F[1]\to(j_*M)[1]\to0$, whose last term is
nonzero, so $B=0$ by simplicity. It remains to see that $M$ is
irreducible. Suppose that $M$ had a proper nonzero
lisse subsheaf $M_1$. Then the object $j_!M_1[1]$ is perverse, because
$j_!M_1\subset j_*M_1$ has no punctual subsheaf, and the image of
$j_!M_1[1]\to P$ in the abelian heart is proper and nonzero, as one
sees on $U$. This contradicts simplicity. Finally, if $P$ is punctual, then by the
long exact cohomology sequence its subobjects in the heart are
punctual sheaves in degree zero, so $P$ is simple exactly when it is
irreducible as a punctual sheaf.

We write $Rf_*L$ as the dual of $Rf_!N$ for a suitable constructible
$N$. The point is that constructibility and base change are known for $Rf_!N$, and over a dense open of $S$ the cohomology sheaves of $Rf_!N$ are locally
constant, and there dualizing preserves both properties.

By Proposition [proposition-locally-constant-sheaves-finite-presentation], the locally
constant sheaf $L$ comes from a locally constant sheaf on the étale
site, and we work with the latter.

Since $X$ is the disjoint union of finitely many open pieces of pure
relative dimension, we may assume that $f$ has pure relative dimension
$d$. Let $\omega_f=f^!\mathbf F_{\ell,S}$ as in
Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism], and let

$$
N=\cHom_X(L,\mathbf F_{\ell,X})\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f .
$$

By Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism], $\omega_f$ is locally
$\mathbf F_{\ell,X}(d)[2d]$. Hence $N$ is bounded constructible and
$\cHom_X(N,\omega_f)=L$.

*Duality.* Consider the pairing

$$
Rf_!N\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_*L
\longrightarrow Rf_!(N\otimes^{\mathbf L}L)
\longrightarrow Rf_!\omega_f
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_{\mathbf F_{\ell,S}}}\mathbf F_{\ell,S},
\tag{6.15}
$$

where the first arrow is the projection formula followed by the counit
$f^*Rf_*L\to L$, and the second is evaluation. Its adjoint is a map

$$
\delta_L:Rf_*L
\longrightarrow \cHom_S(Rf_!N,\mathbf F_{\ell,S}),
\tag{6.16}
$$

and we claim that it is an isomorphism.
Since the map is an adjoint transpose, we test it on Hom groups out of a
family of generators, where adjunctions turn one side into the other.
To this end we write $L=\cHom_X(N,f^!\mathbf F_{\ell,S})$, and test
$\delta_L$ on the objects $P[n]$, where $P=u_!\Fell$
and $u:V\to S$ is quasi-compact, separated and étale. The objects $u_!\Fell$ are constructible of finite Tor amplitude, and their shifts detect
isomorphisms in $D(S_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$. Since
$f^*P\otimes^{\mathbf L}N$ lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Fell)$, we may use tensor-Hom
adjunction, the adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ of
Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image] between
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Fell))$ and $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(S,\Fell))$, and the projection
formula. With Hom groups in $D(S_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$, we then obtain

$$
\Hom(P,Rf_*\cHom(N,f^!\mathbf F_{\ell,S}))
=\Hom(Rf_!(f^*P\otimes^{\mathbf L}N),\mathbf F_{\ell,S})
=\Hom(P\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_!N,\mathbf F_{\ell,S}).
$$

By tensor-Hom adjunction, the last group is
$\Hom(P,\cHom_S(Rf_!N,\mathbf F_{\ell,S}))$. Unwinding the
adjunctions, one sees that the composite bijection is the map induced by
$\delta_L$, for every shift of $P$. Hence $\delta_L$
is an isomorphism.

*Shrinking the base.* Since $\delta_L$ is an isomorphism, it now suffices to
understand the dual of $Rf_!N$. By the finiteness theorem for $Rf_!$
[Stacks, [0GL0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL0), [0G2A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0G2A)], the complex $Rf_!N$ is bounded constructible. A
constructible sheaf on the integral scheme $S$ is locally constant on a
nonempty open subset. Thus each of the finitely many nonzero cohomology
sheaves of $Rf_!N$ is locally constant on a nonempty open of $S$. Let $S_0$
be the intersection of these opens; it is nonempty because $S$ is
irreducible.

Over the field $\Fell$, a finite locally constant sheaf is locally free of
finite rank. Its dual is exact, and evaluation identifies it with its
double dual. We now argue by induction on the number of nonzero cohomology
sheaves, using that the relevant canonical maps form morphisms of the
truncation triangles. In this way we see that a bounded complex with finite
locally constant cohomology is dualizable, that its dual is again of this
kind, and that forming the dual commutes with every pullback. Through
$\delta_L$, this proves the first assertion over $S_0$.

*Base change.* The duality $\delta_L$ exchanges $Rf_*L$ with
the dual of $Rf_!N$, and $Rf_!N$ satisfies base change. We show that the
duality is compatible with base change; then $Rf_*L$ satisfies base change
too. Let $v:T\to S_0$ be a
$k$-scheme of finite type over $S_0$, and let $f_T:X_T\to T$ and
$v_X:X_T\to X$ be the base changes. First, base change for $Rf_!$ and (6.1) identify $v_X^*N$, $v^*Rf_!N$ and $v_X^*\omega_f$ with the
corresponding objects for $f_T$. Next, the base change map $v^*Rf_*L\to Rf_{T,*}v_X^*L$ is characterized by the fact that it
carries the pullback of the counit $f^*Rf_*L\to L$ to the counit for
$f_T$. Hence the pullback of (6.15) is the pairing for
$f_T$, composed with this base change map. Finally, the complex $v^*Rf_!N$ is dualizable with dual $v^*\cHom(Rf_!N,\mathbf F_{\ell,S})$. Therefore the
base change map for $Rf_*L$ is identified with the dual of the base change
isomorphism for $Rf_!N$, and it is an isomorphism.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-smooth-morphisms-locally-constant-sheaves], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The adjunction is a composite of two standard adjunctions of ringed topoi.
For the equivalence we check that the unit is an isomorphism on $\Dbc$ and
that the counit is an isomorphism on normalized constructible towers. The
second is the substantial point, since there we must show that the limit of such
a tower is again constructible.

The adjunction is $Lh^*p^{-1}\dashv Rp_*h_*$, for the change of rings $h$ from towers to
constant inverse systems of $\mathcal O_{E,T}$-modules and the morphism $p$ to $T_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$
with $p_*=\varprojlim$ [Stacks, [06YV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YV), [07A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07A6)]. By
Proposition [proposition-sp-integral-towers](1), $\operatorname{red}_T$ maps
$\Dbc(T,\mathcal O_E)$ into normalized constructible towers. On $\Dbc$ the
unit is an isomorphism, since objects of $\Dbc$ are derived complete.

Conversely, let $C_\bullet$ be normalized and put $C=R\varprojlim C_n$. The
key point is that $C/\ell^m\simeq C_m$. Indeed, the complex $C/\ell^m$ differs from
$C_m$ by the derived limit of the tower $(C_m[1])_n$ with transition maps
multiplication by $\ell$, and this limit vanishes, because $\ell^m$ kills $C_m$
and so any $m$ consecutive transition maps compose to zero. Consequently
$C$ is derived complete and $C/\ell\simeq C_1$ is constructible. Moreover
$C$ is bounded, because the $C_n$ have cohomology in a fixed interval, and
on the replete topos $T_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ derived limits of such towers increase the
range by at most one [Stacks, [0940](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0940)]. Therefore
$C\in\Dbc(T,\mathcal O_E)$ by Proposition [proposition-sp-integral-towers](2). Finally, the counit
$\operatorname{red}_TC\to C_\bullet$ is at level $m$ the reduction map
$C/\ell^m\to C_m$, which is an isomorphism by what we just showed. Since
evaluations detect isomorphisms, the counit is an isomorphism.

Since weakly étale means that a morphism and its diagonal are flat,
each assertion about weakly étale morphisms comes down to writing the
relevant diagonal in terms of diagonals and base changes that we already
know to be flat.

Base change preserves flatness of a morphism and its diagonal. For a
composite $V\to U\to X$, the morphism $V\to X$ is flat as a composite of
flat morphisms. Its diagonal $\Delta_{V/X}$ is $\Delta_{V/U}$ followed by
$V\times_UV\to V\times_XV$, and the second map is a base change of
$\Delta_{U/X}$. Both maps are flat, and hence so is $\Delta_{V/X}$.

Let $h:U\to V$ be an $X$-morphism between weakly étale $X$-schemes. We
factor $h$ as the graph $U\to U\times_XV$ followed by the projection
$U\times_XV\to V$. The graph is a base change of the diagonal of $V/X$,
which is flat, and the projection is a base change of $U\to X$, which is also
flat. Their composite $h$ is therefore flat. Similarly, the diagonal $\Delta_h:U\to
U\times_VU$ is the base change of $\Delta_{U/X}$ along the monomorphism
$U\times_VU\to U\times_XU$, so it is flat as well. Finally, Zariski locality
follows from the fact that flatness is Zariski local.

On affine charts, the diagonal of
$\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is the closed immersion
$\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_RB)$ given by the
multiplication map, so the morphism is weakly étale exactly when
$R\to B$ and $B\otimes_RB\to B$ are flat. By Zariski locality on source and
target, this describes weakly étale morphisms on any affine charts.

For ind-étale ring maps, base change is clear because tensor products
commute with filtered colimits. For composition, let $R\to B$ and $B\to C$
be ind-étale, with $B=\varinjlim_\alpha B_\alpha$. Each étale
$B$-algebra $C'$ occurring in a presentation of $C$ is of finite
presentation over $B$, hence is the base change of an étale algebra
$C'_\alpha$ over some $B_\alpha$. Since $B_\alpha$ is étale over $R$,
so is $C'_\alpha$, and $C'$ is the filtered colimit of the étale
$R$-algebras $C'_\alpha\otimes_{B_\alpha}B_\beta$ for $\beta\geq\alpha$.
Thus $C$ is a filtered colimit of ind-étale $R$-algebras, and such a
colimit is again ind-étale [Stacks, [097L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097L)].

The morphism obtained by base change is flat because flatness is stable under base change. Its diagonal is the corresponding base change of the original diagonal and is therefore flat. These are exactly the two conditions for weak étaleness.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

For $V\to U\to X$, the composite $V\to X$ is flat. Its diagonal factors as $\Delta_{V/U}$ followed by $V\times_UV\to V\times_XV$. The second map is a base change of $\Delta_{U/X}$. Both factors are flat, hence so is the diagonal of $V\to X$.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

Flatness of $U\to X$ is local on $U$. The diagonal can be checked near every point of its source $U$; after replacing $U$ by an open neighbourhood, its restriction is the diagonal for that neighbourhood. Thus the two required flatness conditions hold on $U$ if they hold on a Zariski cover.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

A Zariski cover of $X$ pulls back to a cover of $U$ and of $U\times_XU$. On these covers the morphism and its diagonal are the corresponding base changes. Since flatness is local on the target, their flatness is equivalent to flatness after this cover.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

Let $h:U\to V$ be an $X$-morphism between weakly étale $X$-schemes. We
factor $h$ as the graph $U\to U\times_XV$ followed by the projection
$U\times_XV\to V$. The graph is a base change of the diagonal of $V/X$,
which is flat. The projection is a base change of $U\to X$, which is also
flat. Their composite $h$ is therefore flat. The diagonal $\Delta_h:U\to
U\times_VU$ is the base change of $\Delta_{U/X}$ along the monomorphism
$U\times_VU\to U\times_XU$, so it is flat as well. Zariski locality
follows from the fact that flatness is Zariski local.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

Write $B=\varinjlim_\alpha B_\alpha$ with $B_\alpha$ étale over $R$. For an $R$-algebra $R'$, tensor product gives $B\otimes_RR'=\varinjlim_\alpha(B_\alpha\otimes_RR')$. Each algebra in the latter system is étale over $R'$, so the base-changed map is ind-étale.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

be ind-étale, with $B=\varinjlim_\alpha B_\alpha$. Each étale
$B$-algebra $C'$ occurring in a presentation of $C$ is of finite
presentation over $B$, hence is the base change of an étale algebra
$C'_\alpha$ over some $B_\alpha$. Since $B_\alpha$ is étale over $R$,
so is $C'_\alpha$, and $C'$ is the filtered colimit of the étale
$R$-algebras $C'_\alpha\otimes_{B_\alpha}B_\beta$ for $\beta\geq\alpha$.
Thus $C$ is a filtered colimit of ind-étale $R$-algebras, and such a
colimit is again ind-étale [Stacks, [097L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097L)].

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

The diagonal of $\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is the closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_RB)$ given by the multiplication map. Hence the morphism and its diagonal are flat exactly when $R\to B$ and $B\otimes_RB\to B$ are flat, which is the definition of weak étaleness.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-stability].

In both assertions we compare a closed subgroup with $G$, namely the
stabilizer of a subspace in the first and the kernel of the adjoint
representation in the second. We compute the Lie algebra of this
subgroup with dual numbers and conclude with
Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms](3).

Let $U\subseteq M$ be a subspace. In a basis of $M$ extending a basis
of $U$, the scheme-theoretic stabilizer $S\subseteq G$ of $U$ is the
closed subgroup defined by the vanishing of the lower-left block of
$r(g)$. Since the lower-left block of $r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X)$
is $\varepsilon$ times that of $dr(X)$, we find

$$
\operatorname{Lie}(S)
=\{X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G):dr(X)U\subseteq U\}.
$$

If $U$ is $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$-stable, then
$\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, and
Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms](3) shows that $S=G$. Conversely, if
$U$ is $G$-stable, then $S=G$, and the displayed formula shows that $U$
is $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$-stable.

Put $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. We claim that the kernel of the
adjoint representation $G\to\GL(\mathfrak g)$ is the center. Indeed, if
$g$ acts trivially on $\mathfrak g$, consider the centralizer $C_G(g)$.
It is a closed subgroup scheme whose Lie algebra is the fixed space of
$\operatorname{Ad}(g)$, that is, all of $\mathfrak g$. So $C_G(g)=G$
by Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms](3). Conversely, a central element
acts trivially. Since the kernel and the center are reduced by
Cartier's theorem, their equality on $\Omega$-points is an equality of
schemes.

The Lie algebra of the center is now the kernel of a differential. The formula

$$
\operatorname{Ad}(1+\varepsilon X)(Y)=Y+\varepsilon[X,Y]
$$

shows that the differential of $\operatorname{Ad}$ is $\operatorname{ad}$.
The center is a closed subgroup of $\GL(V)$, so the dual-number
description applies to it. By this description, the Lie algebra of
the kernel of a representation is the kernel of its differential. Hence
$\operatorname{Lie}(Z(G))=\ker(\operatorname{ad})=Z(\mathfrak g)$.
By Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem], $Z(G)^\circ$ has the
same Lie algebra as $Z(G)$.

Every group scheme of finite type over a field is quasi-projective
[Stacks, [0BF7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BF7)]. A quasi-projective
proper scheme is projective [Stacks, [0B45](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B45)]. If $\mathcal L$ is ample, then
so is $[-1]^*\mathcal L$, since $[-1]$ is an automorphism, and the
tensor product $\mathcal N=\mathcal L\otimes[-1]^*\mathcal L$ of two ample
sheaves is ample. It is symmetric because $[-1]$ is an involution, which
interchanges the two factors.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-symmetric-ample-sheaf], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The two covers descend to finite flat morphisms $C_i'\to C_i$ of degree $d$
between smooth curves, where $C_i$ is an étale neighbourhood of $y$ in
$X$, étale away from $y$ and with a single point $y_i'$ over $y$
(Lemma [lemma-covers-degree-prime-to-ell](1)). Their product $C_1'\times C_2'\to C_1\times C_2$ is a finite flat morphism of degree $d^2$
of smooth surfaces, étale away from the two fibres through $y$, with
$y'$ the only point over $(y,y)$. Base change to the strict localization
$T$ of $C_1\times C_2$ at $(y,y)$ gives a scheme finite over $T$ with one
point over the closed point, hence local and strictly henselian, and this
is $T'$. This proves the assertions about $T'$ and $T'\to T$.

Choose uniformizers $\xi$ of $X_1'$ and $\eta$ of $X_2'$, so that the completed
local ring of $T'$ at $y'$ is $k[[\xi,\eta]]$. Since the residue field $k$
is algebraically closed, both covers are totally ramified, so $u$ is a unit
of $k[[\xi]]$ times $\xi^d$, and similarly for $v$. Multiplying $\xi$ and
$\eta$ by suitable $d$th roots of nonzero constants, we may assume that

$$
u\equiv\xi^d,\qquad v\equiv\eta^d\pmod{(\xi,\eta)^{d+1}}.
$$

Since $\Phi_X^m$ is purely inseparable of degree $q^m$ and fixes $y$, we
have $\operatorname{ord}_v\varphi=q^m>1$, and hence
$\varphi(v)\in(\eta)^{dq^m}\subseteq(\xi,\eta)^{d+1}$. It follows that the
pulled-back equations of $\Gamma'$, $V'$, $\Delta'$ and $H'$ have initial
forms

$$
\xi^d,\qquad\xi^d,\qquad\xi^d-\eta^d,\qquad\eta^d,
$$

respectively. The support of the tangent cone of a curve is the zero set of
the initial form of its equation, and it does not change when we pass to
the reduction, since if $J$ is the radical of $I$ and $J^n\subset I$ then
the ideals of initial forms satisfy $\mathrm{in}(J)^n\subset\mathrm{in}(I)
\subset\mathrm{in}(J)$. Thus the tangent cone of
$(\Gamma'\cup V')_{\mathrm{red}}$ is supported on the line $\xi=0$, that
of $H'_{\mathrm{red}}$ on $\eta=0$, and that of $\Delta'_{\mathrm{red}}$
on the lines $\xi=\zeta\eta$ with $\zeta^d=1$. This holds also when
$p\mid d$ and $\xi^d-\eta^d$ is a $p$th power. Away from the origin the
first support meets neither of the others. Finally $H'_{\mathrm{red}}$
is the curve $\eta=0$, which is regular.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-tangent-cones-on-cover], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Because $\varepsilon^2=0$, the map $a\mapsto1+\varepsilon a$ is a homomorphism,
and it gives an exact sequence of sheaves of groups on $X$

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow
\mathcal O_{X_\varepsilon}^\times\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X^\times
\longrightarrow1,
$$

split by the inclusion $\mathcal O_X^\times\subset
\mathcal O_{X_\varepsilon}^\times$. The schemes $X$ and
$X_\varepsilon$ have the same underlying space, so
$\operatorname{Pic}(X_\varepsilon)=H^1(X,\mathcal O_{X_\varepsilon}^\times)$.
Since the sequence is split, taking $H^1$ gives
$H^1(X,\mathcal O_{X_\varepsilon}^\times)=H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\oplus\operatorname{Pic}(X)$,
in which the restriction map is the projection to the second summand.
Hence the kernel is $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-tangent-space-picard-functor], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We construct the two filtrations and then compare simple factors by
the Jordan–Hölder argument. The tensor product is filtered
by the filtration on $V$, and each quotient
$A_a\otimes V'$ by the filtration on $V'$; since tensoring over a
field is exact, the quotients are as asserted.

For the exterior power we cannot simply filter factor by factor,
because a wedge product may use several vectors from the same
composition factor. Instead we sort wedges of basis vectors by how many
vectors they take from each factor, after lifting bases of the
$A_a$ to a basis of $V$ adapted to its filtration. Thus a wedge of basis vectors determines a tuple
$(n_a)$, by counting how many vectors it uses from each lifted basis.
Since the basis is adapted, the group $W(U_0)$ carries a lifted basis vector of $A_a$ into the span of the
lifted bases of $A_1,\ldots,A_a$. Hence the action is block upper triangular:
each term of the image of a basis wedge either has the same tuple or has a
tuple obtained from it by moving some of its vectors to smaller indices $a$.
Choose a total order on the tuples
compatible with these moves. Then the spans of the initial segments of
basis wedges form a stable filtration, and on the quotient indexed by
$(n_a)$ the diagonal blocks act as on
$\bigotimes_a\bigwedge^{n_a}A_a$, a space of dimension
$\prod_a\binom{\dim A_a}{n_a}>0$. For example, for $V$ an extension of $A_2$ by
$A_1$, both of dimension one, and $r=1$, the tuples are $(1,0)$ and
$(0,1)$, and the filtration is the given one. For $r=2$ there is the
single tuple $(1,1)$, and $\bigwedge^2V=A_1\otimes A_2$.

The graded pieces of the filtrations just built need not be simple, so to
compare simple factors we refine. By the Schreier refinement
theorem, any two finite filtrations have refinements with isomorphic
graded pieces, matched by the Zassenhaus isomorphism
$(V_{i-1}+V_i\cap W_j)/(V_{i-1}+V_i\cap W_{j-1})\simeq
(W_{j-1}+W_j\cap V_i)/(W_{j-1}+W_j\cap V_{i-1})$; for two
composition series this is the Jordan–Hölder theorem. Applying the same refinement to a composition series and to the tensor or
exterior filtration, we obtain the statement about simple factors. In
particular, these multisets do not change when $V$ and $V'$ are
replaced by their semisimplifications.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-tensor-exterior-powers-filtered-representations], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Write the group as $\nu_X^*G_0$. We may work on an affine open of $X$.
Using Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale] and finite affine
refinements, we refine a trivializing covering to a single faithfully
flat ind-étale affine $U\to X$, and we write $U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ with
$U_i$ affine étale over $X$. A trivialization over $U$ determines a
transition element in $\nu_X^*G_0(U\times_XU)$. By continuity for affine
limits it descends to $G_0(U_i\times_XU_i)$ for some $i$, and the cocycle
identity on the triple product holds after enlarging $i$. Since
$U\to X$ is surjective, each $U_i\to X$ is an étale covering. Gluing the
trivial torsor along this cocycle, we get an étale torsor whose
pullback is isomorphic to the given torsor. Hence the given torsor is
classical by Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image], and it is trivialized by
the étale covering $U_i\to X$. See [Stacks, [099X](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099X)].

The proof uses only that $P_t$ is proper and integral with
$H^0(P_t,\mathcal O_{P_t})=\kappa(t)$, which holds by [Stacks, [0BUG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BUG)]
because $P$ is proper and geometrically integral.

For (1), a trivial sheaf and its inverse both have the nonzero section
$1$, so only the converse needs an argument. On $\mathbf P^1$, for
instance, $\mathcal O(d)$ and $\mathcal O(-d)$ both have nonzero
sections only when $d=0$, and the general argument is the same. Let $s$ and $s'$ be nonzero
sections of $\mathcal L_t$ and $\mathcal L_t^{-1}$. Since $P_t$ is
integral, the product $ss'$ is a nonzero element of
$H^0(P_t,\mathcal O)=\kappa(t)$, hence a unit. Since $ss'$ would
vanish wherever $s$ does, the section $s$ vanishes nowhere, and it
trivializes $\mathcal L_t$.

For (2), note that by (1) the set in question is the intersection of
the loci where $\dim H^0(P_t,\mathcal L_t)$ and
$\dim H^0(P_t,\mathcal L_t^{-1})$ are positive. These loci are closed
because the functions $t\mapsto\dim H^0(P_t,\mathcal L_t^{\pm1})$ are
upper semicontinuous [Stacks, [0BDN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BDN)], as $\mathcal L$ is flat over $T$
and $f$ is proper.

We want a section of $\mathcal L$ over $X\times U$, where $X=P\times Q$,
that does not vanish on the fibre over $t$. Its zero locus then misses a
neighbourhood of that fibre. Such a section exists as soon as
$f_*\mathcal L$ is free of rank one near $t$, with formation compatible
with passage to the fibre.

To get this, we represent $Rf_*\mathcal L$, and the pushforwards of the
restrictions of $\mathcal L$ to the two slices, by complexes of free
modules whose differentials vanish at $t$. By the Künneth formula,
restriction from $H^1$ of the fibre to $H^1$ of the two slices is an
isomorphism. This forces the first differential of $Rf_*\mathcal L$ to
vanish after shrinking $T$. Then $H^0$ of $Rf_*\mathcal L$ is free of
rank one, as we need.

*Setup.* Since $X_{\bar k}=P_{\bar k}\times Q_{\bar k}$ is a
product of integral varieties, $X$ is geometrically integral
[Stacks, [05P3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/05P3)]. We may assume that $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ is affine,
and we let $\mathfrak p$ be the prime of $t$. Below, “shrinking $T$”
means replacing $R$ by $R_g$ for some $g\notin\mathfrak p$; everything
already constructed survives this. Consider the projections

$$
f:X\times T\to T,\qquad f_1:P\times T\to T,\qquad f_2:Q\times T\to T,
$$

and the restrictions $\mathcal L_1$ and $\mathcal L_2$ of $\mathcal L$ to
$P\times q_0\times T$ and $p_0\times Q\times T$, which are trivial. The complexes $E=Rf_*\mathcal L$ and
$E_i=Rf_{i*}\mathcal L_i$ are perfect, and their formation commutes
with base change [Stacks, [0B91](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B91)]. Restriction of sections gives a map
$E\to E_1\oplus E_2$, also compatible with base change.
Since $T$ is affine, $H^0(X\times T,\mathcal L)=H^0(E)$ and likewise for
$E_i$.

*Minimal complexes.* A perfect complex over a local ring can be
represented by a complex of free modules whose differentials vanish
modulo the maximal ideal; the ranks are then the dimensions of the
cohomology of the fibre. We use this to read off the ranks from the
fibre over $t$, where everything is trivial. To do so, put $h^j=\dim H^j(X_t,\mathcal O)$ and
$h_i^j=\dim H^j$ of $\mathcal O$ on the fibres $P_t$ and $Q_t$. Since
$\mathcal L$ is trivial on $X_t$ and the $\mathcal L_i$ are trivial,
$E\otimes^{\mathbf L}_R\kappa(t)$ and $E_i\otimes^{\mathbf L}_R\kappa(t)$
have cohomology of dimensions $h^j$ and $h_i^j$, with $h^0=h_i^0=1$.
After shrinking $T$ we may therefore represent $E$ and $E_i$ by
complexes of finite free modules

$$
R\xrightarrow{d}R^{h^1}\to R^{h^2}\to\cdots,\qquad
R\xrightarrow{d_i}R^{h_i^1}\to R^{h_i^2}\to\cdots
$$

whose differentials vanish modulo $\mathfrak p$ [Stacks, [0BCD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BCD)]. We
represent the map $E\to E_i$ by a map of complexes [Stacks, [064B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/064B)], with
components $a_i:R\to R$ in degree $0$ and $b_i:R^{h^1}\to R^{h_i^1}$ in
degree $1$. Since the differentials vanish modulo $\mathfrak p$, the map
$b_i\otimes\kappa(t)$ is the restriction map on $H^1$ of the fibre
over $t$.

We want to show that $d=0$ after shrinking $T$, since then
$H^0(E)=\ker d=R$ is free of rank one. The maps $b_i$ will let us
transfer this question to the $d_i$, which are easier because
$\mathcal L_i$ is trivial.

*The differentials $d_i$ vanish.* Fix a trivialization
$\mathcal L_1\simeq\mathcal O$, and let $u\in H^0(E_1)=\ker d_1\subset R$
be the section corresponding to $1$. Its image in
$H^0(E_1\otimes^{\mathbf L}\kappa(t))=H^0(P_t,\mathcal O)$ is $1\ne0$,
so $u\notin\mathfrak p$. Since $d_1(u)=u\,d_1(1)=0$, after inverting
$u$ we get $d_1=0$. The same argument gives $d_2=0$.

*The differential $d$ vanishes.* This step uses the two slices
together. If the map $(b_1,b_2)$ is an isomorphism, then $d$ is
determined by $d_1$ and $d_2$, and this condition can be checked on
the fibre. The map $(b_1,b_2)\otimes\kappa(t)$ is restriction from
$H^1(P_t\times Q_t,\mathcal O)$ to the slices $P_t\times q_0$ and
$p_0\times Q_t$. It is an isomorphism by
Lemma [lemma-h-1-structure-sheaf-product], and in particular
$h^1=h_1^1+h_2^1$. Hence the square matrix $(b_1,b_2)$ has determinant
outside $\mathfrak p$. After inverting this determinant, $(b_1,b_2)$ is
an isomorphism. Since the maps form a map of complexes, we have
$b_i\circ d=d_i\circ a_i=0$, and therefore $d=0$.

*Conclusion.* A generator of $H^0$ gives the trivialization. We
have $H^0(X\times T,\mathcal L)=H^0(E)=\ker d=R$, and
its generator $\sigma$ maps to a generator of
$H^0(E\otimes^{\mathbf L}\kappa(t))=H^0(X_t,\mathcal L_t)$. Since
$\mathcal L_t\simeq\mathcal O_{X_t}$ and $H^0(X_t,\mathcal O)=\kappa(t)$,
the section $\sigma$ vanishes nowhere on $X_t$. Its zero locus is
closed in $X\times T$ and disjoint from $X_t$. Since $f$ is proper,
its image in $T$ is a closed set not containing $t$. On the complement
$U$ of this image, $\sigma$ trivializes $\mathcal L$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-triviality-near-fibre], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

By left completeness (Proposition [proposition-left-completeness]),
$L\simeq R\varprojlim_n\tau_{\geq-n}L$, and derived sections preserve
derived inverse limits, so
$R\Gamma(W,L)\simeq R\varprojlim_nR\Gamma(W,\tau_{\geq-n}L)$. Each
$\tau_{\geq-n}L$ is bounded with classical cohomology sheaves in degrees
at most $b$, so by the hypothesis and the hypercohomology spectral
sequence, $R\Gamma(W,\tau_{\geq-n}L)$ has no cohomology above $b+e$. The
Milnor sequence for this tower of complexes of abelian groups, proved as
in Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence], expresses $H^j$ of the derived
limit through $\varprojlim^1$ of $H^{j-1}$ and $\varprojlim$ of $H^j$ of
the terms. Both vanish for $j>b+e+1$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-truncation-pro-etale-sections], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

As in the proof of Proposition [proposition-twisting-weight-zero-adding-dual], the local
eigenvalues of $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal L$ have absolute value one
after applying $\iota$, and those of the second summand are their
inverses, hence their complex conjugates. The extension by zero is
real as well, because its stalks outside the open are zero, and so its

This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-twisted-envelope], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first twist by a large power of an ample sheaf on $C$, which kills
$H^1$ and leaves many sections. Then we remove $k$-rational points one
at a time, each time lowering $h^0$ by one and keeping $H^1=0$, until
$h^0=1$. The twist is defined over $k$ because the points are.

Choose an ample invertible sheaf $\mathcal M$ on $C$. For $r\gg0$, Serre vanishing
and Riemann–Roch show that $\mathcal L\otimes\mathcal M_{k'}^{\otimes r}$
has vanishing $H^1$ and a positive-dimensional space of sections.
As long as $h^0$ is larger than $1$, we choose a nonzero section and
a point $x\in C(k)$ where that section is nonzero. Such a point exists:
the zero divisor of the section is finite, so its image in $C$ is a
finite set, and the complement of this set is a nonempty open of $C$.
This open contains a point of $C(k)$, because the $k$-rational points of a smooth
$k$-scheme are dense when $k$ is separably closed [Stacks, [056U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/056U)].
For the current sheaf $\mathcal F$, consider the sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathcal F(-x_{k'})
\longrightarrow\mathcal F
\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_{x_{k'}}\longrightarrow0
$$

The chosen section does not vanish at $x_{k'}$, so the map
$H^0(C_{k'},\mathcal F)\to\mathcal F|_{x_{k'}}$ is onto the one-dimensional
fibre. By the long exact sequence, subtracting $x_{k'}$ lowers $h^0$ by
exactly $1$ and preserves $H^1=0$. We continue in this way until $h^0=1$. Since all
subtracted points come from $k$, the resulting twist has the form
$\mathcal M_0=\mathcal M^{\otimes r}(-x_1-\cdots-x_s)$ on $C$.
Finally, normalizing along $P$ does not change the dimensions of fibre
cohomology, so the rigidified twist satisfies the same conditions
(see [Stacks, [0B9Y](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9Y)]).
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-twisting-h-0-1-h], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

*Reduction to a lattice.* The vanishing statement is stable under
extensions: if $R^qp_*$ vanishes for $q>2d+1$ on two
sheaves, it vanishes on every extension of one by the other. By Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](3), every
$M\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is a finite extension of sheaves $a_!L$, with
$a:S\hookrightarrow X$ a locally closed immersion and $L$ lisse. Moreover, for $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, $L$ is the scalar extension $\QbarX\otimes_{E}L_E$ of a
lisse $E_S$-module $L_E$ for some finite $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$
(Lemma [lemma-descent-lisse-qbar-sheaves-finite]). For $\Lambda=E$, we simply put $L_E=L$. In both cases we may refine $S$ by a finite stratification, since this
replaces $a_!L$ by a finite extension of sheaves of the same form. By
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification], after such a
refinement $L_E$ contains a lattice $L_0$,
locally free of finite rank over $\mathcal O_{E,S}$, with $L_0[1/\ell]=L_E$. Hence it is
enough to prove the bound for $a_!L_0$, and then to pass to
$a_!L_E=(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$ and, if $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, to its scalar
extension $a_!L$.

In the passage to the limit below we use that the sheaf $a_!L_0$ is
derived $\pi_E$-complete. To see this, note that $a$ is a closed
immersion composed with a quasi-compact open immersion. Closed pushforward
is exact and preserves products [Stacks, [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)], and extension by zero is
exact and preserves limits [Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)]. Therefore both functors preserve
the derived inverse limit that expresses the completeness of $L_0$.

*The torsion bound.* Over the objects $V$ that compute $R^qp_*$,
the reductions $a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)$ have cohomology only up to degree $2d$. Fix an affine weakly contractible $V\to Y$ and
let $p_V:X_V\to V$ be the base change of $p$, which is proper with the same
bound $d$. Since $L_0$ is flat, $a_!L_0\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}
\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ is the sheaf $a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)$, which is the pullback
to the pro-étale site of a classical constructible étale sheaf of
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$-modules. Since the scheme $V$ is not Noetherian, we use the proper vanishing theorem in the generality of [Stacks, [095U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095U)]: if a
proper morphism has geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, then its
higher direct images of torsion sheaves vanish in degrees $q>2d$.
With the comparison [Stacks, [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)] of étale and pro-étale direct
images, this theorem for $p_V$ says that $R^qp_{V,*}$ of this sheaf
vanishes for $q>2d$. As $V$ is weakly contractible, $\Gamma(V,-)$ is
exact on all pro-étale sheaves [Stacks, [0991](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0991)]. Hence
$H^q(X_V,-)=\Gamma(V,R^qp_{V,*}(-))$, and

$$
H^q\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)=0\quad(q>2d).
$$

*The limit.* Derived completeness lets us pass from the reductions
to $a_!L_0$. Since restriction to $X_V$ is exact and commutes with products, hence with derived inverse limits, completeness gives
$(a_!L_0)|_{X_V}\simeq R\varprojlim_n a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)|_{X_V}$.
Derived global sections, too, commute with derived inverse limits, since a
product of K-injective complexes is K-injective and sections preserve
products. The Milnor exact sequence of Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence]

$$
0\to{\textstyle\varprojlim^1_n}H^{q-1}\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)
\to H^q(X_V,a_!L_0)
\to\varprojlim_nH^q\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)\to0
$$

then shows that $H^q(X_V,a_!L_0)=0$ for $q>2d+1$, since for such $q$ both
outer terms vanish by the torsion bound.

*Back to $\Lambda$.* The remaining passages are filtered colimits.
By Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], cohomology on the
quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme $X_V$ commutes with them. For instance, the sheaf $(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$ is the filtered colimit of $a_!L_0$ along multiplication
by $\ell$, and so it has the same vanishing. For $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, scalar extension from $E$ to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is the
filtered colimit of the extensions to finite $E'\supset E$. Since $E'$ is
finite free over $E$, each of these
is, as a sheaf of abelian groups, a finite direct sum of copies of the
original sheaf. Hence the continuity lemma again gives the bound. As $V$ was an
arbitrary affine weakly contractible object, formula
(5.5) shows that
$R^qp_*(a_!L)=0$ for $q>2d+1$. By the first step, $R^qp_*M=0$ for $q>2d+1$
and every $M\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$.

*Passage to $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$.* For constructible $M$ we have
$R^qp_*M\in\Cons(Y,\Lambda)$, because $Rp_*$ maps
$\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ into $\Dbc(Y,\Lambda)$ by
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-constructible-complexes].
Moreover, every object of $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ is a filtered colimit of
constructible sheaves, and $R^qp_*$ commutes with filtered colimits and
direct sums by Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]. All three assertions for $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ therefore follow.

*Reduction to a lattice.* The vanishing statement is stable under
extensions: if $R^qp_*$ vanishes for $q>2d+1$ on two
sheaves, it vanishes on every extension of one by the other. By Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](3), every
$M\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is a finite extension of sheaves $a_!L$, with
$a:S\hookrightarrow X$ a locally closed immersion and $L$ lisse. For
$\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, $L$ is the scalar extension $\QbarX\otimes_{E}L_E$ of a
lisse $E_S$-module $L_E$ for some finite $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$
(Lemma [lemma-descent-lisse-qbar-sheaves-finite]). For $\Lambda=E$, we put
$L_E=L$. We may refine $S$ by a finite stratification, since this
replaces $a_!L$ by a finite extension of sheaves of the same form. By
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification], after such a
refinement $L_E$ contains a lattice $L_0$,
locally free of finite rank over $\mathcal O_{E,S}$, with $L_0[1/\ell]=L_E$. Hence it is
enough to prove the bound for $a_!L_0$, and then to pass to
$a_!L_E=(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$ and, if $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, to its scalar
extension $a_!L$.

In the passage to the limit below we use that the sheaf $a_!L_0$ is
derived $\pi_E$-complete. To see this, note that $a$ is a closed
immersion composed with a quasi-compact open immersion. Closed pushforward
is exact and preserves products [Stacks, [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)], and extension by zero is
exact and preserves limits [Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)]. Therefore both functors preserve
the derived inverse limit that expresses the completeness of $L_0$.

*The torsion bound.* Over the objects $V$ that compute $R^qp_*$,
the reductions $a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)$ have cohomology only up to degree $2d$. Fix an affine weakly contractible $V\to Y$ and
let $p_V:X_V\to V$ be the base change of $p$, which is proper with the same
bound $d$. Since $L_0$ is flat, $a_!L_0\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}
\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ is the sheaf $a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)$, which is the pullback
to the pro-étale site of a classical constructible étale sheaf of
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$-modules. The scheme $V$ is not Noetherian, so we use
the proper vanishing theorem in the generality of [Stacks, [095U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095U)]: if a
proper morphism has geometric fibres of dimension at most $d$, then its
higher direct images of torsion sheaves vanish in degrees $q>2d$.
With the comparison [Stacks, [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)] of étale and pro-étale direct
images, this theorem for $p_V$ says that $R^qp_{V,*}$ of this sheaf
vanishes for $q>2d$. As $V$ is weakly contractible, $\Gamma(V,-)$ is
exact on all pro-étale sheaves [Stacks, [0991](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0991)]. Hence
$H^q(X_V,-)=\Gamma(V,R^qp_{V,*}(-))$, and

$$
H^q\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)=0\quad(q>2d).
$$

*The limit.* Derived completeness lets us pass from the reductions
to $a_!L_0$. Restriction to $X_V$ is exact and commutes with
products, hence with derived inverse limits. Completeness therefore gives
$(a_!L_0)|_{X_V}\simeq R\varprojlim_n a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)|_{X_V}$.
Derived global sections also commute with derived inverse limits, since a
product of K-injective complexes is K-injective and sections preserve
products. The Milnor exact sequence of Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence]

$$
0\to{\textstyle\varprojlim^1_n}H^{q-1}\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)
\to H^q(X_V,a_!L_0)
\to\varprojlim_nH^q\bigl(X_V,a_!(L_0/\pi_E^n)\bigr)\to0
$$

then shows that $H^q(X_V,a_!L_0)=0$ for $q>2d+1$, since for such $q$ both
outer terms vanish by the torsion bound.

*Back to $\Lambda$.* The remaining passages are filtered colimits.
By Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], cohomology on the
quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme $X_V$ commutes with them. The sheaf
$(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$ is the filtered colimit of $a_!L_0$ along multiplication
by $\ell$, and so it has the same vanishing. For $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, scalar extension from $E$ to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is the
filtered colimit of the extensions to finite $E'\supset E$. Since $E'$ is
finite free over $E$, each of these
is, as a sheaf of abelian groups, a finite direct sum of copies of the
original sheaf. The continuity lemma again gives the bound. As $V$ was an
arbitrary affine weakly contractible object, formula
(5.5) shows that
$R^qp_*(a_!L)=0$ for $q>2d+1$. By the first step, $R^qp_*M=0$ for $q>2d+1$
and every $M\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$.

*Passage to $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$.* For constructible $M$ we have
$R^qp_*M\in\Cons(Y,\Lambda)$, because $Rp_*$ maps
$\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ into $\Dbc(Y,\Lambda)$ by
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-constructible-complexes].
Every object of $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ is a filtered colimit of
constructible sheaves, and $R^qp_*$ commutes with filtered colimits and
direct sums by Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]. All three
assertions for $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ follow.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image].

Compute $R^qp_*$ on the weakly contractible affine basis used in clause [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image--1]. Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology] makes these cohomology functors commute with filtered colimits. Every direct sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums, and cohomology is additive on finite sums. The direct-sum comparison is therefore an isomorphism on that basis and hence an isomorphism of sheaves.

*Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image].

We write both cohomologies as colimits of étale cohomology of
schemes of finite type over $k$ and bound these uniformly. Write
$U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ and $V=\varprojlim_iV_i$ with $U_i$ affine
étale over $X$ and $V_i$ affine étale over $Y$, and write
$F=\nu_X^*F_{\acute{e}t}$ (Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image]).
By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], applied
to the schemes $U$ and $X\times_YV$, the cohomology of $F$ on them is the
étale cohomology of $F_{\acute{e}t}$. As $U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ and
$X\times_YV=\varprojlim_iX\times_YV_i$ are limits of qcqs schemes with
affine transition maps, [Stacks, [03Q6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q6)] identifies this with the colimit of
the étale cohomology on the $U_i$, respectively on the $X\times_YV_i$.
Each $U_i$ is affine of finite
type over $k$ with $\dim(U_i)\leq\dim(X)$, so by [Stacks, [0F0V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0V)] we have
$\operatorname{cd}_\ell(U_i)\leq d$ for sheaves of $A$-modules. To bound
cohomology on $X\times_YV_i$ independently of $i$, we choose a finite
affine open cover of $X$, with $r$ members. Since $X$ and $Y$ are
separated over $k$, its intersections and their pullbacks to the affine
$V_i$ are affine; each pullback is étale over the corresponding
intersection and has dimension at most $\dim(X)$. The alternating
Čech complex has length $r-1$, so the Čech spectral sequence
gives the bound $c=d+r-1$. The last assertion is [Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)], which
applies because $g$ is of finite type over a field with
$\operatorname{cd}_\ell(k)<\infty$
(Lemma [lemma-cohomological-dimension-base-field]).

Write $U=\varprojlim_iU_i$, with $U_i$ affine étale over $X$, and $F=\nu_X^*F_{\acute{e}t}$. The bounded-below cohomology comparison and [Stacks, [03Q6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q6)] identify $H^q(U,F)$ with the filtered colimit of $H^q(U_i,F_{\acute{e}t})$. *Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-uniform-bounds-pro-etale-affines].

Choose a finite affine cover of $X$ with $r$ members and write $V=\varprojlim_iV_i$, with $V_i$ affine étale over $Y$. *Source:* the proof of Lemma [lemma-uniform-bounds-pro-etale-affines].

Lemma [lemma-ext-bound-lattices] and inverting $\pi_E$, and reduce

*Reduction to strata.* Bounds pass to extensions in either variable.
Indeed, if $0\to C'\to C\to C''\to0$ is exact, then in the long exact
sequence $\Ext^q(C'',N)\to\Ext^q(C,N)\to\Ext^q(C',N)$ the outer groups
vanish above the larger of the two bounds for $C'$ and $C''$, and so the
middle one does too. Hence a bound that holds for every subquotient of a finite
filtration of the source holds for the source, if we take the maximum.
The same sequence in the second variable shows that a bound that holds
for every subquotient of a finite filtration of the target holds for the
target, with the same value.
In view of Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](3), we may therefore assume
$C=a_!L$, with $a=i\circ u:S\hookrightarrow Z\hookrightarrow X$ as in
Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme] and $L$ lisse. It suffices
to find an integer $d$, depending only on $a$ and $L$, with
$\Ext^q(a_!L,b_!M)=0$ for $q>d$, for all locally closed
$b:T\hookrightarrow X$ and lisse $M$ on $T$. Let
$j:X\setminus Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the open complement of $Z$. When $L$
contains a lisse $\mathcal O_E$-lattice, we show that
$d=\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+\operatorname{cd}_\ell(S)+2$ works.

*Lattices.* First take $\Lambda=E$. Since torsion arguments need
integral structures, we choose lattices. After refining the
stratifications (Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification]),
$L$ and $M$ contain lisse $\mathcal O_E$-lattices $L_0$ and $M_0$.
Refining is harmless, because it replaces $a_!L$ and $b_!M$ by finite extensions of sheaves of the same form, and the first step handles finite extensions.
Moreover, the refinement of the source stratum depends only on $L$, and that of the
target only on $M$. So the bound obtained for the refined source strata
is still independent of $N$.

The lattices are locally free of finite rank over $\mathcal O_E$. Indeed,
being lisse, they are locally of the form
$\mathcal O_{E,U}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P$ with $P$ finitely generated
(Definition [definition-lisse-sheaves]). As subsheaves of $E$-modules
they are torsion free, so $P$ is free. Lemma [lemma-ext-bound-lattices]
now gives $\Ext^q_{\mathcal O_E}(a_!L_0,b_!M_0)=0$ for

*Inverting $\pi_E$.* Inverting $\pi_E$ is a filtered colimit. By

$$

=R\!\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_E}\bigl(a_!L_0,(b_!M_0)[1/\pi_E]\bigr).

(5.1) implies the bound for $E$.

$$

The equalizer of the two maps is a closed
subscheme of $T$, since it is the inverse image of the diagonal of $Y/S$.
Its ideal restricts to zero on $U$, because the two maps agree there.
As a section of $\mathcal O_T$ that vanishes on a scheme-theoretically
dense open is zero, the ideal is zero and the equalizer is all of $T$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-uniqueness-maps-dense-open], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

A finite universal homeomorphism is a homeomorphism of underlying spaces,
so we may remove from $S$ the closed image of $S'\setminus U'$. The remaining
open $U$ is nonempty, and its inverse image $S'_U$ lies in $U'$. Over $U$
the morphisms $X'_U\to X_U$ and $Y'_U\to Y_U$ are finite universal
homeomorphisms, and pullback along them is therefore an equivalence of étale
topoi [Stacks, [03SI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SI)]. Such equivalences preserve constructibility in both
directions and commute with $Rj_*$. Hence pullback along these morphisms
detects boundedness and constructibility, and we get
$Rj_{U,*}(F|_{X_U})\in\Dbc(Y_U,\Fell)$.

For base change, let $T\to U$ be a $k$-scheme of finite type, with
projections $g_X:X_T\to X$ and $g_Y:Y_T\to Y$, and let

$$
\beta_T:g_Y^*Rj_*F\longrightarrow Rj_{T,*}g_X^*F
$$

be the base change map for $j$ along $T$. Put $T'=T\times_US'_U$. Then
$v:T'\to T$ is again a universal homeomorphism, and so are the induced maps
$v_X:X'_{T'}\to X_T$ and $v_Y:Y'_{T'}\to Y_T$, each a thickening followed by
a base change of $v$. Let $\beta'_{T'}:g_{Y'}^*Rj'_*F'\to Rj'_{T',*}g_{X'}^*F'$ be the
base change map for $j'$ along $T'$. Base change maps compose
[Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)], and $v_Y^*Rj_{T,*}\simeq Rj'_{T',*}v_X^*$ because $v_X^*$ and
$v_Y^*$ are equivalences of étale topoi [Stacks, [03SI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SI)]. Hence $v_Y^*\beta_T$ is
identified with $\beta'_{T'}$. The map $\beta'_{T'}$ is an isomorphism by
assumption, so $v_Y^*\beta_T$ is one. Since $v_Y^*$ is an equivalence, it is
conservative, and therefore $\beta_T$ is an isomorphism.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-universal-homeomorphism-base], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For $a\ne0$ the sheaf $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ is ramified at infinity,
and the trivial character is excluded because $M$ is irreducible and
not geometrically constant, its geometric restriction being semisimple. For the first
point, write $t=1/x$ and express the character by
the Artin–Schreier equation $u^p-u=c/t$ with $c\ne0$. Let $v$ be the
normalized valuation of the field generated by a root $u$ over the
completion $k((t))$ at infinity, and let $e$ be the ramification
index, so that $v(t)=e$ and $e\le p$. Since $v(c/t)=-e<0$, we must
have $v(u)<0$, so that $v(u^p)=pv(u)<v(u)$ and
$v(u^p-u)=pv(u)$. Now $pv(u)=-e$ forces $p\mid e$, and so
$e=p$: the cover is totally ramified. Inertia at
infinity therefore maps onto the Galois group $\mathbf F_p$ of this cover, on
which $\psi$ is nontrivial. Since $M$ is unramified at infinity, this
proves the first point, because a character that is nontrivial on
inertia cannot be a constituent of a representation on which
inertia acts trivially.

For the trivial character, we apply
Lemma [lemma-restriction-normal-subgroup] to the geometric
fundamental group, which is normal in the Weil group: the restriction
of $M$ to it is semisimple, and so a
trivial geometric constituent gives nonzero geometric invariants.
Since this space of invariants is Weil-stable, the irreducibility of
$M$ shows that $M$ is geometrically constant.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-unramified-at-infinity-no-linear-characters], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For a constant sheaf extended by zero, a smooth map
$X\to\mathbf A^1$ near the generic point reduces the claim to
Lemma [lemma-case-z-v-x-m]. Near the generic point, a general sheaf
is $j_!G$ with $G$ locally constant. After a finite étale cover, $G$
becomes constant, while the cokernel of the unit of the cover is again of
the form $j_!G'$. Passing to this cokernel shifts the cohomological
degree by one, so an induction on the degree proves the claim for all
$G$ at once.

Since the question is local at a generic point $\zeta$ of $Z$, we may
discard the other irreducible components of $X$ and $Z$.  Consider first
$L=j_!M_U$, where $U=X\setminus Z$ and $M$ is a finite $A$-module.
Since $X$ is normal, it is regular in codimension one.  After shrinking
around $\zeta$, both $X$ and $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ are smooth over $k$,
and a local equation $h$ of $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$ defines a smooth map
$h:X\to\mathbf A^1$.  The local ring $\mathcal O_{X,\zeta}$ is a
discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $h$, so a local equation $g$
of $Z$ can be written $g=wh^m$ with $m\geq1$ and $w$ a unit of
$\mathcal O_{X,\zeta}$.  The function $w$ is regular and invertible on a
neighbourhood of $\zeta$, and there the ideal of $Z$ is $(h^m)$, that
is, $Z=h^{-1}(V(x^m))$ schematically.  By the base change isomorphism
for smooth maps and Lemma [lemma-case-z-v-x-m], we see that $C_{X,Z}(M_X)=0$
there, and the last assertion of Lemma [lemma-base-change-cone-x-z]
yields the same vanishing for $j_!M_U$.

For general $L$, truncation triangles reduce us to a
constructible sheaf $F$ with $F|_Z=0$.  Shrinking around $\zeta$, we may
assume that $F=j_!G$ for a finite locally constant sheaf $G$ on $U$,
since the closure in $X$ of the locus in $U$ where $F$ is not
locally constant cannot contain a generic point of the divisor $Z$.
We prove by induction on $r$, simultaneously for all such normal
pairs and all $G$, that $H^r(C_{X,Z}(j_!G))$ vanishes generically.
As nearby cycles are left $t$-exact and $i^*j_!G=0$, we have

$$
C_{X,Z}(j_!G)=
z^*\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(j_!G)[1]\in D^{\geq-1}.
$$

Therefore the statement holds for every $r<-1$, which starts the induction.

For the induction step, we compare $F=j_!G$ with a sheaf to which the
first part of the proof applies. To construct it, choose a finite étale surjection $f_U:U'\to U$ trivializing $G$,
and let $f:X'\to X$ be the normalization of $X$ in $U'$; it
is finite since $X$ is excellent, and $X'$ is normal.  With
$Z'=f^{-1}Z$ and $j':U'\hookrightarrow X'$,
the sheaf $f^*F=j'_!f_U^*G$ is $j'_!$ of a sheaf that is constant on
each component of $U'$, and $Z'$ is a principal divisor in the normal
scheme $X'$. Since $f$ is finite, the points of $Z'$ over a generic
point of $Z$ are generic points of $Z'$, so the first part of the
proof, applied to $(X',Z')$, and the base change isomorphism for proper maps show that
$C_{X,Z}(f_*f^*F)$ vanishes generically on $Z$.

On a geometric stalk, the unit of the finite étale cover is the
diagonal inclusion into a nonempty finite product, so it is injective
and there is a short exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow f_*f^*F
\longrightarrow j_!G'\longrightarrow0,
$$

where $G'$ is again finite locally constant on $U$.  Applying $C_{X,Z}$
and taking the long exact sequence at a generic point where the middle
term vanishes, we find

$$
H^r(C_{X,Z}(F))\simeq
H^{r-1}(C_{X,Z}(j_!G')).
$$

By the induction hypothesis, the right side vanishes.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-vanishing-generic-points-principal-divisor], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We use the notation introduced before
Lemma [lemma-covers-degree-prime-to-ell] and compute on the étale
model: we identify $\rho$ with a restriction map $r$ away from $y$, kill
$r$ on a cover with $\ell$-group monodromy, and descend.

*Step 1: reduction to $r$.* Let $N=(\mathbb D_XK)|_{X_1-y}$, the dual
of $K|_{X_1-y}$ with respect to the restriction of $\omega_X$, and let
$Q=K|_{X_2-y}$. Write $j_1:X_1-y\hookrightarrow X_1$ and
$j_2:X_2-y\hookrightarrow X_2$ for the inclusions. As $K_{\bar y}=0$,
localization gives $K|_{X_2}=j_{2!}Q$, and $(\mathbb D_XK)|_{X_1}=Rj_{1*}N$
because the dual of an extension by zero is the direct image of the dual.
The ordinary external Künneth comparison therefore
identifies $P=(\mathbb D_XK\boxtimes K)|_T$ with $Rj_*j'_!(N\boxtimes Q)$,
where

$$
j:T-V\hookrightarrow T,\qquad
j':T-(H\cup V)\hookrightarrow T-V.
$$

Both $R\Gamma(T,P)$ and $R\Gamma(\Delta,\delta^*P)$ are zero, because the
schemes are strictly local and the stalk at the closed point is
$(\mathbb D_XK)_{\bar y}\otimes^{\mathbf L} K_{\bar y}=0$. So the
localization triangles identify $\rho$, shifted by one, with the ordinary
restriction $R\Gamma(T-\Gamma,P)\to R\Gamma(\Delta-y,\delta^*P)$, which
under the Künneth identification is

$$
r:R\Gamma(T-(V\cup\Gamma),j'_!(N\boxtimes Q))
\longrightarrow R\Gamma(\Delta-y,(N\boxtimes Q)|_{\Delta-y}).
$$

*Step 2: the restriction vanishes on a cover.* Choose bounded finite
projective lisse models of $N$ and $Q$ by
Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators]; their terms are finite locally
constant, as a punctured strictly local trait is its generic point.
Then Lemma [lemma-covers-degree-prime-to-ell], applied to the terms of the
model of $N$ on $X_1-y$ and to those of $Q$ on $X_2-y$, gives integers
$d_1,d_2$ prime to $\ell$. With $d=\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,d_2)$ we then obtain covers $X_1'\to X_1$ and $X_2'\to X_2$ of the same degree $d$. We want equal
degrees so that $u$ and $v$ become $d$th powers for the same $d$ in
Lemma [lemma-tangent-cones-on-cover]. Let $T'$, $\Gamma'$, $V'$,
$\Delta'$, $H'$ be as in that lemma, and let $N'$ and $Q'$ be the pullbacks
of $N$ and $Q$ to $X_1'-y_1'$ and $X_2'-y_2'$. By construction, the complex $N'\boxtimes Q'$ has finite $\ell$-group monodromy on $T'-(H'\cup V')$, hence also on the
smaller open set obtained by removing $\Gamma'$. Then the restriction $r'$ on $T'$, defined like $r$, is zero by
Lemma [lemma-vanishing-restrictions-after-blowing-up], applied to $T'$
with $D=(\Gamma'\cup V')_{\mathrm{red}}$, the regular curve
$H'_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $C=\Delta'_{\mathrm{red}}$; its hypotheses hold by
Lemma [lemma-tangent-cones-on-cover], and passing to reductions changes
neither the open complements nor the étale cohomology.

*Step 3: descent.* The map $r$ followed by pullback to $\Delta'-y'$
equals pullback to $T'$ followed by $r'=0$, because pullback along
$T'\to T$ commutes with restriction and with extension by zero. As $\Delta$
meets $H\cup V$ only at $y$, Lemma [lemma-tangent-cones-on-cover] shows
that $\Delta'-y'\to\Delta-y$ is finite étale of degree $d^2$. This degree is
invertible in $A$, so Lemma [lemma-descent-vanishing-finite-etale] gives
$r=0$, and hence $\rho=0$. By the comparison theorems, this identity on the
classical étale models of these strictly local schemes also holds in the
pro-étale formulation.
Finally, by Lemma [lemma-local-term-restriction-map],
$\operatorname{LT}_y(\psi)$ is the image of $[\psi]$ under a composite that
begins with $\rho$, so it is zero.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

After blowing up $t$, the three curves are separated along the
exceptional divisor, which then plays the role of $D_2$ in the previous
lemma.

Let $\widetilde T\to T$ be the blowup in $t$, with exceptional divisor
$E\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$, and let $D',H',C'$ be the strict transforms.
In these terms, the hypotheses on tangent cones say that $D'\cap E$ is disjoint
from both $C'\cap E$ and $H'\cap E$. We therefore apply Lemmas [lemma-cohomology-near-two-transverse-divisors] and [lemma-restriction-punctured-curve] to the surface $X=\widetilde T-D'$ with the divisors $D_1=H'\cap X$ and
$D_2=E\cap X=E-D'$. Here the divisor $E-D'$ is connected, since it is a
projective line with finitely many points removed, and $H'\cap X$ meets it
transversely in the single point $z$ corresponding to the tangent
direction of $H$. Since the blowup is an isomorphism off $E$, the source
of the map is $R\Gamma(X-E,j'_!N')$ for the pulled-back complex $N'$.

The strict transform $C'$ is proper and quasi-finite over the
strictly local curve $C$, hence finite. Its closed fibre is the
finite set of tangent directions of its branches, so $C'$ is a
finite disjoint union of strictly local curves $C'_w$, each meeting
$E$ at a single point $w$ of $E-D'$. Each restriction to $C'_w-w$ is
zero by Lemma [lemma-restriction-punctured-curve]. Since
$C'-E\simeq C-t$, the given restriction map is the direct sum of
these zero maps.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-vanishing-restrictions-after-blowing-up], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The lemma follows from the stability of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ under the six operations.
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf] shows that $a_X^!$ and
internal Hom preserve $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$. As $\Lambda_s$ lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$,
both $\omega_X=a_X^!\Lambda_s$ and $\mathbb D_XK$ lie in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ for $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$. We also give a direct
argument with finite coefficients and smooth strata, because the proof of
Lemma [lemma-restriction-geometric-generic-fibre] uses its
dévissage to generators $t_!P$ again.

*Dévissage.* The complex $K$ is built by finitely many cones from
complexes $t_!P$, for locally closed $t:T\hookrightarrow X$ with $T$
smooth and $P$ a locally constant perfect complex. To see this, choose a
finite stratification by smooth strata, disregarding nilpotents, on which
the restrictions $P$ of $K$ are locally constant perfect complexes, and
use the localization triangles. The bounded flat models of
Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators] and their stupid filtrations make
this precise. Since $\mathbb D_X$ is exact and $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is closed
under cones, it suffices to show that $\mathbb D_X(t_!P)$ lies in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$.

*The generators.* Internal adjunction (10.3)
for $t$ gives

$$
\mathbb D_X(t_!P)\simeq Rt_*\mathbb D_TP.
$$

On a smooth stratum of dimension $r$,
Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] identifies
the dual $\mathbb D_TP$ with $P^\vee(r)[2r]$, which is locally a perfect
complex. By Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf]
its ordinary direct image lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-verdier-duality-preserves-constructibility], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For the equivalence of the three conditions on an object $W$: by the
Yoneda lemma, $h_W$ is projective exactly when every epimorphism $F\to G$
induces a surjection $F(W)=\Hom(h_W,F)\to\Hom(h_W,G)=G(W)$. If every
epimorphism onto $h_W$ splits, pull an epimorphism $F\to G$ back along a
section $h_W\to G$; the resulting epimorphism onto $h_W$ splits, so the
section lifts to $F$. Conversely, if every epimorphism is surjective on
sections over $W$, then $\mathrm{id}_{h_W}$ lifts along any epimorphism
onto $h_W$.

To see that covers of $U$ split, note that by
Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale] a
faithfully flat weakly étale $D$-algebra can be refined to a faithfully
flat ind-étale $D$-algebra. This
refinement splits by Proposition [proposition-splitting-ind-etale-covers], and hence so does the original map. Now, given a cover of the
affine $U$, we refine it by a finite affine cover $\{V_j\to U\}$. Its disjoint union
$\coprod_jV_j$ is a single faithfully flat weakly étale affine cover,
which therefore has a section $s:U\to\coprod_jV_j$. The sets
$s^{-1}(V_j)$ then form a finite clopen partition of $U$, and on
$s^{-1}(V_j)$ the inclusion into $U$ factors through $V_j$.

If $F\to h_U$ is an epimorphism, then by the definition of an
epimorphism of sheaves $\mathrm{id}_U$ lifts after passing to a covering
of $U$. We refine this covering by the clopen partition just
constructed, so that on each piece $s^{-1}(V_j)$ we have a lift. Since the
pieces are disjoint and cover $U$, the sheaf condition glues these lifts
with no compatibility to check, and the result is a global lift of
$\mathrm{id}_U$, that is, a section. The same argument,
after pulling back an arbitrary epimorphism along a map from $h_U$,
proves projectivity. See [Stacks, [098F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/098F), [0990](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0990)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-w-contractible-affines-projective], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

An extension of degree $m$ of the constant field does not change the
geometric scheme $X$, the sheaf on it, or its cohomology, and it
replaces the Frobenius of $k_0$ by its $m$th power. So the eigenvalues
$\beta$ are the $\alpha^m$, and $|\iota\alpha^m|\le q^{mu/2}$
holds if and only if $|\iota\alpha|\le q^{u/2}$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-weight-bound-constant-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Let $a:F'\to F$ and $b:F\to F''$ be the maps. Exactness at $F$ gives a
short exact sequence

$$
0\to\operatorname{im}(a)\to F\to\operatorname{im}(b)\to0,
$$

where $\operatorname{im}(a)$ is a quotient of $F'$ and
$\operatorname{im}(b)$ a subobject of $F''$. Since mixed sheaves of
weights at most $u$ are closed under subquotients by
Lemma [lemma-subobjects-quotients-weil-sheaves] and under extensions by
Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations], $F$ is
mixed of weights at most $u$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-weights-exact-sequence], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

A constructible Weil sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec}k_0$ is a
finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with an automorphism $F$, the
geometric Frobenius. In both cases we may assume that $V$ is defined over
a finite extension $E'$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ containing the eigenvalues of $F$. For
$w\in\mathbf R$ let $V_w\subset V$ be the sum of the generalized
eigenspaces of $F$ for the eigenvalues $\alpha$ with
$|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{w/2}$. These subspaces are $F$-stable, only finitely many are
nonzero, and $V=\bigoplus_wV_w$. Let $w_1<\dots<w_m$ be the weights that
occur. Then the subspaces $V_{w_1}\oplus\dots\oplus V_{w_j}$ form a finite
filtration by Weil subsheaves with quotients $V_{w_j}$, and $V_{w_j}$ is
pure of weight $w_j$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-weil-sheaves-point-mixed], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The projection formula and proper base change reduce each of the two
triangle identities to the identity $s_i=1$ of
Lemma [lemma-class-diagonal-projective-line], tensored with the
identity of a coefficient complex.

*First triangle identity.* This is the equation
$\varepsilon_{Rp_*M}\circ Rp_*(\eta_M)=1_{Rp_*M}$. Using composition of
direct images, $pp_1=pp_2$, proper base change and the projection
formula, this composite equals

$$
\begin{split}
Rp_*M
&=R(pp_1)_*\Delta_*M\\
&\longrightarrow R(pp_1)_*p_1^*M(1)[2]\\
&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
Rp_*\bigl(M\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}
Rp_{1*}A_{\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S}(1)[2]\bigr)\\
&\xrightarrow{Rp_*(1_M\otimes \operatorname{Tr}_{p_1})}Rp_*M .
\end{split}
\tag{6.10}
$$

Here the first arrow is $Rp_*$ of the first arrow of (6.7), with
$R(pp_2)_*$ rewritten as $R(pp_1)_*$. The middle isomorphism is the
projection formula for $p_1$. It replaces the proper base change
isomorphism of (6.7), after $Rp_*$, followed by the projection formula
isomorphism of (6.8). The last arrow replaces $1\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_p$
in (6.8) by $\operatorname{Tr}_{p_1}$, the base change of
$\operatorname{Tr}_p$ along $p$ (Lemma [lemma-cohomology-projective-line-trace]).
In this form, the trace is applied to $Rp_{1*}\delta$, that is, to the
factor $\Delta_*A$, and $M$ only appears as a coefficient.

This rewriting is an equality of maps because the projection formula
isomorphism is compatible with proper base change. To see this, recall
that the proper base change map is the adjoint transpose of the counit of
$g^*\dashv Rg_*$ for the relevant pullback $g$. The projection map is the adjoint transpose of the same counit tensored with the identity, and the counit of a composite adjunction is the composite of the counits.
Therefore the two routes from $R(pp_2)_*p_1^*M=R(pp_1)_*p_1^*M$ to
$Rp_*M\otimes Rp_*A(1)[2]$ have the same adjoint transpose, as in
the pasting Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].

On the route through (6.10) we identify
$Rp_{1*}A=p^*Rp_*A$ by proper base change and then use the
projection formula for $p$. By naturality of the projection formula in its
second variable, the first arrow of (6.10) is then
$1_M\otimes Rp_{1*}\delta$ under the projection identification. The
composite is therefore $Rp_*(1_M\otimes s_1)$, which is $1_{Rp_*M}$ by
Lemma [lemma-class-diagonal-projective-line].

*Second triangle identity.* Here the roles of the two projections
are exchanged: we must show that
$p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]\circ\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}$ is the identity.
Take $M=p^*N(1)[2]$ in (6.7). Since $N$ and the Tate twist are
pulled back from $S$, both $p_1^*M$ and $p_2^*M$ are
$(pp_1)^*N(1)[2]=(pp_2)^*N(1)[2]$. The projection formula moves this common
factor outside $Rp_{2*}$, and $\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}$ becomes
$1\otimes Rp_{2*}\delta$. By the base change compatibility of (6.5),
$p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]$ becomes $1\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_{p_2}$,
applied to the target of $Rp_{2*}\delta$. We obtain

$$
p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]\circ\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}
=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}\otimes
(\operatorname{Tr}_{p_2}\circ Rp_{2*}\delta)
=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}\otimes s_2=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}.
\tag{6.11}
$$

All shifts moved in (6.10) and (6.11) are even, so no Koszul signs appear.

The unit is constructed from $\delta$ and proper base change, and
the counit from (6.5) and the projection formula. All of these ingredients are compatible with base change and change of coefficients, and hence so
are $\eta$ and $\varepsilon$. Transported by $\nu^*$, the same then holds for the corresponding adjunction
on the pro-étale categories.

*First triangle identity.* This is the equation
$\varepsilon_{Rp_*M}\circ Rp_*(\eta_M)=1_{Rp_*M}$. Using composition of
direct images, $pp_1=pp_2$, proper base change and the projection
formula, this composite equals

$$
\begin{split}
Rp_*M
&=R(pp_1)_*\Delta_*M\\
&\longrightarrow R(pp_1)_*p_1^*M(1)[2]\\
&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
Rp_*\bigl(M\otimes_\Lambda^{\mathbf L}
Rp_{1*}\Lambda_{\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S}(1)[2]\bigr)\\
&\xrightarrow{Rp_*(1_M\otimes \operatorname{Tr}_{p_1})}Rp_*M .
\end{split}
$$

Here the first arrow is $Rp_*$ of the first arrow of (6.7), with
$R(pp_2)_*$ rewritten as $R(pp_1)_*$. The middle isomorphism is the
projection formula for $p_1$. It replaces the proper base change
isomorphism of (6.7), after $Rp_*$, followed by the projection formula
isomorphism of (6.8). The last arrow replaces $1\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_p$
in (6.8) by $\operatorname{Tr}_{p_1}$, the base change of
$\operatorname{Tr}_p$ along $p$ (Lemma [lemma-cohomology-projective-line-trace]).
In this form, the trace is applied to $Rp_{1*}\delta$, that is, to the
factor $\Delta_*\Lambda$, and $M$ only appears as a coefficient.

This rewriting is an equality of maps because the projection formula
isomorphism is compatible with proper base change. To see this, recall
that the proper base change map is the adjoint transpose of the counit of
$g^*\dashv Rg_*$ for the relevant pullback $g$. The projection map is the
adjoint transpose of the same counit tensored with the identity. The
counit of a composite adjunction is the composite of the counits.
Therefore the two routes from $R(pp_2)_*p_1^*M=R(pp_1)_*p_1^*M$ to
$Rp_*M\otimes Rp_*\Lambda(1)[2]$ have the same adjoint transpose, as in
the pasting Lemma [lemma-identity-pasting].

On the route through (6.10) we identify
$Rp_{1*}\Lambda=p^*Rp_*\Lambda$ by proper base change and then use the
projection formula for $p$. By naturality of the projection formula in its
second variable, the first arrow of (6.10) is then
$1_M\otimes Rp_{1*}\delta$ under the projection identification. The
composite is therefore $Rp_*(1_M\otimes s_1)$, which is $1_{Rp_*M}$ by
Lemma [lemma-class-diagonal-projective-line].

*Second triangle identity.* Here the roles of the two projections
are exchanged: we must show that
$p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]\circ\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}$ is the identity.
Take $M=p^*N(1)[2]$ in (6.7). Since $N$ and the Tate twist are
pulled back from $S$, both $p_1^*M$ and $p_2^*M$ are
$(pp_1)^*N(1)[2]=(pp_2)^*N(1)[2]$. The projection formula moves this common
factor outside $Rp_{2*}$, and $\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}$ becomes
$1\otimes Rp_{2*}\delta$. By the base change compatibility of (6.5),
$p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]$ becomes $1\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_{p_2}$,
applied to the target of $Rp_{2*}\delta$. We obtain

$$
p^*(\varepsilon_N)(1)[2]\circ\eta_{p^*N(1)[2]}
=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}\otimes
(\operatorname{Tr}_{p_2}\circ Rp_{2*}\delta)
=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}\otimes s_2=1_{p^*N(1)[2]}.
$$

All shifts moved in (6.10) and (6.11) are even, so no Koszul signs appear.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line].

The unit is constructed from the diagonal class $\delta$ and the proper base-change comparison. The diagonal class pulls back to the diagonal class, and proper base-change maps satisfy pasting. Pulling back the unit composite therefore gives the unit composite over the new base, with the specified comparisons.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line].

The counit is the projection-formula isomorphism followed by the trace (6.5). The trace commutes with base change by Lemma [lemma-cohomology-projective-line-trace--4], and the projection formula commutes with proper base change by the adjoint-transpose calculation in the proof of clause [proposition-adjunction-projective-line--1]. Thus their composite is the base-changed counit.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line].

The unit is defined from the diagonal class and proper base change. Finite extension of scalars carries the Cartier–Kummer diagonal class to the class over the new ring and carries the base-change comparison to that comparison. Applying extension of scalars to the defining composite consequently gives the new unit.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line].

The counit is formed from the trace and the projection formula. The trace is the projection onto the distinguished summand of the projective-line decomposition, and finite coefficient change carries that decomposition and projection to the corresponding ones. The projection-formula map is defined by tensor and adjunction, which commute with this coefficient comparison. Their composite is therefore the new counit.
