We describe $R^qh_*$ as a sheafification and show that each local class
dies after a suitable étale covering. In degrees at least two this is
the cohomological dimension of affine curves. In degree one we first
descend the class to $C_L$, then trivialize it on a finite étale Galois
cover of $C_L$, and finally extend this cover over $C$.

*Step 1: reduction to local classes.* We may work on the étale
site, because $h$ is qcqs and direct images can be compared
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images]). There, [Stacks, [03Q8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q8)]
identifies $R^qh_*\underline{\mathbf Z/m}$ with the
sheafification of the presheaf

$$
U\longmapsto H^q(U\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\Omega,
\mathbf Z/m),
\qquad U\to C\text{ \'etale},
$$

so we must show that every such class vanishes on an étale covering
of $U$.

*Step 2: degrees $q\geq2$.* In these degrees the groups themselves
vanish for affine $U$, which we may assume because the question is local
on $U$. Indeed, $U_\Omega$ is then affine and étale over $C_\Omega$.
Hence it is empty or a finite disjoint union of smooth affine curves over
the algebraically closed field $\Omega$, and $(C_2)$ of
Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] kills its cohomology in
degrees $q\geq2$.

*Step 3: a section and connected fibres.* From now on $q=1$. The
extension theorem we want to use requires a section and geometrically
connected fibres. The map $U\to S$ need not have them, but we may arrange
them locally. By [Stacks, [0EY4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EY4)], after an étale covering of $U$ the map
$U\to S$ factors as $U\to V\to S$ with $U$ and $V$ affine, $V\to S$ étale,
and $U\to V$ smooth with geometrically connected fibres and a section.
Moreover, the separated étale map $V\to S$ is a finite disjoint union of
open immersions [Stacks, [09Z9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09Z9)], because $S$ is normal and integral with
separably closed function field. As we only have to kill classes on
$U_\Omega$, we may therefore replace $S$ by one of these opens and $C$ by
the part of $U$ over it, which does not change the fraction field $L$.
Afterwards there
is a section $s:S\to C$ and the fibres are geometrically connected.

*Step 4: descent to $C_L$ and a trivializing cover.* Let
$\xi\in H^1(C_\Omega,\mathbf Z/m)$. It is the pullback of a unique class
$\xi_L\in H^1(C_L,\mathbf Z/m)$, because the pullback
$H^1(C_L,\mathbf Z/m)\to H^1(C_\Omega,\mathbf Z/m)$ is an isomorphism by
$(C_6)$ of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves], applied to the affine
curve $C_L$ as in [Stacks, [03SC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SC)]; this step uses that $m$ is prime to the
characteristic. Next, the classification of $H^1$ by torsors [Stacks, [03AJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03AJ)] and
Lemma [lemma-torsors-under-classical-groups] show that $\xi_L$ is the
class of a finite étale $\mathbf Z/m$-torsor $P\to C_L$. Choose a
connected component $Z$ of $P$ and let $G\subseteq\mathbf Z/m$ be its
stabilizer. As the curve $C_L$ is connected, $Z\to C_L$ is a finite
étale Galois cover with group $G$. The class $\xi_L$ vanishes on $Z$,
because the pullback of $P$ to $Z$ has the diagonal section.

*Step 5: extending the cover over $C$.* We use the extension theorem
for generic Galois covers [Stacks, [0EZJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZJ)]: let $S$ be
integral, normal and qcqs with generic point $\eta$, and let $C\to S$
be qcqs and smooth with geometrically connected fibres and a section
$s$. If $Z\to C_\eta$ is a finite étale Galois cover with group
$G$ of order invertible on $S$, and $Z$ has a $\kappa(\eta)$-rational point
over $s(\eta)$, then $Z$ extends to a finite étale Galois cover
$\widetilde Z\to C$ with group $G$. The idea is that a cover of order
prime to the residue characteristics ramifies only tamely, and splitting over the section then rules out ramification
along the irreducible special fibres, and at points of codimension at least two
the cover extends by purity of the branch locus.

The hypotheses hold with $C_\eta=C_L$. Indeed, the order $|G|$ divides $m$
and is therefore invertible on $S$. Moreover, the fibre of $Z$ over
$s(\eta)$ is nonempty, as $Z\to C_L$ is finite étale and surjective, and
it has an $L$-rational point because $L$ is algebraically closed. So
$\widetilde Z$ exists.

We check that $\widetilde Z\to C$ is an étale covering, that is, that it
is surjective. The scheme $C$ is connected, since $C\to S$ is open and
surjective with connected fibres over a connected base. Hence
the image of $\widetilde Z$ in $C$, which is open and closed and contains the
generic fibre, is all of $C$. Finally, $\xi$ dies on this covering. Indeed,
$\widetilde Z\times_C C_\Omega=Z\times_{C_L}C_\Omega$, so the pullback of
$\xi$ to $\widetilde Z\times_CC_\Omega$ is the pullback of $\xi_L|_Z=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-base-change-larger-algebraically-closed], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We bound the poles of $L(U_0,\mathcal G^{\otimes2m},t)$ by determinant
weights through $H^2_c$, and positivity then passes the bound to each local
factor.

We may assume that $\mathcal G$ is semisimple. Indeed, by
Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra], replacing $\mathcal G$ by its
semisimplification changes neither its local characteristic polynomials
nor the determinant weights of its constituents.

*The top cohomology.* Fix $m\ge1$ and put
$\mathcal T=\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$. We show that every eigenvalue $\mu$ of
$F$ on $H_c^2(U,\mathcal T)$ satisfies $|\iota(\mu)|\le q^{m\beta+1}$; these
eigenvalues determine the possible poles of the $L$-function. First, every
constituent of $\mathcal T$ has determinant weight at most $2m\beta$, by
Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations](1).
Next, Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology] identifies
$H_c^2(U,\mathcal T)$ with $T_{\pi_1(U)}(-1)$, where
$T$ is the generic fibre of $\mathcal T$. The geometric fundamental group
acts trivially on $T_{\pi_1(U)}$, so its simple Weil factors are
one-dimensional, as one sees by triangularizing the operator induced by a
degree-one lift. Let $b$ be the eigenvalue on such a factor. Since
$T_{\pi_1(U)}$ is a Weil quotient of $T$, the factor is a constituent of
$\mathcal T$, and its determinant weight is $\lambda_\iota(b)$. From
$\lambda_\iota(b)=2\log_q|\iota(b)|\le2m\beta$ we get
$|\iota(b)|\le q^{m\beta}$. The twist $(-1)$ multiplies eigenvalues by $q$,
and the claim follows.

*The local factors.* The bound on $H^2_c$ makes the $L$-function
holomorphic on a disc, and positivity passes this to each local
factor. As $H_c^0=0$ by Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology],
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product] gives

$$
L(U_0,\mathcal T,t)
=\prod_{x\in|U_0|}\det(1-\operatorname{Frob}_x t^{\deg(x)}\mid\mathcal T_{\bar x})^{-1}
=\frac{\det(1-Ft\mid H_c^1(U,\mathcal T))}
{\det(1-Ft\mid H_c^2(U,\mathcal T))}.
$$

This is an identity of formal power series, and the product is
coefficientwise locally finite because there are only finitely many
closed points of bounded degree. Now put $R_m=q^{-m\beta-1}$. By the bound on
$H_c^2$, the denominator has no zero on the disc $|t|<R_m$ after applying
$\iota$, so the rational function, and with it its Taylor series, is
holomorphic on this disc.

Each local factor
$\det(1-\operatorname{Frob}_x t^{\deg(x)}\mid\mathcal T_{\bar x})$ has no zero
on the same disc. Indeed, after applying $\iota$ the local factors of
$L(U_0,\mathcal T,t)$ are power series with nonnegative coefficients and
constant coefficient one by Lemma [lemma-positivity-euler-factors], so
that Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence] applies.

Now let $\alpha$ be a local eigenvalue of $\mathcal G$. Then $\alpha^{2m}$ is
an eigenvalue on $\mathcal T$ by Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra], and
$1-\iota(\alpha)^{2m}t^{\deg(x)}$ divides the local factor. Its roots
have absolute value $|\iota(\alpha)|^{-2m/\deg(x)}$, so by the previous paragraph this number must be at
least $R_m$, that is,

$$
|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_x^{\beta+1/m}.
$$

Letting $m$ tend to infinity proves the bound.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first show, using translations, that the reduced subscheme
$G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a smooth group scheme. It then suffices to show
that $G$ has the same tangent space at $1$ as $G_{\mathrm{red}}$, that
is, that nilpotent functions at $1$ lie in $\mathfrak m^2$, and this is
where we divide by an integer.

*Step 1: $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a smooth subgroup scheme of $G$.*
Multiplication and inversion restrict to $G_{\mathrm{red}}$. This is
because products of reduced schemes of finite type over the perfect
field $\Omega$ are reduced [Stacks, [035Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/035Z)], and a morphism from a
reduced scheme to $G$ factors through $G_{\mathrm{red}}$. The reduced scheme
$G_{\mathrm{red}}$ contains a dense
smooth open subscheme [Stacks, [056V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/056V)]. It is smooth everywhere, since a
translation moves a closed point of this open to any other closed point of
$G_{\mathrm{red}}$.

*Step 2: nilpotent functions at $1$ lie in $\mathfrak m^2$.* Let
$R=\mathcal O_{G,1}$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and nilradical
$I$, and let $\widehat R$ be its completion. At the point $(1,1)$ the
multiplication induces a continuous comultiplication

$$
\Delta:\widehat R\longrightarrow
\widehat R\,\widehat\otimes_\Omega\widehat R.
$$

The counit is evaluation at $1$, and composing $\Delta$ with evaluation at $1$
in either factor gives the identity (the counit identities), because $1$ is a
two-sided unit for the group law.
We claim that $I\subseteq\mathfrak m^2$.
As completion is faithfully flat, it suffices to prove that every
nilpotent $b\in\widehat R$ lies in $\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,2}$.
Suppose that $b\notin\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,2}$, and let $n\ge2$ be
the least integer with $b^n=0$. By the counit identities,

$$
\Delta(b)=b\otimes1+1\otimes b+w,
\qquad
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak m}\,\widehat\otimes_\Omega
\widehat{\mathfrak m}.
$$

Now reduce the second factor modulo $\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,2}$. Every
term in the binomial expansion of $\Delta(b)^n$ with at least two
factors from $1\otimes b+w$ vanishes, because
$1\otimes b+w$ has its second factor in $\widehat{\mathfrak m}$, and as $b^n=0$
we are left with

$$
n b^{n-1}\otimes b+n(b^{n-1}\otimes1)w=0.
$$

If we now also reduce the first factor modulo
$b^{n-1}\widehat{\mathfrak m}$, the second term vanishes, and we get

$$
n\,\overline{b^{n-1}}\otimes\overline b=0
\quad\text{in}\quad
(\widehat R/b^{n-1}\widehat{\mathfrak m})
\otimes_\Omega(\widehat R/\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,2}).
$$

This identity is impossible, which proves the claim. Indeed, the class
$\overline{b^{n-1}}$ is nonzero by Nakayama's lemma, because the module
$(b^{n-1})$ is nonzero by the choice of $n$. The class $\overline b$ is
nonzero by assumption. A tensor product of nonzero vectors over a field
is nonzero, and $n\ne0$ in characteristic zero.

*Step 3: $G$ is smooth.* The schemes $G$ and $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ have the
same cotangent space at $1$. Indeed, by Step 2 the kernel of
$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\to(\mathfrak m/I)/(\mathfrak m/I)^2$ is
$(I+\mathfrak m^2)/\mathfrak m^2=0$. They also have the same local
dimension at $1$, because a nilpotent ideal does not change the
underlying space. As the local ring $R/I$ of $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ at $1$
is regular by Step 1, we get

$$
\dim_\Omega\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=\dim R,
$$

so $R$ is regular, and in particular a domain [Stacks, [00NP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NP)].
By translation the local rings of $G$ at all closed points are
regular. Since $\Omega$ is perfect, $G$ is smooth at every closed point.
The nonsmooth locus is closed and contains no closed point, and hence it
is empty. Being smooth, $G$ is reduced, and its tangent
space at $1$ has dimension $\dim G$. Finally, the open subgroup $G^\circ$ has the
same tangent space at $1$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We write a power of $\rho(s)$ as a central torus element times an
element of $H$, by Lemma [lemma-identity-component], and average
the torus part over the components of $G$ so that it becomes central
in all of $G$. The factors from $H$ that accumulate in this
process are collected in $h$; their determinants are roots of unity, so by
Lemma [lemma-determinant-weight-from-central-scalar] they do no harm. Note that the
direct sum $V$ of the $V_i$ is again semisimple, so
Lemma [lemma-identity-component] applies to it.

Since the component group of
$G$ is finite (Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms]), we may choose
$m>0$ with $\rho(s)^m\in G^\circ$. By Lemma [lemma-identity-component], we
can write $\rho(s)^m=ct$ with $c\in Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ and $t\in H^\circ$.
Choose representatives $g_1,\ldots,g_b$ of the components of $G$ and
set

$$
z=\prod_{j=1}^bg_jcg_j^{-1},\qquad N=mb.
$$

The element $c$ is central in $G^\circ$ but perhaps not in $G$, since
the other components may conjugate it nontrivially. The product $z$ of its
conjugates, one for each component, is however central in $G$.
Indeed, the factors lie in the abelian group $Z(G^\circ)^\circ$, and since replacing
$g_j$ by $g_ju$ with $u\in G^\circ$ does not change the corresponding
factor, conjugation by an element of $G$ permutes the
factors. Next, every commutator lies in $H$, so each factor has the same image
as $c$ in $G/H$. Since $c\in H\rho(s)^m$, we get $z\in H\rho(s)^{mb}$, which
gives $h$ and $N=mb>0$.

Being central in $G$, the element $z$ commutes with the action of $W(U_0)$ on
tensor constructions. Moreover, as noted after the definition of tensor constructions,
every $W(U_0)$-stable subspace of a tensor construction is $G$-stable. Hence
$z$ acts on the $W(U_0)$-stable subquotients and commutes with the action of
$W(U_0)$ on them. On a simple subquotient, therefore, an eigenspace of $z$ is nonzero and
$W(U_0)$-stable, hence is the whole space; in other words, $z$ acts by a scalar.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We treat sheaves killed by a prime first, where
Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-closed-fibre] applies, and then reach all torsion
sheaves by extensions, direct sums and filtered colimits.

Suppose first that $\ell F=0$ for a prime $\ell$.  Take an injective resolution
$F\to I^\bullet$ in sheaves of $\mathbf F_\ell$-modules on $\mathbf P^1_{R,\acute{e}t}$.
Since $i^*$ is exact, $F_0\to I_0^\bullet$ is again a resolution, and by
Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-closed-fibre] its terms are
$\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,-)$-acyclic. Moreover, Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree]
shows that the two complexes of sections agree term by term:

$$
\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_R,I^\bullet)\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,I_0^\bullet).
$$

The left complex computes $R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_R,F)$, and the right computes
$R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,F_0)$. Hence the natural restriction map between them is a
quasi-isomorphism.

By the long exact cohomology sequences and the five lemma, the sheaves
for which the statement holds form a class closed under extensions. Since a
sheaf killed by $\ell^a$ has a finite filtration with quotients killed by
$\ell$, and a sheaf killed by an integer $n$ is the finite direct sum of
its primary parts, the class contains all sheaves of bounded torsion.
An arbitrary torsion $F$ is the colimit
$\varinjlim_n F[n]$, with positive integers ordered by divisibility, and the
comparison passes to this colimit, because the cohomology of the
quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes $\mathbf P^1_R$ and
$\mathbf P^1_\kappa$ commutes with filtered colimits [Stacks, [03Q5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q5)]. Finally, all
maps used are restriction maps, which gives naturality in $F$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-cohomology-p-1-over-henselian], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

By the Kummer sequence, the vanishing above degree one follows from the
divisibility of $\operatorname{Pic}(U)$ and the vanishing of
$H^q(U,\mathbf G_m)$ for $q\geq2$ (Lemma [lemma-cohomology-multiplicative-group]). For $H^1$ we describe
$\mu_n$-torsors as line bundles $L$ with a trivialization of
$L^{\otimes n}$. After extending $L$ to $\overline C$, the orders at the
punctures measure the failure of the torsor to extend. These orders give
the residue map $\partial$. We prove exactness at each place, and then deduce the rank
and the invariance under field extension.

Since $\overline C$ is regular, we may use divisors to see that

$$
\operatorname{Pic}(U)=\operatorname{Pic}(\overline C)/
\langle\mathcal O_{\overline C}(x):x\in D\rangle.
$$

One of these line bundles has degree one. Every class in
$\operatorname{Pic}(\overline C)$ is therefore congruent, modulo the
subgroup generated by it, to a class of degree zero. Hence
$J(\overline C)(k)$ surjects onto $\operatorname{Pic}(U)$. As $J(\overline C)(k)$ is
$n$-divisible (Corollary [corollary-torsion-jacobian-field-extension]), so is
$\operatorname{Pic}(U)$.
By the Kummer sequence and Lemma [lemma-cohomology-multiplicative-group], we have
$H^2(U,\mu_n)=\operatorname{Pic}(U)/n=0$ and $H^q(U,\mu_n)=0$ for
$q\geq3$.

We construct the sequence (D.1) using line
bundles.  Recall that a $\mu_n$-torsor on $U$ is given by a pair
$(L,\alpha:L^{\otimes n}\simeq\mathcal O_U)$ of a line bundle and a
trivialization of its $n$th power.  To define its residues, we extend $L$ to a line
bundle $\overline L$ on $\overline C$ and let $s=\alpha^{-1}(1)$ be the
corresponding rational section of $\overline L^{\otimes n}$.  The
divisor of $s$ is supported on $D$, since $s$ generates on $U$. Its
orders modulo $n$ do not depend on the extension. Indeed, two
extensions differ by $\mathcal O(E')$ with $E'$ supported on $D$, and
this changes the divisor of $s$ by $nE'$. These orders define
$\partial(L,\alpha)$. Their sum is zero modulo $n$, since the divisor of
$s$ has degree $\deg\overline L^{\otimes n}=n\deg\overline L$.

Suppose all orders are divisible by $n$, and write
$\operatorname{div}(s)=nE$ with $E$ supported on $D$. Then $s$ is a
nowhere vanishing section of
$(\overline L(-E))^{\otimes n}=\overline L^{\otimes n}(-nE)$. So the
trivialization extends to a torsor with line bundle $\overline L(-E)$ on
$\overline C$, and this torsor restricts to $(L,\alpha)$ on $U$. This
proves exactness at $H^1(U,\mu_n)$.

To prove
injectivity, note that a trivialization on $U$ of a torsor on $\overline C$
gives a rational section of its line bundle whose $n$th power has no
zero or pole on $\overline C$.  Therefore the divisor of the section is
zero, and the section trivializes the torsor on $\overline C$.

To see that $\partial$ maps onto the kernel of $\sum$, we lift a
residue vector with sum zero modulo $n$ to an integral divisor $B$
supported on $D$. Its degree is divisible by $n$ because the residues sum
to zero. We claim that, as a consequence, there is a line bundle $\overline L$ with
$\overline L^{\otimes n}\simeq\mathcal O_{\overline C}(B)$. To find it, choose
$P\in\overline C(k)$ and put $L_1=\mathcal O_{\overline C}((\deg B/n)P)$, so that the
line bundle $\mathcal O_{\overline C}(B)\otimes L_1^{\otimes-n}$ has degree
zero. By divisibility of $J(\overline C)(k)$ it is $N^{\otimes n}$
for some $N$ of degree zero, and $\overline L=L_1\otimes N$ works. It remains to
produce the torsor. The
canonical section of $\mathcal O_{\overline C}(B)$ has divisor $B$ and is
nowhere zero on $U$. It therefore defines a trivialization of
$\overline L^{\otimes n}|_U$, that is, a Kummer torsor on $U$ whose
residues are the orders of $B$. Finally, the
summation map is surjective since $D$ is nonempty. This proves that the
sequence is exact (see also [Stacks, [03RR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RR)]).

The left term and the kernel of summation are free $\mathbf Z/n$-modules of
ranks $2g$ and $\#D-1$. Hence the resulting short exact sequence
splits noncanonically. For naturality, note that the formation of the
compactification, the boundary points, the line bundles and the orders
of vanishing commutes with base change. The
leftmost pullback map is an isomorphism by
Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime], and the residue groups and their
summation maps are unchanged. By the five lemma applied to the two
exact sequences, the middle pullback map is an isomorphism.

The idea is to glue $M$ to each compactification $X_i$ of $M_i$ after
removing from $X_i$ the closure of the part lying over $M\setminus M_i$.
This gives separated schemes $W_i$ containing $M$, and a common
modification combines them into one separated $W$. It remains to check that $W$ is proper, and for this we use the valuative criterion. Separating the closures of the
boundaries, we obtain
(A.1), and from it we deduce that every
valuation of $D$ extends into one of the $W_i$.

*Separating the boundaries.* Since the subsets to be removed from $X_i$ are defined by points of
$M$ outside $M_i$, we must relate each $X_i$ to $M$ itself. Choose dense compactifications $M_i\subseteq X_i$. By
Lemma [lemma-extending-graph-from-compactification], after admissible blow-ups
there are opens $M_i\subseteq V_i\subseteq X_i$ and proper maps
$\psi_i:V_i\to M$ that are isomorphisms above $M_i$.
Put, for $\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}$,

$$
Z_i=M\setminus M_j,\qquad
Z_{i,r}=\psi_i^{-1}(Z_r),\qquad
B_{i,r}=\overline{Z_{i,r}}\subseteq X_i.
$$

The subsets $Z_{i,1},Z_{i,2}$ are disjoint and closed in $V_i$.
By Lemma [lemma-separation-closures], after a further
$V_i$-admissible blow-up we may assume that
$B_{i,1}\cap B_{i,2}=\varnothing$, and subsequent $V_i$-admissible
blow-ups preserve this disjointness.

Let $X_{12}$ be the schematic closure of
$V_1\times_MV_2$ in $X_1\times_SX_2$, with proper projections
$p_i$. Above $V_1$, the first projection is the base change of
$\psi_2$, so it is an isomorphism near $Z_{1,2}$. By
Lemma [lemma-extending-isomorphism-over-closure-closed] it becomes
an isomorphism near $B_{1,2}$ after a blow-up. We replace $X_{12}$ by its strict transform, or
equivalently by the closure of the new graph. Since $p_1$ is now an
isomorphism over a neighbourhood of $B_{1,2}$ and $Z_{1,2}$ is dense in
$B_{1,2}$, the inverse image of $Z_{1,2}$ is dense in $p_1^{-1}(B_{1,2})$. The second
projection maps that inverse image into $Z_{2,2}$. By density it
maps all of $p_1^{-1}(B_{1,2})$ into $B_{2,2}$, which is disjoint
from $B_{2,1}$. This gives the disjointness used in the valuative
argument below:

$$
X_{12}\cap(B_{1,2}\times_SB_{2,1})=\varnothing.
\tag{A.1}
$$

*The separated schemes $W_i$.* We glue

$$
W_i=M\coprod_{M_i}(X_i\setminus B_{i,j}).
$$

We claim that these schemes are separated over $S$. The scheme $W_i$
is covered by $M$ and $X_i\setminus B_{i,j}$, both separated, and they
are glued along $M_i$. It therefore suffices to show that the graph of
the inclusion $M_i\to X_i\setminus B_{i,j}$, which is the mixed part of
the diagonal, is closed in $M\times_S(X_i\setminus B_{i,j})$.

Suppose that a point of the graph of $M_i$ specializes in
$M\times_S(X_i\setminus B_{i,j})$. Since $\psi_i$ is proper, its graph
is closed in $M\times_SX_i$. Hence the specialized point lies in the
graph of $\psi_i$, over a point of $V_i$. If its image in $M$ lay in
$M\setminus M_i=Z_j$, the lifted point would lie in
$Z_{i,j}\subseteq B_{i,j}$, contradicting the second coordinate. So
the specialization remains in the graph. The graph is an immersion with
constructible image, and in the Noetherian situation a constructible
subset that is closed under specialization is closed. Therefore the
graph is a closed immersion, which proves separatedness.

*Valuations of $D$.* For properness we use the valuative criterion, and we show first that
every valuation of $D$ extends into one of the $W_i$.
Let $R$ be a valuation ring with fraction field $K$, and let
$\operatorname{Spec}(K)\to D$ be an $S$-map over a given
$\operatorname{Spec}(R)\to S$. It extends to both $X_i$, since they are proper, and the pair of extensions factors through $X_{12}$, because the
closure of the graph contains its generic point and
$\operatorname{Spec}(K)$ is schematically dense in
$\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. By
(A.1), the closed point cannot map into
both of the removed closed subsets $B_{1,2}$ and $B_{2,1}$. We may therefore choose $i$ such that the closed point does not map into $B_{i,j}$. Since an open containing the closed point of a local scheme contains the whole scheme, the extension factors through $X_i\setminus B_{i,j}\subseteq W_i$.

*Gluing and properness.*
Lemma [lemma-gluing-after-admissible-blow-ups], applied to
$M\subseteq W_i$, gives a separated $W$ of finite type, covered by
admissible modifications $W_i'$. Since the modification is proper, the
lift of the valuation into $W_i$ lifts further into $W_i'$, hence
into $W$. Such lifts are unique because $W$ is separated. The valuative
criterion [Stacks, [0894](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0894)], in the form that only requires lifts of maps
from $\operatorname{Spec}(K)$ into the dense open $D$, then shows that
$W\to S$ is universally closed. As $W$ is also of finite type and
separated, it is proper over $S$. Its open $M$ yields the desired
compactification, which becomes dense after we take the schematic
closure of $M$. This is [Stacks, [0F40](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F40)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-compactifying-union-two-opens], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The plan is to prove compactness on the étale
site against arbitrary objects of $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$, where the commutation of
cohomology with direct sums that we need is classical, and then transfer the
result to $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ by $\nu_X^*$.

Recall that compact objects are closed under shifts,
finite extensions and direct summands. Hence, by
Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators], it suffices to treat $a_!L$. To do so, factor $a=i\circ u$ with $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ closed and $u:S\hookrightarrow Z$ open, and let
$j:X\setminus Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the complementary open immersion.
The idea is then to write $R\!\operatorname{Hom}(a_!L,-)$ as a composite of functors each of
which commutes with direct sums. Since $L$ has finite projective stalks, it is dualizable with dual
$L^\vee=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(L,A_S)$, and the étale form of
Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme](2) shows that for $K\in D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ we have

$$
R\!\operatorname{Hom}_X(a_!L,K)
=R\Gamma\bigl(S,L^\vee\otimes_A u^*R\underline\Gamma_ZK\bigr),
\qquad R\underline\Gamma_ZK=i^*\fib\bigl(K\to Rj_*j^*K\bigr),
$$

where $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ denotes sections with support in $Z$.
We claim that every functor on the right, viewed as a functor between étale
derived categories, preserves arbitrary direct sums. For $Rj_*$
and $R\Gamma(S,-)$, this is [Stacks, [0F11](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F11)], which says that a derived direct image
of finite cohomological dimension commutes with direct sums of unbounded
complexes. It applies to $A$-modules because derived direct
image and global sections commute with forgetting the coefficient ring
[Stacks, [0D6J](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D6J)]. The remaining functors are inverse images, tensor products with finite projective sheaves, and a fibre, and these also preserve direct sums: inverse images are left adjoints, tensor products commute with direct sums, and the fibre of a
map between functors that preserve direct sums again preserves them.
Hence $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_X(a_!L,-)$ commutes with direct sums. Taking $H^0$, we see
that $\Hom(a_!L,-)$ commutes with direct sums, that is, $a_!L$ is compact.
By Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators] it follows that every object of
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ is compact.

On the pro-étale site, Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison] and
Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients] show that the inverse image
$\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$ is exact, fully
faithful and preserves direct sums. Such a functor identifies the localizing
subcategories generated by $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ on the two sites. Compactness against
all étale complexes therefore implies compactness in $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$.

For the last assertion we have to show that there are no other compact
objects. Since constructibility and finite Tor amplitude are preserved by direct
summands, the category $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ is thick. It is essentially small,
because it is a full subcategory of the essentially small bounded constructible
category, and by definition a skeleton generates $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$. In a
triangulated category with direct sums generated by a set of compact
objects, the compact objects form the thick closure of that set
[Stacks, [09SM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09SM), [09SN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09SN)]. In our case this closure is $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$.

There are two statements: $\nu_X^*$ identifies the two localizing
categories, and on the étale side the localizing category is
everything. The first follows formally from the comparison results for
the pro-étale site. For the second we exhibit compact generators of
$D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ that lie in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$.

An exact fully faithful functor that preserves direct sums identifies
the localizing subcategories generated by corresponding generators.
In our case, Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients] shows that $\nu_X^*$ is such a
functor on unbounded complexes and that it is compatible with direct
images, and on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ it is the equivalence of
Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison]. Finally, inverse images commute with $\nu^*$ because both composites are
inverse images along the same morphism of topoi.

For the equality with the whole étale derived category, let
$u:U\to X$ range over a basis of quasi-compact separated étale
objects. The free representable module sheaves $u_!A_U$ are flat
constructible, hence belong to $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$. We have
$R\!\operatorname{Hom}_X(u_!A_U,K)=R\Gamma(U,K)$. It follows that their shifts
detect zero objects of $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$. Indeed, if $H^n(U,K)=0$ for all such $U$
and all $n$, then every cohomology sheaf of $K$ vanishes, being the sheafification
of $U\mapsto H^n(U,K)$. These objects are also compact in all of
$D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$. The reason is that $R\Gamma(U,-)$ commutes with
direct sums, since $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(U)<\infty$, as in the étale part of the
proof of Proposition [proposition-compactness-finite-coefficients]. A set of
compact objects whose shifts detect zero objects generates a
triangulated category with direct sums as a localizing subcategory.
Hence these objects generate the entire étale derived category.

As for base change, we compare orientations and the maps $\mu_{f,K}$, first
over any finite admissible ring and then for towers. The orientations are
compared on a chart adapted to both $f$ and $g$, where each is iterated
integration along affine lines, with the coordinates ordered so that the
two iterated integrals are the same. Applying $R\varprojlim$ then gives the
integral identity, and inverting $\ell$ and descending to a finite extension of
$\mathbf Q_\ell$ give the identities for coefficient fields.

*Orientation, finite coefficients.* Both orientations are maps of
rank one locally constant sheaves after removing twist and shift, so it
suffices to compare them on a cover of $X$ by charts, and we choose charts
adapted to both morphisms. That is, choose an open $W\subset Y$ with
an étale $Z$-map $W\to\mathbf A^e_Z$, and an open $U\subset f^{-1}(W)$
with an étale $W$-map $U\to\mathbf A^d_W$. Then the composite
$U\to\mathbf A^d_W\to\mathbf A^d_{\mathbf A^e_Z}=\mathbf A^{d+e}_Z$ is
étale, and we order the coordinates of $\mathbf A^{d+e}_Z$ with the $e$
coordinates of $g$ first and the $d$ coordinates of $f$ last. Over this
chart, both orientations are adjoint to iterated integration along affine
lines, in the same order: first the $d$ coordinates of $f$, then the $e$
coordinates of $g$. Since the recursive construction preceding
(9.11) integrates the last coordinate first, the
integration on $\mathbf A^{d+e}_Z$ is exactly this composite. Each diagonal
orientation agrees on a chart with the integration in its coordinates, so the two
orientations agree on the cover.

*The maps $\mu_{f,K}$, finite coefficients.* The two maps
agree because their transposes under the composite adjunction do. Indeed, the
transpose of the iterated map applies the projection formula and the
counit for $f$, then the projection formula and the counit for $g$, whereas the
transpose of the map for $g\circ f$ applies the projection formula for
$g\circ f$ and its counit. The two isomorphisms given by the projection
formula agree by associativity of tensor products, and the counit of the
composite adjunction is the composite of the two counits.

$\gamma_{f,\bullet}$ and its composite adjunction. Since the orientations are maps of
sheaves of towers of rank one, we may test their equality at each level, while the maps

For composition, the only new ingredient is a map that moves an
extension by zero past a proper direct image. It is an isomorphism by
the same argument as for refinements: it restricts to the identity on
an open, and both sides vanish on the closed complement by proper base
change. For base change of $Rf_!$ we combine proper base change with the
elementary fact that extension by zero commutes with pullback.

*The composition isomorphism.* Choose compactifications $f=p\circ j$
and $g=q\circ j_Y$, with $j:X\to\overline X$ and $j_Y:Y\to\overline Y$ open and
$p,q$ proper. In the composite $Rq_*j_{Y!}Rp_*j_!$, the middle factor $j_{Y!}Rp_*$
applies a proper direct image before an extension by zero, and we
want to interchange the two.
To do this, compactify the morphism $j_Y\circ p:\overline X\to\overline Y$ as
$\overline X\xrightarrow{j'}W\xrightarrow{r}\overline Y$, with $j'$ open,
$r$ proper and $\overline X$ dense in $W$. Then $r^{-1}(Y)=\overline X$,
because the open immersion $\overline X\to r^{-1}(Y)$ is a morphism from a proper
$Y$-scheme to a separated $Y$-scheme, hence proper, and its image is
closed, open and dense.

The interchange map is defined as follows. For $M$ in $D(\overline X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, restriction to the open
$Y\subset\overline Y$ identifies $j_Y^*Rr_*j'_!M$ with $Rp_*M$, because
$r^{-1}(Y)=\overline X$, the restriction of $r$ over $Y$ is $p$, and
$j'_!M$ restricts to $M$ on $\overline X$. By the adjunction $j_{Y!}\dashv j_Y^*$, we obtain a map

$$
\iota_M:j_{Y!}Rp_*M\longrightarrow Rr_*j'_!M,
\tag{5.9}
$$

which is the unique map restricting to the identity of $Rp_*M$ over $Y$.

For $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\overline X,\Lambda)$, this map is an isomorphism. Indeed, over $Y$ it is the identity, and over $\overline Y\setminus Y$ both sides vanish.
For the right-hand side, the vanishing follows from proper base change on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-localizing-categories]) for the inclusion
of $\overline Y\setminus Y$ into $\overline Y$, since $j'_!M$ vanishes on
$r^{-1}(\overline Y\setminus Y)=W\setminus\overline X$. Both sides preserve
direct sums on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\overline X,\Lambda))$
(Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-extension-zero]). Hence
Lemma [lemma-checking-isomorphisms-constructible-complexes] shows that
$\iota_M$ is an isomorphism for all
$M\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\overline X,\Lambda))$. For $M=j_!K$ it gives

$$
Rq_*j_{Y!}Rp_*j_!K\simeq Rq_*Rr_*j'_!j_!K=R(qr)_*(j'j)_!K,
$$

and the right side is $R(gf)_!K$ computed with the compactification
$gf=(qr)\circ(j'j)$.

*Verification of canonicity and associativity.* Every map used is characterized by
its restriction to an open subscheme, since the refinement maps
(5.7) and the maps
$\iota_M$ restrict to identities. For example,
replacing any of the chosen compactifications by a refinement commutes with
$\iota_M$, because both composites restrict to
the same identity and are then equal by adjunction. For associativity, given three composable morphisms, we choose common refinements (by graph closure) of the finitely
many compactifications that occur in the composites of two of them. On these, each of the two bracketings is built from composites of proper direct images,
composites of extensions by zero, and maps of the form
$\iota_M$. The first two kinds of pieces are associative: the isomorphisms $Rq_*Rr_*\simeq R(qr)_*$ are associative because they are the
isomorphisms of derived functors of composites of left exact functors
(equivalently, they are adjoint to the composition isomorphisms of the
inverse images), and composition of extensions by zero is associative by
adjunction. Moreover, interchanging two adjacent open and proper steps in either order gives the same map by the uniqueness of
$\iota_M$. So the two bracketings agree.

from one for each factor, so we treat $j_!$ and $Rp_*$ separately. Since open immersions and proper
morphisms are stable under base change, we may pull back a compactification
$f=p\circ j$ along $v$ to a compactification $f'=p'\circ j'$, where now
$j'$ and $p'$ denote the base changes of $j$ and $p$. For $j_!$, extension by zero commutes with inverse image, as shown before the proposition. Combining this with proper base change
on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\overline X,\Lambda))$
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-localizing-categories]),
we obtain the isomorphism $v^*Rp_*j_!\simeq Rp'_*v'^*j_!\simeq Rp'_*j'_!u^*$
on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$. This isomorphism is
compatible with change of compactification because the refinement maps are
characterized by their restriction to the open subscheme.
It is also compatible with composing two cartesian squares, because both factors are. For the first factor, a map between extensions by zero from an
open is determined by its restriction to that open, since
$\Hom(j_!B,j_!B')=\Hom(B,B')$. For the second, a base change map is the adjoint transpose of a counit, and the counit of a composite adjunction
is the composite of the counits. Finally, compatibility with the composition isomorphisms of (1) follows in the same way as canonicity: both composites
are built from refinement maps, maps
$\iota_M$ and proper base change maps, and
they agree because their restrictions to the open part are the same
identity.

*The composition isomorphism.* Choose compactifications $f=p\circ j$
and $g=q\circ j_Y$, with $j:X\to\overline X$ and $j_Y:Y\to\overline Y$ open and
$p,q$ proper. In the composite $Rq_*j_{Y!}Rp_*j_!$, the middle factor $j_{Y!}Rp_*$
applies a proper direct image before an extension by zero, and we
want to interchange the two.
Compactify the morphism $j_Y\circ p:\overline X\to\overline Y$ as
$\overline X\xrightarrow{j'}W\xrightarrow{r}\overline Y$, with $j'$ open,
$r$ proper and $\overline X$ dense in $W$. Then $r^{-1}(Y)=\overline X$,
because the open immersion $\overline X\to r^{-1}(Y)$ is a morphism from a proper
$Y$-scheme to a separated $Y$-scheme, hence proper, and its image is
closed, open and dense.

The interchange map is defined as follows. For $M$ in $D(\overline X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, restriction to the open
$Y\subset\overline Y$ identifies $j_Y^*Rr_*j'_!M$ with $Rp_*M$, because
$r^{-1}(Y)=\overline X$, the restriction of $r$ over $Y$ is $p$, and
$j'_!M$ restricts to $M$ on $\overline X$. By the adjunction $j_{Y!}\dashv j_Y^*$, we obtain a map

$$
j_{Y!}Rp_*M\longrightarrow Rr_*j'_!M,
$$

which is the unique map restricting to the identity of $Rp_*M$ over $Y$.

(Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-extension-zero]). Hence

compactifications are compared through a third one that refines both,
by the argument described at the start of this subsection.

For independence it suffices to
compare a compactification with a refinement of it. Indeed, the
schematic closure of $X$ in a compactification is a refinement of it,
since its inverse image over $X$ is $X$. Moreover, any two dense
compactifications have a common refinement
(Proposition [proposition-dense-compactifications-form-cofiltered-category]).

*Refinements.* Let $j:X\to Z$ and $j':X\to Z'$ be
compactifications over $Y$, and let $h:Z'\to Z$ be a refinement
(Definition [definition-compactification-refinement]), that is, a proper $Y$-morphism
with $h\circ j'=j$ and $h^{-1}(X)=X$. To construct the comparison
map, note that restriction to the open subscheme
$X$ commutes with $Rh_*$. This holds because $h^{-1}(X)=X$ and
restriction is exact and preserves K-injectives, its left adjoint $j_!$
being exact. As $j'^*j'_!K=K$, we get $j^*Rh_*j'_!K\simeq K$. By adjunction this isomorphism
corresponds to a map

$$
e_{h,K}:j_!K\longrightarrow Rh_*j'_!K
\tag{5.7}
$$

whose restriction to $X$ is the identity. We claim that it is an isomorphism
for $K\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$. By
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-extension-zero], both sides are exact
functors of $K$ preserving direct sums, so by
Lemma [lemma-checking-isomorphisms-constructible-complexes] we may assume that
$K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$, where proper base change is available.

By the exact sequence for an open and its closed complement, applied in
each degree [Stacks, [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH)], a morphism in $D(Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ that is an isomorphism on $X$ and on $Z\setminus X$ is an isomorphism. On $X$ our map is the identity, so it remains to see that on $Z\setminus X$ both sides vanish. For $j_!K$ this holds by definition of extension by zero, while for $Rh_*j'_!K$ we use proper base change on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-localizing-categories]) for the inclusion
of $Z\setminus X$ into $Z$. It shows that the restriction of $Rh_*j'_!K$
is the direct image of the
restriction of $j'_!K$ to $h^{-1}(Z\setminus X)=Z'\setminus X$, which is
zero. This proves the claim. Applying $Rp_*$
and using $R(p\circ h)_*=Rp_*Rh_*$, we obtain an isomorphism between the two
candidate functors $Rf_!$, namely $Rp_*j_!$ and $R(ph)_*j'_!$.

If $Z''\xrightarrow{k}Z'\xrightarrow{h}Z$ are two successive refinements,
with $j'':X\to Z''$ the open immersion, then $Rh_*(e_{k,K})\circ e_{h,K}$ and $e_{hk,K}$ are maps from $j_!K$ to
$R(hk)_*j''_!K$ that both restrict to the identity on $X$. By the
observation before the proposition, they are equal.

*Common refinements.* Two arbitrary compactifications need not be related by a refinement, but they have a common one. Indeed, given dense compactifications $Z_1$ and
$Z_2$, Proposition [proposition-dense-compactifications-form-cofiltered-category] provides a dense
compactification $Z$ with proper maps $h_i:Z\to Z_i$ satisfying
$h_i^{-1}(X)=X$, and similarly for finitely many compactifications. The refinement isomorphisms for $h_1$ and $h_2$ then compose to an isomorphism
between the functors defined by $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, and transitivity of the refinement maps on a common refinement shows that this comparison does
not depend on the chosen refinement and satisfies the cocycle
condition.

For $\mathcal O_E$, and hence for $\mathbf Z_\ell$, this is the equivalence of (1)
and (4) in the criterion above. For the fields we show that every
constructible sheaf is flat, which bounds the Tor amplitude of a bounded
complex by its cohomological amplitude.

For a field $\Lambda(*)$, a constructible sheaf $M$ is, on each stratum and locally on
a cover $\{U_i\}$, of the form $\Lambda_{U_i}\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P_i$
with $P_i$ a finite-dimensional vector space, so it is locally a finite free
$\Lambda_{U_i}$-module. Restriction to the strata is exact and the restrictions
are jointly conservative, as in the proof of the criterion. Hence every
constructible sheaf has Tor amplitude in $[0,0]$. Finally, a bounded complex whose finitely many cohomology
sheaves have finite Tor amplitude has finite Tor amplitude, by the

An equivalence with a $2$-colimit amounts to two statements, essential
surjectivity on objects and a bijection on morphisms. Both are parts of
Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field], and we recall how each
is proved before putting them together.

The statement about objects is
Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field](2). Its proof first descends the
lisse sheaves on the strata, together with their transition matrices. It
then descends the connecting morphisms of a finite Postnikov tower, and in
this way the complexes themselves descend. The bijection
on morphisms is Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field](1) with
$r=0$, since $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ is a full subcategory. Its proof uses the continuity of
Ext out of a constructible complex
(Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex]), applied to the filtered
colimit $\QbarX=\varinjlim_F F_X$. Surjectivity says that
every morphism descends to a finite stage, and injectivity says that two
morphisms with the same image agree at a later finite stage. Now consider the
category whose objects are the pairs $(E,K)$ with $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,E)$ and whose
Hom sets are these colimits. Together with descent of objects, the statements
above say exactly that the functor from this category to $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ is
fully faithful and essentially surjective.

Consider the ordinary category whose objects are pairs $(E,K)$ and whose Hom sets are filtered colimits of the Hom sets after finite coefficient extension. Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field](1), in degree zero, identifies those colimits bijectively with the Hom sets after extension to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Its part (2) makes every target object isomorphic to one represented by a pair $(E,K)$. Thus the comparison is fully faithful and essentially surjective, and is an equivalence of ordinary categories.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-dctf-x-qbar-2-colimit].

It then descends the finitely many connecting morphisms in a Postnikov tower, enlarging that field finitely many times. The resulting complex extends to the prescribed object, with its constructibility and Tor bound unchanged.

A common refinement of two compactifications is the closure of $X$ in
their fibre product, as in the example of $\mathbf A^2$ above. The
properties of morphisms then follow from density.

Given two compactifications, let $Z$ be the schematic closure of the
image of $X$ in $\overline X_1\times_S\overline X_2$ under the diagonal map.
The map from $X$ is a quasi-compact immersion, because over the open
$X\subseteq\overline X_1$ it is the graph of a morphism to $\overline X_2$, and $\overline X_2$ is
separated over $S$. By Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness], $X$ is an open
subscheme of $Z$ and is scheme-theoretically dense in $Z$. Since the
product is proper over $S$, the scheme $Z$ and its projections are proper.

The projections are refinements, that is, $X$ is its own inverse image
in $Z$. By Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness] the
formation of the schematic closure commutes with restriction to opens.
Over $X\subseteq\overline X_1$ we may therefore compute it on the open
$X\times_S\overline X_2$. There the immersion is the graph of
$X\to\overline X_2$, which is closed, so the closure is this graph. This means that the inverse image of $X$
under the first projection is $X$, on which the first projection is the
identity. The same holds for the second projection. The assertion
for finite families follows by induction.

Let $h:\overline X'\to\overline X$ be a
morphism of dense compactifications restricting to the identity on
$X$. To see that $h$ is proper, note that it factors through its graph.
This graph is closed in $\overline X'\times_S\overline X$ because
$\overline X$ is separated over $S$, and the projection of this product to
$\overline X$ is proper because $\overline X'$ is proper over $S$.

Next, the inclusion $X\to h^{-1}(X)$ is a section of the separated map
$h^{-1}(X)\to X$. It is therefore closed, as well as open. Since $X$ is
schematically dense in $\overline X'$, it is schematically dense in the
open $h^{-1}(X)$. A closed subscheme containing it must be all of
$h^{-1}(X)$, and we conclude that $h^{-1}(X)=X$. Two parallel morphisms
are equal by Lemma [lemma-uniqueness-maps-dense-open]. Finally, the
category is nonempty by Nagata's theorem. Since any two objects have a
common refinement and parallel morphisms are equal, it is cofiltered.

We use one central element for $V$ and $V'$ simultaneously, so that
its scalars on the factors of $V\otimes V'$ are products of its scalars
on the factors of $V$ and of $V'$. Since
Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group] requires
semisimple representations, we apply it to
$V^{\mathrm{ss}}\oplus V'^{\mathrm{ss}}$. This changes nothing,
because by Lemma [lemma-tensor-exterior-powers-filtered-representations] the simple factors of
$V\otimes V'$ and $\bigwedge^rV$ depend only on the composition factors
of $V$ and $V'$. Now let $c_a$ and $c'_b$ be the
scalars by which its central element of degree $N$ acts on the
composition factors $A_a$ of $V$ and $A'_b$ of $V'$. By
Lemma [lemma-determinant-weight-from-central-scalar],
$\gamma_a=\lambda_\iota(c_a)/N$ and
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(A'_b)=\lambda_\iota(c'_b)/N$.

(1) The central element acts by $c_ac'_b$ on $A_a\otimes A'_b$, and hence
on every simple factor of it. By the same lemma, each such factor has
determinant weight $\gamma_a+\operatorname{dw}_\iota(A'_b)$. Moreover, each
$A_a\otimes A'_b$ is nonzero, and Lemma [lemma-tensor-exterior-powers-filtered-representations]
identifies the simple factors of these tensor products with those of
$V\otimes V'$.

(2) The central element acts on $\bigotimes_a\bigwedge^{n_a}A_a$ by
$\prod_ac_a^{n_a}$. So each simple factor of this nonzero representation
has determinant weight $\sum_an_a\gamma_a$, and
Lemma [lemma-tensor-exterior-powers-filtered-representations] identifies these factors with those of
$\bigwedge^rV$.

(3) We have $\det(s\mid A^\vee)=\det(s\mid A)^{-1}$, and duality carries a
composition series of $V$ to one of $V^\vee$ whose factors are the duals
$A_a^\vee$.

For $\mathcal O_E$ we use the criterion of
Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion], which
asks for derived completeness and constructible reduction. Let
$K\in\Dbc(U,\mathcal O_E)$. Since $Rj_*$ commutes with $R\varprojlim$
[Stacks, [099L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099L)], $Rj_*K$ is derived complete. Since $Rj_*$ also commutes with
cones, the reduction of $Rj_*K$ modulo $\pi_E$ is $Rj_*$ of the reduction
of $K$. That reduction comes from $U_{\acute{e}t}$. Its direct image is
therefore the pullback of the étale one [Stacks, [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)], which is bounded
constructible by Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field]. Both
conditions of the criterion hold, and so $Rj_*K\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$.

For $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we reduce to the integral case. Since $Rj_*$ is
exact, the objects $K$ with $Rj_*K\in\Dbc$ form a triangulated
subcategory. It therefore suffices to treat the generators of
Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4). These come from integral objects by
inverting $\ell$ and by a colimit over finite extensions of $E$. Both
operations are filtered colimits of systems with a common lower bound,
and $Rj_*$ commutes with such colimits
(Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]). Hence $Rj_*$ of a generator
is obtained from $Rj_*$ of an integral object by the same operations, and
it lies in $\Dbc$.

We construct mutually inverse maps: a divisor gives its invertible sheaf,
normalized along $P$, and a family in $F$ has, up to units on $T$, a
unique section in each fibre, whose zero scheme is a family of divisors of
degree $g$.

*From divisors to sheaves.* On $C\times \operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$,
normalize the universal invertible sheaf as

$$
\mathcal L_g=\mathcal O(D_g)\otimes
f_{\operatorname{Hilb}^g}^*(P_{\operatorname{Hilb}^g}^*\mathcal O(D_g))^{-1}.
$$

Let $W$ be the open locus where $Rf_{\operatorname{Hilb}^g,*}\mathcal L_g$ is a line
bundle in degree $0$; then $\mathcal L_g$ defines a morphism $W\to F$.

*From sheaves to divisors.* Let $\mathcal L$ be a rigidified class in
$F(T)$ and set $\mathcal N=f_{T,*}\mathcal L$. By assumption
$Rf_{T,*}\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal N'[0]$ for an invertible $\mathcal N'$,
so $\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal N'$ is invertible. The
evaluation map $f_T^*\mathcal N\to\mathcal L$ is a section $s$ of
$\mathcal L\otimes f_T^*\mathcal N^{-1}$. It is determined by $\mathcal L$
up to a unit on $T$, and such a unit does not change its zero scheme $D$.

This $D$ is a relative effective Cartier divisor. Indeed, the formation
of $\mathcal N$ commutes with base change
(Lemma [lemma-coherent-base-change-invertible-sheaves]). Hence on each
fibre $C_{\kappa(t)}$ the section $s$ is a nonzero element of the
one-dimensional space of sections. The fibre is integral because $C$ is
geometrically integral, so the zero scheme of $s$ on the fibre is an
effective Cartier divisor.
Moreover, the fibres of $D$ have degree $g$: for a point $t$ of $T$ we have
$h^0(\mathcal L_t)=1$ and $H^1(C_t,\mathcal L_t)=0$, so Riemann–Roch
gives

$$
\deg\mathcal L_t
=\chi(\mathcal L_t)-(1-g)=1-(1-g)=g.
$$

The morphism $D\to T$ is proper, since $D$ is closed in the proper scheme
$C_T$. It has finite fibres, and it is flat, as is every relative
effective Cartier divisor. A proper, flat, finitely presented morphism
with finite fibres is finite locally free. Its rank at $t$ is the degree
$g$ of the fibre $D_t$, the divisor of zeros of a section of
$\mathcal L_t$. Hence $D$ defines a morphism
$T\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$.

*The constructions are inverse.* Normalizing $\mathcal O(D)$ along
$P_T$ recovers $\mathcal L$, because
$\mathcal O(D)\simeq\mathcal L\otimes f_T^*\mathcal N^{-1}$.
The two constructions are therefore inverse to each other,
and they commute with base change, which proves that $W\simeq F$ (see [Stacks, [0B9X](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9X)]).

The cycle class comes from a single map defined with
$\mathbf Z$-coefficients, the boundary of the divisor sequence. Hence all
its reductions are reductions of one map of systems.

The diagonal is an effective Cartier divisor, which gives a boundary
morphism $\Delta_*\mathbf Z\to\mathbf G_m[1]$ (Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor]).
Tensoring with the system $(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_n$ and using the Kummer
sequence, we get one morphism of systems
$\Delta_*\mathbf Z/\ell^\bullet\to\mathbf Z/\ell^\bullet(1)[2]$. Its level
$n$ is the class of Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor] for
$\mathbf Z/\ell^n$. The transition maps between levels are part of
the data, and this is what a family of separately constructed
classes would lack. Next we take $R\varprojlim$. The site is replete with
exact products
(Propositions [proposition-repleteness-pro-etale-topos] and [proposition-exact-products]).
Hence $R\varprojlim\circ(-\otimes\mathbf Z/\ell^\bullet)$ is derived
$\ell$-completion [Stacks, [099M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099M)], and the limit $\Delta_*\mathbf Z_\ell\to\mathbf Z_\ell(1)[2]$
is the completion of the boundary map of
Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor]. It is linear over the
completed coefficient sheaf by [Stacks, [099I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099I)]. We obtain the trace in the
same way from the decomposition of $Rq_*\mathbf Z/\ell^\bullet$.

$\mathbf Z/\ell^\bullet$ in degree $0$, that is, a family of endomorphisms

scalars to $\mathcal O_E$, invert $\ell$ and take the colimit over finite
extensions (Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]). Base change holds
because the Cartier and Kummer maps are natural and pullback commutes with
$R\varprojlim$ here (Lemma [lemma-inverse-image-coefficient-sheaves]).

The first implication in (1) is immediate from the definition, since an
étale algebra is the colimit of the constant system on itself. For the
second, a filtered colimit of étale algebras is flat, and its
multiplication map is the filtered colimit of the multiplication maps
$B_\alpha\otimes_RB_\alpha\to B_\alpha$, which are flat; see
[Stacks, [092A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/092A)].

For (2) we show that $R\to B$ is unramified, which together with
flatness and finite presentation means that it is étale. The
multiplication map $B\otimes_RB\to B$ is surjective, and it is flat by
assumption. It is of finite presentation because $B$ is of finite
presentation over $R$. Hence the diagonal of
$\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is a closed immersion
that is flat and of finite presentation. Its ideal $I$ is then finitely
generated with $I=I^2$, hence generated by an idempotent, so the diagonal
is also an open immersion. A morphism locally of finite type whose diagonal is
an open immersion is unramified, and this proves (2).

presentation over $R$. Hence the diagonal of
$\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is a closed immersion
that is flat and of finite presentation. Its ideal $I$ is then finitely
generated with $I=I^2$, hence generated by an idempotent, so the diagonal
is also an open immersion. A morphism locally of finite type whose diagonal is
an open immersion is unramified, and this proves (2).

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-etale-implications].

By Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects](3),
exactness of sheaves can be checked on affine weakly contractible $W$, and
by part (1) evaluation at such $W$ is exact. Since limits are computed on sections, a
product of short exact sequences therefore evaluates on $W$ to a product of short exact
sequences of $\mathcal R(W)$-modules, which is exact because by the axiom
of choice we may lift a tuple coordinate by coordinate. This proves the
first assertion.

The derived product is the termwise product of K-injective
representatives (complexes $I$ such that maps from acyclic complexes to
$I$ are null-homotopic, the unbounded analogue of bounded-below injective
complexes). Since products are exact, a product of quasi-isomorphisms is a
quasi-isomorphism: its cone is the product of the cones, which is
acyclic. We may therefore replace the K-injective representatives by any
quasi-isomorphic ones. Hence termwise products compute the product in
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal R)$, and they commute with cohomology because
products are exact; see [Stacks, [0947](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0947), [08TB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08TB)].

Applying $j_*$ to the short exact sequence gives the long exact sequence

$$
0\to j_*F_1\to j_*F\to j_*F_2\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }R^1j_*F_1,
$$

so it suffices to show that the connecting map $\delta$ vanishes. It is
Frobenius-equivariant, and we show that its source and target have
disjoint weights.
Since $R^1j_*F_1$ is zero on $U$, we look at a point of
$C\setminus U$. There the stalk of the source has weights at most $w$
by Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]. For the target, note that the dual
$F_1^\vee$ is pure of weight $-w$, so the same result shows that the
stalk of $j_*F_1^\vee$ has weights at most $-w$. By
Lemma [lemma-local-duality-point-c-u] the stalk of the target is
the dual of this stalk twisted by $(-1)$, and hence the target has weights
at least $w+2$. Now the image of $\delta$ is a
quotient of the source and a submodule of the target, so its
eigenvalues would have weights both at most $w$ and at least $w+2$.
Hence $\delta$ vanishes at each point of $C\setminus U$. As
$R^1j_*F_1$ is zero on $U$, it follows that $\delta=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-exactness-fixed-pure-weight], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both sides of $\alpha$ are exact in each variable, so by dévissage it is
enough to check $\alpha$ on generators.
First, for constant coefficients we compute $f_i^!$ by
Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] for smooth maps and by localization, and check $\alpha$ directly. Next, general coefficients are built from extensions by zero $j_!F$ of lisse sheaves.
Since $f^!$ does not commute with $j_!$, we replace $j_!$ by
$Rj_*$, which does. The difference has smaller support, and we treat it
by induction. For the classical statements we refer to
[sga5, III, (1.6.4), (1.7.3), Proposition 1.7.4 and (3.1.1)].

*Constant and lisse coefficients.*
First let the coefficients be constant. For smooth $f_i$ of relative
dimensions $d_i$, Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] identifies $f_i^!L_i$
with $f_i^*L_i(d_i)[2d_i]$, and $(f_1\times f_2)^!$ with
$(f_1\times f_2)^*(d_1+d_2)[2d_1+2d_2]$, so both sides of $\alpha$ become
the same twisted pullback. That $\alpha$ is this identification follows from
the compatibility of the trace map (Definition [definition-trace-map])
with products. Indeed, $\alpha$ is defined through the counits, and for
a smooth map the trace map is the counit composed with $\gamma_f$.

For closed immersions we use the localization triangle and the case of
ordinary external Künneth where one factor is the identity, applied
to the complementary open immersions. In general, every map factors locally as a
closed immersion followed by a smooth projection of affine spaces. Since
$\alpha$ is compatible with composition of morphisms and with
restriction to open subschemes, Zariski localization gives the constant case for general
maps. Next, lisse finite flat coefficients become constant with finite projective values on an étale cover, so descent gives the lisse case, and then the case of bounded perfect lisse models. In each of these steps the isomorphism we obtain is $\alpha$ itself:
for smooth maps because $\gamma_f$ identifies the counit with the trace map, and for localization and descent because $\alpha$ is natural
and compatible with restriction.

*General coefficients.*
A constructible complex is lisse on a dense open, and the rest has
smaller support. We therefore argue by induction on the sum of the dimensions of the supports
of $L_1,L_2$. Pushforward along closed immersions is compatible with
$\alpha$ by proper base change and the exceptional exchange of
Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas]. Hence we may first assume that the
support is the entire base. As both sides of $\alpha$ are exact in each
variable, a finite constructible stratification,
bounded flat models and two-out-of-three reduce us to generators
$j_{i!}F_i$ for dense open $j_i:U_i\hookrightarrow Y_i$, with $F_i$
a lisse sheaf with finite projective stalks
(Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators]).

Since $f_i^!$ does not commute with $j_{i!}$ in
general, we pass through $Rj_{i*}$. Let $j'_i$ and $f_{i,U}$ be
the base changes of $j_i$ and $f_i$. The exceptional exchange
$f_i^!Rj_{i*}\simeq Rj'_{i*}f_{i,U}^!$ is the mate, under the right
adjoints, of base change for $Rf_{i!}$ along the open immersion. Hence
it is compatible with the counits used to define $\alpha$. By this
exchange and the ordinary external Künneth formula, the comparison on
$(Rj_{1*}F_1,Rj_{2*}F_2)$ is the pushforward of the lisse comparison.
Let $z_i:Z_i\hookrightarrow Y_i$ be the closed complement of $U_i$. In
the triangles

$$
j_{i!}F_i\longrightarrow Rj_{i*}F_i\longrightarrow
z_{i*}z_i^*Rj_{i*}F_i\xrightarrow{+1},
$$

the third term is still constructible of finite Tor amplitude by
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], and its support has smaller dimension.
Since $\alpha$ is natural, it maps the corresponding
triangles to each other in each variable. By induction and two-out-of-three, first
in one variable and then in the other, we obtain $\alpha$ for
$(j_{1!}F_1,j_{2!}F_2)$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-exceptional-external-kunneth], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The maps
$\mu_N$ and $\beta_N$ are defined globally as adjoint
transposes. Since being an isomorphism is local on $X$, respectively on $X'$, we show that on a chart both maps become identifications of inverse images
under the explicit identification (6.14). For this we follow
the counits through the factorization $U\to\mathbf A^d_V\to V$.

We write
$\varepsilon_N:Rf_!f^!N\to N$ for the counit of
$Rf_!\dashv f^!$ (for $f=p$ this is (6.8)). The map $\mu_N$ is the
transpose of the morphism

$$
Rf_!(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
N\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_!\omega_f
\xrightarrow{1\otimes\varepsilon_{A_S}}N ,
$$

where the first arrow is the projection formula. The map $\beta_N$ is the
transpose, for $f'$, of the morphism (6.2)
(Definition [definition-exceptional-base-change-finite]).

*Local charts.* The computation of $f^!$ on a chart also
proves (1). Zariski locally on $X$ and $S$, a smooth morphism
is an étale map to affine space followed by the projection
[Stacks, [054L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054L)]. Thus every point of $X$
has an affine open neighbourhood $u:U\hookrightarrow X$ mapping into
an affine open $v:V\hookrightarrow S$, together with a separated
étale map $e:U\to\mathbf A^d_V$ such that $fu=vp_de$, where
$p_d:\mathbf A^d_V\to V$ is the projection. By
Lemma [lemma-affine-space-etale-localization] and uniqueness of right adjoints,
we have

$$
u^*f^!N=e^*p_d^*v^*N(d)[2d],\qquad
u^*\omega_f=A_U(d)[2d].
\tag{6.14}
$$

In particular, $\omega_f$ has a single nonzero cohomology sheaf, in
degree $-2d$, which is locally free of rank one. This proves (1), because
the counit on $U$ is the composite of the étale counit for $e$ and the
counit for $p_d$. The first of these is the sum over the fibres.

*$\mu_N$ is an isomorphism.* On each such $U$, under
(6.14), the source and the target of $\mu_N$
are both $e^*p_d^*v^*N(d)[2d]$. We claim that the map is the
identification obtained by reassociating tensor product and twist. It
suffices to compare the transposes. Both are the projection formula
followed by the counit for $v$, the $d$ counits for the affine lines, and
the étale counit for $e$. They agree by the formula for the counit of a
composite in Lemma [lemma-affine-space-etale-localization]. Hence
$\mu_N$ is an isomorphism on $X$.

*$\beta_N$ is an isomorphism.* For each type of chart,
under the explicit description of $f^!$ as a
twisted inverse image, $\beta_N$ is the evident identification of
inverse images. For the projective line, the transpose of
(6.2) is the usual identification
$g'^*p^*N(1)[2]=p'^*g^*N(1)[2]$ of pullbacks. This holds because the unit
(6.7) and counit (6.8) commute with base change.
By restriction to the affine line and composition, the same holds for
affine space. For a separated étale map $u$, the transpose is again the
usual identification of inverse images. Indeed, the stalk of $u_!M$ at a
geometric point is the direct sum of the stalks of $M$ at the geometric
points over it. This description is compatible with base change, and under
it the counit $u_!u^*N\to N$ is the sum of the identity maps of the stalks
of $N$.

The cases combine, because base change for $Rf_!$ is compatible with
composition (Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek](2)) and the counit of a composite is the composite of
the counits. The open immersions $u$ and $v$ are étale, so the étale case covers them as well. Substituting these facts into (6.2), we see that the restriction of
$\beta_N$ to $U\times_XX'$ is the composite of the étale and
affine-space cases just treated. Hence $\beta_N$ is an
isomorphism on a cover of $X'$, and therefore it is an isomorphism.

*Compatibilities.* Taking $N=A_S$, we see that
$\beta_N$ identifies $g'^*\omega_f$ with $\omega_{f'}$, because
$g^*A_S=A_{S'}$. The compatibility of $\mu_N$ with
$\beta_N$ says that two maps $g'^*(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f)\to f'^!g^*N$ agree. Here the first is
$\mu_N$ followed by $\beta_N$, and the second is the identification
$g'^*(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f)=f'^*g^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_{f'}$,
coming from $g'^*f^*=f'^*g^*$ and the case $N=A_S$, followed by
$\mu_N$ for $f'$. Their transposes are maps
$Rf'_!g'^*(f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f)\to g^*N$. Both are given by the
projection formula followed by the counit, once before and once after
the base change isomorphism for $Rf_!$. They agree for two reasons. First, the projection formula isomorphism is compatible with the base change
isomorphism for $Rf_!$. Second, by the definition (6.2) of
$\beta_N$, the counit for $f'$ composed with $Rf'_!$ of
$\beta_N$ is $g^*$ of the counit for $f$ under that
isomorphism.

*Local charts.* The computation of $f^!$ on a chart also
proves (1). Zariski locally on $X$ and $S$, a smooth morphism
is an étale map to affine space followed by the projection
[Stacks, [054L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/054L)]. Thus every point of $X$
has an affine open neighbourhood $u:U\hookrightarrow X$ mapping into
an affine open $v:V\hookrightarrow S$, together with a separated
étale map $e:U\to\mathbf A^d_V$ such that $fu=vp_de$, where
$p_d:\mathbf A^d_V\to V$ is the projection. By
Lemma [lemma-affine-space-etale-localization] and uniqueness of right adjoints,
we have

$$
u^*f^!N=e^*p_d^*v^*N(d)[2d],\qquad
u^*\omega_f=\Lambda_U(d)[2d].
$$

In particular, $\omega_f$ has a single nonzero cohomology sheaf, in
degree $-2d$, which is locally free of rank one. This proves (1), because
the counit on $U$ is the composite of the étale counit for $e$ and the
counit for $p_d$. The first of these is the sum over the fibres.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism].

The special feature of the pro-étale site is that $i^*$ preserves
limits; we prove this first, deduce exactness of $j_!$ from the
localization sequence, obtain the statement about products and derived
limits from a triangle expressing $j_!$ through $Rj_*$, $i^*$ and $i_*$,
and check base change by adjunction.

*Step 1: the functors $i^*$ and $i_*$.* The functor $i^*$ preserves
limits, because evaluating $i^*M$ on a weakly contractible affine over $Z$
is the same as evaluating $M$ on an affine object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, and
evaluation commutes with limits. The assertion is local on $X$. Let $V$
be a weakly contractible object of the affine ind-étale basis of $Z$. It
determines an affine object $v(V)$ in the corresponding basis of $X$,
henselian along its inverse image of $Z$: the functor $v$ is the fully
faithful left adjoint to base change of these affine bases, and
$v(V)\times_XZ\simeq V$ [Stacks, [09A9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A9)]. The pullback of a sheaf, evaluated
on $V$, is its evaluation on $v(V)$, because every covering of a weakly
contractible object splits, so that sheafification does not change values
there. Since evaluation commutes with limits and these objects detect
isomorphisms, $i^*$ preserves limits. Being a left adjoint, it also
preserves colimits. Since it preserves both limits and colimits, it is exact. Lifting covers
along $v$ shows that $i_*$ is exact and that $i^*i_*=\mathrm{id}$ and
$j^*i_*=0$. Finally, the localization sequence is exact on the
pro-étale site [Stacks, [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH)], that is, the adjunction map
$M\to i_*i^*M$ is surjective with kernel $j_!j^*M$.

*Step 2: exactness of $j^*$ and $j_!$.* The functor $j^*$ is
restriction to $U_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, hence exact. The functor $j_!$ is exact
because its composites $j^*j_!$ and $i^*j_!$ are exact and the pair
$(j^*,i^*)$ detects exactness. Here the first composite is $j^*j_!=\mathrm{id}$,
and the second is $i^*j_!=0$. Indeed, in the localization sequence of $j_!N$
the first map $j_!j^*j_!N\to j_!N$ is an isomorphism since $j^*j_!N=N$.
Hence $i_*i^*j_!N=0$, and $i^*j_!N=0$ because $i_*$ is fully faithful. The pair
$(j^*,i^*)$ detects exactness, because both functors are exact, hence
commute with taking homology of a complex of sheaves, while a sheaf $M$
with $j^*M=0$ and $i^*M=0$ is zero by the localization sequence.

*Step 3: products and derived inverse limits.* For
$K\in D(U_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},j^*\mathcal R)$, applying the localization sequence to a
complex representing $Rj_*K$ and using $j^*Rj_*K\simeq K$, we obtain the
triangle

$$
j_!K\longrightarrow Rj_*K\longrightarrow i_*i^*Rj_*K
\longrightarrow j_!K[1].
$$

The last two terms preserve products and derived inverse limits, because
$Rj_*$ and $i_*$ are right adjoints and $i^*$ is exact and preserves
limits by Step 1; hence so does their fibre $j_!$. As $j_!$ is exact and
products are exact, the corresponding statements about limits of sheaves
of modules follow.

*Step 4: base change.* The map $j'_!g'^*\to g^*j_!$ is an isomorphism
because its right adjoint is. Indeed, $j'_!g'^*$ is left adjoint to
$g'_*j'^*$ and $g^*j_!$ is left adjoint to $j^*g_*$, and the right adjoint
of the map is the base change map $j^*g_*\to g'_*j'^*$, which is an
isomorphism since both sides send a sheaf on $X'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ to its
restriction to the objects lying over $U'$. The same holds on derived
categories, since the coefficient rings are inverse images, so that
$g^*$, $g'^*$ and $j'_!$ are exact.
The argument with the functor $v$ is [bhatt-scholze15, §6.1]; see also
[Stacks, [09AA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AA), [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH), [09BM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BM)] and [Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)].

along $v$ shows that $i_*$ is exact and that $i^*i_*=\mathrm{id}$ and

pro-étale site [Stacks, [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH)], that is, the adjunction map

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme].

*Step 3: products and derived inverse limits.* For
$K\in D(U_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},j^*\mathcal R)$, applying the localization sequence to a

triangle

$$
j_!K\longrightarrow Rj_*K\longrightarrow i_*i^*Rj_*K
\longrightarrow j_!K[1].
$$

The last two terms preserve products and derived inverse limits, because
$Rj_*$ and $i_*$ are right adjoints and $i^*$ is exact and preserves
limits by Step 1; hence so does their fibre $j_!$. As $j_!$ is exact and
products are exact, the corresponding statements about limits of sheaves

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme].

*Step 4: base change.* The map $j'_!g'^*\to g^*j_!$ is an isomorphism
because its right adjoint is. Indeed, $j'_!g'^*$ is left adjoint to
$g'_*j'^*$ and $g^*j_!$ is left adjoint to $j^*g_*$, and the right adjoint
of the map is the base change map $j^*g_*\to g'_*j'^*$, which is an
isomorphism since both sides send a sheaf on $X'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ to its
restriction to the objects lying over $U'$. The same holds on derived
categories, since the coefficient rings are inverse images, so that
$g^*$, $g'^*$ and $j'_!$ are exact.

be a weakly contractible object of the affine ind-étale basis of $Z$. It
determines an affine object $v(V)$ in the corresponding basis of $X$,
