We argue by induction on
$n=\dim(X_{\bar\eta}\times_{\bar\eta}Y_{\bar\eta})$, simultaneously for
all such traits.  Before slicing we need two reductions: global sections require proper families, and
bounding fibre dimensions after slicing requires flatness, so we
arrange both.  For properness, note first that the assertion is local on $X_s\times_kY_s$.  We may therefore pass to
affine neighbourhoods of the two factors, take projective closures
over $S$ and extend the coefficients by zero on their generic fibres.
By the base change isomorphism for nearby cycles along open immersions,
the restriction of the new map is the original map, so we may assume
that $X$ and $Y$ are projective.  For flatness, the base change isomorphism for
the closed immersions of the closures of their generic fibres, together with
invariance under nilpotent thickenings, lets us also assume that they are
reduced with dense generic fibres, hence flat
over the trait.  Moreover, none of these reductions increases $n$.

Let $Q$ be the cone of (E.4). For proper
families, global sections of nearby cycles on the special fibre are
cohomology of the geometric generic fibre, so by the base change
isomorphism for the proper structure maps and
Lemma [lemma-kunneth-map-proper-direct-image], the map of global
complexes induced by $\Pi_{L,M}$ is the ordinary Künneth isomorphism

$$
R\Gamma(X_{\bar\eta},L)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}
R\Gamma(Y_{\bar\eta},M)
\xrightarrow{\sim}
R\Gamma(X_{\bar\eta}\times Y_{\bar\eta},L\boxtimes M),
$$

and therefore

$$
R\Gamma(X_s\times_kY_s,Q)=0.
\tag{E.5}
$$

By Lemma [lemma-finite-support-global-sections], $Q=0$ as soon as
$Q$ has finite support.  When $n=0$, the special fibres are
zero-dimensional by flatness, so the support is finite. Let $n>0$.
By Lemma [lemma-quasi-finite-coordinates], $X_s\times_kY_s$ is
covered by finitely many products $V_s\times W_s$ of open subschemes
with quasi-finite maps $b:V\to\mathbf A^q_S$ and $c:W\to\mathbf A^r_S$,
where $q+r\leq n$ and $\dim V_{\bar\eta}\leq q$,
$\dim W_{\bar\eta}\leq r$. The restriction of $Q$ to $V_s\times W_s$ is
the cone of $\Pi_{L|_V,M|_W}$. If $q+r<n$, it vanishes by the induction
hypothesis. By symmetry we may therefore
assume $q+r=n$ and $q>0$, and compose $b$ with one of
the coordinate projections $\mathbf A^q_S\to\mathbf A^1_S$. In the
notation of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-map-slice] for $V$, $W$ and this
map, the map $V'\to\mathbf A^q_S\times_{\mathbf A^1_S}S'=\mathbf
A^{q-1}_{S'}$ is a base change of $b$, hence quasi-finite, and
therefore

$$
\dim V'_{\bar\eta'}\leq q-1,\qquad
\dim W'_{\bar\eta'}\leq r.
$$

By the induction hypothesis $\Pi_{L',M'}$ is an isomorphism. By
Lemma [lemma-kunneth-map-slice], the restriction of $Q$ over $s'$
is therefore zero. In other words, the support of $Q$ has no point over
the generic point of this coordinate line in the special fibre. Its
image in that line is constructible and does not contain the generic
point, so it is a finite set of closed points.

We repeat this argument for each of the $q$ coordinates of $b$. After
interchanging the factors, we do the same for each of the $r$
coordinates of $c$; the analogue of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-map-slice]
with the roles of $X$ and $Y$ exchanged holds by symmetry of
$\boxtimes$. The support of $Q$ on $V_s\times W_s$ is then contained in
the inverse image under $b_s\times c_s$ of a finite set. This inverse
image is finite, because $b_s\times c_s$ is quasi-finite. With finite
support, (E.5) and
Lemma [lemma-finite-support-global-sections] show that $Q=0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-kunneth-map-slice], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

All maps involved are maps out of an extension by zero, so each of them
is determined by its restriction to the open subscheme, where it is
an identity or an inverse counit. We use this repeatedly.

Independence of the compactification reduces to a refinement $h:Z'\to Z$. The two maps
$j_!K\to Rh_*Rj'_*K=Rj_*K$ obtained from
(5.7) and from $j_!K\to Rj_*K$ have the same
adjoint under $j_!\dashv j^*$, namely the inverse of $j^*Rj_*K\to K$.
Hence they are equal. Applying $Rp_*$ gives independence.

The square is checked on the compactifications that define $c^!_{g,f}$
and the interchange map (5.9). Apart from composition
and naturality squares for ordinary direct images, it comes down to
comparing the two maps

$$
j_{Y!}Rp_*M\longrightarrow Rr_*j'_!M
\longrightarrow Rr_*Rj'_*M=Rj_{Y*}Rp_*M,
\qquad
j_{Y!}Rp_*M\longrightarrow Rj_{Y*}Rp_*M.
$$

Their adjoints under $j_{Y!}\dashv j_Y^*$ are both the inverse
counit for $j_Y^*\dashv Rj_{Y*}$, because the interchange map restricts
to the identity on $Y$. So the two maps agree. Applying $Rq_*$ with $M=j_!K$,
and using naturality for $j_!K\to Rj_*K$, we get the displayed
square for the chosen compactifications. The refinement calculation
extends it to any choices. If $f$ is proper, the
compactification with $j=\mathrm{id}$ has $\eta_f$ equal to the
identity, and the last assertion follows from the square.

For $f=pj$, the inverse counit $K\to j^*Rj_*K$ has under $j_!\dashv j^*$ a unique adjoint $j_!K\to Rj_*K$. Applying $Rp_*$ and the composition comparison $Rp_*Rj_*\simeq Rf_*$ gives the displayed map. All three constructions are natural in $K$, so they define the required transformation.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-forgetting-supports-composition].

The composite of two transforms is again an integral
transform, and we compute its kernel. It will turn out to be the
constant sheaf on the diagonal, twisted by $(-r)$, which up to this twist
is the kernel of the identity functor. Let $r_{ij}$ be the projections of
$V\times_SV^\vee\times_SV$ onto pairs of factors. By base change and
the projection formula, the composite of two transforms is the
transform with the convolution kernel

$$
Rr_{13!}(r_{12}^*\mathcal K_\psi\otimes
r_{23}^*\mathcal K_{\psi^{-1}})[2r].
$$

At a point $(x,z)$, the unshifted integral over the middle factor is
the cohomology of the character sheaf attached to
$y\mapsto\psi\langle x-z,y\rangle$, and hence it vanishes for $x\ne z$
by Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character]. Thus the unshifted convolution
is supported on the diagonal, so the localization triangle identifies
it canonically with the direct image of its restriction to the
diagonal. There the unit trivialization of the character sheaf and
the trace map for the vector bundle identify the restriction with
$E(-r)[-2r]$. Since the shift $[2r]$ cancels $[-2r]$, we obtain the first
inversion formula. If instead the two kernels use the same character, then
$x-z$ is replaced by $x+z$, the support is the antidiagonal, and we
obtain the second formula. Since the traces and unit trivializations
used here are defined over $k_0$, these isomorphisms commute with the
Weil structures.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-fourier-inversion], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

By Fourier inversion, a punctual transform would force every geometric
constituent of $M$ to be a linear character sheaf, and the hypothesis
excludes this.

By Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart], the transform of the simple
object $(j_*M)[1]$ is simple, and so by
Lemma [lemma-simple-objects] it is either punctual or of the
displayed form. Restricting the kernel to $\{a\}\times\mathbf A^1$
shows that the inverse transform of a geometric skyscraper at $a$ is
$\mathcal L_{\psi(-ax)}(1)[1]$. Now, if the transform were punctual, it
would geometrically be an iterated extension of skyscrapers at
finitely many points $a$, so by Fourier inversion and exactness
$(j_*M)[1]$ would be geometrically an iterated extension of the
objects $\mathcal L_{\psi(-ax)}(1)[1]$. Restricting to $U$, we see
that every geometric constituent of $M$ would be one of these linear
characters, which the hypothesis excludes. Finally, the open $U'_0$ and
the sheaf $M'$ are defined over $k_0$, since we may choose a
Weil-stable open on which the constructible transform is lisse.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We show that the geometric transform and its inverse preserve
${}^pD^{\le0}$. Being mutually inverse, they then preserve
${}^pD^{\ge0}$ by orthogonality, and the Weil statement follows by
Lemma [lemma-perverse-weil-sheaves], since the forgetful functor on
perverse Weil sheaves is exact and reflects exactness. For the first
step, the key point is
that the stalks of the transform are compactly supported cohomology
groups on the affine line, in degrees $0,1,2$, and that the group in degree two is
nonzero only at the finitely many points $y$ for which the twisted sheaf
has a geometrically constant quotient.

*Right exactness.* Since the transform is triangulated and
${}^pD^{\le0}$ is stable under extensions and
positive shifts, ordinary truncation reduces this to punctual sheaves
in degree zero and to objects $G[1]$ with $G$ constructible. Indeed, an
object of ${}^pD^{\le0}$ is an iterated extension of its shifted
ordinary cohomology sheaves $\mathcal H^a(K)[-a]$ with $a\le0$; the one
with $a=0$ is punctual, and the others are of the form $G[1]$ shifted
by a nonnegative amount.
Punctual sheaves map into ${}^pD^{\le0}$, since by the stalk formula
the transform of a geometric skyscraper is a lisse sheaf shifted by one.

For $G[1]$ we show that the transform lies in ordinary degrees
$-2,-1,0$ and that its degree-zero sheaf has finite support. The first
assertion follows from the stalk formula and
Lemma [lemma-cohomological-range-curve]. For the second, note that the degree-zero stalk at a closed
geometric point $y$ is

$$
H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,G\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)}).
$$

On a dense open where $G$ is lisse with generic representation $V$,
write $\chi_y$ for the character of $\pi_1$ given by the restriction of
$\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)}$. By localization we may discard the finitely many
remaining points, which contribute only in degree zero, and
Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve] (whose proof of the
formula for $H^2_c$ uses only the geometric curve) shows that this stalk is
$(V\otimes\chi_y)_{\pi_1}(-1)$. In particular, it is nonzero only if
$V$ has the rank-one quotient $\chi_y^{-1}$, and we show that this
happens for only finitely many $y$.
First, the characters $\chi_y$ are pairwise distinct. Indeed, if
$\chi_y=\chi_{y'}$ with $y\ne y'$, then $\mathcal L_{\psi((y-y')x)}$ is
trivial on the dense open, hence on the line by the surjectivity of
fundamental groups. This is impossible, because its compactly
supported cohomology vanishes by Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character],
whereas the constant sheaf has nonzero top cohomology with compact
support. Second, if $V$ has pairwise nonisomorphic rank-one quotients
$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$, then the induced map
$V\to\chi_1\oplus\dots\oplus\chi_n$ is surjective. To see this, note
that its image is a subrepresentation of a sum of pairwise nonisomorphic simple
representations, hence the sum of some of the $\chi_i$, and it maps
onto each $\chi_i$. So $n\le\dim V$,
and $\chi_y^{-1}$ is a quotient of $V$ for at most $\dim V$ points $y$.
The degree-zero sheaf therefore has only finitely many nonzero closed
geometric stalks. Since it is constructible, it has finite support, and the
transform of $G[1]$ belongs to ${}^pD^{\le0}$.

*Exactness.* The argument for $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ applies
equally to $\psi^{-1}$, and a Tate twist does not affect supports or
degrees. Both $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ and its quasi-inverse
$\operatorname{FT}_{\psi^{-1}}(-)(1)$ of
Proposition [proposition-fourier-inversion] therefore preserve
${}^pD^{\le0}$. Since
${}^pD^{\ge0}$ is the right orthogonal of ${}^pD^{\le-1}$, the two
mutually inverse equivalences also preserve ${}^pD^{\ge0}$. Both
functors are therefore t-exact, and they induce exact equivalences of
the geometric hearts. With their canonical Frobenius compatibilities and
the equivariant inversion isomorphisms of
Proposition [proposition-fourier-inversion], they then give quasi-inverse
functors on perverse Weil sheaves, which are exact because the forgetful
functors are exact and reflect exactness.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Let $i:\{y\}\hookrightarrow X$ and $j:U=X\setminus\{y\}\hookrightarrow X$.
We split $\psi$ along the localization triangle and compute the two local
terms separately.

*Splitting $\psi$.* Both pieces are stable under $\Phi_X^m$, and in
fact $((\Phi_X^m)^{-1}\{y\})_{\mathrm{red}}=\{y\}$. In the enhanced derived
category, the functorial localization triangle is a two-step filtered
object,

$$
K_U=j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K
\xrightarrow{+1},
$$

and $\psi$ induces a coherent map from the $(\Phi_X^m)^*$-pullback of this
filtration to the filtration itself, with induced correspondences

This is the projectivity theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces; see
[Stacks, [08YN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08YN)]. Here we sketch the implication from extremal disconnectedness
to projectivity, which is the direction used later. To lift a map
$S\to T_2$ along a surjection $T_1\to T_2$, one pulls the surjection back to
$S$ and chooses a minimal closed subspace of the fibre product that
still surjects onto $S$. Then extremal disconnectedness forces this
irreducible surjection to be a homeomorphism, and its inverse gives the
lift.

The isomorphism comes from the Kummer sequence and the identification
of the preceding proposition. The point is that both are compatible with
the Galois action and with the transition maps. Then they pass to the
inverse limit.

We compute on the étale site and transport the result to the
pro-étale site by Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison].
Since that comparison is natural, it preserves all the maps and Galois
actions below. The Kummer sequence gives

$$
0\longrightarrow
H^0(C,\mathbf G_m)/\ell^n
\longrightarrow H^1(C,\mu_{\ell^n})
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)[\ell^n]
\longrightarrow0.
$$

The first term vanishes. Indeed, $C$ is proper and connected, so
$H^0(C,\mathbf G_m)=\bar k^{\times}$, and this group is divisible. For the
last term, note that the degree map takes values in the torsion-free group $\mathbf Z$, so
$\operatorname{Pic}(C)[\ell^n]=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)[\ell^n]$, and
Proposition [proposition-jacobian-over-ground-field] identifies this
group with $J_0[\ell^n](\bar k)$. It remains to check Galois equivariance. The map induced by
$\mu_{\ell^n}\to\mathbf G_m$ and the identification of
Proposition [proposition-jacobian-over-ground-field] are natural in the
curve and in the field, and hence Galois-equivariant.

To check the transition maps, we map the Kummer sequence for
$\ell^{n+1}$ to that for $\ell^n$ by $[\ell]$ on the first
$\mathbf G_m$ and by the identity on the second. On the kernels this is
$z\mapsto z^\ell$. On the Picard group it sends an invertible sheaf
to its $\ell$-th tensor power, which is $[\ell]$ on $J_0$. Therefore the
displayed isomorphisms identify the two inverse systems, including
their transition maps.

The proof uses one property of constructible sheaves: maps out of them
commute with filtered colimits. Because of this, the formal colimits of
the ind-category behave like actual colimits. Each closure property in (2)
then reduces to the same property of $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$, once the objects
and maps involved are written as filtered colimits of constructible
sheaves and maps between them.

*Finite presentation.* Constructible sheaves are finitely
presented in $\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. Indeed,
Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex] in degree zero
shows that $\Hom(C,-)$ commutes with filtered colimits for $C$ constructible.
By Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](1),(2), the
category $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is essentially small, abelian, and closed
under extensions. We fix a small skeleton, so that the ind-category in (1) is defined.

*Full faithfulness.* For filtered diagrams $(C_\alpha)$ and
$(D_\beta)$ of constructible sheaves, finite presentation implies

$$
\Hom(\varinjlim_\alpha C_\alpha,\varinjlim_\beta D_\beta)
=\varprojlim_\alpha\varinjlim_\beta\Hom_{\Cons(X,\Lambda)}(C_\alpha,D_\beta),
$$

which is the Hom set in the ind-category. This proves (1), since the
essential image is $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ by definition.

*Canonical presentations.* The closure properties below involve
several ind-constructible sheaves at once, so to compare their
presentations we use a presentation that involves no choices. Namely, for $B\in\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$, let $J(B)$ be
the category of constructible sheaves $C$ with a map $C\to B$; we show that
$B=\varinjlim_{J(B)}C$.

The category $J(B)$ is filtered. Indeed, two objects $C_1\to B$ and $C_2\to B$
both map to $C_1\oplus C_2\to B$, and two parallel arrows $C\rightrightarrows C'$
over $B$ are equalized by the cokernel of their difference, which is
constructible and still maps to $B$. Now write
$B=\varinjlim_\alpha C_\alpha$. By finite presentation, every
$C\to B$ factors through some $C_\alpha$, and two factorizations agree at
a later stage. This means that the given diagram is cofinal in $J(B)$, and
hence $B=\varinjlim_{J(B)}C$.

*Filtered colimits and direct sums.* Let $B=\varinjlim_\lambda B_\lambda$
be a filtered colimit with $B_\lambda\in\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$. To present $B$, consider the category of pairs $(\lambda,C\to B_\lambda)$ with $C$ constructible. It is filtered:
we move finitely many indices to a common upper bound, and then use direct
sums and cokernels in $J(B_\lambda)$. Moreover, the colimit of the $C$ over this category is $\varinjlim_\lambda\varinjlim_{J(B_\lambda)}C=B$. A direct sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums, so it lies in $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$
as well.

*Kernels and cokernels.* Let $f:B\to B'$ be a map in
$\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$. It suffices to write $f$ as a filtered colimit of maps $v$ of
constructible sheaves. Since filtered colimits are exact, $\ker f$
and $\coker f$ are then the filtered colimits of the constructible sheaves
$\ker v$ and $\coker v$. Let $P_f$ be the category of commutative squares

$$
\begin{matrix} C&\xrightarrow{v}&D\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ B&\xrightarrow{f}&B',\end{matrix}
\qquad C,D\in\Cons(X,\Lambda).
$$

This category is filtered, because finite colimits of such squares are
formed by finite colimits of the arrows $v$ in the abelian category
$\Cons(X,\Lambda)$. We claim that the functor $P_f\to J(B)$,
$(v)\mapsto(C\to B)$, is cofinal. Indeed, every $C\to B$ is the source of a square, namely $v=\mathrm{id}_C$ with $C\to B'$ the composite. If
$C\to C_1\xrightarrow{v_1}D_1$ and $C\to C_2\xrightarrow{v_2}D_2$ are two
squares under the same $C\to B$, then both map to the square with source
$C_1\amalg_CC_2$ and target $D_1\amalg_CD_2$. Here the pushouts are taken in $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$, and they map to $B$ and $B'$ because the two maps
from $C$ to $B$, and the two maps from $C$ to $B'$, agree.

Similarly, the functor $P_f\to J(B')$, $(v)\mapsto(D\to B')$, is cofinal.
Every $D\to B'$ is the target of a square, namely $v:0\to D$. If
$C_1\xrightarrow{v_1}D_1$ and $C_2\xrightarrow{v_2}D_2$ are two squares
under the same $D\to B'$, then both map to the square with source
$C_1\oplus C_2$ and target $D_1\amalg_DD_2$. The two cofinality statements give
$f=\varinjlim_{P_f}v$, and exactness of filtered colimits gives

$$
\ker f=\varinjlim_{P_f}\ker v,\qquad
\coker f=\varinjlim_{P_f}\coker v,
$$

both of which lie in $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$.

*Extensions.* Let $0\to N\to M\to B\to0$ be exact in
$\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, with $N=\varinjlim_\beta D_\beta$ and
$B=\varinjlim_\alpha C_\alpha$ ind-constructible. We show that $M$ is a
filtered colimit of extensions of constructible sheaves. First, the pullback
of the extension along $C_\alpha\to B$ is ind-constructible. Its class lies in
$\Ext^1(C_\alpha,N)$, and
Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex] gives

$$
\Ext^1(C_\alpha,N)
=\varinjlim_\beta\Ext^1(C_\alpha,D_\beta).
$$

So the pulled-back extension is pushed out from an extension $M_{\alpha\beta}$
of $C_\alpha$ by some $D_\beta$. Since
$\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is closed under extensions, $M_{\alpha\beta}$ and each of its
pushouts along $D_\beta\to D_{\beta'}$ are constructible. Their colimit over
$\beta'$ is the pullback of $M$ to $C_\alpha$. Second, since filtered
colimits are exact, $M$ is the colimit over $\alpha$ of these pullbacks.
By closure under filtered colimits, $M\in\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$.

*Grothendieck.* The category $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ is Grothendieck abelian
in the sense of [Stacks, [079A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079A)]. Indeed, by the above its colimits
exist and are computed in $\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, so filtered
colimits are exact. The direct sum of the objects of the skeleton of
$\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is a generator.

*Finite presentation.* Constructible sheaves are finitely
presented in $\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. Indeed,
Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex] in degree zero
shows that $\Hom(C,-)$ commutes with filtered colimits for $C$ constructible.
By Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](1),(2), the
category $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ is essentially small, abelian, and closed
under extensions. We fix a small skeleton. Part (1) follows from finite
presentation.

$(D_\beta)$ of constructible sheaves, finite presentation implies

$$
\Hom(\varinjlim_\alpha C_\alpha,\varinjlim_\beta D_\beta)
=\varprojlim_\alpha\varinjlim_\beta\Hom_{\Cons(X,\Lambda)}(C_\alpha,D_\beta),
$$

which is the Hom set in the ind-category.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-ind-constructible-sheaves].

The substantial implication is (2)$\Rightarrow$(3), which is
Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes]. The others hold because
the complexes $\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$ are complete, have finite Tor amplitude, and have
constructible reductions. These properties survive extension by zero
from strata. We prove (1)$\Rightarrow$(2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(1) and
(3)$\Leftrightarrow$(4).

*(1) implies (2).*
We first treat a single constructible sheaf, locally on a stratum, then
extend by zero from the strata, and finally pass to complexes.

A finitely generated $\mathcal O_E$-module is a finite sum of copies of
$\mathcal O_E$ and of modules $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^r$, so its sheaf has a
two-term finite free resolution. The coefficient sheaf
$\mathcal O_{E,U_i}$ on a member $U_i$ of the cover in
Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves](1) is derived complete. Indeed, it is
the limit of its finite quotients by Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients],
and since the transition maps between these quotients are surjective, this
limit agrees with the derived limit by Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence].
As completeness is preserved by finite sums and cones, the
modules $\mathcal O_{E,U_i}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P_i$ of
Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves](1) are complete, and their
reductions are bounded locally constant finite complexes. We may check
these assertions on a pro-étale cover, because restriction to an object
is a localization of the topos, and it preserves limits and the cones
defining the reductions.

For a constructible sheaf, choose a finite stratification as in the
definition. Then for a stratum $a:S\hookrightarrow X$, factored as
$a=i\circ j$ as in Section [sec-Derived-functors], the open immersion $j$ is
quasi-compact because $X$ is Noetherian. Extension by zero $a_!=i_*j_!$ preserves
completeness, because it is exact, commutes
with the cones defining the reductions, and preserves limits. Here, for $j_!$ the
last point is the assertion about limits in Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme], see
[Stacks, [09BP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BP)], while for $i_*$ it holds because $i_*$ is exact and
a right adjoint. Using
the finite filtration by open and closed pieces, we see that the whole
sheaf is complete with constructible finite reductions. Applying this to
the finitely many cohomology sheaves of $K$ and
using the bounded Postnikov triangles, we obtain (2).

*(2) implies (3).*
This is Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes].

*(3) implies (1).*
Each of the finitely many strata is quasi-compact, so the local isomorphisms of (3)
can be taken on a finite covering by quasi-compact pro-étale objects,
and their bounds give a common cohomological interval. Since the map from
the constant sheaf with value the discrete ring $\mathcal O_E$ to
$\mathcal O_{E,S}$ is flat [Stacks, [099L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099L)], the cohomology of
$\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$ is
$\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}H^q(P^\bullet)$. Here
$H^q(P^\bullet)$ is finitely generated over $\mathcal O_E$, so these sheaves satisfy
the condition of Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves](1). This proves (1).

*(3) is equivalent to (4).*
The complexes $\mathcal O_{E,S}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$ have finite Tor
amplitude, and since the stratification is finite there is a common interval.
Since the restrictions to the strata are exact and jointly conservative, they
detect vanishing after tensoring with any sheaf of modules, and (3) implies (4).
Conversely, (4) implies (1) by definition of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, and hence (3) by
the implications already proved.

A finite abelian group of order $\ell^{2gn}$ killed by $\ell^n$ need not
be free over $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$; for $g\geq1$ the group
$(\mathbf Z/\ell^2)^{2g-2}\oplus(\mathbf Z/\ell)^{4}$ has order $\ell^{4g}$
and is killed by $\ell^2$. For $A[\ell^n]$, however, this cannot happen because
we know the orders at every level together with the exact
sequences given by $[\ell]$. Indeed, we use them to lift a basis of the
$\ell$-torsion step by step and check by counting that the lifts form
a basis at each level.

*The $\ell$-torsion and the exact sequences.* The group
$A[\ell](\bar k)$ is a vector space of dimension $2g$ over $\Fell$, since
it is killed by $\ell$ and has order $\ell^{2g}$ by
Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n]. Moreover there are exact
sequences

$$
0\longrightarrow A[\ell](\bar k)
\longrightarrow A[\ell^{n+1}](\bar k)
\xrightarrow{[\ell]}A[\ell^n](\bar k)\longrightarrow0,
$$

whose surjectivity holds because $A(\bar k)$ is divisible: every point of
$A[\ell^n](\bar k)$ is $\ell$ times a point, which then lies in
$A[\ell^{n+1}](\bar k)$.

*Lifting bases.* Choose a basis of $A[\ell](\bar k)$ and lift it
successively along $[\ell]$; the lifts form a basis at each level.
Suppose that $x_1,\ldots,x_{2g}\in A[\ell^{n+1}](\bar k)$ lift
a basis of $A[\ell^n](\bar k)$ obtained in this way, so that
$\ell^nx_1,\ldots,\ell^nx_{2g}$ is the chosen basis of $A[\ell](\bar k)$.
To see that the $x_i$ are independent, note first that all coefficients of a relation between them are divisible by
$\ell^n$, as we see by applying $[\ell]$ to it. The relation then becomes a
relation between the elements $\ell^nx_i$ of the chosen basis of
$A[\ell](\bar k)$, so the coefficients are even divisible by $\ell^{n+1}$.
As $A[\ell^{n+1}](\bar k)$ has order $\ell^{2g(n+1)}$, the $x_i$ therefore
form a basis of it over $\mathbf Z/\ell^{n+1}$.
Passing to the inverse limit of these compatible bases, we obtain both
isomorphisms and the description of $T_\ell A/\ell^nT_\ell A$.

*Equivariance and independence of $\bar k$.* The groups and maps in
the statement commute with the action of $\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)$,
because the group schemes $A[\ell^n]$ and the maps $[\ell]$ are defined
over $k$. In particular the projection
$T_\ell A/\ell^nT_\ell A\to A[\ell^n](\bar k)$ is equivariant. The
chosen bases need not be equivariant, which is why the isomorphisms
with $(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)^{2g}$ and $\mathbf Z_\ell^{2g}$ are noncanonical.
Finally, the points of $A[\ell^n]$ and the multiplication maps do not
change under a further algebraically closed extension, because
$A[\ell^n]$ is finite étale and hence a finite disjoint union of points
over $\bar k$.

We show that both sides reduce modulo $\pi_E^n$ to the two sides of
the finite formula, by identifying the reductions of the complexes, of the
operators and of the traces. This suffices, since an element of
$\mathcal O_E$ that vanishes modulo every $\pi_E^n$ is zero.

*Complexes and operators.* By Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point],
$R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K)$ and the geometric stalks are perfect, and
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients] provides canonical isomorphisms

$$
\begin{aligned}
R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n
&\simeq R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K_n),\\
K_{\bar y}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n&\simeq(K_n)_{\bar y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Under these isomorphisms the reductions of the integral operators are the operators
of $\bar\theta_n$, because extension of scalars commutes with the
pullbacks, with the units defining the endomorphisms $T_{c_m}$, and with
composition, and hence with the iterates $\theta_m$. Moreover
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence] applies for every $n$,
because $K_n\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$.

*Traces.* Represent each of the two integral complexes by
a bounded complex $P^\bullet$ of finite projective
$\mathcal O_E$-modules and its endomorphism by a chain map
$v^\bullet$. By Proposition [proposition-properties-trace] its trace is

$$
\operatorname{tr}_{\mathcal O_E}(v)
=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}(v^i\mid P^i).
$$

The reduction of this
expression modulo $\pi_E^n$ is the trace on
$P^\bullet\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$, as each $P^i$ is finite projective.

*Conclusion.* The
reduction of each side of (12.1) is therefore the corresponding
side of the finite formula for $(K_n,\bar\theta_n)$. Hence the
difference of the two sides lies in
$\pi_E^n\mathcal O_E$ for every $n$. It is zero because
$\mathcal O_E\hookrightarrow\varprojlim_n\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ is
injective.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-integral-trace-formula], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Both assertions are [bhatt-scholze15, Proposition 6.8.14(2)]. We prove the first,
which is where the Noetherian hypothesis enters. Let $K\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$.
By Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves], there is a finite stratification such
that the restriction of each of the finitely many cohomology sheaves of
$K$ to each stratum $S$ is, on quasi-compact pro-étale charts $U$, of
the form $\mathcal O_{E,U}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P$ with $P$ finitely
generated. Suppose that $K[1/\ell]=0$. Extension of scalars to $E_X$ is
exact, so $E_U\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P=0$, and each such $P$ is torsion.
The underlying space of $X$ is Noetherian, so each stratum is
quasi-compact and finitely many charts suffice. With finitely many $P$, one power of $\ell$ kills the restrictions of all
cohomology sheaves of $K$ to all strata. By the localization sequences of
Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme], a larger power kills every cohomology
sheaf of $K$. Since $K$ is bounded, a further power kills $K$ itself,
by induction along its truncation triangles.

Full faithfulness says that for $K,L\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ every morphism
$E_X\otimes K\to E_X\otimes L$ is $\ell^{-c}$ times the image of a
morphism $K\to L$ for some $c\geq0$, and that a morphism $K\to L$ becomes
zero after extension of scalars only if some power of $\ell$ kills it.
For essential
surjectivity, recall from Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4) that
$\Dbc(X,E)$ is generated by objects coming from $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$. By the
description of the Hom groups, a connecting morphism between them lifts to an
integral one after multiplication by a power of $\ell$. Hence finite cones of
the generators also have integral models.

A functor with a fully faithful right adjoint is the Verdier localization
at its kernel, so we show that restriction of scalars is fully faithful
and compute the kernel.

Inverting $\ell$ is a filtered colimit along multiplication by $\ell$,
hence exact. Therefore $E_X=\mathcal O_{E,X}[1/\ell]$ is flat over
$\mathcal O_{E,X}$, and $H^q(E_X\otimes K)=H^q(K)[1/\ell]$. Restriction of
scalars is right adjoint to extension of scalars, and the counit is an isomorphism,
because $\ell$ already acts invertibly on an $E_X$-module. Restriction is
therefore fully faithful, and extension of scalars is the Verdier localization
at its kernel. By the formula for $H^q(E_X\otimes K)$, this kernel consists of
the complexes $K$ with $H^q(K)[1/\ell]=0$ for all $q$.

The three kinds of coefficients are reached from finite ones in three
different ways: $\mathcal O_E$ by completion, $E$ by inverting $\ell$, and
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ as a colimit over finite extensions. We treat them in this order,
each case using the previous one.

Let $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E$, and put $C=\Cone(\theta(K))$; we must show
$C=0$. Since the complexes $F(K)$ and $G(K)$ lie in $\Dbc(Y,\mathcal O_E)$, they are derived $\pi_E$-complete by
Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]. Moreover, derived complete complexes are closed under cones, and so $C$ is derived complete
too. Derived Nakayama (Lemma [lemma-reduction-derived-nakayama]) therefore reduces $C=0$ to $C/\pi_E=0$. Now reduction modulo $\pi_E$ is a change of coefficients along $\mathcal O_E\to\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$. By the
compatibility assumed in the statement, it identifies $\theta(K)/\pi_E$
with $\theta_{\mathcal O_E/\pi_E}(K/\pi_E)$. This is an isomorphism by the
hypothesis for finite rings, applied to $A=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$. Thus
$C/\pi_E=0$, and so $C=0$. In particular, the case $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ gives $\Lambda=\mathbf Z_\ell$.

Let $\Lambda=E$. Here completeness is of no help, since a complex over
$E$ is killed by reduction modulo $\pi_E$. Instead we use integral models.
Both $F_E$ and $G_E$ are exact and $\theta_E$ is a transformation of exact
functors. Hence the objects $K$ for which $\theta_E(K)$ is an isomorphism
form a triangulated subcategory. By Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4),
every object of $\Dbc(X,E)$ is built by finitely many cones and shifts from
objects $K_0[1/\ell]$ with $K_0\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$. It therefore
suffices to treat these. Inverting $\ell$ is the change of coefficients
along $\mathcal O_E\to E$. By hypothesis, $\theta_E(K_0[1/\ell])$ is
therefore identified with $\theta_{\mathcal O_E}(K_0)[1/\ell]$. This is an
isomorphism by the integral case.

Let $\Lambda=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. By Proposition [proposition-dctf-x-qbar-2-colimit], every $K$ is
isomorphic to $K_E\otimes_E\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ for some finite $E$ and some
$K_E\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,E)$. By hypothesis, applied to $E\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, the map
$\theta_{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}(K)$ is identified with $\theta_E(K_E)\otimes_E\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, which
is an isomorphism by the case of $E$. Again $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ is included.

The coefficient comparisons for the six operations are those of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients]. Thus any comparison obtained from the specified units, counits, composition and tensor maps commutes with scalar extension: apply these equalities to each constituent map and then compose them. This verifies the compatibility input without assuming that the comparison itself is an isomorphism.

We descend the Jacobian of $C_{0,k_s}$, where $k_s\subseteq\bar
k$ is a separable closure of $k$. In general $k_s/k$ is infinite, hence
not an fppf cover. For this reason we move the descent datum on the
Jacobian over $k_s$ by limit arguments to a finite Galois extension, and
descend along that extension. A second limit argument shows that the
descended scheme represents the degree-zero Picard sheaf.

Let $F=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C_0/k}$ be the degree-zero part of the
fppf Picard sheaf. Here we use that the fibrewise degree is locally
constant, by coherent base change and Riemann–Roch. Since the Picard
sheaf and the degree commute with base change,
Theorem [theorem-picard-scheme-jacobian-over-separably] gives an
abelian variety $J_s$ over $k_s$ representing the restriction of $F$ to
$k_s$-schemes; $J_s$ is projective. Over $k_s\otimes_kk_s$ the two
pullbacks of $J_s$ represent the same functor, so by the Yoneda lemma we
get an isomorphism between them. All identifications are induced by $F$.
Hence this isomorphism satisfies the cocycle condition over
$k_s\otimes_kk_s\otimes_kk_s$ and respects the group structures.

To move this descent datum to a finite extension, note that $k_s$ is
the filtered union of its finite separable subextensions, and
$k_s\otimes_kk_s$ and the triple tensor product are the corresponding
unions. By the limit theorems for schemes of finite
presentation [Stacks, [01ZM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZM)], the defining equations of $J_s$ in a
projective space, the descent isomorphism, its inverse and the group
operations are defined over some finite stage. The finitely many
identities among them (inverse, cocycle, group axioms) hold after
enlarging the stage. Finally, we enlarge it further to a Galois extension. In
this way we obtain a finite Galois extension $K/k$ in $k_s$ and a
projective $K$-scheme $J_K$ with a group structure and a compatible
descent datum for $K/k$, whose base change to $k_s$ is the datum on $J_s$.
Since $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite locally free
and surjective, the descent datum on the projective scheme $J_K$ is
effective [Stacks, [0CCJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CCJ)]. This gives a commutative group scheme $J_0$ over
$k$ with $J_0\times_kk_s\simeq J_s$. Properness and smoothness descend
along $K/k$, and connectedness and dimension may be checked over $\bar
k$. Hence $J_0$ is an abelian variety of dimension $g$.

The functors $J_0$ and $F$ are fppf sheaves that agree after base
change to $k_s$. Since $k_s/k$ is not finite, we need a limit argument
to show that they agree. Both functors are
locally of finite presentation. For $J_0$ this is [Stacks, [01ZC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZC)]. For $F$
it follows from Lemma [lemma-rigidification-along-section] once the
finite stages contain a field of definition of a point of $C_0$,
because invertible sheaves, rigidifications and their isomorphisms are
of finite presentation. Hence, for affine $T$ over $k$, a section of
either functor over $T_{k_s}$, or over $T_{k_s\otimes_kk_s}$, comes from
a finite stage. Likewise, two sections that agree over $T_{k_s}$ agree over
a finite stage.

The identification $J_0(T_{k_s})\simeq F(T_{k_s})$ is compatible with the
descent data. Let a section of one functor over $T$ be given. We
transport its image over $T_{k_s}$ and descend the result to some
$T_L$ with $L/k$ finite. After enlarging $L$, its two pullbacks to
$T_{L\otimes_kL}$ agree. Since both functors are fppf sheaves, it then
descends to $T$. The same argument applied to equalities shows that the
result is unique. We obtain inverse bijections $J_0(T)\simeq F(T)$,
natural in affine $T$, and hence an isomorphism of sheaves.

The Picard sheaf and the degree commute with field extension. Hence
$J_0\times_kk'$ represents the degree-zero Picard sheaf of
$C_0\times_kk'$ for every $k'/k$. Over $\bar k$ the value of the Picard
sheaf is the Picard group, by rigidification and
$\operatorname{Pic}(\bar k)=0$. This gives the displayed identification.
For $\gamma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)$, naturality with respect to
$\operatorname{Spec}(\gamma)$ says that this group isomorphism
intertwines the Galois action on points with pullback of invertible
sheaves. Here $\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)=\operatorname{Gal}(k_s/k)$
because $\bar k/k_s$ is purely inseparable.

By the Kummer sequence, $H^1(C,\mu_{\ell^n})$ is
the $\ell^n$-torsion of the Picard group, and Poincaré duality
turns this into a statement about the untwisted $H^1$.

The first identification is
Proposition [proposition-h-1-curve-tate-module], which also
gives its Galois equivariance, and it shows that the coefficient map
$z\mapsto z^\ell$ from $\mu_{\ell^{n+1}}$ to $\mu_{\ell^n}$ corresponds to
$[\ell]$ on the Jacobian.

For the dual Tate module, Poincaré duality at finite level pairs the
untwisted $H^1$ with the twisted one that we have just identified with
$J[\ell^n](k)$. Derived duality gives a statement about the single group
$H^1$ because all the groups involved are free $A_n$-modules. Indeed, we have
$H^0(C,A_n)=A_n$ and $H^2(C,A_n(1))=A_n$ by
Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime], while the group
$H^1(C,A_n(1))$ is free of rank $2g$ by the identification above and
Corollary [corollary-torsion-jacobian-field-extension]. Since
$A_n(1)\simeq A_n$ over $k$, the untwisted $H^1$ is free of rank $2g$ as well.
Finally, a bounded complex with projective cohomology modules is the sum of its
shifted cohomology modules in the derived category, so $A_n$-duality acts
degree by degree. In this situation derived Poincaré duality,
Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality], applied to the
constant sheaf, induces in degree one an isomorphism

$$
H^1(C,A_n)\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Hom_{A_n}(H^1(C,A_n(1)),A_n).
$$

This map is the adjoint of cup product followed by the trace map of
the duality theorem, and both cup product and trace commute with
reduction of coefficients and with the action of
$\operatorname{Gal}(k/k_0)$.  Because of the twist on the second
factor, Frobenius acts trivially on the target $A_n$.

In the limit, the finite-level dualities combine into a duality with the
Tate module. Since the transition maps $[\ell]$
are surjective, we have $J[\ell^n](k)=T_\ell J/\ell^nT_\ell J$. Moreover
$T_\ell J$ is finite free by Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module], and a
homomorphism of finite free $\mathbf Z_\ell$-modules is determined by its reductions
modulo all $\ell^n$, and every compatible system of reductions lifts.
Hence the inverse limit of the adjoints at finite level is the dual of
$T_\ell J$. We obtain a perfect pairing

$$
\varprojlim_nH^1(C,A_n)\times T_\ell J\longrightarrow\mathbf Z_\ell,
$$

invariant under Frobenius.  Since geometric Frobenius acts on $T_\ell J$
by $B^{-1}$, its matrix on $\varprojlim_nH^1(C,A_n)$ in the dual
basis is $(B^{-1})^{-t}=B^t$.

Let $M\subset L$ be as in the statement, with reductions $M_n=M/\pi_E^nM$.
The fibres of these reductions define a continuous action of
$\pi_1(X,\bar x)$ on the finite free completed fibre

$$
M_{\bar x}:=\varprojlim_n(M_n)_{\bar x}.
$$

The fibre functor of the proposition takes $L$ to the rational fibre
$M_{\bar x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}E$; in other words, we apply the fibre functor of finite
covers to the finite reductions and complete the result.

Full faithfulness comes from
the Galois theory of finite étale covers of the connected scheme $X$. It says that
taking the fibre at $\bar x$ is an equivalence between finite locally
constant sheaves on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ and finite sets with continuous
$\pi_1(X,\bar x)$-action, compatible with module structures.
To pass from the finite reductions to $L$ we need to clear denominators.
Let $M\subseteq L$ and $M'\subseteq L'$
be lattices in two lisse $E_X$-modules. Then a morphism
$\phi:L\to L'$ has a uniform denominator: $\pi_E^c\phi$ maps $M$ into $M'$
for some $c\geq0$. To see this, bound the finitely many matrix entries on a
quasi-compact pro-étale covering trivializing both lattices.

For faithfulness, suppose the fibre of $\phi$ vanishes. Then the fibres of all
the reductions of $\pi_E^c\phi$ vanish, so these reductions vanish by the Galois
correspondence. Since $M'=\varprojlim_nM'_n$, it follows that $\pi_E^c\phi=0$.
For fullness, take an equivariant map between the rational fibres. After
multiplication by some $\pi_E^c$, it maps $M_{\bar x}$ into $M'_{\bar x}$. Its
reductions are then equivariant maps of finite fibres, so by the Galois
correspondence they come from compatible maps $M_n\to M'_n$. The
inverse limit of these is a map $M\to M'$ whose rationalization,
divided by $\pi_E^c$, has the given fibre.

The same uniform denominator, applied to the identity of $L$, shows that
the rational fibre does not depend on the lattice. Indeed, if $M_1$ and $M_2$ are
two lattices in $L$, then $\pi_E^c\,\mathrm{id}_{L}$ sends
$M_1$ into $M_2$ for some $c\geq0$, and symmetrically.
On fibres these maps, divided by $\pi_E^c$, therefore give mutually inverse
equivariant isomorphisms between the two rational fibres.

For essential surjectivity we build a stable lattice and glue its
reductions. A continuous
representation of the profinite group $\pi_1(X,\bar x)$ on $E^r$ has
compact image. Hence the $\mathcal O_E$-span of the translates of a
lattice is bounded and contains that lattice. As $\mathcal O_E$ is
noetherian, this span is a stable finite free lattice, and its reductions define
compatible finite locally constant étale sheaves. These sheaves become
constant simultaneously on the surjective pro-étale cover obtained
as the inverse limit of the finite étale covers corresponding to
their kernels. Their inverse limit is therefore lisse over
$\mathcal O_E$, and its rationalization is lisse over $E$. Finally, this
construction is inverse to the fibre functor.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-lattices-representations-normal-scheme], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We compute the cohomology sheaves of the derived limit with the Milnor
sequence and find that they are those of $K$.

Represent $K$ by a complex and form its canonical truncation tower,
with maps $K\to\tau_{\geq-n}K$ and
$\tau_{\geq-(n+1)}K\to\tau_{\geq-n}K$. For fixed $q$, the sheaves
$H^q(\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ and $H^{q-1}(\tau_{\geq-n}K)$ are eventually
constant, with identity transition maps, equal to the corresponding
cohomology sheaves of $K$, so the $R^1$ term in
(2.2) vanishes and the limit term is $H^q(K)$. As the natural
map induces this identification in every degree, it is an
isomorphism; see [Stacks, [0947](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0947)](2).
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-left-completeness], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We follow the two halves described at the start of this section:
first the radical is central, and then the quotient by the center
equals its derived algebra.

Put $\mathfrak r=\operatorname{rad}\mathfrak l$, and write the
faithful module as a direct sum of simple modules. Let $M$ be one of
them. By Lemma [lemma-lie-s-theorem], there is a nonzero
simultaneous $\lambda$-eigenspace $M_\lambda$ for $\mathfrak r$. We
claim that $M_\lambda$ is $\mathfrak l$-stable. To prove this, fix $x\in\mathfrak l$ and
$0\ne v\in M_\lambda$, and consider
$U=\operatorname{span}\{v,xv,x^2v,\ldots\}$. For
every $a\in\mathfrak r$ we have $[a,x]\in\mathfrak r$, and the identity

$$
ax^j=x^ja+\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}x^i[a,x]x^{j-1-i}
$$

shows, by induction on $j$, that $a$ preserves $U$ and acts on it by a
triangular matrix with constant diagonal $\lambda(a)$ in the basis
$v,xv,x^2v,\ldots$ of $U$. Indeed, the identity gives
$ax^jv=\lambda(a)x^jv$ plus terms $x^i[a,x]x^{j-1-i}v$, and by induction
applied to $[a,x]\in\mathfrak r$ these lie in the span of
$v,\ldots,x^{j-1}v$. With this, the trace of $[x,a]$ on $U$ can be computed in two
ways. Since $x$ and $a$ preserve $U$, the restriction of $[x,a]$ to $U$
is a commutator, whose trace is zero. On the other hand,
$[x,a]\in\mathfrak r$ acts on $U$ with constant diagonal
$\lambda([x,a])$. Comparing,

$$
0=\operatorname{tr}_U[x,a]=\dim(U)\lambda([x,a]),
$$

and $\lambda([x,a])=0$ because $\Omega$ has characteristic zero. It
follows that
$a(xv)=\lambda(a)xv+\lambda([a,x])v=\lambda(a)xv$, which proves the
claim.

Since $M$ is simple, the claim gives $M_\lambda=M$. Thus $\mathfrak r$
acts on $M$ by scalars, and in particular $[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak r]$
acts as zero on $M$. This holds for every simple summand, and the module
is faithful, so $[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak r]=0$, that is,
$\mathfrak r\subseteq Z(\mathfrak l)$. The reverse inclusion holds
because the center is an abelian ideal.

For the second equality, we show that the quotient
$\overline{\mathfrak l}=\mathfrak l/Z(\mathfrak l)$ has zero radical and
apply Lemma [lemma-killing]. The inverse image of a solvable ideal of the
quotient is a central extension of a solvable Lie algebra, hence
solvable. So it is contained in $\mathfrak r=Z(\mathfrak l)$. The
lemma now gives $[\overline{\mathfrak l},\overline{\mathfrak l}]
 =\overline{\mathfrak l}$. In other words, every element of $\mathfrak l$ is
congruent modulo $Z(\mathfrak l)$ to a sum of brackets, and
$\mathfrak l=Z(\mathfrak l)+[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak l]$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We first trivialize each $K_n$ locally, separately for each $n$, and then make
the trivializations compatible. To begin, choose a finite stratification on which all cohomology sheaves of
$K_1$ are locally constant, and refine it by connected components;
there are finitely many of these, since the strata are Noetherian.

For every stratum $S$ the restriction $K|_S$ is again derived complete with
constructible first reduction. Indeed, restriction to an open subscheme
preserves limits, and so does restriction to a closed subscheme on the
pro-étale site
(Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme]).
Moreover, both restrictions are exact and commute with the two-term cones defining the
reductions. From now on we fix a connected stratum $S$.

*Local trivializations at each finite level.*
By Lemma [lemma-bounds-finite-reductions], each $K_n|_S$ is classical and
of finite Tor amplitude, with locally constant finite cohomology, so we
may work on $S_{\acute{e}t}$. Fix a geometric point $\bar s$. Then the stalk complex at
$\bar s$ has a minimal finite free model $M_n$ in the common interval
$[a,b]$. By Lemma [lemma-local-constancy-finite-level] the complex
$K_n|_S$ is étale locally isomorphic to the constant complex $(M_n)_S$.

On stalks at $\bar s$, the reduction maps $K_{n+1}\to K_n$ induce maps
$M_{n+1}\to M_n$ inducing isomorphisms
$M_{n+1}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n+1}}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n\simeq M_n$, because
the étale stalk functor is exact and symmetric monoidal.
By Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-over-oe] there is a bounded finite free
complex $P^\bullet$ with $P^\bullet/\pi_E^n\simeq M_n$. Back on
$S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, we get for each $n$ local isomorphisms
$(P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_S\simeq K_n|_S$ in
$D(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$, chosen separately for
each $n$.

*The integral isomorphism.*
Choose an affine weakly contractible cover $W\to S$. For each $n$, the
local isomorphism becomes an isomorphism
$(P^\bullet/\pi_E^n)_W\simeq K_n|_W$ on all of $W$, since by weak
contractibility a covering by trivializing charts splits. Moreover, the restriction
$K|_W$ is derived complete, and its reductions are the $K_n|_W$. By
Lemma [lemma-integral-model-weakly-contractible] we conclude that
$K|_W\simeq\mathcal O_{E,W}\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}P^\bullet$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

A locally constant sheaf with model $M$ is the same as a torsor under the
automorphism sheaf of the constant sheaf $\underline M$, so the
proposition follows from the lemma once we know that this automorphism
sheaf is classical.

Decompose $X$ into the open pieces on which the constant model has a
fixed isomorphism type, and fix a finitely presented module $M$. A
presentation $\Lambda^m\to\Lambda^n\to M\to0$ identifies the internal
endomorphism sheaf of $\underline M$ with the kernel of
$\underline M^{\,n}\to\underline M^{\,m}$. Since the constant sheaf
functor is exact, this kernel is the constant sheaf on
$\operatorname{End}_\Lambda(M)$, and so the automorphism sheaf of
$\underline M$ is the constant discrete group
$\operatorname{Aut}_\Lambda(M)$. Hence
$\mathit{Isom}(\underline M,F)$ is a torsor under this classical group,
and by Lemma [lemma-torsors-under-classical-groups] it has sections étale locally.
Since $F$ is obtained from this torsor by twisting $\underline M$, it is
the pullback of the corresponding twist of the constant étale sheaf,
and so it is classical. This is the descent argument of [Stacks, [099Y](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099Y)].

Everything follows from the triangle (2.1). Indeed, for a tower of
modules, $R\varprojlim_nM_n$ is the fibre of a map between two sheaves in
degree $0$, so it has cohomology only in degrees $0$ and $1$, namely the
kernel and the cokernel of $1-T$. Here the kernel is $\varprojlim_nM_n$, and
the cokernel is $R^1\varprojlim_nM_n$, which proves the first two
assertions. Similarly, for a tower of complexes, the long exact cohomology sequence
of (2.1) reads

$$
\prod_nH^{q-1}(K_n)\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nH^{q-1}(K_n)
\to H^q(R\varprojlim_nK_n)\to\prod_nH^q(K_n)\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nH^q(K_n),
$$

where we used that by Proposition [proposition-exact-products] the cohomology of each
product is the product of the cohomology sheaves. The cokernel on the left
is $R^1\varprojlim_nH^{q-1}(K_n)$ and the kernel on the right is
$\varprojlim_nH^q(K_n)$, which gives (2.2).

Suppose now that the transition maps of a tower of modules are
epimorphisms. We show that $1-T$ is an epimorphism; then
$R^1\varprojlim_nM_n=0$ and the derived limit is $\varprojlim_nM_n$. By
Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects] it suffices to check surjectivity on sections
over every weakly contractible $W$, where the maps $t_n$ are surjective.
Given $(a_n)$, choose $m_0$ arbitrarily and then, recursively, $m_{n+1}$
with $t_n(m_{n+1})=m_n-a_n$. Then $(1-T)(m_n)_n=(a_n)_n$. See
[Stacks, [0947](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0947)].

Everything follows from the triangle (2.1). The cone
is formed on the level of complexes, so the triangle
$\Cone(1-T)[-1]\to\prod_nK_n\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nK_n\to$ is functorial in
the tower, and its long exact cohomology sequence reads

$$
\prod_nH^{q-1}(K_n)\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nH^{q-1}(K_n)
\to H^q(\Cone(1-T)[-1])\to\prod_nH^q(K_n)\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nH^q(K_n),
$$

where we used that by Proposition [proposition-exact-products] the
cohomology of each product is the product of the cohomology sheaves. The
kernel of $1-T$ on the right is $\varprojlim_nH^q(K_n)$. Let $a_K$ be the
map induced on the cokernel on the left and $b_K$ the map to this kernel;
both are natural in the tower because the triangle and its long exact
sequence are. This gives the first sequence. By clause [proposition-milnor-sequence--1],
applied to the tower of sheaves $(H^{q-1}(K_n))$, the isomorphism $e_1$
identifies $R^1\varprojlim_nH^{q-1}(K_n)=H^1(R\varprojlim_nH^{q-1}(K_n))$
with the cokernel on the left, and $\Cone(1-T)[-1]=R\varprojlim_nK_n$ by
(2.1). This gives (2.2).

For the general statement, the homotopy limit $L$ sits in a distinguished
triangle $L\to\prod_nF_n\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nF_n\to L[1]$ in
$D(\mathcal A)$, whose first map has the maps $L\to F_n$ as components.
The product in $D(\mathcal A)$ is the termwise product of K-injective
representatives. Since countable products in $\mathcal A$ are exact, they
commute with cohomology, so $H^i(\prod_nF_n)=\prod_nH^i(F_n)=P$, and
$H^i(1-T)$ is $1-T$ for the endomorphism $T$ of the statement. The long
exact cohomology sequence of the triangle,

$$
P\xrightarrow{1-T}P\to H^j(L)\to\prod_nH^j(F_n)\xrightarrow{1-T}\prod_nH^j(F_n),
$$

then gives the asserted sequence, since the kernel on the right is
$\varprojlim_nH^j(F_n)$.

We use the isomorphism $[n]^*\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2}$
twice: on curves in the fibres of $[n]$ it shows that $[n]$ is finite,
and in Euler characteristics it computes the degree. In between, translation invariance shows that all fibres have the same length, which
makes $[n]$ finite locally free. Finally, whether $[n]$ is étale is decided by its differential.

Since finiteness, flatness and the degree may be checked after base
change to an algebraic closure, we may assume that $k$ is
algebraically closed. Choose a symmetric ample $\mathcal N$
(Lemma [lemma-symmetric-ample-sheaf]); then
$[n]^*\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2}$ by
Proposition [proposition-pullback-multiplication-n]. If a fibre of $[n]$ had positive
dimension, it would contain a proper integral curve. Since $[n]$ maps
that curve to a point, the restriction of
$[n]^*\mathcal N$ to it is trivial, whereas the restriction of
$\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2}$ has positive degree. Hence every fibre has
dimension zero, and since $[n]$ is proper, it is finite. Its image is a
closed subset of dimension $g$, hence equal to the integral variety $A$
(Lemma [lemma-abelian-variety-commutative]).
After base change to an algebraic closure of its residue field, every
fibre of $[n]$ becomes a translate of $A[n]$. Indeed, if $y=nx_0$, then
translation by $x_0$ carries $A[n]=[n]^{-1}(0)$ isomorphically onto
$[n]^{-1}(y)$, because $[n]$ is a homomorphism. Hence all fibres have the
same degree $r=\dim_k\Gamma(A[n],\mathcal O_{A[n]})$.

To get flatness from the constancy of the fibre degree, we use the
following general fact. A finite morphism $f$ to a reduced Noetherian
scheme whose fibres all have degree $r$ is finite locally free of rank
$r$. Indeed, near any point Nakayama's lemma gives a surjection
$\mathcal O^{\oplus r}\to f_*\mathcal O$, since the fibre at that point
has dimension $r$. This surjection is an isomorphism at each generic
point, where the local ring is a field and both sides are vector
spaces of dimension $r$. Hence on an affine open every coordinate of a
section of its kernel lies in all minimal primes, and is therefore zero
because the ring is reduced. Since $A$ is smooth, hence
reduced, $[n]$ is finite locally free.

Recall that for a locally free sheaf $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ on $A$,
the function $m\mapsto\chi(A,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal N^{\otimes m})$
is a polynomial of degree $g$ with leading coefficient
$r\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)/g!$. Here
$\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)=(\mathcal N^g)$ is the degree of $A$ with respect
to $\mathcal N$, a positive integer because $\mathcal N$ is ample. We
compare the coefficients of $m^g$ in two expressions for
$\chi(A,[n]^*\mathcal N^{\otimes m})$. Since $[n]$ is finite, this
Euler characteristic equals
$\chi(A,[n]_*[n]^*\mathcal N^{\otimes m})$, which by the projection
formula is $\chi(A,\mathcal N^{\otimes m}\otimes[n]_*\mathcal O_A)$.
As $[n]_*\mathcal O_A$ is locally free of rank $\deg[n]$, the
coefficient is $\deg[n]\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)/g!$. Since
$[n]^*\mathcal N^{\otimes m}\simeq\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2m}$, it is also
$n^{2g}\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)/g!$. Hence

$$
\deg[n]\,\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)
=n^{2g}\deg_{\mathcal N}(A).
$$

Since $\deg_{\mathcal N}(A)>0$, we conclude that $\deg[n]=n^{2g}$; compare [Stacks, [0BFG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BFG)].
It remains to treat étaleness. The differential of the group law at
$(0,0)$ is addition of tangent vectors. By induction, the differential
of $[n]$ at the identity is $n\operatorname{id}$. Since $[n]$ commutes
with translations, the same holds at every point. If $n$ is invertible,
$[n]$ is therefore étale. Base change along the identity section
gives the assertion for $A[n]$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We argue by induction on $n=\dim X_{\bar\eta}$, simultaneously for all
traits $S$ as above, and show that the cone of $\delta_{X,M}$ has zero
global sections and finite support.

*Reductions.* We may assume that $X$ is projective, reduced, and flat
over $S$, by reductions none of which increases $n$. The assertion is
local and, by Lemma [lemma-nearby-duality-proper-direct-image],
compatible with restriction to opens. So we may pass to a projective
compactification and extend $M$ by zero on its generic fibre. Next we
use the compatibility with proper direct image
(E.13) for the closure of that
generic fibre, together with invariance under nilpotent thickenings.
This lets us assume that $X$ is reduced and flat over $S$.

Put $Q=\Cone(\delta_{X,M})$. It is bounded and constructible by the
finiteness theorem for nearby cycles and ordinary Verdier duality. By
(E.14), $R\Gamma(X_s,Q)=0$.

*Finite support.* By Lemma [lemma-finite-support-global-sections],
it remains to show that the support of $Q$ is finite. By
Lemma [lemma-quasi-finite-coordinates], $X_s$ is covered by
finitely many opens $V_s$ with quasi-finite coordinate maps
$V\to\mathbf A^q_S$, $q\leq n$, and $\dim V_{\bar\eta}\leq q$. As the
vanishing of $Q$ is local, we may replace each $V$ by finitely many
affine opens covering it, with the restricted coordinate maps. Then for
each coordinate map $V\to\mathbf A^1_S$ there is a closed immersion of
$V$ into some $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1_S}$ over $\mathbf A^1_S$, as
required in Lemma [lemma-nearby-duality-slice].

We claim that $Q$ vanishes over the generic point of each coordinate line
in the special fibre. The slice $V'$ has generic fibre of dimension at
most $q-1<n$. Hence the claim follows from the induction hypothesis and
Lemma [lemma-nearby-duality-slice]. The support of $Q$ therefore
lies over finitely many closed points of each coordinate line. Since the
coordinate map is quasi-finite, the support is finite. This argument
also covers $n=0$, where $q=0$ and $V_s$ is finite.

*Pro-étale formulation.* The comparison for constructible complexes
with finite coefficients transports both the pairing and this isomorphism
to the small pro-étale site.
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-nearby-duality-slice], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

On the compactification the vanishing holds because
$J_0(k_0)$ is finite, and on the boundary it holds because Frobenius
acts by a power of $q$, which is not $1$. The residue sequence reduces the
open case to the proper one, and at the end we pass from integral to
rational coefficients.

*The proper case.* Let $U_0=C_0$ be proper, with Jacobian $J_0$.
Here the cohomology is the dual of the Tate module, and the question is
whether $1$ is an eigenvalue of Frobenius on it.  By
Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector], arithmetic Frobenius has no
fixed vector on $T_\ell J$; indeed, a fixed compatible tuple would
consist of $\ell$-power torsion points of the finite group $J_0(k_0)$.
This means that $B-1$ is invertible on $V_\ell J$.  On the other side, geometric Frobenius
acts on the untwisted $H^1$ by $B^t$
(Proposition [proposition-kummer-duality-integral-tate-module]). Since
$\det(B^t-1)=\det(B-1)\ne0$, it fixes neither a nonzero rational vector
nor a nonzero integral compatible tuple.  The argument applies to
every power of Frobenius, so the same holds over every finite
extension of $k_0$, which we need in the open case.

*The open case.* A fixed class has zero residues at
the boundary points, so it extends to the compactification, where the
proper case shows that it is zero. To make this precise, choose $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ as in
Lemma [lemma-proper-smooth-model], with boundary $i:D\hookrightarrow C$.
At each finite level there is then a canonical residue sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow H^1(C,A_n)\longrightarrow H^1(U,A_n)
\longrightarrow H^0(D,A_n(-1)).
$$

To obtain it with the correct twist and Frobenius action, we use the
dualizing complexes.  By transitivity, $i^!\omega_C=\omega_D=A_n$.
Since $\omega_C=A_n(1)[2]$, it follows that
$i^!A_{n,C}=A_{n,D}(-1)[-2]$.  The localization triangle
$i_*i^!A_{n,C}\to A_{n,C}\to Rj_*A_{n,U}$ now yields the displayed
sequence, and all its maps are natural in the coefficients and under
automorphisms of the model.

Choose $m>0$ such that $F^m$ fixes all geometric boundary points, and
put $Q=q^m$.  On $\varprojlim_nH^0(D,A_n(-1))$, which is finite free
over $\mathbf Z_\ell$, the operator $F^m$ acts as $Q$. Since $Q-1\ne0$, it has no
nonzero fixed element. A fixed compatible class on $U$ therefore has zero
residues at every level, so by exactness it lifts uniquely to
$H^1(C,A_n)$. By uniqueness the lifts are compatible and fixed by
$F^m$, and the proper case over $\mathbf F_Q$ shows that they vanish.

*Rational coefficients.* To pass from compatible systems of classes
to $H^1(U,E)$, we identify $H^1(U,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ with the rationalization of the
inverse limit and check that rationalizing does not create fixed vectors. By
Proposition [proposition-continuous-cohomology-pro-etale-cohomology], applied to the constant
sheaves $A_n$, we have $R\Gamma(U,\mathbf Z_\ell)=R\varprojlim_nR\Gamma(U,A_n)$,
and hence an exact sequence

$$
0\to\varprojlim\nolimits^1_nH^0(U,A_n)\to H^1(U,\mathbf Z_\ell)
\to\varprojlim_nH^1(U,A_n)\to0.
$$

The $\varprojlim^1$-term vanishes because the groups $H^0(U,A_n)=A_n$
have surjective transition maps.  On $U_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ the sheaf $\mathbf Q_\ell$ is
$\mathbf Z_\ell[1/\ell]$ (Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients]), a filtered
colimit of copies of $\mathbf Z_\ell$, and cohomology on the quasi-compact and
quasi-separated scheme $U$ commutes with filtered colimits of sheaves
(Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], applied to sheaves placed
in degree zero).  So $H^1(U,\mathbf Q_\ell)=H^1(U,\mathbf Z_\ell)\otimes\mathbf Q_\ell$ is the
rationalization of the inverse limit.

The inverse limit of the residue sequences is exact on the left, and
rationalization is exact, so we obtain an exact sequence of finite-dimensional
$\mathbf Q_\ell$-spaces $0\to H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)\to H^1(U,\mathbf Q_\ell)\to I\to0$, where $I$ is the image
of the residue map inside the rationalized boundary term. By the proper case,
$F^m-1$ is invertible on $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$. On the boundary term, $F^m-1$ acts by
$Q-1$, so it is injective on the $F^m$-stable subspace $I$. Now let $v$ be a
vector of $H^1(U,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ killed by $F^m-1$. Its image in $I$ is killed by
$F^m-1$, hence zero. Thus $v$ comes from $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$, where it is zero by the
proper case. Since a vector fixed by $F$ is fixed by $F^m$, it follows that Frobenius
has no fixed rational vector, and extending scalars to $E$ gives the assertion
over $E$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

A fixed vector is a compatible system of torsion points, each rational
over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$. But the rational points form a finite group, so the orders of the $\ell$-power torsion points in it are bounded, and
compatibility under $[\ell]$ then forces the system to vanish. The statement for $V_\ell A$ then follows by clearing denominators.

Since an automorphism and its inverse have the same fixed vectors, we
may use arithmetic Frobenius instead. On $A(\overline{\mathbf F}_q)$
its $m$th power fixes exactly $A_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$. This group is
finite, because on each affine open of a finite affine cover a rational
point is determined by finitely many coordinates in the finite field.
Hence the $\ell$-primary part of $A_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ is killed by
some $\ell^e$. Let $(t_n)$ be a fixed compatible sequence. Each
$t_{n+e}$ lies in this $\ell$-primary part, and since the transition
maps are $[\ell]$, we find

$$
t_n=\ell^e t_{n+e}=0
$$

for every $n$. This proves that $(T_\ell A)^{F^m}=0$.

Since $T_\ell A$ is free by
Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module], it injects into
$V_\ell A$. A suitable power of $\ell$ times a fixed vector of
$V_\ell A$ is a fixed vector of $T_\ell A$, and so it vanishes. Hence
$(V_\ell A)^{F^m}=0$. In other words, $F^m-1$ is injective on the
finite-dimensional space $V_\ell A$, and therefore bijective.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We test Tor amplitude by tensoring with modules. By a projection formula
for constant modules we may move the tensor product inside $Rj_*$. There
the complex $K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\underline M$ has amplitude $[a,b]$, and
$Rj_*$ adds at most $d$ degrees.

The complex $Rj_*K$ is bounded constructible by
Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field], and $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)$ is finite
by Theorem [theorem-results-from-etale-theory](3). To bound
the Tor amplitude, we work on the étale site, where geometric points are
conservative. By
Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison], we have
$K\simeq\nu_U^*K_{\acute{e}t}$ for some
$K_{\acute{e}t}\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(U_{\acute{e}t},A)$. By
Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients], the
pro-étale pullback of $Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}$ is $Rj_*K$.

We first prove the projection formula for constant coefficients. Namely,
for every $A$-module $M$, viewed as a constant sheaf, the projection
morphism

$$
(Rj_*K)\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}\underline M_X
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
Rj_*\bigl(K\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}\underline M_U\bigr)
\tag{6.23}
$$

is an isomorphism. Recall that for a scheme $V$
with $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(V)<\infty$, the projection formula of
[Stacks, [0F12](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F12)] identifies
$R\Gamma(V,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_AM$ with
$R\Gamma(V,K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_A\underline M)$. Moreover, a map of complexes of sheaves is an isomorphism if it induces isomorphisms on derived
sections over a basis of the site. Since the sections of $Rj_*$ over $V$ are the sections over $V\times_XU$, we apply the projection formula to
every quasi-compact étale $V\to X$ and to $V\times_XU$. This gives
isomorphisms between the derived sections of the two sides of the étale
version of (6.23), compatibly with the
projection morphism. Hence the étale version holds. Finally, inverse image is exact and symmetric monoidal, and it commutes with unbounded direct image, so the pullback of the étale isomorphism is
(6.23).

On the étale site it suffices to bound Tor against constant $A$-modules.
Indeed, let $G$ be an étale sheaf of $A$-modules and $\bar x$ a geometric
point. The stalk of $Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_AG$ at $\bar x$
is that of $Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_A\underline M$ with
$M=G_{\bar x}$, and geometric stalks are conservative. Now
$K\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}\underline M_U$ has cohomology in $[a,b]$. Hence the
étale version of the right-hand side of
(6.23) lies in $[a,b+d]$. By the
projection formula, so does
$Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_A\underline M$. In other words,
$Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}$ has Tor amplitude in $[a,b+d]$.

To pass to $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, we pull back a bounded flat constructible model
of $Rj_{\acute{e}t,*}K_{\acute{e}t}$ in degrees $[a,b+d]$ [Stacks, [0F4M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F4M)]. Since pullback
preserves flatness, its pullback to $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is again a complex of flat
sheaves in degrees $[a,b+d]$. Hence its tensor product with any sheaf of
$A$-modules on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is computed termwise and lies in degrees
$[a,b+d]$. This argument also covers the sheaves on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ that are not pulled
back from $X_{\acute{e}t}$, for which geometric stalks would not detect the Tor amplitude.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-open-direct-image-preserves-finite], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We apply Lemma [lemma-kunneth-one-identity-factor] once in each factor
of the factorization

$$
X_1\times X_2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}_{X_1}\times f_2}
X_1\times Y_2\xrightarrow{f_1\times\operatorname{id}_{Y_2}}
Y_1\times Y_2
$$

of $f_1\times f_2$. We apply it to $f_1$ with second coefficient
$Rf_{2*}M_2$, which lies in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y_2,A)$ by
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf]. After interchanging the
factors, we apply it to $f_2$ with coefficient $M_1$. Then the composite of
$R(f_1\times\operatorname{id}_{Y_2})_*$ of the second isomorphism with the
first is an isomorphism
from $Rf_{1*}M_1\boxtimes Rf_{2*}M_2$ to
$R(f_1\times f_2)_*(M_1\boxtimes M_2)$. Since its adjoint transpose is
$\varepsilon_{f_1}\boxtimes\varepsilon_{f_2}$, it is the Künneth map
(8.3).
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-ordinary-external-kunneth], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The Artin–Schreier sequence turns the question into one about
$\varphi-1$ on $H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k$ and on $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. The
key fact is that on a finite-dimensional space over an algebraically
closed field, a Frobenius-linear map minus the identity is surjective
with finite kernel.

*Step 1: the Artin–Schreier sequence.* Write also $\varphi$ for the
endomorphism $a\mapsto a^p$ of the sheaf
$\mathbf G_a$ on $C_{\acute{e}t}$.  The Artin–Schreier sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathbf F_p\longrightarrow\mathbf G_a
\xrightarrow{\varphi-1}\mathbf G_a\longrightarrow0
$$

is exact, because surjectivity is a local question and $T^p-T-a$ has
derivative $-1$. The étale cohomology of $\mathbf G_a$ is the
coherent cohomology of $\mathcal O_C$. Indeed, quasi-coherent sheaves have
the same cohomology on the étale and on the Zariski site, by faithfully
flat descent on affine opens and the Čech resolution. This coherent
cohomology vanishes in degrees above one, since $C$ is a curve. Since $C$
is proper, $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space.

*Step 2: linear algebra.* Let $\varphi$ be a Frobenius-linear endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$; we show that $\varphi-1$ is surjective and that
its kernel is the set of $k$-points of a finite étale scheme of
order $p^f$ with $f\leq\dim_k V$.  To prove this, we reduce along a finite
filtration to the part where $\varphi$ is nilpotent and the part where $\varphi$ is
bijective.  On the nilpotent part, $\varphi-1$ is an automorphism given by an
additive polynomial, with inverse $-(1+\varphi+\varphi^2+\cdots)$, a
finite sum; in particular its kernel there is zero.  On a bijective part of dimension $f$, by contrast, we choose a
basis, invert the matrix of $\varphi$, and write the equations of the fibres as

$$
x_i^p-\sum_j b_{ij}x_j=c_i\qquad(1\leq i\leq f),
$$

where $(b_{ij})$ is invertible.  The coordinate algebra is free of
dimension $p^f$, with basis the monomials having each exponent less
than $p$.  Moreover, the Jacobian matrix of these equations
is $-(b_{ij})$, because $p=0$ in $k$, and it is invertible; so each fibre is finite
étale of degree $p^f$ and has $p^f$ points over the algebraically
closed field $k$ [Stacks, [0A3L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3L)]. In particular every fibre is nonempty,
so $\varphi-1$ is surjective, and the kernel has $p^f$ elements.

*Step 3: conclusion.* We apply Step 2 to $H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k$ and to
$H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ in the long
exact sequence associated to the Artin–Schreier sequence. Surjectivity
of $\varphi-1$ on $H^0$ gives $H^1(C,\mathbf F_p)=\ker(\varphi-1)$ on
$H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$, with the bound on its dimension, and surjectivity on
$H^1$ together with $H^2(C,\mathcal O_C)=0$ gives $H^q(C,\mathbf F_p)=0$ for
$q>1$. Finally, the pullback map under an extension $k'/k$ is an isomorphism
[Stacks, [0HAN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0HAN), [0A3P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3P)]: flat base change for coherent cohomology identifies the
vector space and its Frobenius-linear map with their scalar
extensions, and the kernel is a finite étale scheme, whose $k$-points
and $k'$-points agree. As always,
Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison] carries the
statement over to $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.
