Comparing the $L$-functions of $\mathcal F$ and of $j_*\mathcal F$
gives the weaker bound $a+2$ at the boundary, and tensor powers
remove the extra $2$.

The assertion is local at a point of $X_0-U_0$, so we may replace $X_0$ by an
affine neighbourhood of that point. The complement of $U_0$ is an effective
Cartier divisor, so after shrinking this neighbourhood it is cut out by one
equation $f$, and then $U_0=D(f)$ is affine as well. Write
$i:Z_0=X_0-U_0\hookrightarrow X_0$. The hypotheses are preserved by this
replacement. Indeed, forming $j_*$ commutes with restriction to open
subschemes, and the restriction of $\mathcal F$ is still punctually of weights
$\le a$. Moreover, a nonempty open of $X_0$ is still geometrically connected.

The boundary Euler factors of $j_*\mathcal F$ are the ratio
$L_X/L_U$ of the two $L$-functions defined below. We show that $L_U$
has no zero and $L_X$ no pole on the disc $|t|<q^{-a/2-1}$, so that the
boundary factors have no pole there, and this bounds their eigenvalues.

*The $L$-function on $U_0$.* Put $L_U(t)=L(U_0,\mathcal F,t)$.
We show that $\iota L_U$ is holomorphic and nonvanishing on the disc,
by bounding the coefficients of its logarithm.
The logarithm of the Euler product has coefficients

$$
\log\iota L_U(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c_n}{n}t^n,
\qquad
c_n=\sum_{d\mid n}d\sum_{\deg(x)=d}
\iota\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x^{n/d}\mid\mathcal F_{\bar x}).
$$

Let $r=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal F$. For a closed point $x$ of
degree $d\mid n$, the bound on the weights gives
$|\iota\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x^{n/d}\mid\mathcal F_{\bar x})|
\le rq_x^{(n/d)a/2}=rq^{na/2}$. Since
$\sum_{d\mid n}d\cdot\#\{x\in|U_0|:\deg(x)=d\}=\#U_0(k_n)$,
Lemma [lemma-point-count-bound] gives $|c_n|\le rDq^{n(a/2+1)}$. Hence the
logarithm converges on the disc $|t|<R=q^{-a/2-1}$, and its exponential
is a nonvanishing holomorphic function there. By the trace formula,
its Taylor series is that of the rational function $\iota L_U(t)$, so
the two agree on the whole disc.

*The $L$-function on $X_0$.* Let $L_X(t)=L(X_0,j_*\mathcal F,t)$.
We show that $\iota L_X$ is holomorphic on the same disc. By the trace
formula its poles come from $H^0_c$ and $H^2_c$ of $j_*\mathcal F$, and
we compute both groups.

The group $H^0_c$ vanishes. Indeed, the support of a compactly supported
section of $j_*\mathcal F$ on $X$ is closed and proper over $k$, and since $X$ is
an affine curve, the support is finite. So the section vanishes on a dense
open subset of $U$, and as $\mathcal F$ is lisse and $U$ is connected, it vanishes
on all of $U$. Since a section of $j_*\mathcal F$ is determined by its restriction
to $U$, the section is zero.
For $H^2_c$, note that the quotient sheaf in

$$
0\longrightarrow j_!\mathcal F\longrightarrow j_*\mathcal F
\longrightarrow i_*i^*j_*\mathcal F\longrightarrow0
$$

is supported on the finite boundary, whose cohomology is concentrated
in degree zero.  From the long exact sequence we obtain
$H_c^2(X,j_*\mathcal F)=H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)$, and by
Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology] its eigenvalues have absolute value at most
$q^{a/2+1}$.  By the trace formula, every pole of $\iota L_X$ is the
inverse of a Frobenius eigenvalue on $H^0_c$ or $H^2_c$. Since
$H^0_c=0$, the poles have absolute value at least $q^{-a/2-1}=R$. Hence
$\iota L_X$ is holomorphic on $|t|<R$.

*The boundary factors.* On $U_0$ the sheaves $\mathcal F$ and
$j_*\mathcal F$ have the same stalks, so the two Euler products differ
only by the factors at the points of $Z_0$, and we get

$$
L_X(t)=L_U(t)\prod_{z\in Z_0}
\det(1-\operatorname{Frob}_z t^{\deg(z)}\mid(j_*\mathcal F)_{\bar z})^{-1}.
$$

Since $L_U$ has no zero on the disc, the finite product on the right
is holomorphic there. As it is the reciprocal of a product of
polynomials with constant term one, none of these polynomials has
a zero on the disc.  Now, for an eigenvalue $\alpha$ at $z$, the roots of
$1-\iota(\alpha)t^{\deg(z)}$ have absolute value
$|\iota(\alpha)|^{-1/\deg(z)}$. This number is therefore at least $R$, which
is the preliminary bound

$$
|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_z^{a+2}.
$$

*Tensor powers.* The error $2$ in the exponent comes from the
twist $(-1)$ on $H^2_c$. Since it does not grow with the weight, it
becomes negligible for high tensor powers. We therefore apply the
preliminary bound to $\mathcal F^{\otimes m}$ for every $m\ge1$, a sheaf
punctually of weights $\le ma$.  Let $V$ be the local generic fibre of
$\mathcal F$ at $z$. By Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk], the eigenvalue
$\alpha$ of $\operatorname{Frob}_z$ on $(j_*\mathcal F)_{\bar z}$ has an
eigenvector $v\in V^{I_z}$, and then $v^{\otimes m}$ is a nonzero
invariant eigenvector in $V^{\otimes m}$ with eigenvalue $\alpha^m$.
By the same lemma, $\alpha^m$ is therefore an eigenvalue on the stalk of
$j_*(\mathcal F^{\otimes m})$ at $\bar z$, and the preliminary bound for
$\mathcal F^{\otimes m}$ gives $|\iota(\alpha)|^{2m}\le q_z^{ma+2}$.  Taking
$m$th roots and letting $m$ tend to infinity, we obtain
$|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_z^a$ at every boundary point. On $U_0$, finally, the bound is
the hypothesis.
This clause is proved by the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Each assertion has two parts: a statement about eigenvalues at closed
points, which follows from Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra], and, for
mixedness, the construction of a filtration with pure quotients.

An extension is filtered by a filtration of its
subobject followed by the inverse images of a filtration of its
quotient. The graded pieces of the result are those of the two given
filtrations, so a common upper bound persists.

For tensor products we use that the coefficients form a field, so that the
associated graded of the tensor product of two filtrations is the tensor
product of the two associated gradeds. By
Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra], the eigenvalues of tensor
products and duals are the products $\alpha_i\beta_j$ and the
inverses $\alpha_i^{-1}$, whose weights are $a+b$ and $-a$.

For the dual of a mixed lisse sheaf $G$ with mixed filtration
$(G_i)$, suppose first that the graded pieces $G_i/G_{i-1}$ are lisse.
Dualizing is exact on lisse sheaves, so the annihilator filtration
$G_i^\perp=\ker(G^\vee\to G_i^\vee)$ has graded pieces
$(G_i/G_{i-1})^\vee$, which are pure of the negated weights by the
computation above. In general the graded pieces need not be lisse: on a
curve, a pure lisse $G$ has the filtration $j_!j^*G\subseteq G$, whose
quotient $i_*i^*G$ is a skyscraper with dual zero. We then argue by
Noetherian induction on $X$. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a dense open, stable
under Frobenius, on which all graded pieces are lisse, and let
$i:Z\to X$ be its closed complement. On $U$ the first case applies to
$j^*G$. Since $G$ is lisse, $i^*(G^\vee)\simeq(i^*G)^\vee$, and $i^*G$ is a
mixed lisse sheaf on $Z$, so $i^*(G^\vee)$ is mixed by induction, of the
negated weights. Extension by zero and direct image along a closed
immersion are exact and do not change stalks, so they carry mixed
filtrations to mixed filtrations of the same weights, and the exact
sequence

$$
0\to j_!j^*(G^\vee)\to G^\vee\to i_*i^*(G^\vee)\to 0
$$

shows that $G^\vee$ is mixed, of the negated weights.

Inverse images do not change weights, because the weight is normalized
by the degree. Indeed, at a closed point of an inverse image the Frobenius is a
positive power of the Frobenius at the image point, and the residue field
degree is multiplied by the same integer. For shifts, $\mathcal H^i(K[r])=\mathcal H^{i+r}(K)$ is mixed of weights
at most $w+i+r$, which is the bound $w+r$ for $K[r]$.

The local eigenvalue of $\mathcal B_b$ at $x$ is $b^{\deg(x)}$,
of weight $2\log_q|\iota(b)|$, and tensoring by $\mathcal B_b$ multiplies every
eigenvalue by it. For the Tate sheaf, recall that
arithmetic Frobenius acts on roots of unity by raising to the $q$th
power. Geometric Frobenius is its inverse, so it acts on
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ by $q^{-1}$, of weight $-2$.

For an extension $0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\to\mathcal H\to0$, start with a mixed filtration of $\mathcal F$ and append the inverse images in $\mathcal G$ of a mixed filtration of $\mathcal H$. The successive quotients are exactly those of these two filtrations, hence are pure.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

By definition, $\mathcal H^j(K)$ has weights at most $w+j$. Since $\mathcal H^i(K[r])=\mathcal H^{i+r}(K)$, its bound is $w+i+r=(w+r)+i$, which is the bound defining weight at most $w+r$ for $K[r]$.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

At a closed point $x$, the rank-one twist has eigenvalue $b^{\deg(x)}$. Its normalized weight is $2\log_q|\iota(b)|$. Tensoring multiplies each eigenvalue by this number, so its weight increases by that constant. The same calculation on each graded piece proves the assertion for mixed weights.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Arithmetic Frobenius raises roots of unity to their $q$th powers. Geometric Frobenius is its inverse, and therefore acts by $q^{-1}$ on the Tate module and on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

By clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--13], the twist $(r)$ has degree-one Frobenius $q^{-r}$. Apply clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--12]: its weight contribution is $2\log_q(q^{-r})=-2r$.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Use the filtration constructed in clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--1]. Every graded weight is a weight from one of the two given filtrations, so none exceeds their common upper bound.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

The eigenvalues on the tensor-product stalk are the products of the two sets of eigenvalues by Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra]. Multiplication of their absolute values adds the normalized weights, giving $a+b$.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

The eigenvalues on a dual stalk are the reciprocals of the original nonzero eigenvalues by Lemma [lemma-filtrations-spectra]. Their absolute values therefore give the negative weight $-a$. The lisse hypothesis ensures that the sheaf dual has these dual stalks.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Tensor the two finite mixed filtrations. Over a field tensor product is exact, and the associated graded is the tensor product of the associated gradeds. By clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--3], each such graded tensor is pure of the sum of its two weights, at most $a+b$.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Let $(G_i)$ be a mixed filtration of the mixed lisse sheaf $G$. If the graded pieces $G_i/G_{i-1}$ are lisse, dualizing is exact on lisse sheaves, so the annihilator filtration $G_i^\perp=\ker(G^\vee\to G_i^\vee)$ has graded pieces $(G_i/G_{i-1})^\vee$. Clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--4] makes them pure of the negated weights. This proves the second assertion, and the first one in this case.

In general the graded pieces need not be lisse, and we argue by Noetherian induction on $X$. Let $j:U\to X$ be a dense open, stable under Frobenius, on which all graded pieces are lisse, and let $i:Z\to X$ be its closed complement. On $U$ the first case applies to $j^*G$. Since $G$ is lisse, $i^*(G^\vee)\simeq(i^*G)^\vee$ with $i^*G$ mixed lisse on $Z$, so $i^*(G^\vee)$ is mixed of the negated weights by induction. Extension by zero and direct image along a closed immersion do not change stalks, so they carry mixed filtrations to mixed filtrations of the same weights. Clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--1], applied to $0\to j_!j^*(G^\vee)\to G^\vee\to i_*i^*(G^\vee)\to0$, shows that $G^\vee$ is mixed of the negated weights.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

At a closed point over a closed point of residue degree $e$, the new Frobenius is the corresponding positive power of the old Frobenius. The residue degree is multiplied by that same power. Thus the absolute-value condition normalized by residue degree, and hence the weight, is unchanged.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Pull back a mixed filtration. Inverse image is exact on these sheaves, so its graded pieces are the inverse images of the original graded pieces. They remain pure by clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--7].

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

The filtration in clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--8] has exactly the same graded weights as the original one by clause [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations--7]. Therefore the same upper bound applies.

*Source:* the proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

We compute $R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*K$ with an injective resolution of $K$ on
the étale site. By the lemma its pullback is still acyclic for
$\nu_{X,*}$, and by full faithfulness on sheaves the result is
the resolution itself.

Choose a bounded-below injective resolution $K\to I^\bullet$. Since
$\nu_X^*$ is exact, $\nu_X^*I^\bullet$ represents $\nu_X^*K$, and by
Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-pulled-back-injectives] its terms are $\nu_{X,*}$-acyclic,
so $R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*K$ is computed by the complex
$\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*I^\bullet$. By Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image] the
unit $I^q\to\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*I^q$ is an isomorphism for every $q$, so
this complex is $I^\bullet$, which proves (2.7).
Since $\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},-)=\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},-)\circ\nu_{X,*}$, the statement on
global sections follows by composing the derived functors; see
[Stacks, [099V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099V), [099W](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/099W)].

The category $\Sh(X_{\acute{e}t},\mathcal A)$ is Grothendieck abelian, so we may
choose a bounded-below injective resolution $K\to I^\bullet$. Since
$\nu_X^*$ is exact, $\nu_X^*I^\bullet$ represents $\nu_X^*K$.

Each $\nu_X^*I^q$ is $\nu_{X,*}$-acyclic. For sheaves of
$\Lambda$-modules this is Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-pulled-back-injectives].
Its proof applies verbatim to an injective sheaf $I$ with values in
$\mathcal A$, once the free sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules on the nerve of a
covering are replaced as follows. For an object $a$ of $\mathcal A$ and an
étale object $U$, let $a_U$ be the sheaf associated with
$V\mapsto\bigoplus_{\Hom(V,U)}a$, so that
$\Hom(a_U,I)=\Hom_{\mathcal A}(a,I(U))$. For an étale covering of $V$,
the augmented complex of the sheaves $a_U$ on its nerve is exact: locally
the covering has a section, and then the complex is $a$ tensored with the
chain complex of the Čech nerve of a nonempty set, which is
contractible. As $I$ is injective, applying $\Hom(-,I)$ shows that
$\Hom_{\mathcal A}(a,-)$ of the augmented Čech complex of $I$ is exact
for every $a$. Taking for $a$ the cycles in a given degree shows that the
Čech complex of $I$ itself has no positive cohomology, and the rest of
the argument is unchanged.

By Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image], $\nu_X^*$ is
fully faithful on $\mathcal A$-valued sheaves, so the unit
$I^q\to\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*I^q$ is an isomorphism for every $q$. Hence
$R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*K$ is computed by the complex
$\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*I^\bullet\simeq I^\bullet$, and the derived unit is
identified with the resolution $K\to I^\bullet$. This proves
(2.7). For $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Mod}(\Lambda)$ the derived
categories involved are $D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and
$D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison].

Since $\nu_X^*$ is exact, applying it termwise preserves acyclic complexes
and quasi-isomorphisms, so it defines
$\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ on the unbounded derived
categories. As in clause [proposition-unbounded-functors-products--1], sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules on
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ form a Grothendieck category, every complex $N$ has a K-injective
resolution $N\to J$ [Stacks, [079P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079P)], and $R\nu_{X,*}N$ is represented by
$\nu_{X,*}J$.

We first check that $R\nu_{X,*}$ is right adjoint to $\nu_X^*$ on the
unbounded derived categories. Write $[C,C']$ for maps of complexes up to
homotopy. The adjunction $\nu_X^*\dashv\nu_{X,*}$ on sheaves of modules gives,
for complexes $C$ on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ and $J$ on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, an isomorphism of Hom
complexes, hence a bijection $[C,\nu_{X,*}J]\simeq[\nu_X^*C,J]$. If $J$ is
K-injective and $C$ is acyclic, then $\nu_X^*C$ is acyclic, so
$[\nu_X^*C,J]=0$ and therefore $[C,\nu_{X,*}J]=0$. Thus $\nu_{X,*}J$ is
K-injective. Maps in the derived category into a K-injective complex are
maps up to homotopy, so for every $K$ and every $N$ with K-injective
resolution $N\to J$ we obtain bijections, natural in $K$ and $N$,

$$
\Hom(K,R\nu_{X,*}N)=[K,\nu_{X,*}J]\simeq[\nu_X^*K,J]
=\Hom(\nu_X^*K,N).
$$

For any adjunction with unit $\eta$, the map $f\mapsto\nu_X^*f$ is the
composite of $f\mapsto\eta_M\circ f$, from $\Hom(K,M)$ to
$\Hom(K,R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*M)$, with the adjunction bijection; this is one of
the triangle identities. It therefore suffices to show that
$\eta_M:M\to R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*M$ is an isomorphism for
$M\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. For such $M$ the complex $\nu_X^*M$ is bounded
below, and a bounded-below complex of injectives is K-injective. So
$R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*M$ and $\eta_M$ are the object and the map of
(2.7), and clause [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison--1] shows that $\eta_M$ is an
isomorphism. Restricting to $K\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ gives the final
assertion.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison].

Apply $R\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},-)$ to the unit isomorphism of clause [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison--1]. Composition of derived right adjoints identifies $R\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},R
u_{X,*}
u_X^*K)$ with $R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},
u_X^*K)$, giving the asserted comparison.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison].

We take the immersion into projective space given by the Stacks
Project and show that properness of $X$ makes it closed. The second
assertion then follows by writing $i_X$ as a graph followed by a base
change of $i_S$.

The version of Chow's lemma in [Stacks, [0202](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0202)] gives a proper
surjection $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and an immersion
$i_S:\widetilde X\to\mathbf P^n_S$ for every separated
$X\to S$ of finite type with $S$ qcqs. It is deduced from the Noetherian
case by the approximation argument in the proof of
Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem], using the embedding of $X$ into a
scheme of finite presentation [Stacks, [01ZJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZJ)]. In our situation, moreover, $f$ and $\pi$ are proper, so $\widetilde X$
is proper over $S$. Now a map from a proper $S$-scheme to a separated
$S$-scheme is proper, because its graph is closed and the projection of
the product to the target is proper. Hence $i_S$ is a proper immersion. Its image is therefore closed, and
$i_S$ is a closed immersion.

For the second assertion, we factor $i_X$ as the graph of $\pi$
followed by the base change of $i_S$:

$$
\widetilde X\longrightarrow\widetilde X\times_SX
\longrightarrow\mathbf P^n_S\times_SX.
$$

The first arrow is closed because $X\to S$ is separated, and the
second is closed because $i_S$ is. Their composite is $i_X$. Since
$\pi$ is $i_X$ followed by the projection $\mathbf P^n_X\to X$, it is
projective, and so is $f\pi=q_Si_S$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-chow-s-lemma-projective-form], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-chow-s-lemma-projective-form], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Embed $X$ as a closed subscheme of a separated scheme $Y$ of finite
presentation over $S$. Apply Noetherian approximation to $S$ and
descend $Y\to S$ to a separated morphism $Y_0\to S_0$ of finite
presentation over a Noetherian scheme $S_0$, as in the proof of
Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem]. The Noetherian
Chow construction, using [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness] and
[lemma-uniqueness-maps-dense-open], supplies a proper surjection
$Y'_0\to Y_0$ and an immersion of $Y'_0$ into a projective space over
$S_0$.

Pull back this diagram to $S$ and then to the closed subscheme $X$ of
$Y$. Properness and surjectivity are preserved. The cartesian square
for projective space identifies the base-changed immersion, and its
restriction to the inverse image of $X$ is still an immersion. Its
composite with the projection is $f\pi$.

The Noetherian construction uses a projective space whose homogeneous
coordinates are indexed by a finite set. A linear closed immersion puts
this space inside $\mathbf P^n_S$ for some $n\geq 0$. Composing with it
gives the assertion.

If $f$ is proper, then $q_Si_S=f\pi$ is proper. Since $q_S$ is
separated, $i_S$ is proper, hence a proper immersion and therefore a
closed immersion. This recovers the closed immersion of
[theorem-chow-s-lemma-projective-form--1] over a general qcqs base.

A left adjoint is fully faithful exactly when its unit is an isomorphism,
and the essential image is then the set of objects on which the counit is
an isomorphism. We check both on pro-étale affines, where
(2.6) computes $\nu_X^*$.

Evaluating (2.5) on an étale object
$V$ gives $F(V)$, so $F\xrightarrow{\sim}\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*F$, which proves
full faithfulness. Moreover,
every $\nu_X^*F$ is classical by (2.6).
Conversely, let $G$ be classical. On a pro-étale affine the counit
$\nu_X^*\nu_{X,*}G\to G$ is

$$
(\nu_X^*\nu_{X,*}G)(U)
=\varinjlim_iG(U_i)\longrightarrow G(U),
$$

which is an isomorphism by (2.4). Since
pro-étale affines form a covering basis
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-affines-form-basis]), the counit is an
isomorphism of sheaves.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For constructible sheaves we reduce to the explicit calculations, and
arbitrary torsion sheaves are filtered colimits of these. The reduction
has four steps: dévissage to constructible $\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaves,
extension by zero from an open on which the sheaf is locally constant,
a cover of degree prime to $\ell$ that makes it unipotent, and
normalization, which leaves constant coefficients on smooth curves.

By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], we may work on $C_{\acute{e}t}$, and
since a universal homeomorphism does not change the étale topos, we may
replace $C$ by $C_{\mathrm{red}}$.  A constructible torsion sheaf has a
finite exponent, because it has finitely many isomorphism types of
finite stalks.  It is therefore the direct sum of its finitely many primary
parts, and a finite filtration of an $\ell$-primary part has constructible
$\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaves as graded pieces.  By the stability under
extensions just proved, it suffices to treat such sheaves.

Choose a dense smooth open $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ on which the
sheaf is finite locally constant.  By Lemma [lemma-removing-finitely-many-points]
we may replace the sheaf by its extension by zero.  On the connected
components of $U$, Lemma [lemma-reduction-unipotent-local-system] and finite
direct images reduce us to constant $\mathbf F_\ell$ extended by zero on
curves finite over $C$; this is allowed because the assertions pass to
direct summands and because, by Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms-cohomology], finite
direct images are exact and do not change cohomology.  Finally, normalization and Lemma [lemma-sheaves-finite-support-finite-morphisms] reduce these sheaves to the
calculations with constant coefficients on smooth curves, namely the
Kummer sequence for $\ell\ne p$ and the Artin–Schreier
sequence for $\ell=p$.  Since all reductions preserve the
hypothesis that $C$ is proper or affine, the theorem holds for
constructible torsion sheaves.

An arbitrary torsion sheaf on the qcqs scheme $C$ is a filtered
colimit of constructible torsion sheaves, and cohomology commutes with
filtered colimits [Stacks, [03SA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SA), [03Q5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q5)].  For torsion prime to
the characteristic or $p$-primary torsion, we may take the constructible
sheaves with the same kind of torsion, by splitting off primary
parts before passing to the colimit. Pullback and restriction also
commute with filtered colimits. Hence vanishing and the pullback
isomorphisms pass to the colimit. So does surjectivity in $(C_8)$,
because a representative of a class already occurs at some
stage. Finiteness is asserted only for constructible sheaves.
Finally, Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison] carries these conclusions and their maps over to $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.

The idea is that, by Lemma [lemma-reduction-finitely-many-degrees], maps out of a
constructible sheaf depend only on the cohomology of the target in $d_C+1$
consecutive degrees, uniformly in the family. For targets with cohomology in a
fixed bounded interval the claim follows from the case of
ind-constructible sheaves by induction on the length.

The first assertion follows from the second, since
$\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))\subset\Dic(X,\Lambda)$
(Corollary [corollary-ambient-ind-derived]) and direct sums in
$\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$ are those of $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

First let $C\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$, and suppose that all $K_\lambda$ have
cohomology in a fixed interval $[a,b]$. We prove the claim, for all
shifts of the $K_\lambda$ at once, by induction on $b-a$. If $a=b$, then
$K_\lambda=B_\lambda[-a]$ with $B_\lambda\in\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$, and the
claim is that $\Ext^q(C,-)$ commutes with direct sums of objects of
$\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$, which is Corollary [corollary-ind-heart-b]. In
general, the triangles
$\tau_{\leq b-1}K_\lambda\to K_\lambda\to H^b(K_\lambda)[-b]\to$ are
compatible with direct sums, because $H^n$ commutes with direct sums. We
apply $\Hom(C,-)$ to these triangles and take the direct sum over
$\lambda$; since direct sums of abelian groups are exact, the result is
again a long exact sequence. It maps to the long exact sequence of the
summed triangle. The outer terms are of the form covered by the
induction hypothesis (cohomology in $[a,b-1]$ and in $[b,b]$), and so
the five lemma gives the claim for cohomology in $[a,b]$.

For arbitrary $K_\lambda$, we apply Lemma [lemma-reduction-finitely-many-degrees] with
$m=0$, which allows us to replace each $K_\lambda$, and
$\bigoplus_\lambda K_\lambda$, by its truncation to degrees $[-d_C,0]$.
Since the interval is the same for the whole family and truncation
commutes with direct sums, the bounded case applies.

From constructible sheaves $C$ we pass to complexes by dévissage.
For fixed $(K_\lambda)$, the objects $C$ for which the map is an
isomorphism are closed under shifts. They are closed under cones by the
five lemma, applied to the long exact sequences of $\Hom(-,K_\lambda)$
summed over $\lambda$ and of $\Hom(-,\bigoplus_\lambda K_\lambda)$. A bounded constructible complex is a
finite extension of shifts of its constructible cohomology sheaves, and
hence it belongs to this class.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-compactness-rational-coefficients], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The preceding proposition treats the case of a single stratum. For a finite
stratification we argue locally, by induction on the number of strata.
Once the sheaves are known to be classical, the equivalences follow from
full faithfulness of $\nu_X^*$ and its version for $D^+$.

Given a point, we shrink to an affine open on which the stratum
containing it is closed, with inclusion $i$ and open complement $j$.
The exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow j_!j^*F\longrightarrow F
\longrightarrow i_*i^*F\longrightarrow0
$$

reduces the assertion to fewer strata, because on pro-étale sheaves of
modules the functors $j_!$ and $i_*$ preserve classical sheaves, by
(2.10) and Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images],
and classical sheaves are closed under extensions
(Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]). Since $\nu_X^*$ is
fully faithful, sheaves that are classical on the members of a Zariski
covering are classical, so the local statement suffices. The
derived statement follows from Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]
and bounded truncation; see [Stacks, [09AK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AK), [09AL](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AL)].

On one stratum use Proposition [proposition-locally-constant-sheaves-finite-presentation--1]; induct on the number of strata.

Given a point, we shrink to an affine open on which the stratum
containing it is closed, with inclusion $i$ and open complement $j$.
The exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow j_!j^*F\longrightarrow F
\longrightarrow i_*i^*F\longrightarrow0
$$

reduces the assertion to fewer strata, because on pro-étale sheaves of
modules the functors $j_!$ and $i_*$ preserve classical sheaves, by
(2.10) and Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images],
and classical sheaves are closed under extensions
(Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]). Since $\nu_X^*$ is
fully faithful, sheaves that are classical on the members of a Zariski
covering are classical, so the local statement suffices. The
derived statement follows from Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]
and bounded truncation; see [Stacks, [09AK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AK), [09AL](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AL)].

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves].

By clause [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves--1], every constructible pro-étale sheaf is classical. The comparison is fully faithful by Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image] and preserves the finite stratifications and finite-presentation local systems defining constructibility. It is therefore an equivalence on these sheaf categories.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves].

Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes] characterizes the bounded-below derived essential image by classical cohomology sheaves and gives full faithfulness. Clause [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves--2] identifies the constructible cohomology sheaves on both sites. Bounded truncation yields the asserted equivalence of bounded constructible derived categories; see [Stacks, [09AK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AK), [09AL](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AL)].

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves].

We work over an affine open of $Y$ and evaluate on the
covering basis $V=\varprojlim_iV_i$, with $V_i$ affine and étale
over $Y$. By (2.6) and
Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], for a sheaf $F$ the map in
degree $q$ is the continuity map

$$
\varinjlim_i H^q_{\acute{e}t}(X\times_YV_i,F)
\longrightarrow
H^q_{\acute{e}t}(X\times_YV,F).
$$

Since $g$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so are its base
changes, and the map is an isomorphism by continuity of étale
cohomology under affine limits [Stacks, [03Q6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q6)]. Using bounded-below
resolutions, or the convergent hypercohomology spectral sequences, we
pass from sheaves to $K$; see [Stacks, [09A6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09A6)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

This is the proper henselian-pair theorem [Stacks, [0A0C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A0C)], quoted in the reference. Its hypotheses are exactly that $(R,J)$ is henselian and $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is proper, and its comparison is restriction to $Z_0$. It applies to arbitrary sheaves of sets on $Z_{\acute{e}t}$ and gives the asserted bijection. Restriction commutes with morphisms of sheaves, which gives naturality in $F$.

We split $K$ by the triangle $j_!j^*K\to K\to Ri_*i^*K$ and use
additivity of trace classes. The piece supported on $Z$ gives the trace
of $u_Z$. The piece $j_!j^*K$, on the other hand, has zero trace, which we show by deforming
to the normal cone.

*Reductions.* We may assume that $W=C$, that $\Fix(c)=F_0$ and that
the ideal inclusions hold on $C$. Indeed, by
Remark [remark-reduction-connected-fixed-point-scheme], restricting $C$ to $W$
and removing the other connected components of $\Fix(c)$ changes neither
the trace class on $F_0$ nor $u_Z$ near $F_{0,Z}$.
By Lemma [lemma-fixed-point-scheme-deformation], the common map
$\Fix(c)\to X$ maps set-theoretically into $Z$. The same lemma shows
that after base change from $T$ to $S$ the reduction of the fixed scheme
of the deformed correspondence is $(\Fix(c)\times S)_{\mathrm{red}}$, as
Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme] requires.

*The case $i^*K=0$.* We show that $\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)=0$. First,
the specialized complex vanishes on the zero section,

$$
\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(K)|_Z=0,
$$

because Verdier's theorem on the zero section
(Theorem [theorem-verdier-s-theorem-specialization-zero]) identifies the restriction of
$\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(K)$ to the zero section with the restriction
of $K$ to $Z$, and invariance under the nilpotent thickening
$Z_{\mathrm{red}}\to Z$ passes from $Z$ to $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$.

Next, consider the leg $\gamma_2$ of the correspondence on the special
fibre, along which we take ordinary pullback. It maps set-theoretically
into the zero section by
Lemma [lemma-normal-cones-contracting-ideals](2). Invariance under
nilpotent thickenings therefore gives $\gamma_2^*\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(K)=0$.
So the specialized morphism has zero source, and its trace is zero.

Finally, we relate this trace to $\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)$. The generic
fibre of the deformed correspondence is $c$ over $\eta$. So
Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class] identifies the
zero trace with the specialization of the pullback of
$\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)$ to the generic fibre. By
Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme],
specialization is the identity under the identifications for constant
families, and these carry that pullback to $\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)$.
Hence $\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)=0$.

*General $K$.* We apply Proposition [proposition-additivity-trace-classes](2)
to the triangle

$$
j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Ri_*i^*K,
\qquad j:X\setminus Z_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow X,
$$

whose hypothesis $c_1^{-1}(Z_{\mathrm{red}})\subset c_2^{-1}(Z_{\mathrm{red}})$
follows from $I_2\subset I_1$.
The open piece has zero trace by the case just treated, while the closed
graded piece is the proper pushforward of $u_Z$ along $i$ and $i'$, by
Lemma [lemma-closed-piece-pushforward], and
Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier] identifies its trace with the
pushforward of the trace class of $u_Z$.
To compare with $F_0$, note that the map $h_{F_0}$ is an isomorphism after reduction, because $\Fix(c)$ lies
in $c_1^{-1}(Z)$ set-theoretically by
Lemma [lemma-fixed-point-scheme-deformation]. This proves the displayed formula.
If $F_0$ is proper, then so is $F_{0,Z}$, and pushing both sides forward to
$\operatorname{Spec}k$ and composing with the trace map of
Definition [definition-trace-class-local-terms] gives the equality of
local terms.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-contracting-correspondences-local-terms], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Say that a morphism has the property if the conclusion holds for it,
for every $w$ and every mixed $F$ of weights at most $w$. Quasi-finite
maps and projections of relative affine lines have the property, and by
Lemma [lemma-relative-noether-normalization-over-stratification]
every $f$ is built from these two kinds of maps. So it suffices to show
that the property is stable under composition and under finite partitions.

For composition, let $X_0\xrightarrow{h}Z_0\xrightarrow{g}Y_0$ and consider the Leray
spectral sequence for compact supports,

$$
E_2^{a,b}=R^ag_!(R^bh_!F)\ \Longrightarrow\ R^{a+b}(gh)_!F.
$$

It is Frobenius-equivariant by the naturality of the truncation tower
and of the composition isomorphism for direct image with compact
support. If both maps have the property, then $E_2^{a,b}$ is mixed of
weights at most $w+a+b$. Since each later page is a subquotient of the
previous one, the same holds for $E_\infty^{a,b}$. The abutment
filtration of $R^n(gh)_!F$ is finite, because the operations preserve
bounded constructible complexes. Its quotients are the
$E_\infty^{a,n-a}$, and by Lemma [lemma-weights-exact-sequence]
$R^n(gh)_!F$ is mixed of weights at most $w+n$.

For partitions, we apply Lemma [lemma-relative-noether-normalization-over-stratification] and refine the
partitions to filtrations by open and closed pieces. After this
refinement we can order the pieces so that each is open in the union
of itself and the later ones. This lets us apply the localization
sequences one piece at a time. On the pieces, the restriction
of $F$ to each source piece is again mixed of weights at most $w$, and on
every refined source piece the finite map to $\mathbf A^d_V$ restricts
to a separated quasi-finite map, which has the property by
Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images]. Moreover, the projection
$\mathbf A^d_V\to V$ is a composition of $d$ projections of relative
affine lines. Each of them has the property by
Proposition [proposition-relative-affine-line], and by the
composition argument the map from the piece to $V$ has the property.
Finally, we assemble the pieces one at a time in the chosen order. By
Lemma [lemma-weight-bounds-partitions](1) on the source and
Lemma [lemma-weight-bounds-partitions](2) on the target, the bound
for the pieces implies the bound for $R^if_!F$ on $Y_0$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

This is [Stacks, [081S](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/081S)]. The idea is to view the inverse of
$W_U\to U$ as a partial section of $W\to T$ and to extend it by
Theorem [theorem-extension-partial-section]; the strict transform is then the graph
of the extension.

Choose a finite type ideal $\mathcal I_0$ cutting out $T\setminus U$.
Its blow-up $T_1\to T$ makes $U$ schematically dense by
Lemma [lemma-making-open-schematically-dense]. Over $T_1$, the base change of $W\to T$ to
$T_1$ is separated and of finite type, and the inverse of
$W_U\to U$ is a section of it over $U$. We may therefore apply Theorem [theorem-extension-partial-section] over $T_1$, with $V=U$, which gives a further blow-up and an extension of
this section, with closed graph, over an open containing the inverse
image of $U$. By Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow] the
composite is a $U$-admissible blow-up
$\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}(T)$. Let $b:T'\to T$ be the blow-up of
$\mathcal I\mathcal I_0$, which dominates both. Pulling back to $T'$ gives
an open $W_0\subseteq T'$ containing $b^{-1}(U)$ and a map $W_0\to W$
over $T$ whose graph $\Gamma$ is closed in $W\times_TT'$. As the zero set
of $\mathcal I\mathcal I_0$ is exactly $T\setminus U$,
$b^{-1}(U)$ is schematically dense in $T'$, hence in $W_0$.

We included the factor $\mathcal I_0$ so that the center of $b$ is
exactly $T\setminus U$. Then the strict transform $W'$ is the schematic
closure of $W_U$ in $W\times_TT'$. Over $U$, the
subscheme $W_U$ is the graph of the original section, so it lies in
$\Gamma$ and $W'\subseteq\Gamma$. Conversely, $\Gamma\simeq W_0$
contains the inverse image of $U$ as a schematically dense open. Hence
the schematic closure of $W_U$ in $\Gamma$ is $\Gamma$. We conclude that
$W'=\Gamma\simeq W_0$, and $W'\to T'$ is an open immersion.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-elimination-indeterminacy], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Cover the given object by pro-étale affines

The construction is that of [bhatt-scholze15, Theorem 2.4.9] and
[Stacks, [0983](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0983)]. We first make the local rings strictly henselian, and
then replace the profinite space of components by an extremally
disconnected one surjecting onto it, which does not change the local
rings.

In the first stage we construct
a faithfully flat ind-étale $R$-algebra $C$ that is w-strictly local.
To do so we first replace $R$ by an ind-Zariski algebra whose spectrum is
w-local, and then take a filtered colimit of étale neighbourhoods of
the closed points, which makes the local rings at the closed points
strictly henselian. This is the construction of simultaneous strict
localizations in [Stacks, [097X](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097X)]. Each step is a filtered colimit of
étale algebras, so $C$ is ind-étale over $R$ by
Lemma [lemma-stability].

For the second stage, choose a surjection
$S\to\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}(C))$ with $S$ extremally disconnected using
Lemma [lemma-extremally-disconnected-covers], and realize this map by an ind-Zariski
$C$-algebra $D$ such that

$$
|\operatorname{Spec}(D)|
\simeq |\operatorname{Spec}(C)|
\times_{\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}(C))}S
$$

as topological spaces. Concretely, write $S$ as a limit of finite
quotients, use finite products of $C$, restrict to the relevant
closed sets of components by idempotent localizations, and take a
filtered colimit; see [Stacks, [097D](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097D)]. This construction identifies local
rings, is surjective when $S$ is, and preserves w-locality. Hence
$C\to D$ is faithfully flat and the local rings at closed points of
$D$ remain strictly henselian. The space of components of
$\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ is $S$, so $D$ is
w-contractible, and the composite $R\to C\to D$ is ind-étale and
faithfully flat.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We construct $f^!N$ one object at a time as the object representing
maps out of $Rf_!(-)$ into $N$, and then check direct sums on the compact
generators.

For $N\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$, the functor

$$
\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ab},
\qquad M\longmapsto\Hom(Rf_!M,N)
$$

is cohomological and sends direct sums to products. By
Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability], $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ is
compactly generated, and Brown representability [Stacks, [0A8F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8F)] says
that on such a category every cohomological functor sending direct sums
to products is representable, say by $f^!N$. By the
Yoneda lemma, these objects form a right adjoint, and a right adjoint of an
exact functor of triangulated categories is exact [Stacks, [0A8G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8G)].

To see that $f^!$ preserves direct sums, we test the canonical map
$\bigoplus_\alpha f^!N_\alpha\to f^!(\bigoplus_\alpha N_\alpha)$
on a compact generator $G\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ and its shifts.
On the source, compactness of $G$ and adjunction give

$$
\Hom\Bigl(G[n],\bigoplus_\alpha f^!N_\alpha\Bigr)
=\bigoplus_\alpha\Hom(G[n],f^!N_\alpha)
=\bigoplus_\alpha\Hom(Rf_!G[n],N_\alpha).
$$

On the target, adjunction and compactness of $Rf_!G\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$
give the same group. The map therefore induces bijections on
$\Hom(G[n],-)$ for all compact generators $G$ and all $n$. Applying the
detection property to its cone, we see that it is an isomorphism.

For $N\in\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$, the functor

$$
\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ab},
\qquad M\longmapsto\Hom(Rf_!M,N)
$$

is cohomological and sends direct sums to products. By
Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability], $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ is
compactly generated, and Brown representability [Stacks, [0A8F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8F)] says
that on such a category every cohomological functor sending direct sums
to products is representable, say by $f^!N$. By the
Yoneda lemma, these objects form a right adjoint, and a right adjoint of an
exact functor of triangulated categories is exact [Stacks, [0A8G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8G)].

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image].

Clause [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image--1] constructs $f^!$ as a right adjoint to the exact triangulated functor $Rf_!$. The adjoint exactness theorem [Stacks, [0A8G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8G)], applied with this adjunction, gives its shift comparison and preservation of distinguished triangles. Hence $f^!$ is exact.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image].

For any object $N$, both proposed right adjoints represent the same functor $M\mapsto\Hom(Rf_!M,N)$. Yoneda gives a unique isomorphism that identifies the representing Hom bijections. Applying uniqueness to maps of $N$ makes these isomorphisms natural, and identifying the Hom bijections identifies the unit and counit. This is the stated adjunction-compatible uniqueness.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image].

Locally on $X$ and $Y$, the morphism $f$ is a closed immersion followed by
the projection from an affine space. We therefore treat these two cases and
then glue.

*Closed immersions.* Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed immersion with open
complement $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, and let $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ be the
local cohomology functor of Section [sec-Extension-by-zero-and-completion]. We show that $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ and that it is $i^!$. For
$K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$, there is a triangle

$$
i_*R\underline\Gamma_ZK\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K
\longrightarrow i_*R\underline\Gamma_ZK[1].
$$

By Proposition [proposition-open-direct-image-preserves-finite], the two terms on the right lie in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, and hence so does $i_*R\underline\Gamma_ZK$. Since
$i^*i_*=\mathrm{id}$ and $i^*$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, we get
$R\underline\Gamma_ZK\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Z,A)$. Explicitly, if $K$ has Tor
amplitude in $[a,b]$, then $R\underline\Gamma_ZK$ has Tor amplitude in
$[a,b+\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+1]$. The functor
$R\underline\Gamma_Z:D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)\to D(Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$ is right adjoint
to $i_*$ (Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme](1)), and
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,A))$ is a full subcategory of $D((-)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$. By
uniqueness of right adjoints, $R\underline\Gamma_ZK$ is therefore $i^!K$ in
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Z,A))$.

*Projections.* Let $p:\mathbf A^d_Y\to Y$ be the projection. From the
adjunction $Rq_*\dashv q^*(1)[2]$ for the projective line
$q:\mathbf P^1_Y\to Y$
(Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]) and from
Lemma [lemma-affine-space-etale-localization], we deduce that
$p^!\simeq p^*(-)(d)[2d]$ on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,A))$. This functor preserves
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, since pullback preserves a bounded constructible flat model and
the Tate twist is locally free of rank one.

For example, for the origin $i:0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ over $\bar k$
and $K=A$, the triangle gives $i^!A\simeq A(-1)[-2]$
(Example [example-closed-support] below). Its Tor amplitude $[2,2]$ lies in the

considered. Thus $f^!K$ is bounded constructible of finite Tor amplitude

amplitude valid everywhere. Finally, $Rf_!$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ by
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients].
Both sides of the adjunction therefore lie in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, and its Hom
bijections restrict.
