The equivalence is [Stacks, [0GS2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GS2)], proved by algebraization, approximation,
and descent of finite presentation. For the consequence, note that the groups in
(4.8) classify $M$-torsors, which are finite
étale schemes with an action of $M$ satisfying the equations of a simply
transitive action. The equivalence transports these schemes, their actions
and the equations, so it induces a bijection on isomorphism classes of
$M$-torsors.

We work with the étale sheaf corresponding to $F$, in
$D^+(-_{\acute{e}t},\Fell)$, and prove (6.19) and $\beta_T$
together by induction on
$n=\dim X_{k(S)}$, allowing at each stage all integral bases $S$ of
finite type over $k$. We first handle the complement of a finite set by
passing to the base $\mathbf A^1_S$, then the smooth, locally constant
case, and finally the general case by dévissage.

*Preliminary reductions.* Several modifications of the data are
harmless, and we will make them freely in the induction. First, the
assertions extend from open to locally closed immersions with the same
source. Indeed, such an immersion factors as an open immersion into its
scheme-theoretic closure followed by a closed immersion. Since closed direct
image is exact, preserves constructibility, and commutes with arbitrary
pullback [Stacks, [0959](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0959)], the assertions pass along this factorization. We will use the induction hypothesis in this form.
Next, replacing $Y$ by the scheme-theoretic closure of $X$, we may assume
that $X$ is dense in $Y$. We may also shrink $S$ to be affine, and we may
remove the closures of the images of the irreducible components of $Y$
that do not dominate $S$, since there are finitely many of them and none
contains the generic point of $S$. Finally, the assertions are local on
$Y$. Since we only use finite affine covers, the finitely many resulting
opens of $S$ can be intersected.

*Base case.* If the generic fibre is empty or zero-dimensional,
then after shrinking $S$ the immersion $j$ becomes an isomorphism or $Y$
becomes empty. Suppose first that $X_{k(S)}$ is empty. By density
$Y_{k(S)}$ is empty. On a finite affine cover, a coordinate algebra that
vanishes over $k(S)$ has its unit killed by a nonzero element of
$\mathcal O(S)$. Hence $Y$ becomes empty after shrinking $S$. If $n=0$,
the dense open $X_{k(S)}$ of the zero-dimensional Noetherian space
$Y_{k(S)}$ is all of $Y_{k(S)}$. The same argument applied to
$Y\setminus X$ shows that $j$ becomes an isomorphism after shrinking $S$.

Now let $n\geq1$, and assume the theorem, including $\beta_T$, for
generic fibres of dimension less than $n$.

*Step 1: for $Y$ projective over $S$, both assertions hold on
an open $G\subset Y$ whose complement is finite over $S$.* We replace the
base $S$ by the larger base $\mathbf A^1_S$, over which the generic fibre is
smaller, so that the induction hypothesis applies. To do this, choose charts and
coordinates as in Lemma [lemma-coordinate-projections]. Via
$t_{\alpha r}$, we regard $X\cap Y_\alpha\hookrightarrow Y_\alpha$ as an
open immersion of schemes over the integral base $\mathbf A^1_S$, which is
of finite type over $k$. By part (1) of that lemma, its generic fibre has
dimension less than $n$. Therefore the induction hypothesis, applied over the base
$\mathbf A^1_S$ to the restriction of $F$, gives a dense open
$V_{\alpha r}\subset\mathbf A^1_S$ over which both assertions hold.

Since $Rj_*$ commutes with restriction to the open $Y_\alpha$, the
assertions hold for $Rj_*F$ on $t_{\alpha r}^{-1}(V_{\alpha r})$. They
continue to hold after a base change $T\to S$ with $T$ of finite type over
$k$, as we see by applying the hypothesis to the inverse image of
$V_{\alpha r}$ in $\mathbf A^1_T$. Let $G$ be the finite union of the opens
$t_{\alpha r}^{-1}(V_{\alpha r})$. Then on $G$ the map $\beta_T$ is an isomorphism, and the complex $Rj_*F$ is bounded constructible. For the
boundedness, note that there are finitely many pieces, and therefore the
cohomology lies in a common finite range of degrees. Finally, part (2) of
the lemma shows that, after shrinking $S$, the reduced complement
$Z=Y\setminus G$ is finite over $S$.

*Step 2: the theorem holds in dimension $n$ when $X$ is
smooth over $S$ and $F$ is locally constant.* We may assume that $Y$ is
projective over $S$. Indeed, let $Y_\beta$ be a member of a finite affine
cover of $Y$, embed it in some $\mathbf A^m_S$ over the affine base,
and let $\overline Y$ be the closure of $X\cap Y_\beta$ in
$\mathbf P^m_S$. Then $X\cap Y_\beta$ is open and dense in
$\overline Y$, which is projective over $S$. Moreover $X\cap Y_\beta$ is
still smooth over $S$, with generic fibre of dimension at most $n$. The
result for $X\cap Y_\beta\subset\overline Y$ gives it on $Y_\beta$, because
$Rj_*$ and its base change maps commute with restriction to opens of the
target.

For $Y$ projective, Step 1 gives an open $G\subset Y$ with complement
finite over $S$ on which both assertions hold. Since $X$ is smooth over $S$
and $F$ is locally constant,
Lemma [lemma-extension-across-finite-subset] applies. It shows that
the assertions hold on all of $Y$ after shrinking $S$.

*Step 3: the general case in dimension $n$.* We find a dense open
$V\subset X$ to which Step 2 applies, and treat the difference between
$F$ and $Rv_*v^*F$, which lives on the smaller set $X\setminus V$, by the
induction hypothesis. Let $S'\to S$ and $V$ be as in
Lemma [lemma-generic-smooth-open].
Lemma [lemma-universal-homeomorphism-base] shows that it suffices to prove
the theorem for $(X_{S'})_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow(Y_{S'})_{\mathrm{red}}$
and the pullback of $F$ over $S'$. Its generic fibre still has dimension
$n$ because $S'\to S$ is a universal homeomorphism. We therefore replace
$S$ by $S'$ and all schemes by these reductions. Then $V\subset X$ is a
dense open, smooth over $S$, on which $F$ is locally constant. The
generic fibre of $X\setminus V$ has dimension less than $n$.

Let $v:V\hookrightarrow X$ be the open immersion and
$i:X\setminus V\hookrightarrow X$ its reduced closed complement. By
Step 2, after shrinking the base, both $v$ and $jv$ have bounded
constructible direct images of $v^*F$. Their base change maps are
isomorphisms after every base change $T\to S$ with $T$ of finite type
over $k$. Complete the unit of
$v^*\dashv Rv_*$ to a triangle

$$
\Delta_F:\ F\longrightarrow Rv_*v^*F\longrightarrow D
\longrightarrow F[1].
\tag{6.21}
$$

The first term is the constructible sheaf $F$, and the second is
bounded constructible by Step 2. Hence $D$ is bounded constructible too.
Indeed, by the long exact cohomology sequence, its cohomology sheaves are
extensions of kernels by cokernels of maps between constructible sheaves,
and these are constructible [Stacks, [09BH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BH)]. Moreover $v^*D=0$, as the unit
is an isomorphism on $V$. The localization triangle
(6.18) for $v$ and $i$ now shows that

$$
D=i_*i^*D.
$$

The locally closed immersion $ji:X\setminus V\to Y$ has generic fibre
of dimension less than $n$. We apply the induction hypothesis to each of
the finitely many constructible cohomology sheaves of $i^*D$, together
with their truncation triangles. This gives

$$
R(ji)_*i^*D=Rj_*D\in\Dbc(Y,\Fell),
$$

with base change maps that are isomorphisms. Now apply $Rj_*$ to
the triangle $\Delta_F$. In the resulting triangle, the middle term
$R(jv)_*v^*F$ is bounded constructible by Step 2, and the third term
$Rj_*D$ was treated just now. Hence $Rj_*F$ is bounded constructible.

To see that the base change map $\beta_T$ is an isomorphism, we
compare the triangle $\Delta_F$ with its analogue over $T$. Let
$g_X:X_T\to X$, $g_Y:Y_T\to Y$ and $g_V:V_T\to V$ be the projections, and
$v_T:V_T\to X_T$ the base change of $v$. The base change map

$$
\beta_v:g_X^*Rv_*v^*F\longrightarrow Rv_{T,*}g_V^*v^*F
$$

is an isomorphism by Step 2, and it carries $g_X^*$ of the first arrow of
the triangle $\Delta_F$ to the unit $g_X^*F\to Rv_{T,*}v_T^*g_X^*F$ of
$v_T^*\dashv Rv_{T,*}$. Since cones are not functorial, we have to choose the
triangles compatibly, and we take as triangle for this unit the pullback of
the triangle $\Delta_F$, transported through $\beta_v$. Now the base change map

$$
\beta_j:g_Y^*Rj_*\longrightarrow Rj_{T,*}g_X^*
$$

is a natural transformation of exact functors. It therefore induces a morphism from
$g_Y^*$ of $Rj_*$ of the triangle $\Delta_F$ to $Rj_{T,*}$ of this
triangle. On the second term it is $\beta_j$ at $Rv_*v^*F$ followed by
$Rj_{T,*}\beta_v$. Since base change maps compose [Stacks, [0EZR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZR), [0EZS](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EZS)], this
composite is the base change map for $jv$, an isomorphism by Step 2. On the third term it is $\beta_j$ at $D$. It is an isomorphism because,
composed with $Rj_{T,*}$ of the base change isomorphism for the closed
immersion $i$ [Stacks, [0959](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0959)], it is the base change map for $ji$ at $i^*D$
treated above. Hence, by the five lemma for triangles, it is an
isomorphism on the first term, which is $\beta_T$.

This completes the induction.

We prove clauses [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj--1] and [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj--2] together. Since
$S_0\subset S$ is open, a morphism $t:T\to S$ with image in $S_0$ factors
through $S_0$, and then $X_T=(X_{S_0})_T$ and $Y_T=(Y_{S_0})_T$. Write
$F_0=F|_{X_{S_0}}$.

*Step 1: $\Lambda=\Fell$ and $T$ of finite type over $k$.* The prime
$\ell$ is invertible on $S$. The argument of
the proof of Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj], applied to the étale sheaf
$F$, gives a nonempty open $S_0$ for which (6.19) holds and
(6.20) is an isomorphism for every $k$-scheme $T\to S_0$ of
finite type.

*Step 2: finite $\Lambda$ and $T$ of finite type over $k$.* Let $N$
be a positive integer killing $\Lambda$ and invertible on $S$. Then
$\Lambda$ is the product of its $p$-primary parts for the primes $p$
dividing $N$, and $F$, $Rj_*$, the inverse images and the base change maps
decompose accordingly. So we may assume that $\Lambda$ is killed by $p^r$
for a prime $p$ invertible on $S$. The functors $Rj_*$ commute with the
forgetful functors to $\mathbf Z/p^r$-modules [Stacks, [0D6J](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D6J)], the base
change maps are built from units and counits and so commute with them
too, and a $\Lambda$-sheaf is constructible if and only if its underlying
sheaf is, as shown in the proof of Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field]. So we
may assume $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/p^r$. The filtration
$F\supset pF\supset\cdots\supset p^rF=0$ has constructible
$\mathbf F_p$-sheaves as successive quotients. Apply Step 1 to each of
these $r$ quotients and intersect the resulting opens to get $S_0$. The
short exact sequences of the filtration are triangles, and $Rj_{S_0,*}$
and $Rj_{T,*}g_{X,0}^*$ carry them to triangles. By induction on $r$ and
the long exact cohomology sequences, $Rj_{S_0,*}F_0$ is bounded with
constructible cohomology sheaves, these being extensions of kernels by
cokernels of maps between constructible sheaves [Stacks, [09BH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09BH)]. The base
change maps form morphisms between these triangles, so they are
isomorphisms by the five lemma.

*Step 3: noetherian $T$.* Let $T\to S_0$ with $T$ noetherian. By
[Stacks, [09MV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09MV)], $T=\varprojlim_\lambda T_\lambda$ for a directed system of
$S_0$-schemes $T_\lambda$ of finite presentation over $S_0$, hence of
finite type over $k$, with affine transition morphisms. Write
$F_\lambda$ and $F_T$ for the pullbacks of $F_0$ to $X_{T_\lambda}$ and $X_T$, and
$h_\lambda:Y_T\to Y_{T_\lambda}$, $h_{\mu\lambda}:Y_{T_\mu}\to Y_{T_\lambda}$
for the projections. Base change maps are compatible with composition of
cartesian squares. Hence the base change map (6.20) for $T$
is $h_\lambda^*$ of the one for $T_\lambda$ followed by the base change map
$\gamma_\lambda:h_\lambda^*Rj_{T_\lambda,*}F_\lambda\to Rj_{T,*}F_T$ for
$T\to T_\lambda$, and similarly for $T_\mu\to T_\lambda$. By Step 2 the
base change maps for $T_\lambda$ and $T_\mu$ are isomorphisms, and so
$h_{\mu\lambda}^*R^ij_{T_\lambda,*}F_\lambda\to R^ij_{T_\mu,*}F_\mu$ is an
isomorphism for $\mu\geq\lambda$. The open immersions $j_{T_\lambda}$ are base changes of $j$, which is
quasi-compact because $Y$ is Noetherian, so they are quasi-compact and
quasi-separated; and $X_T=\varprojlim_\lambda X_{T_\lambda}$,
$Y_T=\varprojlim_\lambda Y_{T_\lambda}$ with affine transition morphisms.
So by [Stacks, [0EYM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYM)]

$$
R^ij_{T,*}F_T=\varinjlim_\mu h_\mu^{-1}R^ij_{T_\mu,*}F_\mu,
$$

a colimit whose transition maps are isomorphisms. Thus $H^i(\gamma_\lambda)$
is an isomorphism for every $i$, and so is (6.20) for $T$.

Finally, (6.20) identifies $Rj_{T,*}g_X^*F$ with
$g_{Y,0}^*Rj_{S_0,*}F_0$. By (6.19) and since inverse image
preserves boundedness and constructibility, this lies in
$\Dbc(Y_T,\Lambda)$.

That (6.20) is an isomorphism for every noetherian
$T\to S_0$ was shown, with the same $S_0$, in the proof of
clause [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj--1]. The two formulations agree: $g_Y$ factors as
$Y_T\to Y_{S_0}\subset Y$, the restriction of $Rj_*F$ to the open
$Y_{S_0}$ is $Rj_{S_0,*}F_0$, and by the compatibility of base change maps
with composition of cartesian squares, the base change map over $S$ is the
one over $S_0$ composed with the base change map for the open immersion
$Y_{S_0}\subset Y$, which is an isomorphism.

Both isomorphisms are the first two Verdier exchange formulas of
Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas] for $f=a_X$, so we only have to recognize the Verdier dual on the point as the linear dual. On $s$ the dualizing complex is
$\Lambda_s$, so $\mathbb D_s=\cHom_s(-,\Lambda_s)$. Since $k$ is
algebraically closed, Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point] identifies
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ with $\operatorname{Perf}(\Lambda)$. Under this identification, then, $\mathbb D_s$ becomes $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,\Lambda)$, and the two exchange
formulas read (10.5) and
(10.6). As for the pairing,
Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas]
constructs the exchange formula (10.3) from
evaluation and the counit of $Rf_!\dashv f^!$. For $f=a_X$ it is therefore
the adjoint of the displayed pairing.

Apply the compact-direct-image exchange formula of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--1] to $a_X:X\to s$. The dualizing object on $s$ is $\Lambda_s$. By Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point], global sections identifies constructible complexes on this geometric point with perfect $\Lambda$-complexes and their internal dual with $R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,\Lambda)$. The exchange formula is therefore the asserted first global isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality].

Apply the ordinary-direct-image exchange formula of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas--2] to $a_X$. The same point-category identification as in clause [theorem-global-verdier-duality--1] makes the dual on $s$ the linear derived dual. This gives the second global isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality].

The internal-adjunction comparison in Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas] is defined by transposing evaluation after the projection formula and the counit. For $f=a_X$ this composite is cup product with mixed supports, evaluation into $\omega_X$, and $\varepsilon_{a_X}$. Thus its adjoint is exactly the first global isomorphism of clause [theorem-global-verdier-duality--1].

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality].

In each case we turn the Weil structure into a Frobenius correspondence
by composing with $\kappa_1$, and we use
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] to see that this does not change
the operators. We then treat the coefficient rings in the order
finite, integral, rational, algebraic, each case using the
previous one.

For finite $A$, we apply Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence]
to $\psi=\phi\kappa_1$. Then Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] identifies $T_{c_m}(\psi_m)$ with $\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m$ and, at each fixed
point, $\psi_{m,\bar y}$ with $\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}$. Similarly, for $\mathcal O_E$, composing the Weil structure with
$\kappa_1$ we get a
Frobenius correspondence $\Phi_X^*K\to K$. By the integral form of
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius], the endomorphisms it induces on $R\Gamma_c$ and on the stalks
are those induced by the Weil structure. The identity therefore follows from
Proposition [proposition-integral-trace-formula]. In particular, taking $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ gives the case of $\mathbf Z_\ell$.

For coefficients $E$, the Weil structure composed with $\kappa_1$ is a
Frobenius correspondence $\psi_E$, and by the rational form of
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] the endomorphisms it induces on $R\Gamma_c$ and on the stalks
are those induced by the Weil structure. We apply
Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences] to $\psi_E$, apply (12.1) to $(K_0,\theta)$,
extend scalars to $E$, and multiply by $\pi_E^{-Nm}$. By linearity of
categorical traces and their compatibility with extension of scalars
(Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]), together with
(12.2), this gives the identity for every $m$.
The case $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ gives the case of $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, complexes and morphisms are colimits of their versions over
finite extensions, so it is enough to find the Weil complex over some
finite $E$ and to check that the answer does not depend on the choice.
By Proposition [proposition-dctf-x-qbar-2-colimit] the complex $K$, its
Weil structure $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ descend to a common finite extension
$E/\mathbf Q_\ell$. After a further finite extension the two identities saying
that these maps are inverse to each other hold as well. Thus we get a
Weil complex at a finite stage, and by extension
of scalars its formula over $E$ gives (12.3). If we
choose another representative, any isomorphism compatible with the Weil structures descends to a common finite extension, so the resulting
operators are conjugate. Since the trace is compatible with extension of scalars and invariant under conjugation, the result does not depend
on the stage or on the representative.

The complexes are perfect by Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point]. Compatibility
with the change-of-coefficients maps holds because the pullbacks, the
endomorphisms $T_{c_m}$ and the iterated Frobenius correspondences commute with the
comparisons of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients]. Finally, over a field
the categorical trace is the alternating trace on cohomology by
Proposition [proposition-properties-trace], and this proves
(12.4).

Put $\psi=\phi\kappa_1$. Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] identifies $T_{c_m}(\psi_m)$ with $\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m$ and its fixed-point endomorphisms with $\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}$. Apply Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence] with these finite coefficients. Substituting the identified endomorphisms gives exactly the asserted equality.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

Compose the integral Weil structure with $\kappa_1$ to obtain $\Phi_X^*K\to K$. The integral comparison in Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] identifies its global and stalk operators with those of the Weil structure. Proposition [proposition-integral-trace-formula], obtained by applying the finite formula to every reduction and passing to the complete coefficient ring, therefore gives this identity.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

For coefficients $E$, the Weil structure composed with $\kappa_1$ is a
Frobenius correspondence $\psi_E$, and by the rational form of
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] the endomorphisms it induces on $R\Gamma_c$ and on the stalks
are those induced by the Weil structure. We apply
Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences] to $\psi_E$, apply (12.1) to $(K_0,\theta)$,
extend scalars to $E$, and multiply by $\pi_E^{-Nm}$. By linearity of
categorical traces and their compatibility with extension of scalars
(Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]), together with
(12.2), this gives the identity for every $m$.
The case $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ gives the case of $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, complexes and morphisms are colimits of their versions over
finite extensions, so it is enough to find the Weil complex over some
finite $E$ and to check that the answer does not depend on the choice.
By Proposition [proposition-dctf-x-qbar-2-colimit] the complex $K$, its
Weil structure $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ descend to a common finite extension
$E/\mathbf Q_\ell$. After a further finite extension the two identities saying
that these maps are inverse to each other hold as well. Thus we get a
Weil complex at a finite stage, and by extension
of scalars its formula over $E$ gives (12.3). Now
choose another representative. An isomorphism compatible with the Weil
structures descends to a common finite extension, so the resulting
operators are conjugate. The trace is compatible with extension
of scalars and invariant under conjugation. Hence the result does not depend
on the stage or on the representative.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

Apply the compactly supported cohomology assertion of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point] to $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. Its hypotheses are exactly the finite-type hypothesis on $X$ and the constructibility and finite Tor-amplitude of $K$. It identifies $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ with a perfect $\Lambda$-complex.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

Apply the stalk assertion of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point] to each geometric point $\bar y$. Restriction of a constructible finite-Tor-amplitude complex to that point is a bounded complex with finite coefficients and finite Tor-amplitude, hence a perfect $\Lambda$-complex.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

The pullbacks, $T_{c_m}$, and iterated Frobenius correspondences commute with the coefficient comparisons of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients]. The scalar-extension identity for categorical traces in Proposition [proposition-properties-trace--3] therefore transports every term of the equality to the corresponding term over the new ring. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, independence of the chosen finite stage follows from the conjugacy and common-extension argument in clause [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula--4].

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

The complexes are perfect by clauses [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula--5] and [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula--6]. Over a field apply the cohomological trace identity of Proposition [proposition-properties-trace--6] to the global operator and to every stalk operator in the categorical trace formula. Their alternating cohomological traces are precisely the displayed terms.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula].

Representability is a general theorem, once we know that finite sets of
points lie in affine opens. We then obtain the geometric properties from the addition map $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}\times C\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$, which we show to be finite
locally free. Starting from $\operatorname{Hilb}^{1}_{C/k}=C$, we get smoothness and the
dimension by induction on $d$, and properness and irreducibility from
the finite surjection $C^d\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$.

Every finite set of points of $C$ lies in an affine open. Indeed, if $Q$
is a closed point outside the set, then $\mathcal O_C(Q)$ has positive
degree, hence is ample by Riemann–Roch, and so $C\setminus\{Q\}$ is
affine. Hence $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$ is represented by a scheme, separated and locally
of finite type over $k$ [Stacks, [0B9A](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9A)]. The universal closed subscheme
is the divisor $D_d$.

Let $T$ be a $k$-scheme and $t\in T$ a point. Since the local rings of
$C_{\kappa(t)}$ at closed points are discrete
valuation rings, every finite closed subscheme of a fibre is an
effective Cartier divisor. By the fibrewise criterion for relative
effective Cartier divisors, every $D\in \operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}(T)$ is a relative effective
Cartier divisor on $C_T/T$. This gives the description of $T$-points
and the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O(D_d)$. Multiplying ideals adds
such divisors, and we obtain the addition map

$$
\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}\times C\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k},\qquad (D,x)\longmapsto D+\Gamma_x.
$$

It identifies $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}\times C$ with the universal divisor over
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$: if a divisor $E$ contains the graph $\Gamma_x$, then dividing a local
equation of $E$ by one of $\Gamma_x$ gives a relative effective
Cartier divisor $D$ with $E=D+\Gamma_x$, of degree $d$ by the exact
sequence for a sum of divisors. In other words, the addition map is the
projection to $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$ of the universal divisor
$D_{d+1}\subset C\times \operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$. By definition of
the Hilbert functor, $D_{d+1}$ is finite locally free of degree $d+1$ over
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$. Hence the addition map is finite
locally free of degree $d+1$ [Stacks, [0B9G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9G)], in particular faithfully
flat.

We now argue by induction on $d$, starting from
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{0}_{C/k}=\operatorname{Spec}k$ and
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{1}_{C/k}=C$. The scheme $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d+1}_{C/k}$
is smooth because regularity descends along faithfully flat maps, also
after extending $k$. It has dimension $d+1$ because the addition map is
finite and surjective [Stacks, [0B9H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9H)].

Properness comes from the finite surjective map $C^d\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$
given by iterated addition. This map makes $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$
quasi-compact. It also makes $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$ universally
closed, because $C^d$ is proper and surjectivity is stable under base
change. Since $C^d$ is geometrically integral, $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$
is geometrically irreducible. Being smooth, it is then geometrically
integral [Stacks, [0B9I](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9I)].

For $C=\mathbf P^1$, the map $C^d\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}=\mathbf P^d$ sends $d$ points to
the binary form with these zeros, that is, the product of $d$ linear
forms; it is the quotient by the symmetric group, of degree $d!$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-hilbert-schemes-points-smooth-curve], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

If $S$ is Noetherian, we choose a cover as in
Lemma [lemma-affine-covers-dense-intersection] and argue by induction on the
unions $X_r=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_r$. For $r=1$, the lemma gives a
compactification of $U_1$. If $X_r$ has a compactification, we apply
Proposition [proposition-compactifying-union-two-opens] to
$M=X_{r+1}$, with $M_1=X_r$ and $M_2=U_{r+1}$. Each piece has a
compactification, by induction and by the lemma. The overlap
$X_r\cap U_{r+1}$ is dense in $X_{r+1}$, since it contains the total
intersection, which contains all generic points of $X$. Hence $X_{r+1}$
has a compactification. The last union is $X$ itself, and taking the
schematic closure of $X$ makes the compactification dense.

Now let $S$ be a general qcqs scheme, and suppose first that $X\to S$
is separated and of finite presentation. By absolute Noetherian
approximation we can write

$$
S=\varprojlim_i S_i
$$

with $S_i$ Noetherian and affine transition maps [Stacks, [01ZA](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZA)].
Since $X\to S$ is of finite presentation, it descends to a model
$X_i\to S_i$ for some $i$, and after increasing $i$ the model is
separated [Stacks, [01ZM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZM), [01ZQ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZQ)]. We then compactify this model by the Noetherian case and base change the compactification to $S$. The result is a compactification, because open immersions and proper morphisms are stable under base change, and taking
the schematic closure of $X$ makes the result dense.

Finally, let $X\to S$ be separated of finite type. By [Stacks, [01ZJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01ZJ)],
there is a closed immersion $X\hookrightarrow X_0$ with $X_0\to S$
separated of finite presentation. We compactify $X_0$ by the case
already proved, and take the schematic closure of $X$ in that
compactification. This closure is proper over $S$. Its restriction to
the open $X_0$ is the closed subscheme $X$ itself, so $X$ is open in
the closure, and it is schematically dense there by
Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness].
This clause is proved by the proof of Lemma [lemma-affine-covers-dense-intersection], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We prove (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).
The step (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is the main one: it applies the
degree-zero isomorphism termwise to an injective resolution.

*(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii).* Condition (ii) is the case of
(i) where $F$ sits in degree zero. Suppose (ii) holds, and let $I$ be an
injective sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules. Then $R^qf'_*g'^*I\simeq g^*R^qf_*I$
by (ii). The right hand side vanishes for $q>0$ because $I$ is injective,
and this is (iii).

*(iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii).* Let $F$ be a sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules. We
compare the two sides of the base change map through an injective
resolution $F\to I^\bullet$ by sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules. The complex
$f'_*g'^*I^\bullet$ computes $Rf'_*g'^*F$. Indeed, since $g'^*$ is exact,
$g'^*I^\bullet$ is a resolution of $g'^*F$, and its terms are
$f'_*$-acyclic by (iii), so Lemma [lemma-acyclic-resolutions] applies.
Similarly, the complex $g^*f_*I^\bullet$ computes $g^*Rf_*F$, because inverse image is
exact. Between the two, Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-degree-zero] gives an
isomorphism

$$
g^*f_*I^m\xrightarrow{\sim} f'_*g'^*I^m
$$

in each degree, and these form an isomorphism of complexes by naturality. By
(4.4) this isomorphism is the derived base
change map for $F$, which proves (ii).

*(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).* Let $K\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. For bounded $K$
we argue by induction on the cohomological length. A complex of length one
is a shifted sheaf, which (ii) covers, while a longer one is, by a canonical
truncation triangle, an extension of two complexes of smaller length.
Since the base change map is a morphism of triangles, the five lemma on
cohomology sheaves shows that it is an isomorphism for $K$.
An unbounded $K$ reduces to the bounded case, because a given
cohomology sheaf only depends on a bounded truncation. More precisely, fix a degree $m$
and choose $N\geq m$, so that $\tau_{\leq N}K$ is bounded and has the desired
comparison. Both functors $g^*Rf_*$ and $Rf'_*g'^*$ send
$D^{\geq N+1}(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ into $D^{\geq N+1}(Y'_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, since inverse images are exact
and derived direct images are left $t$-exact. Applying them to

$$
\tau_{\leq N}K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow
\tau_{\geq N+1}K\xrightarrow{+1}
$$

we see that the comparison for $K$ in degree $m$ is the comparison for
$\tau_{\leq N}K$, hence an isomorphism. As $m$ was arbitrary, (i) follows.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-pbc-injective-acyclicity], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Representability is Lemma [lemma-representability-picard-functor].
The tangent space is given by
Lemma [lemma-tangent-space-picard-functor]. Fix the point
$P\in C(k)$ used to define $F$.

For an invertible sheaf $\mathcal L$ on $C_T$, the Euler characteristic
$\chi(C_t,\mathcal L_t)$ is a locally constant function of $t\in T$.
This holds because $C_T\to T$ is proper and flat and $Rf_{T,*}\mathcal L$
is perfect (Lemma [lemma-coherent-base-change-invertible-sheaves]).
By Riemann–Roch the degree of $\mathcal L_t$ is locally constant as well.
This gives the displayed decomposition into open and closed pieces. The
charts in $\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$ and their translates show
that the scheme is smooth of dimension $g$.

It remains to see that the scheme is separated. A $k$-rational point of a
scheme locally of finite type over a field is closed. Hence the unit
section of the group scheme is a closed immersion. The diagonal is the
preimage of the unit section under $(x,y)\mapsto xy^{-1}$, so it is
closed as well.

The universal divisor defines the Abel map

$$
\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}^g_{C/k},
\qquad D\longmapsto\mathcal O_C(D).
$$

For a line bundle $\mathcal L$ of degree $g$ on $C_{k'}$, with $k'$
algebraically closed, Riemann–Roch gives
$h^0(\mathcal L)\geq\chi(\mathcal L)=g+1-g=1$. A nonzero section has an
effective divisor $D$ of degree $g$ with $\mathcal O(D)\simeq\mathcal L$.
Hence the Abel map is surjective on points over algebraically closed
fields, and this suffices for surjectivity. It follows that
$\operatorname{Pic}^g_{C/k}$ is quasi-compact. It is of finite type since
the charts are locally of finite type. A separated scheme of finite
type that is the surjective image of the proper scheme
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$ is proper. It is geometrically irreducible
because $\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$ is.
Translation by $\mathcal O_C((d-g)P)$ identifies
$\operatorname{Pic}^g_{C/k}$ with the component of each degree $d$. In
particular, the component of degree zero is smooth, proper, connected and
commutative. Such a group scheme is an abelian variety
(see [Stacks, [0BA0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BA0)]).

The tangent space $T_0J(C)$ is the kernel of
$\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k[\varepsilon])\to\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}(k)$,
where $\varepsilon^2=0$. Since $\operatorname{Pic}(k[\varepsilon])=0$, this is
the kernel of $\operatorname{Pic}(C_{k[\varepsilon]})\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)$,
which is $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ by
Lemma [lemma-tangent-space-picard-functor].

For a field extension $k'/k$, the Picard functor of $C_{k'}$ is the
restriction of $\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$ to $k'$-schemes. Hence its
representing scheme is the base change. The degree of $\mathcal L_t$ is
computed on the fibre $C_t$, so the decomposition by degree, and with it
$J(C)$, is compatible with this base change.

The theorem is global duality rewritten by means of smooth purity: once
$\omega_X$ and $\mathbb D_XK$ are identified, the pairing of
Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality] becomes $\beta_K$.

Corollary [corollary-dualizing-complex-smooth-scheme] identifies $\omega_X$.
Since internal Hom commutes with tensoring its second variable by an
invertible Tate twist and a shift, we get the
displayed description of $\mathbb D_XK$. If $K$ is locally
perfect, then locally $K$ is represented by a bounded complex of finite projective
modules, whose dual is the termwise dual, with the usual evaluation.

Next, $\beta_K$ is the pairing of
Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality] for $K$, transported along the
isomorphism $\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$. Indeed, under this isomorphism evaluation
$K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb D_XK\to\omega_X$ becomes evaluation on
coefficients $K\otimes^{\mathbf L}K^\vee(d)[2d]\to\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$.
Moreover, the trace map of Definition [definition-trace-map] is by definition the
counit $\varepsilon_{a_X}$ precomposed with $\gamma_{a_X}$, so the
counit becomes $\operatorname{Tr}_X$. Hence the adjoint of $\beta_K$ is
the isomorphism (10.5), which is
(10.8). By Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point]
both factors of $\beta_K$ are perfect complexes. Since the adjoint of
$\beta_K$ is an isomorphism, $\beta_K$ is perfect.

For proper $X$ we have $Ra_{X!}=Ra_{X*}$, which gives the
assertion on proper $X$. The last statement holds because the pairing is built from tensor
products, the two direct images, evaluation, the isomorphism $\gamma_{a_X}$ and
the trace map, all of which Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients] and
Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] show to be
compatible with every coefficient map.

Apply smooth purity, Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients], to the structural smooth morphism $a_X$ of pure relative dimension $d$. It identifies $a_X^!\Lambda=\omega_X$ with $\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$ by its specified purity map.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

By definition $\mathbb D_XK=\cHom_X(K,\omega_X)$. Substitute clause [theorem-poincare-duality--1]. Tensoring the second argument with an invertible rank-one Tate twist commutes with internal Hom, as does shifting that argument. This gives the displayed isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

Locally represent $K$ by a bounded complex of finite projective coefficient modules. Its dual is computed by the termwise dual complex, again bounded and finite projective. Thus $K^\vee$ is locally perfect.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

For the finite-projective local model of clause [theorem-poincare-duality--4], each ordinary Hom functor into the coefficient ring computes the corresponding derived Hom. The termwise dual complex therefore represents $\cHom_X(K,\Lambda_X)$ with its usual evaluation. These identifications are natural and glue, so it is the ordinary perfect-complex dual.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

We show below that $\beta_K$ is the pairing of
Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality] for $K$, transported along the
isomorphism $\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$. Granting this, the adjoint of $\beta_K$ is
the isomorphism (10.5), which is
(10.8). To show it, note
that under this isomorphism evaluation
$K\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbb D_XK\to\omega_X$ becomes evaluation on
coefficients $K\otimes^{\mathbf L}K^\vee(d)[2d]\to\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$.
The trace map of Definition [definition-trace-map] is by definition the
counit $\varepsilon_{a_X}$ precomposed with $\gamma_{a_X}$. Hence the
counit becomes $\operatorname{Tr}_X$, and $\beta_K$ is the transported
pairing. By Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point]
both factors of $\beta_K$ are perfect complexes. Since the adjoint of
$\beta_K$ is an isomorphism, $\beta_K$ is perfect.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

By clause [theorem-poincare-duality--6], $\beta_K$ is the global Verdier pairing transported by the purity identification $\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$. The adjoint of that pairing is the isomorphism in Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality--1]. Transporting the adjunction gives exactly the displayed canonical isomorphism.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

For proper $X$, the comparison $Ra_{X!}\to Ra_{X*}$ is an isomorphism by Proposition [proposition-forgetting-supports-composition--3]. Replacing compact direct image by ordinary direct image through this comparison in the construction of the pairing and its adjoint gives the asserted proper version.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

The pairing is the composite of cup product, evaluation, the purity map $\gamma_{a_X}$ and the trace. Tensor, internal Hom and both direct images commute with the coefficient comparisons by Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients]. Purity and trace do so by Proposition [proposition-compatibility-purity-change-coefficients]. Applying these compatibilities to each factor transports the composite to $\beta_{K_{\Lambda'}}$, including its adjoint.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality].

The pairing $\beta_K$ is a composite of maps each of which commutes with
pullback along Frobenius, so it is equivariant. Over a
field the remaining statements then follow by linear algebra, because the
pairing is perfect.

Cup product with mixed supports and evaluation are natural for pullback
by Frobenius, and the isomorphism $\gamma_{a_X}$ and the trace map are equivariant
by Proposition [proposition-purity-trace-commute-frobenius]. Moreover, the contragredient Weil structure on $K^\vee$ is chosen so that evaluation
$K\otimes K^\vee\to\Lambda_X$ is a morphism of Weil complexes, with the
trivial structure on $\Lambda_X$. It follows that the composite $\beta_K$ is equivariant, which gives $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=\langle
x,y\rangle$ for the first pairing. The second pairing is obtained by moving the
twist from the second factor to the values. Now geometric Frobenius acts on $\Lambda(d)$ by $q^{-d}$ and on
$\Lambda(-d)$ by $q^d$, so for $y$ in $H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee)$ the
operator $F$ on $y\otimes\zeta$, with $\zeta$ a generator of
$\Lambda(d)$, is $q^{-d}(Fy)\otimes\zeta$. Removing the twist, we get the
displayed identity $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^d\langle x,y\rangle$.

For field coefficients, Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields] identifies
$H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee)$, via the untwisted pairing, with the dual of
$H_c^i(X,K)$ tensored with $\Lambda(-d)$. Moreover, Frobenius on $H_c^i(X,K)$ is invertible, because $\phi_K$ is an isomorphism and pullback along the
automorphism $\operatorname{Fr}_X$ is invertible on cohomology.
In matrix terms, choose dual bases for the perfect pairing, let $F_i$ be the
matrix of $F$ on $H^i_c(X,K)$ and $F_{2d-i}$ that on $H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee)$. Then the identity $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^d\langle x,y\rangle$ reads ${}^tF_iF_{2d-i}=q^d$. In other words, Frobenius on
$H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee)$ is $q^d$ times the inverse transpose of Frobenius on
$H_c^i(X,K)$. Since a matrix and its transpose have the same characteristic polynomial, this proves the eigenvalue statement with algebraic multiplicities. Finally, taking determinants of
$F_{2d-i}=q^d\,{}^t(F_i)^{-1}$ on spaces of dimension $b$, we get
$\det F_{2d-i}=q^{db}(\det F_i)^{-1}$.

Cup product with mixed supports and evaluation commute with Frobenius pullback. Purity and trace commute with Frobenius by Proposition [proposition-purity-trace-commute-frobenius]. By the contragredient structure of clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--1], evaluation intertwines the two Weil structures with the constant Weil structure. Their composite $\beta_K$ therefore intertwines Frobenius.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

Take degree $i$ on the compactly supported factor and degree $2d-i$ on the other factor in clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--2]. The target is $\Lambda$ with trivial Frobenius action, so equivariance is precisely the asserted equality.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

Move the twist $(d)$ in clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--3] from the second factor to the values. Geometric Frobenius acts on $\Lambda(d)$ by $q^{-d}$ and hence on $\Lambda(-d)$ by $q^d$. The equivariance equality becomes the asserted formula.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

The Weil structure $\phi_K$ is an isomorphism, and pullback by the Frobenius automorphism is invertible on compactly supported cohomology. Their composite defining $F$ is therefore invertible.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields] makes the untwisted pairing perfect. In dual bases let $F_i$ and $F_{2d-i}$ be the two Frobenius matrices. Clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--4] gives $F_i^tF_{2d-i}=q^d I$. By clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--5], $F_i$ is invertible. Solving gives $F_{2d-i}=q^d(F_i^{-1})^t$.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

The perfect pairing of Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields] identifies the second space with the linear dual of the first tensored with the one-dimensional space $\Lambda(-d)$. Their dimensions agree.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

After extending scalars to an algebraic closure, transposition preserves the characteristic polynomial, while inversion replaces each nonzero eigenvalue by its reciprocal with algebraic multiplicity. Apply these facts to clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--6]; multiplication by $q^d$ gives the listed eigenvalues.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

Take determinants in clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--6]. The common dimension is $b$ by clause [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius--7], so $\det F_{2d-i}=q^{db}(\det F_i)^{-1}$. Multiplying by the nonzero determinant $\det F_i$ proves the identity.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius].

Weakly étale and ind-étale maps differ only in
how local rings are glued. Namely, after strict localization of the base a
weakly étale map identifies local rings, that is, for every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ lying over
$\mathfrak p\subset R$ the induced map of local rings $R_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism.
Such a map becomes ind-Zariski after refinement.

Applying the construction of simultaneous strict localizations to the pair
$R\to B$ we obtain compatible ind-étale refinements $R\to C$
and $B\to D$, with both spectra w-local and with closed points of
$D$ mapping to closed points of $C$. The map $C\to D$ is still weakly
étale by Lemma [lemma-stability], and the local rings
of $C$ at closed points are strictly henselian. Olivier's rigidity
theorem says that a weakly étale local map out of a strictly
henselian local ring is an isomorphism; see [Stacks, [092Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/092Z)]. Applying it at
the closed points of $D$, which lie over closed points of $C$, we get
isomorphisms of local rings there. Every point of the w-local
$\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ is a generalization of a closed point, and its
local ring is a localization of the local ring at that closed point.
Hence $C\to D$ identifies all local rings. For a ring map that identifies
local rings there is a faithfully flat ind-Zariski refinement of the target
over which the map becomes ind-Zariski [Stacks, [097G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097G)]. Applied to $C\to D$,
this gives a faithfully flat ind-Zariski map $D\to D'$ such that
$C\to D'$ is ind-Zariski, and we take $B'=D'$.

The algebra $B'$ has the two required properties. The map $B\to B'$ is the
composite $B\to D\to D'$ of two faithfully flat ind-étale maps, and
$R\to B'$ is the composite $R\to C\to D'$ of an ind-étale and an
ind-Zariski map. Both composites are ind-étale by
Lemma [lemma-stability]. For details see [Stacks, [097Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097Z)].
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We work on the étale site, where Propositions [proposition-proper-base-change-projective-line]
and [proposition-proper-base-change-etale-site] apply to the torsion rings
$\Lambda/p\Lambda$. By dévissage we reach all torsion sheaves of
$\Lambda$-modules, and the comparison theorems then bring us back to the
pro-étale site.

By Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes], we may write $K=\nu_X^*K_{\acute{e}t}$
with $K_{\acute{e}t}\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, and the cohomology sheaves of $K_{\acute{e}t}$
are torsion. Indeed, $\nu_X^*$ is exact, commutes with colimits and is fully
faithful on sheaves, and therefore detects the condition $F=\varinjlim_nF[n]$
of Definition [definition-torsion-sheaves]. We must show that the base change
map for $K_{\acute{e}t}$ is an isomorphism in $D^+(Y'_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, and then
pass to the pro-étale site.

We reduce to the rings $\Lambda/p\Lambda$, $p$ prime. These are killed by
$p$, so $\mathrm{PBC}_{\Lambda/p\Lambda}(f)$ holds by
Propositions [proposition-proper-base-change-projective-line] and [proposition-proper-base-change-etale-site]. Now a sheaf $F$ of
$\Lambda$-modules with $pF=0$ is a sheaf of $\Lambda/p\Lambda$-modules, and
restriction of scalars along $\Lambda\to\Lambda/p\Lambda$ is exact and
conservative. Moreover, it commutes with inverse images, derived direct images
and base change maps, since both derived direct images are computed on
underlying abelian sheaves
(Lemma [lemma-cohomology-modules-underlying-abelian]). Hence the base change map for $F$ is an
isomorphism.

If $nF=0$, we argue by induction on the number of prime
factors of $n$. For a prime $p\mid n$, the outer terms of
$0\to F[p]\to F\xrightarrow{p}pF\to0$ are killed by $p$ and by $n/p$,
so the five lemma applies to the long exact cohomology sequences. Finally, a torsion
sheaf is the filtered colimit $\varinjlim_nF[n]$. Since
(4.7) applies to the qcqs morphisms $f$ and $f'$,
the base change map is an isomorphism for every torsion sheaf of
$\Lambda$-modules. The truncation argument at the end of the proof of
Theorem [theorem-pbc-injective-acyclicity] then passes from sheaves to bounded below complexes with
torsion cohomology, in particular to $K_{\acute{e}t}$.

To return to the pro-étale site we apply $\nu_{Y'}^*$. Since $f$ and
$f'$ are proper, hence qcqs, the comparison of direct images in
Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images] applies. Using it together with the
comparison of inverse images $g_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}^*\nu_Y^*\simeq\nu_{Y'}^*g_{\acute{e}t}^*$, we
identify $\nu_{Y'}^*g^*Rf_*K_{\acute{e}t}$ and
$\nu_{Y'}^*Rf'_*g'^*K_{\acute{e}t}$ with $g^*Rf_*K$ and $Rf'_*g'^*K$ in
$D^+(Y'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. By the last assertion of
Lemma [lemma-naturality-pasting-comparison], under these identifications the
base change map of $K$ is the inverse image on $Y'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ of the étale
base change map of $K_{\acute{e}t}$. We have shown that the latter is an isomorphism.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

The trace class of $u$ is built in three steps: $u$ becomes a map into
$P_X=K\boxtimes\mathbb D_XK$, evaluation maps $P_X$ to the
dualizing complex on the diagonal, and $c^!$ moves the result to
the fixed locus. We check that each step commutes with pushforward. For the first two steps this means identifying the map adjoint to $u'$ with the
pushforward of the map adjoint to $u$, and evaluation for $K'$ with the
pushforward of evaluation for $K$. The third step needs more care. The squares $c'_ig=fc_i$ are only required to commute, so in general $\Fix(c)\ne C\times_{C'}\Fix(c')$, and we compare the two fixed loci through an intermediate scheme.

*Maps into $P$.* Put $P_Y=K'\boxtimes \mathbb D_YK'$, and
let $\tau_f:Rf_*\omega_X\to\omega_Y$ be the counit.
By the Künneth formula for the proper map $f\times f$ and the exchange
$\mathbb D_YRf_*\simeq Rf_*\mathbb D_X$ of Verdier duality, we obtain an isomorphism

$$
\rho_f:R(f\times f)_*P_X\xrightarrow{\sim}P_Y.
$$

A cohomological correspondence $u$ defines a map
$\theta_u:Rc_!A_C\to P_X$, obtained by exceptional adjunction from the
section $A_C\to c^!P_X$. Under
$Rc'_!Rg_*\simeq R(f\times f)_*Rc_!$, the map defined by the pushforward $u'$ is

$$
\theta_{u'}=
\rho_f\,R(f\times f)_*\theta_u\,
(Rc'_!Rg_*\simeq R(f\times f)_*Rc_!)\,Rc'_!\eta_g.
$$

To verify this identity, we apply tensor–Hom adjunction and then the
exceptional adjunction for $c'_1$. After this both sides become
$Rc'_{1!}\alpha$, followed by $Rf_*Rc_{1!}u$ and
$Rf_*\varepsilon_{c_1}$. The two sides use the projection formulas
for $c_1$ and for $c'_1$ in different orders, but they agree because
$c'_1g=fc_1$ and projection formulas are compatible with composition.

*Evaluation.* Evaluation is compatible with $\rho_f$, in the sense that

$$
e_{K'}\rho_f=
R\Delta_{Y*}\tau_f\,R(f\times f)_*e_K,
\qquad (f\times f)\Delta_X=\Delta_Yf.
$$

After restricting to the diagonal and taking tensor–Hom
adjoints, this says that Verdier duality for the proper map $f$ identifies
evaluation against $Rf_*K$ with the pushforward of evaluation against
$K$, followed by $\tau_f$. This holds because that duality is defined
by means of the counit $\tau_f$.

*Fixed loci.* The two maps into $P_Y$ and the two evaluations therefore
match. The trace classes, however, live on two different fixed loci, and we
must see that passing from $\Fix(c)$ to $\Fix(c')$
is the map $h_*$ of Definition [definition-pushforward-correspondence].
Recall that the fixed loci are the pullbacks of the diagonals,
$\Fix(c)=C\times_{X\times X}X$ and $\Fix(c')=C'\times_{Y\times Y}Y$.
To compare them, we factor $h$ through the fibre product $C\times_{C'}\Fix(c')$:

$$
\Fix(c)\xrightarrow{i'}C\times_{C'}\Fix(c')\xrightarrow{\pi}\Fix(c'),
$$

where the closed immersion $i'$ is the pullback of $X\to X\times_YX$ and $\pi$
is the base change of $g$. We use proper base change for the
square defining $C\times_{C'}\Fix(c')$, and the exceptional counit for $i'$.
Since counits are compatible with composition, the integration map for $h$ is
$\tau_h=\tau_\pi R\pi_*\tau_{i'}$.
Applying the identity for $\theta_{u'}$ and the compatibility of
evaluation, together with these base change maps, we identify the map
$A_{C'}\to Ri_{c'*}\omega_{\Fix(c')}$ defining the left-hand trace with

$$
A_{C'}\xrightarrow{\eta_g}Rg_*A_C
\longrightarrow Rg_*Ri_{c*}\omega_{\Fix(c)}
=Ri_{c'*}Rh_*\omega_{\Fix(c)}
\xrightarrow{Ri_{c'*}\tau_h}Ri_{c'*}\omega_{\Fix(c')}.
$$

Taking the $i_{c'}^*$-adjoint by means of the identity of composite units
$Rg_*\eta_{i_c}\,\eta_g=Ri_{c'*}\eta_h\,\eta_{i_{c'}}$, we obtain the
first formula (compare
[sga5, III, Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.7]).

*The trace formula.* For proper $X$ and $C$, we push forward to the identity correspondence on $s$, using
$f=a_X$ and $g=a_C$. Then the pushed cohomological correspondence is $T_c(u)$.
Indeed, for $g=a_C$ the map $\alpha$ is the pullback
$R\Gamma(X,K)\to R\Gamma(C,c_2^*K)$ and $\beta$ is the counit of
$c_1$ after $R\Gamma$, and these are the outer arrows in the definition of
$T_c(u)$. Moreover, the fixed locus of the identity correspondence of $s$ is $s$ itself. Hence the left side of the first formula is the local term of
$T_c(u)$ on $s$, which by Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point] is the
trace of $T_c(u)$. On the right, $h_*$ is integration over $\Fix(c)$, and since integration over a disjoint union is the sum of the integrations, this
gives the second assertion.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We bound the stalks of $R^ih_!F$ by the curve case, we show that these
sheaves are mixed by twisting to weight zero and adding the dual, and
we combine the two facts using
Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf].

*The stalks.* Fix a closed point $y$ of $Y_0$. Base change for
direct images with compact support
(Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek]) gives
an identification

$$
(R^ih_!F)_{\bar y}=H_c^i(U_{\bar y},F)
$$

compatible with the local Frobenius operators. The restriction of $F$ to
the fibre is again pure of weight $w$, because a residue extension
raises both an eigenvalue and the residue cardinality to the same
power. The fibre is a smooth affine curve over $\kappa(y)$, so
Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve] shows that $H_c^i(U_{\bar y},F)$ has
weights at most $w+i$. After a finite extension of $\kappa(y)$ the
components of the fibre are geometrically connected.
Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve], applied to each of them
with $j$ the identity, shows that these groups vanish outside degrees
$1$ and $2$.

*Mixedness.* We prove that $R^ih_!F$ is mixed. This is trivial
for $F=0$, so we may assume $F\ne0$. Let $G=F^0\oplus(F^0)^\vee$, with
$F^0=F\otimes\mathcal B_b$, be the sheaf of
Proposition [proposition-twisting-weight-zero-adding-dual]. It is
lisse, real and pure of weight zero. At a closed point $y$
write

$$
P_{i,y}(T)=\det(1-T\operatorname{Frob}_y\mid H_c^i(U_{\bar y},G)).
$$

Applying Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve] to the components of the
fibre after a finite extension of $\kappa(y)$, as above, we see that
$P_{0,y}=1$ and that every reciprocal root of $P_{2,y}$ has modulus
$q_y$. By the bound just proved, every reciprocal root of $P_{1,y}$
has modulus at most $q_y^{1/2}$.

We claim that $\iota P_{1,y}$ and $\iota P_{2,y}$ have real
coefficients. By the Euler product and the determinant identity of
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product], after applying $\iota$ we have

$$
L_\iota(U_y,G,T)=\frac{\iota P_{1,y}(T)}{\iota P_{2,y}(T)}.
$$

Since the Euler factors are real, this rational function has real
Taylor coefficients. Both it and its complex conjugate are regular at
zero, so they are equal as rational functions. Moreover, the numerator and the
denominator are coprime: a common root would give an eigenvalue having
both permitted moduli, whereas $q_y^{1/2}<q_y$. Since a reduced fraction whose
numerator and denominator have constant coefficient one is unique,
comparing it with its conjugate we find
$\iota P_{1,y},\iota P_{2,y}\in\mathbf R[T]$, which proves the claim.
Without the curve case this step would fail, because a common factor of
numerator and denominator could cancel, and we would only know that the
quotient is real, not each polynomial.

The sheaves $R^ih_!G$ are constructible by the finiteness theorems,
and we have shown that they are real at every closed point. By
Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed] each of them
has a finite mixed filtration.

To return from $G$ to $F$, note that by additivity $R^ih_!F^0$ is a
direct summand of $R^ih_!G$. A direct summand is a Weil subsheaf, and
so it is mixed by
Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations]. By the
projection formula for the constant twist, it is isomorphic to
$R^ih_!F\otimes\mathcal B_b$. Removing the twist preserves the finite
Weil filtration and shifts the weight of every pure quotient by $w$.
Hence $R^ih_!F$ is mixed.

*Conclusion.* The sheaf $R^ih_!F$ is mixed, and by the bound on the
stalks all its local eigenvalues have modulus at most $q_y^{(w+i)/2}$.
Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf], with
$w+i$ in place of $w$, shows that every nonzero quotient in the
filtration has weight at most $w+i$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-pure-lisse-sheaves-over-relative], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

Since $f_0$ is proper, the definition of $Rf_{0!}$ by
compactification identifies it with $Rf_{0*}$. This identification
commutes with the base change maps that define the Weil structures,
which proves the first assertion.

Fix a closed point $y$. By proper base change, the stalk at $\bar y$
with its local Frobenius is $H^i(X_{\bar y},F)$. By
Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf], $R^if_{0*}F$ is mixed
of weights at most $w+i$, so every eigenvalue $\alpha$ there
satisfies

$$
|\iota(\alpha)|\leq q_y^{(w+i)/2}.
$$

The opposite inequality comes from duality. The dual $F^\vee$ is
lisse of weight $-w$, so $F^\vee(d)$ has weight $-w-2d$. On the
smooth proper geometric fibre, Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields] and
Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius] give a Frobenius-equivariant perfect
pairing

$$
H^i(X_{\bar y},F)\times
H^{2d-i}(X_{\bar y},F^\vee(d))\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell.
$$

Since the pairing is perfect and takes values in the trivial Weil
line, it identifies the second factor with the dual of the first as a
Frobenius module, so the eigenvalues on the second factor are the
$\alpha^{-1}$, with multiplicities. Applying
Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf] once more, now to the
structure map of the fibre over $\kappa(y)$ and to $F^\vee(d)$, of
weight $-w-2d$, and to its cohomology in degree $2d-i$, we get

$$
|\iota(\alpha)|^{-1}
\leq q_y^{(-w-2d+2d-i)/2}=q_y^{(-w-i)/2}.
$$

The two inequalities give $|\iota(\alpha)|=q_y^{(w+i)/2}$ at every
closed point $y$. Every nonzero pure quotient in a mixed filtration of
$R^if_{0*}F$ has a nonzero stalk at some closed point, so its weight is
$w+i$. This proves the last assertion.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-purity-higher-direct-images-under], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We group the constituents by determinant weight and
place each group, tensored with the determinants of the groups of
larger weight, in an exterior power where it carries the largest
determinant weight. There Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] bounds the
eigenvalues of the group by its own determinant weight, and the same
argument applied to the dual gives the reverse bound.

Let $\mathcal G$ be an $\iota$-real lisse Weil sheaf on the curve. We
first prove the assertion when the curve is affine. There, replacing
$\mathcal G$ by its semisimplification changes neither its local characteristic
polynomials nor its irreducible constituents, and it keeps the sheaf
real, so we may assume that $\mathcal G$ is semisimple and write

$$
\mathcal G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^t\mathcal G_i,
\qquad \gamma_1>\cdots>\gamma_t,
\qquad r_i=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal G_i,
$$

where $\mathcal G_i$ is the sum of the irreducible constituents with
determinant weight $\gamma_i$.

Fix $i$, and let us find the exterior power in which $\mathcal G_i$,
together with the determinants of $\mathcal G_1,\dots,\mathcal G_{i-1}$,
carries the largest determinant weight. To this end set $m=\sum_{j<i}r_j$, and put
$B=\sum_{j<i}r_j\gamma_j$.  By
Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations](2), the largest determinant weight of a
constituent of $\bigwedge^{m+1}\mathcal G$ is $B+\gamma_i$.  Indeed,
it is obtained by taking $n_j=r_j$ for every $j<i$ and $n_i=1$, and
every other choice gives a smaller sum, because the $\gamma_j$ are
strictly decreasing.  Moreover, exterior powers of a real sheaf are real. Indeed,
their eigenvalues are the products of eigenvalues with distinct
indices, and complex conjugation permutes this multiset.  Hence
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] applies to $\bigwedge^{m+1}\mathcal G$.

The eigenvalues of $\mathcal G_i$ appear in
$\bigwedge^{m+1}\mathcal G$ not by themselves but multiplied by the
eigenvalues of the determinants of the groups of larger weight, and those
eigenvalues are known.
To make this precise, let $x$ be a closed point of the curve and $\alpha$ an eigenvalue of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on $(\mathcal G_i)_{\bar x}$.
The decomposition of the exterior power of a direct sum shows that
$\bigwedge^{m+1}\mathcal G$ contains the summand

$$
(\det\mathcal G_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\det\mathcal G_{i-1})
\otimes\mathcal G_i.
$$

If $\beta_j$ is the eigenvalue of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on
$(\det\mathcal G_j)_{\bar x}$, then the product $\alpha\beta_1\cdots\beta_{i-1}$ is
an eigenvalue of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on the stalk of this summand
at $\bar x$. Since $\det\mathcal G_j$ is pure of weight $r_j\gamma_j$, we have
$|\iota(\beta_1\cdots\beta_{i-1})|^2=q_x^B$. Now
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] gives

$$
|\iota(\alpha)|^2q_x^B\le q_x^{B+\gamma_i},
\qquad |\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_x^{\gamma_i}.
$$

For the reverse bound, note that the dual $\mathcal G^\vee$ is real as well, with determinant weights
$-\gamma_t>\cdots>-\gamma_1$. Applying the same argument to the
summand $\mathcal G_i^\vee$, we get
$|\iota(\alpha^{-1})|^2\le q_x^{-\gamma_i}$, and hence
$|\iota(\alpha)|^2=q_x^{\gamma_i}$. Since every
irreducible constituent of $\mathcal G$ is a summand of exactly one
$\mathcal G_i$, this proves the theorem on an affine curve.

On an arbitrary curve we restrict to an affine neighbourhood of a
given closed point $x$, which suffices because purity is a condition at
each closed point. It remains to check that the restriction changes neither the
constituents nor their determinant weights.
The neighbourhood is a nonempty open subscheme of a smooth geometrically
integral curve, so it is geometrically connected, and restriction to it preserves
irreducibility. Indeed, a connected finite étale cover of a normal connected
curve is integral, and hence remains connected after restriction to a dense
open. So the maps of geometric and of arithmetic fundamental groups are
surjective, and since restriction preserves the degree map, the map of Weil groups
is surjective too. Hence a subspace of the fibre is stable on the open
if and only if it is stable on the curve.

The restriction of a real sheaf is real, and by
Corollary [corollary-rank-one-weights] the determinant keeps its
weight. The affine case therefore applies at $x$, and since $x$ was
arbitrary, we obtain purity on the whole curve. Finally, the sheaf is mixed
because a composition series is a finite filtration with pure quotients.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We show that a fixed power of $\chi$ is trivial on $\pi_1(U)$, by
applying Lemma [lemma-invariant-additive-characters] to its logarithm.
For this we need a subgroup $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$ of finite index in
$\mathcal O_E^\times$ on which the logarithm is an injective homomorphism,
and a power of $\chi$ that lands in it.

*Step 1: the logarithm.* The compact group
$\chi(\pi_1(U))$ lies in $\mathcal O_E^\times$, because its image under the normalized
valuation is a finite subgroup of $\mathbf Z$ and therefore zero.
Now write $e=v_E(\ell)$ and choose an integer
$r>e/(\ell-1)$. We claim that $\log$ is injective on $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$.
For $x\in\mathfrak m_E^r$ and $n\ge1$ we have
$v_E(n)=e\,v_\ell(n)$ and, by Legendre's formula,
$v_\ell(n!)\le(n-1)/(\ell-1)$, so that

$$
v_E(x^n/n)\ge nr-e\,v_\ell(n),
\qquad
v_E(x^n/n!)\ge r+(n-1)\bigl(r-e/(\ell-1)\bigr).
$$

Both bounds tend to infinity with $n$ and are at least $r$: for the
second this is clear, and for the first it follows from
$n-1\ge\ell^{v_\ell(n)}-1\ge(\ell-1)v_\ell(n)$ and $(\ell-1)r>e$, which
give $(n-1)r\ge e\,v_\ell(n)$. The logarithm and exponential
series therefore converge on $\mathfrak m_E^r$; the logarithm maps
$1+\mathfrak m_E^r$ into $\mathfrak m_E^r$, and the exponential maps
$\mathfrak m_E^r$ into $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$. By the usual identities of formal
power series, $\log:1+\mathfrak m_E^r\to\mathfrak m_E^r$ and $\exp$ are
mutually inverse continuous group homomorphisms.

*Step 2: a power of $\chi$.* The quotient
$\mathcal O_E^\times/(1+\mathfrak m_E^r)$ is finite, being isomorphic to
$(\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak m_E^r)^\times$; let $N>0$ be an integer that
kills it. As $\chi(\pi_1(U))\subset\mathcal O_E^\times$, we have
$\chi(g)^N\in1+\mathfrak m_E^r$ for $g\in\pi_1(U)$. Hence
$a(g)=\log(\chi(g)^N)$ defines a continuous homomorphism
$\pi_1(U)\to E$, which is invariant under conjugation by $s$ because $\chi$ takes
values in an abelian group.

*Step 3: conclusion.* Lemma [lemma-invariant-additive-characters]
gives $a=0$, so $\chi(g)^N=1$ for every $g\in\pi_1(U)$, the logarithm being
injective. The theorem follows, since $T^N-1$ has only finitely many roots
in $E$.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-rank-one-sheaves-have-finite], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

We join a fixed point $x_*$ to an arbitrary point $x$ by a
curve on which the geometrically irreducible constituents stay
irreducible. On that curve each constituent is pure by
Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves]. Its weight can be
read off at $x_*$, so it does not depend on the curve. This handles a
lisse sheaf on a smooth affine scheme, and stratifying handles an
arbitrary constructible sheaf. Descent along constant extensions and
gluing of strata preserve mixedness
(Lemmas [lemma-mixedness-descends-constant-extension]
and [lemma-mixedness-open-closed]), so nothing about curves is used
beyond Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves].

*The lisse case.* Suppose that $X_0$ is smooth, geometrically
connected and affine, and that the sheaf $G$ is lisse. Since the curves
of Corollary [corollary-curve-preserving-geometric-irreducibility]
preserve geometric irreducibility, we first split $G$ into
geometrically irreducible pieces. To do so, we make the constant
extension of
Lemma [lemma-geometric-constituents-after-constant-extension] and
write $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ for the quotients of its Weil filtration. Note that the
sheaf $G$ remains real after this extension, because the powers of a
conjugation-stable multiset of eigenvalues again form a
conjugation-stable multiset.

Fix a closed point $x_*$ of $X_0$, and let $x$ be any other closed
point. By Corollary [corollary-curve-preserving-geometric-irreducibility], there is a curve
through chosen geometric points above $x_*$ and $x$ on which every
$S_j$ remains irreducible. The restriction of $G$ to this curve is
real, and Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves] says that the
irreducible constituents of a real sheaf on a curve are pure. Since the
restriction of $S_j$ is irreducible, it is one of them, and so
it is pure. Let $\alpha$ be an eigenvalue of $S_j$ at $x_*$, and let
$e$ be the residue degree over $\kappa(x_*)$ of the point of the curve
above $x_*$. At that point, then, the corresponding eigenvalue is $\alpha^e$
and the residue cardinality is $q_{x_*}^e$. If the restriction is pure
of weight $u$, then $|\iota(\alpha)|^e=q_{x_*}^{eu/2}$, so the weight of
the restriction of $S_j$ must be

$$
w_j=2\log_{q_{x_*}}|\iota(\alpha)|,
$$

which does not depend on the curve. In particular, all eigenvalues of $S_j$ at $x_*$
have this modulus. At $x$, the same calculation with powers
shows that $S_j$ is pure of weight $w_j$. As $x$ was arbitrary, each
$S_j$ is pure of weight $w_j$ on $X_0$. The chosen Weil filtration then
shows that $G$ is mixed after the constant extension, and by
Lemma [lemma-mixedness-descends-constant-extension], $G$ is mixed.

*The general case.* Now let $G$ be an arbitrary constructible
real sheaf. Since nilpotents do not change the étale site, we may
assume that $X_0$ is reduced. In each irreducible component, choose a
dense smooth affine open on which $G$ is lisse and which avoids the
other components. Since the complement has smaller dimension, iterating we
obtain a finite chain of closed subschemes whose differences are
disjoint unions of smooth connected affine pieces on which $G$ is
lisse. After one finite constant extension these pieces are
geometrically connected, and such an extension is allowed by
Lemma [lemma-mixedness-descends-constant-extension], and it keeps
$G$ real. The lisse case then applies
to the positive-dimensional pieces, while at a zero-dimensional piece a
Frobenius-stable full flag of each stalk has quotients of rank one,
which are pure. The restriction of $G$ to every piece is therefore mixed,
and Lemma [lemma-mixedness-open-closed], applied successively along
the chain of closed subschemes, shows that $G$ is mixed.
This clause is proved by the proof of Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed], with the hypotheses and choices shared there.

For bounded below complexes, (1) is
Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro] together with the
comparison of direct images (Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images]);
for unbounded complexes it is [Stacks, [0F0C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0C)], whose finiteness hypothesis
on $f$ is part (3). Part (2) is [Stacks, [0GL0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL0)]. As for part (3), for $Rf_*$ it is [Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)], and for $Rf_!$ we write $f=\bar f\circ j$ with $\bar f$ proper
and $j$ an open immersion; then $Rf_!=R\bar f_*j_!$ with $j_!$ exact, and
[Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)] applies to $\bar f$. Finally, the last assertion follows by the comparison of direct images, since classical sheaves are of the form
$\nu_X^*F$.

Apply Riemann–Roch for the smooth proper curve $C$ and the invertible sheaf $\mathcal L$, in the form [Stacks, [0B5B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5B)] quoted in the reference. With $g=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ and the degree convention fixed in this appendix, it gives exactly $\chi(C,\mathcal L)=\deg\mathcal L+1-g$.

The Serre-duality part of [Stacks, [0B5B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5B)], quoted in the reference, uses the residue trace on the canonical sheaf $\omega_{C/k}$. It identifies the dual of $H^1(C,\mathcal L)$ with $H^0(C,\mathcal L^{-1}\otimes\omega_{C/k})$. Symmetry of tensor product gives the displayed order of factors.

Serre duality gives $h^0(C,\omega_{C/k})=g$ and $h^1(C,\omega_{C/k})=h^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=1$, under the standing hypotheses on $C$. Thus $\chi(C,\omega_{C/k})=g-1$. Apply clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--1] to $\omega_{C/k}$ to obtain $g-1=\deg\omega_{C/k}+1-g$, which is equivalent to the claim.

If $\deg\mathcal L>2g-2$, clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--3] implies that $\omega_{C/k}\otimes\mathcal L^{-1}$ has negative degree. A nonzero section of a line bundle on an integral curve has an effective zero divisor, so a negative-degree line bundle has no nonzero section. Clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--2] therefore gives $H^1(C,\mathcal L)=0$.

Under the degree hypothesis carried by this clause, clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--4] gives $H^1(C,\mathcal L)=0$. Hence $h^0(C,\mathcal L)=\chi(C,\mathcal L)$. Substitute the Riemann–Roch value from clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--1] to obtain the formula.

Apply clause [theorem-riemann-roch-coherent-serre-duality--2] to $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_C$. It gives $H^0(C,\omega_{C/k})\simeq H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)^\vee$, so $\dim_kH^0(C,\omega_{C/k})=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)=g$.

For finite rings the theorem is the torsion theorem once we know that $K$
is classical, and the other rings follow by the reduction principle. By
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf], both sides lie in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y',\Lambda)$, so we only have to show that the canonical map
(4.5) is invertible.

*Finite rings $A$.* The torsion theorem is stated for classical
complexes, so we first check that $K$ is one. By Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves], constructible
pro-étale sheaves with discrete Noetherian coefficients are
classical, and since the cohomology sheaves of $K$ are constructible, $K$ is a bounded classical complex. Since $A$ is
killed by a power of $\ell$, which is invertible on $Y$, smooth base change
for torsion complexes (Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-classical-torsion-2]) applies to $K$.

*Other rings.* We apply Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients] with
$F_\Lambda=g^*Rf_*$, $G_\Lambda=Rf'_*g'^*$ and $\theta_\Lambda$ the base
change map. Both functors are exact, as the proposition requires, and
the base change map commutes with change of coefficients, which is
Lemma [lemma-change-coefficients]. Since $\theta_A$ is an isomorphism for every finite
$A$ by the first case, the proposition shows that $\theta_\Lambda$ is an
isomorphism for every admissible $\Lambda$.

The inverse image $\nu_X^*$ is exact and its values are classical, so the
cohomology sheaves $H^q(K)\simeq\nu_X^*H^q(K_{\acute{e}t})$ are classical and
vanish for all but finitely many $q$. Thus $K$ lies in
$D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$. Since $N$ is invertible on $Y$,
smooth base change for classical torsion complexes
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-classical-torsion-2], with
$\Lambda=A$ and $n=N$) shows that (8.2) is an
isomorphism. Neither finite Tor amplitude nor a finite type hypothesis
enters.

For the last assertion, let $A$ be finite and killed by a power of $\ell$,
which is invertible on $Y$, and let $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$. Then $K$ is
bounded with constructible cohomology, $X$ is of finite type over $k$,
hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated, $f$ is a morphism of schemes of
finite type over $k$, hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and $A$
is Noetherian. By
Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]
(clause [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves--3]) there are a $K_{\acute{e}t}\in\Dbc(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ and an
isomorphism $\nu_X^*K_{\acute{e}t}\simeq K$, so the first part applies.

*Source:* the proof of Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-all-admissible].
