Let $X$ be a nonempty connected normal scheme of finite type over a
field, let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be finite, and fix a geometric point $\bar x$. By
Lemma [lemma-global-lattice-normal-scheme], every lisse $E_X$-module $L$
contains a lisse $\mathcal O_{E,X}$-submodule $M$ with $M[1/\ell]=L$ and
$M\simeq\varprojlim_nM/\pi_E^nM$, whose reductions are finite locally
constant étale sheaves. The fibre functor at $\bar x$,
$L\mapsto\bigl(\varprojlim_n(M/\pi_E^nM)_{\bar x}\bigr)\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}E$,
does not depend on the choice of $M$ up to canonical isomorphism, and it
gives an equivalence between lisse $E_X$-modules and finite-dimensional
continuous $E$-representations of the ordinary profinite group
$\pi_1(X,\bar x)$.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero, let $\mathfrak l$ be a
finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $k$, and let $M$ be a faithful
finite-dimensional semisimple representation of $\mathfrak l$. Assume
that each $x\in\mathfrak l$ acts on $M$ by a triangularizable
endomorphism. Then

$$
\operatorname{rad}\mathfrak l=Z(\mathfrak l).
$$

Here semisimplicity means that every $\mathfrak l$-stable subspace of
$M$ has a $\mathfrak l$-stable complement. The triangularizability
condition is automatic over $k=\Omega$.

If $k$ has characteristic zero, then also

$$

$$

composite with $1-T$, is an isomorphism in
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal R)$. Thus the derived limit is
the ordinary limit in degree zero.

Let $C$ be a smooth proper connected curve of genus $g$ over an
algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $\varphi$ be
the Frobenius-linear endomorphism of $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ induced by
$a\mapsto a^p$ on $\mathcal O_C$.  Then

$$
H^0(C,\mathbf F_p)=\mathbf F_p,\qquad
H^1(C,\mathbf F_p)=
\ker(\varphi-1:H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\to H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)),
$$

and $H^q(C,\mathbf F_p)=0$ for $q>1$.  The group $H^1(C,\mathbf F_p)$
is finite, of $\mathbf F_p$-dimension at most $g$, and its pullback map
is an isomorphism under algebraically closed extension.

Let $\Omega$ be a separably closed field. The category of pro-étale
affines over $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is equivalent to the category
of profinite sets, with finite jointly surjective families as covers.
Consequently its topos is, up to a set-theoretic cutoff, the topos of condensed sets. A discrete
ring $A$ defines the classical constant sheaf, while a profinite
or locally profinite coefficient ring defines its sheaf of continuous
functions on profinite sets.

attrs.title: The pro-étale site of a separably closed field

objects.body:
Let $\Omega$ be a separably closed field, and fix a universe containing
$\Omega$. For a profinite set $S$ in this universe, put

$$
(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega)[S]
=\operatorname{Spec}LC(S,\mathbf Z)
\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega,
$$

where $LC$ denotes locally constant functions. The functor
$S\mapsto(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega)[S]$ is an equivalence from the
category $\operatorname{ProFin}$ of profinite sets onto the category of
pro-étale affines over $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, and it identifies
$\operatorname{ProFin}$ with a dense subsite of $(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.
The topology on this subsite is the coherent topology on profinite sets,
generated by finite jointly surjective families, including the empty
cover of the empty set.

Let $X$ be a scheme and $A$ a discrete abelian group. The constant
pro-étale sheaf with value $A$ is canonically isomorphic to the sheaf
$U\mapsto C(U,A)$ of continuous functions, by the map sending a
constant section to the corresponding constant function. In particular,
this identifies the underlying abelian sheaf of a discrete coefficient
ring with its sheaf of locally constant functions.

For any topological ring $R$, the functor

$$
\underline R(S)=C(S,R)
$$

on profinite sets is a sheaf of rings for the coherent topology, with
pointwise ring operations and restriction by precomposition. This
applies in particular to profinite and locally profinite rings.

Let $p:X\to Y$ be proper, let $g:Y'\to Y$ be any morphism, and let
$p':X'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$ be the projections from $X'=X\times_YY'$.

$$

$$

belongs to $D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)$. Then
$Rp_*K$ is derived $\pi_E$-complete.

More generally, let $p:X\to Y$ be any morphism of schemes, and put $\kappa_E=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$. For every
$M\in D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$, the canonical comparison
between inverse image and derived reduction is an isomorphism

$$
(p^*M)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,X}}(\kappa_E)_X
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
p^*\bigl(M\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,Y}}(\kappa_E)_Y\bigr).
$$

For every $K\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$, its adjoint
comparison, obtained using the inverse of this isomorphism and the counit
$p^*Rp_*K\to K$, is an isomorphism

$$
(Rp_*K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,Y}}(\kappa_E)_Y
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
Rp_*\bigl(K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,X}}(\kappa_E)_X\bigr).
$$

If $K$ is derived $\pi_E$-complete, then $Rp_*K$ is derived
$\pi_E$-complete. Here neither properness nor classicality of the reductions is needed.

$$
G'(c_F(M))\circ c_G(FM)\circ T_1(\eta_M)=\eta'_{T_1M}.

For $F=f^*$ and $G=Rf_*$, with $T_1,T_2$ scalar extension along $\Lambda\to\Lambda'$, the comparisons of Definition [definition-change-of-coefficients-maps](1) and (4) form such a mate square by construction, and on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ they are invertible by [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients--2] and [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients--3]. objects.body: *Shared context.* Throughout this source block, schemes and morphisms satisfy the standing hypotheses of the reference. The symbol $\Lambda$ ranges over $A,\mathcal O_E,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, with $A$ finite admissible and $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ finite. All six operations below are on the pro-étale sites, with the indicated coefficient ring. Each restricted adjunction uses the same ambient units and counits.

Let $C$ be smooth, proper and connected over an algebraically closed
field $k$, with genus $g$, and let $n\geq1$ be invertible in $k$.
There are canonical identifications

$$
\begin{aligned}
H^0(C,\mu_n)&=\mu_n(k),&
H^1(C,\mu_n)&=J(C)[n](k),\\
H^2(C,\mu_n)&=\mathbf Z/n,&
H^q(C,\mu_n)&=0\quad(q>2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The isomorphism in degree two sends the Kummer boundary of a line bundle
$L$ to $\deg L\bmod n$.  These identifications commute with extension
of algebraically closed fields.

Let $\mathcal C$ and $\mathcal D$ be categories, let
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G,J:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ be functors,
and fix adjunctions $F\dashv G$ and $F\dashv J$ with counits
$\varepsilon^G$ and $\varepsilon^J$. There is a natural isomorphism
$\rho:G\xrightarrow{\sim}J$ such that, for every $K\in\mathcal D$,

$$
\varepsilon^J(K)\circ F(\rho(K))=\varepsilon^G(K).
$$

Its underlying natural transformation is uniquely determined by this equation.

In particular, let $\Lambda$ be an admissible coefficient ring and let $J$
be a right adjoint of
$Rf_!:D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)\to D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$ with
counit $\varepsilon^J$. Taking $F=Rf_!$ and $G=f^!$ with counit
$\varepsilon_f$, there is a unique natural isomorphism
$\rho:f^!\xrightarrow{\sim}J$ with
$\varepsilon^J(K)\circ Rf_!(\rho(K))=\varepsilon_f(K)$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes in a universe $u$, and take
sheaves of sets in universe $u+1$. Base change
$b_f:V\mapsto V\times_YX$ preserves finite limits and covering families
on the small pro-étale sites. It induces a geometric morphism

$$
f_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}:\Sh(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})\longrightarrow\Sh(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}),
\qquad f^{-1}\dashv f_*.
$$

Here $f_*$ is restriction along $b_f$, so that
$(f_*\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V\times_YX)$, and $f^{-1}$ is left Kan extension along
$b_f^{\mathrm{op}}$ followed by sheafification. The functor
$f^{-1}:\Sh(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})\to\Sh(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})$
preserves finite limits and all colimits. The same construction for
abelian sheaves in universe $u+1$ agrees with $f^{-1}$ on underlying
sheaves of sets and is exact.

For morphisms $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ of schemes in a universe $u$,
the inverse images on sheaves of sets in universe $u+1$ have a canonical
isomorphism

$$
(g\circ f)^{-1}\simeq f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}.
$$

It is the isomorphism of left adjoints corresponding, under the
adjunctions of [proposition-topos-functoriality--2], to the canonical
isomorphism $g_*\circ f_*\simeq(g\circ f)_*$.

Let $\mathcal F\ne0$ be lisse and pure of weight $w$ on a nonempty
finite-type scheme over $k_0$.  There is $b\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$ with
$|\iota(b)|=q^{-w/2}$.  Put

$$
\mathcal F^0=\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B_b,
\qquad \mathcal E=\mathcal F^0\oplus(\mathcal F^0)^\vee.
$$

Then $\mathcal E$ is real and pure of weight zero, contains
$\mathcal F^0$ as a direct summand, and at points over $k_n$ its trace
is twice the real part of the trace of $\mathcal F^0$.

Let $U$ be a quasi-compact, quasi-separated object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.
There is a hypercover $W_\bullet\to U$ whose term in every simplicial
degree is one affine weakly contractible object. If
$K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal R)$ is represented by a complex
$K^\bullet$ vanishing below degree $a$, then

$$
R\Gamma(U,K)
\simeq \operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K^b(W_r)\bigr)_{r\geq0,\ b\geq a}.
\tag{2.3}
$$

The cosimplicial differential is the alternating sum of pullbacks
along face maps, combined with $(-1)^r$ times the differential of
$K^\bullet$. In total degree $q$ this complex has the finite sum
$\bigoplus_{0\leq r\leq q-a}K^{q-r}(W_r)$.

$K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal R)$ is represented by a complex
$K^\bullet$ vanishing below degree $a$, then

$$
R\Gamma(U,K)
\simeq \operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K^b(W_r)\bigr)_{r\geq0,\ b\geq a}.
\tag{2.3}
$$

The cosimplicial differential is the alternating sum of pullbacks
along face maps, combined with $(-1)^r$ times the differential of
$K^\bullet$. In total degree $q$ this complex has the finite sum
$\bigoplus_{0\leq r\leq q-a}K^{q-r}(W_r)$.

Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow X_0$ be a dense open of a smooth
geometrically connected curve.  If a lisse Weil sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$U_0$ is punctually of weights $\le a$, so is $j_*\mathcal F$ on
$X_0$.

attrs.title: Weights of $j_*$ at the boundary points (1)

objects.body:
Extensions of mixed sheaves are mixed, and an extension of two sheaves with a common upper bound has the same
bound.  Tensor products of pure sheaves of weights $a$ and $b$ are pure
of weight $a+b$, and the dual of a pure lisse sheaf of weight $a$ is
pure of weight $-a$. A tensor product of mixed sheaves of weights at
most $a$ and at most $b$ is mixed of weights at most $a+b$. The dual of
a mixed lisse sheaf is mixed, of the negated weights; when its filtration
has lisse graded pieces, their duals are the graded pieces of the
annihilator filtration of the dual.  Inverse image preserves purity,
mixedness and their upper bounds.  If a complex $K$ has weights at most
$w$, then $K[r]$ has weights at most $w+r$.

For $b\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$, let $\mathcal B_b$ be the geometrically constant
rank-one Weil sheaf on which a degree-one Frobenius acts by $b$.
Tensoring by $\mathcal B_b$ adds
$\lambda_\iota(b)=2\log_q|\iota(b)|$ to every weight.  The Tate sheaf
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ has geometric Frobenius $q^{-1}$, so twisting by $(r)$
subtracts $2r$ from every weight.
An extension of mixed Weil sheaves is mixed.

If a bounded constructible Weil complex $K$ has weights at most $w$,
then $K[r]$ has weights at most $w+r$ for every $r\in\mathbf Z$.

For $b\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$, let $\mathcal B_b$ be the geometrically constant
rank-one Weil sheaf on which a degree-one Frobenius acts by $b$.

Let $b\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$ and put
$c=\lambda_\iota(b)=2\log_q|\iota(b)|$. If $\mathcal F$ is
punctually pure of weight $w$, then $\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B_b$
is punctually pure of weight $w+c$. If $\mathcal F$ is mixed of
weights at most $w$, then $\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B_b$ is mixed
of weights at most $w+c$.

The scalar by which geometric Frobenius acts on the cyclotomic Tate
module is $q^{-1}$ in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$.
Thus $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ has degree-one geometric Frobenius
$q^{-1}$; at a closed point $x$ its local Frobenius is $q_x^{-1}$.
Twisting by $(r)$ subtracts $2r$ from every weight.

Let $i:\mathcal G\hookrightarrow\mathcal F$ be a monomorphism of Weil
sheaves. If $\mathcal G$ and $\operatorname{coker}(i)$ are mixed of
weights at most $w$, then $\mathcal F$ is mixed of weights at most $w$.
The tensor product of pure sheaves of weights $a,b$ is pure of weight $a+b$.

For a lisse Weil sheaf $\mathcal F$ and a closed point $x$, there is
a Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism

$$
(\mathcal F^\vee)_{\bar x}\simeq(\mathcal F_{\bar x})^\vee,
$$

where the Frobenius on the right is the inverse transpose. In
particular, if $\mathcal F$ is punctually pure of weight $a$, its dual
is punctually pure of weight $-a$.

objects.body: The tensor product of mixed sheaves of weights at most $a,b$ is mixed of weights at most $a+b$.
The dual of a mixed lisse sheaf is mixed, of the negated weights. When its filtration has lisse graded pieces, their duals are the graded pieces of the annihilator filtration of the dual.

attrs.title: Dual of a mixed lisse sheaf

objects.body:
Let $f:X_0\to Y_0$ be a morphism of schemes locally of finite type
over $k_0$. If $\mathcal F$
is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ on $Y_0$, then $f^*\mathcal F$
is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ on $X_0$.

Let $f:X_0\to Y_0$ be a morphism between $k_0$-schemes locally of
finite type. If $\mathcal F$ is mixed on $Y_0$, then $f^*\mathcal F$
is mixed on $X_0$.
Inverse image preserves upper weight bounds.

*Shared context.* Let $k_0=\Fq$, let $\ell\nmid q$ be prime, and fix
$\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$.
Weights are real and have the normalization of [definition-weights].
Weil sheaves have coefficients in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.
The assertions below are stated on schemes locally of finite type over
$k_0$; they do not require separatedness or quasi-compactness. Mixed
complexes are bounded constructible Weil complexes on such schemes.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety of dimension $d$ over $\mathbf F_q$.
The Weil conjectures assert that its zeta function, which counts the points
of $X$ over all the fields $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, is a rational function, that it
satisfies a functional equation, and that its zeros lie on the circles
$|T|=q^{-i/2}$ with $i$ odd and its poles on those with $i$ even, an analogue
of the Riemann hypothesis. The points over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$ are the fixed
points of the $m$th power of Frobenius. Weil therefore expected the first two
statements to follow from a Lefschetz fixed point formula and Poincaré
duality in a cohomology theory with coefficients of characteristic zero.
These notes construct such a theory and prove all three statements.

The theory is $\ell$-adic cohomology. Étale cohomology works best with the
torsion coefficients $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, but traces must be taken in
characteristic zero. On the pro-étale site of Bhatt and Scholze,
$\mathbf Z_\ell$ and $\mathbf Q_\ell$ define sheaves of rings just as
$\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ does, so one set of definitions and one formalism of six
operations serve every coefficient ring. The trace formula and Poincaré
duality then give rationality and the functional equation.

The Riemann hypothesis follows from the Deligne–Laumon theorem, which bounds
the absolute values of Frobenius eigenvalues, the weights, on the cohomology
of sheaves. We follow Laumon's proof: fibring by curves reduces the theorem to
curves, where the $\ell$-adic Fourier transform and a positivity argument that
Deligne took from Rankin bound the weights.

The documents speak some of the most important definitions and theorems in our lean formalization. They quote some
foundational results from algebraic geometry and from étale cohomology with
torsion coefficients, each stated precisely. We assume a first course in
algebraic geometry and some familiarity with derived categories and singular
cohomology, but no étale cohomology.

These notes prove the Weil conjectures, which concern the number of
solutions of polynomial equations over finite fields. Weil saw that
rationality and the functional equation would follow from a cohomology
theory for varieties over finite fields with a Lefschetz fixed point
formula and Poincaré duality, while the deepest conjecture, an analogue of the
Riemann hypothesis, needs in addition a bound on the eigenvalues of
Frobenius. Following this plan, we construct such a theory, $\ell$-adic cohomology, and prove the
trace formula and Poincaré duality for it. Then we prove the bound, which
is the Deligne–Laumon theorem.

Let $X_0$ be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus
$g$ over the finite field $\mathbf F_q$, and let $N_m$ be the number of
its points with coordinates in $\mathbf F_{q^m}$. The projective line has
exactly $1+q^m$ such points, and the *Hasse–Weil bound* says that
every curve of genus $g$ comes close to this count:

$$
|N_m-(1+q^m)|\le 2g\,q^{m/2}.
$$

Hasse proved it for elliptic curves [hasse36] and Weil for all
curves [weil48-courbes].

To state Weil's conjectures in higher dimension we put all the numbers
$N_m$ into one generating function. For a separated scheme $X_0$ of
finite type over $\mathbf F_q$, its *zeta function* is

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\exp\Bigl(\sum_{m\ge 1}\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\frac{T^m}{m}\Bigr)
\in 1+T\mathbf Q[[T]].
$$

A closed point $x$ of $X_0$ with residue field $\mathbf F_{q^{\deg x}}$
accounts for exactly $\deg x$ points of $X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ when
$\deg x$ divides $m$, and for none otherwise. Hence
$\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})=\sum_{\deg x\mid m}\deg x$, so

$$
\sum_{m\ge1}\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\frac{T^m}{m}
=\sum_{x\in|X_0|}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{T^{k\deg x}}{k}
=-\sum_{x\in|X_0|}\log\bigl(1-T^{\deg x}\bigr).
$$

Only finitely many closed points have a given degree, so exponentiating
gives the Euler product

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\prod_{x\in|X_0|}\bigl(1-T^{\deg x}\bigr)^{-1},
$$

whose factors are power series with integer coefficients. So the
coefficients of $Z(X_0,T)$ are integers. For example,
$\#\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_{q^m})=1+q^m$ gives
$Z(\mathbf P^1,T)=1/((1-T)(1-qT))$. Set $T=q^{-s}$. Since the residue
field of $x$ has $N(x)=q^{\deg x}$ elements, the Euler product becomes

$$
\zeta_{X_0}(s)=Z(X_0,q^{-s})=\prod_{x\in|X_0|}\bigl(1-N(x)^{-s}\bigr)^{-1},
$$

the analogue of Riemann's

$$
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}=\prod_{p}\bigl(1-p^{-s}\bigr)^{-1},
$$

in which the closed points of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ have residue
fields with $p$ elements. Riemann conjectured that the nontrivial zeros of
$\zeta(s)$ lie on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$.
Weil conjectured the following.

1. *Rationality.* $Z(X_0,T)$ is a rational function of $T$.
2. *Functional equation.* If $X_0$ is smooth and proper of pure
   dimension $d$, then $Z(X_0,1/(q^dT))=\pm q^{d\chi/2}T^{\chi}Z(X_0,T)$,
   where $\chi=\sum_i(-1)^ib_i$ is the Euler characteristic, with $b_i$
   as in (4). For a curve of genus $g$ it equals $2-2g$.
3. *Riemann hypothesis.* If $X_0$ is smooth and proper of pure
   dimension $d$, then
   $$
   Z(X_0,T)=\frac{P_1(T)P_3(T)\cdots P_{2d-1}(T)}
   {P_0(T)P_2(T)\cdots P_{2d}(T)},
   $$
   where $P_i\in\mathbf Z[T]$ has constant term $1$, and its reciprocal
   roots (the numbers $\alpha$ with $P_i(1/\alpha)=0$) are algebraic
   integers all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value $q^{i/2}$.
4. *Betti numbers.* The degree $b_i$ of $P_i$ behaves like a
   Betti number. For instance, $b_i=b_{2d-i}$, as for Poincaré duality
   on a compact manifold of real dimension $2d$. More precisely, suppose
   that $X_0$ comes from characteristic zero: there is a smooth projective
   variety $Y$ over a number field $K$ and a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $K$
   with residue field $\mathbf F_q$ such that $Y$ extends to a smooth
   projective scheme over the local ring $\mathcal O_{K,\mathfrak p}$ whose
   special fibre is $X_0$. Then $b_i$ is the $i$th Betti number of the compact
   complex manifold $Y(\mathbf C)$, for any embedding $K\subset\mathbf C$.
   For a curve of genus $g$ this gives $b_0=b_2=1$ and $b_1=2g$.

For a curve the conjectures recover the Hasse–Weil bound. Here
$Z(X_0,T)=P_1(T)/((1-T)(1-qT))$ with $P_1$ of degree $2g$, and statement
(3) says that $P_1(T)=\prod_{j=1}^{2g}(1-\alpha_jT)$ with
$|\alpha_j|=q^{1/2}$. Comparing the logarithmic derivatives of both sides
with the definition of $Z$ gives

$$
N_m=1+q^m-\sum_{j=1}^{2g}\alpha_j^m,
$$

and since each $|\alpha_j^m|=q^{m/2}$, the Hasse–Weil bound follows. This
is also why (3) is called the Riemann hypothesis. In the variable $s$ with
$T=q^{-s}$, the zeros of $P_1(q^{-s})$ satisfy $|q^{-s}|=q^{-1/2}$, that is,
they lie on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$, exactly where Riemann
conjectured the zeros of $\zeta(s)$ to lie.

We follow one example through the notes, the elliptic curve

$$
C_0\colon\ y^2=x^3-x\qquad\text{over }\mathbf F_3 .
$$

Counting points, including the point at infinity, gives $N_1=4$, $N_2=16$
and $N_3=28$. Suppose the Weil conjectures hold for $C_0$. Then
$Z(C_0,T)=P_1(T)/((1-T)(1-3T))$, where $P_1$ has degree $b_1=2g=2$. Its
leading coefficient is $q=3$, because by duality it is the determinant of
Frobenius on $H^1$ (Example [example-running-example-duality]). So
$P_1=1-aT+qT^2$, and comparing the coefficients of $T$ in $Z$ gives
$a=1+q-N_1=0$. Hence $P_1(T)=1+3T^2$, whose reciprocal roots $\pm i\sqrt3$
have absolute value $3^{1/2}$. Statements (1)–(4) alone would not fix the
leading coefficient: $1-3T^2$ also satisfies them, with the sign $-$ in (2),
and it is the count $N_2=16$ that excludes it. As a check, the formula
$N_m=1+3^m-\bigl((i\sqrt3)^m+(-i\sqrt3)^m\bigr)$ gives $16$ and $28$ for
$m=2,3$. We return to this curve after duality, after the
trace formula and at the end
(Examples [example-running-example-duality], [example-running-example-trace-formula] and [example-running-example-purity]).

Write $X=X_0\times_{\mathbf F_q}\overline{\mathbf F}_q$, and let
$F:X\to X$ be the *Frobenius*: if $X_0$ is cut out of an affine space by
equations with coefficients in $\mathbf F_q$, then $F$ raises each
coordinate to its $q$-th power. A point of $X$ is fixed by $F^m$ exactly
when its coordinates lie in $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, so
$\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ is the number of fixed points of $F^m$. Weil's
idea was to count these fixed points as in topology.

Suppose that we had a cohomology theory with compact supports, assigning to
$X$ finite-dimensional vector spaces $H^i_c(X)$ over a field of
characteristic zero on which $F$ acts. Compact supports are needed because
the trace formula below has to hold for every $X_0$, proper or not: point
counts are additive when $X_0$ is cut into an open subscheme and its
complement, and compactly supported cohomology has the matching long exact
sequence. For proper $X_0$ we write $H^i(X)=H^i_c(X)$; for the conjectures,
which concern smooth proper varieties, this is the only cohomology we need.
Suppose that the theory satisfies the following.

- (a) *Finiteness.* $H^i_c(X)=0$ unless $0\le i\le 2\dim X$.
- (b) *Trace formula.* The fixed points of $F^m$ are counted by a
  Lefschetz formula,
  $$
  \#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F^m\mid H^i_c(X)\bigr).
  $$
- (c) *Poincaré duality.* For smooth proper $X_0$ of pure dimension
  $d$, cup product gives a perfect pairing between $H^i$ and $H^{2d-i}$,
  and $\langle Fx,Fy\rangle=q^d\langle x,y\rangle$. The factor $q^d$ is
  the degree of $F$. It is the scalar by which $F$ acts on the
  one-dimensional space $H^{2d}$ when $X$ is connected.
- (d) *Purity.* For smooth proper $X_0$, the eigenvalues of $F$ on
  $H^i(X)$ are algebraic integers all of whose complex conjugates have
  absolute value $q^{i/2}$.

Then the conjectures follow. For rationality we compare logarithms. For an
endomorphism $F$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ we have

$$
\log\det(1-TF\mid V)^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge1}\operatorname{Tr}(F^m\mid V)\frac{T^m}{m},
$$

as one sees by triangulating $F$: if $F$ has eigenvalues $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_b$,
both sides equal $\sum_j\sum_m\alpha_j^mT^m/m$. Substituting the trace formula
(b) into the definition of $Z$ therefore gives

$$
\log Z(X_0,T)=\sum_{m\ge1}\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F^m\mid H^i_c(X)\bigr)\frac{T^m}{m}
=\sum_i(-1)^{i+1}\log\det\bigl(1-TF\mid H^i_c(X)\bigr),
$$

and so

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\prod_i\det\bigl(1-TF\mid H^i_c(X)\bigr)^{(-1)^{i+1}},
$$

a finite product by (a). In particular $Z(X_0,T)$ is rational, and for
smooth proper $X_0$ the polynomial $P_i(T)$ of the conjectures is
$\det(1-TF\mid H^i(X))$. By duality, the
eigenvalues in degree $2d-i$ are the numbers $q^d/\alpha$ for the
eigenvalues $\alpha$ in degree $i$, and this gives the functional equation.
Purity gives the Riemann hypothesis.

Purity also shows that the factors do not depend on the cohomology theory.
Indeed, the factors in different degrees have reciprocal roots of different
absolute values, so no cancellation can occur in the alternating product.
Each factor is therefore determined by $Z(X_0,T)$ alone, and so is its
degree $b_i$.

Which cohomology could this be? On an irreducible scheme a constant sheaf
is flasque, so its Zariski cohomology vanishes in positive degrees. It
cannot see the $2g$ independent loops of a curve of genus $g$. Coherent
cohomology sees $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$, of dimension $g$. But this is a
vector space over $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$, and traces on it determine
numbers of points only modulo $p$.

An argument of Serre (see [deninger22]) shows that the coefficient field
cannot be $\mathbf Q$, $\mathbf R$ or $\mathbf Q_p$ either. Let $C$ be a
supersingular elliptic curve over $\overline{\mathbf F}_p$. Then
$D=\operatorname{End}(C)\otimes\mathbf Q$ is a quaternion algebra over
$\mathbf Q$, and $D\otimes\mathbf R$ and $D\otimes\mathbf Q_p$ are still
division algebras [deuring41].
Endomorphisms of $C$ would act on $H^1(C)$, a vector space of dimension
$2g=2$ over the coefficient field $K$. This gives a map of
four-dimensional $K$-algebras $D\otimes K\to M_2(K)$. The map is injective
because $D\otimes K$ is simple, hence it is an isomorphism. That is impossible if
$D\otimes K$ is a division algebra. For $\ell\neq p$, on the other hand,
$D\otimes\mathbf Q_\ell\simeq M_2(\mathbf Q_\ell)$, and the argument does not exclude $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

The theory that works is étale cohomology. Its idea is to replace the
open subsets of the Zariski topology by étale maps $U\to X$, which play the
role of small open neighbourhoods in topology: like a covering space, an
étale map is a local isomorphism in the sense of the implicit function
theorem. A sheaf in this topology assigns a group to every étale map
$U\to X$, compatibly with restriction, and étale cohomology is the derived
functor of global sections. Because there are many more étale maps than
open subsets, a sheaf can now have nonzero cohomology in positive degrees.

For a curve we can already see the missing loops in degree one. Let $C$ be
a smooth projective connected curve of genus $g$ over $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$,
and let $n$ be prime to $q$. Three étale sheaves are involved: $\mathbf G_m$,
which sends $U\to C$ to the unit group $\mathcal O(U)^\times$; the same sheaf
with the $n$th power map $t\mapsto t^n$; and its kernel $\mu_n$, the sheaf of
$n$th roots of unity. The sequence

$$
0\to\mu_n\to\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{\;t\mapsto t^n\;}\mathbf G_m\to0
$$

is exact in the étale topology. Indeed, surjectivity of a map of sheaves
only has to hold locally, and an $n$th root of a unit $a$ exists on the
étale cover defined by $t^n=a$, which is étale because $n$ is invertible.
(In the Zariski topology the last map is not surjective.) As in the Zariski
topology, $H^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf G_m)$ is the Picard group of $C$ (Hilbert's
Theorem 90). The global units of $C$ are $\overline{\mathbf F}_q^\times$, in which
$n$th roots exist, so $H^0(\mathbf G_m)\xrightarrow{n}H^0(\mathbf G_m)$ is
surjective. The long exact sequence therefore identifies
$H^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mu_n)$ with the kernel of multiplication by $n$ on
$H^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf G_m)=\operatorname{Pic}(C)$.

To compute this kernel we use the degree. It gives an exact sequence
$0\to\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\to\operatorname{Pic}(C)\xrightarrow{\deg}\mathbf Z\to0$,
and since $\mathbf Z$ has no torsion, every line bundle killed by $n$ has
degree zero. So $\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)[n]$. The group
$\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$ is the group of points of the *Jacobian* $J$ of
$C$, an abelian variety of dimension $g$ (Section [sec-The-Jacobian]), and on an
abelian variety of dimension $g$ the $n$-torsion points form a group
$(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}$ when $n$ is prime to the characteristic
(Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module]). Altogether,

$$
H^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mu_n)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]=J[n]\simeq(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}
$$

(Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime]), which is the
size of $H^1$ of a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$ with coefficients
$\mathbf Z/n$. Now let $n=\ell^k$ and let $k\to\infty$. The groups $J[\ell^k]$, with the
maps $J[\ell^{k+1}]\to J[\ell^k]$ given by multiplication by $\ell$, form the
*Tate module* $T_\ell J=\varprojlim_kJ[\ell^k]$, free of rank $2g$ over
$\mathbf Z_\ell$ (Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module]). On the cohomology
side these maps correspond to $\mu_{\ell^{k+1}}\to\mu_{\ell^k}$, $z\mapsto z^\ell$,
so the identification above passes to the limit:

$$
\varprojlim_kH^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mu_{\ell^k})\simeq T_\ell J
$$

(Proposition [proposition-h-1-curve-tate-module]). In other words, the
Tate module is the first cohomology of $C$ with coefficients in the inverse
system $(\mu_{\ell^k})_k$, which is written $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$ (we come back to what
this limit means below). Weil used $T_\ell J$ in his proof for curves, in
place of an $H^1$ that was not yet available.

Frobenius acts on both sides. Let $\pi$ be the endomorphism of $J$ induced by
Frobenius; it raises the coordinates of torsion points to the $q$-th power,
and under the isomorphism above it is the action of the arithmetic
Frobenius $\sigma:z\mapsto z^q$ in $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbf F}_q/\mathbf F_q)$
on the torsion points. The map $F$ on cohomology is pullback along the
Frobenius of $C$, which is the inverse of this Galois action on
$\overline{\mathbf F}_q$-points (we compare the two Frobenius maps in
Section [sec-Frobenius-correspondences]). Hence $F$ acts on
$\varprojlim_kH^1(C_{\acute{e}t},\mu_{\ell^k})$ by $\pi^{-1}$. Weil showed [weil48-av] that the characteristic polynomial of $\pi$ on
$T_\ell J$ has integer coefficients, and that the numerator of the zeta
function is

$$
P_1(T)=\det(1-T\pi\mid T_\ell J).
$$

Because of the twist, $F$ acts on the untwisted group $H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ by
$q\pi^{-1}$ (Section [sec-Weil-complexes]). Its eigenvalues $q/\alpha$ run
through the eigenvalues $\alpha$ of $\pi$ again, by the functional equation, so
also $P_1(T)=\det(1-TF\mid H^1(C,\mathbf Q_\ell))$, as predicted in
Section [sec-The-Weil-conjectures]. For the curve $C_0$ above,
$\pi$ acts on $T_\ell J$ with characteristic polynomial $T^2+3$, and indeed
$P_1(T)=1+3T^2$.

The example suggests how to obtain a theory with coefficients of
characteristic zero: compute étale cohomology with the finite coefficients
$\mathbf Z/\ell^k$, where the theory works, take the inverse limit over $k$
to obtain $\mathbf Z_\ell$-modules, and finally invert $\ell$. The limit has to be
taken with care, as $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ already shows. On it, étale sheaves are sets with a continuous action of
the Galois group $\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, and $H^1$ with coefficients in an
abelian group $A$ is the group of continuous homomorphisms
$\widehat{\mathbf Z}\to A$. For $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^k$ this is $\mathbf Z/\ell^k$,
and the limit of these groups is $\mathbf Z_\ell$. But the étale topology sees $\mathbf Z_\ell$
only as a discrete group, and a continuous homomorphism from the compact group
$\widehat{\mathbf Z}$ to the discrete torsion-free group $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is zero, so
the constant sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ has $H^1=0$. What one wants, therefore, is the limit of the
cohomology groups, not the cohomology of the limit sheaf. After inverting
$\ell$ this gives a theory with coefficients in $\mathbf Q_\ell$. However, the eigenvalues of
Frobenius lie in an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ rather than in $\mathbf Q_\ell$
itself, and so we also allow coefficients in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, where characteristic
polynomials split.

The resulting theory is $\ell$-adic cohomology, for a prime $\ell$ not dividing $q$. It was
constructed by Grothendieck and his collaborators, who proved (a), (b) and
(c) for it in SGA 4 and SGA 5 [sga4], [sga5]. Purity (d) is the hard part,
and Deligne proved it [deligne74], [deligne80]. The general form of
his theorem, on weights of $Rf_!$, was later reproved by Laumon with the
$\ell$-adic Fourier transform [laumon87] (see also [katz88], [kiehl-weissauer01]); we call it the
Deligne–Laumon theorem. Our proof uses the Fourier transform as Laumon does,
but it is organized differently in places.

Of statement (4) we prove that $b_i=b_{2d-i}$. We also prove that
$b_i=\dim H^i(X,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ for every $\ell$ not dividing $q$; in particular this
dimension does not depend on $\ell$
(Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes]). The comparison
with the Betti numbers of a lift to characteristic zero needs the comparison
theorem between étale and singular cohomology, which we do not prove.

The proof of purity does not treat one variety at a time. It cuts a
variety into pieces and fibres it over other varieties, and point counts
behave simply under both operations. If $Z_0\subset X_0$ is closed with
complement $U_0$, then $\#X_0(\mathbf F_q)=\#U_0(\mathbf F_q)+\#Z_0(\mathbf F_q)$,
and for a morphism $f:X_0\to Y_0$,

$$
\#X_0(\mathbf F_q)=\sum_{y\in Y_0(\mathbf F_q)}\#f^{-1}(y)(\mathbf F_q).
$$

On the right we sum a function on $Y_0$ that is not constant. To follow
such sums with cohomology, we replace functions by sheaves.

The sheaves in question are *constructible*: there is a decomposition
of $X$ into finitely many locally closed pieces on each of which the sheaf
is locally constant with finite stalks. After passing to the limit, the
stalks are finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q_\ell$-vector spaces instead. A *Frobenius
structure* on a constructible sheaf $K$ on $X$ is an isomorphism
$F^*K\simeq K$, and a sheaf with a Frobenius structure is a *Weil
sheaf*. The same definitions apply to complexes of sheaves
(Section [sec-Weil-complexes]). Let $x$ be a point of $X_0$ over
$\mathbf F_{q^m}$. The corresponding point $\bar x$ of $X$ is fixed by $F^m$,
so the stalk of $(F^m)^*K$ at $\bar x$ is $K_{\bar x}$. Iterating the
Frobenius structure gives an isomorphism $(F^m)^*K\simeq K$, and on the
stalk at $\bar x$ it becomes an endomorphism $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ of
$K_{\bar x}$. Its trace defines the *trace function*

$$
t_K:X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})\longrightarrow\mathbf Q_\ell,\qquad x\longmapsto
\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid K_{\bar x}),
$$

where for a complex the trace is the alternating sum of the traces on the
cohomology groups. The constant sheaf has trace function $1$.

Operations on functions correspond to operations on sheaves. For example, pulling back
a function along $f$ corresponds to the inverse image $f^*K$, and the
product of two functions to the tensor product. Similarly, summing a function over
the fibres of $f$ corresponds to the direct image with compact supports
$Rf_!K$, whose stalk at a point $\bar y$ is the compactly supported
cohomology of $K$ on the fibre over $\bar y$. The resulting identity
$t_{Rf_!K}(y)=\sum_{f(x)=y}t_K(x)$ is a form of the trace formula
(Corollary [corollary-trace-functions-direct-image-compact]). When $f$ is the
map to a point, it is (b) with coefficients in $K$. The one further operation
we need is a Fourier transform, explained in Section [sec-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem].
This correspondence between functions and sheaves is Grothendieck's
*function–sheaf dictionary* [sga4-5, Sommes trig.]:

| functions on $X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ | Weil complexes on $X$ |
|---|---|
| $t\mapsto t\circ g$ | $g^*K$ |
| $t\cdot t'$ | $K\otimes^{\mathbf L}L$ |
| $t\mapsto\bigl(y\mapsto\sum_{f(x)=y}t(x)\bigr)$ | $Rf_!K$ |
| $t=t|_{U}+t|_{Z}$ | $j_!j^*K\to K\to i_*i^*K\to$ |
| $\sum_xt(x)$ | $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ with its Frobenius |
| $t\mapsto\bigl(y\mapsto-\sum_xt(x)\psi(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^m}/\mathbf F_q}(xy))\bigr)$ | $Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)[1]$ |

Proposition [proposition-function-sheaf-dictionary] states and proves the
first five lines. The last line is built from the first three, as we explain
in Section [sec-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem]. Since $Rf_!$ of a sheaf is a
complex, we work in derived categories throughout.

Duality has no simple counterpart for functions, and it needs two more
operations: the internal Hom of sheaves and the *exceptional inverse
image* $f^!$, a right adjoint of $Rf_!$. With $f^*$, $Rf_*$, $Rf_!$ and
$\otimes$ these are Grothendieck's *six operations*. Part I
of these notes, roughly their first third, constructs them for all the
coefficient rings we need. To see why $f^!$ is the right tool, consider Poincaré
duality for a smooth variety $X$ of pure dimension $d$ over an
algebraically closed field $k$, with coefficients
$\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n$. It should say that cup product

$$
H_c^i(X,\Lambda)\times H^{2d-i}(X,\Lambda(d))\longrightarrow
H^{2d}_c(X,\Lambda(d))\longrightarrow\Lambda
$$

is a perfect pairing. Here $\Lambda(d)=\mu_{\ell^n}^{\otimes d}$ is the
*Tate twist* (Definition [definition-tate-twists]). The twist is
needed because Frobenius does not act trivially on top cohomology. For
instance, the map $F:\mathbf P^1\to\mathbf P^1$ has degree $q$. It pulls the
class of a point back to $q$ times itself, so $F$ acts on
$H^2(\mathbf P^1,\Lambda)$ by $q$. With our conventions $F$ acts on
$\Lambda(1)$ by $q^{-1}$ (Section [sec-Coefficient-rings]), and therefore
it acts trivially on $H^2(\mathbf P^1,\Lambda(1))$. In general the twist
$(d)$ removes the factor $q^d$ from the pairing.

For an oriented manifold $V$ of dimension $r$ there is a clean proof, due to
Verdier. Let $a:V\to\mathrm{pt}$ be the map to a point. The functor $Ra_!$,
cohomology with compact supports, has a right adjoint $a^!$, and the
adjunction gives, for every sheaf $G$ on $V$,

$$
R\!\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(R\Gamma_c(V,G),\Lambda\bigr)\simeq R\!\operatorname{Hom}(G,a^!\Lambda).
$$

This isomorphism comes from the adjunction alone and holds for every $V$;
what makes it a duality theorem is a computation of $a^!\Lambda$.
It is a complex of sheaves on $V$, and its restriction to an open subset
$U$ is the corresponding complex for $U$. So it can be computed in a chart
$\mathbf R^r$. There its only cohomology sheaf sits in degree $-r$, with
stalks $\Hom(H^r_c(\mathbf R^r,\Lambda),\Lambda)\simeq\Lambda$. An orientation
identifies these stalks consistently, and this gives
$a^!\Lambda\simeq\Lambda[r]$. For $G=\Lambda$ the displayed isomorphism then
reads $R\!\operatorname{Hom}(R\Gamma_c(V,\Lambda),\Lambda)\simeq R\!\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda,\Lambda[r])=R\Gamma(V,\Lambda)[r]$.
Taking cohomology in degree $-i$ and using that $\Lambda$ is a field or, for
$\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, a self-injective ring, this says
$\Hom(H^i_c(V,\Lambda),\Lambda)\simeq H^{r-i}(V,\Lambda)$, which is
Poincaré duality for $V$.

We follow the same route. For the structure morphism $a$ of a smooth
variety $X$ of dimension $d$ we show $a^!\Lambda\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$,
again by a local computation (*smooth purity*). Poincaré duality
follows.

The main theorem of Part I is that $f^!$
exists and carries constructible complexes to constructible complexes
(Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image]). Existence is a general
fact. Indeed, to give a right adjoint of $Rf_!$ is to find, for each $N$, an object
$f^!N$ with $\Hom(M,f^!N)=\Hom(Rf_!M,N)$, naturally in $M$, and Brown's
representability theorem provides such objects for an exact functor between
triangulated categories that commutes with arbitrary direct sums. It needs
one hypothesis on the source: it must be *compactly generated*, that is,
built by shifts, cones and direct sums from a set of objects $M$ for which
$\Hom(M,-)$ commutes with direct sums. Such objects are called compact; in the
derived category of a ring, for example, the perfect complexes are the
compact objects. Constructible complexes are such objects, but they are not closed
under direct sums. We therefore apply the theorem to the larger category
built from them in this way.

It remains to show that $f^!$ carries constructible complexes to
constructible complexes, and this is geometric. Locally $f$ is a closed
immersion followed by a projection from affine space, and affine space is
open in a product of projective lines, so two cases remain. For the projection
$\mathbf P^1_Y\to Y$, we compute $f^!$ explicitly, whereas for a closed immersion
$i$ with open complement $j$, a distinguished triangle computes $i^!K$ from
$K$ and $Rj_*j^*K$. This case therefore comes down to the theorem of
Deligne that the ordinary direct image $Rj_*$ preserves constructible
complexes.

The six operations must also be available for $\mathbf Z_\ell$- and $\mathbf Q_\ell$-coefficients,
compatibly with reduction modulo $\ell^n$. This is a problem, because inverse limits behave badly on the étale
site: on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, as we saw in
Section [sec-Weil-cohomology], the constant sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ has $H^1=0$,
although the limit of the groups $H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z/\ell^k)$
is $\mathbf Z_\ell$. For this reason the classical theory works with compatible systems of
sheaves modulo $\ell^n$ and builds the derived categories by
hand [ekedahl90]. We use instead the pro-étale site of Bhatt and Scholze [bhatt-scholze15]. Its
objects over $X$ include, besides the étale maps $U\to X$, inverse limits
$\varprojlim_iU_i\to X$ of affine étale maps, for example the spectrum of an
algebraic closure of $\mathbf F_q$ over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, and
its coverings are the families that are jointly surjective in a strong sense.
Every étale sheaf defines a sheaf on it, and every bounded below complex of étale
sheaves has the same cohomology on the two sites (Chapter [chap-The-pro-etale-site]).
The gain is that $\mathbf Z_\ell$, with its topology, becomes a sheaf whose cohomology
is the limit: on the pro-étale site
$H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z_\ell)=\mathbf Z_\ell$
(Example [example-first-cohomology-finite-field]). On it, $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is
a sheaf of rings whose sections are continuous functions to $\mathbf Z_\ell$, so that an
$\ell$-adic sheaf is simply a sheaf of modules over it, and we use the usual
derived category of these modules, with no inverse systems. In this setting all the
geometric arguments are made with coefficients $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, where the
classical theory applies, and the pro-étale site then carries them over to
$\mathbf Z_\ell$, $\mathbf Q_\ell$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

Part II proves Poincaré duality and the trace formula.
Why should the Lefschetz formula hold for Frobenius? For a self-map $\varphi$ of a compact manifold $V$ whose fixed points
are transverse, the Lefschetz fixed point formula reads

$$
\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\varphi^*\mid H^i(V,\mathbf Q)\bigr)
=\sum_{\varphi(x)=x}\operatorname{sign}\det\bigl(1-d\varphi_x\bigr),
$$

so each fixed point $x$ is counted with the sign of $\det(1-d\varphi_x)$.
In our case the differential of Frobenius is zero, because $d(u^q)=qu^{q-1}du=0$ in
characteristic $p$. So every fixed point should count with $+1$. On a curve
one can see this directly. Let $u$ be a local coordinate at a fixed point,
and $v$ the same coordinate on the second factor of $X\times X$. In these coordinates the graph
of $F^m$ is $v=u^{q^m}$, and it meets the diagonal $v=u$ with multiplicity one.

The Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula states that for every Weil
complex $K$,

$$
\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F^m\mid R\Gamma_c(X,K)\bigr)
=\sum_{y\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})}t_K(y)
$$

(Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula]). For the constant
sheaf it is axiom (b). In
Example [example-running-example-trace-formula] we apply it to the
elliptic curve $C_0\colon y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ of
Section [sec-The-Weil-conjectures], where it reads $N_m=1-\operatorname{Tr}(F^m\mid H^1)+3^m$. Since
$N_1=4$, the trace of $F$ on $H^1$ is $0$. Duality gives
$\det(F\mid H^1)=3$, and we recover $Z(C_0,T)=(1+3T^2)/((1-T)(1-3T))$.

We deduce the trace formula, as in SGA 5 [sga5, III, III B, XV], from a general
Lefschetz formula. A *correspondence* on $X$ is a pair of maps
$c_1,c_2:C\to X$. For instance, the graph of a map $\varphi$ is a
correspondence with $c_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $c_2=\varphi$. To act on the
cohomology of $K$, a correspondence needs a map $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$, and for
the graph of $F$ this is the Frobenius structure $F^*K\to K$. For such data the
Lefschetz–Verdier formula
(Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]) holds when $X$ and
$C$ are proper. It writes the trace on cohomology as a sum, over the fixed
points, of *local terms*, numbers computed from $K$ and $u$ near each
fixed point. In general, however, a local term is not the trace on the stalk.

To apply this to Frobenius on a curve $X$, which need not be proper, we
compactify $X$ by adding finitely many points and extend $K$ by zero. The
added points are again fixed by Frobenius, but there $K$ is no longer locally
constant: its stalk is zero, while nearby stalks need not be. The main computation of Part II
shows that even so, at every fixed point $y$ of Frobenius on a curve, the
local term is the trace of $\operatorname{Frob}_y$ on $K_{\bar y}$
(Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve]). To prove this,
we cut $K$ into its restrictions to $y$ and to the complement of $y$. Local terms are additive
for this decomposition, and for the piece supported at $y$ the local term is
the trace. It therefore suffices to show that the local term vanishes when
$K_{\bar y}=0$.

Here $dF=0$ is used once more. Because of it, at $(y,y)$ the graph $v=u^{q^m}$ is tangent
to the axis $v=0$, that is, to $X\times\{y\}$, while the diagonal $v=u$ is
not. Blowing up the point $(y,y)$ of $X\times X$ therefore separates the two
curves. After the blow-up the local term is a map between cohomology groups
supported near two disjoint curves meeting the exceptional divisor, and such
a map factors through the stalk of $K$ at $y$; so it vanishes when
$K_{\bar y}=0$ (Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk]). (In Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula] we
use instead the transposed graph $\{(F^mx,x)\}$, which is tangent to
$\{y\}\times X$.)

Curves suffice for the general case. Indeed, the trace formula is
compatible with $Rf_!$, and a variety can be fibred in curves over a
variety of smaller dimension.

Part III proves purity. Fix an embedding
$\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to\mathbf C$, and write $q_x$ for the number of elements of the
residue field of a closed point $x$ of $X_0$. A Weil sheaf with coefficients
in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is *pure of weight $w$* if every eigenvalue $\alpha$ of
Frobenius on every stalk satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|=q_x^{w/2}$, and *mixed*
if it has a finite filtration whose quotients are pure. Similarly, a complex has
*weights at most $w$* if each cohomology sheaf $\mathcal H^i$ is mixed with
weights at most $w+i$ (Definition [definition-weights]). The shift by $i$ is chosen so that both the constant sheaf, pure of weight
$0$, and its cohomology complex $R\Gamma(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$, whose $H^i$ should have
weight $i$, have weights at most $0$.

The *Deligne–Laumon theorem* (Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek]),
proved by Deligne in Weil II [deligne80] and reproved by Laumon with
the Fourier transform [laumon87], says that
if $K$ has weights at most $w$, so does $Rf_!K$ for every morphism $f$ of
separated $\mathbf F_q$-schemes of finite type. It gives only an upper
bound. For the constant sheaf on a smooth proper $X_0$, duality supplies
the lower one. With $f$ the map to a point, the theorem says that the eigenvalues
on $H^i$ satisfy $|\iota(\alpha)|\le q^{i/2}$. Since Poincaré duality pairs
$\alpha$ on $H^i$ with $q^d/\alpha$ on $H^{2d-i}$, the same bound in degree
$2d-i$ gives $|\iota(\alpha)|\ge q^{i/2}$. The two bounds together are purity.
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes] deduces the
Weil conjectures from it.

The proof has four steps, each of which has a model in classical
mathematics.

**Step 1: from varieties to curves.** The theorem is stated for all
sheaves, not only the constant one, because the proof is an induction on
dimension. Away from a closed subset, a variety is fibred in curves over a
variety of smaller dimension, much as one computes the cohomology of a fibre
bundle by the Leray spectral sequence from the cohomology of the fibres and
of the base. Along such a fibration, however, the direct image of the
constant sheaf is no longer constant, so the induction needs the theorem for
all sheaves. It thereby reduces to curves, provided the direct images that
occur along the way are mixed
(Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed]). On a curve the
statement says: if $\mathcal F$ is a lisse sheaf, pure of weight $w$, on a
smooth curve $U_0$, then $H^1_c(U,\mathcal F)$ has weights at most $w+1$
(Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve]). Since every curve, after removing
finitely many points, maps to the affine line by a finite map, it is enough
to treat open subsets of $\mathbf A^1$. The proof on curves combines two ideas: Rankin's positivity argument,
which Deligne used in Weil I and Weil II [deligne74], [deligne80],
and the Fourier transform, which Laumon [laumon87] used in place of
Deligne's monodromy arguments.

**Step 2: positivity bounds the eigenvalues at points.** The model is Rankin's method for the coefficients of modular
forms [rankin39]: the Dirichlet series $\sum|\tau(n)|^2n^{-s}$ has
nonnegative coefficients, so the position of its first pole bounds each
individual coefficient. Here the role of the Dirichlet series is played by an
$L$-function. Let $\mathcal G$ be a *lisse* sheaf on an affine curve
$U_0$, that is, a locally constant one. Such a sheaf is the same as a
representation of the fundamental group, and its *monodromy* is the
image of that representation. Call $\mathcal G$ *real* if the
characteristic polynomials of Frobenius on its stalks have real
coefficients (Definition [definition-real-sheaves]). Its $L$-function is
the product, over closed points $x$, of the *Euler factors*
$\det(1-\operatorname{Frob}_x T^{\deg x}\mid\mathcal G_{\bar x})^{-1}$. On an
affine curve $H^0_c=0$ and $H^i_c=0$ for $i>2$, so the trace formula shows
that the $L$-function equals $\det(1-TF\mid H^1_c)/\det(1-TF\mid H^2_c)$. Two
facts make this useful.

- Consider an even tensor power $\mathcal G^{\otimes 2m}$. The logarithm of
  an Euler factor has coefficients
  $\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x^n\mid\mathcal G_{\bar x})^{2m}/n$, and
  these are nonnegative because the traces are real. Each Euler factor
  therefore has nonnegative coefficients bounded by those of the whole
  product. In particular it converges wherever the product does
  (Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence]).
- The product has poles only where $\det(1-TF\mid H^2_c)$ vanishes, and
  $H^2_c$ is easy to compute: it is the largest quotient of a stalk on which
  the monodromy acts trivially, twisted by $(-1)$.

The second fact bounds the eigenvalues on $H^2_c$ of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$,
and the first turns this into a bound at every point. To state the result,
let $\beta$ be the largest *determinant weight* of the irreducible
constituents of $\mathcal G$; the determinant weight of a constituent of
rank $r$ is the weight of its determinant divided by $r$
(Definition [definition-determinant-weight]). The eigenvalues on $H^2_c$ of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ have absolute value at
most $q^{m\beta+1}$. Indeed, by the second fact $H^2_c$ is a quotient of a
stalk of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ on which the geometric monodromy acts
trivially, twisted by $(-1)$. On such a quotient Frobenius acts through
one-dimensional pieces, each a constituent of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$, and the
determinant weight of every constituent of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ is at most
$2m\beta$ (Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations]).
So these eigenvalues have absolute value at most $q^{m\beta}$, and the twist
$(-1)$ multiplies them by $q$. The product therefore
converges for $|T|<q^{-m\beta-1}$, and by the first fact the Euler factor at
$x$ converges there too. This factor has a pole where
$T^{\deg x}=\alpha^{-2m}$, for each eigenvalue $\alpha$ of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on $\mathcal G_{\bar x}$. Hence
$|\iota(\alpha)|^{2m}\le q_x^{m\beta+1}$ for every $m$, and taking $2m$-th roots
and letting $m\to\infty$ gives the intermediate result:

> *every Frobenius eigenvalue $\alpha$ at a point of a real lisse sheaf
> satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_x^\beta$*

(Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight]).

**Step 3: rank one, and purity of real sheaves.** The bound of Step 2
is only useful if the determinants have weights, that is, if lisse sheaves of
rank one are pure. A rank-one sheaf is a character of the fundamental group,
the analogue of a Hecke character, and it is pure as soon as its restriction
to the geometric fundamental group has finite image. We show that this image
is finite. If it were not, the logarithm of a power of the character would
give a nonzero class in $H^1$ of the curve fixed by Frobenius. This class
cannot come from the removed points, since Frobenius acts on those classes
by powers of $q$. So it comes from the compactification, and it gives a
nonzero vector in the Tate module of its Jacobian fixed by Frobenius. Such a
vector is a compatible system of rational $\ell$-power torsion points of
unbounded order, which is impossible because the Jacobian has only finitely
many rational points (Section [sec-Sheaves-of-rank-one]). With the determinants under control, Step 2 bounds the eigenvalues of
$\mathcal G$ by its largest determinant weight. To bound those of a single
constituent we apply Step 2 to exterior powers of $\mathcal G$, in which that
constituent is multiplied by the determinants of the others, which are now
known; this isolates its weight (as in the example
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\oplus\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ of Chapter [chap-Purity-of-real-sheaves]). Applied also to
the dual, which gives the lower bound, it yields the second intermediate
result:

> *each irreducible constituent of a real lisse sheaf on a curve is pure*

(Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves]).

**Step 4: the Fourier transform turns cohomology into a stalk.** Steps 2 and 3 bound eigenvalues at the points of a curve, but we must bound
eigenvalues on its cohomology. The Fourier transform turns one into the
other. Its model is the discrete Fourier transform
$\hat t(y)=\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_q}t(x)\psi(xy)$ of a function $t$ on
$\mathbf F_q$, where $\psi$ is a nontrivial additive character. Two
properties matter. The value $\hat t(0)$ is the sum of all values of $t$, so
a sum over the line becomes a single value. And Plancherel's formula
$\sum_y|\hat t(y)|^2=q\sum_x|t(x)|^2$ holds.

The classical example is the Gauss sum. Let $\chi$ be a nontrivial
multiplicative character, extended by $\chi(0)=0$, and let
$g=\sum_x\chi(x)\psi(x)$ be its Gauss sum. Substituting $x\mapsto x/y$ shows
that $\hat\chi(y)=\overline\chi(y)g$ for $y\neq0$, so the transform has the
same absolute value $|g|$ at all $q-1$ nonzero points, and $\hat\chi(0)=0$.
Plancherel now reads $(q-1)|g|^2=q(q-1)$, and we find $|g|=\sqrt q$. In other
words, a function of absolute value $1$ is carried to one of absolute value
$\sqrt q$, that is, weight $0$ to weight $1$. This is the shape of the whole
argument: first the transform is shown to have a single absolute value (to be
pure), and then Plancherel finds which one.

Grothendieck's dictionary turns the transform into an operation on sheaves
on the affine line. Read the formula for $\hat t$ from the inside out: pull
$t$ back to the plane along $p_1(x,y)=x$, multiply by the function
$\psi(xy)$, and sum over the fibres of $p_2(x,y)=y$. Each step is a line of
the table in Section [sec-The-function-sheaf-dictionary]. So if $\mathcal K_\psi$ is a
sheaf on the plane with trace function $\psi(xy)$ and we put

$$
\operatorname{FT}_\psi K=Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)[1],
$$

then for $y\in\mathbf F_q$ the table gives

$$
t_{\operatorname{FT}_\psi K}(y)
=-\,t_{Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)}(y)
=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_q}t_{p_1^*K}(x,y)\,t_{\mathcal K_\psi}(x,y)
=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_q}t_K(x)\,\psi(xy)
=-\,\hat t_K(y).
$$

The sign comes from the shift $[1]$, which changes the sign of every trace.

Now let $M$ be an irreducible lisse sheaf, pure of weight $w$, on a dense
open $j:U_0\to\mathbf A^1$, and let $j_*M$ be its direct image to
$\mathbf A^1$. Its compactly supported cohomology lives in degrees $1$ and
$2$; as in Step 2, $H^2_c$ is easy, and the group we must bound is
$H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$. Just as $\hat t(0)$ is the sum of $t$, the stalk
at $0$ of the Fourier transform of $j_*M$ is the compactly supported
cohomology of $j_*M$. The sheaves $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ with trace function
$x\mapsto\psi(ax)$ are exceptions, as the characters $\psi(ax)$ are for the
discrete transform: their transform is concentrated at one point. Suppose
that no constituent of $M$ over $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ is of this form. Then
the transform is again of the form $j'_*M'$ for a lisse sheaf $M'$ on a dense
open of the dual line
(Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension]). The
hypothesis excludes in particular constant constituents (the case $a=0$), so
the monodromy of $M$ has no coinvariants and $H^2_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)=0$. This
gives the third intermediate result:

> *the stalk of $j'_*M'$ at $0$ is exactly $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$.*

It remains to find the weight of $M'$, and here the two halves of the Gauss
sum argument return. To show that $M'$ is pure we use Step 3: we twist $M$ to
weight $0$ and add its dual, whose eigenvalues are the complex conjugates.
The transform of the result is again a real sheaf, and it maps onto a
twist of $M'$, which is irreducible. So a twist of $M'$ is an irreducible
constituent of a real sheaf, hence pure by Step 3, and therefore $M'$ is
pure
(Proposition [proposition-purity-lisse-part-fourier-transform]). The
weight of $M'$ is then found from the sheaf version of Plancherel's
formula, which compares the sums of $|t_M(x)|^2$ and $|t_{M'}(y)|^2$ over
$\mathbf F_{q^m}$ as $m$ grows: it is $w+1$
(Theorem [theorem-weight-fourier-transform]). By
Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points], the stalk of $j'_*M'$
at $0$ has weights at most $w+1$, and this is the bound we want. For
genus-one curves over $\mathbf F_3$, the resulting purity gives
$1\le N_1\le7$ (Example [example-running-example-purity]).

The main theorem is the Weil conjectures for smooth proper varieties over
$\mathbf F_q$ (Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes]),
with the statement on Betti numbers as above. The proof follows Weil's plan:
it constructs a cohomology theory satisfying the properties (a)–(d) of a
Weil cohomology listed in Section [sec-Weil-cohomology]. Each part uses the
one before it.

- Part I (Chapters [chap-The-pro-etale-site]–[chap-Smooth-base-change])
  constructs the six operations for $\ell$-adic coefficients
  (Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image]). It ends with smooth base
  change and the Künneth formula.
- Part II (Chapters [chap-Smooth-purity]–[chap-The-trace-formula])
  proves smooth purity
  (Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients]), Verdier and
  Poincaré duality (Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality]), which is (c),
  and the trace formula, which is (b). It ends with rationality and the
  functional equation. As for (a), the groups $H^i_c$ are finite because
  $Rf_!$ preserves constructibility. They vanish outside $[0,2\dim X]$, and
  Theorem [theorem-trace-isomorphism-top-degree] treats the smooth proper
  case used for the Weil conjectures.
- Part III (Chapters [chap-Weights]–[chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures])
  defines weights, proves purity of real sheaves on curves, introduces the
  Fourier transform and proves the Deligne–Laumon theorem, first on curves and then
  in general. It ends with the Weil conjectures.

Most appendices prove results from algebraic geometry that the main text
uses: Nagata compactification and Chow's lemma, abelian varieties, the
Picard scheme of a curve, the cohomology of curves with torsion
coefficients, and facts on algebraic groups. Appendix [chap-Specialization-and-contracting-correspondences]
is of a different kind. It is not a preliminary but a second, independent
theory of local terms, by specialization to the normal cone, which computes
the local terms of contracting correspondences; the main line of the proof
does not use it.

We assume a first course in algebraic geometry: schemes, quasi-coherent
sheaves and their cohomology, curves and divisors, and étale morphisms;
some homological algebra (derived functors, derived and triangulated
categories); and singular cohomology with Poincaré duality and the
Lefschetz fixed point formula, which serve as models. We do not assume
étale cohomology. The results from the étale theory with torsion
coefficients that we need [sga4], [sga4-5] are stated where they are used,
with references.

On a first reading one can take the foundations on trust and follow the
main line:

- the statements of Chapter [chap-Constructible-complexes] and of the main
  theorem of Part I, Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image];
- the base change map and the statement of proper base change
  (Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro]);
- Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f] on why $f^!$ preserves
  constructibility with torsion coefficients;
- smooth purity with finite coefficients (Section [sec-The-tensor-product-map]),
  which is where the twist $(d)$, the shift $[2d]$ and the trace map
  come from;
- Chapter [chap-Verdier-and-Poincare-duality] on duality;
- Frobenius and Weil complexes (Section [sec-Weil-complexes]); in
  Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula], the local
  calculation at a fixed point of Frobenius on a curve;
- Chapters [chap-Weights]–[chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures], beginning with
  the plan in the opening of Part III.

The passages between coefficient rings (most of which are applications of
Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients]), the coherence of the various
comparison maps, smooth base change (Chapter [chap-Smooth-base-change]),
and the pro-étale foundations of Chapter [chap-The-pro-etale-site]
can be read when needed.

We fix a prime $\ell$ and a field $k$ that is finite or algebraically
closed, of characteristic different from $\ell$. Unless said otherwise,
schemes are separated and of finite type over $k$, and morphisms are
$k$-morphisms. The hypothesis on $k$ is needed to bound the
$\ell$-cohomological dimension of $k$
(Lemma [lemma-cohomological-dimension-base-field]), while the constructions of
Sections [sec-Coefficient-rings] and [sec-Derived-functors] make sense for arbitrary
schemes. Finally, a citation such as [Stacks, [0F0C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0C)] refers to the tag of a result in the
Stacks Project [stacks].

On the pro-étale site we regard every coefficient ring $\Lambda$ as a
condensed ring, that is, as a sheaf of rings on profinite sets, which
remembers the topology of $\Lambda$. (On the étale site, which we use only
with finite coefficients, a finite ring is simply a ring.) The coefficient sheaf $\Lambda_X$ on $X$ is then the pullback
of $\Lambda$ along the map from $X$ to a point
(Section [sec-Coefficient-rings]). For a finite ring $A$ this pullback
is the classical constant sheaf.

Derived categories are the classical ones. Namely, $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is
the derived category of the abelian category of sheaves of
$\Lambda_X$-modules. On these categories all functors are derived, and we write them $f^*$,
$Rf_*$, $Rf_!$ and $f^!$. Unless another category is named, we have
$f^*:D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and
$Rf_*:D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, whereas the
categories on which $Rf_!$ and $f^!$ act are fixed where these functors
are defined. To avoid set-theoretic problems, we take sizes with respect to a fixed universe that is large
enough to contain the w-contractible covers of
Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers].

On the étale site the constant sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ forgets that $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is
profinite. The pro-étale site $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ of Bhatt and Scholze [bhatt-scholze15]
repairs this. Its objects are the weakly étale $X$-schemes, and its
coverings are fpqc coverings
(Definition [definition-small-pro-etale-site]).

We need three properties of this site.

- (a) *Limits.* For a tower $\cdots\to F_2\to F_1$ of surjections of
  sheaves, cohomology commutes with the limit:
  $R\Gamma(X,\varprojlim_nF_n)\simeq R\varprojlim_nR\Gamma(X,F_n)$.
- (b) *Topology.* The sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ remembers the topology of $\mathbf Z_\ell$.
- (c) *Comparison.* Sheaves coming from the étale site keep their
  étale cohomology, so that the results of SGA 4 still apply to them.

Property (b) can be seen on a point. Over a separably closed field the topos
of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is, up to a set-theoretic cutoff, that of condensed sets
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed], proved in
Subsection [subsec-Condensed-rings] below), and there the sections of $\mathbf Z_\ell$ over a
profinite set $S$ are all continuous maps $S\to\mathbf Z_\ell$, not only the locally
constant ones.

|  | on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ | on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ |
|---|---|---|
| objects | étale $X$-schemes | weakly étale $X$-schemes |
| local objects | strictly henselian local rings | w-contractible rings |
| topos of a geometric point | sets | condensed sets |
| the sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ on a point | $\mathbf Z_\ell$ with discrete topology | continuous maps to $\mathbf Z_\ell$ |

Property (a) fails on $X_{\acute{e}t}$, for the following reason. A surjection of
sheaves is surjective on sections only after refining the cover. A countable
product of surjections needs one refinement for each factor, and these
infinitely many refinements need not have a common refinement among étale
covers. So a countable product of surjections need not be surjective,
$R^1\varprojlim_nF_n$ need not vanish, and $\varprojlim_nF_n$ differs from
$R\varprojlim_nF_n$. For $F_n=\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$
this is the lost $H^1$. On $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ there are enough objects
on which no refinement is needed: the spectra of w-contractible rings, roughly
families of strictly henselian local rings parametrized by an extremally
disconnected profinite set. Every cover of such a spectrum splits, so every
surjection of sheaves is surjective on its sections there, and limits of
sheaves can be computed there as limits of sets and modules. However, building these
objects takes two theorems from outside algebraic geometry: Gleason's theorem
on extremally disconnected spaces and Olivier's theorem on weakly étale
maps. Once we have them, property (a) follows in a few lines
(Proposition [proposition-continuous-cohomology-pro-etale-cohomology]).
In particular, over $\mathbf F_q$ it gives back $H^1=\mathbf Z_\ell$
(Example [example-first-cohomology-finite-field]).

For property (c) we compare the two sites through the pullback functor
$\nu_X^*$ from sheaves on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ to sheaves on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. Its image
consists of the sheaves that we call *classical*: a sheaf on
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is classical if its sections over a limit
$U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ of affine étale $X$-schemes are the colimit of its
sections over the $U_i$ (Definition [definition-classical-pro-etale-sheaves]).
In other words, a classical sheaf is determined by its values on étale
$X$-schemes, as an étale sheaf is. The comparison has four parts.

- $\nu_X^*$ is an equivalence from étale sheaves onto classical sheaves
  (Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image]).
- It preserves the cohomology of bounded below complexes
  (Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison]).
- It commutes with direct images along quasi-compact quasi-separated
  morphisms (Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images]).
- For a finite coefficient ring, a constructible sheaf on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$
  is classical, and $\nu_X^*$ is an equivalence from
  $D^b_c(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ onto $\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$
  (Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]). So with finite
  coefficients the two sites have the same constructible complexes.

Later, $f^!$ is built by Brown representability on the unbounded derived
category, so we also need the comparison for unbounded complexes. With finite
coefficients it holds as well, because affine schemes étale over a scheme
of finite type over $k$ have uniformly bounded cohomological dimension. Each
cohomology group of an unbounded complex therefore depends only on a bounded
below truncation, where the comparison is already known
(Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients]). The
sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$, however, is not classical
(Example [example-coefficient-sheaf-outside-classical-part]). This is
what the computation of $H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z_\ell)$ in
Section [sec-Weil-cohomology] needs: $H^1$ comes out as $\mathbf Z_\ell$ only when
sections see the topology of $\mathbf Z_\ell$. So the comparison applies to the
$\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ but not to $\mathbf Z_\ell$ itself, and we reach $\mathbf Z_\ell$ from them by derived completion
(Section [sec-Extension-by-zero-and-completion]).

Throughout this chapter, schemes are arbitrary unless a result states a
finiteness hypothesis, because objects of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ are in general neither
Noetherian nor of finite type, even when $X$ is a variety. The standing
assumption that schemes are of finite type over $k$ resumes in
Chapter [chap-Constructible-complexes].

The objects we want are inverse limits of étale $X$-schemes.
Being such a limit is a condition on a presentation, which is awkward to
work with, so we take as objects the weakly étale $X$-schemes of the
following definition. This class is defined by flatness conditions. For this
reason it is stable under base change and composition, and membership in it
is local for the Zariski topology (Lemma [lemma-stability]). We lose
little by the change: after a faithfully flat refinement every weakly
étale scheme becomes a limit of étale schemes
(Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale]).

Typical examples are the schemes that the étale site can only reach
through colimits. The strict henselization
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X,\bar x}$ is the limit of
the affine étale neighbourhoods of $\bar x$, and on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ it
appears only through the stalk at $\bar x$. On $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ it is an
object. Similarly
$\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbf F}_q=\varprojlim_m\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^m}$
is an object over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, and for a profinite
set $S=\varprojlim S_i$ the scheme $X\times S=\varprojlim_i\coprod_{S_i}X$
is an object over $X$. Through the last family the site sees
profinite sets, and hence the topology of $\mathbf Z_\ell$.
The three classes of ring maps are related as follows.

For instance, $\mathbf F_q\to\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ is ind-étale, as
the colimit of the finite fields $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, but it is not
étale, because $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ is not of finite type over
$\mathbf F_q$.

In (2) the flatness of the diagonal takes the place of unramifiedness;
flatness of $R\to B$ alone would not suffice. The converse of the second
implication in (1) fails in general: a weakly étale map need not be a
filtered colimit of étale maps. It does become ind-étale after a
faithfully flat refinement
(Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale] below, and
[Stacks, [097Z](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/097Z)]). Geometrically, a weakly étale scheme over $X$ is covered,
in the pro-étale topology, by a limit of étale $X$-schemes.

The finite refinement condition is part of the topology, and a jointly
surjective family that does not satisfy it is not a covering. We record
two consequences of the definition.

By (2) the pro-étale topology is finer than the étale topology. By (1),
over an affine object a covering may always be replaced by a single
faithfully flat map. For example, the single map
$\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbf F}_q\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$
is a pro-étale covering, although it is not an étale one. These
coverings define a topos with the expected functoriality in $X$.

To compute limits of sheaves by taking sections, we want objects over
which every cover splits, so that sheafification changes nothing there.
On the étale site the spectrum of a strictly henselian local ring,
such as the étale local ring of a variety at a geometric point, has
this property, but such spectra do not cover $X$. Instead, the rings we need are
families of strictly henselian local rings over a profinite set of
components. Moreover, we require this set to be extremally disconnected, which means
that the closure of every open subset is open, because under this condition a cover
splits. Namely, over each component of $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ we choose a
component of the cover lying above it, and extremal disconnectedness lets us
make this choice continuously. The model case is the ring of locally
constant functions from a profinite set to a separably closed field
(Example [example-locally-constant-functions-w-local]), which is a family
of copies of one field indexed by the profinite set. Below we define these
rings, the w-contractible rings, by a hierarchy of local conditions, and we show that every
ring has a faithfully flat ind-étale cover by one of them
(Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers]).

Recall that spectral spaces are quasi-compact and sober, with a basis
of quasi-compact opens closed under finite intersections, and that the space of
connected components of a spectral space is profinite.

Closedness of
$T^c$ does not follow from uniqueness of closed specializations, which is
why the definition requires it separately. The basic properties of these
notions are as follows.

So a w-strictly local ring is a family of strictly henselian local rings
indexed by the profinite set of its components, and a w-contractible ring
is such a family indexed by an extremally disconnected profinite set.

The constructions below change the set of components while keeping the
local rings, and for this we use the following class of maps. A ring map
$R\to A$ is a *local isomorphism* if $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ is
covered by principal opens $D(g)$, each mapping isomorphically onto an
open subscheme of $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ [Stacks, [096E](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/096E)], and it is
*ind-Zariski* if it is a filtered colimit of local isomorphisms
[Stacks, [096M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/096M)]. For instance,
$R\to R\times R$ is a local isomorphism. Taking the colimit over the finite
quotients $S_i$ of a profinite set $S$, we see that
$R\to\varinjlim_iR^{S_i}=LC(S,R)$ is ind-Zariski. Its spectrum is
$\operatorname{Spec}(R)\times S$. A localization $R\to R_{\mathfrak p}$ at a
prime is ind-Zariski as well, as the colimit of the $R_f$ with
$f\notin\mathfrak p$. The property we use is that an ind-Zariski map does
not change local rings: each local ring of $A$ is a local ring of $R$.

We use extremally disconnected spaces through their projectivity. In
Proposition [proposition-splitting-ind-etale-covers] we use it to split a surjection of component
spaces, and in Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers] we cover a profinite component
space by an extremally disconnected one
(Lemma [lemma-extremally-disconnected-covers]).

To use the proposition we need enough extremally disconnected spaces.
They come from Stone–Čech compactifications of discrete sets.

A finite discrete space is extremally disconnected, while the Cantor set
$\{0,1\}^{\mathbf N}$ is not. To see this, let $V_n$ be the clopen set of
sequences beginning with $0^n1$, and let $U$ be the union of the $V_n$
for odd $n$. The closure of $U$ is $U\cup\{000\cdots\}$, and it is not
open, because every neighbourhood of $000\cdots$ contains some $V_n$ with
$n$ even, which is disjoint from the closure. More generally, infinite extremally
disconnected compact spaces have no nontrivial convergent sequences, and
therefore they are never metrizable. In practice they arise as
Stone–Čech compactifications.

Over a w-contractible ring an ind-étale cover splits at each closed
point by strict henselianity, and Gleason's theorem lets us choose these
local splittings continuously in the point.

The proposition would be of little use if w-contractible rings were rare.
The next theorem shows that every ring has a faithfully flat ind-étale
cover by one, so that, after a single refinement, every affine object of
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is replaced by one over which covers split.

To compute on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ we want the limits of étale affines to form a
basis (Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-affines-form-basis]), so that
étale sheaves can be evaluated on every object by a colimit. Objects of
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ are only weakly étale, while the covers above are ind-étale,
and the next theorem bridges the two.

To compute with sheaves on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ it suffices to evaluate on two
kinds of affines. Every object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is covered by pro-étale
affines (Theorem [theorem-pro-etale-refinements-weakly-etale]), and
these are in turn covered by w-contractible affines
(Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers]), over which taking
sections is exact.

The two kinds of affines are used for different purposes. On a
pro-étale affine $U=\varprojlim_iU_i$, a sheaf pulled back from
$X_{\acute{e}t}$ can be evaluated by a colimit, and for this reason the comparison theorems of
Section [sec-Classical-sheaves] are proved on such affines. On a w-contractible
affine, by contrast, every epimorphism of sheaves is surjective on sections, so the
homological results of the next three sections are proved there.

In Lemma [lemma-w-contractible-affines-projective] we turn the splitting
of ring maps in Proposition [proposition-splitting-ind-etale-covers]
into a statement about sheaves. The idea is this. A finite cover of a
w-contractible affine has a section. Such a section amounts to a
