decomposition of the affine into finitely many clopen pieces, each mapping
into one member of the cover. Local lifts along an epimorphism can then be
glued over these pieces without any further refinement.

Over $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, for example, the weakly étale
$X$-scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ is already a
pro-étale affine, and $X$ itself is covered by it. Applying
Theorem [theorem-existence-contractible-covers] to the charts of such a
basis, we pass from pro-étale affines to w-contractible ones. The next two
results show that the spectra of w-contractible rings have the splitting
property for sheaves and that they cover every object.

On a topological space we check exactness at points, and on the étale
site at geometric points. On $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, instead, we check exactness, and compute
limits and colimits, by evaluating on weakly contractible objects. Over
these objects we can compute in the ordinary derived categories of
sheaves of modules by taking sections. Until
Section [sec-Classical-sheaves], $\mathcal R$ denotes a sheaf of rings on
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, for instance the pullback of a condensed ring
(Section [sec-Coefficient-rings]).

The main result is
Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects]. On a weakly
contractible affine $W$, taking sections is exact and commutes with all
limits and colimits of module sheaves. Moreover, these functors, for all
such $W$, are jointly conservative.

Stalk functors behave worse. Indeed, a stalk functor is exact and commutes with
colimits, but not with infinite products. Moreover, products of sheaves on $X_{\acute{e}t}$
need not be exact either, because a section of a product of
surjections lifts in each factor only after its own refinement of the
cover, and infinitely many refinements cannot in general be made at once.
Evaluation at $W$ avoids both problems: it commutes with products because
limits of sheaves are computed on sections, and it is exact because covers of
$W$ split.

In the simplest case, $X$ a geometric point, the site is that of profinite
sets (Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed], proved
in Subsection [subsec-Condensed-rings] below). The
weakly contractible affines are then the extremally disconnected ones, among
them $\beta(T^\delta)$ for a set $T$. Indeed, a surjection of profinite sets
onto such an $S$ has a section by Gleason's theorem.
This is the categorical definition of [bhatt-scholze15, §3.2].

Note that the splitting condition concerns a covering family as a whole. If $W$
is disconnected, a lift of $\mathrm{id}_{h_W}$ along a covering family
may use different members of the family on different clopen pieces
of $W$.

By Lemma [lemma-w-contractible-affines-projective], the spectrum of a
w-contractible ring is weakly contractible. By
Theorem [theorem-enough-affine-weakly-contractible-objects], such
affines cover every object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. For abelian sheaves we use these
two facts in the following form.

The quasi-compactness used here is quasi-compactness as an object of the
site: coverings admit finite refinements. Affine objects of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$
have this property. The affine weakly contractible objects are
quasi-compact, quasi-separated and projective, and they cover every object.

Cohomology on other objects need not vanish. For instance, a fibre product
of two weakly contractible affines need not be weakly contractible, and for this
reason the Čech complex of a cover by them does not in general compute
cohomology.

We need inverse limits to pass from torsion to adic coefficients, for
example to form $\varprojlim_n\mathbf Z/\ell^n$, and the first use of weakly
contractible objects is to show that such limits are well behaved. In a
general topos a limit of epimorphisms need not be an epimorphism, because
the local lifts at each stage may require ever finer covers. On
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, however, this does not happen, since surjectivity and exactness can be
checked on sections over weakly contractible objects, and there no
refinement is needed. As a result, the limit of a tower of epimorphisms maps
epimorphically onto each term
(Proposition [proposition-repleteness-pro-etale-topos]). For the same
reason products are exact (Proposition [proposition-exact-products]).

Exactness of products means that derived limits can be computed as for
abelian groups. Namely, the derived limit of a tower is the fibre of $1-T$ on the
product. Its cohomology is therefore given by the Milnor sequence of
Proposition [proposition-milnor-sequence], and $R^p\varprojlim$
vanishes for $p\geq2$. For a tower of epimorphisms, such as
$(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_X$, moreover $R^1\varprojlim$ vanishes, and the derived limit is the ordinary limit. In the next
section we also deduce left completeness from the Milnor sequence. With these
facts we compute the cohomology of $\mathbf Z_\ell$ as continuous cohomology
(Proposition [proposition-continuous-cohomology-pro-etale-cohomology]).

For sheaves of modules the same lifting argument, applied coordinatewise
rather than along a tower, shows that products are exact. This lets us
compute derived limits by termwise products of complexes.

Derived limits of countable towers have an explicit model. For a
countable tower of modules, write $t_n:M_{n+1}\to M_n$ and let
$T:\prod_nM_n\to\prod_nM_n$ be $T((m_n)_n)=(t_n(m_{n+1}))_n$. For a
tower $(K_n)$ in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal R)$, represented by a tower of
complexes $K_{n+1}\to K_n$, the same formula defines $T$ termwise, and the
derived inverse limit is the homotopy fibre of $1-T$

$$
R\varprojlim_n K_n
=
\fib\Bigl(
\prod_n K_n\xrightarrow{\,1-T\,}\prod_n K_n
\Bigr)=\Cone(1-T)[-1].
\tag{2.1}
$$

The cone is formed on the level of complexes, so that the
construction is functorial in the tower. By Proposition [proposition-exact-products]
the termwise products are the derived products, and so, by [Stacks, [0940](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0940)],
this cone agrees with the derived inverse limit.

More generally, the $R^1\varprojlim$ term vanishes if, on every affine
weakly contractible $W$, the tower of section modules satisfies the
Mittag–Leffler condition. To see this, note that evaluation on $W$
preserves cokernels
(Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects]). So the
cokernel of $1-T$ evaluated on $W$ is the cokernel of $1-T$ on the tower
$(M_n(W))$, which vanishes by the Mittag–Leffler lemma [Stacks, [07KV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07KV)]. As
evaluation on these $W$ detects vanishing, the $R^1\varprojlim$ term
vanishes.

An unbounded complex on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is determined by its
bounded-below truncations, and its cohomology is computed from theirs
by a derived limit. On the étale site of a scheme of infinite
cohomological dimension this can fail, whereas on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ it holds because
products are exact, so that the Milnor sequence applies.

Left completeness (Proposition [proposition-left-completeness]) lets
us treat an unbounded complex as the derived limit of bounded below ones,
to which injective resolutions and the comparison theorems apply. In
this way we prove the unbounded comparison of
Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients].

For bounded below complexes we also give an explicit model of cohomology.
On a quasi-compact quasi-separated object $U$,
Proposition [proposition-weakly-contractible-hypercovers] provides a
hypercover all of whose terms $W_r$ are affine weakly contractible. Since these
terms have no higher cohomology, the hypercover spectral sequence
collapses, and $R\Gamma(U,K)$ is the total complex of the sections
$K^b(W_r)$. This model has a consequence we use later. Namely, in each total degree
only finitely many terms occur, and evaluation on each $W_r$ commutes with
filtered colimits. Hence cohomology commutes with filtered colimits of
uniformly bounded below complexes
(Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]). We use this to show that
cohomology and direct images commute with inverting $\ell$ and with
extension of scalars to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, the colimit over the finite extensions
$E'$ of $E$.

To compute the cohomology of an unbounded complex from its
truncations, we need derived functors on the whole unbounded derived
category that commute with derived inverse limits.

For bounded-below complexes, weakly contractible objects provide explicit
cochain complexes computing cohomology.

For a single sheaf this is the cochain complex
$M(W_0)\to M(W_1)\to M(W_2)\to\cdots$. It may be nonzero in every degree,
so the hypercover gives no bound on cohomological dimension.
For unbounded $K$, by left completeness
(Proposition [proposition-left-completeness]) and since
$R\Gamma(U,-)$ commutes with derived inverse limits, we get
$R\Gamma(U,K)\simeq
R\varprojlim_n R\Gamma(U,\tau_{\geq-n}K)$, and the hypercover complex
computes each term.

In particular, $H^q(U,-)$ commutes with direct sums of sheaves of
modules. Quasi-compactness of $U$ is needed already for $H^0$. Let $X$ be a
geometric point and $U=\coprod_{n\in\mathbf N}X$, and consider the direct
sum $\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbf N}\mathbf Z$ of copies of the constant sheaf.
Its sections over $U$ are $\prod_n\bigoplus_i\mathbf Z$, which contains the
element whose $n$th component is the $n$th basis vector, whereas
$\bigoplus_i H^0(U,\mathbf Z)=\bigoplus_i\prod_n\mathbf Z$ consists of the
elements with only finitely many nonzero indices $i$.

For direct sums of unbounded complexes the common lower bound is replaced
by uniform bounds on cohomological dimension
(Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients]).

From here until Section [sec-Continuous-cohomology], $\Lambda$ denotes a discrete
commutative ring and $\Lambda_X$ its constant sheaf on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. To use
the torsion arguments of étale cohomology, we must know which pro-étale
sheaves come from étale sheaves. The main result answers this: étale sheaves
embed fully faithfully, and the essential image consists of the sheaves
whose sections on a limit $\varprojlim U_i$ are the colimit of the sections
on the $U_i$. In particular, the reductions $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ lie in this image, while the
$\ell$-adic coefficient sheaves themselves, such as $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$, do
not (Example [example-coefficient-sheaf-outside-classical-part]).

The colimit condition is forced on us by the way étale sheaves extend
to limits. If $F$ is an étale sheaf and $\bar x$ a geometric point, the
only reasonable value of the pullback of $F$ on the strict henselization
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X,\bar x}=\varprojlim(U,\bar u)$
is $\varinjlim F(U)=F_{\bar x}$. In this way stalks of étale sheaves
become sections of pro-étale sheaves.
Proposition [proposition-comparison-morphism-inverse-image] defines
the pullback $\nu_X^*$ by this rule, and
Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image] characterizes its
image by it. The part that is not formal is cohomology, because pro-étale covers
are not étale covers. In the next section we show that they create
no new cohomology classes for classical sheaves.

For $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbf F}_q$,
formula (2.6) says that $(\nu_X^*F)(U)$ is the
colimit of the $F(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^m})$, that is, the
underlying set of the Galois module corresponding to $F$. Formula
(2.6) also shows at once that every sheaf
$\nu_X^*F$ is classical. The next theorem says that there are no other
classical sheaves.

For a bounded-below complex $K$ on $X_{\acute{e}t}$, the pro-étale
cohomology of $\nu_X^*K$ is the étale cohomology of $K$
(Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison]). Bounds on
cohomological dimension are needed only for unbounded complexes
(Section [sec-Unbounded-complexes]). With this theorem, statements of SGA 4
about the cohomology of torsion sheaves, such as $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ on a
variety, can be quoted on the pro-étale site.

The theorem rests on two facts. A pro-étale cover of an affine can be
refined to a limit of étale covers, and sections of a classical sheaf on
a limit are the colimit of sections. It follows that the Čech complex
of a pro-étale cover is a filtered colimit of étale Čech
complexes. Because of this, an injective étale sheaf stays acyclic after
pullback (Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-pulled-back-injectives]), and
resolving by injectives gives the theorem. For non-classical coefficients
the comparison fails, as the computation of
$H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z_\ell)$ in Section [sec-Weil-cohomology]
shows.

It follows that the cohomology of a pro-étale affine is the colimit of the
cohomology of its étale approximations
(Corollary [corollary-cohomology-pro-etale-affine]). Moreover, classical
complexes in $D^+$ are exactly the pullbacks of étale ones
(Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]), and this is
what we need for proper base change on the pro-étale site.

Since injective sheaves compute derived functors, the lemma suffices
to compare derived direct images, and we obtain the comparison of cohomology
by resolving a bounded-below complex by injectives.

Applied to a pro-étale affine, the theorem computes its cohomology from
the étale schemes of which it is the limit.

To apply statements proved on the étale site, such as proper base
change, on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, we also need the essential image of $\nu_X^*$
on $D^+$. It consists of the classical complexes.
Write $D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ for the full
subcategory of $D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ of classical complexes.

Proper base change is proved on the étale site
(Chapter [chap-Proper-base-change]), while $Rf_!$ is defined by direct
images on the pro-étale site. To transfer proper base change, and to
compute these direct images, we compare direct images on the two sites.

Let $g:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Base change of objects of the
sites defines a commutative square of topoi

$$
\begin{CD}
X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}@>{\nu_X}>>X_{\acute{e}t}\\
@V{g_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}}VV @VV{g_{\acute{e}t}}V\\
Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}@>{\nu_Y}>>Y_{\acute{e}t}.
\end{CD}
$$

It induces an isomorphism
$g_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}^*\nu_Y^*\simeq\nu_X^*g_{\acute{e}t}^*$ of functors
$\operatorname{Mod}(Y_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, compatible with
composition. Since all four functors are exact, it is also an
isomorphism of functors $D(Y_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.
For direct images the comparison needs a hypothesis on $g$. The
comparison map
$\nu_Y^*Rg_{\acute{e}t,*}\to Rg_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t,*}\nu_X^*$ of functors
$D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D^+(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is defined as the
adjoint of the composite of
$g_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}^*\nu_Y^*Rg_{\acute{e}t,*}\simeq\nu_X^*g_{\acute{e}t}^*Rg_{\acute{e}t,*}$ with
$\nu_X^*$ applied to the counit of the adjunction $g_{\acute{e}t}^*\dashv Rg_{\acute{e}t,*}$.

Evaluated on a pro-étale affine $V=\varprojlim_iV_i$ over $Y$, the
comparison map is the map from $\varinjlim_iH^q(X\times_YV_i,F)$ to
$H^q(X\times_YV,F)$. So the theorem below is the continuity of étale
cohomology under affine limits, and like it, it needs $g$ to be
quasi-compact. Without this the map fails to be surjective already for $q=0$.
For example, let $Y$ be affine and connected, $X=\coprod_{n\in\mathbf N}Y$ and $F$ the
constant sheaf $\mathbf Z/2$. Then $g_*F$ is the product of countably many
copies of $\mathbf Z/2$ on $Y$. On $V=Y\times S$ with $S$ an infinite
profinite set, the pro-étale side has as sections all sequences of
locally constant functions $S\to\mathbf Z/2$, while the classical side
only has the sequences that factor through a common finite quotient of
$S$.

Since every bounded-below classical complex is of the form $\nu_X^*K$
(Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]), the theorem
shows that, for $g$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated, $Rg_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t,*}$
carries bounded-below classical complexes to classical complexes.

In later arguments we transport maps built from units, counits and composition
from the étale to the pro-étale site, and for this we record how the
comparison map behaves under these operations. Write
$\beta_g:g_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}^*\nu_Y^*\simeq\nu_X^*g_{\acute{e}t}^*$ for the isomorphism
above and $c_g$ for the map (2.9).

In the comparison for constructible sheaves below we argue by induction on
strata, using the functors of localization triangles. The next proposition
identifies these functors on the two sites.

The six operations act on constructible complexes, and their finiteness
theorems are proved on the étale site. To use these theorems we show that
constructible pro-étale sheaves are classical, so that they correspond to
constructible étale sheaves, and that the comparison preserves finite Tor
amplitude.

A sheaf of modules on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is locally constant if it is trivialized by
a pro-étale covering, and it is of finite presentation if its constant
models are finitely presented $\Lambda$-modules. Building on this, for Noetherian
$\Lambda$, a sheaf is constructible if, locally on $X$, there is a finite
partition into constructible locally closed strata such that it is locally
constant of finite type on each stratum. We write $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ for the
category of constructible sheaves and $\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ for the bounded
complexes with constructible cohomology sheaves. For a discrete ring these notions
agree with Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves], which is stated
for all coefficient rings in Section [sec-Constructibility] below. These conditions
refer only to pro-étale covers, so the main step is to descend torsors
from pro-étale to étale covers.

A priori there could be more pro-étale local systems than étale
ones, since the covers are larger. For finite groups, however, there are not. Indeed, a
torsor under a finite group is described by a cocycle on one pro-étale
affine cover. That cover is a limit of étale covers and the group is
classical, so the cocycle is defined at a finite stage. For $\mathbf Z_\ell$, by contrast, there
are more local systems, and this is the reason for using the pro-étale
site. For example, over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$, a rank-one $\mathbf Z_\ell$-local system
on which Frobenius acts by a unit $u\in\mathbf Z_\ell^\times$ of infinite order is
trivialized by a pro-étale cover but by no étale one. Our comparison
therefore concerns only finite coefficients, and we study $\ell$-adic
local systems through their reductions.

What we use later is the case of a finite ring $A$. For such $A$,
Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves] and
Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison] identify the
category $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ on the pro-étale site with the classical one.

The hypothesis that the group is classical is essential. For instance, the group
$\mathbf Z_\ell^\times$ is not classical, and the rank-one $\mathbf Z_\ell$-local system on
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ described above is a $\mathbf Z_\ell^\times$-torsor
with no étale trivialization. On the other hand, for locally constant sheaves with finitely
presented constant models over a discrete ring, the relevant group is the
automorphism group of the model, which is discrete, and the lemma applies.

To pass from a single stratum to arbitrary constructible sheaves, note
that for a finite ring $A$ the proposition applies to every finite local
system of $A$-modules. A constructible sheaf is built from such local
systems on the strata of a stratification, by extension by zero and
extensions. Both operations preserve classical sheaves. For extension by
zero this follows from the comparisons of Section [sec-Direct-images].
For extensions it is
Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes], which uses that
$R^1\nu_{X,*}$ vanishes on classical sheaves.

The six operations act on complexes of finite Tor amplitude, so we also
need to know that the equivalence just proved respects this condition. A
priori the pro-étale condition is stronger, since it requires a Tor
bound against all pro-étale modules, most of which are not classical.

In particular, the corollary applies to every finite commutative
$\ell$-primary ring $A$.

Proper base change needs the comparison with the étale site only for
bounded-below complexes. Brown representability, however, takes place in the
unbounded derived category, so we extend the comparison to unbounded
complexes. The difficulty is that a morphism from a sheaf into an unbounded
complex $K$ involves in principle all the cohomology sheaves of $K$ at once,
and so does a cohomology sheaf of $Rg_*K$. Both depend on only finitely many
of them if Ext groups and cohomology of sheaves vanish above a fixed degree,
uniformly in the sheaf. The smallest such degree is the cohomological
dimension defined below.

Without such a bound, $\Hom$ out of the constant sheaf need not commute with
direct sums. For example, take
$\ell=2$ and $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf R$. Here étale cohomology is
the cohomology of $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbf C/\mathbf R)=\mathbf Z/2$, and
$H^q(\mathbf Z/2,\mathbf F_2)=\mathbf F_2$ for every $q\geq0$. Thus
$\operatorname{cd}_2(S)=\infty$, and $\Hom(\mathbf F_2,-)$ does not commute
with the direct sum $\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbf F_2[n]$ (see the opening of
Chapter [chap-Construction-of-f]).

Over a field of finite cohomological dimension, the étale cohomology of
schemes of finite type is uniformly bounded. In that case every computation
in a fixed degree can be carried out on a bounded-below truncation. We use
the bounds in this way in
Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients] below and, later, in the proofs of
compactness and of the preservation of direct sums by $Rp_*$
(Lemmas [lemma-uniform-ext-bound]
and [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image]).

By Theorems [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison] and [theorem-comparison-direct-images],
these are the usual $\ell$-cohomological dimensions computed on the
étale sites. So the classical bounds apply. If $k'$ is a field with $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(k')<\infty$, then
$\operatorname{cd}_\ell(S)$ and $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(g)$ are finite for all
schemes $S$ and morphisms $g$ of finite type over $k'$ [Stacks, [0F10](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F10)].
For our field $k$ the hypothesis holds by the following lemma.

Over $\overline{\mathbf F}_q$, for example, a variety of dimension $n$
has $\ell$-cohomological dimension at most $2n$, and the curve $\mathbf P^1$
attains this bound, since $H^2(\mathbf P^1,\mathbf Z/\ell)\neq0$. Over
$\mathbf F_q$, however, one more degree is possible. Indeed, for $\ell\neq p$ the
Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence gives
$H^3(\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf F_q},\mu_\ell)\simeq
H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,H^2(\mathbf P^1_{\overline{\mathbf F}_q},\mu_\ell))
=H^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z/\ell)=\mathbf Z/\ell$.

To extend the comparison theorems to unbounded complexes with these
bounds, we need two facts. First, the bounds hold uniformly over the affine
objects on which we take sections
(Lemma [lemma-uniform-bounds-pro-etale-affines]). Second, on the
pro-étale side a cohomology group of an unbounded complex in a fixed
degree only sees a bounded-below truncation
(Lemma [lemma-truncation-pro-etale-sections]).

Since by Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image] the
classical sheaves of $A$-modules are the essential image of $\nu_X^*$ on
sheaves, and $\nu_X^*$ commutes with direct sums of sheaves, classical
sheaves of $A$-modules are closed under arbitrary direct sums in
$\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$.

We want pullback along morphisms and change of coefficients to be
compatible without any bookkeeping. For this we define each coefficient
ring once, on a point, and pull it back to every scheme along a single
morphism of topoi. This gives $A_X$, $\mathcal O_{E,X}$, $E_X$ and
$\QbarX$. Here $A$ is a finite commutative ring killed by a power of
$\ell$, with the discrete topology, and $A_X$ is the usual constant sheaf.
For the point we take the site of profinite sets described below. By
Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed] it is the
pro-étale site of a separably closed field. Unlike the étale site of
the field, it keeps the topology of the coefficient rings.

The constant sheaf with value the abstract ring $\mathbf Z_\ell$ forgets the topology
of $\mathbf Z_\ell$, and on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ it has $H^1=0$
(Section [sec-Weil-cohomology]). We therefore need a notion
of coefficient ring on a geometric point that retains the topology. The
pro-étale site of a separably closed field is the site of profinite sets
(Proposition [proposition-pro-etale-site-separably-closed] below). So a
coefficient ring must at least be a sheaf of rings on profinite sets, that
is, a condensed ring. The continuous maps from profinite sets into $\mathbf Z_\ell$ form
such a sheaf. With it, $H^1$ of $\mathbf F_q$ becomes $\mathbf Z_\ell$
(Example [example-first-cohomology-finite-field]).

Let $*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ be the site of profinite sets, with finite jointly
surjective families as covers. A *condensed ring* is a sheaf of
rings on $*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. A topological ring $V$ defines a condensed ring
$\underline V$, whose sections over $S$ are the continuous maps $S\to V$.
This is a sheaf because a surjection of profinite sets is a quotient map.

The étale topos of $\Omega$ is the topos of sets, whereas by the
proposition its pro-étale topos is the topos of condensed sets. The final
object of $*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is weakly contractible, so taking global sections is
exact. However, a condensed sheaf is not determined by its global sections.
For classical sheaves geometric stalks still suffice, whereas a general sheaf of
modules on the pro-étale site has to be evaluated on all
weakly contractible affines
(Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects]). For example, the
completed coefficient sheaf $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$ of
Example [example-coefficient-sheaf-outside-classical-part] is of this
general kind: its sections on a profinite set $S$ are all continuous
functions $S\to\mathbf Z_\ell$.

Fix an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$. Throughout, $E$ denotes a
finite extension of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ inside $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, with ring of integers
$\mathcal O_E$ and uniformizer $\pi_E$. For $\mathcal O_E$ and $E$ the $\ell$-adic topologies define condensed rings
$\underline{\mathcal O_E}$ and $\underline E$. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, however, the
topology causes a problem. To see why, recall that classically a $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaf is an $E$-sheaf for
some finite $E$ with scalars extended, and all arguments with lattices and
reduction modulo $\pi_E$ take place over that $E$. They cannot be made over
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ itself, because $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is not complete and its valuation ring is not
a discrete valuation ring. But the sheaf of all continuous maps to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$
has sections that are defined over no finite $E$ (see below), so it would
lose this reduction. To keep it available, we take instead the filtered
colimit over the finite coefficient fields.
Using the valuation topology on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, we put

$$
\underline{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}(S)=
\{a:S\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\text{ continuous}:a(S)\subset E\text{ for some finite }E/\mathbf Q_\ell\}
=\varinjlim_E\underline E(S).
$$

This is already a sheaf, because a cover of a profinite set can be refined by a
finite one, and finitely many finite extensions of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ lie in a common
one. Since
filtered colimits of sheaves on $*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ are computed sectionwise,
$\underline{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}=\varinjlim_E\underline E$ as condensed rings.

This condensed ring is smaller than $\underline V$ for $V=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ with the valuation
topology. Indeed, algebraic numbers of unbounded degree can tend to $0$.
Such a sequence is a continuous map from a convergent sequence to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$
with image in no finite extension. With our choice,
Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field] shows that every
constructible $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-complex and every morphism between such complexes
descends to a finite $E$.

A profinite set $S$ defines a pro-étale scheme
$\operatorname{Spec}LC(S,\mathbf Z)$ over $\mathbf Z$, where
$LC(S,\mathbf Z)$ is the ring of locally constant functions. The functor
$S\mapsto\operatorname{Spec}LC(S,\mathbf Z)$ is continuous and preserves
finite limits, as one checks on finite quotients of $S$, so it induces a
morphism of topoi $\Sh((\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})\to
\Sh(*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})$ [Stacks, [00X6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00X6)]. Composing with the structure morphism of
$X$, we obtain

$$
p_X:\Sh(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t})\longrightarrow\Sh(*_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}),
$$

and for a condensed ring $\Lambda$ we write $\Lambda_X=p_X^*\Lambda$.
For a morphism $f:X\to Y$ we have $p_Y\circ f=p_X$, and hence a canonical
isomorphism $f^{-1}\Lambda_Y\simeq\Lambda_X$, compatible with identities
and composition. Likewise, a morphism $\Lambda\to\Lambda'$ of condensed
rings pulls back to $\Lambda_X\to\Lambda'_X$, which defines extension of
scalars $\Lambda'_X\otimes_{\Lambda_X}-$ from $\Lambda_X$-modules to
$\Lambda'_X$-modules on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. Thus both pullback along morphisms
and change of coefficients are obtained from $p_X^*$.

The next lemma identifies these rings with the completed coefficient
rings of classical $\ell$-adic cohomology.

The first isomorphism describes $\mathcal O_{E,X}$ as a limit of its
finite quotients. To compute derived reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$ we also
need these quotients as cokernels of multiplication by $\pi_E^n$, which
the next corollary provides.

Using the two-term resolution we see that, for every
complex $K$ of $\mathcal O_{E,X}$-modules, the derived reduction
$K\otimes^{\mathbf L}(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X$ is the cone of
$\pi_E^n:K\to K$ (Lemma [lemma-reduction-derived-nakayama]).

We call the rings $A,\mathbf Z_\ell,\mathcal O_E,\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ the *admissible*
coefficient rings. Here $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ is allowed, so that $\mathbf Z_\ell$ and $\mathbf Q_\ell$ are the
case $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ of $\mathcal O_E$ and $E$. For $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$
we write $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}=\mathcal O_{\mathbf Q_\ell,X}$ and
$\mathbf Q_{\ell,X}=(\mathbf Q_\ell)_X$. By the comparison lemma above,

$$
\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}\simeq\varprojlim_n(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_X,
\qquad
\mathbf Q_{\ell,X}\simeq\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}[1/\ell].
$$

For a condensed ring $\Lambda$ we write $\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ for the
category of $\Lambda_X$-modules. Its derived category is
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

Duality and the trace map need, besides the constant sheaf, its twists
by roots of unity. The reason is already visible on $\mathbf P^1$ over an
algebraically closed field $k$, for $n$ invertible in $k$. The Kummer
sequence $0\to\mu_n\to\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{n}\mathbf G_m\to0$ gives
an isomorphism
$H^2(\mathbf P^1,\mu_n)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1)/n=\mathbf Z/n$,
given by the degree of a line bundle. This isomorphism involves no choice,
and it sends the class of a point to $1$. An identification of
$H^2(\mathbf P^1,\mathbf Z/n)$ with $\mathbf Z/n$, on the other hand,
requires an isomorphism $\mu_n\simeq\mathbf Z/n$, that is, a choice of a
primitive $n$th root of unity. Frobenius does not respect such a choice.

To see this, let $k$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbf F_q$. The
arithmetic Frobenius acts on $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ by $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^q$.
The geometric Frobenius is the inverse of the arithmetic Frobenius in
$\operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbf F_q)$. Hence it acts on $\Lambda(1)$ by
$q^{-1}$, and on $H^2(\mathbf P^1,\Lambda)\simeq\Lambda(-1)$ by $q$. This
agrees with $\#\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_q)=1+q$.

Over $\mathbf C$ the twist is $2\pi i\mathbf Z$. The exponential sequence
identifies $H^2(\mathbf P^1(\mathbf C),2\pi i\mathbf Z)$ with $\mathbf Z$.
An identification of $H^2(\mathbf P^1(\mathbf C),\mathbf Z)$ with
$\mathbf Z$, by contrast, is a choice of orientation, and the complex
orientation depends on the choice of $i$.

With twists, the trace map of $\mathbf P^1$
(Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]) and smooth
purity $f^!\simeq f^*(d)[2d]$
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients]) are
canonical and commute with Frobenius
(Proposition [proposition-purity-trace-commute-frobenius]). This is
where the factor $q^d$ in Poincaré duality (c) comes from.

Every base change argument below compares a module over $\Lambda_Y$ with
its pullback to $X$, and for this we want the pullback of a
$\Lambda_Y$-module to be its inverse image as a sheaf, with no tensor
product. For coherent sheaves this fails, since
$f^*M=\mathcal O_X\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}f^{-1}M$ and
$f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y\ne\mathcal O_X$ in general. For our coefficient sheaves
the two notions agree, because all coefficient sheaves are pulled back
from the point. The same holds for their Tate twists, where $\ell$
is invertible.

The second part of the next lemma says that extension of scalars to a
finite extension $E'/E$ is a finite direct sum. We use this, for instance,
in the proof of
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-constructible-complexes].

By (1), the pullback of modules over these sheaves, defined in
Section [sec-Derived-functors] below, is the exact functor $f^{-1}$.

The comparison theorems above concern discrete coefficients, whereas the integral
and rational $\ell$-adic coefficient rings of Section [sec-Coefficient-rings]
are defined directly on the pro-étale site, because the discrete constant
sheaves with the same values have the wrong cohomology
(Example [example-first-cohomology-finite-field]). The main result of
this section,
Proposition [proposition-continuous-cohomology-pro-etale-cohomology],
says that pro-étale cohomology with coefficients $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is
the classical continuous cohomology, that is, the derived limit of
cohomology with coefficients $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$.

The sheaf $\mathbf Z_{\ell,X}$ is the inverse limit of the classical sheaves
$(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_X$, with surjective transition maps
(Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients]). For such a limit,
the cohomology is the derived limit of the cohomology of the terms. When
the terms are classical, this is continuous étale cohomology.

When the $F_n$ come from the étale site, as the sheaves
$(\mathbf Z/\ell^n)_X$ do, each term on the right is étale cohomology
by the comparison theorem, and the proposition identifies pro-étale
cohomology of the limit with continuous étale cohomology
$R\varprojlim_nR\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},F_n)$.

Applying the Milnor sequence (2.2) to the
tower of complexes $R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},F_n)$ and using the proposition, we
obtain for every $q$ a natural exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow R^1\varprojlim_nH^{q-1}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},F_n)
\longrightarrow H^q(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},F)
\longrightarrow\varprojlim_nH^q(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},F_n)
\longrightarrow0.
\tag{2.11}
$$

The first term can be nonzero, because the transition maps between the
cohomology groups need not be surjective even if those between the
sheaves $F_n$ are. It vanishes if the groups
$H^{q-1}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},F_n)$ satisfy the Mittag–Leffler condition. This
holds for instance if they are finite, since then descending chains of
images stabilize at each level.

The integral coefficient sheaves are inverse limits. To restrict integral
complexes to the strata of a stratification, and to extend them by zero,
we therefore need the functors $j_!$, $j^*$, $i^*$ and $i_*$ to commute
with limits. On the pro-étale site this holds, even for inverse image
along a closed immersion, and from this we deduce the localization triangles
and construct the local cohomology functor. With these tools we can argue with
closed supports before the exceptional inverse image and proper base
change are available.

That $i^*$ commutes with limits is special to the pro-étale site. On
$X_{\acute{e}t}$ the stalk of $i^*F$ at a point of $Z$ is the stalk of $F$. This
is a colimit, and colimits do not commute with infinite products. On
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, by contrast, the value of $i^*M$ on a weakly contractible affine over $Z$
is the value of $M$ on one affine object of $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, henselian along
$Z$ (Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme]),
and evaluation on one object preserves limits.
For $\mathcal O_{E,X}=\varprojlim(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X$ this means that
$i^*$ applied to the limit is the limit of the restrictions
$(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_Z$. The same holds for any integral complex given
as a derived limit of its reductions.

A complex over $\mathcal O_E$ is determined by its reductions modulo
$\pi_E^n$ when it is derived complete
(Definition [definition-derived-adic-completeness] below). Combined
with the computation of the cohomology of these reductions on the étale
site, this is how we reduce integral statements to finite coefficients
throughout the notes.

For arguments with closed supports we need a right adjoint of $i_*$
before $i^!$ is constructed by Brown representability. We build it from
$i^*$, $j^*$ and $Rj_*$ alone. We keep the notation of
Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme].

Once $i^!$ exists, it agrees with $R\underline\Gamma_Z$ on the
localizing category on which $i^!$ is defined, since both are right
adjoints of $i_*$ there.

We treat integral coefficients through their reductions modulo
powers of $\pi_E$. This is possible for complexes that are recovered
from their reductions, the derived complete ones. Derived completeness
is the analogue for complexes of the condition $M=\varprojlim_nM/\pi_E^nM$
on a module. For example, $\mathcal O_{E,X}$ itself is derived complete.
The sheaf $E_X$ is not, since all its reductions vanish.

We write $K_n=K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,X}}(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n})_X$
for the reductions of $K$. The canonical transition maps
$K_{n+1}\to K_n$ induce isomorphisms
$K_{n+1}\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n+1})_X}(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^{n})_X\simeq K_n$,
by associativity of the derived tensor product. We call $(K_n)$, with these isomorphisms, the *tower of reductions*
of $K$.

Over a point, for $K=\mathcal O_E$ placed in degree $0$, the reductions
are $K_n=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$, and the lemma is the classical Nakayama
lemma for the complete local ring $\mathcal O_E$. The hypothesis of
completeness cannot be dropped, since $E\neq0$ but $E/\pi_E=0$.

Let $K$ be derived complete. Since $R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},-)$ is a right
adjoint, it commutes with the derived limit, and therefore

$$
R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K)
\simeq R\varprojlim_nR\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K_n).
$$

When the $K_n$ are classical bounded-below complexes, each term on the
right can be computed on the étale site by
Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison]. In this way
we compute the cohomology of $K$ from its tower of reductions $(K_n)$.

In Section [sec-Constructibility] we define constructible complexes over
$\mathcal O_E$, and we show that for Noetherian $X$ they are exactly the
derived complete complexes $K$ whose reduction $K_1$ is constructible
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]).
Derived complete complexes can equally be studied over the constant sheaf
with value the discrete ring $\mathcal O_E$
(Lemma [lemma-integral-models](1)).

The rational coefficient sheaves are obtained by inverting $\ell$ and
passing to the colimit over $E$:
$E_X\simeq\mathcal O_{E,X}[1/\ell]$ and $\QbarX\simeq\varinjlim_E E_X$
(Lemma [lemma-comparison-completed-coefficients]).
Chapter [chap-Constructible-complexes] also compares constructible
complexes over $E_X$ and $\QbarX$ with the classical adic categories. It
does so by lattices and by descent to a finite extension.

A lisse $E$-sheaf is the analogue of a local system: pro-étale locally it is
isomorphic to $E_X^r$ for some $r$ (Definition [definition-lisse-sheaves] below).
Inside such a sheaf $L$, a lattice is a locally free $\mathcal O_E$-subsheaf
$L_0$ with $L_0[1/\ell]=L$, and the first point of this chapter is that a lattice need
not exist. For an example, glue $0$ and $\infty$ on $\mathbf P^1$ to obtain a nodal curve $X$. Then the infinite
chain $Y$ of projective lines, with $\infty$ on each line glued to $0$ on the next,
maps to $X$ by an étale covering. Moreover, the group $\mathbf Z$ acts on $Y$ by
translation, simply transitively on the fibres, so $Y\to X$ is an étale
$\mathbf Z$-torsor. Using this torsor and letting
the generator of $\mathbf Z$ act on $E$ by multiplication by $\ell$, we obtain a
lisse $E$-sheaf of rank one. It has no lattice, because $\ell$ is not a unit of
$\mathcal O_E$, so that multiplication by $\ell$ does not carry any lattice onto
itself. The sheaf comes from the character
$n\mapsto\ell^n$ of $\mathbf Z$, and since this character does not extend continuously to
$\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, the sheaf has no classical counterpart as a system $(F_n)$
(see the discussion before Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification];
the example is in [bhatt-scholze15]).

This matters because every geometric input to the
next chapters (proper base change, the cohomology of curves, Deligne's generic
base change) is a theorem about torsion sheaves, whereas a rational sheaf has no
reduction modulo $\ell$: since $E_X$ is $\ell$-divisible, we have
$E_X\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E=0$. To use the torsion theory we must
therefore find integral objects inside rational ones, and then pass to their
torsion reductions. The example above shows that this cannot be done globally.

Classically each coefficient ring comes with its own theory:

| coefficients | classical constructible objects |
|---|---|
| finite ring $A$ | constructible étale sheaves of $A$-modules |
| $\mathbf Z_\ell$, $\mathcal O_E$ | systems $(F_n)$ of constructible   $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$-sheaves |
|  | with $F_{n+1}\otimes\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n\simeq F_n$ |
| $\mathbf Q_\ell$, $E$ | the same systems up to isogeny, that is, with $\ell$ inverted |
| $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ | a colimit of the categories for all finite $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ |

On the pro-étale site, by contrast, one local condition covers all of them. Namely, a
$\Lambda_X$-module is constructible if, on the strata of a finite stratification
of $X$, it is pro-étale locally of the form $\Lambda_X\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P$ for
a finitely presented module $P$ over $\Lambda(*)$, the ring of sections over the
point
(Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves]). For finite $A$ these are the
classical constructible sheaves, while for $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ they are lisse on the strata.
For $\mathcal O_E$, on the other hand, the modules $P$ may have torsion, for
example $P=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$.

The six operations will act on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$, bounded complexes with
constructible cohomology and finite Tor amplitude. For $\Lambda$ not a finite
ring the Tor condition is automatic, that is, $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)=\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$
(Proposition [proposition-ctf-equals-bc]). For a finite ring, however, it
matters: over $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ the constructible sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$ has
infinite Tor dimension (Section [sec-Constructibility] below).

Over $\mathcal O_E$ the passage to torsion is a criterion: for Noetherian $X$, a
complex is constructible exactly when it is derived complete and its reduction
modulo $\pi_E$ is constructible
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]). The criterion
is not formal, because the local models of the reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$ must be
made compatible in $n$
(Proposition [proposition-local-structure-integral-constructible-complexes],
Section [sec-Integral-constructible-complexes]). This description is due to Bhatt and
Scholze [bhatt-scholze15].

Over $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, as the nodal curve shows, lattices exist only after
stratifying, and this is enough. After descending from $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ to a finite
extension $E$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ and refining a stratification, a lisse sheaf has a
lattice on each stratum
(Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification]), and the reductions
of the lattice modulo $\pi_E^n$ are classical torsion sheaves
(Lemma [lemma-integral-models]).

On a connected normal scheme no stratification is needed: there a lattice exists
globally, and lisse $E$-sheaves are continuous representations of
$\pi_1(X,\bar x)$
(Proposition [proposition-lattices-representations-normal-scheme], proved in
Part III).

Dévissage along strata also shows that $\Hom$ out of a constructible
complex commutes with filtered colimits of complexes bounded below
by a common degree
(Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex]); this continuity is
used, together with descent to a finite $E$, in
Chapter [chap-Construction-of-f].

Throughout this chapter
schemes are again separated and of finite type over $k$, as in our conventions.

Four of the six operations, $f^*$, $Rf_*$, $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ and
internal Hom, exist for every condensed ring $\Lambda$ on the whole unbounded
derived categories by the usual resolutions. The remaining two need more work: $Rf_!$ is built
from proper direct image and extension by zero
(Section [sec-Direct-image-with-compact-support]), and its right adjoint comes from Brown
representability.

Sheaves of $\Lambda_X$-modules can be viewed as module objects over the
ring object $\Lambda_X$ in $\Sh(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\operatorname{Ab})$, with the tensor product
over $\Lambda_X$ given by the coequalizer of the two actions
$M\otimes\Lambda_X\otimes N\rightrightarrows M\otimes N$. The category of
$\Lambda_X$-modules is Grothendieck abelian. Hence complexes have K-injective
resolutions, which define $Rf_*$ and $\cHom$ [Stacks, [07A5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07A5), [08J7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08J7)]. They also
have K-flat resolutions, which define $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$, and
$K\otimes^{\mathbf L}-$ is left adjoint to $\cHom(K,-)$ [Stacks, [06YL](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06YL)].

The pullback of a $\Lambda_Y$-module $M$ along $f:X\to Y$ is
$f^*M=\Lambda_X\otimes_{f^{-1}\Lambda_Y}f^{-1}M$. Since
$f^{-1}\Lambda_Y\simeq\Lambda_X$ (Lemma [lemma-inverse-image-coefficient-sheaves]), this is just $f^{-1}M$. Therefore $f^*:\operatorname{Mod}(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to
\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is exact, and on derived
categories it is left adjoint to $Rf_*:D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to
D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. For an open immersion $j:U\to X$, extension by
zero $j_!:\operatorname{Mod}(U_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is
exact and left adjoint to $j^*$.

Constructible sheaves will be built from lisse sheaves on the strata of a
stratification, each extended by zero to all of $X$
(Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves] and
Corollary [corollary-coefficient-heart-b]). We fix this extension by
zero now. Let $a:S\hookrightarrow X$ be a locally closed immersion, for
instance the inclusion of a stratum. Then $S$ is open in its closure, so $a$
factors as $a=i\circ j$, with $j:S\hookrightarrow\overline S$ the open
immersion into the closure and $i:\overline S\hookrightarrow X$ the closed
immersion. We put

$$
a_!=i_*j_!:\operatorname{Mod}(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda).
$$

For a $\Lambda_S$-module $L$, the sheaf $a_!L$ restricts to $L$ on $S$,
and its restrictions to $\overline S\setminus S$ and to $X\setminus\overline S$
are zero. Indeed $a^*a_!=j^*i^*i_*j_!=\mathrm{id}$, the sheaf $j_!L$
vanishes on $\overline S\setminus S$, and $i_*$ of a sheaf vanishes on
$X\setminus\overline S$
(Proposition [proposition-extension-zero-restriction-closed-subscheme],
which applies because the open immersions involved are quasi-compact, $X$
being Noetherian). The same proposition shows that $j_!$ and $i_*$ are
exact, so $a_!$ is exact. It therefore acts on complexes term by term and defines
$a_!:D(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ with no derived functor
needed. Once $Rf_!$ is constructed (Section [sec-Direct-image-with-compact-support]), this
functor is $Ra_!$.

With finite coefficients a constructible sheaf is, on the strata of a
finite stratification, locally constant with finite stalks. The six
operations, however, will act on constructible complexes of finite Tor amplitude
for every coefficient ring, so we need a definition of constructibility that covers all coefficient
rings at once. We give it by a local condition
(Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves]). This condition has two parts, a
stratification and a local model that replaces local constancy, and the
complexes we use must in addition have finite Tor amplitude. As we explain below, each of the
three conditions answers a specific need. For $\mathcal O_E$ we then
show that constructibility can be tested on the reduction modulo $\pi_E$
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]). For a
morphism $g:Z\to X$ and a $\Lambda_X$-module $M$ we write $M|_Z=g^*M$, a
$\Lambda_Z$-module.

A stratification
cannot be avoided, already for sheaves coming from geometry: for
$j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$, the sheaf $j_!\Lambda$ is zero at
the origin and $\Lambda$ elsewhere, so it is not locally constant on
$\mathbf A^1$.

Local constancy itself has to be rephrased. For instance, for $\Lambda=\mathbf Z_\ell$,
“locally constant” with value a $\mathbf Z_\ell$-module would mean locally a constant
sheaf with value the discrete group, but on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$
such a sheaf has $H^1=0$ (Section [sec-Weil-cohomology]), whereas the
answer we want is $\mathbf Z_\ell$. We therefore ask instead that $M$ be locally of the
form $\Lambda_U\otimes_{\Lambda(*)}P$, with $P$ a finitely presented module over the ring $\Lambda(*)$ of sections
over the point, as in the opening of this chapter. This keeps the $\ell$-adic topology. For finite $\Lambda$
it is local constancy, and for $E$ it says that $M$ is locally free of
finite rank. In this formulation, finite presentation of $P$ replaces finiteness of the stalks.

Finally, the six operations should commute with change of coefficients, and
this needs finite Tor amplitude. Over $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ the sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$
is constructible, but
$\mathbf F_\ell\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^2}\mathbf F_\ell$ has
cohomology $\mathbf F_\ell$ in every degree $\leq0$. With the Tor condition imposed, by contrast,
the category
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ is stable under change of coefficients and under
$\otimes^{\mathbf L}$, and for $\mathcal O_E$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ the
Tor condition is automatic (Proposition [proposition-ctf-equals-bc]).

The modules that satisfy the condition of (1) on all of $X$ are the
analogue of local systems, and they are the building blocks on the
strata.
For the individual coefficient rings the definitions take a familiar form.

Part (5) is special to the admissible coefficients. For a general condensed ring, kernels of maps between constructible
sheaves can fail to be constructible, and then $\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ is not
triangulated.

Constructibility over $\mathcal O_E$ is defined by a local condition, but in
practice we know a complex $K\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$ through
its reductions
$K_n=K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathcal O_{E,X}}(\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n)_X$ of
Definition [definition-derived-adic-completeness]. The criterion below says that
$K$ is constructible exactly when it is derived complete and $K_1$ is
constructible. Write $\mathbf F_E=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$ for the residue
field, so that $K_1\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf F_E)$.

To prove the criterion we must produce, on each stratum, one complex of
finite free $\mathcal O_E$-modules that is locally a model for all the
$K_n$ at once. Each $K_n$ separately is easy to control: its bounds and
its stratification are inherited from $K_1$ by dévissage along the
powers of $\pi_E$, and on a stratum it is locally isomorphic to a
constant perfect complex. The difficulty is that these local isomorphisms
are chosen independently at each level, so they have to be made
compatible before we pass to the limit. On a weakly contractible cover
we do this by a Mittag–Leffler argument, which needs a uniform
rate. Such a rate exists because a bounded complex of finite free modules over the
discrete valuation ring $\mathcal O_E$ has finitely generated
cohomology, and the torsion of this cohomology is killed by a fixed power of
$\pi_E$.
Throughout, we use the étale site only at the finite levels, through
Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves].

To make the local trivializations of the $K_n$ compatible, we need two facts about
complexes over $\mathcal O_E$:
a compatible system of perfect complexes over the rings
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ comes from a single bounded finite free complex, and
the images of the cohomology at finite levels stabilize at a uniform rate.

The second fact is used in the proof of
Lemma [lemma-integral-model-weakly-contractible] for the internal Hom
complex $(P^\bullet)^\vee\otimes P^\bullet$, whose $H^0$ at level $n$
consists of the maps $P^\bullet/\pi_E^n\to P^\bullet/\pi_E^n$ in the derived
category. There it says that a map at level $n$ which lifts far enough lifts
to all levels, and how far is enough depends only on the torsion of the
cohomology.

Such an $e$ exists, since $\mathcal O_E$ is a Noetherian discrete
valuation ring and $H^{q+1}(Q^\bullet)$ is finitely generated.

The bound $m\geq n+e$ cannot be improved. To see this, take
$Q^\bullet=[\mathcal O_E\xrightarrow{\pi_E^e}\mathcal O_E]$ in degrees
$0,1$, so that $H^0(Q^\bullet)=0$ and $H^1(Q^\bullet)=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^e$.
For $m\geq e$ the group $H^0(Q^\bullet/\pi_E^m)$ is $\pi_E^{m-e}\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^m$,
and its image at level $n$ is generated by $\pi_E^{m-e}$ modulo $\pi_E^n$.
This image is zero exactly when $m\geq n+e$, in agreement with the image of
$H^0(Q^\bullet)=0$.

At a single finite level the local structure is a statement about the
étale site: a perfect complex with locally constant cohomology is
locally constant. On a connected scheme its local model is moreover the same
at every point.

On a weakly contractible object the local isomorphisms of the finite
levels become global, and the only remaining problem is to choose them
compatibly. For this we use the uniform rate of
Lemma [lemma-images-cohomology-finite-levels].
The local structure is the hard half of the following criterion.

In the classical adic setting, this description of the integral
constructible category is [bhatt-scholze15, Proposition 6.8.11] and
[Stacks, [09C7](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C7)].

Lemma [lemma-integral-models] compares $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathcal O_E)$ with
the classical category of constructible $\mathcal O_E$-complexes
[Stacks, [09C1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C1)], which is defined with modules over the constant sheaf with
value the discrete ring $\mathcal O_E$.

For the integral and rational rings the finite Tor amplitude condition is
automatic.

For a finite ring that is not regular the condition is needed, as the
$\mathbf Z/\ell^2$-module $\mathbf F_\ell$ of Section [sec-Constructibility]
shows. Moreover, finite Tor amplitude is a condition on the whole complex, not on its
cohomology sheaves. The category
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ is thick, but in general it is not stable under standard truncations.
For example, for $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$ the complex $[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ is
perfect, whereas its nonzero cohomology modules are $\mathbf F_\ell$,
which are not perfect. For this reason, the compactness proofs for
finite $A$ work with bounded flat constructible models, and standard
truncations are taken in $\Dbc$. The models exist by the next lemma.

Until the end of this section, $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, so that
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}=\Dbc$ and we can argue with constructible cohomology sheaves
and standard truncations. Recall (after
Definition [definition-lisse-sheaves]) that a $\Lambda_X$-module is
constructible exactly when it is lisse, that is locally free of
finite rank for the pro-étale topology, on each stratum of a finite
stratification of $X$. By dévissage we reduce statements about
$\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ to the simplest constructible sheaves, namely lisse sheaves
extended by zero from a stratum, the sheaves $a_!L$ of
Section [sec-Derived-functors]. This dévissage first splits a complex into its
cohomology sheaves by truncation, and then filters each constructible sheaf by
strata.

For this dévissage we need constructible sheaves to form an
abelian category (Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves]). In the proof we
reduce a morphism of lisse $E$-sheaves to a morphism of integral lattices,
and for $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we first descend the morphism to a finite $E$. To prepare for this, in the next two
lemmas we construct the lattices locally and carry out the descent.

For example, in rank one the lattices in $E$ are the
$\pi_E^m\mathcal O_E$ for $m\in\mathbf Z$, so the discrete set of lattices
is $E^\times/\mathcal O_E^\times\simeq\mathbf Z$. Hence for $L=E_X$ the
representing scheme is $\coprod_{m\in\mathbf Z}X$.

With lattices we pass from $E$ to $\mathcal O_E$. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we
first need to come down to a finite extension $E$, and on a quasi-compact
scheme this only involves finitely many matrix entries.

With these two lemmas we can show that constructible sheaves with field
coefficients form an abelian category, and obtain the filtration by
extensions by zero of lisse sheaves that the dévissage uses.

If $X$ is a curve, part (3) amounts to an exact sequence
$0\to j_!L\to F\to i_*i^*F\to0$, where $j$ is the inclusion of a dense
open subset on which $F$ is lisse, $L=j^*F$, and $i$ is the inclusion of
the finitely many closed points of the complement.

**Exercises.** (1) Compute the stalks of $a_!L$ for a locally
closed immersion $a$ and a lisse $L$. (2) For $K=\Lambda_X[1]$, in
which degree is the nonzero cohomology sheaf? (3) Show that
$j_!\Lambda_{\mathbf G_m}$ has no nonzero global sections on
$\mathbf A^1_k$.

For complexes we get the following. Since constructible sheaves form an
abelian subcategory, complexes with constructible cohomology are stable under
cones, and the filtration of part (3) together with the truncation triangles generates
them from the sheaves $a_!L$.

A morphism of $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-complexes should be defined over some finite
extension $E$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$. Since $\QbarX=\varinjlim_EE_X$, this amounts to asking
that Hom out of a constructible complex commute with a filtered colimit, where a
filtered colimit of complexes means the termwise colimit of a filtered
diagram of complexes of sheaves. We prove this continuity for complexes with
a common lower bound. In this form it is the pro-étale analogue of the classical fact that
cohomology of a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme commutes with filtered
colimits. Besides the descent to a finite coefficient field below, continuity
is used in two places. The first is the uniform bound for Ext groups, which
is proved first for integral lattices, so we need continuity for $\mathcal O_E$
as well. The second is the compactness argument for $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$
(Section [sec-Compactness-of-constructible-complexes]).

For cohomology and higher direct images the statement is
Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], which holds for every sheaf of
rings. To reach Hom, recall that a constructible sheaf has a finite filtration by sheaves $a_!L$ with
$L$ lisse on a stratum $S$ (Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves](3)). Using
sections with support in a closed subscheme, we turn Hom out of $a_!L$ into
cohomology on $S$ of a complex built from the target by $Rj_*$ and
restrictions, and the comparison then goes through a hypercohomology spectral
sequence. Because of the common lower bound, only finitely many of its
terms contribute to a given degree, and each of these terms commutes with
the colimit.

Formula (3.1) expresses Hom out of $a_!L$ through
cohomology on the stratum $S$ and the functors $i^*$, $u^*$ and $Rj_*$.
Each of these commutes with filtered colimits of uniformly bounded below
complexes, and from this we deduce the continuity of Ext.

Applied to sheaves, which are complexes in degree $0$, the lemma says that
for $M\in\Cons(X,\Lambda)$, $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, the functors
$\Ext^n(M,-)$ commute with filtered colimits of $\Lambda_X$-modules.

The lattice arguments below need the discrete valuation ring
$\mathcal O_E$ with its uniformizer $\pi_E$, but the valuation ring of
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is not of this kind. Since $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is the filtered union of the
finite extensions $E$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, we show instead that every object and every
morphism of $\Dbc(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ is defined over some finite $E$.

For $C\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},E)$ and a finite extension $E'/E$, the
extensions of scalars are the complexes $C_{E'}=E'_X\otimes_{E_X}C$ and
$C_{\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell}=\QbarX\otimes_{E_X}C$. These tensor products need not be derived, since
$E'_X$ and $\QbarX$ are flat over $E_X$.

The classical counterpart is the fact that a continuous representation of
a profinite group on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^r$, with the $\ell$-adic topology, takes
values in $\GL_r(E)$ for some finite $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$. Similarly, a constructible complex, or a morphism
between two of them, is described by finitely many matrices with entries
in $\QbarX$, and on a quasi-compact scheme finitely many such entries
already lie in a single $E_X$. We use the next lemma whenever a statement for
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is reduced to one for a finite $E$, as in
Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4) and in the uniform Ext bound
(Lemma [lemma-uniform-ext-bound]).

We pass from statements with coefficients $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ to
statements with coefficients $E$ through integral lattices. A lisse
$E_X$-module may fail to have a lattice on all of $X$, but it has one on
each stratum of a finite stratification
(Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification]), and this is enough for
dévissage arguments. In particular, from the stratified statement we obtain the integral
generators of Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4).
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification] is also the
first step in the proofs of the uniform Ext bound and of the degree bound for
proper direct image in Chapter [chap-Construction-of-f]. On a
connected normal scheme, by contrast, there is a global lattice, and lisse $E$-sheaves are
representations of $\pi_1(X,\bar x)$; we prove this where it is used, in
Proposition [proposition-lattices-representations-normal-scheme].

On the nodal curve $X$ of Example [example-lattices-nodal-curve], the
sheaf $L$ has no global lattice, and one stratification step
repairs this. On the open stratum
$X\smallsetminus\{\text{node}\}\simeq\mathbf G_m$ the torsor is
trivial, so $L$ is constant there and has a lattice. The node, with its
reduced structure, is the spectrum of a field, which is normal, and hence the
restriction of $L$ to the node has a lattice as well.

In the proof we first find a lattice after a surjective étale base change
and then push it down by the trace. For the first step we use that the
lattices in $E^r$ form a discrete set on which $\GL_r(E)$ acts continuously,
which makes the sheaf of lattices in $L$ an étale $X$-scheme. For the
second step the base change must be finite étale, which we arrange by
restricting to the strata of a finite stratification.

To deduce statements over $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ from statements over
$\mathcal O_E$, we need integral objects that generate $\Dbc(X,E)$ and
$\Dbc(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$. We also want to know that our integral constructible
complexes are those of the Stacks Project, so that results proved there
apply, and we prove both in the next lemma.
Recall from
Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion] in Section [sec-Integral-constructible-complexes] that an object lies in
$\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)=D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathcal O_E)$ precisely when it is derived complete and its
reduction modulo $\pi_E$ is a bounded constructible complex pulled back
from $X_{\acute{e}t}$.
The Stacks Project works instead with the category $\Dc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ of
[Stacks, [09C1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09C1)], built from modules over the constant sheaf $\mathcal O_E$
rather than over $\mathcal O_{E,X}$.

In (4) each $L_0$ satisfies the condition of
Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves](1), so it lies in
$\Cons(S,\mathcal O_E)$. By (3) the objects $a_!L_0$ then lie in
$\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$. Their reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$ are
bounded constructible complexes with coefficients in
$\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$, which are pulled back from $X_{\acute{e}t}$
(Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison]).

On $\mathbf A^1$, part (4) is visible in the running example. There the constant
sheaf $E_{\mathbf A^1}$ is the cone of a map $i_*E[-1]\to j_!E_{\mathbf G_m}$,
and up to shift both terms are of the form $(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$ with $L_0$ the constant
lattice $\mathcal O_E$ on the stratum.

Passing from $\mathcal O_E$ to $E$ means inverting $\ell$, and on derived
categories this is a Verdier localization.

The kernel contains more than the complexes killed by a power of $\ell$,
for example $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathcal O_{E,X}/\ell^n$. It does so even
among constructible sheaves: on $\bigsqcup_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Spec}k$,
the sheaf equal to $\mathcal O_E/\ell^n$ on the $n$-th point is killed by
inverting $\ell$ but by no power of $\ell$. When the underlying space of
$X$ is Noetherian, however, this cannot happen in $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$, and there
inverting $\ell$ amounts to tensoring the Hom groups with $E$.

The function–sheaf dictionary
(Section [sec-The-function-sheaf-dictionary],
Proposition [proposition-function-sheaf-dictionary]) turns the identity
$\#X_0(\mathbf F_q)=\sum_y\#f^{-1}(y)(\mathbf F_q)$ into a statement about
sheaves, and for this the trace function of $Rf_!K$ at a point $y$ must be
the sum of $t_K$ over the fibre $f^{-1}(y)$. This requires the stalks of
$Rf_!K$ to be the cohomology of the fibres, but nothing in the definition of
the derived direct image says so.

For a proper map $f:X\to Y$ of locally compact Hausdorff spaces the answer
is yes. Indeed, the sets $f^{-1}(V)$, for $V$ a neighbourhood of $y$, form a basis
of neighbourhoods of the compact fibre, and the cohomology of a compact
subset is the colimit of the cohomology of its neighbourhoods.

In the étale topology, however, the stalk of $R^qf_*F$ at a geometric point
$\bar y$ is the cohomology of $X\times_YY_{(\bar y)}$, where
$Y_{(\bar y)}$ is the spectrum of the strict henselization of $Y$ at
$\bar y$. This scheme is much larger than the fibre $X_{\bar y}$. For
instance, if $f$ is the identity of a curve and $\bar y$ lies over a
closed point, then it is the spectrum of a strictly henselian local ring
of dimension one, not a point.

Properness cannot be dropped. For example, let $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$
be the inclusion, $i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ the origin, and $A$
the constant sheaf on $\mathbf G_m$ with value a nonzero finite abelian
group. Then the sheaf $i^*j_*A$ is nonzero, while the base change of
$\mathbf G_m$ to the origin is empty.

For proper $f$, nevertheless, the answer is yes. More generally, pulling a proper
family back to a new base and taking its cohomology can be done in either
order. Precisely, for a cartesian square with $f$ proper, $g:Y'\to Y$ arbitrary and
$X'=X\times_YY'$, the base change map

$$
g^*Rf_*K\longrightarrow Rf'_*g'^*K
$$

is an isomorphism for every bounded below classical complex $K$ with
torsion cohomology sheaves (Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro]).
In particular, taking for $g$ a geometric point gives the stalk formula
(Corollary [corollary-cohomology-geometric-fibres]). The theorem is due to
Artin [sga4, XII–XIII], and unlike smooth base change
(Chapter [chap-Smooth-base-change]), it holds for torsion of every
order, including torsion divisible by the residue characteristics.

The content of the theorem is already visible in degree zero, where it is
a statement about connectedness. Indeed, sections of the constant sheaf $\{0,1\}$
are open and closed subsets, and for a proper scheme over a henselian
local ring, the open and closed subsets correspond to those of the closed
fibre. When $X$ is finite over a henselian local ring $R$, this says
that idempotents of the finite $R$-algebra lift from its reduction
modulo the maximal ideal, which is one form of Hensel's lemma.
Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree] extends the
statement to sections of every étale sheaf of sets. Higher degrees
then reduce to degree zero and the projective line, and from $\mathbf P^1$ the
general case follows by formal steps, through $(\mathbf P^1)^n$,
$\mathbf P^n$ and Chow's lemma
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-etale-site]).

We make these calculations on the étale site, where the classical
tools are available, and transport them to
classical complexes on the pro-étale site by the comparison
theorems of Chapter [chap-The-pro-etale-site]. For $\mathcal O_E$ we pass
to the limit over the reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-complete-integral]). Since pullback need not
preserve derived completeness, at this stage the statement for
$\mathcal O_E$ involves the completed inverse image. Once we know that
$Rp_*$ preserves constructibility
(Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-constructible-complexes]), however, the completion is
unnecessary, and we obtain the ordinary base change isomorphism on
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ for every admissible coefficient ring.

We use proper base change three times later. First, it computes the stalks of
$Rf_!$ in the trace formula
(Corollary [corollary-trace-functions-direct-image-compact]). Second, it makes
$Rf_!=Rp_*j_!$ independent of the compactification
(Proposition [proposition-construction-independence-rf-shriek]). Finally,
it bounds the Tor amplitude of $Rp_*$ with finite coefficients
(Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients]).

Proper base change asserts that a specific map, from the pullback of the
direct image to the direct image of the pullback, is an isomorphism. We
define this map and describe it on sections, so that we can compute
it on stalks.

From Definition [definition-torsion-pbc-property] on, we fix the
coefficient ring. Integral and rational coefficients are treated in Section [sec-ell-adic-coefficients].
Results for abelian sheaves apply to sheaves of modules, by the following
lemma.

Equivalently, first apply the unit
$g^*f_*F\to f'_*f'^*g^*f_*F$, and then apply $f'_*$ to
the displayed composite. This construction is natural in $F$, and it applies
equally to sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules.

On sections the map has the following simple description. A section of $g^*f_*F$ over an
étale $V\to Y'$ is represented by an étale $W\to Y$, a map $V\to
Y'\times_YW$, and a section over $X\times_YW$. Given such data, the base change map restricts
this section along

$$
X'\times_{Y'}V\longrightarrow X\times_YW,
$$

and it is the sheafification of this map of presheaves.

The derived adjunction exists because inverse image is exact and its
right adjoint preserves injectives. Note that the construction of the base change
map uses only that the square commutes; the cartesian hypothesis
is needed only when we ask whether the map is an isomorphism.

To compute (4.3), choose a bounded below
injective resolution $K\to I^\bullet$ and an injective replacement
$g'^*I^\bullet\to J^\bullet$. Then the base change map is represented by the
morphism of complexes

$$
g^*f_*I^\bullet
\longrightarrow
f'_*g'^*I^\bullet\longrightarrow f'_*J^\bullet.
\tag{4.4}
$$

Here the first arrow is the underived base change map in each degree. By
exactness of $g^*$ the source is $g^*Rf_*K$, and the last complex
computes $Rf'_*g'^*K$. The formula does not depend on the choices,
since comparison maps between injective resolutions
are unique up to homotopy. Moreover, it is the adjoint map of Definition [definition-derived-base-change-map], because
under adjunction the first arrow corresponds to the square isomorphism
followed by the counit, and the replacement map is the canonical passage
to the derived direct image.

Base change maps for composite squares are composites of base change
maps.

On the pro-étale site we use the same construction, but here $\Lambda$ may
be any coefficient ring pulled back from the point, not only a torsion
ring. For such $\Lambda$ inverse images are exact
(Lemma [lemma-inverse-image-coefficient-sheaves]), and the adjunction
$f^*\dashv Rf_*$ exists on the unbounded derived categories.

Equivalently, with $\eta_{f'}$ the unit of $f'^*\dashv Rf'_*$, it is
the composite

$$
g^*Rf_*K\xrightarrow{\eta_{f'}}
Rf'_*f'^*g^*Rf_*K\simeq Rf'_*g'^*f^*Rf_*K
\xrightarrow{Rf'_*g'^*\varepsilon_f}Rf'_*g'^*K.
$$

This is the pro-étale form of the base change map of
Definition [definition-derived-base-change-map]. It is defined for every cartesian
square (4.1), and the same construction applies to any
commutative square. Since proper and smooth base change are proved on the
étale site and then transported to the pro-étale site, we
need to know that the two maps correspond.

For a proper morphism, the underived base change map is an isomorphism
for every étale sheaf of sets, with no torsion hypothesis. The reason is
that, for a proper scheme over a henselian pair, restriction of sections to
the closed fibre is bijective
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree]).

Recall that a pair $(R,I)$, with $I$
an ideal of the ring $R$, is *henselian* if $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R$
and Hensel's lemma holds for it: every factorization modulo $I$ of a
monic polynomial into coprime monic factors lifts to a factorization in
$R$ [Stacks, [09XE](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09XE)]. A local ring with its maximal ideal
is a henselian pair exactly when it is henselian. For example, a complete
local ring is henselian.

The theorem is [Stacks, [0A0C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A0C)]. At heart it is a statement about
connectedness: every irreducible closed subset of a scheme proper
over a henselian pair meets the closed fibre in a nonempty connected subset.
This follows from Stein factorization and the
connectedness properties of henselian pairs [Stacks, [0A0B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A0B)]; over a general
affine base, Stein factorization only produces an algebra integral over
$R$, but that suffices. A topological argument on spectral spaces then turns
connectedness into bijectivity of restriction for Zariski sheaves.

Passing to étale sheaves uses finite covers, which are harmless here: a
finite cover of $Z$ remains proper over $R$, so the connectedness statement also holds after
every finite cover. Given an étale covering of $Z$, we choose a finite surjection
$Z'\to Z$ that factors through the covering Zariski locally on $Z'$, and
sections then descend along $Z'\times_ZZ'\rightrightarrows Z'$
[Stacks, [09ZF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09ZF)].

The stalks of $f_*F$ are sections over geometric fibres. Indeed, a stalk
is the set of sections over the strict localization, and the henselian
comparison identifies these with the sections over the closed fibre.

In degree zero we needed no hypothesis on the sheaf. In higher degrees we
do: proper base change fails for the constant sheaf $\mathbf Z$.
We therefore restrict to torsion sheaves.

If $\Lambda$ is torsion as an abelian group, it is
killed by the additive order of $1$, so every sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules
is torsion. The two descriptions of torsion in
Definition [definition-torsion-sheaves] agree. Indeed, the colimit is
taken in sheaves, and geometric stalks commute with colimits and finite
limits and detect isomorphisms, so the equivalence reduces to the case
of abelian groups.

Torsion is a local condition on sections: every section is killed by an
integer after passing to an étale covering. However, the integer may vary
between members of the covering. For example, the
constant sheaf $\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z$ on a nonempty scheme is torsion, but on the
disjoint union of countably many copies of the scheme its sections
include $(1/2^n)_{n\geq1}$, which has infinite order.

From now until the end of Section [sec-Proper-morphisms], $\Lambda$ denotes a
commutative ring that is torsion as an abelian group, unless another ring
is specified. For such $\Lambda$ and proper $f$ we prove
$\mathrm{PBC}_\Lambda(f)$ in Propositions [proposition-proper-base-change-projective-line]
and [proposition-proper-base-change-etale-site], and Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro] then removes the
condition on $\Lambda$.

To pass from degree zero to higher degrees we apply the degree-zero
result to an injective resolution $F\to I^\bullet$ of a sheaf $F$ on
$X$. By
Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-degree-zero]
the base change map is an isomorphism $g^*f_*I^m\simeq f'_*g'^*I^m$ in
each degree. Here the complex $g^*f_*I^\bullet$ computes $g^*Rf_*F$. The
complex $f'_*g'^*I^\bullet$, on the other hand, is $f'_*$ applied to a
resolution of $g'^*F$ that need not be injective, since $g'^*$ does not
preserve injectives. It still computes $Rf'_*g'^*F$ if every $g'^*I^m$
is $f'_*$-acyclic. We call this condition injective acyclicity, and
Theorem [theorem-pbc-injective-acyclicity] shows that it is
equivalent to proper base change. Its advantage is that, unlike the base change statement,
injective acyclicity is a vanishing condition on single sheaves.

In general $g'^*I$ is not injective, and injective acyclicity only asks
that it be $f'_*$-acyclic. By the next lemma this suffices to compute
$Rf'_*$ of the pullback of an injective resolution term by term.

To pass from sheaves killed by an integer to all torsion sheaves, we
use continuity of étale cohomology: if $u:T\to S$ is quasi-compact
and quasi-separated, then

$$
\varinjlim_i R^qu_*F_i\xrightarrow{\sim}
R^qu_*\bigl(\varinjlim_i F_i\bigr)\qquad(q\geq0)
\tag{4.7}
$$

for every filtered system of abelian
étale sheaves on $T$. The same
holds after any base change of $u$ [Stacks, [09Z1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09Z1)]. Indeed,
$R^qu_*F$ is the sheafification of
$V\mapsto H^q(T\times_SV,F|_{T\times_SV})$ on affine étale $V\to S$, and
the étale cohomology of the quasi-compact and quasi-separated
scheme $T\times_SV$ commutes with filtered colimits of abelian sheaves
[Stacks, [03Q5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q5)].
