The following criterion reduces proper base change in higher degrees to
injective acyclicity, a vanishing statement that can be checked on curves.

Let $\pi:\mathbf P^1_S\to S$ be the projection. A geometric stalk of
$R^q\pi_*F$ is the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1$ over a strictly henselian
local ring, and proper base change for $\pi$ says that it is the cohomology
of the geometric fibre, and that this group does not change under base
change.

The model case is a complete discrete valuation ring $R$. Think of
$\operatorname{Spec}R$ as a small disc around its closed point, and of
$\mathbf P^1_R$ as a family of projective lines over the disc. In
topology such a family retracts onto the central fibre, and we expect
that, for torsion sheaves, the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1_R$ is that of
its closed fibre. Besides the comparison in degree zero of
Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree], the proof
uses two theorems about henselian pairs from the Stacks Project. The first
is the affine analogue of what we want to prove.

This is [Stacks, [09ZI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09ZI)]; Gabber proves it by an effacement argument on affines.
The second fact concerns finite étale covers of a proper scheme. In degree
one it says that $\mathbf Z/n$-torsors, like sections, are determined by the
closed fibre.

The last step of the proof, the change of separably closed ground
field, uses the following facts about curves over an algebraically
closed field, which we also need later. For torsion divisible by the
characteristic, proper and affine curves behave differently, which is
why some of the assertions require $C$ to be proper.

In characteristic zero, the condition that $F$ be prime to the
characteristic in $(C_4)$ and $(C_6)$ is automatic.

The final step for the projective line compares cohomology over the
residue fields of two strict localizations, which are separably closed
but in general not algebraically closed. For this we need the following
form of $(C_7)$.

Let $R$ be a henselian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and
residue field $\kappa$, and let $i:\mathbf P^1_\kappa\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^1_R$ be the
inclusion of the closed fibre. For a sheaf $G$ on $\mathbf P^1_{R,\acute{e}t}$ write
$G_0=i^*G$. To compare the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1_R$ with that of its
closed fibre, we apply the comparison in degree zero of
Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree] to an
injective resolution. This works once we know that the restriction $I_0$
of an injective sheaf $I$ is acyclic on $\mathbf P^1_\kappa$
(Lemma [lemma-acyclicity-closed-fibre]). However, an injective sheaf is too
large to work with directly, so we approximate it by constructible sheaves
and embed these into direct images along finite morphisms, using three
standard finiteness facts about small étale topoi of quasi-compact
quasi-separated schemes.

The sheaves on the right of (4.9)
are direct images along finite morphisms, and by
Lemma [lemma-finiteness-small-etale-topoi](3) such direct
images are exact functors and commute with restriction to the closed fibre.

With this acyclicity, an injective resolution on $\mathbf P^1_R$ restricts
to an acyclic resolution on the closed fibre. Applying the degree-zero
comparison of Theorem [theorem-comparison-over-henselian-pair-degree] term by term, we obtain
the comparison in all degrees. Since the lemma only concerns sheaves killed by
a prime $\ell$, we then extend the result to all torsion sheaves by dévissage.

For example, let $R$ be strictly henselian and $n$ invertible in $R$. Then the
residue field $\kappa$ is separably closed, and passing to its algebraic
closure does not change the étale topos [Stacks, [03SI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SI)]. Hence
$H^2(\mathbf P^1_\kappa,\mu_n)\simeq\mathbf Z/n$, generated by the Kummer
class of $\mathcal O(1)$
(Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime], in
Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves]), and the proposition
says that $H^2(\mathbf P^1_R,\mu_n)$ is also $\mathbf Z/n$, generated by the
class of $\mathcal O(1)$.

Let $\pi:\mathbf P^1_S\to S$ be the projection and $\bar s$ a geometric
point of $S$. The stalk of $R^q\pi_*F$ at $\bar s$ is the cohomology of
$\mathbf P^1$ over the strict localization at $\bar s$, by
(4.12) below. By
Proposition [proposition-cohomology-p-1-over-henselian] it is therefore
the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1_{k_s}$, where $k_s$ is the separably
closed residue field. Along a base change $g:T\to S$ the residue field
grows from $k_s$ to $k_t$, so on stalks the base change map becomes the
pullback from $\mathbf P^1_{k_s}$ to $\mathbf P^1_{k_t}$, which is an
isomorphism by Lemma [lemma-extension-separably-closed-ground-field].
This is the second place where properness enters: for $\mathbf A^1$ and
$p$-torsion coefficients the corresponding map is not surjective.

The stalk formula holds for every
quasi-compact quasi-separated morphism $f:Z\to S$. For a geometric point $\bar s$ of $S$ and an abelian sheaf
$G$ on $Z_{\acute{e}t}$ we have

$$
(R^qf_*G)_{\bar s}
\simeq H^q(Z\times_SS_{(\bar s)},G|),\qquad
S_{(\bar s)}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,\bar s}.
\tag{4.12}
$$

Indeed, the stalk is the filtered
colimit of $H^q(Z\times_SV,G|)$ over pointed étale neighbourhoods
$(V,\bar v)$ of $\bar s$, and by continuity of étale cohomology this
colimit is the cohomology of the indicated limit scheme
[Stacks, [03Q9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03Q9)].

Proper base change for an arbitrary proper morphism follows from the
case of the projective line
(Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-projective-line]) by
formal steps. Finite morphisms satisfy proper base change
directly, and Lemma [lemma-composition-cancellation] shows that the
property is stable under composition and descends along proper
surjections. Descent along a proper surjection $u:X\to Y$ works because
every injective sheaf on $Y$ is a direct summand of $u_*J$ for an
injective sheaf $J$ on $X$, and the hypotheses on $u$ and on the
composite keep $u_*J$ acyclic after base change.

The steps are then as follows. First, composition gives the projection of
$(\mathbf P^1)^n$. Then descent along the finite surjection
$(\mathbf P^1)^n\to\mathbf P^n$ gives the projection of $\mathbf P^n$,
and with it every projective morphism. Finally, by Chow's lemma every proper
morphism is dominated by a projective one through a proper surjection,
so a last descent covers all proper morphisms.

For instance, if $u:\operatorname{Spec}k'\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a
separable extension of degree $d$ and $\bar w$ is a geometric point, the
formula says that $(u_*F)_{\bar w}$ is the product of the $d$ stalks of $F$
at the $d$ embeddings of $k'$ into $\Omega$ over $k$.

Stability under composition and descent along proper surjections are
best proved on the level of injective acyclicity, since by
Theorem [theorem-pbc-injective-acyclicity] it is equivalent to proper
base change and it lends itself to a spectral sequence argument.

Part (i) already gives proper base change for $(\mathbf P^1_S)^n\to S$, a
composite of projections of projective lines. To reach $\mathbf P^n_S$ we
use part (ii), and for this we need a finite surjection from
$(\mathbf P^1_S)^n$ onto $\mathbf P^n_S$ over $S$.

For $n=1$ the map $\sigma_1$ is the identity of $\mathbf P^1_S$. For $n=2$
it sends $([x_1:y_1],[x_2:y_2])$ to
$[x_1x_2:x_1y_2+y_1x_2:y_1y_2]$, and over a field it is the quotient by
swapping the two factors, of degree $2$.

We can now treat projective morphisms, since they factor as a closed
immersion followed by the projection of a projective space. By Chow's lemma
an arbitrary proper morphism is dominated by a projective one through a proper
surjection, and the cancellation of
Lemma [lemma-composition-cancellation](ii) then passes proper base
change to the proper morphism.

The six operations live on the pro-étale site, where we also meet torsion
sheaves of modules over rings that are not torsion, such as $\mathcal O_E$. So far
$\mathrm{PBC}_\Lambda(f)$ is known on the étale site only when $\Lambda$ is
torsion
(Propositions [proposition-proper-base-change-projective-line] and [proposition-proper-base-change-etale-site]).
We therefore drop the condition on $\Lambda$, keeping torsion
cohomology sheaves, and pass to classical pro-étale complexes by the
comparison theorems of Chapter [chap-The-pro-etale-site].

The reduction to torsion rings is possible because a torsion sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules is a
filtered colimit of sheaves killed by an integer $n$. Such a sheaf
has a finite filtration with quotients killed by primes $p$, and these
quotients are modules over $\Lambda/p\Lambda$. Moreover, the cohomology of a sheaf
of modules is that of its underlying abelian sheaf, so the base change
map does not depend on which ring we regard as the coefficients.

For the passage to the pro-étale site we use two facts: a classical
complex in $D^+$ is $\nu_X^*$ of an étale one
(Corollary [corollary-bounded-below-classical-complexes]), and $\nu^*$
commutes with $g^*$ and with direct images along proper maps
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images]). Taking for $g$ a geometric
point then shows that the stalks of $Rf_*K$ are the cohomology of the
geometric fibres (Corollary [corollary-cohomology-geometric-fibres]).

Suppose $\Lambda$ is killed by a positive integer, for instance that
$\Lambda$ is a finite ring. Then every complex of $\Lambda_X$-modules has
torsion cohomology sheaves, and the theorem applies to every
$K\in D^+_{\mathrm{class}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

Taking for $g$ a geometric point, we answer the question at the start of
the chapter. The only additional point is to make sense of a stalk on the
pro-étale site, where the stalk is the value of $\bar y^*Rf_*K$ on the
point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, whose topos is that of condensed sets.
We check that for a classical complex this value is the étale stalk.

Let $A$ be a finite admissible coefficient ring and $p:X\to Y$ a proper
morphism of separated schemes of finite type over the standing field $k$.
For $C\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$, proper base change identifies the geometric stalks of
$Rp_*C$ with the cohomology of the fibres. From this identification and the
classical finiteness theorem we obtain that $Rp_*C$ is constructible, with
a bound on its Tor amplitude. Both facts are needed for the passage to
integral and rational coefficients below, whereas direct sums in the unbounded
localizing categories are treated in
Section [sec-Compactness-for-finite-coefficients].

Pro-étale proper base change
(Theorem [theorem-proper-base-change-classical-pro]) concerns
classical complexes with torsion cohomology sheaves. For a finite ring $A$
it therefore applies, with $\Lambda=A$, to every $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ for
schemes of finite type over $k$, because bounded constructible complexes
on quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes are classical
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]). For
$\mathcal O_E$, however, the theorem gives proper base change only at each finite
level $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$, and we must pass to the limit. Later
statements of this kind make this passage once and for all, by the reduction
principle of Section [sec-Reduction-to-finite-coefficients]; here we make it directly.

The difficulty is completeness: the inverse image
$g^*:D(Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)\to D(Y'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$,
which is exact on sheaves of modules, need not preserve derived
completeness. We therefore complete after pulling back.

The natural map $g^*M\to\hat g^*M$ is the completion map of $g^*M$, since
$g^*$ commutes with the reductions. For constructible $M$ the completion
does nothing. Indeed, let $Y$ and $Y'$ be of finite type over
$k$ and $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\mathcal O_E)$. Then $g^*M$ lies in
$\Dbc(Y',\mathcal O_E)$ by Lemma [lemma-integral-models](3), hence it is
derived complete by
Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]
((1)$\Rightarrow$(2)), and $\hat g^*M=g^*M$. However, until we know that proper direct
image preserves constructibility, we can only state base change with the
completed inverse image.

In the proof we use the following map, which also appears in the
projection formula.

When the pullbacks are already complete, the completed base change
isomorphism is the ordinary one.

We will show that $Rp_*K$ is again constructible when $K$ is constructible.
Once this is known, the completed inverse images in
Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-complete-integral] agree with $g^*$ and $g'^*$, and the
proposition becomes the ordinary base change
isomorphism

$$
g^*Rp_*K\xrightarrow{\sim}Rp'_*g'^*K
\qquad(K\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)).
$$

Let $p:X\to Y$ be proper. We need to know, for every admissible
coefficient ring, that $Rp_*$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ and satisfies proper
base change and the projection formula there, because the construction
of $Rf_!=Rp_*\circ j_!$ in Section [sec-Direct-image-with-compact-support] starts from
these facts. For $Y=\operatorname{Spec}k$ with $k$ algebraically closed,
they say that the cohomology groups $H^i(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ of a proper $X$ are
finite-dimensional and vanish outside a bounded range of degrees.

For finite coefficients, constructibility and the Tor bound are
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients], and
the other admissible rings reduce to this case.

For $\mathcal O_E$, the complex $Rp_*K$ is derived
complete, and its reduction modulo $\pi_E$ is $Rp_*$ of the reduction of
$K$, so the integral constructibility criterion
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]) and derived Nakayama
(Lemma [lemma-reduction-derived-nakayama]) reduce everything to torsion
coefficients. For $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ it suffices to treat the
generators $(a_!L_0)[1/\ell]$. Indeed, on bounded below complexes $Rp_*$
commutes with inverting $\ell$ and with extension of scalars to finite
extensions and to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, since both are filtered colimits
(Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology]).

Verdier duality, Poincaré duality and the trace formula all rest on a
right adjoint $f^!$ of $Rf_!$. Indeed, Verdier duality (Chapter [chap-Verdier-and-Poincare-duality])
is duality with respect to the dualizing complex $a_X^!\Lambda$, where
$a_X:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the structure map, and Poincaré duality
follows from it once smooth purity
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients]) computes
$f^!$ for smooth morphisms. Similarly, the local terms of the trace formula
(Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula]) are built from $f^!$ for the two
projections of a correspondence.

The functor $Rf_!$ itself is easy to
write down. A separated morphism of finite type $f:X\to Y$ has a
compactification $f=p\circ j$, with $j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$ an
open immersion and $p:\overline X\to Y$ proper
(Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem]), and we put
$Rf_!=Rp_*\circ j_!$. This definition stays within constructible complexes because, for every admissible $\Lambda$, the functor $Rp_*$ maps $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(\overline X,\Lambda)$ into $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$. The resulting functor satisfies proper base
change and the projection formula
(Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-constructible-complexes]).

The right adjoint of $Rf_!$ is another matter. The factor $j_!$ has the right
adjoint $j^*$, but for $Rp_*$ with $p$ proper no formula for a right
adjoint is available. Even where a formula exists, it is not computed
pointwise: for a closed immersion $i$ the functor $i^!$ takes sections with
support in the closed subscheme, so the value of $i^!K$ at a point depends
on $K$ near the point, not only on its stalk there.

Grothendieck and Hartshorne built the coherent $f^!$ from local formulas
and then had to glue them. Neeman noticed, instead, that $D_{\mathrm{qc}}(X)$
is generated by compact perfect complexes and that $Rf_*$ preserves direct
sums, so that Brown representability produces $f^!$ with no formula. We follow his approach, with $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ in place of the perfect complexes.

The theorem we use is the following. Let $\mathcal T$ be a triangulated
category with arbitrary direct sums, and suppose that $\mathcal T$ is
compactly generated: there is a set $\mathcal G$ of compact objects $G$
(that is, $\Hom(G,-)$ commutes with direct sums) such that $K=0$ whenever
$\Hom(G[n],K)=0$ for all $G\in\mathcal G$ and $n\in\mathbf Z$. Then every
exact functor out of $\mathcal T$ that preserves direct sums has an exact
right adjoint [Stacks, [0A8F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8F), [0A8G](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A8G)]. The category $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is not closed
under infinite direct sums. We therefore apply the theorem to the localizing
category $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ that it generates
(Section [sec-Existence-and-finiteness-of-f]). The result is
Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image]: for every
admissible $\Lambda$ and every separated morphism of finite type $f:X\to Y$
there is an exact functor

$$
f^!:\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))\to\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)),
\qquad
\Hom(Rf_!M,N)\simeq\Hom(M,f^!N).
$$

For finite coefficients nothing is lost
by passing to the localizing category, since
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$ is equivalent to the classical derived category
$D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ (Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category]).

Everything therefore rests on the two hypotheses of the theorem: that
the objects of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ are compact in $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$,
and that $Rp_*$ preserves direct sums for proper $p$. Neither is formal,
because the summands of a direct sum may live in degrees going off to
$-\infty$. If the Ext groups out of a sheaf do not vanish in high degrees,
compactness fails even for the constant sheaf. Here is an example, outside
our conventions because $\mathbf R$ is neither finite nor algebraically
closed. Take $\ell=2$ and $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf R$. Then sheaves on $X_{\acute{e}t}$ are modules over
$\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbf C/\mathbf R)=\mathbf Z/2$, and
$\Ext^n(\mathbf F_2,\mathbf F_2)=H^n(\mathbf Z/2,\mathbf F_2)=\mathbf F_2$
for all $n\geq0$. Since products of modules are exact and the complexes
$\mathbf F_2[n]$ live in distinct degrees, the sum
$\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbf F_2[n]$ in $D(X_{\acute{e}t},\mathbf F_2)$ is also the
product. Hence

$$
\Hom\Bigl(\mathbf F_2,\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathbf F_2[n]\Bigr)
=\prod_{n\ge0}\mathbf F_2
\ne\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathbf F_2
=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\Hom(\mathbf F_2,\mathbf F_2[n]).
$$

By our conventions (Section [sec-Conventions]) the base field is finite or
algebraically closed, so its
$\ell$-cohomological dimension is finite
(Lemma [lemma-cohomological-dimension-base-field]). For finite
coefficients this rules out such examples. In that case both hypotheses
reduce to the fact that classical étale cohomology commutes with direct
sums of unbounded complexes (Section [sec-Compactness-for-finite-coefficients]).
For $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ a bound on the base is not enough, and we
prove instead a bound on $\Ext$ that depends only on the source
(Lemma [lemma-uniform-ext-bound]).

We construct $f^!$ by Brown representability, as outlined at the beginning
of this chapter, without writing it down. Brown representability needs a
category with arbitrary direct sums, and $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is not closed
under them. We therefore enlarge it to the smallest category that has them
and show that $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ compactly generates it.

For integral and rational coefficients, this is also
$\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$, by Proposition [proposition-ctf-equals-bc].

For $\mathcal O_E$ the objects of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathcal O_E)$ are derived
complete, but the localizing subcategory they generate also contains complexes that are
not. For this reason the proof of Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image](4) must show, for
integral constructible $K$, that $f^!K$ is derived complete.

By Proposition [proposition-ctf-equals-bc], the theorem holds with $\Dbc$ in
place of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ for $\Lambda=\mathbf Z_\ell,\mathcal O_E,\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

For proper $p$ we may use the trivial compactification, so that $Rp_!=Rp_*$.
By part (4), the functor $Rp_*:D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)\to D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$ then has the
right adjoint $p^!$.

Parts (1)–(3) are proved in this chapter and part (4) in
Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f]. For smooth $f$, smooth purity
(Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity]) gives a global isomorphism
$f^!\simeq f^*(d)[2d]$, compatible with trace and composition.

Brown representability produces $f^!$ once the bounded constructible
complexes are known to be compact, that is, once $\Hom(C,-)$
commutes with direct sums for constructible $C$. The difficulty is that the
summands may have cohomology in degrees going off to $-\infty$, so that
$\Hom(C,-)$ sees all the groups $\Ext^n(C,-)$ at once. For instance, over
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf R$ these groups never stop, and we saw at the
beginning of this chapter that compactness fails there. By contrast, over a finite
field they stop, as the following example shows.

The general argument rests on the same mechanism: a bound $d_C$, valid
for all constructible targets at once, beyond which $\Ext^q(C,-)$
vanishes. Until the end of Section [sec-Compactness-of-constructible-complexes], $\Lambda$ is $E$
or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, and we show that bounded constructible complexes are compact
in $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$. Since $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)=\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$,
these are the proposed compact generators. The advantage of working with $\Dbc$ is that we can use truncations
and the constructible heart, which is abelian by
Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves]. As for notation, $\Hom$ and
$\Ext$ without decoration are taken in $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, also when both arguments are
constructible sheaves, and a subscript indicates the coefficient ring where
it changes, as in the lattice arguments over $\mathcal O_E$.

By dévissage it suffices to show, for a constructible sheaf $C$ and a
family $(K_\lambda)$ of objects of $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$, that
$\bigoplus_\lambda\Hom(C,K_\lambda)\to\Hom(C,\bigoplus_\lambda K_\lambda)$
is bijective. Besides the uniform bound
$\Ext^q(C,N)=0$ for $q>d_C$ and all constructible $N$
(Lemma [lemma-uniform-ext-bound] below), we use that $\Ext^q(C,-)$
commutes with filtered colimits of complexes that vanish below a fixed
degree, in particular of sheaves
(Lemma [lemma-continuity-ext-out-constructible-complex], proved in
Section [sec-Continuity-of-Ext]).

The idea of the bound is to count cohomological dimensions modulo
$\pi_E^n$, add one degree for the derived limit over $n$, and invert
$\pi_E$ by passing to a colimit. For torsion coefficients the count is
direct. By (3.1), $R\!\operatorname{Hom}(a_!L,N)$ is the cohomology
on the stratum $S$ of a complex obtained from $N$ by restriction and
$Rj_*$. Each of these steps raises degrees by a bounded amount that
does not depend on $N$. With coefficients $E$ we cannot count in this
way, because $E$-sheaves are not torsion and $\operatorname{cd}_\ell$
only controls torsion sheaves. This is why we choose lattices on the
strata. Inverting $\pi_E$ at the end then needs the continuity of Ext
from Section [sec-Continuity-of-Ext].

The bound $d_C$ on $\Ext^q(C,-)$ is a sum of the cohomological
dimensions $\operatorname{cd}_\ell$ of Definition [definition-cohomological-dimension]. In the
proof we compute $R\!\operatorname{Hom}(a_!L_0,K)$, for a derived complete
$K\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal O_E)$, as a derived inverse limit over the
reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$. For this, the functors in
(3.1) have to commute with derived inverse limits, and
we use the next lemma with $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E$.

The main case is that of lattices. There we count cohomological
dimensions for the reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$, and we pass to the limit
by Lemma [lemma-limits-sections-support].

Suppose $C=a_!L$, with $a$ factored as $S\hookrightarrow Z\hookrightarrow X$
and $j$ the open complement of $Z$, and suppose that $L$ contains a lisse
$\mathcal O_E$-lattice. By
Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification], this holds after
refining $S$. In this case the proof gives
$d_C=\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)+\operatorname{cd}_\ell(S)+2$. One of the two extra
degrees comes from the cone defining $R\underline\Gamma_Z$, and the other from
a derived inverse limit over the reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$.

The targets in the compactness statement are direct sums of objects of
$\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$, and their cohomology sheaves need not be
constructible. Already the sheaf $\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf N}\Lambda_X$ is
not constructible, since its stalks are not finitely generated. Such
sheaves are, however, filtered colimits of constructible sheaves, and both
continuity and the uniform bound for Ext groups extend to these colimits.

Recall that the ind-category
$\operatorname{Ind}(\mathcal C)$ of a small category $\mathcal C$ has as
objects the filtered diagrams in $\mathcal C$ (“formal filtered colimits”), with
$\Hom(\varinjlim_\alpha C_\alpha,\varinjlim_\beta D_\beta)
=\varprojlim_\alpha\varinjlim_\beta\Hom(C_\alpha,D_\beta)$.
Proposition [proposition-ind-constructible-sheaves] below says that for
constructible sheaves the formal and the actual colimits agree.

The dévissage arguments need a class of sheaves that is abelian and
closed under extensions and direct sums, and on which $\Ext^q(C,-)$
behaves as on constructible sheaves. By
Proposition [proposition-ind-constructible-sheaves], the category
$\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ has the first three properties, and
Corollary [corollary-ind-heart-b] gives the last.

Since every ind-constructible sheaf is a filtered
colimit of constructible ones, the continuity of $\Ext^q(C,-)$ lets us
extend the uniform bound of Lemma [lemma-uniform-ext-bound] to the
whole category $\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$. Writing a direct sum as the filtered
colimit of its finite subsums, we also see that $\Ext^q(C,-)$ commutes
with direct sums of ind-constructible sheaves.

Objects of $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$ can be unbounded, and we do not know
a priori that their truncations stay in $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$. For this
reason, here and in
Section [sec-Direct-image-with-compact-support], we carry out truncation arguments among
complexes with ind-constructible cohomology sheaves.

On ind-constructible sheaves, $\Ext^q(C,-)$ vanishes above $d_C$ and
commutes with direct sums (Corollary [corollary-ind-heart-b]). Because
the bound $d_C$ is uniform, maps from a constructible sheaf $C$ into an
unbounded complex depend only on its cohomology sheaves in degrees
$[-d_C,0]$. This is the step that fails over $\mathbf R$ in the example
at the beginning of this chapter, where
$\Ext^n(\mathbf F_2,\mathbf F_2)\neq0$ for all $n$. Since the window has the same length for a whole family of targets, compactness follows from
the case of sheaves by induction on the length of the window.

The window $[m-d_C,m]$ in (5.3) depends on $C$ and
$m$ only, not on $K$, and so we can treat a whole
family $(K_\lambda)$ at once in the compactness theorem.

Lemma [lemma-hypotheses-brown-representability] combines this theorem with the
corresponding statements for the other coefficient rings and shows that a
small skeleton of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ is a set of compact generators of
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$.

In this section the coefficient ring is a finite admissible ring $A$.
Proper direct image preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ by Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients], and we now show that the constructible generators are compact and that proper
direct image preserves direct sums on the localizing categories. In both
cases we reduce to the classical étale theory, using bounded flat
constructible models and the fact that étale cohomology commutes with
direct sums of unbounded complexes.

Finite Tor amplitude is a property of the complex, not of its cohomology
sheaves: the cohomology sheaves of an object of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ can have infinite
Tor amplitude (Section [sec-Finite-Tor-amplitude]). The property can,
however, be read off from a flat model. This is why we work with the
bounded flat models of Lemma [lemma-flat-models-generators].

For finite coefficients the localizing category is a familiar one: the
next proposition shows that it is the classical unbounded derived
category of the étale site. In particular, $f^!$ with finite
coefficients is defined on all of $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$. The proposition also
shows that $Rf_!$, once it is defined as $Rp_*j_!$ by a compactification in
Section [sec-Direct-image-with-compact-support], is computed by the classical functor
$Rp_{\acute{e}t,*}j_{\acute{e}t,!}$ on the étale site.

Proper direct image already preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ by
Proposition [proposition-proper-direct-image-finite-coefficients].
Its extension to the localizing categories therefore only needs preservation of
arbitrary direct sums. By the comparison just proved, this reduces
to the unbounded étale statement.

The trace formula needs a relative version of cohomology with compact
supports, whose stalks are the groups $H^i_c$ of the fibres. Consider
first a locally compact Hausdorff space
$X$ with an open embedding $j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$ into a compact
space. A section of $j_!F$ is a section of $F$ that vanishes near
$\overline X\setminus X$, and $H^i_c(X,F)=H^i(\overline X,j_!F)$. For
example, for $X=\mathbf R$ and $\overline X$ the circle, we find
$H^1_c(\mathbf R,\mathbf Z)=\mathbf Z$.

The definition by sections with compact support has no direct analogue
for schemes, because every scheme of finite type over $k$ is quasi-compact, and the
algebraic substitute for compactness is properness, which is a property
of a morphism and not of a subset. The two-step form, however, does carry over.
In it, the functor $j_!$ imposes compact support along the open immersion, while for
a proper map $p$, as for a map of spaces with compact fibres, the direct
image with compact supports is the ordinary direct image $Rp_*$. By
proper base change, the result does not depend on the compactification
(Proposition [proposition-construction-independence-rf-shriek]).
Proper base change also identifies
the stalks of $Rf_!$ with the compactly supported cohomology of the
fibres (Corollary [corollary-trace-functions-direct-image-compact]).

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a separated morphism of finite type. For a
compactification $f=p\circ j$, with $j$ an open immersion and $p$ proper,
we define $Rf_!=Rp_*\circ j_!$. We must show that this functor
preserves direct sums. In the following subsection we take
$\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, so that
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))=\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$.

To apply Brown representability, we need $Rf_!$ to preserve arbitrary
direct sums. Since $j_!$ is a left adjoint, it does. The question is
therefore whether $Rp_*$ preserves direct sums for proper $p$.
For complexes with a common lower and upper bound, this would follow from
finiteness of $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(p)$. However, the summands of a direct
sum in $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ need not have any common bound. As in the
proof of compactness, we use a uniform bound instead. Let $d$ bound
the fibre dimensions of $p$. We show that $R^qp_*$ vanishes on
$\IndCons(X,\Lambda)$ for $q>2d+1$. This means that $\mathcal H^q(Rp_*K)$ depends
only on the cohomology of $K$ in degrees $[q-2d-1,q]$.

We prove the bound on sections over
affine weakly contractible objects and then pass to colimits. For this
we use the continuity of pro-étale cohomology,
Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], applied to sheaves, which
are complexes vanishing below degree $0$. It says that for a quasi-compact
and quasi-separated morphism $p$ the functors $R^qp_*$ on sheaves of
modules commute with filtered colimits. Since a direct sum is the
filtered colimit of its finite subsums, they also commute with direct sums.

We also use the following description of $R^qp_*$. If $V\to Y$ is an
affine weakly contractible object and $X_V=X\times_YV$, then
$\Gamma(V,-)$ is exact (Corollary [corollary-evaluation-weakly-contractible-objects](1)), and hence

$$
(R^qp_*M)(V)=H^q((X_V)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},M|_{X_V}).
\tag{5.5}
$$

Since such $V$ form a basis of $Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, a sheaf on $Y_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$
vanishes if its sections over all of them vanish.

By a stratification we reduce the lemma to the extension
by zero of a lisse $\mathcal O_E$-lattice on a stratum. Its reductions
modulo $\pi_E^n$ are torsion sheaves, for which the classical bound $2d$ holds. In the passage to the limit over $n$, the $\varprojlim^1$ term raises the bound by one, to $2d+1$. The remaining steps, inverting $\ell$, extending scalars to $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ and passing to ind-objects, are filtered colimits. By
Corollary [corollary-continuity-cohomology], the bound survives each of them.

The bound $2d+1$ is not sharp. For example, for the structure map of a smooth projective curve over $\bar k$, where $d=1$, the lemma only says that
cohomology vanishes above degree $3$, while in fact it vanishes above
degree $2$. The extra degree does no harm, because the arguments
below only need a bound that does not depend on the sheaf. As in the
compactness argument, such a bound passes from sheaves to unbounded complexes.

For $\mathcal O_E$ the rational arguments for compactness
(Theorem [theorem-compactness-rational-coefficients]) and for direct
sums (Lemma [lemma-proper-direct-image-unbounded-complexes]) go
through with one change. Integral constructible sheaves are no
longer locally free on strata; for example,
$\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E$ is constructible. But $\mathcal O_E$ is a
discrete valuation ring, so they have free resolutions of length one.
The estimates only use the resulting Tor amplitude $[-1,0]$.

For instance, $\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E$ is the cokernel of
$\pi_E:\mathcal O_{E,X}\to\mathcal O_{E,X}$, so it has Tor amplitude
$[-1,0]$. Its dual $\cHom(\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E,\mathcal O_{E,X})=
(\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E)[-1]$ has Tor amplitude $[0,1]$, as in (3).

The dévissage in the proof of compactness also needs that the operations it
uses preserve $\Dbc(-,\mathcal O_E)$.

With these two lemmas, the integral case of the two hypotheses of Brown
representability can be checked by following the rational proofs.

These are the facts about $\mathcal O_E$ that we use in the construction
of $Rf_!$ below.

From now on, $\Lambda$ is any admissible coefficient ring.
Lemmas [lemma-uniform-bound-proper-direct-image] and [lemma-proper-direct-image-unbounded-complexes] only treat $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, but we use them only through the fact that $Rp_*$ preserves direct
sums for proper $p$. For finite and integral coefficients this fact was proved separately, and the next proof collects the references.

Proper base change shows, by one and the same argument, that $Rp_*\circ j_!$
does not depend on the compactification and is compatible with
composition and base change. The comparison maps are maps out of an
extension by zero $j_!K$. They are therefore determined by their restriction to
$X$, where they are the identity. On the closed complement of $X$,
proper base change shows that both sides vanish, and so the map is an
isomorphism. For instance, if $h:Z'\to Z$ is proper and
$h^{-1}(X)=X$, then $Rh_*j'_!K$ restricted to $Z\setminus X$ is the direct
image of the restriction of $j'_!K$ to $Z'\setminus X$, which is zero.
Since proper base change is only known on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$, we first show that all
the functors involved preserve direct sums, so that it suffices to check
isomorphisms on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ (Lemma [lemma-checking-isomorphisms-constructible-complexes]).

That both factors of $Rp_*\circ j_!$ preserve the localizing
categories comes from the definition of $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ in the following
form: if the objects of $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ with some property form
a triangulated subcategory that is closed under direct sums and contains
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$, then every object of $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$ has the
property.

The proper base change map and the comparison maps between compactifications
are natural transformations between exact functors on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda))$
that preserve direct sums. To show that such a transformation is an
isomorphism, it suffices to check this on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda)$.

For a cartesian square with $p$ proper, the base change map
$g^*Rp_*\to Rp'_*g'^*$ of (4.5) is a map of functors
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(Y'_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. The lemma lets us pass
from $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$, where it is an isomorphism, to
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))$.

The comparisons between compactifications below are the proper direct
images of the unique maps out of $j_!K$ that restrict to the identity on
$X$. They are unique because, for an open immersion $j:X\to Z$, the functor
$j_!$ is left adjoint to $j^*$ on the pro-étale derived categories, so
that a map out of $j_!K$ is determined by its restriction to $X$.

To make $Rf_!$ functorial in $f$, and for the base change
theorems later on, we need composition and base change isomorphisms. The
base change map is defined as follows. Let $f:X\to Y$ be separated of
finite type with compactification $f=p\circ j$, let $v:Y'\to Y$ be a
morphism, and let $f':X'\to Y'$, $u:X'\to X$, $p':\overline X'\to Y'$,
$j':X'\to\overline X'$ and $v':\overline X'\to\overline X$ be the base
changes, so that $f'=p'\circ j'$ is a compactification. For
$K\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, the isomorphism
$j'^*v'^*j_!K\simeq u^*j^*j_!K=u^*K$ corresponds under $j'_!\dashv j'^*$ to
a map $j'_!u^*K\to v'^*j_!K$. This map is an isomorphism: it is the identity
on the open $X'$, and both sides vanish on the closed complement
$v'^{-1}(\overline X\setminus X)=\overline X'\setminus X'$ [Stacks, [09AH](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09AH)]. The
base change map for $Rf_!$ is the composite

$$
v^*Rp_*j_!K\longrightarrow Rp'_*v'^*j_!K\simeq Rp'_*j'_!u^*K
\tag{5.8}
$$

of the base change map (4.5) for $p$ and $Rp'_*$ of the
inverse of this isomorphism.

On a space, a section with compact support is in particular a section,
and so compactly supported cohomology maps to ordinary cohomology. The algebraic counterpart is a map $Rf_!\to Rf_*$, which is an isomorphism for proper $f$, and we need it to be compatible with the composition maps
just constructed: in Section [sec-Conventions-2] this is one of the compatibilities that the comparison with the étale site has to respect.

Let $\Lambda$ be an admissible coefficient ring and fix $N$ in
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))$. Since the functor $Rf_!$ preserves direct sums (Proposition [proposition-construction-independence-rf-shriek]),
the functor $M\mapsto\Hom(Rf_!M,N)$ turns direct sums into products. If
the objects of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ are compact generators of the
localizing category, Brown representability produces an object $f^!N$
representing it. The next lemma checks this hypothesis for every admissible $\Lambda$; for $\mathcal O_E$ it uses the compactness proved in
Subsection [subsec-Integral-coefficients] by reduction to torsion coefficients.

Compactness enters a second time. The functor $Rf_!$ also maps
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ into $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$, so it sends the compact
generators to compact objects. For this reason the adjoint $f^!$
preserves direct sums (Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image]).

With the hypotheses checked, the theorem below follows from Brown
representability in the form recalled at the start of the chapter.

Brown representability gives $f^!$ one morphism at a time. To compute it in Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f], however, we factor $f$ locally. The two are linked by uniqueness of adjoints: an isomorphism between composites of left adjoints, such as $Rg_!\circ Rf_!\simeq R(gf)_!$ or
$Rf_!=Rp_*\circ j_!$, gives an isomorphism between the right
adjoints, composed in the opposite order. Since $j^!=j^*$ for an open
immersion $j$, it follows that $f^!$ is local on $X$ and on $Y$. For example, a smooth $f$ is
locally the composite of an étale map and a projection
$\mathbf A^n_Y\to Y$. By composition and locality, $f^!$ is then
determined by its values on these two kinds of maps.

Base change for $f^!$ does not follow in this way. Passing to right
adjoints in the base change isomorphism $v^*Rf_!\simeq Rf'_!u^*$ relates
$f^!Rv_*$ and $Ru_*f'^!$. These involve direct images, not the
inverse images $u^*f^!$ and $f'^!v^*$ that one wants to compare. We prove
base change for smooth morphisms in
Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism]. That
$f^!$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ is proved in
Theorems [theorem-f-shriek-finite-coefficients] and [theorem-f-shriek-ell-adic-coefficients].

Once we know that $f^!$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda)$
(Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f]), these isomorphisms restrict to the
full subcategories $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda)$, and the same statements hold for
the adjunction between $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ and $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$.

Brown representability gave us $f^!$
(Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image]), but only as a
functor

$$
f^!:\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda))\longrightarrow\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda))
$$

for $f:X\to Y$ separated of finite type and $\Lambda$ an admissible coefficient
ring. It tells us nothing about the values of $f^!$. A priori, $f^!$ of a
constructible complex is just some object of the large category on the right,
possibly unbounded and with cohomology sheaves that are not constructible.

The rest of the notes needs more than this. For example, Verdier duality (Chapter [chap-Verdier-and-Poincare-duality]) says that
$\mathbb D_X=\cHom(-,a_X^!\Lambda)$ is an involution of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$,
and this makes sense only if the dualizing complex $a_X^!\Lambda$ lies in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$. Similarly, the local terms of the trace formula are defined through the isomorphism
$\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)\simeq c^!(K\boxtimes\mathbb D_XK)$ for a
correspondence $c=(c_1,c_2)$
(Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism]), which also needs $f^!$
to preserve constructible complexes. In this chapter we prove what both need
(part (4) of Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image]): $f^!$ maps
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$ into $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$. A universal property cannot give this, so we have to compute $f^!$, and the computation is local.

By
Proposition [proposition-composition-open-restriction-compactifications-f],
the functor $f^!$ is compatible with composition, equals $j^*$ for an open
immersion $j$, and is local on $X$ and on $Y$. We may therefore assume that
$Y$ is affine and that $f$ is a closed immersion into some $\mathbf A^n_Y$
followed by the projection to $Y$. Since $\mathbf A^n_Y$ is open in
$(\mathbf P^1_Y)^n$, and $(\mathbf P^1_Y)^n\to Y$ is a composite of $n$
projections $\mathbf P^1_T\to T$, two cases remain.

For the projection $p:\mathbf P^1_T\to T$ we can write the adjunction
down, and we find $p^!=p^*(1)[2]$
(Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]). Here the counit is the trace $Rp_*\Lambda(1)[2]\to\Lambda$, and the unit is the cycle class of the diagonal in $\mathbf P^1_T\times_T\mathbf P^1_T$. The triangle identities then hold because the diagonal meets each fibre of either projection
in a single point. For a closed immersion $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ with open complement $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, on the other hand, the functor $i^!$ takes sections with support in
$Z$, and it sits in the localization triangle

$$
i_*i^!K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K\longrightarrow .
$$

Let $K$ be constructible. Then $j^*K$ is constructible, and since $i^*i_*\simeq\mathrm{id}$ and
$i_*$ preserves constructibility, $i^!K$ is constructible exactly when the
third term $Rj_*j^*K$ is. So the constructibility of $f^!$ comes down to one
question: does direct image along an open immersion preserve bounded
constructible complexes and, with finite coefficients, finite Tor
amplitude? Proper base change does not help here, since $j$ is not
proper.

The answer is not formal, because $Rj_*$, and with it $i^!$, sees more
than the stalks of $K$ on $Z$: it sees the cohomology of $K$ on a punctured
neighbourhood of $Z$. For the origin $i:0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ over
an algebraically closed field, the stalk of $Rj_*\Lambda$ at $0$ is the
cohomology of a punctured disc, which the Kummer covers of $\mathbf G_m$
compute to be $\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-1]$, and the triangle gives
$i^!\Lambda\simeq\Lambda(-1)[-2]$, whereas $i^*\Lambda=\Lambda$
(Example [example-closed-support] below).

Over a field the answer is Deligne's finiteness theorem in
SGA 4$\tfrac12$ [sga4-5], and we follow his proof. Its induction on dimension leads to fibrations over bases of positive dimension, so
Deligne proves a statement in families over a base $S$. In families,
however, the formation of $Rj_*$ need not commute with base change. Let
$S=\mathbf A^1$ with coordinate $t$, let $Y=\mathbf A^2$ with coordinates
$(t,x)$, viewed over $S$, and let $j$ be the inclusion of
$X=Y\setminus\{(0,0)\}$. By purity
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients], proved in
Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity] below), the punctured strict henselization of
$Y$ at the origin has cohomology $\Lambda$ in degree $0$ and
$\Lambda(-2)$ in degree $3$ only. Hence $R^1j_*\Lambda=0$. On the fibre
over $t=0$, however, $j$ becomes $\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$,
whose $R^1j_*\Lambda$ is $\Lambda(-1)$ at the origin. Since over $t\neq0$ the map $j$ is an isomorphism, base change fails only at $t=0$.

Deligne's generic base change theorem says that this is the general
picture. Let $j:X\hookrightarrow Y$ be an open immersion of schemes of
finite type over an integral base $S$ of finite type over $k$, and let $F$
be a constructible $\Fell$-sheaf on $X$. Then there is a nonempty open
$S_0\subset S$ over which $Rj_*F$ is bounded constructible and its
formation commutes with base change along every $T\to S_0$ of finite type
(Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj]; Deligne
proves more). Over $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$ the only nonempty open is $S$
itself, so we obtain the finiteness and base change of $Rj_*$
over a field (Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field]).

The projective line returns in the proof of the generic theorem. There we
must control $Rf_*L$ for smooth $f$ and locally constant $L$, and we do so
through the formula for $f^!$ of a smooth morphism (Section [sec-Smooth-morphisms]).

For finite coefficients
(Theorem [theorem-f-shriek-finite-coefficients]) we also bound the Tor
amplitude of $Rj_*K$: it grows by at most $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)$
(Proposition [proposition-open-direct-image-preserves-finite]). For
integral and rational coefficients we have $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}=\Dbc$, and we reduce
modulo a uniformizer. This works because an integral complex is
constructible if it is derived complete with constructible reduction
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]). Only the
adjunction for the projective line resists this reduction. Its unit and
counit must be constructed as single morphisms with
$\mathcal O_E$-coefficients
(Proposition [proposition-ell-adic-cycle-class-diagonal]). The result is
Theorem [theorem-f-shriek-ell-adic-coefficients].

Until Section [sec-Finite-coefficients-2] the coefficient ring is a finite
commutative $\ell$-primary ring, which we denote by $A$. With such coefficients nothing is lost by computing on the étale site. For $X$ of
finite type over $k$, the comparison functor

$$
\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)\longrightarrow D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)
$$

is fully faithful
(Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients]),
and it identifies $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ with the localizing category
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A))$ on which $f^!$ was constructed
(Proposition [proposition-comparison-etale-derived-category]). It also
identifies the constructible complexes on the two sites
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]). In the following
sections we therefore work in $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$, and every result is
transported to the pro-étale site by $\nu_X^*$.

This transport is harmless because $\nu^*$ identifies all the operations we use with their étale
counterparts, compatibly with units and counits
(Lemma [lemma-comparison-direct-images-compatibilities]). These
operations are the cohomology
(Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison]); the direct
images and their base change maps, also for unbounded complexes
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-direct-images] and
Proposition [proposition-unbounded-comparison-finite-coefficients]); and
the inverse images, tensor products, extension by zero and the localization
triangles (Section [sec-Direct-images]). Moreover, by
Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison], finite Tor
amplitude can be checked on the étale site.

We write $\Dbc(X,A)$ also for the bounded constructible objects of
$D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$, which correspond to those of the pro-étale category.
For a separated morphism of finite type $f:X\to S$, the
functor $Rf_!$ and its right adjoint $f^!$ of
Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image] correspond to
the functors $Rf_!$ and $f^!$ between $D(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ and $D(S_{\acute{e}t},A)$,
and the two adjunctions correspond. Accordingly, from now on $g^*$, $Rf_*$, $Rf_!$, $f^!$ and $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ denote the functors on the étale derived
categories.

Below we apply
Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek], stated on
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,A))$, to the étale functors. This is legitimate because the
comparison identifies the composition maps of
Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek] on the two
sites: the refinement maps (5.7) and the
open–proper interchange (5.9) are
characterized by their restriction to the open. The comparison also preserves the counits defining base change and the inverse counits defining
forgetting supports
(Proposition [proposition-forgetting-supports-composition]). Taking right adjoints, we see that it identifies the composition maps for $f^!$ as well.

Except in Lemmas [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor], [lemma-cohomology-projective-line-trace]
and [lemma-coordinate-projections], which allow more general bases as stated
there, all schemes and base changes are of finite type over $k$.

We use three classical theorems about the étale site.

It is an isomorphism for smooth $f$
(Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism]).
The global isomorphism $f^!\simeq f^*(d)[2d]$ for smooth $f$ of relative
dimension $d$, and its compatibility with composition, are treated with smooth purity in
Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity].
Here we need only its restriction to charts $U\to\mathbf A^d_S$.

Let $p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S$ be the projection. We construct the adjunction $Rp_*\dashv p^*(1)[2]$ from two maps: the counit is a trace
$Rp_*A(1)[2]\to A$, obtained from the cohomology of $\mathbf P^1$, and the unit is the cycle class of the diagonal in
$\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S$, a special case of the cycle class of
an effective Cartier divisor. Both triangle identities say that pushing the
class of the diagonal forward along either projection
$\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1\to\mathbf P^1$ and applying the trace gives
$1$. This holds because the diagonal meets each fibre of either projection
in a single point.

In topology the same two maps appear. For instance, for a bundle $E\to B$ with fibre
$S^2$, integration over the fibre $H^2(S^2)\to\mathbf Z$ is the counit of
Poincaré duality on the fibres, and the unit is the Thom class of the
diagonal of $E\times_BE$, which is Poincaré dual to the identity
correspondence. In étale cohomology, by contrast, the fundamental class of a point on
$\mathbf P^1$ comes from a line bundle through the Kummer sequence. So both maps are
built from line bundles: the trace comes from $c_1(\mathcal O(1))$, and the
class of the diagonal comes from the divisor $x_0y_1-x_1y_0=0$.

For every other morphism, we shall compute $f^!$ from this adjunction, from
$j_!\dashv j^*$ for open immersions and from localization.

The lemma will be applied twice: to the section at infinity of $\mathbf P^1_S$,
which gives the trace, and to the diagonal of
$\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S$, which gives the unit. The
first application enters the computation of $Rp_*A$.

Over $S=\operatorname{Spec}\bar k$, (6.4) reads
$R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_{\bar k},A)\simeq A\oplus A(-1)[-2]$.
Here the shift $[-2]$ places the second summand in degree $2$, so that it is
$H^2$, and the twist $(-1)$ records how Galois acts on $H^2$: the
Kummer map identifies $H^2$ with
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1)\otimes\mu_{\ell^r}^{\otimes-1}$, that is, with
$A(-1)$. Twisting by $(1)$ and shifting by $[2]$ therefore moves this summand to degree $0$ with trivial twist. The map $\operatorname{Tr}_p$ is the projection onto this summand, and it sends the class
of a point to $1$. It is the counit of
$Rp_*\dashv p^*(1)[2]$ in
Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]. After its lift to
$\mathcal O_E$ in Subsection [subsec-The-projective-line], it is also the trace
map $\operatorname{Tr}_p$ of $\mathbf P^1$ in
Section [sec-Compatibilities].

As a check of the twist, let us work over $\mathbf F_q$. The geometric
Frobenius acts by $1$ on $H^0$ and by $q$ on $H^2=A(-1)$. The
alternating sum of the traces is $1+q=\#\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_q)$, as in
Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function].

**Exercise.** Using the localization sequence of
Example [example-running-example], show that
$H^1_c(\mathbf G_{m,\bar k},A)\simeq A$ and
$H^2_c(\mathbf G_{m,\bar k},A)\simeq A(-1)$, and that these
are the only nonzero groups.

The adjunction is built from the trace
$\operatorname{Tr}_p$ of (6.5) and the cycle class of the
diagonal provided by Lemma [lemma-cycle-class-cartier-divisor]. As in all of this part of the section, we compute on the étale sites
(Section [sec-Conventions-2]). Let
$p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S$ be the projection, let $p_1,p_2:\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S\to\mathbf P^1_S$ be the
two projections and let
$\Delta:\mathbf P^1_S\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^1_S\times_S\mathbf P^1_S$
be the diagonal. For $i=1,2$, the projection $p_i$ is a projective line over
the other factor, with trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{p_i}$ given by
(6.5). Both triangle identities rest on the following
computation.

We build the unit and counit of the adjunction from $\delta$ and from
the trace. For $M\in D((\mathbf P^1_S)_{\acute{e}t},A)$,
let

$$
\begin{split}
\eta_M:M
&=Rp_{2*}\Delta_*M\\
&\longrightarrow Rp_{2*}\bigl(p_1^*M(1)[2]\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }p^*Rp_*M(1)[2] .
\end{split}
\tag{6.7}
$$

Here the first arrow is $Rp_{2*}$ applied to $\delta\otimes p_1^*M$,
where we use the projection formula
$\Delta_*M=\Delta_*A\otimes^{\mathbf L}p_1^*M$, and the second arrow is the proper base change isomorphism $p^*Rp_*\simeq Rp_{2*}p_1^*$. For $N\in D(S_{\acute{e}t},A)$,
let

$$
\varepsilon_N:Rp_*\bigl(p^*N(1)[2]\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }N\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}
Rp_*A_{\mathbf P^1_S}(1)[2]
\xrightarrow{1\otimes \operatorname{Tr}_p}N,
\tag{6.8}
$$

where the first arrow is the projection formula. These maps exist for
unbounded complexes by [Stacks, [0F0C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F0C), [0GL5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GL5)].

Let $f:X\to S$ be smooth of relative dimension $d$. Extending the formula
$p^!=p^*(1)[2]$ for $p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S$, we show in
Proposition [proposition-exceptional-inverse-image-smooth-morphism] that
$f^!N\simeq f^*N\otimes^{\mathbf L}\omega_f$ with $\omega_f$ locally
isomorphic to $A(d)[2d]$. We need this formula in the proof of generic constructibility below, because
it must control $Rf_*L$ for a locally constant sheaf $L$. Indeed, we know nothing about $Rf_*L$ directly, whereas the finiteness theorem and proper base change control $Rf_!$. With the formula, however, the adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ becomes a duality between
$Rf_*L$ and $Rf_!$ of the twisted dual of $L$
(Lemma [lemma-smooth-morphisms-locally-constant-sheaves]). On a manifold, Poincaré duality exchanges ordinary and compactly supported cohomology in the same way.

For example, let $f:\mathbf G_m\to\operatorname{Spec}\bar k$ and
$L=A=\Fell$. The localization triangle for the origin of
$\mathbf A^1$ and $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1_{\bar k},A)\simeq A(-1)[-2]$
give $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf G_m,A)\simeq\fib\bigl(A(-1)[-2]\to A\bigr)$.
Hence $H^1_c=A$ and $H^2_c=A(-1)$ are the only nonzero groups, and
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf G_m,A(1)[2])$ has cohomology $A(1)$ in degree
$-1$ and $A$ in degree $0$. Its dual has $A$ in degree $0$ and
$A(-1)$ in degree $1$. This is indeed $R\Gamma(\mathbf G_m,A)$,
with $H^1=A(-1)$ given by the Kummer torsors.

The duality must also commute with base change. This requires the base
change isomorphism $g'^*f^!\simeq f'^!g^*$ for smooth $f$, and for it the
local form $\omega_f|_U\simeq A_U(d)[2d]$ on charts suffices. A global identification of $\omega_f$ with $A_X(d)[2d]$, by contrast, needs a trace map for $f$; it is part of smooth purity
(Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity]). For the local form we use that, Zariski locally on $X$ and $S$, a smooth morphism $f:X\to S$ factors as an étale morphism to some
$\mathbf A^d_S$ followed by the projection to $S$, and the next lemma treats these two kinds of morphisms.

Part (2) generalizes $j^!=j^*$ from open immersions to étale maps.
For $d=1$, $k$ algebraically closed and $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$, part (1) says that
$\Hom(R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,F),M)=\Hom(F,M_{\mathbf A^1}(1)[2])$. For
$F=A$ both sides are $\Hom(A,M(1)[2])$, consistent with the example above: the left
side because $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1_{\bar k},A)\simeq A(-1)[-2]$, and the right side because
$R\Gamma(\mathbf A^1_{\bar k},A)=A$.

Applied along local charts $U\xrightarrow{e}\mathbf A^d_S\to S$, the two
parts of the lemma compute $f^!$ locally on $X$ for every smooth $f$. The
proposition below turns this into two global statements, a tensor formula
and base change.

In Step 2 of the proof of Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj], the next
lemma is applied to $f=bj$, with $b:Y\to S$ projective and
$j:X\hookrightarrow Y$ open.

To control $Rj_*F$ for an open immersion $j:X\hookrightarrow Y$ over $S$,
with $Y$ projective over $S$, we cover most of $Y$ by opens where the
induction hypothesis applies and treat the rest separately. On a chart $Y_\alpha$, a coordinate function $t:Y_\alpha\to\mathbf A^1_S$ lets us view $X\cap Y_\alpha$ over the new base $\mathbf A^1_S$, over which its generic fibre has one
dimension less. Hence the induction hypothesis in
Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj] gives
constructibility and base change over a dense open of $\mathbf A^1_S$.
The preimages of these opens, however, do not cover $Y$. Take for instance
$Y=\mathbf P^1_S$ with the two standard charts: there a point is missed only if
each of the coordinates $x$ and $1/x$ defined there takes an excluded
value. After shrinking $S$, the leftover set is therefore a closed subset
finite over $S$. Lemma [lemma-coordinate-projections] shows that the same holds in general.

On the leftover finite part we cannot argue by dimension again. We do not
have to, since a finite direct image is exact and conservative. This means
that on a subset finite over $S$, the constructibility of a sheaf can be
read off from its direct image to $S$.
Lemma [lemma-detection-proper-direct-image] turns this into a
criterion. If a complex is already constructible away from such a subset,
a proper direct image to $S$ detects whether it is constructible
everywhere. In the smooth case this direct image is $R(bj)_*F$, which
Lemma [lemma-smooth-morphisms-locally-constant-sheaves] controls. For
this reason the induction passes through the smooth case first.

The next lemma produces such a finite complement. Projections to
coordinate lines lower the dimension of the generic fibre, and the
subset that they do not cover becomes finite over a smaller base.

Let $j:X\hookrightarrow Y$ be an open immersion of schemes over an
integral base $S$, and let $F$ be a constructible $\Fell$-sheaf on $X$.
For such data, Deligne's generic base change theorem says that over a dense open of $S$
the complex $Rj_*F$ is bounded constructible and its formation commutes
with base change. In particular, over a field it gives the finiteness of $Rj_*$ (Corollary [corollary-open-direct-image-over-field]), and this is all that the
computation of $f^!$ requires. On the other hand, the punctured plane over the $t$-line, discussed at the beginning of this chapter, shows that we cannot ask for
more than a dense open.

In characteristic $p$ the generic fibre need not contain a smooth dense
open. For example, let $X=\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_p}$ map to the $t$-line
by $x\mapsto x^p$. The generic fibre is
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_p(t^{1/p})$, which is not smooth over
$\mathbf F_p(t)$. For this reason Step 3 of the proof of
Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj] below allows a finite universal
homeomorphism of the base. Such a map changes neither the étale topoi
nor the conclusion.

We fix notation for base change. With $j$ as above and a morphism $T\to S$, we write
$j_T:X_T\hookrightarrow Y_T$ for the base change and
$g_X:X_T\to X$, $g_Y:Y_T\to Y$ for the projections. The base change map $g_Y^*Rj_*K\to Rj_{T,*}g_X^*K$ is then the map (4.5).

The proof of Theorem [theorem-generic-constructibility-base-change-rj]
is an induction on the dimension of the generic fibre, in three steps. The next three lemmas are the parts of this proof that do not use the
induction hypothesis, and each serves one step.
First, Lemma [lemma-extension-across-finite-subset] is Step 2: if $X$ is smooth and $F$ locally constant, it extends the conclusion from an open
$G$ with complement finite over $S$, provided by Step 1, across that complement.
Next, Lemma [lemma-universal-homeomorphism-base] allows Step 3 to replace
$S$ by a finite universal homeomorphism, as the example above requires.
Lemma [lemma-generic-smooth-open] then provides, after this
replacement, the dense open $V$ of Step 3, smooth with $F$ locally
constant, whose complement has a smaller generic fibre.

The only nonempty open of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is
$\operatorname{Spec}k$ itself, and hence over a field the theorem holds
without any shrinking.

Let $A$ be a finite commutative $\ell$-primary ring and $f$ a separated
morphism of finite type. We show that the right adjoint $f^!$ of
Theorem [theorem-existence-exceptional-inverse-image] preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,A)$
(Theorem [theorem-f-shriek-finite-coefficients]). By the reduction at the start
of this chapter and by the previous section, we only have to show
that direct image along an open immersion $j$ preserves finite Tor
amplitude. The upper end of the Tor amplitude grows by at most the
$\ell$-cohomological dimension $\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)$ of
Definition [definition-cohomological-dimension]. This dimension is
finite for morphisms of finite type over $k$.

Finite Tor amplitude cannot be checked on cohomology sheaves, since these
may have infinite Tor dimension over $A$: for $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$, already the
constant sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$ has infinite Tor dimension. We therefore obtain the Tor
bounds below from flat models. By [Stacks, [0F4M](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F4M)], every object of
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ is represented by a bounded complex of constructible flat
$A$-sheaves. On the strata of a finite stratification, such a model is
locally a bounded complex of finite projective $A$-modules.

For $j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ over $\bar k$ and $K=A$, the
stalk of $Rj_*A$ at the origin is the cohomology of the punctured
strict henselization. It has cohomology $A$ in degree $0$ and $A(-1)$ in
degree $1$, both free. It is therefore isomorphic to $A\oplus A(-1)[-1]$.
The Tor amplitude grows from $[0,0]$ to $[0,1]$, and the bound of the
proposition, with $d=\operatorname{cd}_\ell(j)=1$, is attained.

Combining the proposition with the computation of $p^!$ for affine space,
we obtain the main theorem for finite coefficients.

For $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we have $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}=\Dbc$, and we
show that $f^!$ preserves $\Dbc$. The argument of
Section [sec-Finite-coefficients-2] uses two geometric facts, namely the finiteness of
$Rj_*$ for an open immersion and the adjunction for the projective line, and we deduce both from the case of torsion coefficients. This is possible because an integral complex lies in $\Dbc$ if it is derived complete with constructible reduction modulo
$\pi_E$ (Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]), and rational
complexes are built from integral ones (Lemma [lemma-integral-models](4)).

For $Rj_*$ this reduction is immediate, since $Rj_*$ commutes with
$R\varprojlim$ and with cones (Proposition [proposition-direct-image-along-open-immersion]).
For the projective line it is not, because the unit and counit are morphisms, and a compatible family of morphisms modulo $\ell^n$ need not come from a
morphism of the limits. We therefore construct the class of the diagonal
and the trace once, at the level of inverse systems
(Subsection [subsec-The-projective-line]). Besides this, the integral case uses the structure of integral constructible complexes and the fact that proper
direct image preserves direct sums (Subsection [subsec-Integral-coefficients]).

With torsion coefficients, $Rq_*\dashv q^*(1)[2]$ is built from the cycle
class $\delta:\Delta_*\Lambda\to\Lambda(1)[2]$ of the diagonal of
$\mathbf P^1_Y\times_Y\mathbf P^1_Y$, the trace
$\operatorname{Tr}_q:Rq_*\Lambda(1)[2]\to\Lambda$ and two identities between
them (Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line]). The classes modulo $\ell^n$, however, are morphisms in different derived categories, compatible under reduction. Since morphisms in a derived category are not computed levelwise,
such a family need not give a morphism after $R\varprojlim$. We therefore
construct the class once, in the derived category of inverse systems of
sheaves, and then pass to the limit.

To turn $\delta_\Lambda$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_q$ into an adjunction we
repeat the torsion calculation. It used the projection formula and
proper base change on the categories where $Rq_*$ and $q^*(1)[2]$ act.
Proper base change on $\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}})$ is
Proposition [proposition-proper-base-change-localizing-categories], and we extend the projection
formula in the same way.

Now the torsion proof of the adjunction for $\mathbf P^1$ can be run
with $\delta_\Lambda$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_q$, once $s_1=s_2=1$ is known.

For admissible $\Lambda$ and a closed immersion $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$
with complement $j$, the local cohomology functor $R\underline\Gamma_Z$
is right adjoint to $i_*=Ri_!$
(Lemma [lemma-sections-support-closed-subscheme](1)). Hence
$i^!\simeq R\underline\Gamma_Z$, and $i^!$ is computed by the localization triangle

$$
i_*i^!K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K
\longrightarrow i_*i^!K[1].
$$

For $\mathcal O_E$ we also need the projection formula on the localizing
categories, which follows from the case of $\Dbc$ and the results of
Subsection [subsec-Integral-coefficients].

We can now repeat the argument for finite coefficients with
$\mathcal O_E$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

The parts of Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image] were proved
separately for each kind of coefficient ring, and we collect the references.

Smooth base change and Verdier biduality will be proved with torsion
coefficients, as were proper base change and Deligne's theorem on $Rj_*$.
The Weil conjectures, however, need them over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, where Frobenius
eigenvalues live. This chapter provides the principle that carries every
such statement across. A canonical map built from the six operations is an
isomorphism for all admissible $\Lambda$ as soon as it is one for every
finite ring (Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients]).

For $\mathcal O_E$ both sides are derived complete, and by derived Nakayama
it suffices to check the map modulo $\pi_E$. For instance, let $K$ be in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathcal O_E)$. Both sides of the biduality map
$K\to\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK$ are derived complete. Modulo $\pi_E$, moreover, the map is biduality with $\mathbf F_E$-coefficients, which is an isomorphism.
Hence the biduality map is an isomorphism. From there we pass to $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$: every object over $E$ is built by cones from integral models with $\ell$ inverted, and every object over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is defined over a finite extension $E$
(Proposition [proposition-dctf-x-qbar-2-colimit]). In this way smooth base
change (Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-all-admissible]) and Verdier
biduality (Theorem [theorem-verdier-biduality]) pass from torsion to
$\ell$-adic coefficients.

The principle needs two things, and neither is formal. First, both sides
must lie in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda)$. Thus all six operations must preserve these
categories, and not only $Rf_!$ and $f^!$, which we now control
(Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image],
Section [sec-Proof-of-the-theorem]). Second, each operation must commute with
change of coefficients. For $f^*$ and $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ this is clear, since a change of coefficients is itself a tensor product. For a right adjoint, however, it is a real statement. For example, consider a map of finite rings $A\to B$; then the isomorphism $R\Gamma(X,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_AB\simeq
R\Gamma(X,K\otimes^{\mathbf L}_AB)$ is a projection formula, and it uses
finite cohomological dimension. Next consider $\mathcal O_E\to E$. Since
$E$ is the colimit of the modules $\pi_E^{-n}\mathcal O_E$, the comparison
says that $Rf_*$ commutes with a filtered colimit. This holds because the
terms are uniformly bounded below.

Internal Hom causes a further difficulty, because it hides the exceptional
inverse image. For a closed immersion $i$ we have

$$
\cHom(i_*\Lambda,K)\simeq i_*i^!K .
$$

Before we can say anything about $\cHom(K,L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}\Lambda'$, we
must therefore know how $i^!$ behaves under change of coefficients. The comparison map for $f^!$ is defined by adjunction, and to show that it is an isomorphism we compute $f^!$ once more, for a closed immersion and for
$\mathbf P^1$. For $\mathbf P^1$, for instance, it comes down to the compatibility of the
cycle class of the diagonal and of the trace with change of coefficients
(Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients]).

The first requirement needs no construction: on the pro-étale site the
six operations are the ordinary derived functors of sheaves of modules, and
we only check that they preserve $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda)$
(Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf]).
For torsion coefficients on the étale site, these finiteness theorems are in SGA 4 and
SGA 4$\tfrac12$ [sga4], [sga4-5]. In general, the work is in $Rf_*$ and in $\cHom$ (Section [sec-Stability-of-Dbctf]). There, a compactification reduces $Rf_*$ to proper direct image and $Rj_*$, while the formula above and its
analogue for open immersions express $\cHom$ through $Ra_*$, $a^!$ and
tensor products. Tensor products, finally, are handled by the local description of a
complex of finite Tor amplitude: on the strata of a finite stratification
it is locally $\Lambda_S\otimes P$ with $P$ perfect
(Section [sec-Finite-Tor-amplitude]).

From now on we work in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ without further comment and pass between
$\mathcal O_E$, $E$, $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ and finite rings whenever a statement is easier for
one of them, as in the trace formula and in the proof of the Weil conjectures.

Pullback and tensor product are local, and they preserve the description
of a complex of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ on the strata of a stratification as
$\Lambda_S\otimes P$ with $P$ perfect. The direct images and internal Hom
are not local. For the direct images a compactification $f=pj$ helps.
Since $Rf_*=Rp_*Rj_*$, it suffices to know proper direct image and direct
image along an open immersion. Internal Hom hides both of these
operations and also $f^!$. For an open immersion $j$ we have
$\cHom(j_!\Lambda,K)=Rj_*j^*K$, and for a closed immersion $i$ we have
the formula $\cHom(i_*\Lambda,K)\simeq i_*i^!K$ recalled at the beginning
of this chapter. If $a$ is the locally closed immersion of a
stratum and $P$ is a perfect complex on it, the formula

$$
\cHom(a_!P,K)\simeq Ra_*\bigl(P^\vee\otimes^{\mathbf L}a^!K\bigr)
$$

combines the two. Every constructible complex is built from objects
$a_!P$ by finitely many cones. By this formula, internal Hom is therefore
expressed through $Ra_*$, $a^!$ and tensor products. This is one reason we
needed $f^!$ on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ first. The result is Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf].

Smooth base change for $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is deduced from the integral case
by extending scalars (Chapter [chap-Smooth-base-change]), and later proofs
often argue in the same way, through the reduction principle of
Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients]. For
this the six operations must commute with extension of scalars. For pullback, extension by zero and tensor product this is formal, since
extension of scalars is itself a tensor product. For $Rf_*$, by contrast, it rests on finite cohomological dimension and on continuity, and for $f^!$ it rests on a
second computation of $f^!$, for closed immersions and for $\mathbf P^1$.
These results are collected in Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients].

A change of coefficients is derived extension of scalars along a map
of condensed rings, pulled back to $X$. For a map $\Lambda\to\Lambda'$ write

$$
K_{\Lambda'}=\Lambda'_X\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\Lambda_X}K.
$$

This functor $D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda')$ is left
adjoint to the exact restriction of scalars
$D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda')\to D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.
We consider the following maps of coefficient rings:

1. any homomorphism $A\to B$ of finite admissible rings;
2. the maps $\mathcal O_E\to\mathcal O_F$ and $E\to F$ for a
   finite extension $F/E$ inside $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$;
3. localization $\mathcal O_E\to E$, inclusions $E\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$,
   and continuous maps $\mathcal O_E\to A$ to finite admissible rings,
   such as the reductions $\mathcal O_E\to\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ (continuity
   is needed for the map to define a map of condensed rings);
4. composites of these maps.

For $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$, the list contains $\mathbf Z_\ell\to\mathcal O_F$, $\mathbf Q_\ell\to F$, $\mathbf Z_\ell\to\mathbf Q_\ell$,
$\mathbf Z_\ell\to A$ and $\mathbf Q_\ell\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Thus these maps connect all the admissible
coefficient rings. Note that the map $A\to B$ in (1) need not be flat, and for this reason extension of scalars is derived. As a consequence, the comparison isomorphisms below hold for complexes but not degree by degree, as the following example
shows.

Before stating the result we fix the comparison maps. Items (1)–(3) below, for $f^*$, $j_!$ and $\otimes^{\mathbf L}$, are identifications of
two composites of left adjoints. The remaining items are derived from these: items (4) and (6), for $Rf_*$ and $\cHom$, are adjoint transposes of the inverse of (1), respectively (3),
composed with the extension of scalars of the counit, and item (5)
combines (4) for $p$ with (2).

The map for $f^!$ is defined in the same way, as the transpose of a
counit, once we know that (5) is an isomorphism; see
(7.1) below. We now show, one
operation at a time, that these maps are isomorphisms on $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$.

In the lemmas below it suffices to treat the maps in items (1)–(3) of the
list of coefficient maps, that is, all maps except composites. Indeed,
extension of scalars along a composite of two maps of the list is the
composite of the two extensions. Each map in
Definition [definition-change-of-coefficients-maps] for the composite
is the composite of the maps for the two factors. For (1)–(3) this holds by the coherence of the associativity isomorphisms, and for (4)–(6) it holds because the adjoint transpose of a composite of such maps is the composite
of the transposes.

We can now define the comparison map for $f^!$. Let $f:X\to Y$ be
separated of finite type and $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$. Then
$f^!K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ by Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image],
and we let

$$
\beta_{f,K}:(f^!K)_{\Lambda'}\longrightarrow f^!(K_{\Lambda'})
\tag{7.1}
$$

be the transpose, under the adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ on
$\Loc(D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(-,\Lambda'))$, of the morphism

$$
Rf_!((f^!K)_{\Lambda'})
\xrightarrow{\sim}(Rf_!f^!K)_{\Lambda'}
\xrightarrow{(\varepsilon_K)_{\Lambda'}}K_{\Lambda'},
$$

whose first arrow is the inverse of the isomorphism of
Lemma [lemma-change-coefficients-compact-support].

The proof below uses three properties of $\beta$. First, the maps $\beta$
are compatible with composition: under $(gf)^!\simeq f^!g^!$ we have
$\beta_{gf,K}=f^!(\beta_{g,K})\circ\beta_{f,g^!K}$. This holds because the
counit of a composite adjunction is the composite of the counits, and
because the comparison for $Rf_!$ is compatible with the composition
isomorphisms of
Proposition [proposition-composition-base-change-rf-shriek]; both are
determined by their restrictions to the open subscheme. Second, let
$\Lambda\to\Lambda'\to\Lambda''$ be a composite of two maps of the list.
Then $\beta$ for the composite is $\beta$ for $\Lambda'\to\Lambda''$
composed with the extension of scalars to $\Lambda''$ of $\beta$ for
$\Lambda\to\Lambda'$. Indeed, both are transposes of the composite of the
extended counits and the comparisons for $Rf_!$. Third, for an open
immersion $u$, under $u^!\simeq u^*$, the map $\beta_{u,K}$ is the
isomorphism of Definition [definition-change-of-coefficients-maps](1).
Both are transposes of the same map under $u_!\dashv u^*$.

The lemmas combine into the following statement, which is the form in
which change of coefficients is used later.

Without the condition on Tor amplitude, change of coefficients would not
preserve the categories. For instance, let $X$ be a geometric point. The
sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$ belongs to $\Dbc(X,\mathbf Z/\ell^2)$ but not to
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\mathbf Z/\ell^2)$. Its extension of scalars
$\mathbf F_\ell\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{\mathbf Z/\ell^2}\mathbf F_\ell$ is
unbounded.

For coefficients in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$,
Lemma [lemma-descent-finite-coefficient-field] expresses $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$
in terms of the categories $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,E)$ for finite $E$. As a statement about
ordinary categories, it reads as follows.
