$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$ be smooth of pure relative dimensions
$d$ and $e$. Composing the finite adjunctions, we identify
$(g\circ f)_A^!$ with $f_A^!g_A^!$, compatibly with
$R(g\circ f)_{!,A}\simeq Rg_{!,A}Rf_{!,A}$, and the counit of the
composite adjunction is the composite of the two counits.

The change-of-coefficients maps are compatible with composition: for $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$ and
$K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Z_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$,

$$
b^{g\circ f}(M)=Rg_{!,B}(b^f(M))\circ b^g(Rf_{!,A}M),
\qquad
c^{g\circ f}(K)=f_B^!c^g(K)\circ c^f(g_A^!K).
$$

The first identity holds on each free term of a resolution of $B$ over $A$,
since the composition isomorphism is natural, and the totalization in
Lemma [lemma-sp-reduction] extends it to arbitrary $A\to B$. We get the
second by transposing under the composite adjunction.

On towers, the composition isomorphism for $Rf_{!,\bullet}$ is built from
the same constructions. The isomorphism
$(g\circ f)^!_\bullet\simeq f^!_\bullet g^!_\bullet$ is the isomorphism of
right adjoints given by the composite adjunction on towers. Since evaluation at
level $n$ carries the counits on towers to the finite counits
(Proposition [proposition-sp-tower-geometric]), the level $n$ of
these isomorphisms is the finite one, and by the identities above they commute
with the transition maps, which are built from $b$ and $c$. Applying
$R\varprojlim$ gives the integral composition isomorphisms

$$
R(g\circ f)_{!,\mathcal O_E}\simeq Rg_{!,\mathcal O_E}Rf_{!,\mathcal O_E},
\qquad
(g\circ f)_{\mathcal O_E}^{!}\simeq f_{\mathcal O_E}^{!}g_{\mathcal O_E}^{!},
$$

between $\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ and $\Dbc(Z,\mathcal O_E)$; for $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$ the
coefficients are $\mathbf Z_\ell$. As for base change, inverting $\ell$ and extending
scalars give the composition isomorphisms with coefficients $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.
These isomorphisms $(g\circ f)^!\simeq f^!g^!$ are the composition isomorphisms of
Proposition [proposition-composition-open-restriction-compactifications-f](1).
Indeed, the isomorphism of that proposition is characterized by the following
property: it carries the counit of $R(g\circ f)_!\dashv(g\circ f)^!$,
composed with the composition isomorphism for $Rf_!$, to the composite of
the counits for $f$ and $g$. By uniqueness of adjoints it therefore
suffices to check this property for every coefficient ring. With finite
coefficients it holds by definition. On towers the composition isomorphism
is the one of the composite adjunction, so in $D(\operatorname{Tow})$ it
carries the counit on towers of $g\circ f$ to the composite of the counits
on towers. By the comparison following the construction of $e_{f,\bullet}$
in Subsection [subsec-Base-change-and-composition], $\operatorname{red}$ carries the counits
and the composition isomorphism for $Rf_!$ with coefficients $\mathcal O_E$
to those on towers, and applying $R\varprojlim$ gives the property over
$\mathcal O_E$. Similarly, the same comparison shows that extension of scalars along
$\mathcal O_E\to E$ and $E\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ carries the counits and the
composition isomorphisms for $Rf_!$ to the corresponding ones, which gives
the property over $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

With these composition isomorphisms in place for every coefficient ring,
the statement takes the following form. In topological terms it says that
the orientation of a composite of submersions is the product of the
orientations.

On a compact oriented manifold of dimension $n$, Poincaré duality
pairs $H^i$ with $H^{n-i}$ by cup product followed by integration
$H^n(M)\to\mathbf R$, which sends the class of a point to $1$. To obtain
the Poincaré pairing of Weil's axiom (c) we need the analogue of
integration. By adjunction we already have a map, the counit
$Rf_!f^!K\to K$, but its source involves $f^!$, which we only know
through its universal property. Composing with $\gamma_f$ replaces
$f^!K$ by the twisted and shifted inverse image, so the result is a map out of
compactly supported cohomology of an explicit complex. For example, for $X$ smooth of
dimension $d$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ and $K=\Lambda$, it is
a map $H_c^{2d}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X(d))\to\Lambda$. Here the twist cannot be
dropped, for the reason explained before
Definition [definition-tate-twists]: geometric Frobenius acts on
$H^2(\mathbf P^1_k,\mathbf Z_\ell)$ by $q$, so only the twisted trace map commutes
with Frobenius (Section [sec-Weil-complexes]). The trace map is used in the Poincaré pairing
(Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality]) and the trace isomorphism in top
degree (Theorem [theorem-trace-isomorphism-top-degree]).

Let $f:X\to Y$ be smooth of pure relative dimension $d$, and let
$\Lambda$ be any admissible coefficient ring. We omit $\Lambda$ from
the notation and let $\varepsilon_f(K):Rf_!f^!K\to K$ be the counit
of the adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ between $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$
and $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$.

By the first part of the remark, for affine space the trace map is the explicit integration along lines
built from $\mathbf P^1$. The trace map of a general smooth morphism is
glued from such charts, and the next statement says that the gluing
respects composition, as integration over the fibres of a composite of
submersions is iterated integration.

The last compatibility compares the maps $\gamma_f$ for different coefficient
rings. For a map $A\to B$ of finite rings the comparison
$c_{A,B}$ of Lemma [lemma-sp-reduction] is the change-of-coefficients map
for $f^!$ of Proposition [proposition-six-operations-change-coefficients],
since both are defined as the transpose of the extended counit composed with
the inverse of the comparison for $Rf_!$.

The proof of Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients]
assembles the constructions above; only the trace normalization (1) with
integral coefficients needs a separate argument.

For the structure morphism of a smooth scheme, Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients] computes the
dualizing complex used in Poincaré duality
(Chapter [chap-Verdier-and-Poincare-duality]).

As a check, take $X=\mathbf A^1_k$ with $k$ algebraically closed. The
adjunction gives
$\Hom(R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda),\Lambda[-2])\simeq\Hom(\Lambda_X,a^!\Lambda[-2])
=H^0(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda(1))=\Lambda(1)$, and indeed
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda)=\Lambda(-1)[-2]$.

If $k$ is algebraically closed, taking global sections turns the trace
$\operatorname{Tr}_a(\Lambda_{\operatorname{Spec}k})$ into a map
$R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X(d))[2d]\to\Lambda$, and taking $H^0$ of
it gives the trace map
$H_c^{2d}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X(d))\to\Lambda$.
For example, for $X=\mathbf P^1_k$ it sends $c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ to $1$.

The main estimate in the proof of the Deligne–Laumon theorem, the goal of
Part III, is an upper bound: every Frobenius eigenvalue on $H^i$ of a smooth proper variety has
absolute value at most $q^{i/2}$. The lower bound comes from Weil's axiom (c).
Suppose that the cup product pairs $H^i$ with $H^{2d-i}$ perfectly and that
Frobenius multiplies the pairing by $q^d$. Then the eigenvalues $\alpha$ in
degree $i$ correspond to the eigenvalues $q^d/\alpha$ in degree $2d-i$, so the
upper bound for $q^d/\alpha$ is a lower bound for $\alpha$
(Chapter [chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures]). The same relation gives the functional
equation of the zeta function (Corollary [corollary-functional-equation]). This
chapter proves axiom (c).

For the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ of the introduction,
duality says that the two eigenvalues on $H^1$ have product $3$
(Example [example-running-example-duality]), but it does not bound them
separately.

For a compact oriented manifold $M$ of dimension $n$ the model is Verdier's.
Let $a:M\to\mathrm{pt}$ be the map to a point. Then $\omega_M=a^!\mathbf Z$ is
the orientation sheaf placed in degree $-n$, and the functor
$\mathbb D=\cHom(-,\omega_M)$ is an involution on constructible complexes.
Duality is the isomorphism
$R\Gamma(M,\mathbb DK)\simeq R\!\operatorname{Hom}(R\Gamma_c(M,K),\mathbf Z)$.

We follow the same route. For a scheme $X$ with structure map
$a_X:X\to s=\operatorname{Spec}k$, put $\omega_X=a_X^!\Lambda_s$ and
$\mathbb D_X=\cHom(-,\omega_X)$
(Definition [definition-verdier-dual-evaluation]). The adjunction
$Ra_{X!}\dashv a_X^!$ gives for free a pairing of $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ with
$R\Gamma(X,\mathbb D_XK)$, and it also gives two exchange formulas

$$
\mathbb D_YRf_!\simeq Rf_*\mathbb D_X,\qquad
f^!\mathbb D_Y\simeq\mathbb D_Xf^*
$$

(Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas]). Over an algebraically
closed field the first formula, for $a_X$, is global duality,
$R\Gamma(X,\mathbb D_XK)\simeq R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(X,K),\Lambda)$
(Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality]). For smooth $X$ of pure dimension
$d$, smooth purity gives $\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$, and global duality
becomes Poincaré duality: the pairing

$$
R\Gamma_c(X,K)\otimes^{\mathbf L}R\Gamma(X,K^\vee(d))[2d]
\longrightarrow\Lambda,\qquad K^\vee=\cHom(K,\Lambda_X),
$$

built from evaluation and the trace map, is perfect
(Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality]).

For $X$ smooth, proper and connected and $\Lambda$ a field, this will give a
perfect cup product pairing
$H^i\times H^{2d-i}\to\Lambda(-d)$ compatible with Frobenius
(Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing] and
Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius] in Section [sec-Weil-complexes]).

What the adjunction does not give is that the pairing is perfect. For that we need
Verdier biduality: the map $K\to\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK$ is an isomorphism for every
$K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ and every admissible $\Lambda$
(Theorem [theorem-verdier-biduality]). Then $\mathbb D_X$ is an anti-equivalence, and
applying the first two exchange formulas to $\mathbb D_XK$ gives the other two,
$\mathbb D_YRf_*\simeq Rf_!\mathbb D_X$ and $\mathbb D_Xf^!\simeq f^*\mathbb D_Y$
(Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas]).

Biduality cannot be proved by dévissage, because dualizing a piece $t_!P$,
with $P$ locally constant on a smooth stratum $t:T\hookrightarrow X$, twice needs the exchange formula $\mathbb D_XRt_*\simeq t_!\mathbb D_T$, which
is itself a consequence of biduality (Section [sec-Verdier-biduality]). We argue
instead by induction on dimension, restricting to the geometric generic fibre of
a function, where duality commutes with restriction up to the twist $(1)[2]$
(Lemmas [lemma-restriction-geometric-generic-fibre]
and [lemma-double-dual-geometric-generic-fibre]).

Global duality was announced by Verdier and proved by Deligne
[sga4, XVIII]. Biduality for constructible complexes over a field is due to
Deligne [sga4-5, Th. finitude].

A perfect pairing of complexes induces perfect pairings of cohomology modules
over a field (Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields]), but not
over $\mathcal O_E$ (Remark [remark-duality-cohomology-groups-over-oe]).
For this reason we formulate the duality statements in the derived category, as perfect pairings of
perfect complexes (Definition [definition-perfect-pairing]).

After defining the dualizing complex $\omega_X$,
the Verdier dual $\mathbb D_X$ and the double-dual map
$\delta_K:K\to\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK$, we prove the two exchange
formulas that need only adjunctions
(Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas]). They say
that $\mathbb D$ turns $Rf_!$ into $Rf_*$
and $f^*$ into $f^!$. For example, for $f=a_X$ and $K=\Lambda_X$ the first says that
$R\Gamma(X,\omega_X)$ is the dual of $R\Gamma_c(X,\Lambda)$, as for the
homology of a manifold. The other half, with the roles of $!$ and $*$
reversed, needs biduality.

The induction in the proof of Theorem [theorem-verdier-biduality]
ends on the geometric point, the case $\dim X=0$. There we want duality to be
the duality of finite projective modules, and for this constructible
complexes must be perfect. Over $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ this is a real
condition; for instance, the module $\mathbf Z/\ell$ has infinite projective
dimension over $\mathbf Z/\ell^2$. This is why we require the coefficients to
have finite Tor dimension. With this requirement,
Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point] shows that $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ of the
point is exactly the category of perfect complexes.

On the point, then, duality is the linear duality of perfect complexes,
and the double dual is the identity. On a general $X$, however, we dualize into
$a_X^!\Lambda_s$ instead of $\Lambda$. By the adjunction
$Ra_{X!}\dashv a_X^!$, maps into $a_X^!\Lambda_s$ are the same as
linear forms on compactly supported cohomology.

On the geometric point we have $\omega_s=\Lambda_s$, so $\delta$ is the
evaluation map of Lemma [lemma-perfect-complexes-geometric-point].

The proof of biduality uses only the exchange formulas that follow from
adjunctions. We first write down the comparison maps. Let $f:X\to Y$
be a morphism, $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ and $L\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y,\Lambda)$. The
map

$$
Rf_*\cHom_X(K,f^!L)\longrightarrow\cHom_Y(Rf_!K,L)
\tag{10.1}
$$

is the tensor–Hom adjoint of the composite

$$
\begin{aligned}
Rf_*\cHom_X(K,f^!L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}Rf_!K
&\simeq Rf_!\bigl(f^*Rf_*\cHom_X(K,f^!L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}K\bigr)\\
&\longrightarrow Rf_!\bigl(\cHom_X(K,f^!L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}K\bigr)
\longrightarrow Rf_!f^!L\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_f}L
\end{aligned}
$$

of the projection formula, the counit of $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, evaluation
and the counit $\varepsilon_f$ of $Rf_!\dashv f^!$. In particular, for $L=\omega_Y$, using $f^!\omega_Y=f^!a_Y^!\Lambda_s=\omega_X$, it is a map
$Rf_*\mathbb D_XK\to\mathbb D_YRf_!K$. The map
$f^!\mathbb D_YL\to\mathbb D_Xf^*L$ is the tensor–Hom adjoint of the
map $f^!\mathbb D_YL\otimes^{\mathbf L}f^*L\to f^!\omega_Y=\omega_X$
that corresponds under $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ to

$$
Rf_!(f^!\mathbb D_YL\otimes^{\mathbf L}f^*L)
\simeq Rf_!f^!\mathbb D_YL\otimes^{\mathbf L}L
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_f\otimes1}\mathbb D_YL\otimes^{\mathbf L}L
\longrightarrow\omega_Y,
$$

the last arrow being evaluation.

On a smooth curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field, with
$\omega_C=\Lambda_C(1)[2]$, biduality is easy to see for the two basic kinds of sheaves. Indeed, for a locally constant sheaf $L$ of free
$\Lambda$-modules the dual is $L^\vee(1)[2]$, and dualizing twice gives
back $L$. For a skyscraper $i_*M$ at a closed point $i:x\to C$, the
exchange formula $\mathbb D_Ci_*\simeq i_*\mathbb D_x$ for the proper
map $i$ shows that the dual is $i_*\mathbb D_xM$, so biduality reduces
to biduality on the point. In general, a constructible sheaf is an extension of $i_*M$ by $j_!L$, where
now $i$ is the inclusion of a finite set of closed points and $L$ is
locally constant on its complement $j:U\hookrightarrow C$. The open piece is the difficult one: we have $\mathbb D_C(j_!L)\simeq Rj_*\mathbb D_UL$, and to dualize $Rj_*$ we would need
the second exchange formula. That formula, however, depends on biduality. In dimension one this can still be checked by hand, using the cohomology of the henselian punctured disc, whereas in higher dimension the direct images
$Rj_*$ along the boundary of a stratum have no such description.

The proof of Theorem [theorem-verdier-biduality] needs two preliminary facts. First, Lemma [lemma-verdier-duality-preserves-constructibility] shows that
$\mathbb D_X$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$. Second, Lemmas [lemma-restriction-geometric-generic-fibre] and [lemma-double-dual-geometric-generic-fibre] show that $\mathbb D_X$ and
$\delta$ commute with restriction to a geometric generic fibre up to the
twist $(1)[2]$, and this twist cancels in the double dual.

We prove biduality by induction on dimension, restricting the
double-dual morphism to the geometric generic fibre of a map to
$\mathbf A^1_k$. This needs comparison maps between the operations on
a scheme and on its geometric generic fibre. Let $B/k$ be a
smooth integral curve and $\bar\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\overline{k(B)}$, and for a $B$-scheme $T$ of finite type let
$g_T:T_{\bar\eta}=T\times_B\bar\eta\to T$ be the projection, with
pullback $g_T^*:D(T_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)\to D(T_{\bar\eta,\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$, where $A$
is a finite coefficient ring. First, for a morphism $h:T\to X$ of $B$-schemes
the base change map $g_X^*Rh_*L\to Rh_{\bar\eta,*}g_T^*L$ is
adjoint to $g_T^*$ of the counit $h^*Rh_*L\to L$. Second, for a closed immersion $i:Z\to X$ of $B$-schemes, the pullback
$i_{\bar\eta,*}g_Z^*i^!M=g_X^*i_*i^!M\to g_X^*M$ of the counit
corresponds under $i_{\bar\eta,*}\dashv i_{\bar\eta}^!$ to a map $g_Z^*i^!M\to i_{\bar\eta}^!g_X^*M$. Finally, for internal Hom,
$g_X^*\cHom_X(K,M)\to\cHom_{X_{\bar\eta}}(g_X^*K,g_X^*M)$ is the
tensor–Hom adjoint of $g_X^*$ of evaluation
$\cHom_X(K,M)\otimes^{\mathbf L}K\to M$. The next lemma says that these
maps are isomorphisms.

For $B=\mathbf A^1_k$ the dualizing complex changes by a twist under
restriction to the geometric generic fibre, and this twist cancels in
the double dual.
With these lemmas we can prove biduality.

Since $\mathbb D_X$ is now an anti-equivalence, we can dualize the formulas of
Lemma [lemma-internal-adjunction-two-exchange-formulas]. This gives the two
exchange formulas with the roles of $!$ and $*$ reversed.

Over an algebraically closed field, $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(s,\Lambda)$ is the category
of perfect $\Lambda$-complexes, and on it $\mathbb D_s$ is
$R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,\Lambda)$. For $f=a_X$ the first two Verdier exchange
formulas therefore become dualities between compactly supported and ordinary
cohomology. This is global Verdier duality
(Theorem [theorem-global-verdier-duality]). It holds for every $X$ of
finite type, smooth or not.

For smooth $X$ of pure dimension $d$ we have $\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$.
For locally perfect $K$ the Verdier dual is therefore the ordinary dual $K^\vee$
twisted by $(d)[2d]$, and the counit of $Ra_{X!}\dashv a_X^!$ becomes the trace
map of Definition [definition-trace-map]. In this way global duality becomes
cup product followed by the trace.

Over a finite base field $k$ the same argument gives us isomorphisms
$Ra_{X*}\mathbb D_XK\simeq\mathbb D_sRa_{X!}K$ and
$Ra_{X!}\mathbb D_XK\simeq\mathbb D_sRa_{X*}K$ in $D(s_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$,
with $\mathbb D_s=\cHom_s(-,\Lambda_s)$. These are the first two formulas
of Corollary [corollary-verdier-exchange-formulas] for $f=a_X$. After
base change to an algebraic closure they become the isomorphisms of the
theorem.

The first isomorphism of the theorem is the adjoint of a pairing. We give a
name to pairings whose adjoint is an isomorphism.

For smooth $X$, Corollary [corollary-dualizing-complex-smooth-scheme] identifies $\omega_X$ with
$\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$, and global duality becomes the Poincaré pairing
of Weil's axiom (c).

For $X=\mathbf A^1$ and $K=\Lambda$ the theorem pairs
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda)=\Lambda(-1)[-2]$ with
$R\Gamma(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda(1))[2]=\Lambda(1)[2]$, and the pairing is
the trace $H^2_c(\mathbf A^1,\Lambda(1))\simeq\Lambda$. Over a field we
can pass from this statement about complexes to statements about the
individual cohomology groups.

The only property of a field used in this proof is that
$R\!\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,\Lambda)$ commutes with taking cohomology.

For constant coefficients on a smooth, proper and connected $X$, we expect
$H^{2d}(X,\Lambda_X(d))$ to be free of rank one, generated by the class of a
point, as for a manifold. We use this normalization
in the trace formula and in point counting.

For a compact connected oriented manifold this is the statement that
integration $H^n(M)\to\mathbf R$ is an isomorphism sending a point to
$1$. Here the statement also has an arithmetic meaning, because geometric Frobenius
acts on $\Lambda(-d)$ by $q^d$. Once we know that the trace map
commutes with Frobenius (Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius]), the theorem below
says that Frobenius acts on $H^{2d}$ by $q^d$ and on $H^0$ trivially.
These give the factors $1-T$ and $1-q^dT$ of the zeta function.

Combined with
Corollary [corollary-degreewise-duality-over-fields], the theorem gives the cup product pairing
(Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing]).

By the theorem, $H^{2d}(X,\Lambda_X(d))$ is free of rank one. It is
generated by the class of a point, which we define by the counit of the
exceptional adjunction for the inclusion of the point. Let
$x:\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ be a closed point. Using
$x^!\omega_X=(a_Xx)^!\Lambda_s=\Lambda$ and
$\omega_X\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$, the counit $x_*x^!\omega_X\to\omega_X$
induces a map
$\Lambda\to R\Gamma(X,\omega_X)=R\Gamma(X,\Lambda_X(d))[2d]$, and we let
$[x]\in H^{2d}(X,\Lambda_X(d))$ be the image of $1$.

For a field $\Lambda$ and the constant sheaf, the trace isomorphism in top degree
turns Poincaré duality into the classical cup product pairing. On
$\mathbf P^1$, for instance, the only nontrivial instance is
$H^0\times H^2\to\Lambda(-1)$. After twisting by $(1)$ it pairs the
generators $1$ and $[x]$ to $1$ by Lemma [lemma-class-of-point], so it
is perfect.

The Weil conjectures concern varieties over $\mathbf F_q$, while the six
operations of Part I live on schemes over the algebraic
closure. On $X=X_0\times_{\mathbf F_q}k$, what remains of a variety $X_0$
over $\mathbf F_q$ is an action of Frobenius on $X$ and on every
complex pulled back from $X_0$.

Here $k_0=\mathbf F_q$ and $k$ is an algebraic closure of
$k_0$. In this setting the geometric Frobenius $\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(k/k_0)$ is the inverse of the arithmetic
Frobenius $a\mapsto a^q$. For a scheme $T$ of the form
$T_0\times_{k_0}k$, with $T_0$ over $k_0$, let

$$
\operatorname{Fr}_T:T\longrightarrow T
$$

be the semilinear automorphism induced by $\sigma$. It is a morphism of
schemes covering the automorphism $\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma)$ of
$\operatorname{Spec}k$.

We use $\operatorname{Fr}_T$ to define Weil structures, but we prove the trace formula for the $k$-linear Frobenius
$\Phi_T=F_{T_0/k_0}\times_{k_0}k$, obtained by base change from the
relative $q$-power Frobenius of $T_0$, since its graph is a correspondence over $k$.
The two are compared in Section [sec-Frobenius-correspondences]
(Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius]).

Since $\operatorname{Fr}_T$ is an automorphism of schemes, pullback of
sheaves of modules along it is exact and preserves derived completeness.
Hence for every admissible coefficient ring $\Lambda$ it induces an
autoequivalence

$$
\operatorname{Fr}_T^*:
D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(T,\Lambda)\longrightarrow
D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(T,\Lambda),
$$

which agrees with the derived inverse image along $\operatorname{Fr}_T$.

Instead of complexes on $T_0$ pulled back to
$T$, we keep only the part of that datum that the trace formula sees:
the complex on $T$, where all cohomology is computed, together with an
identification of it with its Frobenius pullback. Every construction on $T$
(direct images, $f^!$, truncations, duals) is compatible with such
identifications by base change, as we check below, so we never have to descend
anything to $T_0$.

There are also more of these pairs than complexes on $T_0$, and we use the extra
ones in Part III. Indeed, for a $\mathbf Q_\ell$-sheaf on $T_0$, the stalk at a geometric point over
a closed point is a continuous representation of a Galois group. It follows that Frobenius preserves a lattice in it, and its eigenvalues are $\ell$-adic units. By contrast, on $\operatorname{Spec}k$ the sheaf $\mathbf Q_\ell$ with
Frobenius acting by $\ell$ is a pair of this kind that does not come
from $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$. Pulled back to a scheme, such
pairs are the sheaves $\mathcal B_b$ that normalize weights in
Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

We require an isomorphism so that the Frobenius operator on cohomology is
invertible over a field (Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius]).
The trace formula itself only needs a morphism
(Definition [definition-frobenius-correspondences-their-operators]), and
it is stated for these pairs
(Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula]).

A Weil structure is the datum needed to define a Frobenius operator on
cohomology. The basic example is a complex $K$ pulled back from a complex
$K_0$ on $T_0$. Since the projection $T\to T_0$ composed with
$\operatorname{Fr}_T$ is again the projection, the pullback of $K_0$ gives a
canonical isomorphism $\operatorname{Fr}_T^*K\simeq K$.

The triangles, truncations and spectral sequences we form in
$D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(T,\Lambda)$ are compatible with Weil structures. Since
$\operatorname{Fr}_T^*$ is exact on sheaves, it commutes with standard
truncations and with the triangle of a short exact sequence of sheaves.
It also commutes with the localization triangle $j_!j^*K\to K\to i_*i^*K$ for an
open immersion $j:U\to T$ obtained by base change from an open
$U_0\subset T_0$, with closed complement $i$. Indeed, for such $U$ we have
$\operatorname{Fr}_T^{-1}(U)=U$, and $\operatorname{Fr}_T$ restricts to
$\operatorname{Fr}_U$ and to the Frobenius of the complement. These constructions
therefore carry Weil structures to Weil structures, and the induced long exact
cohomology sequences are Frobenius-equivariant.

Let $(M,\phi_M)$ be a Weil complex on $X$ and let $f:X\to Y$ come from $f_0$
over $k_0$. The base change map for the cartesian square with horizontal
arrows $\operatorname{Fr}_X$, $\operatorname{Fr}_Y$ identifies
$\operatorname{Fr}_Y^*Rf_{!}M$ with $Rf_{!}\operatorname{Fr}_X^*M$, and the
composite

$$
\operatorname{Fr}_Y^*Rf_{!}M
\simeq Rf_{!}\operatorname{Fr}_X^*M
\xrightarrow{\ Rf_{!}(\phi_M)\ }Rf_{!}M
$$

is a Weil structure on $Rf_!M$. Likewise $f^*$, $Rf_*$, $f^!$,
$\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ and $\cHom$ carry Weil structures, via the corresponding
base change maps. These maps are isomorphisms for every $f$, because
$\operatorname{Fr}_X$ and $\operatorname{Fr}_Y$ are isomorphisms of schemes
and base change along an isomorphism is transport of structure.

For $Rf_!$ this needs a word, since $\operatorname{Fr}_X$ and
$\operatorname{Fr}_Y$ are not $k$-morphisms, while $Rf_!$ is built from
compactifications over $k$. We compute $Rf_!=R\bar f_*j_!$ with a
compactification $X\overset{j}{\hookrightarrow}\bar X\xrightarrow{\bar f}Y$
obtained by base change from a compactification of $f_0$ over $k_0$
(Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem]). Then
$\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}$ is an automorphism of the scheme $\bar X$ with
$\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^{-1}(X)=X$ and
$\bar f\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}=\operatorname{Fr}_Y\bar f$. For an
automorphism $h$ of a scheme, $h^*\simeq(h^{-1})_*$, so transport of
structure gives
$\operatorname{Fr}_Y^*R\bar f_*\simeq R\bar f_*\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^*$
and $\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar X}^*j_!\simeq j_!\operatorname{Fr}_X^*$, and
their composite is the base change map for $Rf_!$. It does not depend on
the compactification. Indeed, two compactifications of $f_0$ are dominated
by a third, the closure of $X_0$ in their fibre product over $Y_0$, and the
refinement isomorphisms of $Rf_!$ come from proper maps over $k_0$, which
commute with the Frobenii. The map for $f^!$ is the mate of the map for
$Rf_!$, and it is an isomorphism because both functors
$\operatorname{Fr}^*$ are equivalences.

Pullback along $\operatorname{Fr}_T$ on compactly supported cohomology is
constructed in the same way. For a morphism of schemes $h:S'\to S$ and
$L\in D(S_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, the *pullback map*

$$
\operatorname{pb}_{h,L}:R\Gamma(S,L)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(S',h^*L)
$$

is $R\Gamma$ of the unit $L\to Rh_*h^*L$, followed by the identification
$R\Gamma(S,Rh_*-)=R\Gamma(S',-)$. We write $\operatorname{pb}_h$ when $L$
is clear. It is natural in $L$, and it is transitive: for $g:S'\to S$ and
$h:S''\to S'$ we have
$\operatorname{pb}_{gh,L}=\operatorname{pb}_{h,g^*L}\circ\operatorname{pb}_{g,L}$
under $(gh)^*\simeq h^*g^*$. Let $j:T\hookrightarrow\bar T$ be the base change of
a compactification of $T_0$ over $k_0$. Then $\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}$
is an automorphism of $\bar T$ with $\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}^{-1}(T)=T$,
and *pullback along $\operatorname{Fr}_T$* is the composite

$$
\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_T}:
R\Gamma_c(T,K)=R\Gamma(\bar T,j_!K)
\xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}}\ }
R\Gamma(\bar T,\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}^*j_!K)
\simeq R\Gamma(\bar T,j_!\operatorname{Fr}_T^*K)
=R\Gamma_c(T,\operatorname{Fr}_T^*K).
$$

It does not depend on $\bar T$. Indeed, a refinement $\pi:\bar T'\to\bar T$
between two such compactifications comes from $k_0$, so
$\pi\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T'}=\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}\pi$. Transitivity
of pullback maps for this composite, together with the base change
$\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T}^*R\pi_*\simeq R\pi_*\operatorname{Fr}_{\bar T'}^*$
along the automorphisms $\operatorname{Fr}$ and with
$R\pi_*j'_!\simeq j_!$, shows that the refinement isomorphism
$R\Gamma(\bar T',j'_!K)\simeq R\Gamma(\bar T,R\pi_*j'_!K)
\simeq R\Gamma(\bar T,j_!K)$ carries one pullback map to the other. In the
same way, the pullback map along $\operatorname{Fr}_T^m$ is defined, and by
transitivity it is the $m$-fold composite
$\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_T^m,K}=\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_T,(\operatorname{Fr}_T^{m-1})^*K}\circ\cdots\circ\operatorname{pb}_{\operatorname{Fr}_T,K}$.

When $T$ and $K$ are clear, we write $F$ for $\operatorname{Frob}_{T,K}$ and
for the endomorphisms it induces on the groups $H^i_c(T,K)$.

For $r\in\mathbf Z$, write
$\Lambda(r)=\Gamma((\operatorname{Spec}k)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},
\Lambda_{\operatorname{Spec}k}(r))$ for the Tate coefficient
module with its induced Frobenius operator. Arithmetic Frobenius
acts on $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$ by $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^q$. Hence geometric Frobenius
acts on $\Lambda(1)$ by $q^{-1}$, and on $\Lambda(-d)$ by $q^d$.
Let $X_0$ be smooth of pure dimension $d$. After removing the twist, the
trace map of Definition [definition-trace-map] is a Frobenius-equivariant
map, by Proposition [proposition-purity-trace-commute-frobenius] below:

$$
H_c^{2d}(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda_X)\longrightarrow\Lambda(-d).
$$

For $X=\mathbf P^1_k$ this says that geometric Frobenius acts on
$H^2(\mathbf P^1_k,\Lambda)=\Lambda(-1)$ by $q$, as checked after
Proposition [proposition-adjunction-projective-line].

Let $X_0$ be smooth of pure dimension $d$ and let $K$ be locally perfect, so
that $\mathbb D_XK\simeq K^\vee(d)[2d]$. In this case cup product pairs $H^i_c(X,K)$
with $H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee)$ and takes values in $H^{2d}_c(X,\Lambda)$. To use this pairing for the Weil conjectures we need to know how $F$ acts on both sides.
The target is not the trivial Weil complex but
$\Lambda(-d)$, as for $\mathbf P^1$ above. If we forgot the twist, we
would predict the relation $\alpha\leftrightarrow1/\alpha$ between
eigenvalues in complementary degrees instead of
$\alpha\leftrightarrow q^d/\alpha$.

We built Poincaré duality from the purity isomorphism $\gamma_f$ and the
trace map. It therefore suffices to check that these two maps commute with
pullback along Frobenius
(Proposition [proposition-purity-trace-commute-frobenius]). This
statement about natural transformations is transport of structure, except
for the identification of Tate twists. There we use that pullback along
$\operatorname{Fr}_T$ respects Kummer classes. The compatibility
of the duality pairing with Weil structures then follows formally
(Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius]).

Let $f$ be obtained from a smooth morphism $f_0:X_0\to Y_0$ over
$k_0=\mathbf F_q$ by extension to $k$, let $\operatorname{Fr}_X$,
$\operatorname{Fr}_Y$ be the geometric Frobenius maps above, and let
$\gamma_f$ be the isomorphism of (9.2).

Weil structures are transported along $f^!$,
$f^*$ and $Rf_!$. On $f^*K(d)[2d]$ the Weil
structure is the pullback of $\phi_K$ combined with the Kummer
identification. By the proposition above and naturality of $\gamma_f$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}_f$ applied to $\phi_K$, the maps $\gamma_f(K)$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}_f(K)$ are morphisms of Weil complexes.

The constant sheaf $\Lambda_Y$ has the Weil structure given by the
identification $\operatorname{Fr}_Y^*\Lambda_Y\simeq\Lambda_Y$ of pullbacks of
constant sheaves. For $K=\Lambda_Y$ with this structure, the previous
paragraph says that the isomorphism
$\omega_f\simeq\Lambda_X(d)[2d]$ and the trace
$\operatorname{Tr}_f(\Lambda_Y)$ are morphisms of Weil complexes.

For $X_0$ proper and geometrically connected and $K=\Lambda_X$,
Theorem [theorem-trace-isomorphism-top-degree] shows that $F$ is the identity on
$H^0(X,\Lambda)=\Lambda$ and acts by $q^d$ on
$H^{2d}(X,\Lambda)\simeq\Lambda(-d)$.

The trace formula has to express the trace of Frobenius on $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ as a
sum over the fixed points of Frobenius, that is, over $X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$. We
do not prove it for Frobenius directly. Instead we first prove a fixed point
formula for every correspondence on a proper scheme. In this generality the
formula is compatible with proper pushforward, and pushing forward to a point
turns it into a tautology.

For a general correspondence, however, the fixed locus need not be discrete
(Section [sec-Trace-classes-and-local-terms]). The local side is then a sum of contributions, one for
each connected component of the fixed locus, each computed in a neighbourhood of
that component.

We use Grothendieck's formalism of cohomological correspondences, written up by
Illusie in [sga5, III]. In this formalism, a correspondence on $X$ is a map
$c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$, and a cohomological correspondence on $K$ is a
morphism $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$. For example, for the graph of an endomorphism $\varphi$ this is a map $\varphi^*K\to K$. In particular, for Frobenius it is the Weil structure
$\phi_K:\operatorname{Fr}_X^*K\simeq K$ of Section [sec-Weil-complexes], up to the
comparison of $\operatorname{Fr}_X$ with the $k$-linear Frobenius in
Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula]. When $c_2$ is proper, $u$ induces an endomorphism
$T_c(u)$ of $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$. In the same way $\phi_K$ induces the Frobenius operator
$\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}$ on $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ and on every stalk at a fixed point.

The local contributions come from duality, as $\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)=V\otimes
V^\vee$ turns an endomorphism into a tensor whose evaluation is the trace. In this
way $u$ gives the trace class $\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)\in H^0(\Fix(c),\omega_{\Fix(c)})$,
supported on the fixed locus. Its integral over a proper open and closed part $B$ of
$\Fix(c)$ is the local term $\operatorname{LT}_B(u)$. The Lefschetz–Verdier formula
(Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]) says that if $X$ and $C$
are proper over $k$, then

$$
\operatorname{tr}\bigl(T_c(u)\mid R\Gamma(X,K)\bigr)
=\sum_B\operatorname{LT}_B(u).
$$

The proof involves no computation, because trace classes commute with proper pushforward of correspondences. After pushing forward to the identity correspondence of the point,
the trace class becomes the trace of $T_c(u)$ on the perfect complex $R\Gamma(X,K)$
(Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point]). The price of this generality, however, is that the formula does not compute the individual local terms; for Frobenius that is done in
Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula].

With coefficients in a finite ring $A$ both sides are traces of endomorphisms of
perfect complexes (Definition [definition-categorical-trace]). They are not
alternating sums of traces on cohomology modules, since these need not be
projective. In fact, the trace is not even determined by the maps induced on cohomology
(Example [example-trace-not-determined-cohomology]). Moreover, finite rings such as $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ cannot be avoided, because the trace formula over
$\mathcal O_E$ is obtained from its reductions.

Throughout, $k_0=\mathbf F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbf F}_q$ and
$s=\operatorname{Spec}k$. For a scheme $X$ over $k$, $a_X:X\to s$
is the structure morphism, and $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$ whenever a model
$X_0$ over $k_0$ is given. From Section [sec-Traces-of-perfect-complexes] until Section [sec-ell-adic-coefficients-5] the coefficient ring is an arbitrary finite commutative
$\ell$-primary ring $A$, with $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$, and we write $\omega_X=a_X^!A_s$ and
$\mathbb D_XK=\cHom_A(K,\omega_X)$ for the dualizing complex and the
Verdier dual of Definition [definition-verdier-dual-evaluation] with coefficients $A$.
Some proofs compute on small
étale sites and transport the result by means of the comparison
theorems for complexes of finite Tor amplitude.

Both sides of the trace formula are traces of endomorphisms of perfect
$A$-complexes, namely of $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ on the global side and of the
stalks of $K$ on the local side.

Over a field the trace of an endomorphism of a complex is the
alternating sum of its traces on cohomology. Over $A=\mathbf Z/\ell^2$, however, the cohomology modules need not be free, so they have no trace, and
Example [example-trace-not-determined-cohomology] below shows that
the maps on cohomology do not determine the trace. We therefore define
the trace on the complex. On a bounded complex of finite projective modules it is the alternating sum of the traces of the components,
but the definition below expresses this sum through evaluation and
coevaluation, so that it depends only on the morphism in $D(A)$. In
this form it is compatible with every change of rings
(Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]), and this is how we pass from the trace
formula over $\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$ to the trace formula over $\mathcal O_E$ and $E$
(Section [sec-ell-adic-coefficients-5]).

For $P=A$ in degree zero and $v$ multiplication by $a$, coevaluation is
$1\mapsto1\otimes1$ and evaluation is multiplication, so the trace is
$a$. The next proposition lists the properties of the trace that we use.
Compatibility with change of rings lets us move the trace formula between coefficient rings, and the chain-level formula is how we compute traces in examples.

In the additivity statement of the proposition we ask for an endomorphism of
the filtered object, and not merely of the three vertices of a triangle.
The reason is that the middle component is not determined by the outer
ones, and even for a morphism of triangles the trace of the middle
component need not be the sum of the outer traces.

The following example shows why the trace has to be taken on the
complex.

As in topology, a pair of maps $c_1,c_2:C\to X$ should act on
$R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ by pulling back along $c_2$ and pushing forward along $c_1$. The pullback $R\Gamma_c(X,K)\to R\Gamma_c(C,c_2^*K)$ exists when $c_2$ is proper. To push forward we then need a map $Rc_{1!}L\to K$, where $L$ is
the complex on $C$ we have arrived at. By the adjunction $Rc_{1!}\dashv c_1^!$ there is
a canonical such map exactly when $L=c_1^!K$, namely the counit. What connects
the two steps is therefore a map $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$. The resulting
endomorphism $T_c(u)$ is defined in Definition [definition-action-correspondence].

With $c_1^*$ in place of $c_1^!$ the second step fails, since there may
be no nonzero map $Rc_{1!}c_1^*K\to K$. For example, for
the inclusion $i$ of a rational point $y$ into a smooth curve $X$,

$$
\operatorname{Hom}(i_*i^*\Lambda_X,\Lambda_X)
=\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda_y,i^!\Lambda_X)
=\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda_y,\Lambda_y(-1)[-2])=0,
$$

so the only map $Ri_!i^*\Lambda_X\to\Lambda_X$ is zero. When $c_1$ is
finite étale, smooth purity gives $c_1^!=c_1^*$, and the counit is
summation over the fibres. Then $T_c(u)$ is pullback along $c_2$
followed by a sum over the fibres of $c_1$, as for a Hecke operator.

The Lefschetz–Verdier formula
(Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]) is stated in this generality.
For the trace formula we apply it to the graph of Frobenius
(Definition [definition-frobenius-correspondences-their-operators]).

Here $c_2$ is the leg along which $K$ is pulled back and $c_1$ is the
leg along which we take $c_1^!$; in [sga5, III, §3] the two names are
interchanged. Since $X$ is separated, $\Delta_X$ and $i_c$ are closed
immersions.

The example to keep in mind is the graph of an endomorphism
$\varphi:X\to X$, that is, $C=X$ with $c_1=\operatorname{id}_X$ and
$c_2=\varphi$. Then $c_1^!K=K$, and a cohomological correspondence is a
morphism $u:\varphi^*K\to K$. In this case the fixed locus $\Fix(c)$ is the fixed point scheme of $\varphi$, which we also denote $\Fix(\varphi)$. For the Frobenius $\Phi_X$ and a Weil complex this is the correspondence whose trace formula we want.

A cohomological correspondence $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ is a morphism on $C$, so to obtain from it a class on the fixed locus we must first view
it as a section of $c^!$ of a single complex on $X\times X$, which can
then be restricted to the diagonal. In linear algebra this is the
identification $\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)=W\otimes V^\vee$, under which
the trace becomes evaluation. Its sheaf version is the isomorphism
$\cHom(p_2^*K,p_1^!K)\simeq K\boxtimes\mathbb D_XK$ of
Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism]. Here $p_1,p_2:X\times X\to X$
are the projections and $M\boxtimes N=p_1^*M\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_2^*N$ is the
external tensor product in $D((X\times X)_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)$. Applying $c^!$ to it, we obtain
$\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$. On the point the isomorphism is exactly
$\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)=V\otimes V^\vee$.

The isomorphism comes from Künneth formulas for $Rf_!$, $Rf_*$, $f^!$,
$\cHom$ and Verdier duals. For $Rf_!$ the formula follows directly from base change for compact supports and the projection formula, and for ordinary direct images from smooth and proper base change
(Proposition [proposition-ordinary-external-kunneth], Section [sec-The-Kunneth-formula]).
The formula for $f^!$ (Proposition [proposition-exceptional-external-kunneth]), by contrast, needs a
dévissage on the coefficients, starting from constant coefficients,
where for smooth $f$ the functor $f^!$ is a twist and a shift.

Let $f_i:X_i\to Y_i$, $i=1,2$, be morphisms of separated $k$-schemes of
finite type. For $M_i\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_i,A)$, using base change for compact
supports and the projection formula, we obtain the Künneth isomorphism

$$
R(f_1\times f_2)_!(M_1\boxtimes M_2)
\simeq Rf_{1!}M_1\boxtimes Rf_{2!}M_2.
$$

For the structure maps it reads
$R\Gamma_c(X_1\times X_2,M_1\boxtimes M_2)\simeq R\Gamma_c(X_1,M_1)\otimes^{\mathbf L} R\Gamma_c(X_2,M_2)$.
For $L_i\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(Y_i,A)$ let

$$
\alpha:f_1^!L_1\boxtimes f_2^!L_2\longrightarrow
(f_1\times f_2)^!(L_1\boxtimes L_2)
$$

be the morphism adjoint, under $R(f_1\times f_2)_!\dashv(f_1\times f_2)^!$,
to the composite

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(f_1\times f_2)_!(f_1^!L_1\boxtimes f_2^!L_2)
&\simeq Rf_{1!}f_1^!L_1\boxtimes Rf_{2!}f_2^!L_2\\
&\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_{f_1}\boxtimes\varepsilon_{f_2}}
L_1\boxtimes L_2,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\varepsilon_{f_i}$ is the counit of $Rf_{i!}\dashv f_i^!$.

Using the Künneth formulas for both kinds of direct image and for $f^!$,
we now identify cohomological correspondences with sections of
$c^!(K\boxtimes\mathbb D_XK)$.

In linear algebra the trace is evaluation $W\otimes W^\vee\to A$ on
the diagonal. Here evaluation takes values in $\omega_X$ on the diagonal, and
by applying $c^!$ we move it to the fixed locus.

We want to write $\operatorname{tr}(T_c(u))$ as a sum of contributions
from the fixed locus. The first guess, a sum over fixed points of the
traces of $u$ on stalks, does not make sense in general, because the
fixed locus need not be finite. For example, for the identity correspondence of $\mathbf P^1$ and $K=A$, every point is fixed. The trace on
$R\Gamma(\mathbf P^1,A)=A\oplus A(-1)[-2]$ is $1+1=2$,
the self-intersection of the diagonal.

What does make sense is a class on $\Fix(c)$. By
Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], $u$ is a section of
$c^!(K\boxtimes\mathbb D_XK)$, and composing with the trace morphism we
obtain a section of $\omega_{\Fix(c)}$. Such a section can be integrated
over a proper piece $B$ of the fixed locus. Indeed,
$H^0(B,\omega_B)=\operatorname{Hom}(Ra_{B!}A_B,A)$, and
$Ra_{B*}A_B=Ra_{B!}A_B$ for proper $B$. Composing with the unit
$A\to Ra_{B*}A_B$ therefore gives an element of $A$. In the example above, $H^0(\mathbf P^1,\omega_{\mathbf P^1})=H^2(\mathbf P^1,A(1))$ and the
degree map $H^2(\mathbf P^1,A(1))\to A$ is an isomorphism, so Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier] shows that the trace class is $2$ times the class of a point.

We will see that the trace class is additive in $K$
(Proposition [proposition-additivity-trace-classes]) and compatible with proper
pushforward (Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]). However, at an isolated fixed point the local term can still differ from the trace on the stalk
(Remark [remark-locality-warning]). For Frobenius the two are
shown to agree in Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve].

On the point, the local term is the categorical trace of
Definition [definition-categorical-trace], and we use this later to
identify the local terms of Frobenius with traces on stalks.

The global side of the trace formula is the trace of the following
endomorphism.

In the first arrow we use the ordinary unit together with
$Rc_{2*}=Rc_{2!}$, which holds since $c_2$ is proper, and the displayed
isomorphism comes from the composition of direct images with compact support.

The Lefschetz–Verdier formula computes the trace of $T_c(u)$ in terms of
the trace class. We obtain it as the special case, for the map to a point, of the
compatibility of trace classes with proper pushforward. This works because $T_c(u)$ is itself a cohomological correspondence: for
proper $X$ and $C$ it is a correspondence on the point with coefficients
$R\Gamma(X,K)$, and on the point the trace class is the trace by
Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point]. The global trace is therefore the trace
class of a pushed-forward correspondence, and it remains to
show that trace classes commute with pushforward along proper maps.

To push a cohomological correspondence forward along proper morphisms,
we must produce from $u$ a map
$c_2'^*Rf_*K\to c_1'^!Rf_*K$. The only maps available for this are the units and counits of the adjunctions on the two legs, used as in the
construction of $T_c(u)$. Here properness of $f$ and $g$ gives $Rf_*=Rf_!$ and $Rg_*=Rg_!$, and this allows us to push forward the
counit for $Rc_{1!}\dashv c_1^!$. We also push forward along closed immersions
(Section [sec-Additivity-of-trace-classes]).

For $Y=s$, $C'=s$ and $f=a_X$, $g=a_C$ with $X$ and $C$ proper, the
pushforward $u'$ is an endomorphism of $R\Gamma(X,K)$. Unwinding $\alpha$ and $\beta$ shows that it is $T_c(u)$, and the following theorem compares
trace classes before and after pushforward. In this special case it
is the Lefschetz–Verdier formula.

To compute local terms, we cut $K$ into pieces along a decomposition of
$X$ into an open and a closed part, both invariant under the
correspondence. For this the trace class must be additive. For
the trace of an endomorphism of a perfect complex, additivity says that
a block triangular matrix has trace equal to the sum of the traces of
its diagonal blocks. By Remark [remark-coherent-additivity] it can
only be expected for filtrations lifted to the filtered derived
category. The trace class needs the same care, and we lift each step of
the construction of the trace morphism to filtered complexes.

In a two-step filtration, for example, a filtered correspondence is a
block triangular matrix
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u_0&*\\0&u_1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ whose
off-diagonal entry has weight $1$. Since $\omega_X$ sits in filtration degree
$0$, the trace class does not see this entry
(Lemma [lemma-filtered-trace-morphism] below).

The operations that enter the
trace morphism have filtered versions, with explicit formulas for their
graded pieces. We use finite decreasing filtrations, the convolution filtration on tensor
products, and the filtration on internal Hom given by

$$
F^r\mathcal Hom(\mathcal M,\mathcal N)
=\{v:v(F^a\mathcal M)\subset F^{a+r}\mathcal N
\text{ for every }a\}.
$$

Write $\cHom_F$, $\otimes_F$ and $\mathbb D_F=\cHom_F(-,\omega_X)$ for
the derived functors on the filtered derived category, where $\omega_X$
carries the filtration concentrated in weight zero, and $M_a$, $N_a$,
$K_a$ for the graded pieces of $\mathcal M$, $\mathcal N$, $\mathcal K$.

With these formulas we lift the trace morphism of
Definition [definition-trace-morphism] to filtered complexes.

To apply this to an open subscheme $U$ and its closed
complement $Z$, we must lift $u$ to the localization triangle. For
this the correspondence must respect the
decomposition: we need $c_1^{-1}(Z)\subset c_2^{-1}(Z)$.
For the graph of an endomorphism $\varphi$, where
$c_1=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $c_2=\varphi$, this says that
$\varphi(Z)\subset Z$.

It is convenient to work with exceptional
adjoints. Put $\Theta=Rc_{1!}c_2^*:D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)\to D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$. In these terms a cohomological correspondence $u$ on $(X,K)$ is the same as a map
$\widehat u:\Theta K\to K$, its adjoint under $Rc_{1!}\dashv c_1^!$.
Under the invariance condition there are no nonzero maps from
$\Theta K_U$ to $K_Z$, so $u$ restricts to $K_U$ in an essentially unique
way. Let

$$
C_U=c_2^{-1}(U),\qquad C_Z=(c_1^{-1}(Z))_{\mathrm{red}},\qquad
i':C_Z\longrightarrow C,
$$

with $i'$ the closed immersion. By the invariance condition both legs of
$C_U$ land in $U$ and both legs of $C_Z$ land in $Z$; we write
$c_U=(c_{1U},c_{2U}):C_U\to U\times U$ and
$c_Z=(c_{1Z},c_{2Z}):C_Z\to Z\times Z$ for the restricted correspondences.

The graded piece on the closed part is a correspondence on $Z$ pushed
forward to $X$. This is the form in which
Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve] uses it,
combined with Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier].

Additivity takes the following form; in
Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve] we apply it with $Z$ a
single fixed point of Frobenius.

Restricting the formula to a proper open and closed part $B$ of the fixed
locus and integrating, we get
$\operatorname{LT}_B(u)=\operatorname{LT}_B(u_U)+\operatorname{LT}_B(u_Z)$.

Let $X_0$ be a separated scheme of finite type over
$\mathbf F_q$, let $X=X_0\times_{\mathbf F_q}\overline{\mathbf F}_q$, and let
$\ell\nmid q$. By Lemma [lemma-frobenius-fixed-scheme], the points of $X_0$ over
$\mathbf F_{q^m}$ are the fixed points of the $m$-th power of the Frobenius $\Phi_X$
on $X$. The Lefschetz–Verdier formula
(Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]) writes a trace on
cohomology as a sum of local terms, but it says nothing about what a local term is.
To count points we need the local term of Frobenius at a fixed point to be the trace
on the stalk.

For a self-map $\varphi$ of a compact manifold with transverse fixed points,
the Lefschetz formula counts each fixed point $x$ with the sign of
$\det(1-d\varphi_x)$. The differential of Frobenius is zero, so we expect every sign to
be $+1$. On a curve this can be seen directly. If $y$ is a fixed point of
$\Phi_X^m$, $u$ is a uniformizer at $y$ defined over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, and $v$ is the
same function on the second factor, then near $(y,y)$ the graph of $\Phi_X^m$ is
$v=u^{q^m}$, and it meets the diagonal $v=u$ with multiplicity one, since
$u^{q^m}-u$ has a simple zero at $u=0$.

For constant coefficients the local term at a transverse fixed point is $1$, so on a
proper $X$ transversality would be enough. Two
things stand in the way in general. First, $X$ need not be proper. If we
compactify, the new fixed points at the boundary have zero stalk for $j_!K$, and
we need their local terms to vanish. Second, a local term is computed from
$\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$ near the fixed point, where $c_1,c_2$ are the two projections
of the graph of Frobenius to $X$ (Definition [definition-correspondence]). The
stalk $K_{\bar y}$ does not determine this complex
(Remark [remark-locality-warning]), so the vanishing of the local term at a
point where the stalk vanishes is a real statement, which transversality alone
does not give.

One computation on a curve settles both problems: Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve] says that for any morphism
$\psi:(\Phi_X^m)^*K\to K$ on a smooth curve, the local term at a rational point $y$
is $\operatorname{tr}(\psi_{\bar y}\mid K_{\bar y})$. The proof, which is Grothendieck's [sga5, XV, §3], uses $d\Phi_X=0$ a second time: the graph $v=u^{q^m}$ is tangent to the axis $v=0$ and the diagonal is not, so blowing up
$(y,y)$ separates them, and near the exceptional divisor the local term becomes a
restriction map that vanishes when $K_{\bar y}=0$
(Remark [remark-outline-local-computation]). Since both sides of the formula
are additive along an open subscheme and its complement
(Lemma [lemma-additivity-open-subscheme-complement]) and compatible with
$Rf_!$ (Lemma [lemma-comparison-via-relative-frobenius]), we never need to
compactify anything but $\mathbf A^1\subset\mathbf P^1$.

The answer is Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula]: for every
Weil complex $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,\Lambda)$ (Section [sec-Weil-complexes]), where
$\Lambda\in\{A,\mathbf Z_\ell,\mathcal O_E,\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\}$ and $A$ is a finite commutative
$\ell$-primary ring, and for every $m\geq1$, we have in $\Lambda$

$$
\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda\bigl(\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m\mid
R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K)\bigr)
=\sum_{y\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})}
\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda\bigl(\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}\mid
K_{\bar y}\bigr).
$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda$ is the trace of an endomorphism of a perfect complex
(Definition [definition-categorical-trace]), and $\operatorname{Frob}_{y,m}$ is the
$m$-th iterate of the Weil structure on the stalk at the fixed point $\bar y$. For
$K=\Lambda_X$ and $\Lambda$ a field the formula is Weil's axiom (b), and it
gives the rationality of the zeta
function (Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function]).

Purity, however, needs the formula for general $K$. For $\Lambda\in\{\mathbf Q_\ell,E,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\}$, in the
form of an Euler product (Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product]), it reads

$$
\prod_{x\in|X_0|}\det\bigl(1-T^{\deg x}\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid K_{\bar x}\bigr)^{-1}
=\prod_i\det\bigl(1-T\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}\mid H^i_c(X,K)\bigr)^{(-1)^{i+1}},
$$

which relates the local eigenvalues of $K$ to the eigenvalues on cohomology.

The conventions of Chapter [chap-The-Lefschetz-Verdier-formula] remain in force.

Two Frobenius maps act on $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$: the $k$-linear scheme
Frobenius $\Phi_X$ and the semilinear geometric Frobenius $\operatorname{Fr}_X$
that defines Weil structures. We prove the trace formula for $\Phi_X$, whose graph is a
correspondence over $k$, and Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius]
translates it to $\operatorname{Fr}_X$.

The operator $T_{c_m}$ on cohomology with compact support defined below
makes sense even when $X$ is not proper, because the second leg
$\Phi_X^m$ of the graph $c_m$ is proper. Indeed, $\Phi_X$ and all its iterates
are finite, since a finitely generated algebra over a perfect field is finite over
its subring of $q$-th powers.

We cannot work with $\operatorname{Fr}_X$ directly. Indeed, the Weil structure $\phi_K$ is a map $\operatorname{Fr}_X^*K\to K$, but
$\operatorname{Fr}_X$ lies over the automorphism $\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma)$
of $s$. Hence its graph is not a morphism $X\to X\times_sX$ of $k$-schemes.
Since the formalism of Chapter [chap-The-Lefschetz-Verdier-formula] uses $c_1^!$ only for $k$-morphisms, it does not apply to this graph. The $k$-linear
$\Phi_X=F_X\circ\operatorname{Fr}_X$, on the other hand, has a graph of the
required kind. Pullback along the absolute Frobenius $F_X$ is the identity on étale sheaves, and this is how
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius]
turns $\phi_K$ into a map $\Phi_X^*K\to K$. For example, on $X=\mathbf A^1_k$ the map
$\Phi_X$ is $t\mapsto t^q$, and the fixed points of $\Phi_X^m$ are the $q^m$ elements of $\mathbf F_{q^m}$. Lemma [lemma-frobenius-fixed-scheme]
describes them in general.

We allow maps $\Phi_X^*K\to K$ that are not isomorphisms,
because the proof over $E$ clears denominators: it multiplies a Weil
structure by a power of $\pi_E$ (Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences]). The
operators below are the two sides of the trace formula in
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence].

The operator $T_{c_m}(\psi_m)$ is defined with the $k$-linear
$\Phi_X$, while the Frobenius operator of Section [sec-Weil-complexes], whose
trace the theorem is about, is defined with $\operatorname{Fr}_X$. The
next lemma says that the two agree, so that the trace formula proved for
$\Phi_X$ is a statement about $\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}$.

For example, if $X_0$ is smooth and geometrically connected of
dimension $d$ and $K=A_X$ with its constant Weil structure, then
$T_{c_1}(\psi)$ acts on $H^{2d}_c(X,A)=A(-d)$ by $q^d$, which agrees
with the action of geometric Frobenius on $A(-d)$ recorded after
Definition [definition-frobenius-operator].

The local terms of the trace formula live on the fixed point scheme
$\Fix(\Phi_X^m)=\Fix(c_m)$ of the graph $c_m$. More precisely, a local term is defined on each open and closed part of this scheme that is proper over $k$. The next lemma
shows that the fixed scheme is a finite reduced set of points, one for each
$\mathbf F_{q^m}$-rational point of $X_0$, so every such point has its own
local term. For Frobenius on a smooth curve we then show that this local term is
the trace on the stalk.

On $\mathbf A^1$ the fixed scheme of $\Phi^m$ is
$\operatorname{Spec}k[t]/(t^{q^m}-t)$. Its $q^m$ points are reduced
because $t^{q^m}-t$ has derivative $-1$. This is the algebraic form
of the transversality seen at the start of
Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula]. Reducedness alone does not determine the
local term, because the stalk does not determine $\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$ near the
fixed point (Remark [remark-locality-warning] below).

Thus every fixed point $y$ is an open and closed point of the fixed
scheme, and its local term $\operatorname{LT}_y$ is defined.

The vanishing of a local term when $K_{\bar y}=0$ is hard to see from the
definition through the trace morphism
(Definition [definition-trace-morphism]), so we first replace that
definition by a description familiar from topology. There the
intersection number of two submanifolds $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ is computed
by restricting the Thom class of $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$. Since the Thom class is supported on $\Gamma$, the result is a class supported on $\Gamma\cap\Delta$.
Similarly, in our setting $\psi$ defines a class supported on the graph. A restriction
map $\rho$ takes it to cohomology of the diagonal supported at $y$, and
the local term is the evaluation of the result. Note that the map $\rho$ does not involve $\psi$. It therefore suffices to show that $\rho$ itself is zero when
$K_{\bar y}=0$ (Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk]), and
then the vanishing holds for every $\psi$, invertible or not.

attrs.title: The local term as a restriction map (1)

objects.body:
In this lemma the two factors of the product are interchanged compared with
the convention $c_m=(\operatorname{id}_X,\Phi_X^m)$ of
Definition [definition-frobenius-correspondences-their-operators].

attrs.title: The local term as a restriction map (2)

objects.body:
The vanishing of the local term is explained by the position of the curves at $(y,y)$. Since
$d\Phi_X=0$, the transposed graph $\Gamma$ is tangent to the vertical
axis $V=\{y\}\times X$. The diagonal $\Delta$ and the horizontal
axis $H$ have other tangent directions. This persists on suitable covers
of degree prime to $\ell$ (Lemma [lemma-tangent-cones-on-cover] below). Blowing up the closed point
separates the curves: the strict transforms of $\Gamma\cup V$, of $\Delta$
and of $H$ meet the exceptional divisor $E\simeq\mathbf P^1$ in
different points.

Let $M$ be the direct image of the coefficients from the complement of $E$.
We consider $M$ on $E$ minus the points of $\Gamma\cup V$, and let $z$ be the
point where $H$ meets $E$. There $M$ is locally constant away from $z$, and its
stalk at $z$ is zero. Both facts use that the monodromy is an
$\ell$-group (Lemma [lemma-cohomology-near-two-transverse-divisors]). Now a branch of $\Delta$ meets $E$ in one point $w$, and the restriction to this
branch factors through the stalk $M_w$. Composing the restriction from $E$ to $M_w$ with the specialization isomorphism from
$M_w$ to the generic stalk of $E$, we get the restriction to the zero stalk $M_z$ followed by specialization. Hence the restriction to $M_w$ is zero.

The transverse case is
Lemma [lemma-cohomology-near-two-transverse-divisors], and
Lemma [lemma-vanishing-restrictions-after-blowing-up] reduces to it by
blowing up the closed point. We compute
on classical étale models of strictly local
schemes, which are filtered limits of schemes of finite type, and in the
proof of Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk] we transport the result
to the pro-étale site.

attrs.title: Vanishing on a strictly local surface (1)

objects.body:
Since the restriction to a curve meeting $D_2$ in one point factors through the
stalk of $M$ at that point, the lemma implies that restrictions to
punctured curves vanish.

attrs.title: Vanishing on a strictly local surface (2)

objects.body:
Near $(y,y)$ the curves we care about do
not meet transversely, since the graph, the diagonal and the axis $H$ all pass
through the same point. The next lemma reduces this configuration to
the transverse one by a single blowup.

attrs.title: Vanishing on a strictly local surface (3)

objects.body:
In the setting of Lemma [lemma-local-term-restriction-map] we compute on the
classical étale models. This is legitimate because the classical comparison
identifies tensor products, duality, exceptional adjunctions and the
pairing between graph and diagonal with their versions there. Let $X_1$
and $X_2$ be two copies of the strict localization of $X$ at $y$. The
strict localization of $X_1\times X_2$ at $(y,y)$ is the strictly local
surface $T$ of Lemma [lemma-local-term-restriction-map]. Write

$$
H=X_1\times\{y\},\qquad V=\{y\}\times X_2,
$$

and keep $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ for the transposed Frobenius graph and the
diagonal in $T$. Let $u$ and $v$ be the pullbacks to the two factors $X_1$
and $X_2$ of the same uniformizer of $X$ at $y$, so that $\Delta$, $V$ and
$H$ have equations $u-v=0$, $u=0$ and $v=0$. Write
$\varphi(v)=(\Phi_X^m)^\#u$, a power series in $v$; the graph $\Gamma$ has
equation $u-\varphi(v)=0$. Since $d\Phi_X=0$, the graph $\Gamma$ is
tangent to $V$, while $\Delta$ and $H$ have other tangent directions.

The next three lemmas prepare the proof of
Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk].

attrs.title: The local term at a zero stalk (1)

objects.body:
The map $\rho$ of Lemma [lemma-local-term-restriction-map] depends on $K$ and on the geometry
of $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ near $(y,y)$, but not on $\psi$. We therefore state
the vanishing of local terms at a zero stalk as a statement about $\rho$ alone.

attrs.title: The local term at a zero stalk (2)

objects.body:
The point $y$ is stable under $\Phi_X^m$,
so additivity of trace classes applies to the localization triangle
for $X\setminus\{y\}$ and $\{y\}$. Here the open piece has zero stalk at $y$, so its local term vanishes by Lemma [lemma-vanishing-local-term-zero-stalk].
The closed piece, in turn, is pushed forward from the point, where the local
term is a trace by Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point]. Note that the argument never uses that $K$ is lisse at $y$. This is why, in the proof of
Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence], we can apply the result to
$j_!K$ at the point at infinity of $\mathbf P^1$.

attrs.title: The local term at a fixed point (1)

objects.body:
For $K=A_X$ on $X=\mathbf A^1_k$ the proposition gives
$\operatorname{LT}_y(\psi_m)=1$ at each of the $q^m$ fixed points of
$\Phi^m_X$. This matches the intersection count at the start of the chapter.
For general $K$ the proposition is not a formal consequence of the
definitions, as Remark [remark-locality-warning] explains.

attrs.title: The local term at a fixed point (2)

objects.body:
The trace formula with finite coefficients is proved by induction on the
number of affine coordinates. We project a closed subscheme of
$\mathbf A^d$ to $\mathbf A^{d-1}$, apply the induction hypothesis to
$Rf_!K$, and identify each stalk of $Rf_!K$ at a rational point with
the cohomology of the fibre, a closed subscheme of $\mathbf A^1$ over a
larger finite field. For this, $Rf_!K$ must carry a Frobenius
correspondence with two properties: its operator on $R\Gamma_c$ is that of
$\psi$, and its stalk maps are the Frobenius operators on the cohomology of the
fibres.

The square formed by $f$ and the two Frobenii commutes, but it is
usually not cartesian. Indeed, already for $f:\mathbf A^1\to s$ the Frobenius of $s$ is the identity, so the fibre product is $\mathbf A^1$ itself,
while $\Phi_{\mathbf A^1}$ has degree $q$. The difference is
measured by the relative Frobenius. It is a universal homeomorphism, so pullback
along it is an equivalence on étale sheaves, and the comparison map
built from it is an isomorphism.

To reduce the trace formula to pieces of $X_0$, we cut $X_0$
into an open subscheme and its closed complement.

The proof uses a single compactification, $\mathbf A^1\subset\mathbf P^1$, so the
Lefschetz–Verdier formula and the curve
computation of Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve]
are applied only on $\mathbf P^1$. This suffices because every affine scheme of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$ is a closed subscheme of some $\mathbf A^d$, and the fibres of a
coordinate projection lie in $\mathbf A^1$. On $\mathbf P^1$ the only new fixed point is the rational point $\infty$, where $j_!K$ has
zero stalk. The fibres over points of $Y_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ are schemes over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, so we prove the theorem for all finite fields at once. The other coefficient rings are treated in Section [sec-ell-adic-coefficients-5].

The base of the induction is the case of finite schemes. There we
can see directly what the formula counts. For example, take $X_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_{q^2}$ and $K=A$. Then the scheme $X$ consists of two points interchanged by $\Phi_X$. Hence
$T_{c_1}$ is the swap of $A\oplus A$, with trace
$0=\#X_0(\mathbf F_q)$, and $T_{c_2}$ is the identity, with trace
$2=\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^2})$. In general $T_{c_m}$ is a block permutation
matrix, and only the points fixed by $\Phi_X^m$ contribute to its trace.

The iterates $\psi_m$, the
endomorphisms $T_{c_m}(\psi_m)$ and the stalk
maps $\psi_{m,\bar x}$ are those of Definition [definition-frobenius-correspondences-their-operators].

To pass from finite coefficient rings to $\mathcal O_E$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$
we follow the steps of
Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients]. Since the statement is now an equality of traces in $\Lambda$ rather than an isomorphism, we carry the steps out
directly. First, for $\mathcal O_E$ we reduce modulo $\pi_E^n$. This works because both sides are traces of
perfect complexes, traces commute with reduction, and $\mathcal O_E$
embeds in $\varprojlim_n\mathcal O_E/\pi_E^n$. Next, for $E$ we clear denominators: a Frobenius correspondence $\psi_E$ with coefficients $E$ need not
come from an integral one; only some multiple $\pi_E^N\psi_E$ does, and this
integral model need not be invertible even when $\psi_E$ is
(Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences]). This is
why we prove the formula for correspondences that are not invertible. Finally, for $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we descend to a finite extension of $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

The Frobenius comparison $\kappa_m$ of
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius] extends to the coefficient rings
$\mathcal O_E$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Let $K\in\Dbc(X,\mathcal O_E)$ have
tower of reductions $(K_n)$ modulo $\pi_E^n$
(Definition [definition-derived-adic-completeness]). Both $(\Phi_X^m)^*$ and
$\operatorname{Fr}_X^{m*}$ preserve derived completeness and commute
with reduction, so each is the derived limit of its values on the
$K_n$. The finite comparisons $\kappa_m$ come from a single functorial
identification on the classical site. Hence they are compatible with
reduction of coefficients, and their derived limit is the integral
$\kappa_m$. The finite comparisons are compatible with iteration and
with the units of the pullbacks, and therefore so is the integral one. It follows that
the integral $\kappa_m$ identifies the endomorphisms $T_{c_m}$ with the geometric Frobenius operators as in
Lemma [lemma-scheme-frobenius-geometric-frobenius].
For $E$ we localize on integral models. By the localized Hom
comparison (9.21) the result does not depend on the choice of model. For $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we
descend from finite extensions.

To pass from $\mathcal O_E$ to $E$ we need an integral Frobenius
correspondence whose rationalization is the given one, up to a power of
$\pi_E$. The next lemma provides it and records how the operators of
both sides of the trace formula change under this rescaling.

With the integral formula and integral models of rational Frobenius
correspondences, we obtain the trace formula stated at the beginning
of this chapter for all coefficient rings.

For finite and integral rings, (12.3) is an identity
of categorical traces of perfect complexes, which makes sense even
when the cohomology modules are not projective.

Under the trace formula, $Rf_!$ becomes summation over fibres and $\otimes$
becomes multiplication of functions on rational points. This is Grothendieck's
function–sheaf dictionary [sga4-5, Sommes trig.]
(Section [sec-The-function-sheaf-dictionary]), and in Part III we compute with
sheaves through their functions in this way.

For $\Lambda$ a field, $t_{K,m}(x)$ is the alternating sum of the traces of
Frobenius on the stalks $\mathcal H^i(K)_{\bar x}$
(Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]). For example, the constant sheaf $\Lambda_X$ with its constant Weil structure has trace function $1$. In terms of trace functions, the theorem says that $\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(\operatorname{Frob}_{X,K}^m
\mid R\Gamma_c(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},K))$ is the sum of $t_{K,m}$ over
$X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$. Applied to the fibres of a morphism, it shows
that direct image with compact support sums trace functions over the fibres.

The other operations on functions also have counterparts on sheaves.
These counterparts, together with the corollary, are the entries of the dictionary that we
use. In this dictionary, morphisms come from morphisms of separated $\mathbf F_q$-schemes
of finite type, and the operations carry the Weil structures described
after Definition [definition-weil-structure].

The Fourier transform of Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform] is one more entry, and
the proposition shows why it corresponds to the discrete transform. Let
$p_1,p_2$ be the projections of $\mathbf A^1\times\mathbf A^1$, let
$\mu(x,y)=xy$, let $\psi:\mathbf F_q\to E^\times$ be a nontrivial additive
character, and let $\mathcal K_\psi=\mu^*\mathcal L_\psi$, where
$\mathcal L_\psi$ is the Artin–Schreier sheaf of
Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf] (proved in
Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform] below). Here $\psi$ is a character, not a
Frobenius correspondence. With this kernel the transform is $\operatorname{FT}_\psi K=Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)[1]$. For
$y\in\mathbf F_{q^m}$ we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{\operatorname{FT}_\psi K,m}(y)
&=-\,t_{Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi),m}(y)
&&\text{(shift)}\\
&=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{q^m}}t_{p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi,m}(x,y)
&&\text{by (3)}\\
&=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{q^m}}t_{p_1^*K,m}(x,y)\,t_{\mu^*\mathcal L_\psi,m}(x,y)
&&\text{by (2)}\\
&=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{q^m}}t_{K,m}(x)\,
\psi\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^m}/\mathbf F_q}(xy)\bigr)
&&\text{by (1) and Lemma~16.1.1.}
\end{aligned}
$$

The first equality holds because a shift changes the sign of a trace, by the
chain formula of Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]. Each of the
other three steps is one operation in the formula
$\hat t(y)=\sum_xt(x)\psi(xy)$: pull $t$ back to the plane, multiply by the
kernel, and sum over the fibres of $p_2$.

Over a field of characteristic zero, the traces of all powers of an
endomorphism determine its characteristic polynomial. Taking the trace
formula for all $m\geq1$, we therefore obtain an identity of power
series: a product over closed points equals an alternating product of
characteristic polynomials of Frobenius on cohomology. This
step divides by $m$, so in the determinant formulas below $\Lambda$ is one of the
fields $\mathbf Q_\ell$, $E$, $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. Characteristic zero is
needed: on $\mathbf F_p^{\oplus p}$ every power of the identity has trace
$p=0$, as for the zero endomorphism, but
$\det(1-T\cdot\operatorname{id})=(1-T)^p=1-T^p$ is not $1$.

For $K=\Lambda_X$ the product over cohomology is finite, so $Z(X_0,T)$ is
rational, and for smooth proper $X_0$ duality pairs the factors in degrees $i$
and $2d-i$ (Corollary [corollary-functional-equation]).

The local factors of the Euler product are indexed by closed points.
A closed point $x\in|X_0|$ of degree $d$ over $\mathbf F_q$
corresponds to a Frobenius orbit of $d$ geometric points, and its
Frobenius on the stalk is the Frobenius going once around this orbit.

For the constant sheaf every local factor is $(1-T^{\deg(x)})^{-1}$, and the
Euler product becomes the zeta function of $X_0$. This proves
rationality of $Z(X_0,T)$ over $\mathbf Q_\ell$. A short argument with linear
recurrences descends it to $\mathbf Q$.

For example, let $X_0=\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_q}$. Then
$\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})=q^m$, so that $Z(X_0,T)=(1-qT)^{-1}$. On the
cohomological side, $H^i_c(X,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ vanishes except for $i=2$, and
$H^2_c(X,\mathbf Q_\ell)\simeq\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$ is a line on which geometric
Frobenius acts by $q$. The only factor is therefore
$(1-qT)^{-1}$, as it should be.

For $X_0=\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf F_q}$ the cohomology is $\mathbf Q_\ell$ in degree
$0$ and $\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$ in degree $2$, so $Z(\mathbf P^1,T)=1/((1-T)(1-qT))$.
This matches $\#\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_{q^m})=1+q^m$. For a curve of positive genus the middle cohomology contributes as well, and for the running example a single point count determines it.

For smooth proper $X_0$, Poincaré duality relates the factors of
the determinant formula in complementary degrees, and this gives a
functional equation.

For the elliptic curve of Example [example-running-example-trace-formula] we have $d=1$ and
$b_0=b_2=1$, $b_1=2$. So $\chi=0$ and $D=\det(F_1)^{-1}\det(F_2)=3/3=1$.
The corollary says $Z(C_0,1/(3T))=Z(C_0,T)$, and indeed

$$
\frac{1+3(3T)^{-2}}{(1-(3T)^{-1})(1-T^{-1})}
=\frac{(3T^2+1)/(3T^2)}{(3T-1)(T-1)/(3T^2)}
=\frac{1+3T^2}{(1-3T)(1-T)}.
$$

For the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ of the introduction,
Frobenius acts on $H^1$ with eigenvalues $\pm i\sqrt3$. The Riemann hypothesis for this curve is then the statement $|\pm i\sqrt3|=3^{1/2}$. But the
eigenvalues live in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, and an $\ell$-adic number has no complex
absolute value until we choose a field embedding
$\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$. Since no choice is preferred, we fix one $\iota$ throughout, and the final theorems hold for every choice.

An eigenvalue $\alpha$ of Frobenius at a closed point of degree $n$ has weight $w$
if $|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{nw/2}$. The factor $n$ makes the weight independent of
the field over which we look at the point: over $\mathbf F_{q^{mn}}$ the
eigenvalue becomes $\alpha^m$ and $q^n$ becomes $q^{mn}$. For example, on $\mathbf P^1$
Frobenius acts on $H^0$ by $1$, of weight $0$, and on $H^2=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ by $q$,
of weight $2$. Similarly, the eigenvalues on $H^1$ of our elliptic curve have weight $1$.
Weil's purity axiom says that this pattern persists: $H^i$ of a smooth proper
variety is pure of weight $i$. The name comes from Hodge theory, where $H^i$
of a compact Kähler manifold carries a Hodge structure of weight $i$.

The proof cannot stay with smooth proper varieties. It fibres them in
curves, and the cohomology of the fibres forms sheaves on the base. So we
need weights for sheaves, and for cohomology that is not pure. Without
smoothness and properness only an upper bound survives. For example, let
$\mathbf G_m=\mathbf P^1\setminus\{0,\infty\}$. The localization sequence gives
$H^1_c(\mathbf G_m,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ with trivial Frobenius and
$H^2_c(\mathbf G_m,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$. This agrees with the trace formula
$q-1=\#\mathbf G_m(\mathbf F_q)$. Thus $H^1_c$ has weight $0$, strictly less
than $1$.

A sheaf is pure of weight $w$ if all its eigenvalues at all closed
points have weight $w$. It is mixed if it has a finite filtration whose
quotients are pure. A bounded complex $K$ has weights at most $w$ if each
$\mathcal H^i(K)$ is mixed with all weights at most $w+i$
(Definition [definition-weights]). Here the shift by $i$ puts the constant sheaf and its cohomology into one statement: $R\Gamma_c(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ has weights
at most $0$ exactly when $H^i_c$ has weights at most $i$, as on
$\mathbf G_m$. In these terms the Deligne–Laumon theorem
(Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek]) says that $Rf_!$ does not increase
weights.

Two warnings will matter later. The first is that weights depend on $\iota$. For example, consider the rank-one Weil sheaf on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ on which
Frobenius acts by $1+\sqrt2\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$. It has weight $2\log_q(1+\sqrt2)>0$ for
an embedding with $\iota(\sqrt2)=\sqrt2$, and weight
$2\log_q(\sqrt2-1)=-2\log_q(1+\sqrt2)$ for the other one. For this reason
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes] needs the
Deligne–Laumon theorem for every $\iota$: only then do the reciprocal roots
of $P_i$ have absolute value $q^{i/2}$ under every complex embedding.

The second warning is that being mixed is not a pointwise condition: it asks
for a filtration with pure quotients, and such a filtration has to be
constructed. Most of Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-in-general] is spent
constructing one for direct images.

We define weights on Weil sheaves, sheaves on $X$ with a Frobenius
structure, rather than on sheaves on $X_0$. The reason is that normalizing weights
requires twisting by the geometrically constant rank-one Weil sheaves $\mathcal B_b$,
on which a degree-one Frobenius acts by a scalar $b\in\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell^\times$. These do not come from
$X_0$ when $b$ is not an $\ell$-adic unit.

Weights are defined by the absolute values of the Frobenius
eigenvalues on stalks at closed points, so we first fix how Frobenius
acts on sheaves.

On a smooth curve $U_0$ we want to treat lisse Weil sheaves as
representations, just as a lisse sheaf on $U_0$ is a continuous
representation of $\pi_1(U_0)$. However, the profinite group $\pi_1(U_0)$ is an extension of $\widehat{\mathbf Z}$ by $\pi_1(U)$, and it has too few
representations for this. Indeed, a continuous representation of a profinite group preserves a lattice, so a lift $s$ of Frobenius acts with
