eigenvalues that are $\ell$-adic units. Hence the rank-one Weil sheaf
$\mathcal B_\ell$, on which $s$ acts by $\ell$ and $\pi_1(U)$ acts trivially,
is not a representation of $\pi_1(U_0)$. Concretely,
$n\mapsto\ell^n$ does not extend continuously to $\widehat{\mathbf Z}$: the
integers $m!$ tend to $0$ in $\widehat{\mathbf Z}$, whereas $\ell^{m!}$ tends
to $0$ in $\mathbf Z_\ell$ and not to $1$.

The Weil group keeps $\pi_1(U)$ with its topology and replaces
$\widehat{\mathbf Z}$ by the discrete group $\mathbf Z$ of integer powers
of Frobenius. Continuity then constrains only the geometric part. These representations of the Weil group are the language of Theorem [theorem-rank-one-sheaves-have-finite] and of the monodromy groups
of Section [sec-Determinant-weights].

Every sheaf defined over $k_0$ is a Weil sheaf. By means of the Weil
isomorphism, Frobenius acts on the stalk at a geometric point over each
closed point $x$, so we can speak of the eigenvalues of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$. In the description by representations the Weil
isomorphism is transport by $s$, and conversely it determines the action
of $s$.

The definition below contains two kinds of bounds. The first, being
punctually of weights $\le w$, bounds the eigenvalues at each closed point;
it is what the curve case yields on each stalk of a direct image. But it
cannot serve as input for the curve case, which needs pure lisse sheaves. The second, mixedness, has the opposite virtue: a mixed sheaf can be treated one pure quotient at a time, and
for a mixed sheaf the bound on weights is again a pointwise condition
(Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf]). In
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-in-general] we use this to turn the stalkwise
bounds into the bound of Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek].

Deligne calls a complex $K$ pure of weight $w$ if $K$ has weights at most
$w$ and its Verdier dual $\mathbb D K$ has weights at most $-w$. Over a point
the two notions agree. In general neither implies the other, and we use ours
only for sheaves and over a point.

The cohomology groups of Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek] are
Weil sheaves on $\operatorname{Spec}k_0$. For them, having weights at most $w$ is just a
condition on the eigenvalues of Frobenius. Indeed, by
Lemma [lemma-weil-sheaves-point-mixed] every Weil $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaf over a point is
mixed, and Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf] reads the bound of a mixed
sheaf off its eigenvalues.

Extending scalars is needed for $E$-sheaves. Suppose $2$ is not a square in $\mathbf Q_\ell$. Then the
rank-two $\mathbf Q_\ell$-sheaf on which Frobenius has eigenvalues $1\pm\sqrt2$ is
irreducible. Its two eigenvalues have different weights, so it has
no filtration with pure quotients over $\mathbf Q_\ell$.

The lemma does not say that a sheaf punctually of weights $\le w$ is
mixed; the filtration has to be found. Nor need the filtration split:
weights see only the characteristic polynomials of Frobenius, so a
Jordan block and its semisimplification have the same weights. The
following example is a mixed sheaf that is not pure and whose filtration
does not split.

The behaviour of weights under the usual operations comes down to the
eigenvalues of an operator on a filtered space, on duals and on tensor
and exterior powers.

At a closed point, each operation in the next lemma and proposition acts on
stalks by one of the constructions of the lemma: a subobject, a
quotient, a tensor product or a dual, or, for an inverse image, a
power of Frobenius. So the behaviour of weights is a matter of
eigenvalues. Mixedness needs in addition some bookkeeping to produce the
filtrations.

Let $X$ be a connected normal scheme of finite type over a field and $L$ a
lisse $E_X$-module. Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification]
gives lattices in $L$ only on the strata of a finite stratification, and the
nodal curve of Section [sec-Lattices-after-stratification] shows that without normality a
global lattice need not exist. On a normal $X$, however, we find a lattice on
all of $X$, and as a consequence lisse sheaves are the same as continuous
representations of the fundamental group. Here normality is used to show that
the étale $X$-scheme representing lattices in $L$ has a component that is
finite étale and surjective. Once we have such a component, we argue as
in Lemma [lemma-lattices-after-finite-stratification].

We apply the lemma to the scheme of lattices in a lisse sheaf. There the
valuative hypothesis says that a lattice defined at the generic point of
a valuation ring extends over the whole ring. This holds because,
locally, lattices form a constant sheaf on a discrete set.

Galois theory of finite étale covers turns statements about the finite
reductions of such an $M$ into statements about representations.

For a separated $k_0$-scheme of finite type $X_0$, we write
$D_{\leq w}(X_0)$ for the category of bounded constructible Weil
complexes $K$ on $X_0$ of weights at most $w$ in the sense of
Definition [definition-weights], that is, such that $\mathcal H^i(K)$ is
mixed of weights at most $w+i$ for every $i$. The Deligne–Laumon theorem says that
for a separated morphism of finite type $f:X_0\to Y_0$, the functor $Rf_!$
maps $D_{\leq w}(X_0)$ into $D_{\leq w}(Y_0)$. The shift by $i$ makes
this one statement for all degrees: for the structure morphism of $X_0$,
one condition on $R\Gamma_c(X,K)$ bounds all the groups $H^n_c(X,K)$ at
once. Moreover, by Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations],
replacing $K$ by $K[r]$ only moves the bound by $r$. The proof occupies
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-in-general] and, for a single curve, the sections
before it, and Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety]
deduces from the theorem the purity of the cohomology of a smooth proper
variety.

In Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] the Fourier transform of a pure sheaf
produces a lisse sheaf $M'$ whose Frobenius eigenvalues we cannot compute.
What we do know is that a twist of $M'$ is a quotient of a sheaf whose traces
are real, and from this alone we must conclude that $M'$ is pure. In
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-in-general] the same need returns for the direct
images of a family of curves, which we can make real but do not know to be
mixed. Both arguments rest on one theorem
(Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves]):

> on a smooth geometrically connected curve, every irreducible
> constituent of a real lisse Weil sheaf is pure, of weight equal to its
> determinant weight.

Before this theorem we know the weights of one kind of sheaf only: a lisse
sheaf of rank one on a curve has finite geometric monodromy, and therefore it is
pure (Section [sec-Sheaves-of-rank-one]). In particular the determinant
of every lisse sheaf is pure, and its weight divided by the rank, the determinant
weight, is the average weight of the eigenvalues at each point. The theorem says that on an
irreducible constituent of a real sheaf no eigenvalue deviates from this
average.

The tool is the trace formula. On an affine curve $U_0$ it expresses the
$L$-function of a lisse sheaf $\mathcal G$ as

$$
L(U_0,\mathcal G,t)
=\prod_{x\in|U_0|}\det(1-\operatorname{Frob}_xt^{\deg(x)}\mid\mathcal G_{\bar x})^{-1}
=\frac{\det(1-Ft\mid H^1_c(U,\mathcal G))}{\det(1-Ft\mid H^2_c(U,\mathcal G))}.
$$

The poles of the right-hand side are controlled by $H^2_c$, which is easy to
compute (Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology]). On the left, a large
eigenvalue at a point $x$ gives a pole of the local factor at $x$ close to the
origin. But this pole could be cancelled by a zero of the product of the other
factors, as in $(1-2t)^{-1}\cdot(1-2t)=1$. Positive factors, however, cannot cancel in
this way. Indeed, suppose all factors are power series with nonnegative coefficients
and constant term $1$. Then the coefficients of each factor are bounded by
those of the product, and Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence] shows that
no factor can converge on a smaller disc than the product.

This idea is Rankin's. In 1939 he improved the bound for Ramanujan's function
$\tau(n)$ to $O(n^{29/5})$ by studying the Dirichlet series
$\sum_n\tau(n)^2n^{-s}$, whose coefficients are nonnegative. Deligne used the
same argument in his first proof [deligne74].

For the Euler factors to be positive, the traces must be real. We therefore call a lisse
Weil sheaf real if its local characteristic polynomials have real coefficients
under the fixed embedding $\iota$ of Convention [situation-weil]
(Definition [definition-real-sheaves]). For example, every sheaf with rational
characteristic polynomials is real, such as a Tate twist of the constant
sheaf. On an even tensor power $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ of a
real sheaf the traces are $2m$th powers of real numbers, and this makes the
Euler factors positive. From this,
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] bounds each
local eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $\mathcal G$ by $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_x^\beta$,
where $\beta$ is the largest determinant weight of the constituents.

This is not yet the theorem, because a real sheaf need not be pure. For
example, the sheaf $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\oplus\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ is real, with constituents of
weights $0$ and $2$, but the bound only gives $2$ for both. To separate the
constituents we pass to exterior powers. In
$\bigwedge^2(\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\oplus\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1))=\det\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)\otimes\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ the factor
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ appears multiplied by the known eigenvalue $q_x$ of $\det\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$,
so the bound $2$ for this summand leaves the bound $0$ for $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ itself.
In general,
Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations](2) finds
the exterior power in which a given group of constituents carries the
largest determinant weight, and the same argument applies there. Positivity,
however, only ever gives upper bounds. The lower bound comes from applying
the same argument to the dual, and in Chapter [chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures] this
role is played by Poincaré duality.

Rankin's argument bounds the local eigenvalues of a sheaf by its
determinant weights, so it needs the determinant of every lisse sheaf to be
pure (Corollary [corollary-determinant-weights]). Since a determinant has rank
one, we prove more generally that every rank-one lisse Weil sheaf on a
smooth geometrically connected curve is pure
(Corollary [corollary-rank-one-weights]), and the later sections
Sections [sec-Determinant-weights]–[sec-Exterior-powers-and-purity] are
built on this fact.

In rank one the question is about characters. Let $U_0$ be a smooth
geometrically connected curve and $s\in W(U_0)$ a lift of Frobenius of
degree one (Convention [situation-weil]). Then a rank-one lisse Weil sheaf is a
character $\chi:W(U_0)\to E^\times$, continuous on $\pi_1(U)$. If $\chi$
is trivial on $\pi_1(U)$, the sheaf is one of the sheaves $\mathcal B_b$
with $b=\chi(s)$; at a closed point $x$ its eigenvalue is
$b^{\deg(x)}$, so it is pure of weight $2\log_q|\iota(b)|$. A Kummer
sheaf is the next simplest case. If $n\mid q-1$, the cover
$t\mapsto t^n$ of $\mathbf G_m$ is a $\mu_n$-torsor, and so a character of
$\mu_n(k_0)$ gives a rank-one sheaf on $\mathbf G_{m,k_0}$ whose
geometric monodromy is cyclic of order dividing $n$. Its eigenvalues
are values of the character on $\mu_n(k_0)$, hence roots of unity, and it is pure of weight $0$.

Up to a twist, every rank-one sheaf behaves like these two. Indeed, by
Theorem [theorem-rank-one-sheaves-have-finite] the image $\chi(\pi_1(U))$
is finite. It follows that $\chi(\operatorname{Frob}_x)$ is $\chi(s)^{\deg(x)}$
times a root of unity, so the sheaf is pure of weight
$2\log_q|\iota(\chi(s))|$.

Finiteness is a statement about Weil sheaves, because on the
geometric curve there are rank-one local systems with infinite
monodromy. For example, the tame fundamental group of
$\mathbf G_{m,k}$ has the quotient $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\simeq\mathbf Z_\ell$, and
$a\mapsto(1+\ell)^a$ is a character of infinite order. But it has no
Weil structure. Indeed, a Weil structure forces $\chi(s^{-1}gs)=\chi(g)$ for
$g\in\pi_1(U)$, while conjugation by $s$ acts on $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$ by multiplication by
a power $q^{\pm1}$. A character of $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$ that extends to the Weil group
therefore satisfies $\chi(g)^{q-1}=1$, and it has finite order.

The general proof follows the same pattern. Since there is no explicit
quotient to compute with, it uses a logarithm instead: a power $\chi^N$ takes
values in $1+\mathfrak m_E^r$, where the $\ell$-adic logarithm converges, and then
$\log\chi^N$ is an additive character of $\pi_1(U)$ invariant under
conjugation by $s$, that is, a class in $H^1(U,E)$ fixed by Frobenius
(Lemma [lemma-invariant-additive-characters]). Such a class is zero
(Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]), so $\chi^N$ is
trivial on $\pi_1(U)$.

For a proper curve, Frobenius fixes no class in $H^1$ because the
Jacobian has only finitely many rational points. If $C_0$ is a proper
curve with Jacobian $J_0$, Kummer theory and Poincaré duality identify
$\varprojlim_nH^1(C,\mathbf Z/\ell^n)$ with the dual of the Tate module
$T_\ell J$ (Proposition [proposition-kummer-duality-integral-tate-module]). A fixed vector in the
dual therefore means that $1$ is an eigenvalue of Frobenius on
$V_\ell J=T_\ell J\otimes\mathbf Q_\ell$, and after scaling, Frobenius would then
fix a nonzero element of $T_\ell J$. Such an element is a compatible system
of $\ell$-power torsion points of $J$ defined over $k_0$, of unbounded order.
These points cannot all lie in the finite group $J_0(k_0)$, and so there is no such
element (Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector]).

For an open curve, the residue sequence contains in addition the boundary term
$H^0(D,E(-1))$. A power of Frobenius acts on it by a power of $q\ne1$, so it
has no fixed vector either. For example, for $\mathbf G_m$ this is the computation above,
since there $H^1(\mathbf G_{m,k},\mathbf Q_\ell)=\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)$, with Frobenius acting by $q$.

Over $\mathbf C$ the link between $H^1$ of a curve and its Jacobian is
classical. There the Jacobian is a torus $V/\Lambda$ with $\Lambda=H_1(C,\mathbf Z)$, and
$H^1(C,\mathbf Z)=\Hom(\Lambda,\mathbf Z)$.
Proposition [proposition-kummer-duality-integral-tate-module] is the $\ell$-adic version, with
$T_\ell J$ in place of $\Lambda\otimes\mathbf Z_\ell$. Here the link with the Jacobian is
Kummer theory, which is a statement about $\mu_{\ell^n}$ and line bundles.
For this reason we work with the coefficients $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ and pass to
$E$ only at the end. Apart from this, the only arithmetic input is the finiteness of
$J_0(k_0)$, which holds because $J_0$ is of finite type over a finite
field.

Once we have a smooth projective model $C_0$, the Jacobian $J_0$ of
$C_0$ exists (Appendix [chap-The-Picard-scheme-of-a-curve]), and we can compare the cohomology of $C$ with its Tate module.
We first make the comparison with finite coefficients, where Kummer
theory applies directly. The proposition ends with a matrix description
of Frobenius, which is the form used in
Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one].

For the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ of the introduction,
arithmetic Frobenius $B$ has eigenvalues $\pm i\sqrt3$ on $T_\ell J$. By the
proposition, geometric Frobenius acts on $\varprojlim_nH^1(C,A_n)$ with the
same eigenvalues. Since $\det(B^t-1)=4\ne0$, it has no fixed vector. The
next proposition proves the same for every smooth curve, including open ones.

With Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one] in hand, the
logarithm argument sketched at the start of Section [sec-Sheaves-of-rank-one]
proves Theorem [theorem-rank-one-sheaves-have-finite].
Corollaries [corollary-rank-one-weights] and [corollary-determinant-weights]
then translate finiteness of monodromy into weights. For a lisse sheaf of
higher rank, however, the determinant weight
(Definition [definition-determinant-weight]) is the only weight we can
attach until Rankin's argument.
Throughout, $U_0$ is a smooth geometrically connected curve over $k_0$ and
$s\in W(U_0)$ is a lift of degree one, as in Convention [situation-weil].
In this setting, the first step identifies the additive
characters to which the logarithm leads.

The invariance hypothesis of the lemma is automatic for characters of
the Weil group. If $\chi:W(U_0)\to E^\times$ is a character, then
$\chi(s^{-1}gs)=\chi(s)^{-1}\chi(g)\chi(s)=\chi(g)$, because $E^\times$
is commutative. So the lemma applies as soon as $\chi$ has been made
additive on $\pi_1(U)$.

Finiteness gives the sheaf a weight, and since the lift $s$ is a
choice, part of the proof checks that the weight does not depend on it.

For a Kummer sheaf on $\mathbf G_{m,k_0}$ the corollary gives weight
$0$, since $\chi(s)$ is then a root of unity. For $\mathcal B_b$ it
gives $\lambda_\iota(b)$, the weight found in
Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].

Before purity is known, the eigenvalues of a lisse sheaf $\mathcal V$
of rank $r$ at a closed point are not controlled individually. Their
product, however, is controlled, since it is the eigenvalue of the rank-one sheaf
$\det\mathcal V$, whose weight is given by Corollary [corollary-rank-one-weights].
Dividing by $r$ we get the average weight of the eigenvalues, which is the only
candidate for a weight of $\mathcal V$. Indeed, if $\mathcal V$ is pure of
weight $w$, then $\det\mathcal V$ is pure of weight $rw$, and the number
defined below is $w$. For a sheaf that is not pure, on the other hand, the number is only an
average. For example, on $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\oplus\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ the determinant is $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$, of
weight $2$, and the number is $1$, the weight of no eigenvalue. For this
reason we apply it to irreducible constituents:
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] bounds the
eigenvalues of a real sheaf by the largest determinant weight of its
constituents, and Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves] then shows that
each irreducible constituent is pure of weight equal to its determinant weight.

The corollary applies to every irreducible constituent of $\mathcal V$
and of every tensor or exterior power of $\mathcal V$. Indeed, a
finite-dimensional representation has a composition series, and each
factor is again lisse and defined over a finite extension of $\mathbf Q_\ell$,
because after enlarging $E$ the invariant subspaces and quotients have
bases defined over $E$.

Before purity is known, the only weight we can attach to an irreducible
lisse Weil sheaf $Q$ on a curve is its determinant weight
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(Q)$, the weight of $\det Q$ divided by the rank
(Definition [definition-determinant-weight] and
Corollary [corollary-determinant-weights]). This section proves the two facts about
determinant weights that Rankin's argument in Section [sec-Rankins-bound] needs for the
tensor and exterior powers of a real sheaf $\mathcal G$. First, every simple
factor of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ has determinant weight at most $2m$ times
the largest determinant weight of the constituents of $\mathcal G$, and this
bounds the weights of $H^2_c$. Second, the determinant weights of the simple
factors of $\bigwedge^r\mathcal G$ are known exactly, and this is what lets
exterior powers separate the constituents.

The difficulty is that a determinant only sees an average. For
irreducible $A$ and $B$ of ranks $a$ and $b$, we have
$\det(A\otimes B)=(\det A)^{\otimes b}\otimes(\det B)^{\otimes a}$. Hence the
determinant weight of $A\otimes B$ as a whole is
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(A)+\operatorname{dw}_\iota(B)$. But $A\otimes B$
is usually reducible, and which subquotients occur depends on the
monodromy. The rank-weighted average of the determinant weights of its
simple factors is the number above, but nothing so far prevents one
factor from lying above it and another below. If the factors were pure,
the determinant weight of each would be its weight, but purity is what we are
trying to prove.

The model to keep in mind is a central character. If a group acts on
$V$ and some central element $z$ acts on $V$ by the scalar $c$, then $z$
acts on every subquotient of $V^{\otimes a}\otimes(V^\vee)^{\otimes b}$
by $c^{a-b}$, without any knowledge of how these representations
decompose. We therefore look for a central element of positive degree in the
monodromy group; its scalars will record weights.

Let $H\subseteq G$ be the Zariski closures in $\GL(V)$ of the
images of $\pi_1(U)$ and of $W(U_0)$, the geometric and arithmetic
monodromy groups. If $H$ were trivial, the image $\rho(s)$ of a
degree-one lift would itself be central. In general we use the structure
of the identity component,

$$
G^\circ=Z(G^\circ)^\circ H^\circ
$$

for $V$ semisimple (Lemma [lemma-identity-component]). The reason is that
the Lie algebra of $G^\circ$ is reductive, hence the sum of its
center and its derived algebra, and since $G/H$ is abelian, the derived algebra
lies in the Lie algebra of $H$. Accordingly, in
Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group] we write a power of
$\rho(s)$ as a central torus element times an element of $H$, and then we take the
product of its conjugates over $G/G^\circ$. The result is an element
$z=h\rho(s)^N$, central in $G$, with $h\in H$ and $N>0$.

On a simple factor $Q$ of any tensor construction, $z$ acts by a scalar
$c_Q$, and taking determinants gives
$c_Q^{\dim Q}=\det(h\mid Q)\det(s\mid Q)^N$. Since determinants have finite
geometric monodromy, $\det(h\mid Q)$ is a root of unity, and from this
Lemma [lemma-determinant-weight-from-central-scalar] concludes that
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(Q)=\lambda_\iota(c_Q)/N$, where
$\lambda_\iota(a)=2\log_q|\iota(a)|$ is the additive function of
Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations].
Since scalars multiply under tensor products, we obtain
Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations].

The facts on algebraic groups that we use, namely the relation between
closed subgroups, their identity components and their Lie algebras, and
the structure of a Lie algebra with a faithful semisimple
representation, are proved in Appendix [chap-Algebraic-groups-in-characteristic-zero].

We treat lisse sheaves as representations of the Weil group. From the
geometry of the curve we use only one fact, proved in
Section [sec-Sheaves-of-rank-one]: the geometric fundamental group acts
through a finite group on every determinant. Everything else is linear
algebra and the structure of algebraic groups.

Throughout, $U_0$ is a smooth geometrically connected curve over $k_0$ and
$s\in W(U_0)$ is a lift of degree one, as in Convention [situation-weil], so that
$W(U_0)=\pi_1(U)\rtimes\langle s\rangle$.

By Convention [situation-weil] the Weil representations are the
lisse Weil $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaves on $U_0$, and so, by
Corollary [corollary-determinant-weights], $\pi_1(U)$ acts through a finite group on
the determinant of every Weil representation. A Weil representation $V$ is
semisimple if it is a direct sum of simple representations, and the semisimplification $V^{\mathrm{ss}}$ of $V$ is the
direct sum of its composition factors.

Two elementary facts are needed. First, semisimplicity is preserved by
restriction to a normal subgroup, which lets us apply Lie theory to the
identity component of the monodromy group below. Second, the composition
factors of tensor and exterior powers are computed from those of the
given representations, so it suffices to prove the formulas for
semisimple representations.

The second fact concerns representations that are not semisimple. A
nonsplit extension of $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ by $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, such as the twist
$\mathcal E(-1)$ of the Kummer extension of
Example [example-kummer-extension], does not decompose. Yet the composition
factors of its tensor and exterior powers are determined by
those of the sheaf, as the next lemma shows by filtering. This is what
lets us pass to semisimplifications in
Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations].

In the arithmetic monodromy group we construct a central element of
positive degree
(Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group]). It acts by a scalar
on each simple factor, and this scalar determines the determinant
weight of the factor. As explained above, we construct the element for semisimple
representations, and then use stable filtrations to obtain the
formulas for arbitrary representations.

The degree must be positive. Indeed, an element of $H$ that is central in
$G$ also acts by a scalar on each simple factor $Q$. But, as for every element
of $H$, its determinant on $Q$ is a root of unity, so under $\iota$ the scalar
has absolute value one, and it records no weight. By contrast, an element
$z=h\rho(s)^N$ with $N>0$ contains $N$ factors of Frobenius, and its
scalar $c_Q$ on $Q$ satisfies
$\lambda_\iota(c_Q)=N\operatorname{dw}_\iota(Q)$
(Lemma [lemma-determinant-weight-from-central-scalar]).

We produce the central element by Lie theory, which applies to
algebraic groups and not to the abstract images of $\pi_1(U)$ and
$W(U_0)$. For $\mathcal B_b$ with $b$ not a root of unity, the image of
$W(U_0)$ in $\GL_1$ is the infinite cyclic group generated by $b$, which
is not an algebraic subgroup; its Zariski closure is all of $\GL_1$,
since the proper closed subgroups of $\mathbf G_m$ are finite. Passing
to the closure loses nothing that we need. Indeed, stabilizers are closed, so
a subspace of $V$ is stable under a group of matrices if and only if it is
stable under its Zariski closure. For this reason Lemma [lemma-identity-component] and
Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group]
are statements about these closures.

We keep the letters $H$ and $G$ for these two groups in the rest of
this section.

For example, for $V=\mathcal B_b$ of Proposition [proposition-weights-under-usual-operations]
the group $H$ is trivial. Hence $\rho(s)=b$ is central in $G$, and the
determinant weight of $\mathcal B_b$ is $\lambda_\iota(b)$.

Rankin's argument needs the determinant weights of the simple factors
of $\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$, of the exterior powers of $\mathcal G$ and
of the dual, so we give a name to the representations built in this way;
the monodromy group acts on all of them.

Since the stabilizer of a subspace is closed, a $W(U_0)$-stable
subspace is $G$-stable, and so $G$ acts on every tensor construction
through its action on $V$.

The central element acts on each simple factor of a tensor construction
by a scalar, and from these scalars we read off determinant weights. Since Weil representations are the lisse Weil
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaves, Definition [definition-determinant-weight] applies
to them.

The lemma reduces determinant weights of tensor constructions to a
computation with the scalars on the composition factors of $V$. By
Proposition [proposition-central-element-arithmetic-monodromy-group], the element $z$ acts
by a scalar on every simple subquotient of a tensor construction on $V$, so the formula
of the lemma applies to each of them. Since the scalars by which a single
element acts multiply under tensor products and exterior powers, this gives
the following formulas.

In particular every simple factor of $V^{\otimes m}$ has determinant weight
at most $m\max\operatorname{DW}(V)$. In Section [sec-Exterior-powers-and-purity] we
use this bound, and part (2), for the constituents of a real sheaf before
we know that they are pure.

We bound the local eigenvalues of a real sheaf by the eigenvalues of
Frobenius on $H^2_c$ of its even tensor powers
(Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight]). Only $H^2_c$ is needed, and
Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology] computes it by Poincaré
duality as the coinvariants of the geometric monodromy.

Rankin's argument uses one fact from each side of the trace
formula. On the cohomological side, an affine curve has $H^0_c=0$, so
only $H^2_c$ can produce poles of the $L$-function, and we can compute
this group without knowing anything about $H^1_c$: its eigenvalues are
$q$ times eigenvalues of Frobenius on a quotient of the generic fibre. On
the side of the Euler product, if the local factors have nonnegative
coefficients, then each of them is holomorphic wherever the product is.

For example, for the constant sheaf on $\mathbf G_m$ we have

$$
L(\mathbf G_m,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell,t)=\prod_{x\in|\mathbf G_m|}(1-t^{\deg(x)})^{-1}
=\frac{1-t}{1-qt},
$$

where $1-t$ comes from $H^1_c$ and the pole at $t=q^{-1}$ from
$H^2_c=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$. Each local factor has its poles on the circle
$|t|=1$, outside the disc $|t|<q^{-1}$, as
Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence] predicts. In general we apply the two facts to
the even tensor powers of a real sheaf, whose $H^2_c$ is bounded by the
determinant weights of Section [sec-Determinant-weights], and this gives
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight].

For the constant sheaf on $\mathbf G_m$ the lemma gives
$H^2_c=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$, of weight $2$, as in the computation at the start
of the section. Now take a Kummer sheaf of a nontrivial character on
$\mathbf G_m$. Then $H^0_c=0$ because $\mathbf G_m$ is affine, and
$H^2_c=0$ because the coinvariants vanish.

The positivity we want is $a^{2m}\ge0$ for the traces $a$ of all powers
$\operatorname{Frob}_x^n$ on $\mathcal G$, and for this all these traces must be
real. It is not enough to ask that the trace of
$\operatorname{Frob}_x$ itself be real. For example, if the eigenvalues at $x$ are $i$
and $1-i$, the trace is $1$, but the trace of the square is
$-1+(1-i)^2=-1-2i$. By the Newton identities, on the other hand, all the power sums are real
exactly when the characteristic polynomial is real, and this is the condition
below. Its basic examples are the constant sheaf, its Tate twists and Kummer
sheaves of quadratic characters. More generally, in Chapter [chap-Pure-sheaves-on-curves],
Proposition [proposition-twisting-weight-zero-adding-dual]
makes every pure sheaf a summand of a real one after a twist. The
condition enters the proof of Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves]
through Lemma [lemma-positivity-euler-factors].

The next lemma is the $\ell$-adic form of Rankin's trick. Since the
even powers of a real trace are nonnegative, the Euler factors of
$\mathcal G^{\otimes2m}$ have nonnegative coefficients.

Without positivity a factor can converge on a smaller disc than the
product, as in the cancellation at the start of this chapter. With
positivity, however, the coefficients of each factor are bounded by those of the product.

In the proposition below, the twist $(-1)$ on $H^2_c$ costs a factor
$q$, and this loss disappears when we take $2m$th roots and let $m$ grow.

Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] only bounds the local eigenvalues
by the largest determinant weight. To bound the eigenvalues of each
constituent by its own determinant weight, we apply the proposition to
exterior powers, which separate the determinant weights of the simple
factors.

Tensor powers cannot do this. For example, suppose $\mathcal G=\mathcal G_1\oplus\mathcal G_2$
with determinant weights $\gamma_1>\gamma_2$. In
$\mathcal G^{\otimes m}$ the largest determinant weight $m\gamma_1$
belongs to the factors of $\mathcal G_1^{\otimes m}$, while every factor
involving $\mathcal G_2$ lies strictly below it. So the bound of
Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight] says nothing sharp about
$\mathcal G_2$.

An exterior power, by contrast, uses each basis vector of $\mathcal G_1$ at most once. Thus if
$r_1$ is the rank of $\mathcal G_1$, every graded piece of
$\bigwedge^{r_1+1}\mathcal G$ involves $\mathcal G_2$, and the summand
$\det\mathcal G_1\otimes\mathcal G_2$ has the largest determinant weight
$r_1\gamma_1+\gamma_2$. Since Corollary [corollary-determinant-weights] gives the
eigenvalues of $\det\mathcal G_1$, a bound for this summand is a
bound for $\mathcal G_2$. We argue on an affine curve, where
the proposition applies, and then pass to an arbitrary curve by
restricting to affine opens, which preserves irreducibility.

How much does the trace function of a sheaf know about its Frobenius
eigenvalues? For a sheaf of rank one, pure of weight $w$, on a dense open
$U_0$ of the line, it knows the weight. Indeed, every trace over $\mathbf F_{q^n}$
has absolute value $q^{nw/2}$, so the sum $S_n$ of the $|t(x)|^2$ over
$U_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})$ is $q^{nw}\#U_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})$, about
$q^{n(w+1)}$, and the growth rate $q^{w+1}$ of these sums therefore determines $w$. In higher rank, however, a
trace is a sum of eigenvalues, and the eigenvalues can cancel. For example, on
$\mathcal B_b\oplus\mathcal B_{-b}$ the trace at a point of degree $n$ is
$b^n+(-b)^n$, which is zero for every odd $n$. We show that the
cancellation cannot persist: for a nonzero pure lisse sheaf of weight $w$
on an affine curve, $\limsup_n\frac1n\log_qS_n=w+1$
(Theorem [theorem-weights-sums-squared-traces]).

The reason is positivity once more. Recall that a sheaf $\mathcal G$ is real
if the characteristic polynomials of Frobenius on its stalks have real
coefficients under $\iota$ (Definition [definition-real-sheaves]). For
such $\mathcal G$, pure of weight $w$, $|t_{\mathcal G}|^2$ is the trace function of
$\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal G$, and hence the generating series of the $S_n$ is the
logarithmic derivative of $L(\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal G,t)$. Positivity of
the Euler factors (Lemma [lemma-positivity-euler-factors]) shows that $L(\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal G,t)$ is not a
polynomial, and Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology] puts its poles
on $|t|=q^{-w-1}$. Together these force the sums $S_n$ to reach the size $q^{n(w+1)}$
infinitely often. The restriction to real sheaves costs nothing, since an arbitrary pure sheaf becomes real
after a twist to weight zero and the addition of its dual
(Proposition [proposition-twisting-weight-zero-adding-dual]).

This is what the Fourier argument of Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves]
needs. That argument starts from a pure lisse sheaf $M$ of weight $w$ on a dense open
$j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ and produces a pure lisse sheaf $M'$ on a
dense open $j'$ of the dual line. It knows the trace function of
$M'$ exactly, as the discrete Fourier transform of that of $M$, but it
cannot see the weight of $M'$ directly. Since Plancherel's formula multiplies the
sums $S_n$ by $q^n$, the theorem shows that $M'$ has weight $w+1$.

The group we finally want to bound, $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$, is the stalk of
$j'_*M'$ at the origin. But the origin may be one of the points where $M'$ is
not lisse, and there we need to know that $j'_*$ does not create larger weights
(Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]).

Let $j$ be the inclusion of a dense open in a smooth curve, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a lisse sheaf on the open. The Fourier argument needs an
extension of $\mathcal F$ to the whole curve that loses nothing at the
boundary points. The ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$ is such an
extension, whereas extension by zero loses something. For example, for the constant
sheaf on $\mathbf G_m\subset\mathbf A^1$, $j_!\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ has stalk $0$ at the
origin, while the constant sheaf on $\mathbf A^1$ is the natural
extension. In general, by Lemma [lemma-boundary-stalk], $j_*\mathcal F$ recovers a lisse
extension whenever one exists, and its stalk at a boundary point is the
space of inertia invariants.

If $\mathcal F$ is punctually of weights $\le a$, then so is
$j_*\mathcal F$, at the boundary points as well
(Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]). In
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] this bounds the weights of
the boundary terms in the Fourier transform of a middle extension.

To bound $j_*\mathcal F$ we compare the $L$-functions of
$\mathcal F$ and of $j_*\mathcal F$ on a disc. To see that the
Euler product converges there, we need a crude bound for the number of
points of a curve.

In the next proof we use the lemma to show that the logarithm of the
Euler product of $\mathcal F$ converges on a disc of radius $q^{-a/2-1}$,
and on this disc we compare it with $j_*\mathcal F$.

The proposition gives only an upper bound at the boundary, and in
general nothing better is true. For example, for a family of elliptic curves with
multiplicative reduction at $z$, the first cohomology of the fibres is
pure of weight $1$, while its inertia invariants at $z$ form a line
of weight $0$. When the inertia acts trivially, however, we get the lower
bound by duality.

The proof of Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points],
together with Lemma [lemma-degree-zero-top-cohomology], also gives the
extreme degrees of the cohomology of a middle extension on an affine
curve.

For the perverse t-structure in Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform] we need
the same range of degrees for arbitrary constructible sheaves.

A constructible Weil sheaf on a curve $C_0$ over $k_0$ gives a
constructible sheaf on $C=C_0\times_{k_0}k$, so the lemma applies to it
as well.

In Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] we know the trace function of the
Fourier transform $M'$ exactly, but not its weight. For a pure sheaf the
trace function determines the weight: it is the growth rate of the sums of
squared traces (Theorem [theorem-weights-sums-squared-traces]).

The number $\nu$ below is the growth exponent of the sums of squared
traces, shifted by $1$ so that it equals the weight. We take a $\limsup$
because the sums can vanish for infinitely many $n$, as the example of
$\mathcal B_b\oplus\mathcal B_{-b}$ at the start of this chapter shows.

A cohomological shift changes the weight of a complex in the sense of
Definition [definition-weights]. But it only multiplies the trace
function by a sign, and so it leaves $\nu$ unchanged.

In the theorem below we find $\nu$ from the radius of convergence of a
generating series, which is a logarithmic derivative of an $L$-function.

To compute $\nu$ we also need upper bounds for lisse sheaves and for
complexes with finite support, as well as the effect of twisting by
$\mathcal B_b$.

A correction at finitely many points of small weight does not change
$\nu$. We use this to discard the boundary terms in
Corollary [corollary-sums-squared-traces-j-shriek].

By counting points, Lemma [lemma-bounds-squared-traces](1) gives
$\nu\le w$ for a sheaf pure of weight $w$. A priori, however, the squared traces could
be much smaller than this trivial bound, through cancellation among the
eigenvalues at each point. The next theorem shows that on average they are
not.

Under the hypothesis of Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension], the
Fourier transform of $(j_*M)[1]$ is again a middle extension. But
Plancherel applies only to complexes on the whole line, boundary points
included, so we need the theorem for $j_*$ and $j_!$ on the larger curve.
This costs nothing: the boundary points do not change $\nu$, because
their weights are small.

Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves] controls the Frobenius
eigenvalues of a real sheaf at the points of a curve. The bound we need
next, however, is of a different kind. Let $M$ be an irreducible lisse sheaf, pure
of weight $w$, on a dense open $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$. The
curve case of the Deligne–Laumon theorem comes down to showing that
$H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$ has weights at most $w+1$. This is a
cohomology group, not the stalk of a sheaf at a point, and Rankin's
argument does not reach it. Is there a sheaf on another curve whose stalk
at one point is this group, and whose weight we can compute from that of
$M$? Up to a shift, the Fourier transform of $(j_*M)[1]$ is such a sheaf.

For functions on $\mathbf F_q$ the discrete Fourier transform already
does what we want. Fix a nontrivial additive character $\psi$ and put
$\hat t(y)=\sum_xt(x)\psi(xy)$. Two properties matter. First, the value
$\hat t(0)$ is the sum of all values of $t$, so a sum over the line
becomes a single value. Second, Plancherel's formula
$\sum_y|\hat t(y)|^2=q\sum_x|t(x)|^2$ holds, by orthogonality of
characters.

To see Plancherel compute an absolute value, let $\chi$ be a
nontrivial character of $\mathbf F_q^\times$, extended by $\chi(0)=0$,
and let $g=\sum_x\chi(x)\psi(x)$ be its Gauss sum. Substituting
$x\mapsto x/y$ shows that $\hat\chi(y)=\overline\chi(y)g$ for $y\ne0$, so
the transform has the same absolute value $|g|$ at all $q-1$ nonzero points,
while $\hat\chi(0)=0$. Plancherel therefore reads $(q-1)|g|^2=q(q-1)$, and we
find $|g|=\sqrt q$. In the language of weights, this means that the transform
carries a function of weight $0$ to one of weight $1$. For the quadratic character of
$\mathbf F_3$, moreover, Example [example-gauss-sum-over-f-3] finds this Gauss
sum, up to sign, as a Frobenius eigenvalue on a cohomology group.

The proof in Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] follows the same two
steps for $M$: first we show that the transform is pure, and then
Plancherel finds its weight.

Grothendieck's function–sheaf dictionary
(Proposition [proposition-function-sheaf-dictionary]) turns the
transform into a functor. Let $\mathcal K_\psi=\mu^*\mathcal L_\psi$ be the pullback of the
Artin–Schreier sheaf (Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf]) along the
multiplication $\mu(x,y)=xy$. Its trace function on $\mathbf F_q$-points is
$\psi(xy)$, and we put

$$
\operatorname{FT}_\psi K=Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)[1].
$$

On trace functions it is the discrete transform up to sign: for
$y\in\mathbf F_q$,

$$
t_{\operatorname{FT}_\psi K}(y)=-\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_q}t_K(x)\,\psi(xy),
$$

because under the dictionary (Section [sec-The-function-sheaf-dictionary-2])
pullback, tensor product and $Rp_{2!}$ become composition, multiplication
and summation over the fibres, the three operations from which $\hat t$
is built, while the shift $[1]$ contributes the sign. Both properties of the
discrete transform carry over. The first becomes the statement that the
stalk at the origin of the dual line is $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,K)[1]$
(Proposition [proposition-base-change-fourier-inversion]), so for
$K=j_*M$ this complex contains the group we want. Plancherel becomes an
identity of trace functions (Corollary [corollary-plancherel]), and
it is what will compute the weight of the transform. In addition,
Fourier inversion,
$\operatorname{FT}_{\psi^{-1}}\operatorname{FT}_\psi K\simeq K(-1)$,
holds because $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal L_\psi)=0$, the sheaf
version of $\sum_x\psi(x)=0$. The $\ell$-adic transform is due to Deligne, and
Laumon's proof [laumon87] of the Deligne–Laumon theorem is built on it.

To speak of the weight of the transform we need it to be a lisse sheaf on
a dense open. But the transform of a sheaf need not be a sheaf. For
example, the transform of the constant sheaf is a skyscraper at the
origin in degree one, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(E)=\delta_0(-1)[-1]$. This
is the sheaf version of $\hat1=q\,\delta_0$, up to the sign coming from
the shift. What the transform does preserve, however, is the category of perverse
sheaves on the line (Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart],
proved in Section [sec-Perverse-t-exactness] below). Since the transform is an exact equivalence of
perverse sheaves, it sends the simple object $(j_*M)[1]$ to a simple object,
which is either punctual or a middle extension. Moreover, only character sheaves
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ are sent to skyscrapers. Hence, if no geometric constituent
of the irreducible sheaf $M$ is such a character, we have

$$
\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\simeq(j'_*M')[1]
$$

for an irreducible lisse $M'$ on a dense open $j'$ of the dual line
(Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension] below).
Comparing stalks at the origin then identifies $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$ with
a stalk of $j'_*M'$, and this is the sheaf we asked for.

We use the six operations on the pro-étale site. At first the
coefficients are a finite extension $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ that contains the
$p$th roots of unity, where $p$ is the characteristic of $k_0$, so that $E$ contains the values of the additive characters of $k_0$. Later the
coefficients are $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

The kernel of the transform is a lisse sheaf whose trace function is
the additive character $\psi$, just as $\psi(xy)$ is the kernel of the
discrete transform. It is cut out of the Artin–Schreier cover of the
line as an eigenspace of the translations. This cover is Galois with
group the additive group $\mathbf F_p$, acting by $u\mapsto u+a$. Let
$u^p-u=x$ with $x\in\mathbf F_{q^n}$. Raising to the powers
$p,p^2,\ldots$ and adding gives $u^{q^n}=u+\operatorname{Tr}(x)$. In
other words, Frobenius acts on the fibre over $x$ by the translation
$\operatorname{Tr}(x)\in\mathbf F_p$. A character $\psi_0$ of
$\mathbf F_p$ then turns this translation into the number
$\psi_0(\operatorname{Tr}x)$. Similarly, the Kummer cover $u^{q-1}=x$ of $\mathbf G_m$ produces the multiplicative
characters in the same way.

Besides the sheaf itself (Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf]), we need the
sheaf version of $\sum_x\psi(x)=0$, namely the vanishing of
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^r,\lambda^*\mathcal L_\psi)$ for a nonzero linear
form $\lambda$ (Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character]). This is stronger than
the statement on trace functions, since the trace formula only says that the
alternating sum of the traces vanishes over every $\mathbf F_{q^n}$.
Fourier inversion and the stalk computations below, however, need each
cohomology group to vanish. This vanishing comes from the eigenspace
decomposition of the cover: the total space of the cover is again an
affine line, and the translations act trivially on the compactly
supported cohomology of a line. Hence the eigenspace of a nontrivial
character is zero.

We check the lemma by hand at two points. Over $\mathbf F_p$ with
$a=1$, the fibre of the cover over $x=1$ is $u^p-u=1$, which has no root in
$\mathbf F_p$. Indeed, Frobenius acts on the
$p$ roots by $u\mapsto u^p=u+1$, a translation of order $p$, and the
trace of $\mathcal L_\psi$ at $x=1$ is therefore $\psi(1)=\psi_0(1)\ne1$.
Over $x=0$, by contrast, the roots are the elements of $\mathbf F_p$, so
they are all fixed and the trace is $1$.

Fourier inversion integrates the kernel over a whole fibre
$\mathbf A^r$ of a vector bundle, so we need the vanishing on
$\mathbf A^r$ and not only on the line. In coordinates in which the
linear form is the first coordinate, the integral over $\mathbf A^r$ is
a product of an integral over the line and one over $\mathbf A^{r-1}$,
and the Künneth formula makes this precise.

Let $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$ be separated morphisms of finite type,
let $p_1:X\times_SY\to X$ and $p_2:X\times_SY\to Y$ be the projections,
and let $h=f\circ p_1:X\times_SY\to S$ be the structure map. For
complexes $K$ on $X$ and $L$ on $Y$ we put
$K\boxtimes_SL=p_1^*K\otimes p_2^*L$.

Over a point, this is the Künneth isomorphism for cohomology with
compact support. All three isomorphisms in the composite are natural,
so when $X$, $Y$, $S$, $f$, $g$, $K$ and $L$ are defined over $k_0$,
the Künneth isomorphism commutes with the Weil structures.

The case $\lambda=0$ of the next lemma is needed as well, since Fourier inversion integrates the
kernel along the diagonal, where the character is trivial.

We integrate with compact supports, $Rp_{2!}$ rather than $Rp_{2*}$,
for two reasons. First, proper base change computes the stalks
of $Rp_{2!}$ as compactly supported cohomology of the fibres, and this
puts $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$ at the origin. Second, the trace formula
holds for $Rp_{2!}$, so that on trace functions the transform becomes the
discrete Fourier transform (16.3) (proved in
Section [sec-The-Plancherel-formula]).

The shift $[r]$ is the one for which the transform preserves the
perverse heart. For example, on the line we will find
$\operatorname{FT}_\psi(E[1])=\delta_0(-1)$, whereas without the shift the
perverse sheaf $E[1]$ would go to $\delta_0(-1)[-1]$, which is not
perverse.

We work with a vector bundle $V\to S$ rather than the line alone,
because the proofs move along the base. For instance, the stalk formula is base change
to a point of the dual bundle, and Fourier inversion is a computation on
$V\times_SV^\vee\times_SV$, which reduces, fibre by fibre, to
Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character] on $\mathbf A^r$. We prove
these two properties in
Propositions [proposition-base-change-fourier-inversion]
and [proposition-fourier-inversion], while the preservation of the heart is
Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart].

Let $S$ be a scheme of finite type over $k_0$ or over $k$, let $V\to S$ be a vector
bundle of rank $r$, and let $V^\vee$ be its dual bundle. Write
$p_1,p_2$ for the projections of $V\times_SV^\vee$, and set

$$
\mathcal K_\psi=\langle\ ,\ \rangle^*\mathcal L_\psi,
\qquad
\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)
=Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi)[r].
\tag{16.1}
$$

The kernel $\mathcal K_\psi$ is lisse of rank one, and since the six
operations preserve constructibility, this defines a triangulated
functor $\operatorname{FT}_\psi:\Dbc(V,E)\to\Dbc(V^\vee,E)$, normalized
by the shift $[r]$.

On the line, the transform exchanges the two simplest perverse sheaves,
the shifted constant sheaf and the skyscraper at the origin, up to a
twist. This is the sheaf version of $\hat 1=q\,\delta_0$ and
$\hat\delta_0=1$.

On trace functions, the Fourier transform is, up to the sign $(-1)^r$, the
discrete Fourier transform over $\mathbf F_{q^n}$ for the character
$\psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/k_0}$
(equation (16.3) below). The Plancherel formula
then says how it changes the growth of squared trace sums, and for a pure sheaf
this growth is the weight
(Theorem [theorem-weights-sums-squared-traces]). This is how we find
the weight of the transform in Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves]: on the
line, Plancherel multiplies the sums of squared traces by $q^n$, and so it
raises the weight read off from their growth by one.

In this section $S=\operatorname{Spec}k_0$ and
$V=\mathbf A^r_{k_0}$.
For a Weil complex $K$ on a $k_0$-scheme $X_0$, we write $t_{K,n}(x)$
for the alternating sum of the Frobenius traces at
$x\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})$, as in Definition [definition-growth-squared-traces].
With this notation, the dictionary (Proposition [proposition-function-sheaf-dictionary])
computes the trace function of the transform step by step. For
$y\in\mathbf F_{q^n}^r$, the shift contributes $(-1)^r$ (chain formula of
Proposition [proposition-properties-trace]), part (3) sums over
the fibre of $p_2$, and part (2) splits the trace of the tensor product:

$$
t_{\operatorname{FT}_\psi K,n}(y)
=(-1)^r\,t_{Rp_{2!}(p_1^*K\otimes\mathcal K_\psi),n}(y)
=(-1)^r\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{q^n}^r}t_{p_1^*K,n}(x,y)\,
t_{\mathcal K_\psi,n}(x,y).
$$

By part (1), $t_{p_1^*K,n}(x,y)=t_{K,n}(x)$, and by part (1) and
Lemma [lemma-artin-schreier-character-sheaf],
$t_{\mathcal K_\psi,n}(x,y)=\psi(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/k_0}\langle x,y\rangle)$.
Hence

$$
t_{\operatorname{FT}_\psi K,n}(y)
=(-1)^r\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{q^n}^r}
t_{K,n}(x)\,
\psi\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbf F_{q^n}/k_0}
\langle x,y\rangle\bigr).
\tag{16.3}
$$

For the constant sheaf $E$ on the line and $n=1$, formula
(16.3) gives the trace $-\sum_x\psi(xy)$, which is $-q$ at
$y=0$ and $0$ elsewhere, in agreement with
$\operatorname{FT}_\psi(E)=\delta_0(-1)[-1]$. Both sides of Plancherel
are then $q^2$, and over $\mathbf F_{q^n}$ they are $q^{2n}$. This gives
$\nu(E)=0$ and $\nu(\operatorname{FT}_\psi E)=1$, as the corollary
predicts.

To apply Theorem [theorem-weights-sums-squared-traces] to the
transform of a pure lisse sheaf $M$, we need to know that the
transform of $(j_*M)[1]$ is again a lisse sheaf on a dense open,
placed in degree $-1$. Although the transform sends the constant sheaf
to a skyscraper (Lemma [lemma-fourier-transform-constant-sheaf]), it preserves
the perverse heart, which on a smooth curve has an elementary
description in terms of ordinary cohomology sheaves and punctual
support.

We can read off the shape of this description from the stalk formula.
The stalk of the transform of $G[1]$ at $y$ is
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,G\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(yx)})[2]$. For a sheaf $G$
without punctual sections $H^0_c$ vanishes, and the proof of
Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart] below shows
that $H^2_c$ is nonzero only at finitely many $y$. So the transform lives in
degrees $-1$ and $0$, with a punctual sheaf in
degree $0$, and this suggests allowing skyscrapers in
degree $0$ in ${}^pD^{\le0}$. Orthogonality then forces the condition on
the other side: a sheaf in degree $0$ lies in ${}^pD^{\ge1}$ only if it
receives no nonzero map from a skyscraper, that is, only if it has no
punctual subsheaf. The perverse t-structure on a curve is the
t-structure built from these two conditions.

What we finally use about it is the list of its simple objects
(Lemma [lemma-simple-objects]). By this list, an exact equivalence
must send an irreducible middle extension to an irreducible middle
extension or to an irreducible punctual sheaf.

Recall that a *t-structure* on a triangulated category $D$ is a
pair of full subcategories $D^{\le0}\supset D^{\le-1}$ and
$D^{\ge0}\supset D^{\ge1}$, where $D^{\le n}=D^{\le0}[-n]$ and
$D^{\ge n}=D^{\ge0}[-n]$, such that $\Hom(A,B)=0$ for $A\in D^{\le0}$
and $B\in D^{\ge1}$, and every object sits in a triangle $A\to K\to
B\to$ with $A\in D^{\le0}$ and $B\in D^{\ge1}$. Its *heart* is
$D^{\le0}\cap D^{\ge0}$; for the ordinary t-structure it is the
category of sheaves. We write $D^{[a,b]}=D^{\ge a}\cap D^{\le b}$.
The triangle is unique up to unique isomorphism, so, as for the
ordinary t-structure, it gives truncation functors and cohomology
objects of $K$ in the heart. Finally, a functor is *t-exact* if it
preserves both subcategories.

Let $C$ be a smooth curve over a perfect field. On $C$ the perverse
t-structure is built from punctual sheaves.

The truncation triangle of the perverse t-structure splits a sheaf into
a punctual part and a part without punctual subsheaves, so we first
construct the largest punctual subsheaf. In the following lemma
“sheaf” means a constructible sheaf with coefficients $E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$.

By Lemma [lemma-perverse-sheaves-curve] below these classes form a
t-structure, the perverse t-structure. We write ${}^pD^{[a,b]}$ and
${}^p\mathcal H^n$ for its subcategories and cohomology objects.

On the line, the two basic examples are $E[1]$ and the skyscraper
$\delta_0$, and by Lemma [lemma-fourier-transform-constant-sheaf] the Fourier
transform exchanges them up to a Tate twist. This is the simplest
instance of the exactness proved in
Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart].

Unwinding the definition, a perverse sheaf on $C$ is a complex in
ordinary degrees $-1,0$ whose $\mathcal H^0$ is punctual and whose
$\mathcal H^{-1}$ has no nonzero punctual subsheaf.

An exact equivalence of abelian categories sends simple objects to
simple objects. Once we know that the transform is exact on the heart,
the following list of simple objects will tell us what the transform
of a middle extension can be.

The transform $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ is
t-exact for the perverse t-structure on the line
(Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-perverse-heart]). By the stalk formula
(16.2), this comes down to the compactly
supported cohomology of sheaves on an affine curve in the extreme
degrees zero and two.

Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be a dense open, and let
$M$ be an irreducible lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$. The argument of
Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-for-curves] needs the transform of the middle
extension of $M$ to be again a middle extension, that is, to come from a
lisse sheaf $M'$ on a dense open of the dual line. This holds unless $M$ has a geometric constituent of the form
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$, and the hypothesis of the next proposition excludes
these. They behave differently: for $a\ne0$ the sheaf $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ has no cohomology
with compact support on the line by
Lemma [lemma-integral-linear-character], and its transform is a
skyscraper rather than a lisse sheaf of weight one. Excluding them, however, costs
nothing in the application, because a sheaf unramified at infinity has no such
constituent other than the constant one, and constant constituents
contribute nothing, since $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)=0$.

The sheaf $M'$ is determined by $M$ up to isomorphism and shrinking of
$U'_0$, since it is the restriction to $U'_0$ of
$\mathcal H^{-1}\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])$. In the application
we check the hypothesis of the proposition with the following
criterion, whose proof is a computation of ramification at infinity.

Let $F$ be a pure lisse Weil sheaf of weight $w$ on a smooth curve $C$.
Why should $H^1_c(C,F)$ have weights at most $w+1$? For the constant
sheaf on a smooth projective curve this is Weil's theorem, proved with
the Jacobian, and for an arbitrary $F$ there is no such object to work
with. Yet the Deligne–Laumon theorem comes down to exactly this bound. The theorem
says that $H^r_c(C,F)$ has weights at most $w+r$
(Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve]), and only $r=1$ requires work.
Indeed, on an affine curve $H^0_c$ vanishes, while by
Lemma [lemma-extreme-degrees-affine-curve] $H^2_c$ is a twist of
the coinvariants of geometric monodromy, pure of weight $w+2$. For
$r=1$ the bound can be strict: on $\mathbf G_m$ the group $H^1_c$ comes from the boundary
and has weight $0$ (see the example of Chapter [chap-Weights]).

For a Gauss sum the answer takes two steps. The transform
$\hat\chi(y)=\overline\chi(y)g$ has the same absolute value for all
$y\ne0$, and Plancherel finds the common value $\sqrt q$. On an open of
the affine line, Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform] makes the same two steps
available for sheaves. More precisely, let $M$ be irreducible on a dense open
$j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$, with no geometric constituent of the
form $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$, and let $M'$ be the lisse sheaf with
$\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\simeq(j'_*M')[1]$
(Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension]). Then

$$
H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)\simeq(j'_*M')_{0'}
$$

(Corollary [corollary-h-1-c-stalk-fourier]). Since a stalk of a middle
extension has weights at most the weight of the lisse sheaf
(Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points]), it
suffices to show that $M'$ is pure of weight $w+1$. Here the second step
is the easy one, because once $M'$ is pure, the sums of squared traces of
Chapter [chap-Pure-sheaves-on-curves] give its weight $w+1$
(Theorem [theorem-weight-fourier-transform]).

The first step, purity of $M'$, is the deep one. The only purity theorem
we have is Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves], for real
sheaves. But the transform of a real sheaf is not real, since $\psi$
takes nonreal values. For example, over $\mathbf F_3$ let $M$ be the
Kummer sheaf of the quadratic character $\chi$ on $\mathbf G_m$, which
is real. By the computation of Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform] and the
signs in (16.3), the trace of $M'$ at
$y\in\mathbf F_3^\times$ is $-\chi(y)g$. Here
$g=\sum_x\chi(x)\psi(x)=\omega-\omega^2=1+2\omega$ is a square root of
$-3$, which is not real. In this case, admittedly, a twist by $\mathcal B_{1/g}$
makes $M'$ real, but in general no twist is known to do this.

The plan is to realize $M'$, up to a twist, as a quotient of a real
sheaf on the dual line, to which that theorem applies. To build it we
add a conjugate. First we twist $M$ to weight zero,
$M^0=M\otimes\mathcal B_b$. Then we transform $j_!M^0$ with the kernel
$\mathcal K_\psi$ and $j_!(M^0)^\vee$ with the kernel
$\mathcal K_{\psi^{-1}}$. At each point the traces of the two transforms
are complex conjugate, so their sum is a real sheaf $H$ on the dual
line. Since the twist $M'\otimes\mathcal B_b$ is a quotient of $H$
(Proposition [proposition-purity-lisse-part-fourier-transform]),
purity of real sheaves then makes $M'$ pure. We use $j_!$ rather than
$j_*$ because its transform is a sheaf, and by
Lemma [lemma-fourier-transform-boundary-sequence] this transform
differs from the transform of $j_*M$ by a lisse sheaf of weights at most
$w$.

Passing from one irreducible $M$ to every pure sheaf needs care, because
$j_*$ is not exact in general. For example, the extension
$0\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)\to F\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to0$ on $\mathbf G_m$ given by the Kummer class
of the coordinate is lisse, but $j_*F\to j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is not surjective at
$0$, since the monodromy of $F$ around $0$ is a nontrivial unipotent
matrix. For sheaves of one weight $w$, however, exactness holds by a weight gap
(Proposition [proposition-exactness-fixed-pure-weight]): by local
duality at the boundary points
(Lemma [lemma-local-duality-point-c-u]), the connecting map
$j_*F_2\to R^1j_*F_1$ goes from weights at most $w$ to weights at least
$w+2$, and so it vanishes.

Throughout this section and the next, $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$
is a dense open and $M$ is a nonzero irreducible lisse Weil sheaf
on $U_0$, pure of weight $w$. We assume that no geometric irreducible
constituent of $M$ is the restriction of $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ for
some $a\in\bar k_0$, and we let $M'$ be the lisse Weil sheaf on a dense
open $j':U'_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^{1\vee}_{k_0}$ with
$\operatorname{FT}_\psi((j_*M)[1])\simeq(j'_*M')[1]$
(Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension]).

We build the real sheaf from extensions by zero, because for them we
can check reality on the trace function. Indeed, at a point of $U_0$ the
eigenvalues of $M^0$ and of its dual have absolute value one, and hence
they are complex conjugate. At a boundary point, however, the
stalk of $j_*M^0$ is the space of inertia invariants, and the stalk of
$j_*(M^0)^\vee$ is the space of invariants of the dual representation,
but nothing we know at this stage makes their Frobenius eigenvalues
conjugate. With $j_!$, by contrast, both stalks vanish there, and the trace function
of the sum of the two transforms is clearly real.

The price is that $j_!M$ is not a simple perverse sheaf, so its
transform $G$ is not $j'_*M'$ but an extension of $j'_*M'$ by the
transform $B'$ of the boundary. This $B'$ is a lisse sheaf of weights at
most $w$ (Lemma [lemma-fourier-transform-boundary-sequence]), and in the
proof of Proposition [proposition-purity-lisse-part-fourier-transform]
we use only that $G$ is a sheaf and that it surjects onto $j'_*M'$.

The argument of Proposition [proposition-twisting-weight-zero-adding-dual]
also applies to twists by the Fourier kernel, and we need this in the
proof of Proposition [proposition-purity-lisse-part-fourier-transform].

In the next proof we use Lemma [lemma-fourier-transform-boundary-sequence]
twice. Applying its vanishing argument to $M^0$ and to its dual, we see
that the transform of the real sheaf is a single sheaf. Then, using
the surjection $G\to j'_*M'$ of the lemma, we exhibit a twist of $M'$
as a quotient of that real sheaf.

By Proposition [proposition-purity-lisse-part-fourier-transform],
$M'$ is pure of some weight $v$, and Plancherel now finds $v$. Purity had
to come first, since the growth exponent $\nu$ of
Definition [definition-growth-squared-traces] is the weight only for
pure sheaves.

attrs.title: The weight of the Fourier transform (1)

objects.body:
In the example of the chapter opening, $M$ is the Kummer sheaf of the
quadratic character over $\mathbf F_3$, of weight $0$, and the trace of
$M'$ at $y\in\mathbf F_3^\times$ is $-\chi(y)g$ with $g^2=-3$. Its
absolute value is $\sqrt3=3^{1/2}$, which is weight $1=w+1$, as the
theorem predicts.

The weight of $M'$ bounds $H^1_c$, because the stalk of the transform
at the origin of the dual line is the compactly supported cohomology of
$j_*M$.

attrs.title: The weight of the Fourier transform (2)

objects.body:
To pass from irreducible sheaves to arbitrary ones we show that $j_*$
is exact on sequences of pure sheaves of one weight. The reason is
a gap in weights. Let $0\to F_1\to F\to F_2\to0$ be an exact sequence of lisse sheaves on
a dense open $U$ of a curve $C$. Applying $j_*$ gives an exact sequence
$0\to j_*F_1\to j_*F\to j_*F_2\to R^1j_*F_1$, and $R^1j_*F_1$ is
supported on $C\setminus U$. Now suppose that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are pure of
weight $w$. Then, by Proposition [proposition-weights-j-boundary-points],
the source of the last map has weights at most $w$ at a point of
$C\setminus U$. On the other hand, by local duality, which we prove first, the stalk of
$R^1j_*F_1$ at such a point is the dual of the invariants of
$F_1^\vee$, twisted by $(-1)$, and this space has weights at least
$w+2$. Since a Frobenius-equivariant map between spaces with disjoint weights
is zero, $j_*$ is exact on such sequences
(Proposition [proposition-exactness-fixed-pure-weight]).

The hypothesis of equal weights is needed. In the Kummer extension
$0\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)\to F\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to0$ of the chapter opening, $F_1=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$
has weight $-2$ and $F_2=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ has weight $0$, so at the origin the
stalks of $j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ and of $R^1j_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(1)$ both have weight $0$, and
the connecting map is indeed nonzero.

Exactness lets us extend Corollary [corollary-h-1-c-stalk-fourier]
from one irreducible sheaf with no geometric constituent of the form
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ to a pure sheaf unramified at infinity
(Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-affine-line]) by induction along a
composition series. Each factor of the series is either geometrically
constant, and then $H^1_c=0$, or it satisfies the hypotheses of the corollary.

For $F$ pure lisse of weight $w$, the pairing shows that
$(R^1j_*F)_{\bar s}$ has weights at least $w+2$. Indeed, it puts this
stalk in duality with a stalk of $j_*F^\vee$, which has weights at most
$-w$, and the pairing takes values in $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$, which has weight $2$.
The next proposition uses this gap between the source and the target
of the connecting map.

All factors of a composition series of a pure lisse sheaf are pure of
the same weight, so the proposition applies to every step of such a
series. In this way we pass from the irreducible sheaves of
Corollary [corollary-h-1-c-stalk-fourier] to arbitrary ones.

The condition at infinity enters only through
Lemma [lemma-unramified-at-infinity-no-linear-characters], to
verify the hypothesis of
Proposition [proposition-fourier-transform-middle-extension]: it
excludes the constituents $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ with $a\ne0$,
whose transforms are skyscrapers rather than middle extensions. In the
last section we remove this hypothesis, together with the
restriction to opens of the line.

Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-affine-line] assumes that the curve is
an open of the affine line and that the sheaf is unramified at infinity.
We remove the second hypothesis by moving a point where the sheaf is
lisse to infinity, and the first by taking the direct image along a
finite map to the line.

For an upper bound it is enough to replace $H^1_c$ by a group that
surjects onto it, and each move does this. For the first move, let $s$ be a point where the
sheaf is lisse. Since a point has no $H^1_c$, deleting $s$ gives a
surjection $H^1_c(W\setminus\{s\},F)\to H^1_c(W,F)$, and after a finite
extension of the constant field and an automorphism of $\mathbf P^1$
sending $s$ to infinity, the sheaf is unramified there. For the second, a finite map
$\pi:C\to\mathbf A^1$ does not change compactly supported cohomology at
all, since $R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\pi_*j_!F)=R\Gamma_c(C,F)$. However,
$\pi_*j_!F$ is lisse and pure only off the branch locus, so we
remove the bad points by one more localization. Such a map $\pi$ exists
by Riemann–Roch, because a function with a single pole of order prime to
$p$ defines a finite generically étale map
(Lemma [lemma-finite-generically-etale-map-line]). Curves that are not
affine, and the degrees $r\ne1$, are treated afterwards in
Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve].

To move a point to infinity we need a rational point, and hence a
finite extension of the constant field. By the lemma this does not
affect a weight bound.

By the lemma, for any open of the projective line and any pure lisse
sheaf on it, we may bound $H^1_c$ with
Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-affine-line]. To reach an arbitrary
affine curve we map it to the line, and we have to choose the map so
that the direct image is again pure and lisse on a dense open.

For example, take for $C_0$ the affine curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over
$\mathbf F_3$, the complement of the point at infinity of the
projective curve. There $g=1$, the point $s=\infty$ is rational, and
$m=2$ satisfies $(m-1)\deg(s)>0$. Accordingly, the function $x$ has a single pole,
of order two, which is prime to $3$, and the map is the double cover
$(x,y)\mapsto x$ of the line, whose extension to the projective curve is
branched over $0$, $\pm1$ and $\infty$.

With both lemmas the bound on the line extends to every affine curve.

To reach a curve that is not affine, we pass to a dense affine open and
view the sheaf on the whole curve as a middle extension.

At this point we know the Deligne–Laumon theorem on curves: a pure lisse sheaf of
weight $w$ on a curve has $H^r_c$ of weights at most $w+r$. For the Weil
conjectures we need the same bound for the cohomology of a variety of
any dimension. In this chapter we prove
Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek], which says that for a separated
morphism of finite type $f:X_0\to Y_0$, the functor $Rf_!$ maps
$D_{\leq w}(X_0)$ into $D_{\leq w}(Y_0)$.

Take a surface fibred in curves over a curve, $f:X_0\to Y_0$. Here the Leray
spectral sequence $H^a_c(Y,R^bf_!\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)\Rightarrow H^{a+b}_c(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$
suggests applying the curve case twice, once on the fibres and once on
the base. On the fibres there is no difficulty: at a closed point $y$
the stalk of $R^bf_!\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is $H^b_c(X_{\bar y},\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$, and the curve
case says that it has weights at most $b$. On the base, however, the
curve case applies only to pure sheaves. So we need a finite filtration
of $R^bf_!\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ with pure quotients, that is, we need $R^bf_!\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ to
be mixed in the sense of Definition [definition-weights], and bounds at
each point separately do not produce such a filtration. In his first
proof [deligne74] Deligne avoided the problem with a Lefschetz
pencil, where the Picard–Lefschetz formula describes the direct image in
the middle degree, but for an arbitrary fibration the sheaves on the base
are not explicit. Once a mixed filtration exists, on the other hand, the pointwise
bound also bounds the weights of its quotients
(Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf]). The question is
therefore whether the direct images are mixed.

The answer comes once more from positivity
(Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed]):

> every constructible real Weil sheaf on a separated scheme of finite
> type over $k_0$ is mixed.

To see why, let $S$ be an irreducible constituent of a real lisse sheaf on a smooth
affine $X_0$. In order to compare the eigenvalues of $S$ at a fixed point $x_*$
with those at an arbitrary point $x$, we restrict to a curve through
both. On the curve each irreducible constituent is pure by
Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves], so if the restriction of
$S$ stays irreducible, its eigenvalues at $x$ have the weight
read off at $x_*$. In order to find curves on which $S$ stays irreducible, we
first show that irreducibility can be detected in one finite quotient of
the fundamental group
(Lemma [lemma-detecting-irreducibility-finite-quotient]), and then Bertini's
theorem gives a curve through the given points that stays connected
in the corresponding finite étale cover
(Lemma [lemma-curve-preserving-finite-cover] and
Corollary [corollary-curve-preserving-geometric-irreducibility]). For
constructible sheaves, finally, we stratify.

By Noether normalization over strata
(Lemma [lemma-relative-noether-normalization-over-stratification]),
an arbitrary $f$ is built from quasi-finite maps and projections of
relative affine lines. The essential case is a smooth family of affine
curves $h:U_0\to Y_0$ with a pure lisse sheaf $F$ on $U_0$. To apply the
theorem on real sheaves we need direct images that are real, and here
the curve case helps a second time. After a twist to weight zero and the
addition of the dual, $F$ becomes a real sheaf $G$, and the curve case on the
fibres makes the direct images of $G$ real, hence mixed. A twist of $F$ is a
direct summand of $G$, so the direct images of $F$ are mixed as well
(Theorem [theorem-pure-lisse-sheaves-over-relative]).

To prove Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed] we
restrict a sheaf to curves, reassemble it over strata and descend it
along constant extensions. For the reassembly and the descent we need
that quasi-finite direct images preserve weights. For the restriction
we need curves on which given lisse sheaves stay geometrically
irreducible.

The first fact is elementary, because a finite direct image only
permutes stalks. Let $y$ be a point downstairs and $x$ a point over $y$
with residue extension of degree $e$. Frobenius at $y$ cycles the $e$
copies of the stalk at $x$, and its eigenvalues are $e$th roots of the
eigenvalues upstairs. Measured against the residue field, absolute
values are therefore unchanged
(Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images]).

The second fact is geometric, since restricting to a curve can lose
monodromy. On $\mathbf G_m\times\mathbf G_m$ with
coordinates $x,y$, in odd characteristic, the double cover $u^2=x$ is
connected, but over the curve $x=1$ it
splits into two copies. Accordingly, the Kummer sheaf of the quadratic
character in $x$ is geometrically nontrivial on the surface but constant
on that curve. In the same way an irreducible sheaf of higher
rank can become reducible on a badly chosen curve. On the other hand, a representation
stays absolutely irreducible on a curve if the image of the
fundamental group of the curve is large enough, and we show that this can
be checked in one finite quotient
(Lemma [lemma-detecting-irreducibility-finite-quotient]). It then
suffices that the curve stays connected in one finite étale cover, and
we find such curves with Bertini's irreducibility theorem
(Lemma [lemma-curve-preserving-finite-cover]).

A lisse sheaf stays geometrically irreducible on a curve $C$ in $X$ as
soon as the image of $\pi_1(C)$ is large enough. The next lemma shows
that it suffices for this image to surject onto one finite quotient of
$\pi_1(X)$, and in Lemma [lemma-curve-preserving-finite-cover] we
construct curves with this property.

For a lisse sheaf on $X$ the finite quotient corresponds to a
connected finite Galois cover $T\to X$. If $C\subset X$ is a curve with
$T\times_XC$ connected, then the fundamental group of $C$ surjects onto
the Galois group of $T$. What we need, then, are curves through given
points whose inverse image in a given connected cover stays connected.

Combining the two lemmas, we obtain the curves we need for real
sheaves. We can treat several sheaves at once, because a single cover
dominates the finite quotients attached to all of them.

With these curves we pass from the purity theorem for real sheaves on
curves (Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves]) to the
mixedness of real sheaves on any base. The curves preserve
geometric irreducibility, so we first split a lisse sheaf into
geometrically irreducible pieces. These pieces need not be Weil
sheaves, because an irreducible Weil sheaf need not be geometrically
irreducible. For example, let $\chi$ be a character of
$\mathbf F_{q^2}^\times$ with $\chi^q\ne\chi$, and let $g$ be the map
from $\mathbf G_m$ over $\mathbf F_{q^2}$ to $\mathbf G_m$ over
$\mathbf F_q$. Geometrically, the direct image under $g$ of the Kummer
sheaf of $\chi$ splits into the Kummer sheaves of $\chi$ and $\chi^q$,
which are distinct. Frobenius exchanges them, and so the direct image
is an irreducible Weil sheaf of rank two. After the quadratic constant
extension the two pieces are Weil sheaves themselves. In general, the
geometric constituents become Weil subquotients after a finite constant
extension
(Lemma [lemma-geometric-constituents-after-constant-extension]).
In the proof of
Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed] we descend
mixedness back along this extension by a trace retraction. We also
reduce constructible sheaves to lisse sheaves on smooth affine strata,
and glue the strata using
Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images].

In the example above, after the quadratic extension the sheaf
$g_*\mathcal K_\chi$ becomes the direct sum of the Kummer sheaves of
$\chi$ and $\chi^q$, and either summand gives a filtration as in the
lemma. Beyond this example, we use the lemma, together with the curves of
Corollary [corollary-curve-preserving-geometric-irreducibility], to
prove that real sheaves are mixed
(Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed]). In that
proof, however, the filtrations with pure quotients exist only after a constant
extension and only on the pieces of a stratification, so the next two
lemmas recover mixedness of the original sheaf.

Let $h:U_0\to Y_0$ be a smooth family of affine curves and $F$ a pure
lisse sheaf on $U_0$. On each stalk of $R^ih_!F$,
Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve] bounds the eigenvalues by
$w+i$. Suppose that $R^ih_!F$ is mixed. Each pure quotient of its
filtration has a nonzero stalk somewhere, and its eigenvalues there are
among those of $R^ih_!F$. By
Lemma [lemma-bounding-weights-mixed-sheaf] the quotients therefore
have weights at most $w+i$. Most of the proof of
Theorem [theorem-pure-lisse-sheaves-over-relative] is devoted to
showing that $R^ih_!F$ is mixed.

An arbitrary $f$ reduces to relative affine curves and quasi-finite
maps. Over a field, Noether normalization makes an affine
variety of dimension $d$ finite over $\mathbf A^d$, and
$\mathbf A^d\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is a composite of $d$ projections
of affine lines. For a separated morphism $f$ of finite type the same
works over a dense open of the target, and we treat the complement by
induction on its dimension
(Lemma [lemma-relative-noether-normalization-over-stratification]).
So we must check the weight bound for two kinds of maps and show
that it survives the gluing.

Quasi-finite maps were treated in
Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images]. For the
projection $\mathbf A^1_Y\to Y$
(Proposition [proposition-relative-affine-line]), consider a sheaf
on the relative line. Over a dense open of the base it is lisse off a
closed subscheme finite over the base. It is therefore glued from a
relative affine curve and a quasi-finite piece. The bound is stable
under composition by the Leray spectral sequence
(Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf]). It is stable under
partitions of the source and of the target by the localization
sequences below. These gluing steps use only that mixed sheaves of
