weights at most $u$ are closed under subquotients and extensions.

By the next lemma, to prove a weight bound for $R^if_!$ of a morphism
$f$, it suffices to prove it over the pieces of finite partitions of
the source and of the target.

To apply the proposition to an arbitrary morphism, we factor it, over
strata, as a quasi-finite map followed by projections of relative
affine lines.

On each piece the map to $V$ is thus a finite map followed by $d$
projections of relative affine lines. The bound holds for the finite
map by Lemma [lemma-finite-quasi-finite-direct-images] and for each
projection by Proposition [proposition-relative-affine-line], and
the next theorem puts the pieces together.

For Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek], stated in
Section [sec-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-2], the case of sheaves is
Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf], and the spectral
sequence of the truncation tower passes to complexes.

The Deligne–Laumon theorem is an upper bound for weights, stated with $\ell$-adic
coefficients and one embedding $\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to\mathbf C$. Weil's
conjectures ask for more: an equality $|\alpha|=q^{i/2}$, for
polynomials $P_i$ with integer coefficients, under every complex
embedding. This chapter closes both gaps.

The lower bound comes from Poincaré duality, and a curve shows how.
Let $X_0$ be a smooth projective curve and $\alpha$ an eigenvalue of
Frobenius on $H^1(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$. Then Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek],
applied to the constant sheaf, gives $|\iota(\alpha)|\le q^{1/2}$. On the other hand, cup
product is a perfect pairing $H^1\times H^1\to H^2=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$, which
Frobenius multiplies by $q$. Hence $q/\alpha$ is an eigenvalue as well,
and the same bound for $q/\alpha$ says that $|\iota(\alpha)|\ge q^{1/2}$.
In dimension $d$ the argument is the same: an eigenvalue $\alpha$ on
$H^i(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|\le q^{i/2}$, while duality makes
$q^d/\alpha$ an eigenvalue on $H^{2d-i}$, of absolute value at most
$q^{(2d-i)/2}$, and we find $|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{i/2}$. This equality is
Weil's axiom (d), and we prove it in Section [sec-The-Riemann-hypothesis],
more generally for the higher direct images of a pure lisse sheaf under
a smooth proper morphism
(Theorem [theorem-purity-higher-direct-images-under]); the case of
the constant sheaf over a point is
Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety]. Since
the Deligne–Laumon theorem holds for every $\iota$, purity holds for all complex
embeddings at once. Indeed, every embedding of a number field into
$\mathbf C$ extends to an isomorphism $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\simeq\mathbf C$.

The polynomials $P_{i,\ell}=\det(1-TF\mid H^i(X,\mathbf Q_\ell))$ are defined with
$\ell$-adic coefficients, and a priori they could depend on $\ell$. The
zeta function does not mention $\ell$. It has a unique expression
$Z(X_0,T)=A/B$ with $A,B\in\mathbf Z[T]$ coprime and $A(0)=B(0)=1$
(Lemma [lemma-reduced-fractions-integer-coefficients];
Sections [sec-Rational-power-series]–[sec-Integrality-and-independence-of-ell]). Can each
$P_{i,\ell}$ be read off from $Z(X_0,T)$? The trace formula writes $Z$
as the alternating product of the $P_{i,\ell}$, but an alternating
product can cancel. For example, $X_0=\mathbf G_m\sqcup
\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ is not proper, and it has $q^m$ points
over $\mathbf F_{q^m}$, as many as $\mathbf A^1$. Hence
$Z(X_0,T)=1/(1-qT)$. Yet $H^0_c$ and $H^1_c$ are both one-dimensional
with eigenvalue $1$, and the factor $1-T$ cancels between them. For a
smooth proper $X_0$ purity rules this out. The reciprocal roots of
$P_{i,\ell}$ have absolute value $q^{i/2}$, so no root of $P_{i,\ell}$
is a root of $P_{j,\ell}$ for $i\neq j$. It follows that the product of
the $P_{i,\ell}$ with $i$ odd is $A$ and the product with $i$ even is
$B$. Grouping the reciprocal roots of $A$ and $B$ by absolute value then
recovers each $P_{i,\ell}$ from $Z(X_0,T)$ alone
(Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes]). In
particular $P_{i,\ell}$ has integer coefficients and does not depend on
$\ell$.

In terms of point counts, purity gives the classical estimates. For a
smooth proper geometrically connected $X_0$ we obtain
$|\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})-(1+q^{dm})|\le\sum_{i=1}^{2d-1}b_iq^{mi/2}$
(Corollary [corollary-point-count-estimates]). In particular, for a curve of genus $g$
this is Weil's bound $2gq^{m/2}$, and for elliptic curves it is Hasse's
theorem. As an illustration, Example [example-running-example-purity] works this out
for genus-one curves over $\mathbf F_3$.

For a proper map we have $Rf_!=Rf_*$, so the upper bound of
Theorem [theorem-direct-image-mixed-sheaf] applies to ordinary
cohomology. If the map is also smooth, Poincaré duality on each fibre
pairs $H^i(X_{\bar y},F)$ perfectly with
$H^{2d-i}(X_{\bar y},F^\vee(d))$. The eigenvalues of the second group
are the inverses of those of the first. The second group has weights at
most $(-w-2d)+(2d-i)=-w-i$, and this upper bound becomes the lower
bound $w+i$ for the first.

Both hypotheses are needed. Without properness, $H^1_c$ of
$\mathbf G_m$ has weight $0$ instead of $1$. Without smoothness duality
fails. For example, the nodal cubic is proper, and its $H^1$ is a line
on which Frobenius acts by $\pm1$, of weight $0$. The relative
statement is no harder than the absolute one, because we check the
bound at one closed point $y$ at a time, on the smooth proper fibre over
$\kappa(y)$. In the proof of
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes] we use
only the case of a point as base and the constant sheaf
(Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety]).

For the Weil conjectures we need only the case where the base is a
point and the sheaf is constant. Then the fibre is $X$ itself, and the
stalk of $R^if_*\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is $H^i(X,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$.

The zeta function has integer coefficients by its definition, but the
trace formula proves its rationality only over $\mathbf Q_\ell$, as an alternating
product of $\ell$-adic characteristic polynomials. To compare these
polynomials for different primes $\ell$, we need a form of the zeta
function that does not mention $\ell$. We show that a rational power
series with integer coefficients is a quotient of integral polynomials
in a unique reduced form.

Lemma [lemma-hankel-rank-rationality] shows that rationality is a
condition of linear algebra on the coefficients, namely that the Hankel
matrix $(c_{r+s})$ has finite rank. Such a condition descends from
$\mathbf Q_\ell$ to $\mathbf Q$. For integrality of the reduced fraction,
Lemma [lemma-reduced-fractions-integer-coefficients] uses a lattice
in the row span of the Hankel matrix that is stable under the shift.
The characteristic polynomial of the shift on this lattice is then
integral. For example, the coefficients $c_n=2^{n+1}-1$ of
$1/((1-2T)(1-T))$ satisfy $c_{n+2}=3c_{n+1}-2c_n$. The shift matrix $S$
on the row span has $\det(1-TS)=(1-2T)(1-T)$, which is the reduced
denominator. In the next section we compare the $\ell$-adic
factorizations with the reduced fraction $A/B$.

Applied with $K=\mathbf Q$ and $K'=\mathbf Q_\ell$, the lemma shows that the zeta
function, which the trace formula writes as a quotient of polynomials
over $\mathbf Q_\ell$, is a quotient of polynomials over $\mathbf Q$. The next
lemma shows that the integrality of its coefficients passes to the
reduced fraction.

By Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function],
$Z(X_0,T)\in\mathbf Q(T)\cap(1+T\mathbf Z[[T]])$ for every
separated $X_0$ of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$. So
Lemma [lemma-reduced-fractions-integer-coefficients] applies. We
write $Z(X_0,T)=A/B$ for the resulting fraction, with $A$ and $B$
coprime in $\mathbf Z[T]$ and $A(0)=B(0)=1$.

Let $X_0$ be smooth and proper over $\mathbf F_q$, of pure dimension
$d$, and let $A/B$ be the reduced fraction of $Z(X_0,T)$
(Lemma [lemma-reduced-fractions-integer-coefficients]). We now
carry out the argument sketched at the start of the chapter. The point is that purity
makes the characteristic polynomials of Frobenius in different degrees
pairwise coprime, so no cancellation can occur, and the polynomials
can be read off from $A$ and $B$.
For a prime $\ell\nmid q$ put

$$
H^i_\ell=H^i(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathbf Q_\ell),\qquad
P_{i,\ell}(T)=\det(1-TF\mid H^i_\ell),\qquad
b_{i,\ell}=\dim_{\mathbf Q_\ell}H^i_\ell.
$$

Since $X_0$ is proper, $H^i_c=H^i$, and the determinant identity of
Corollary [corollary-point-counting-zeta-function] for $\Lambda=\mathbf Q_\ell$ reads

$$
Z(X_0,T)=\prod_{i=0}^{2d}P_{i,\ell}(T)^{(-1)^{i+1}}.
\tag{19.1}
$$

Since Frobenius is invertible, $\deg P_{i,\ell}=b_{i,\ell}$.

Thus the reciprocal roots of $P_{i,\ell}$ are the Frobenius eigenvalues
on $H^i_\ell$, counted with multiplicity. The next lemma shows that $A$
and $B$ sort these eigenvalues by degree, independently of $\ell$ and of
the complex embedding.

In the following examples we read the theorem backwards. For projective
space the point count determines $Z$, and the grouping of the reciprocal
roots by absolute value recovers the $P_i$. For an elliptic curve the
theorem turns one point count into an inequality.

The argument of Hasse's theorem works in every dimension. The
point-counting formula expresses $\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ through the
traces of $F^m$, and purity bounds each trace by the dimension of the
group times the common absolute value of its eigenvalues.

The main text defines cohomology with compact support as in topology:
to push forward along $f:X\to Y$, embed $X$ as an open subset of
something proper over $Y$, extend by zero and push forward, so that
$Rf_!=Rp_*j_!$ (Proposition [proposition-construction-independence-rf-shriek]).
This definition needs every morphism to have a compactification, and it
needs any two compactifications to be dominated by a third, so that
proper base change can show that $Rf_!$ does not depend on the choice.
The second point is elementary once we use compactifications in which
$X$ is scheme-theoretically dense: the closure of $X$ in the fibre
product of two of them dominates both
(Proposition [proposition-dense-compactifications-form-cofiltered-category]).
The first point is Nagata's theorem,
Theorem [theorem-nagata-s-compactification-theorem]: every separated
morphism of finite type $X\to S$ with $S$ quasi-compact and
quasi-separated factors as a quasi-compact open immersion $X\to\overline
X$ followed by a proper morphism $\overline X\to S$.

Why is this hard? Locally a compactification is easy to find: if $S$ and
$X$ are affine, we take the closure of $X$ in projective space over $S$.
The difficulty is to glue. For example, cover $X=\mathbf A^1_k$ by
$U_1=\mathbf A^1\setminus\{0\}$ and $U_2=\mathbf A^1\setminus\{1\}$,
compactify each by $\mathbf P^1$, and glue the two copies of $\mathbf
P^1$ along $U_1\cap U_2$. The result is then $\mathbf P^1$ with the three
points $0$, $1$ and $\infty$ doubled, which is not separated. For curves
blow-ups are not needed, and they would not help either, since blowing up a
point on a regular curve does nothing. In dimension at least two, however, the
closures of $U_1\setminus U_2$ and $U_2\setminus U_1$ can meet in the
boundary, and we pull them apart by blow-ups with centers in the boundary,
which leave $X$ unchanged (Lemma [lemma-separation-closures] and
Proposition [proposition-compactifying-union-two-opens]). Induction
over an affine cover then gives the theorem over a Noetherian base
(Section [sec-Proof-of-Nagatas-theorem]), and Noetherian approximation gives the
general case, which we need because proper base change is proved over
arbitrary qcqs bases.

Proper base change itself is computed on projective space, and Chow's
lemma carries it to every proper morphism
(Section [sec-Proper-morphisms]). We use it in the form of
Theorem [theorem-chow-s-lemma-projective-form]: for a proper
morphism $X\to S$ there is a proper surjection $\widetilde X\to X$ with
$\widetilde X$ projective over $S$.

To show that $Rp_*j_!$ does not depend on the compactification, we must
compare two of them, and in general neither maps to the other. The plane
$\mathbf A^2$ is open in $\mathbf P^2$ and in
$\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$, but the identity of $\mathbf A^2$ extends
to a morphism in neither direction: the map
$(x:y:z)\mapsto((x:z),(y:z))$ is undefined at $(1:0:0)$ and $(0:1:0)$,
and its inverse is undefined at $(\infty,\infty)$. What exists is a third
compactification mapping to both, here the closure of $\mathbf A^2$ in
$\mathbf P^2\times\mathbf P^1\times\mathbf P^1$. So we compare two
compactifications through a common refinement. A refinement $h$ is
required to satisfy $h^{-1}(X)=X$. This is what lets us compute
$Rh_*j'_!$ by restriction to $X$ in the proof of
Proposition [proposition-construction-independence-rf-shriek].

Without density, refinements are not unique. For example, the point
$X=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is open in the compactification
$\operatorname{Spec}k\sqcup\mathbf P^1_k$, which is not dense. Every
automorphism of $\mathbf P^1_k$ gives a refinement of it to itself.
Dense compactifications do not have this problem: morphisms between them
are unique, and with their refinements they form a cofiltered category
(Proposition [proposition-dense-compactifications-form-cofiltered-category]).

For example, $\mathbf A^1_k\subset\mathbf P^1_k$ is a dense
compactification of $\mathbf A^1_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, since a
regular function on an open of $\mathbf P^1_k$ that vanishes on
$\mathbf A^1_k$ is zero. The theorem says that such a factorization
always exists.

This is [Stacks, [0F41](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F41)], and we give the proof in
Section [sec-Proof-of-Nagatas-theorem]. We need it in this generality
because proper base change is proved over arbitrary qcqs bases; for
schemes of finite type over $k$ the Noetherian case of the proof
suffices.

Density is a condition on structure sheaves. For instance, a nilpotent
section supported on the boundary is invisible on $X$, but it prevents
$X$ from being schematically dense. The condition does two things for
us. First, morphisms between dense compactifications are unique and common
refinements exist
(Proposition [proposition-dense-compactifications-form-cofiltered-category]).
Second, passing to a dense compactification does not change the direct
image with proper support (Lemma [lemma-passing-schematic-closure]).
Density is what makes extensions from $U$ unique.

By Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness], every
compactification contains a dense one, the schematic closure of $X$.
For this replacement to be harmless we need that it
does not change $Rp_*j_!$.

For dense compactifications the comparison is formal.
We obtain common refinements by Lemma [lemma-schematic-closure-uniqueness],
and morphisms are unique by Lemma [lemma-uniqueness-maps-dense-open].

Proper base change is applied after a change of base $S'\to S$, so we
also need to know what happens to a compactification under base
change, where density need not survive.

Every modification in the proof of Nagata's theorem is a blow-up whose
center avoids a fixed open, so that this open is not changed.
Here the open $U$ is the scheme being compactified, or a piece of it, and
only the boundary may be modified. For instance, the coordinate axes
minus the origin are disjoint closed subsets of
$U=\mathbf A^2\setminus\{0\}$, but their closures in $\mathbf A^2$ meet at
the origin. The blow-up of the origin is an isomorphism over $U$, and in it
the strict transforms of the axes meet the exceptional line in the two
distinct points of slope $0$ and $\infty$, so they become disjoint.
Lemma [lemma-separation-closures] proves the same in general.

We use blow-ups rather than arbitrary proper modifications that are
isomorphisms over $U$, because a blow-up is given by an ideal. This
makes them easy to combine. Two of them are dominated by the blow-up of
the product ideal, and a composite is again a blow-up
(Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow]). The ideal is
required to be of finite type, so that the blow-up is proper.

On an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$, write
$I=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$. The charts of the blow-up have rings

$$
R[I/a_i]=\bigl((\bigoplus_{m\geq0}I^mt^m)_{a_it}\bigr)_0.
$$

This is the degree-zero part of the localization at $a_it$ of the
Rees algebra, where $t$ is a variable of degree one. It is the quotient
of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(a_ix_j-a_j)_j$ by its $a_i$-power torsion, that
is, by the elements killed by some power of $a_i$, and this torsion can
be nonzero. In the
chart $R[I/a_i]$, the element $a_i$ is a nonzerodivisor and generates
the extended ideal $IR[I/a_i]$. In other words, the center becomes an
effective Cartier divisor. The blow-up is an isomorphism away from the
center. Since $I$ is finitely generated, the blow-up of an affine base
is a closed subscheme of a projective space over it, and therefore $b$
is proper. These constructions glue under restriction to opens.

We first use admissible blow-ups to restore density. A
compactification may contain components or embedded components
supported in the boundary. Blowing up the boundary removes them, because
after the blow-up the boundary is cut out locally by a nonzerodivisor.

After a blow-up, we replace a scheme over $T$ by the part of its
base change that is not concentrated on the exceptional divisor.

Over a chart of $T'$ where $E$ has equation $a$ and $W\times_TT'$ is
affine with ring $B$, the ring of the strict transform is

$$
B/\{b\in B:\ a^nb=0\text{ for some }n\geq0\}.
$$

If $U$ is the complement of the center, this is exactly the schematic
closure of $W_U$ in $W\times_TT'$, the object that occurs in
the elimination of indeterminacy.
By [Stacks, [080E](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080E)], the strict transform is the blow-up of $W$ in the
pulled-back ideal, so it is proper over $W$.

In the proofs below we construct blow-ups locally and one after
another. By the next lemma, finitely many such constructions combine
into a single $U$-admissible blow-up of $T$.

Blow-ups commute with flat base change [Stacks, [0805](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0805)], because flat
pullback preserves the inclusions $\mathcal I^m\subseteq\mathcal O_T$.
Under a base change that is not flat, the pullbacks of these
inclusions can have kernels.
In that case the blow-up of the pulled-back ideal is the strict
transform of the base change, which can be strictly smaller than the
base change itself.

The gluing argument has to extend a morphism defined on a dense open
$U\subseteq X$ as far as possible. When the target $Y$ is not proper,
the extension can stop before reaching all of $X$. We need a way to say
that a partial map is already extended as far as it can be.

Take $X=Y=\mathbf A^1_k$ and $U=\mathbf A^1\setminus\{0\}$. The
inclusion $t\mapsto t$ extends over $0$. Its graph, the diagonal minus
the origin, is not closed in $X\times Y$. The map $t\mapsto1/t$ does not
extend, even after a blow-up, since blowing up a point on a regular
curve does nothing. Its graph $V(ty-1)$ is closed. In general, a closed
graph means that no limit point lies over $X\setminus U$. A map with
closed graph is therefore not the restriction of a map on a larger open.
Both the hypothesis and the conclusion of
Theorem [theorem-extension-partial-section] are stated in this form.
For proper $Y$ the condition forces the domain to be all of $X$, which
gives Corollary [corollary-extension-proper-target].

Since $Y\to S$ is separated, the graph is always closed in
$U\times_SY$; the condition is about its behaviour over $X\setminus U$.
Every map $X\to Y$ is a quasi-domination with domain $X$. Conversely,
if $Y\to S$ is proper, every quasi-domination has domain $X$, because
the projection of the closed graph to $X$ is closed with image the
dense open $U$.

The extension theorem below is proved first for targets that embed in
affine space over the base. We reduce a general target to this form by
Zariski's Main Theorem.

Quasi-affine targets are the ones where a partial section can be
extended by hand, by clearing denominators of finitely many
coordinates. Using the proposition, we reduce the general extension
theorem to this case, once we know that the relevant closure is
quasi-finite over the base.

We quote this theorem from [conrad07, Theorem 2.4], with the
auxiliary base equal to $T$, and explain below the structure of its
proof. Note that $Y$ is qcqs, since $p$ is separated and of
finite type and $T$ is qcqs. The hypothesis on $f$ says that
$f$ is a quasi-domination of $V$ over $Y$. We apply the theorem only
when $V=U$, the case of [conrad07, Remark 2.5]. Then the
hypothesis holds automatically, because a section of a separated
morphism is a closed immersion.

The proof first treats a quasi-affine $Y\to T$. If $Y\to T$ is
quasi-affine and $T$ is affine, then $Y$ is a quasi-affine scheme of
finite type over $T$, and it embeds in some $\mathbf A^n_T$
[Stacks, [04II](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04II)]. The coordinates of $f$ are then finitely many fractions,
and a blow-up clearing their denominators extends $f$. One first makes
$U$ schematically dense, so that the extended coordinates still satisfy
the equations of $Y$. Using a finite affine cover of $T$, we then
obtain the quasi-affine case over a qcqs base. In fact the proof needs this case for opens
$U\subseteq V$ with $U$ not necessarily dense, because the reduction
below applies it to the opens $f^{-1}(Y_i)\subseteq V$, which need not be dense. For
this, a further construction in Conrad's proof keeps the centers outside $V$.

The general case reduces to the quasi-affine one, and this reduction is
where Zariski's Main Theorem enters. The plan is to extend the section
on each affine open of $Y$ separately. The closure of the section is
then quasi-finite over the base, hence quasi-affine, and the
quasi-affine case applies once more.

In detail, choose a finite affine open cover $Y=\bigcup_iY_i$. Since $T$
is quasi-separated, each $Y_i\to T$ is quasi-compact, and as $Y_i$ is
affine it is quasi-affine. Hence the quasi-affine case applies to each
$f|_{f^{-1}(Y_i)}$, and we take a common $V$-admissible blow-up
$T_1\to T$. Let $Z$ be the schematic closure of the image of $f$ in
$Y\times_TT_1$. It meets each $Y_i\times_TT_1$ inside the closed graph
of an extension, which has at most one point over each point of $T_1$.
Since there are finitely many $Y_i$, the fibres of $Z\to T_1$ are
finite. As $Z\to T_1$ is separated and of finite type, it is
quasi-finite, and it is quasi-affine by
Proposition [proposition-relative-form-zariski-s-main]. The quasi-affine case then extends the section into $Z$, and the composite of the two blow-ups is
$V$-admissible by Lemma [lemma-products-composites-u-admissible-blow].

When the target is not proper, the extension is defined only on an
open of the blow-up, and we can still say what it looks like. Suppose
the target is a separated map $W\to T$ of finite type that is an
isomorphism over $U$, and the section is its inverse over $U$. Then the
extension identifies a blow-up of $W$ with an open of a blow-up of $T$.

The blow-up is not uniquely determined. However, on any such
modification with $U$ schematically dense, the graph of the extension
is forced to be the closure of the original section. By
Lemma [lemma-uniqueness-maps-dense-open], the identifications
obtained on common admissible refinements therefore agree.

In the gluing argument below, a compactification of an open $V$ of $M$
is related to $M$ itself by a proper map defined on a larger open of
the compactification.

The inductive step of Nagata's theorem is
Proposition [proposition-compactifying-union-two-opens]. Suppose that $M=M_1\cup M_2$
with $M_1\cap M_2$ dense, and that each $M_i$ has a compactification $X_i$;
we want a compactification of $M$. The natural candidate glues $M$ to each
$X_i$ along $M_i$, after we remove from $X_i$ the closure of the part lying
over $M\setminus M_i$. For the result to be separated, however, and for every
valuation to extend into one of the two pieces, the closures in $X_i$ of
the two disjoint closed subsets over $M\setminus M_1$ and
$M\setminus M_2$ must be disjoint. They need not be, and this is where
Lemma [lemma-separation-closures] enters: it makes them disjoint by an
admissible blow-up, as with the coordinate axes in
Section [sec-Elimination-of-indeterminacy].

We need two other lemmas.
Lemma [lemma-extending-isomorphism-over-closure-closed] keeps an
isomorphism near such a closure, and
Lemma [lemma-gluing-after-admissible-blow-ups] glues two
modifications into one separated scheme. Both use elimination of
indeterminacy from the previous section. Recall that it turns a map
that is an isomorphism over a quasi-compact open $U$ into an open
immersion after a $U$-admissible blow-up.

We quote this from [Stacks, [0F3V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F3V)] and sketch the argument, which
works with closed subschemes of $T$ rather than closed subsets of $V$. Let
$\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2$ be ideals of finite type on $T$ cutting out
closed subschemes $Z_1,Z_2$ that are disjoint over $V$ and restrict
to $F_1,F_2$ there. Producing such ideals on all of $T$ is where
constructibility and finite presentation are needed. Since
$\mathcal I_1+\mathcal I_2$ is the unit ideal over $V$, its blow-up
is $V$-admissible. Moreover, on each affine chart the extended ideal is
generated by a single element of $\mathcal I_1$ or of $\mathcal I_2$. Now, on a chart where it is generated by $f\in\mathcal I_1$, the strict
transform of $Z_1$ is obtained from its inverse image by dividing out
the $f$-power torsion. Since $f$ vanishes on $Z_1$, every element of
the ring of the inverse image is killed by $f$. Hence the strict
transform of $Z_1$ does not meet that chart. The same holds for
$Z_2$ on the other charts, and therefore the strict transforms of $Z_1$
and $Z_2$ are disjoint [Stacks, [080P](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/080P)]. The constructibility needed to produce such ideals causes no trouble for us, because in the Noetherian applications below every closed subset is
constructible and its reduced ideal is of finite type.

For the gluing we also need to know that a proper map that is an
isomorphism near a closed subset of $V$ remains one near its closure in $T$, after a blow-up.

The last ingredient replaces two separated schemes containing a common open
by modifications that glue to a separated scheme.

The gluing lemma produces a separated scheme but says nothing about
properness. In the inductive step we prove properness by the valuative
criterion, using the separation of closures.

Over a Noetherian base, the theorem follows from
Proposition [proposition-compactifying-union-two-opens] by induction over an affine cover
whose members overlap densely. Each affine piece is compactified by its
closure in a projective space. The proposition then compactifies the
union of the first $r$ pieces with the next one. It requires the
overlap to be dense, because its valuative criterion only tests maps
from spectra of valuation rings whose generic point maps into the
overlap. Lemma [lemma-affine-covers-dense-intersection] provides a
cover whose total intersection contains all generic points of $X$.

Over a general qcqs base we use Noetherian approximation. This works because a morphism of finite presentation is the base change of one over a Noetherian scheme,
and compactifications are stable under base change. A morphism that is only of finite type, however, need not descend in this way. We therefore first
embed $X$ as a closed subscheme of a scheme of finite presentation over
$S$, and take the closure of $X$ in a compactification of the latter.

We prove the theorem in three steps of increasing generality: a
Noetherian base, a finitely presented morphism over any qcqs base, and
a morphism of finite type.

Let $f:X\to S$ be proper. In Section [sec-Proper-morphisms] proper base change is first proved for projective morphisms. By
Lemma [lemma-composition-cancellation] it then descends along a
proper surjection $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ as soon as it holds for $\pi$
and for the composite $f\pi$. Chow's lemma says precisely that such a $\pi$ exists with both $\pi$ and $f\pi$ projective. Some modification of $X$ is unavoidable here, since there are proper varieties that are not
projective.

Two steps of the main proof come down to the torsion points of a
Jacobian. By the Kummer sequence, $H^1(C,\mu_n)$ of a curve is the $n$-torsion of its Jacobian. The first step, the finiteness of $H^1$ needed for proper base change, is therefore a count of torsion points. The second step is
the finiteness of geometric monodromy in rank one, where purity begins.
It needs Frobenius to fix no class in $H^1$ of a curve over
$\mathbf F_q$ (Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]).

For a complex torus $\mathbf C^g/\Lambda$ the count is trivial: the
$n$-torsion is $\tfrac1n\Lambda/\Lambda\simeq(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}$. For an abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ over an arbitrary field $k$, however, there is no lattice, and the torsion points must be counted algebraically. This is what we do: we prove that for $n$ invertible in $k$ the group scheme $A[n]$ is finite
étale of rank $n^{2g}$ (Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n]).
It follows that the Tate module $T_\ell A=\varprojlim_mA[\ell^m](\bar k)$
is free of rank $2g$ over $\mathbf Z_\ell$
(Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module]). Moreover, over $\mathbf F_q$, no power of Frobenius has a nonzero fixed vector on
$T_\ell A$ (Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector]).
The reason is short: a fixed vector would be a compatible system of
$\ell$-power torsion points of unbounded order in the finite group
$A_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$.

The count rests on one formula. If $\mathcal N$ is a symmetric ample
invertible sheaf on $A$, then

$$
[n]^*\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2}
$$

(Proposition [proposition-pullback-multiplication-n]). On an elliptic
curve with $\mathcal N=\mathcal O(e)$ this says that the divisor
$[n]^*(e)$ is linearly equivalent to $n^2(e)$. When $n$ is prime to the
characteristic, $[n]$ is étale and $[n]^*(e)$ is the reduced divisor
$E[n]$. Comparing degrees then gives $\#E[n]=n^2$.

In general the formula is used twice. First, it forces $[n]$ to have
finite fibres. Indeed, $\mathcal N^{\otimes n^2}$ has positive degree
on every complete curve in $A$, while $[n]^*\mathcal N$ is trivial on a
curve contracted by $[n]$. Second, we compute the Euler characteristics
$\chi(A,[n]^*\mathcal N^{\otimes m})$ in two ways, and comparing their
leading coefficients gives $\deg[n]=n^{2g}$.

The formula itself comes from the theorem of the cube
(Theorem [theorem-theorem-cube]). Following [Stacks, [0BEZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BEZ)], we prove the theorem of the cube together with the rigidity lemma. As a by-product, from the rigidity lemma we deduce that $A$ is commutative; see also [milne-av].

In this appendix all group schemes are of finite type over a field $k$
of arbitrary characteristic.

The theorem of the cube says that an invertible sheaf $\mathcal L$ on
$X\times Y\times Z$, with $X,Y$ complete varieties and $Z$ connected,
that is trivial on
the three slices through a point $(x,y,z)$ is trivial. To prove it, we
view $\mathcal L$ as a family of invertible sheaves on $X\times Y$
parametrized by $Z$. Following [Stacks, [0BEZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BEZ)], we then consider the set of
points of $Z$ over which the sheaf is trivial. This set is closed, by
semicontinuity. It is also open, by a computation of $H^0$ and $H^1$
near such a point. Since it contains $z$ and $Z$ is connected, it is
all of $Z$. The openness uses the triviality on the two slices
$x\times Y\times Z$ and $X\times y\times Z$, and with only two factors
it fails.

Part (2) is the closed half of the theorem of the cube. If the sheaf
is trivial over the members of an open cover of $T$, then the
evaluation map identifies it with a pullback from $T$, since sections
along the proper factor $P$ are constant.

The open half of the theorem is the substantial step. It uses the fact
that $H^1$ of the structure sheaf of a product is the sum of the $H^1$
of the factors.

With the closed and the open half in hand, it remains to glue the local
trivializations.

The second tool, which we use to show that an abelian variety is
commutative (Lemma [lemma-abelian-variety-commutative]), is a
rigidity statement. It says that a family of maps from a proper variety
that is constant on one member is constant on all nearby members.

Let $\mathcal L$ be an invertible sheaf on an abelian variety $A$. We
pull $\mathcal L$ back to $A\times A\times A$ along the partial sums of
the coordinates. There the theorem of the cube gives a second order
recursion for $n\mapsto[n]^*\mathcal L$, whose solution is

$$
[n]^*\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal L^{\otimes n(n+1)/2}\otimes([-1]^*\mathcal L)^{\otimes n(n-1)/2}
$$

(Proposition [proposition-pullback-multiplication-n]). For symmetric $\mathcal L$ the
formula gives $\mathcal L^{\otimes n^2}$. If
$[-1]^*\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal L^{-1}$, as for an invertible sheaf of
degree zero on an elliptic curve, it gives $\mathcal L^{\otimes n}$.

We apply the formula to a symmetric ample sheaf
(Lemma [lemma-symmetric-ample-sheaf]). It shows that $[n]$ is
finite and flat of degree $n^{2g}$, and that $[n]$ is étale when $n$
is invertible in $k$ (Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n]).
The hypothesis on $n$ cannot be dropped. For example, in characteristic $p$ the
differential of $[p]$ is zero, and as a consequence an elliptic curve has at most $p$
points of order dividing $p$ over $\bar k$, although $E[p]$ has rank
$p^2$.

We use three facts: commutativity, which follows from rigidity; a
symmetric ample sheaf, which follows from projectivity; and the formula
for $[n]^*\mathcal L$, which follows from the cube. Rigidity and the cube require $A$ to be geometrically integral,
which we check together with commutativity.

From now on we write the group law additively. Projectivity is the
one structural fact that we quote.

For a symmetric ample $\mathcal N$, the degree of $[n]$ can be read off from
the growth of $\chi(A,\mathcal N^{\otimes m})$, since pulling back by
$[n]$ multiplies $m$ by $n^2$ and $\chi$ grows like $m^g$.

It follows that the group $A(\bar k)$ is divisible. Indeed, since $[n]$
is finite and surjective, its fibre over a point of $A(\bar k)$ is a
nonempty finite $\bar k$-scheme, and so it has a $\bar k$-point.

Fix a prime $\ell$ invertible in $k$. With this prime, compatible systems of
$\ell$-power torsion points of $A$ form the Tate module $T_\ell A$, a
$\mathbf Z_\ell$-module with an action of $\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)$. For example, for a
complex torus $\mathbf C^g/\Lambda$ it is $\Lambda\otimes\mathbf Z_\ell$, the first
homology with $\ell$-adic coefficients. In general,
Proposition [proposition-integral-tate-module] shows that $T_\ell A$
is free of rank $2g$ over $\mathbf Z_\ell$. The input is the orders of the groups
$A[\ell^n](\bar k)$, which are known from
Proposition [proposition-multiplication-n], and these orders force each of
these groups to be free over $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ of rank $2g$. Moreover, the
transition maps are surjective because $A(\bar k)$ is divisible.

Although Frobenius can have many fixed points on the finite levels, no
power of it has a nonzero fixed vector in the Tate module
(Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector]). For example, for the elliptic curve $E_0:y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$, the three roots
of $x^3-x$ lie in $\mathbf F_3$. So all of $E[2]$ is rational, and
Frobenius acts trivially on it. On $T_2E$, however, a fixed vector would
be an unbounded compatible system of $2$-power torsion points in the
finite group $E_0(\mathbf F_{3^m})$. For the Jacobian of a curve, Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one] turns this into
the statement that Frobenius has no fixed class in $H^1$ of the curve.

Over a finite field, Frobenius acts on $T_\ell A$, and by the last
proposition this action is compatible with its action on each
$A[\ell^n](\bar k)$. The next proposition shows that no power of
Frobenius has a nonzero fixed vector. For the Jacobian of a curve, this is the input to
Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one].

For a curve $C$ proper and connected over a separably closed field and
$n$ invertible in that field, the Kummer sequence shows that
$H^1(C,\mu_n)$ is the $n$-torsion of the Picard group of $C$. But the
Picard group is an abstract group. In particular, nothing about it says that its
$n$-torsion is finite, let alone isomorphic to $(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}$. Nor
does it say why Frobenius should have no fixed vector on the $\ell$-adic
limit, as Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]
requires. Both questions become statements of
Appendix [chap-Abelian-varieties] once we know that
$\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$, the group of invertible sheaves of degree
zero, is the group of points of an abelian variety.

Over $\mathbf C$ this is the Abel–Jacobi theorem, $\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\simeq
H^0(C,\Omega^1)^\vee/H_1(C,\mathbf Z)$. Over an arbitrary field we
construct the Jacobian as a Picard scheme, which represents invertible
sheaves in families.

Let $C$ be a smooth proper connected curve of genus $g$ over a separably
closed field $k$. The idea is that most invertible sheaves of degree $g$
are given by divisors. Suppose $\mathcal L$ has degree $g$ and
$h^0(\mathcal L)=1$. Then the zeros of its unique section up to scalars
form an effective divisor of degree $g$, and this divisor determines
$\mathcal L$. Effective divisors of degree $g$ are the points of the
Hilbert scheme $\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$, a smooth proper variety of
dimension $g$ (Theorem [theorem-hilbert-schemes-points-smooth-curve]).

By Riemann–Roch, every invertible sheaf of degree $g$ has $h^0\geq1$,
with equality exactly when $h^1=0$. This condition is open in families,
by semicontinuity, and it defines an open chart
$W\subset\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$ of the Picard functor
(Proposition [proposition-divisors-degree-g-open-chart]).
Riemann–Roch also moves every invertible sheaf into this chart by a twist
defined over $k$ (Lemma [lemma-twisting-h-0-1-h]). Hence the
translates of $W$ cover the Picard functor, and they glue to the Picard
scheme. Its components are proper because the Abel map
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}\to\operatorname{Pic}^g$ is surjective and
its source is proper.

The Picard functor itself is a sheafified quotient of
$T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C\times T)$. We have to divide out the
invertible sheaves pulled back from $T$, since these are trivial locally
on $T$. When $C$ has a rational point, we describe the Picard functor by
invertible sheaves trivialized along that point
(Lemma [lemma-rigidification-along-section]).

The outcome is
Theorem [theorem-picard-scheme-jacobian-over-separably]: the
component of degree zero, the Jacobian $J(C)$, is an abelian variety of
dimension $g$ with $J(C)(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)$ and tangent space
$H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$ at the origin.
Over a finite field we descend the Jacobian to an abelian
variety $J_0$ over $\mathbf F_q$. Then
Propositions [proposition-jacobian-over-ground-field]
and [proposition-h-1-curve-tate-module] give an isomorphism
$\varprojlim_nH^1(C,\mathbf Z/\ell^n(1))\simeq T_\ell J_0$ compatible
with Frobenius, which is the form in which
Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one] uses the
Jacobian; see also [milne-jv].

attrs.title: The Picard scheme of a curve

objects.body:
We want a scheme whose points over $T$ are families of invertible sheaves
on $C$ parametrized by $T$. The obvious candidate $T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)$, however, contains too much. For example, for $C=\mathbf P^1_k$ and connected $T$, every invertible sheaf on $\mathbf P^1_T$ is
$\mathcal O(d)\otimes f_T^*\mathcal M$ for a unique $d\in\mathbf Z$ and a
unique $\mathcal M\in\operatorname{Pic}(T)$. In other words
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1_T)=\mathbf Z\oplus\operatorname{Pic}(T)$,
whereas the Picard scheme should be the constant scheme $\mathbf Z$. In
fact the functor $T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)$ is not even a
Zariski sheaf, because the pullback $f_T^*\mathcal M$ of a nontrivial invertible sheaf
$\mathcal M$ on $T$ is trivial locally on $T$ but not globally, so no
scheme represents this functor.

The Picard functor is therefore defined as the sheafification of
$T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)/f_T^*\operatorname{Pic}(T)$
(Definition [definition-relative-picard-functor]). When $C$ has a
section, Lemma [lemma-rigidification-along-section] removes the
pullbacks from $T$ in another way, by fixing a trivialization along the
section. We use this rigidified description to construct the chart of
Proposition [proposition-divisors-degree-g-open-chart] and the Picard
scheme of Theorem [theorem-picard-scheme-jacobian-over-separably].

Equivalently, one may sheafify
$T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)$, since an invertible sheaf on $T$
becomes trivial on a Zariski cover. The sheafification is needed: invertible sheaves satisfy effective descent, but their automorphisms can
prevent their isomorphism classes from forming a sheaf. For this reason
neither the displayed quotient nor $T\mapsto\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)$ need
be an fppf sheaf [Stacks, [0B9L](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9L)]. If $f$ has a section, the next lemma
describes the sheafification directly. We also write
$\operatorname{Pic}_{C/S}$ for the Picard scheme when it exists.

For a smooth proper geometrically connected curve $C$ over a field
$k$, we have $H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k$. For every field extension $k'/k$
the curve $C_{k'}$ is again smooth, proper and integral, and flat base change
for coherent cohomology gives $H^0(C_{k'},\mathcal O_{C_{k'}})=k'$ and
$\dim_{k'}H^1(C_{k'},\mathcal O_{C_{k'}})=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. Every
$k$-scheme is flat over $k$, so the same flat base change shows that $(\ast)$
holds for $C\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. If $C$ has a $k$-point $P$, the preceding lemma applies
with $\sigma=P$ (see [Stacks, [0B9U](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B9U)]).

The chart of the Picard scheme in degree $g$ is cut out by the
condition $h^1=0$. Let $\mathcal L$ be an invertible sheaf of degree $g$ on
a curve of genus $g$. Then Riemann–Roch gives $h^0(\mathcal L)-h^1(\mathcal L)=1$,
so $h^1(\mathcal L)=0$ if and only if $\mathcal L$ has exactly one
section up to scalars. In a family over $T$, coherent base change shows
that the condition “$Rf_{T,*}\mathcal L$ is an invertible sheaf in
degree zero” is open on $T$ and compatible with base change. It
therefore defines an open subfunctor of the Picard functor.

The condition is not closed, because $h^0$ can jump up under
specialization. For example, on a curve of genus two a divisor $D$ of
degree two has $h^0(\mathcal O(D))=1$ unless $\mathcal O(D)\simeq\omega_{C/k}$,
in which case $h^0=2$. The chart therefore misses the line of canonical
divisors in $\operatorname{Hilb}^{2}_{C/k}$, and we need its translates
to cover the Picard scheme in degree two.

Fix a smooth proper geometrically connected curve $C$ over $k$, with
structure morphism $f:C\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, and set
$g=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. Such a curve is projective
[Stacks, [0A26](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A26)].

For $C=\mathbf P^1_k$ and $\mathcal L=\mathcal O(d)$ with $d\geq0$, the
sections are the binary forms of degree $d$, a space of dimension
$d+1=\deg\mathcal L+1-0$, and $\omega=\mathcal O(-2)$ has degree $-2=2g-2$.

We quote the theorem from [Stacks, [0B5B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B5B)], where it is proved for smooth
curves and the duality is given by the residue trace on differentials.
We prove its compatibility with field extension in
Corollary [corollary-serre-duality-field-extension] below. For the displayed vanishing, recall that a nonzero
section of an invertible sheaf on an integral curve has an effective
divisor of zeros. Hence an invertible sheaf of negative degree has no
nonzero section. If $\deg\mathcal L>2g-2$, then
$\omega_{C/k}\otimes\mathcal L^{-1}$ has negative degree, and
$H^1(C,\mathcal L)=0$ by duality. The dimension formula then follows from
Riemann–Roch. For $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_C$ the duality gives
$\dim_kH^0(C,\omega_{C/k})=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)=g$.

The Picard scheme is constructed over a separably closed field, but its
points are tested over arbitrary extensions. Hence Riemann–Roch and
coherent base change must be compatible with extension of the ground
field, and for duality we need this for the pairing itself, not only
for the dimensions.

Recall that the chart of the Picard scheme consists of the invertible
sheaves $\mathcal L$ for which $Rf_{T,*}\mathcal L$ is an invertible
sheaf in degree $0$. We use coherent base change in the following form.

On a smooth curve a finite subscheme of length $d$ is the same as an
effective divisor of degree $d$. These divisors are parametrized by the
Hilbert scheme of points $\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$, which is the
symmetric power $C^{(d)}$. Iterated addition of points gives a finite
surjection $C^d\to \operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$, from which
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}$ inherits properness, irreducibility and
dimension $d$ (Theorem [theorem-hilbert-schemes-points-smooth-curve]).
For example, for $C=\mathbf P^1$, an effective divisor of degree $d$ is the zero set of
a binary form of degree $d$ up to scalars, and
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{d}_{C/k}=\mathbf P^d$.

A divisor $D$ gives the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O(D)$ with its
canonical section. Conversely, an invertible sheaf with a section up to
scalars gives a divisor. When $h^0=1$ the section is unique up to
scalars, and then the divisor is determined by the sheaf. In this way the
open part of $\operatorname{Hilb}^{g}_{C/k}$ where $h^0(\mathcal O(D))=1$
and $h^1=0$ becomes an open subfunctor of the Picard functor
(Proposition [proposition-divisors-degree-g-open-chart]).

For $d\geq0$, let $\operatorname{Hilb}^d_{C/k}$ be the
functor on $k$-schemes sending $T$ to the set of closed subschemes
$D\subset C_T$ that are finite locally free of rank $d$ over $T$.

Assume now that $C(k)$ contains a point $P$, and let us describe
$\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$ by rigidified invertible sheaves as in
Lemma [lemma-rigidification-along-section]. We define a subfunctor
$F\subset\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$ as follows. A rigidified class
$\mathcal L$ on $C_T$ lies in $F(T)$ if, in the derived category of
$\mathcal O_T$-modules,

$$
Rf_{T,*}\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal N[0]
\quad\text{for some invertible }\mathcal N\text{ on }T.
$$

By Lemma [lemma-coherent-base-change-invertible-sheaves], this condition defines
an open locus of $T$ compatible with base change, so that
the inclusion $F\subset\operatorname{Pic}_{C/k}$ is representable by
open immersions.

To cover the Picard functor by translates of $F$, we have to move every
invertible sheaf into $F$ by a twist defined over $k$.

We glue the translates of the chart of
Proposition [proposition-divisors-degree-g-open-chart] to the Picard
scheme, whose component of degree zero is the Jacobian. Gluing uses twice
that $k$ is separably closed: to find a rational point for the
rigidification, and to obtain the twists of
Lemma [lemma-twisting-h-0-1-h] over $k$. For an elliptic curve, the Abel map $C=\operatorname{Hilb}^{1}_{C/k}\to\operatorname{Pic}^1_{C/k}$ is
an isomorphism, and translation by $\mathcal O_C(-P)$ identifies $C$ with
its own Jacobian. In general, the tangent space of the Jacobian at the
origin is computed by deforming the trivial sheaf over the dual numbers.

We compute the tangent space with the dual numbers
$k[\varepsilon]$, $\varepsilon^2=0$; the computation works for any
scheme over $k$.

We use the theorem in the following form: over an algebraically closed
field, the Picard group of $C$ is an extension of $\mathbf Z$ by the
group of points of an abelian variety.

The Kummer sequence on a curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field
identifies $H^1(C,\mu_n)$ with $\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]$ and
$H^2(C,\mu_n)$ with $\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n$
(Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime]). To compute these groups, we
combine two facts. First, the exact sequence of Corollary [corollary-degree-jacobian]
separates the discrete part $\mathbf Z$ of the Picard group from the
Jacobian. Second, Appendix [chap-Abelian-varieties] describes multiplication by
$n$ on an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field: it is
surjective on points, and for $n$ invertible in $k$ its kernel is
$(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}$. Now apply the snake lemma to multiplication by $n$
on the degree sequence. Since $\mathbf Z$ is torsion free, the
$n$-torsion of $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$ is $J(C)[n](k)\simeq(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g}$.
Since $J(C)(k)$ is divisible, the cokernel of $n$ on $\operatorname{Pic}(C)$
is $\mathbf Z/n$, given by the degree.

For proper base change we also need these groups to be unchanged under
extension of the algebraically closed field. This holds because
$J(C)[n]$ is finite étale
(Corollary [corollary-torsion-jacobian-field-extension]).

To compare the Galois action on the cohomology of a curve over $\bar k$
with a Tate module, we need the Jacobian over the ground field $k$.
For example, in Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]
we work over a finite field, and Frobenius acts on
$\varprojlim_nH^1(C,\mathbf Z/\ell^n(1))$. It has no fixed vector there
because this module is $T_\ell J_0$ for an abelian variety $J_0$ over
$\mathbf F_q$ (Proposition [proposition-no-frobenius-fixed-vector]).
The construction so far works over a separably closed field and uses a
rational point for the rigidification. However, a curve over $k$ need not
have a $k$-point; for instance, the conic $x^2+y^2+z^2=0$ over $\mathbf R$ has none.
We therefore define $J_0$ as the scheme representing the degree-zero part
of the fppf Picard sheaf. Concretely, we obtain it from the Jacobian over $k_s$
by Galois descent through a finite Galois extension $k'/k$
(Proposition [proposition-jacobian-over-ground-field]). The Kummer sequence then
identifies $H^1(C,\mathbf Z/\ell^n(1))$ with $J_0[\ell^n](\bar k)$
compatibly with the Galois action and the transition maps
(Proposition [proposition-h-1-curve-tate-module]).

Since $J_0$ is defined over $k$, the Galois group acts on its torsion
points. Using the Kummer sequence on $C$, we compare this action with
the Galois action on cohomology.

The last step of proper base change for $\mathbf P^1$ compares the
cohomology of a curve over two separably closed fields, one inside the
other. Smooth base change needs the same comparison for affine
curves, with coefficients prime to the characteristic. Both
rest on Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves], whose assertions we
recall. Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C$ be a separated scheme
of finite type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, and let $F$ be a classical
torsion abelian sheaf on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. Then:

- $(C_{1})$ $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>2$;
- $(C_{2})$ if $C$ is affine, $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>1$;
- $(C_{3})$ if $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ and $F$ is $p$-primary,
  $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>1$;
- $(C_{4})$ if $F$ is constructible with finite stalks and prime to
  $\operatorname{char}k$, all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite;
- $(C_{5})$ if $C$ is proper and $F$ is constructible with finite stalks,
  all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite;
- $(C_{6})$ if $k'/k$ is an extension of algebraically closed fields and $F$
  is prime to $\operatorname{char}k$, the pullback maps
  $H^q(C,F)\to H^q(C_{k'},F|)$ are isomorphisms;
- $(C_{7})$ if $C$ is proper, the maps in $(C_6)$ are isomorphisms for every
  torsion $F$;
- $(C_{8})$ for any open $U\subseteq C$, restriction
  $H^2(C,F)\to H^2(U,F|_U)$ is surjective.

Over $\mathbf C$ the vanishing and finiteness assertions are statements
about a Riemann surface, which has the homotopy type of a CW complex of
dimension two, or of one if it is not compact.

In algebraic geometry we compute the groups. Let $C$ be a smooth proper
connected curve of genus $g$ and let $n$ be invertible in $k$. Three
ingredients compute the cohomology of $\mu_n$: the Kummer
sequence $0\to\mu_n\to\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{n}\mathbf G_m\to0$, the
vanishing of $H^q(C,\mathbf G_m)$ for $q\geq2$, which is a consequence of
Tsen's theorem, and the Jacobian of Appendix [chap-The-Picard-scheme-of-a-curve]. They give

$$
H^0(C,\mu_n)=\mu_n(k),\qquad H^1(C,\mu_n)=J(C)[n](k)\simeq(\mathbf Z/n)^{2g},
\qquad H^2(C,\mu_n)=\mathbf Z/n
$$

(Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime]).
These groups do not change under extension of algebraically closed
fields, because torsion points of an abelian variety do not. For $\mathbf P^1$, which has $g=0$, the computation fixes the normalization of
the class of $\mathcal O(1)$ that
Remark [remark-twists-projective-line] provides for the proof of
proper base change. Removing a nonempty finite set of $r$ points kills
$H^2$ and raises the rank of $H^1$ to $2g+r-1$
(Proposition [proposition-cohomology-smooth-affine-curve]).

Proper base change, however, is needed for all torsion coefficients,
including those divisible by the characteristic $p$, and there the
answer changes. On the affine line,
$H^1(\mathbf A^1_k,\mathbf F_p)=k[t]/\{h^p-h\}$ is infinite, and it grows
when $k$ is enlarged (Example [example-affine-line-characteristic-p]).
Indeed, the Artin–Schreier torsors $y^p-y=at$, for $a\in k$, have
pairwise distinct classes, and over a larger field $k'$ there are new ones
with $a\in k'\setminus k$. So for $p$-torsion coefficients, finiteness
and invariance under field extension hold only for proper curves. This is
why $(C_5)$ and $(C_7)$ of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] assume
properness, and why
Lemma [lemma-extension-separably-closed-ground-field] is stated for
proper curves.

The Artin–Schreier sequence
$0\to\mathbf F_p\to\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\varphi-1}\mathbf G_a\to0$
reduces the cohomology of $\mathbf F_p$ to the coherent cohomology of
$\mathcal O_C$. On the affine line it presents $H^1$ as the cokernel of
$h\mapsto h^p-h$ on $k[t]$, as above. On every curve it gives
$H^q(C,\mathbf F_p)=0$ for $q\geq2$
(Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves], $(C_3)$).

A general torsion sheaf is reduced to a constant one by two observations.
First, a sheaf supported on finitely many points has no cohomology in
positive degrees. Hence passing to the normalization of a curve, or
extending a sheaf by zero from a dense open subset, changes cohomology
only in degrees zero and one, and only by finite groups
(Lemmas [lemma-normalization-constant-sheaf] and [lemma-removing-finitely-many-points]).
Second, a finite $\mathbf F_\ell$-local system becomes a successive
extension of constant sheaves on a finite étale cover of degree $d$
prime to $\ell$. This cover is given by an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup of the
monodromy. Dividing the trace of the cover by $d$ shows that the local
system is a direct summand of the pushforward of its pullback
(Lemma [lemma-reduction-unipotent-local-system]). We follow the
proof of [Stacks, [03SC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SC)].

Throughout this appendix, cohomology means cohomology on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$,
and the sheaves are classical in the sense of
Definition [definition-classical-pro-etale-sheaves]: by
Theorem [theorem-classical-sheaves-essential-image] such a sheaf is the inverse image
$\nu_C^*G$ of a sheaf $G$ on $C_{\acute{e}t}$ along the comparison morphism.
By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], its cohomology, together with
the restriction and pullback maps, agrees with étale cohomology, so
we carry out all calculations on $C_{\acute{e}t}$ and transport them back by
$\nu_C^*$.

Let $p\ge0$ be the characteristic of $k$. In this appendix $\ell$ is
an arbitrary prime, possibly equal to $p$. In characteristic zero the
hypotheses in $(C_4)$ and $(C_6)$ of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] that
$F$ be prime to the characteristic hold automatically.

attrs.title: Cohomology of torsion sheaves on curves

objects.body:
Let $C$ be a smooth curve over an algebraically closed field $k$, and
let $\nu_C^*\mathbf G_m$ be the
pullback of the multiplicative group $\mathbf G_m$ of $C_{\acute{e}t}$ to $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. For $n$ invertible
in $k$, the Kummer sequence $0\to\mu_n\to\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{n}\mathbf G_m\to0$
reduces the cohomology of $\mu_n$ to that of $\nu_C^*\mathbf G_m$, so
we compute the latter first.
In degree one, $H^1(C,\mathbf G_m)$ is the Picard group, as in the
Zariski topology, while the groups $H^q(C,\mathbf G_m)$ vanish for $q\ge2$
(Lemma [lemma-cohomology-multiplicative-group]). In particular the
Brauer group of $C$ is zero. This matches, over $\mathbf C$, the topology of a Riemann surface, whose integral cohomology
vanishes above degree two, and whose $H^2$ is accounted for by the degree of
line bundles. In algebraic geometry the vanishing comes from Tsen's
theorem, which says that forms of low degree over the function field
$k(C)$ have nontrivial zeros. Over a finite field Tsen's theorem fails:
by class field theory the function field of a curve has nonzero Brauer
group. This is one reason why we work over an algebraically closed field.
With the lemma and the Jacobian, the Kummer sequence then computes the
cohomology of $\mu_n$ on a proper curve
(Proposition [proposition-smooth-proper-curves-torsion-prime]).

On a proper curve, the lemma and the Kummer sequence reduce the
cohomology of $\mu_n$ to the groups $\operatorname{Pic}(C)[n]$ and
$\operatorname{Pic}(C)/n$, both computed in Appendix [chap-The-Picard-scheme-of-a-curve].

Every smooth connected curve over an algebraically closed field that
is not proper is affine and is the complement of a finite nonempty set
of closed points in a smooth proper connected curve.  To see this,
take a projective model of its function field and normalize it, and
recall that regular curves over a perfect field are smooth.

On the affine curve $U=\overline C\setminus D$ the Picard group is a
quotient of $\operatorname{Pic}^0(\overline C)$. It is therefore divisible,
and $H^2(U,\mu_n)=0$; this matches the fact that, topologically, a punctured Riemann surface is
homotopy equivalent to a graph. In degree one, on the other hand, new torsors appear, since a
Kummer torsor on $U$ need not extend over $\overline C$. The obstruction to extending it
at each puncture is the residue of the torsor, that is, the order modulo
$n$ of the corresponding rational section. For example, on
$\mathbf G_m=\mathbf P^1\setminus\{0,\infty\}$ the torsor $y^n=x$ has
residues $1$ and $-1$ at the two punctures. It generates
$H^1(\mathbf G_m,\mu_n)\simeq\mathbf Z/n$. In general the residues sum
to zero. The residue sequence of
Proposition [proposition-cohomology-smooth-affine-curve] shows that
$H^1(U,\mu_n)$ is free of rank $2g+\#D-1$ over $\mathbf Z/n$. This is the
first Betti number of a surface of genus $g$ with $\#D$ punctures.

For the constant sheaf $\mathbf F_\ell$, with $\ell$ a prime different
from $\operatorname{char}k$,
the two preceding propositions prove $(C_1)$–$(C_8)$ on smooth curves.
Indeed, a primitive $\ell$th root of unity in $k$ identifies
$\mathbf F_\ell$ with $\mu_\ell$, compatibly with the pullback maps to
$C_{k'}$, since the root of unity stays primitive in $k'$.
For $(C_8)$, note that an open in a smooth connected proper curve is
either the whole curve or an affine curve, which has $H^2=0$, and that
an open in a smooth affine curve is affine.

Since the Kummer cover $T^n=a$ is étale only when $n$ is invertible,
$p$-torsion in characteristic $p$ needs a different sequence.
In the Artin–Schreier sequence the role of $\mathbf G_m$ is played by
the additive group, whose étale cohomology is the coherent cohomology
of the structure sheaf. Since coherent cohomology of a curve vanishes above degree one, this gives $H^q(C,\mathbf F_p)=0$ for $q\geq3$. For
$q=2$ we also need that $\varphi-1$ is surjective on $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$,
which holds over an algebraically closed field. So $H^2(C,\mathbf F_p)=0$
even on a proper curve, and there is no analogue of the class of a point
in $H^2$.

On a proper curve, $H^1(C,\mathbf F_p)$ is the fixed space of the
Frobenius-linear map $\varphi$ on the $g$-dimensional space
$H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. Hence it has dimension at most $g$
(Proposition [proposition-p-torsion-smooth-proper-curve]). The
bound can be strict. For example, for an elliptic curve, $\varphi$ on the line
$H^1(E,\mathcal O_E)$ is bijective when $E$ is ordinary, and zero when
$E$ is supersingular, as is $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\overline{\mathbf F}_3$.
Accordingly $H^1(E,\mathbf F_p)$ has dimension one or zero. On an affine curve, by contrast, the cokernel of $\varphi-1$ on the ring of functions contributes to
$H^1$, and this group is infinite
(Example [example-affine-line-characteristic-p]).

On an affine curve the same sequence is even simpler to use, because
coherent cohomology vanishes in positive degrees. On the other hand,
$H^1$ is now the cokernel of $\varphi-1$ on an infinite-dimensional
space.

For the affine line we can compute the cokernel explicitly, and we see
that it is infinite and grows with the field, unlike in the proper case.

For the constant sheaf $\mathbf F_p$ on smooth curves, we obtain
$(C_1)$, $(C_3)$, $(C_5)$ and $(C_7)$ from the proposition on proper
curves, and $(C_1)$, $(C_2)$ and $(C_3)$ from the lemma on affine
curves, while $(C_8)$ holds because $H^2$ vanishes in both cases.

So far we have computed with constant coefficients on smooth curves,
whereas Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] concerns arbitrary curves of
dimension at most one and arbitrary torsion sheaves. Two reductions close
the gap: normalization and removing finitely many points. Both rest
on Lemma [lemma-sheaves-finite-support-finite-morphisms], which says
that a sheaf supported on finitely many points has no higher cohomology.
Hence passing between a curve, its normalization and a dense open subset
changes cohomology only in degrees zero and one, and only by finite groups
that do not change under field extension.

For example, let $C:y^2=x^3+x^2$ be the nodal cubic. Its normalization
$\mathbf A^1\to C$ has two points over the node. For $M=\mathbf Z/n$ the
normalization sequence of
Lemma [lemma-normalization-constant-sheaf] has cokernel
$M^2/\Delta M\simeq M$ at the node. If $n$ is invertible in $k$, then
$H^1(\mathbf A^1,\mathbf Z/n)=0$, and the long exact sequence gives
$H^1(C,\mathbf Z/n)\simeq\mathbf Z/n$. This is the analogue of the loop
created by the node.

Since a sheaf supported on finitely many points is a direct image from
those points, it has no higher cohomology. All the reductions below use
this vanishing.

The normalization of a curve is finite
and is an isomorphism away from finitely many points, so the constant
sheaf on $C$ differs from the direct image of the constant sheaf on
$C^{\mathrm{nor}}$ only by a sheaf with finite support.

The normalization sequence reduces constant coefficients on a reduced
curve to the smooth case. By
Lemma [lemma-sheaves-finite-support-finite-morphisms], its cokernel term has finite
sections, unchanged under field extension, and no positive cohomology.
Moreover, by Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms-cohomology], $H^q(C,\pi_*\underline M)=H^q(C^{\mathrm{nor}},\underline M)$.
The long exact sequence therefore yields isomorphisms
$H^q(C,\underline M)\simeq H^q(C^{\mathrm{nor}},\underline M)$
for $q\geq2$, while in degrees zero and one it gives a natural exact sequence
relating $C$ and $C^{\mathrm{nor}}$, whose remaining term is a finite
group. From these sequences, vanishing and finiteness pass
from $C^{\mathrm{nor}}$ to $C$, and by the five lemma so does invariance
under field extension.

The normalization of an affine or proper curve is again affine or
proper. Hence all assertions of
Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] for constant $\mathbf F_\ell$ follow from
the calculations on smooth curves. For $(C_8)$, we apply this comparison
to $C$ and to the inverse image of an open subset. The commutative
square of restriction maps then reduces surjectivity to the smooth components.

A constructible sheaf on a curve is locally constant on a dense open
subset. Removing the finitely many remaining points replaces the sheaf
by its extension by zero from this open, and changes cohomology only in
degrees zero and one. Let $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ be a dense open in a
reduced curve, and let $i:Z\hookrightarrow C$ be its finite
complementary closed subscheme. For a classical sheaf $F$ we have the
exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow j_!j^*F\longrightarrow F
\longrightarrow i_*i^*F\longrightarrow0
$$

of an open and its closed complement. We check its exactness on
geometric stalks on $C_{\acute{e}t}$, and then pull it back.

When $j$ is dense, Lemma [lemma-removing-finitely-many-points], together with
the calculation for constant $\mathbf F_\ell$ on $C$ via
Lemma [lemma-normalization-constant-sheaf], shows that $j_!\underline{\mathbf F_\ell}$
satisfies the assertions of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves].
An arbitrary open is dense in the reduced union of the components it
meets, a closed subscheme of $C$, so we can apply the dense case
there and pass back to $C$: direct image along a finite
morphism is exact [Stacks, [0A3Q](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A3Q)] and, by
Lemma [lemma-finite-morphisms-cohomology], does not change cohomology.

We reduce a local system to constant sheaves by pulling it back along
a cover of degree prime to $\ell$, on which it becomes unipotent. To find such a cover, note that a local
system of finite $\mathbf F_\ell$-vector spaces has finite
monodromy: the fundamental group acts on a fibre through a
finite quotient. The local system then becomes a successive extension of
constant sheaves on the cover defined by an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup of the
monodromy group.

On the full cover of its monodromy the local system even becomes
constant. But that cover can have degree divisible by $\ell$, and then
the local system need not be a direct summand of the pushforward of its
pullback. For example, let $v:y^2=x$ be the double cover of $\mathbf G_m$,
in characteristic different from two, and let $\ell=2$. The composite of
the unit $\mathbf F_2\to v_*\mathbf F_2$ and the trace is multiplication by
$2$, which is zero. In fact $\mathbf F_2$ is not a direct summand of
$v_*\mathbf F_2$ at all. The monodromy representation of
$v_*\mathbf F_2$ is the regular representation $\mathbf F_2[\mathbf Z/2]$,
which is indecomposable.

For a cover of degree prime to $\ell$, on the
other hand, Lemma [lemma-reduction-unipotent-local-system] shows that the
trace divided by the degree splits the unit. It therefore suffices to
prove the vanishing, finiteness and invariance statements for the
pullback. The pullback is unipotent, that is, built from constant sheaves
by extensions.

To apply this to $j_!G$ on a reduced curve $C$, we take for $U$ a dense
smooth open on which $G$ is locally constant.  Normalizing $C$ in the
finite extensions of function fields defined by $V$, we get a finite
morphism $\bar v:Y\to C$ with $V$ the inverse image of $U$, and an
open immersion $j':V\hookrightarrow Y$.  From the cartesian square
formed by these maps and the formula for stalks of direct images along
finite morphisms, we find that

$$
j_!v_*v^*G=\bar v_*j'_!v^*G,
$$

which is also the exchange formula of [Stacks, [0GJ1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GJ1)].  If
$C$ is proper, then $Y$ is proper, and if $C$ is affine, then $Y$ is affine.

The assertions travel from constant sheaves to $j'_!v^*G$ on $Y$, then
to $j_!v_*v^*G$ on $C$, and from there to the direct summand $j_!G$.
Since $j'_!$ is exact, the filtration of $v^*G$
gives a filtration of $j'_!v^*G$ with graded pieces $j'_!\mathbf F_\ell$.
The assertions of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] hold for these
pieces by the calculation for constant sheaves extended by zero. As we
show at the start of the next section, they pass along
extensions, so they hold for $j'_!v^*G$. Since
$\bar v_*$ is exact, they hold for $j_!v_*v^*G$. By the splitting
given by the trace, they hold for its direct summand $j_!G$. For
invariance under field extension we use that the unit and the trace
commute with extension of the ground field. Then the pullback map for
$j_!G$ is a retract of the pullback map for $j_!v_*v^*G$, and a retract
of an isomorphism is an isomorphism [Stacks, [03SD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03SD)].

If $C$ is not equidimensional, we choose a dense open that is
smooth and is the disjoint union of the regular loci of the
one-dimensional components and the isolated points.  On the isolated
points taking sections is exact, each connected
one-dimensional piece is treated as above, and finite direct sums
preserve all the assertions.

The assertions of Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves] pass along short
exact sequences.  To see this, let $0\to F_1\to F\to F_2\to0$ be exact, and
suppose that the assertions are known for $F_1$ and $F_2$.  Vanishing and
finiteness follow from the long exact sequence, and invariance under
field extension follows from the map between the two long exact
sequences and the five lemma.
For $(C_8)$ an extra argument is needed. Let $b\in H^2(U,F)$, and lift its image in $H^2(U,F_2)$ to
$c_2\in H^2(C,F_2)$.  The obstruction to lifting $c_2$ to $H^2(C,F)$
lies in $H^3(C,F_1)$, which vanishes by $(C_1)$, so such a lift
$c$ exists. The difference $b-c|_U$ comes from $H^2(U,F_1)$, and by
$(C_8)$ for $F_1$ it lifts to $H^2(C,F_1)$; adding that
lift to $c$ gives the required global class [Stacks, [0A5C](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A5C)].

The trace formula needs the local term at an isolated fixed point to be
the trace on the stalk. This is not a formal fact. A local term is
computed from $\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$ near the fixed point, and the stalk
does not determine this complex (Remark [remark-locality-warning]).
Instead, Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula] proves the equality by a computation
for Frobenius on a smooth curve
(Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve]) and reduces
everything else to that case. In particular, its trace formula
(Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula]) does not
depend on this appendix.

The computation leaves open why Frobenius behaves so well. Topology
suggests that the reason is contraction. If a map $\varphi$ of a manifold
contracts a neighbourhood of a fixed point $y$ into itself, then the local
index at $y$ is $1$. With coefficients in a sheaf, the local index is the
trace of $\varphi$ on the stalk at $y$. Frobenius contracts in the
strongest possible sense: its differential is zero. In this
appendix we make this explanation into a theorem, in any dimension and
for a whole class of correspondences at once.

In algebraic geometry we measure contraction by powers of ideals. Let
$c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$ be a correspondence, $Z\subset X$ a closed
subscheme with ideal $I$, and put $I_i=c_i^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_C$. We say,
as in [varshavsky05], that $c$ contracts towards $Z$ if
$I_2\subset I_1$ and $I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$ for some $n\geq1$.
Frobenius is the model case. Indeed, take $c=(\mathrm{id},\Phi_X^m)$ and $Z$ a
point $y\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$, and choose coordinates $x_i$ of an
affine neighbourhood of $y$ defined over $\mathbf F_q$. Then $y$ has
coordinates $a_i\in\mathbf F_{q^m}$, and
$(\Phi_X^m)^*(x_i-a_i)=x_i^{q^m}-a_i=(x_i-a_i)^{q^m}$. Hence
$I_2\subset I_1^{q^m}$, and $n=1$ works.

The main theorem,
Theorem [theorem-contracting-correspondences-local-terms], says that
near a component of its fixed locus that meets $Z$, the trace class of a
contracting correspondence can be computed on $Z$ alone, from the
correspondence restricted to $Z$. For $Z$ a point,
Corollary [corollary-contracting-local-terms-point] says that the local
term at an isolated fixed point is the trace on the stalk, even when $X$
is singular. The theorem and its proof are due to
Varshavsky [varshavsky05]. They generalize Fujiwara's theorem, conjectured by Deligne, that
the local terms of a correspondence composed with a sufficiently high
power of Frobenius are the naive ones.

The proof makes the contraction literal by deforming $X$ to the normal
cone of $Z$. Over the trait $\operatorname{Spec}k[t]_{(t)}$, the
deformation to the normal cone $\mathcal D_ZX$ has generic fibre $X$ and
special fibre the normal cone $N_ZX$. On the special fibre, the
contraction hypothesis says that the second leg maps everything into the
zero section (Lemma [lemma-normal-cones-contracting-ideals]). There
the part of $K$ away from $Z$ contributes nothing. What remains is the
specialization of $K$ restricted to the zero section, and by Verdier's
theorem (Theorem [theorem-verdier-s-theorem-specialization-zero])
this is $K|_Z$.

It remains to transport the answer back to $X$. We identify the trace
class on the special fibre with the specialization of the trace class of
$c$ (Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class]). The
specialization map is an isomorphism, because the fixed locus does not
move in the family up to nilpotents
(Lemma [lemma-fixed-point-scheme-deformation]). Before any of this,
we must be able to specialize a trace class at all. A trace class is
built from $K\boxtimes\mathbb DK$, so we need nearby cycles to commute
with external products and with Verdier duality.
Propositions [proposition-external-kunneth-formula-nearby-cycles]
and [proposition-nearby-cycles-commute-verdier-duality] prove both,
by a dimension argument of Illusie [illusie94].

We use the six operations and the notation for correspondences and
trace classes of Chapter [chap-The-Lefschetz-Verdier-formula], and classical
results on nearby cycles over a trait, which we recall where they are
first needed. Throughout this appendix, $k$ is algebraically closed,
$\ell$ is invertible in $k$, and $A$ is a finite commutative ring
annihilated by a power of $\ell$. The only exception to these conventions is the base of
nearby cycles in
Sections [sec-Kunneth-formula-for-nearby-cycles]–[sec-Specialization-of-the-trace-class], which
may be any excellent strictly henselian trait, with residue field only
separably closed. As in the rest of the notes, statements about constructible
complexes on $k$-schemes are made on the pro-étale site, but we construct
nearby cycles on the classical étale site and transport them by the
comparison for constructible complexes
(Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves] and
Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison]).

Let $S$ be the strict henselization of $\operatorname{Spec}k[t]_{(t)}$,
with generic point $\eta$. Nearby cycles move a complex from the generic
fibre of a family over $S$ to its special fibre. Since the special fibre
does not lie in the generic fibre, we cannot simply restrict. The obvious
attempt is to extend by $Rj_*$ along the open generic fibre and restrict
by $i^*$ to the special fibre. This fails already for $S$ itself,
because the fraction field of $S$ is not separably closed. Its absolute Galois group is the inertia group, whose tame quotient is
$\prod_{\ell'\neq p}\mathbf Z_{\ell'}(1)$. For $n$ invertible in $k$,
the stalk of $R^1j_*(\mathbf Z/n)$ at the closed point is therefore
$H^1(\eta,\mathbf Z/n)=\mathbf Z/n(-1)\neq0$. This class comes from
the arithmetic of $\eta$, not from the geometry of the family. Passing
first to the geometric generic fibre removes such Galois classes. After
this change, the constant sheaf specializes to itself, in degree zero, by
the first calculation below.

Both specialization to the normal cone and the comparison of trace classes in
Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class] are built from
nearby cycles on the deformation to the normal cone. The key input is
Verdier's theorem,
Theorem [theorem-verdier-s-theorem-specialization-zero]
(see [varshavsky05, §§1.3–1.4 and 3]).

The basic computation is that nearby cycles of a constant family
$Y\times S$ give back the complex we started with
(Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family]). We use it twice. It
makes the map $\tau_{X,Z}$ below land in $i^*L$, and it makes the
specialization of trace classes the identity when the fixed scheme does
not move (Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme]).
Its proof uses only the definition of nearby cycles, their base change
maps and two calculations, which we now recall.

Choose a geometric generic point $\bar\eta$ of $S$, and let $\mathcal Y\to S$ be separated of finite type.
To define nearby cycles, we pull $\mathcal Y$ back to the integral closure of $S$ in
the chosen separable closure of its fraction field, and let $\bar i$
and $\bar j$ be the inclusions of the special fibre and of the
geometric generic fibre of this pullback.  Then, for $L$ on
$\mathcal Y_\eta$ with pullback $L_{\bar\eta}$ to the geometric generic
fibre, the geometric nearby cycles are

$$
R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}(L)=\bar i^{*}R\bar j_*L_{\bar\eta}.
$$

This defines a functor
$R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}:D^b_c(\mathcal Y_{\eta,\acute et},A)\to
D(\mathcal Y_{s,\acute et},A)$. We suppress the inertia action, except
where invariants under the wild inertia group of a finite extension of
traits are taken below.

For a morphism $g:\mathcal Y'\to\mathcal Y$ of separated
$S$-schemes of finite type, there is a base change map for pullback

$$
g_s^*R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}
\longrightarrow R\Psi_{\mathcal Y'}g_\eta^*,
$$

which is invertible for smooth $g$. For proper $g$
there is a base change map for proper direct image

$$
Rg_{s*}R\Psi_{\mathcal Y'}
\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}Rg_{\eta*}.
$$

These base change maps commute with composition and with the specialization
map defined below. Their invertibility follows from two base change
theorems for torsion coefficients. First, proper base change [Stacks, [095T](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095T)] says that restriction to a fibre commutes with proper direct image.
Second, smooth base change [Stacks, [0F09](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F09)] (for sheaves [Stacks, [0EYU](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EYU)]) says that
pullback along a smooth map commutes with direct image along a qcqs
morphism, when the coefficients are torsion of order invertible on the
base. Suppose first that $g$ is proper. The two direct images on the
generic fibres agree because direct image is compatible with composition,
and $\bar i^*$ commutes with the proper direct image by proper base
change. Suppose next that $g$ is smooth. Since $R\bar j_*$ is direct
image along a qcqs morphism, we may apply smooth base change to it and
then restrict to the special fibre. Smooth base change applies because
the coefficients are annihilated by a power of $\ell$, which is
invertible on $S$. The same base change maps appear in
[sga7-2], Exposé XIII, (2.1.7.1)–(2.1.7.3).

We also use two calculations for a finite $A$-module $M$. The first is
$R\Psi_S(M_{\eta})=M$. It holds because the integral closure
$\bar S$ of $S$ in the separable closure is strictly henselian, so the
stalk of $R\bar j_*M$ at its closed point is
$R\Gamma(\bar\eta,M)=M$. The second is the usual calculation for the
affine line with coefficients prime to the characteristic:
$H^r(\mathbf A^1_k,M)=0$ for $r>0$ and $H^0(\mathbf A^1_k,M)=M$. It
follows from [Stacks, [03RR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RR)] applied to the compactification
$\mathbf A^1\subset\mathbf P^1$, which has genus zero and one point at
infinity. To apply that result, note that every finite $M$ is a finite
direct sum of cyclic modules, and over the algebraically closed field $k$
