the cyclic constant coefficients are isomorphic to the corresponding
roots of unity.
By truncation the two calculations extend to a bounded complex
$M^\bullet$ of finite $A$-modules, viewed as a constant complex:

$$
R\Psi_S(M^\bullet_\eta)\simeq M^\bullet,
\qquad R\Gamma(\mathbf A^1_k,M^\bullet_{\mathbf A^1_k})\simeq M^\bullet.
$$

Finally, all complexes stay bounded and constructible. By the finiteness
theorem for nearby cycles with torsion coefficients ([sga4-5],
*Théorèmes de finitude*, §3; [illusie94, §4.1,
pp. 44–45]), $R\Psi_{\mathcal Y}$ takes bounded
constructible complexes of finite Tor dimension to complexes of the same
kind. Finite Tor dimension is what we need when we take traces.
The same holds for an arbitrary bounded constructible complex, without
the Tor condition. To see this, we may forget the $A$-action, since the
underlying torsion sheaves of $A$-linear nearby cycles are the usual
nearby cycles. Bounded constructible complexes are stable under
extensions and truncation, so the filtration by powers of $\ell$ reduces
us to constructible $\mathbf F_\ell$-sheaves. These have finite Tor
dimension over $\mathbf F_\ell$, and the finiteness theorem applies.

For a separated $k$-scheme $Y$ of finite type, the constant family
$Y\times S$ has special fibre $Y$. For $L$ on $Y$, let $L_\eta$ be its
pullback to the generic fibre.  Restricting the adjunction unit of
$\bar j$ on the pullback of $L$ to the special fibre, we get the
specialization map $\sigma_Y(L)$ below.

The contracting argument needs a complex on the normal cone $N_ZX$ that
still remembers $K$ near $Z$. Pulling $K|_Z$ back along the projection
$N_ZX\to Z$ is not enough, since it forgets the directions leaving $Z$.
For example, take $X=\mathbf A^1$, $Z$ the origin, and $K=j_!A$ for
$j:\mathbf A^1\setminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$. Then $K|_Z=0$,
so the pullback is zero. By contrast, the deformation to the normal cone is
$\operatorname{Spec}k[x,t,x/t]$ over the trait, that is, the constant
family $\mathbf A^1\times S$ in the coordinate $x'=x/t$, and on its
generic fibre $K$ is $j_!A$ for $x'\neq0$. Hence, by
Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family], the nearby cycles are $j_!A$ on
$N_ZX=\mathbf A^1$, which is not zero. This construction is the
specialization functor $\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}$ defined below, and by
Verdier's theorem
(Theorem [theorem-verdier-s-theorem-specialization-zero]) it still
recovers $K|_Z$ on the zero section.
Theorem [theorem-contracting-correspondences-local-terms] uses both
properties.

Let $X$ be a separated $k$-scheme of finite type, and let
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed subscheme with ideal $I$.
The deformation to its normal cone, over the chosen trait, is

$$
\mathcal D_ZX=
\operatorname{Spec}_{X\times S}
\bigl(\mathcal O_{X\times S}[I/t]\bigr).
$$

Here $\mathcal O_{X\times S}[I/t]$ is the base change to $S$ of the
subalgebra of $\mathcal O_X[t,t^{-1}]$ generated by $\mathcal O_X[t]$
and the fractions $a/t$ with $a\in I$.  Its generic fibre is $X_\eta$ and its special fibre is

$$
N_ZX=\operatorname{Spec}_Z
\left(\bigoplus_{r\geq0}I^r/I^{r+1}\right).
$$

The quotient by $I$ and all $a/t$ defines a closed immersion
$\widetilde z:Z\times S\hookrightarrow\mathcal D_ZX$, whose special
fibre $z:Z\hookrightarrow N_ZX$ is the zero section.  For $L$ on $X$,
let $L_\eta$ be its pullback to the generic fibre $X_\eta$ of
$\mathcal D_ZX$, and define the specialization functor
$\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}:D^b_c(X_{\acute et},A)\to
D^b_c((N_ZX)_{\acute et},A)$ by

$$
\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(L)=R\Psi_{\mathcal D_ZX}(L_\eta).
$$

The base change map for pullback along $\widetilde z$, followed by the
inverse of the isomorphism of Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family], defines
a natural transformation

$$
\tau_{X,Z}(L):z^*\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}(L)
\longrightarrow R\Psi_{Z\times S}((i^*L)_\eta)
\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*L.
\tag{E.1}
$$

We use this map, in this direction, to specialize trace
classes.

We will apply the base change maps for nearby cycles to the deformations
of different pairs, and for this we need to know how the deformation
depends on the pair.

Theorem [theorem-verdier-s-theorem-specialization-zero] asserts that $\tau_{X,Z}$ is an
isomorphism, that is, that the cofibre

$$
C_{X,Z}(L)=\operatorname{cofib}\bigl(
\tau_{X,Z}(L)\bigr)
$$

vanishes. As for $C_Y$, we compute the cofibre in the stable
$\infty$-category, so that $C_{X,Z}$ is an exact functor. The proof has three steps.  First, the base
change maps of the next lemma reduce us to the case $i^*L=0$ and, after
a blow-up, to the case of an effective Cartier divisor.  Then, for a
principal divisor in a normal scheme, an explicit contraction
of the affine line shows that $C_{X,Z}(L)$ vanishes at the generic points of
$Z$.  Finally, after an embedding into affine space, projection along a line and
induction on the dimension show that the remaining support is empty.

To prove the vanishing at the generic points of $Z$, we first treat a
nonreduced point on the affine line, where an explicit contraction is available.

Near a generic point of a principal divisor in a normal scheme, the
pair $(X,Z)$ is a smooth pullback of $(\mathbf A^1,V(x^m))$, so by
Lemma [lemma-case-z-v-x-m] $C_{X,Z}$ vanishes there on constant
coefficients. The next lemma extends this to all sheaves that vanish on $Z$.

On $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ we define the functor $\operatorname{Sp}_{X,Z}$ and the map
(E.1) by transport of the étale constructions
above along the comparison for constructible complexes with finite
coefficients (Theorem [theorem-comparison-constructible-sheaves]).

To specialize a trace class we have to specialize the external product
$K\boxtimes \mathbb DK$, so we need the comparison
map from the external product of nearby cycles to the nearby cycles of
the external product to be an isomorphism. We prove this on the classical
étale site by the dimension argument of
[illusie94, Theorem 4.7, pp. 51–53].

In this section and the next three, $S$ is an excellent strictly
henselian trait, as announced at the start of this appendix, with separably
closed residue field $k$, generic point $\eta$, and a chosen geometric
generic point $\bar\eta$.  Let $p$ be the characteristic exponent of
$k$.  The coefficients lie in a finite commutative $\ell$-primary ring
$A$, with $\ell$ invertible on $S$.  On the geometric fibres we use the
ordinary external Künneth formula,
Proposition [proposition-ordinary-external-kunneth]. It applies over the
separably closed field $k$, since passing to an algebraic closure is a
purely inseparable extension and does not change the étale topos.

We use two further facts about traits, both from [sga4-5],
*Théorèmes de finitude*, §§3.4 and 3.7.
First, geometric nearby cycles are invariant under extension of
traits, with the corresponding restriction of the inertia action
(loc. cit., 3.7). Second, the calculation in loc. cit., 3.4, describes
them by restriction to the generic point of a coordinate line, as follows.
Let $s'$ be a geometric generic point of the special fibre
$\mathbf A^1_k$ of $\mathbf A^1_S$, and let $S'=(\mathbf A^1_S)_{(s')}$ be
the strict localization of $\mathbf A^1_S$ at $s'$.  This is a
strictly henselian trait with the same uniformizer as $S$.  With
compatible geometric generic points, its inertia group fits into an exact sequence

$$
1\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow I'\longrightarrow I
\longrightarrow1,
$$

where $P$ is pro-$p$ (and is trivial when $p=1$).
For $a:W\to\mathbf A^1_S$, put $W'=W\times_{\mathbf A^1_S}S'$, and let $N'$ be the pullback
of $N\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(W_\eta,A)$.  There is a canonical
identification

$$
(R\Psi_{W/S}N)|_{W_s\times_{\mathbf A^1_k}s'}
\simeq (R\Psi_{W'/S'}N')^P.
\tag{E.2}
$$

Here $(-)^P=R\Gamma(P,-)$ is exact on the discrete
torsion coefficients prime to $p$ under consideration.  The formula comes
from factoring the map from the geometric generic fibre
through the geometric generic point of $S'$, which lies over
$\bar\eta$. The Galois group of the second step is $P$. It is pro-$p$
because the common uniformizer identifies the tame inertia quotients.
The formula is compatible with the base change maps for pullback and
with the product maps obtained from $\bar i^*R\bar j_*$. To see this, we
factor the maps of generic fibres in the same way and use that the
adjunctions for direct image are compatible with composition.

The functor of $P$-invariants commutes with tensoring by an object on
which $P$ acts trivially: for a complex $Q$ with
continuous $P$-action and a complex $B$ with trivial $P$-action, the
projection map is an isomorphism

$$
(Q\mathbin{\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}}B)^P
\simeq Q^P\mathbin{\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}}B.
\tag{E.3}
$$

Indeed, $P$-invariants are exact on discrete torsion
$A$-modules.  For a finite quotient $G$ of $P$, the invariants are the
image of the averaging idempotent $|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}g$, since the
$p$-power $|G|$ is invertible in $A$, and this idempotent commutes with
tensoring by $B$.  By continuity we pass from the finite quotients to
$P$, and resolving $B$ by flat $A$-modules gives the derived identity.

For $X,Y$ separated of finite type over $S$, $L$ on $X_\eta$ and $M$
on $Y_\eta$, the comparison map $\Pi_{L,M}$ below is the restriction to
the special fibre of the map

$$
R\bar j_{X*}L_{\bar\eta}\boxtimes
R\bar j_{Y*}M_{\bar\eta}
\longrightarrow
R\bar j_{X\times Y,*}(L_{\bar\eta}\boxtimes M_{\bar\eta})
$$

defined by the base change maps for pullback and the lax monoidal
structure of direct image.

The proof has the same shape as that of
Lemma [lemma-nearby-cycles-constant-family]: the cone of $\Pi_{L,M}$
has no global sections and finite support, so it vanishes.
When $X$ and $Y$ are projective, the ordinary Künneth formula on the
geometric generic fibres gives zero global sections, once we
know how $\Pi$ behaves under proper direct image. Restricting to
the generic point of a coordinate line by
(E.2) lowers the dimension of the generic fibre,
and induction on the dimension shows that the support is
finite. The next four lemmas supply these ingredients.

A complex supported on finitely many closed points is determined by its
stalks at these points, and we can read off these stalks from global
sections.

To restrict to coordinate lines we need coordinates in which the
special fibre is quasi-finite over an affine space of the right
dimension.

In the slicing step we compare $\Pi$ with the Künneth map over the
trait $S'$ of (E.2). Let $X,Y$ be separated of
finite type over $S$, let $b:X\to\mathbf A^1_S$ be a morphism, and
put

$$
X'=X\times_{\mathbf A^1_S}S',\qquad Y'=Y\times_S S',\qquad
L'=L|_{X'_{\eta'}},\quad M'=M|_{Y'_{\eta'}}.
$$

Let $c$ be a correspondence over the trait $S$ and $u$ a cohomological
correspondence on its generic fibre. Nearby cycles turn $u$ into a map
between $\Psi$ of $c_2^*K$ and $\Psi$ of $c_1^!K$. To obtain a
cohomological correspondence $u_s$ on the special fibre, we must move
$\Psi$ past $c_2^*$ and $c_1^!$. This needs base change maps between
nearby cycles and the operations $f^*$, $Rf_*$, $Rf_!$ and $f^!$. We
make these maps explicit here. We also prove the identities between them
that Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class] uses to
show that the trace of $u_s$ is the specialization of the trace of $u$.

We write
$\Psi_X=R\Psi_{X/S}$ for a separated $S$-scheme $X$ of finite type.
For a morphism $f:V\to W$ of separated $S$-schemes of finite type, put

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
\alpha_f:f_s^*\Psi_W&\longrightarrow&\Psi_Vf_\eta^*,\\
\chi_f:\Psi_WRf_{\eta*}&\longrightarrow&Rf_{s*}\Psi_V,\\
\nu_f:Rf_{s!}\Psi_V&\longrightarrow&\Psi_WRf_{\eta!},\\
\beta_f:\Psi_Vf_\eta^!&\longrightarrow&f_s^!\Psi_W.
\end{array}
$$

The map $\alpha_f$ is the base change map for pullback of $\bar i^*R\bar j_*$, and
$\chi_f$ is its adjoint mate for $f_s^*\dashv Rf_{s*}$ and
$f_\eta^*\dashv Rf_{\eta*}$.

To define $\nu_f$, we choose a
relative Nagata compactification $f=ph$, with
$h:V\hookrightarrow\overline V$ open and $p$ proper.
We define $\nu_h:h_{s!}\Psi_VM\to \Psi_{\overline V}h_{\eta!}M$ using the
adjunction for the open immersion, by requiring that its adjoint be

$$
\Psi_VM=\Psi_Vh_\eta^*h_{\eta!}M
\xrightarrow{\alpha_h^{-1}}h_s^*\Psi_{\overline V}h_{\eta!}M.
$$

Since $p$ is proper, $\chi_p$ is invertible, and we put
$\nu_f=\chi_p^{-1}\,Rp_{s*}(\nu_h)$, using
$Rf_{s!}=Rp_{s*}h_{s!}$ and $Rf_{\eta!}=Rp_{\eta*}h_{\eta!}$.
The map $\nu_f$ does not depend on the compactification. Indeed, if $q$ is a common
proper refinement of two
compactifications, proper base change identifies $Rq_*h'_!$ with
$h_!$ on both fibres. After taking adjoints for the open immersions,
compatibility with this identification reduces to the composition rule
for $\alpha$ and the triangle identity of the ordinary adjunction.
Common refinements also show that $\nu$ is compatible with
composition.

We can also describe $\nu_f$ on the total families. Write $i_V$ and
$j_V$ for the inclusions $\bar i$ and $\bar j$ of the special and
geometric generic fibres of $V$, so that $\Psi_V=i_V^*Rj_{V*}$. By proper
base change, $i_W^*Rf_!\simeq Rf_{s!}i_V^*$ and
$j_W^*Rf_!\simeq Rf_{\eta!}j_V^*$. Consider the map
$Rf_!Rj_{V*}\to Rj_{W*}Rf_{\eta!}$ whose $j_W^*$-adjoint is

$$
j_W^*Rf_!Rj_{V*}\simeq Rf_{\eta!}j_V^*Rj_{V*}
\xrightarrow{Rf_{\eta!}\varepsilon_{j_V}}Rf_{\eta!}
$$

Its restriction by $i_W^*$ is a map $Rf_{s!}\Psi_V\to \Psi_WRf_{\eta!}$,
and we claim that this map is $\nu_f$. As both constructions are
compatible with composition, it suffices to check this for $p$ and for $h$. For proper $p$ the
restricted map is $\chi_p^{-1}$, by proper base change for $i_W^*$.
For the open immersion $h$ we have $h_\eta^*h_{\eta!}=1$, and the
$h_s^*$-adjoint of the restricted map is $\alpha_h^{-1}$, as in the
definition of $\nu_h$.

The map $\beta_f(M)$ is the adjoint, for $Rf_{s!}\dashv f_s^!$, of

$$
Rf_{s!}\Psi_Vf_\eta^!M\xrightarrow{\nu_f}
\Psi_WRf_{\eta!}f_\eta^!M
\xrightarrow{\Psi_W\varepsilon_{f_\eta}}\Psi_WM.
\tag{E.6}
$$

For proper $f$, the maps $\chi_f$ and $\nu_f$ are inverse isomorphisms
after the identification $Rf_*=Rf_!$.

The lax monoidal map
$\mu_Y:\Psi_YM\otimes^{\mathbf L} \Psi_YN\to \Psi_Y(M\otimes^{\mathbf L} N)$ of $R\bar j_*$ is adjoint to the
tensor product of the two counits $j^*Rj_*\to1$. It is associative,
symmetric and unital, with unit $\sigma_Y:A_{Y_s}\to \Psi_YA_{Y_\eta}$,
and $\alpha_f$ is monoidal. For $f:V\to W$ and $g:W\to Y$, we have

$$
\alpha_{gf}=\alpha_f(g_\eta^*)f_s^*\alpha_g,
\qquad \sigma_V=\alpha_f(A)f_s^*\sigma_W,
\qquad\mu(\sigma\otimes1)=1.
\tag{E.7}
$$

For the structure morphism $a_Y:Y\to S$, set
$\theta_Y=\beta_{a_Y}(A):\Psi_Y\omega_{Y_\eta}\to\omega_{Y_s}$,
using $\Psi_SA=A$.

The proof of Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class] moves the
base change maps past the projection formula, composition, external
duality and the cartesian square defining the fixed point scheme.
The following four lemmas give the identities it needs. Each is proved by
taking adjoints until both sides become the same composite of base
change maps and counits, and then using the composition laws for the
base change maps and for the counits. For a morphism $f$ on either
fibre, write $t_f:f^!M\otimes^{\mathbf L} f^*N\to f^!(M\otimes^{\mathbf L} N)$
for the projection-formula mate of the exceptional counit.

Let $p_1,p_2$ be the projections of $X\times_SX$. On either
fibre, let $\xi:p_2^*\omega_X\to p_1^!A_X$ be the isomorphism of
Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism] for $K=A_X$, and for a complex $M$ put
$\kappa_M=t_{p_1}(\xi\otimes1):p_2^*\omega_X\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_1^*M\to p_1^!M$, where
$t_{p_1}:p_1^!A_X\otimes^{\mathbf L} p_1^*M\to p_1^!M$ is the projection-formula mate of
the exceptional counit.

The next identity says that, under the base change maps, the map
$\kappa_M$ of external duality on the generic fibre corresponds to
$\kappa_{\Psi_XM}$ on the special fibre, up to $\theta_X$.

For the last identity, let $c:C\to X\times_SX$ be a correspondence of
separated $S$-schemes of finite type, with fixed scheme $F$, closed
immersion $i:F\hookrightarrow C$, map $d:F\to X$, and closed diagonal
$\Delta:X\hookrightarrow X\times_SX$, so that $F=C\times_{X\times X}X$.
Let $\zeta:c^!R\Delta_*\xrightarrow\sim Ri_*d^!$ be the base change
isomorphism for exceptional inverse image and proper direct image in
this cartesian square, on either fibre.

Since the second factor of $K\boxtimes \mathbb DK$ is a Verdier dual,
specializing a trace class also requires nearby cycles to commute with
Verdier duality, by an explicit map $\delta_{X,M}$ defined below
[illusie94, Theorem 4.2].

The trait $S$ and the coefficient ring $A$ are those of
Proposition [proposition-external-kunneth-formula-nearby-cycles], and
$\mathbb D_{X_{\bar\eta}}$ and $\mathbb D_{X_s}$ are the Verdier duals
relative to the geometric generic point $\bar\eta$ and the closed
point $s$ of $S$. We work on the classical étale site and transport
the result to the pro-étale site at the end.

We use the base change maps $\chi_f$, $\nu_f$, $\beta_f$, the lax monoidal
map $\mu_X$ and the map $\theta_X:\Psi_X\omega_{X_\eta}\to\omega_{X_s}$ of
the preceding section.  Recall that $\beta_f$ is the adjoint, for $Rf_{s!}\dashv f_s^!$, of
(E.6) and that $\nu_f=\chi_f^{-1}$ for proper $f$.
For $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_\eta,A)$, define the morphism
$\delta_{X,M}:\Psi_X\mathbb D_{X_\eta}M\to\mathbb D_{X_s}(\Psi_XM)$
as the tensor–Hom adjoint of the pairing

$$
\Psi_XM\otimes \Psi_X\mathbb D_{X_\eta}M
\xrightarrow{\mu_X}\Psi_X(M\otimes \mathbb D_{X_\eta}M)
\xrightarrow{\Psi_X\operatorname{ev}}\Psi_X\omega_{X_\eta}
\xrightarrow{\theta_X}\omega_{X_s}.
\tag{E.12}
$$

The argument is the one used for
Proposition [proposition-external-kunneth-formula-nearby-cycles].
As there, on a projective $X$ global duality shows that the cone of
$\delta$ has zero cohomology on $X_s$. Restriction to the generic point
of a coordinate line (E.2) and induction on
dimension show that the cone has finite support. For this we need two
compatibilities of $\delta$: with proper direct image, and with
restriction to the generic point of a coordinate line. In the second we
keep track of the twist $A(1)[2]$ on both fibres.

For the slice we need that taking invariants under the pro-$p$ group $P$
of (E.2) commutes with duality.

We fix the notation for the slice. Let $b:X\to\mathbf A^1_S$ be a
coordinate map and let $S'=(\mathbf A^1_S)_{(s')}$ be the trait at the
generic point of the special fibre used in
(E.2).  Set
$X'=X\times_{\mathbf A^1_S}S'$, $M'=M|_{X'_{\bar\eta'}}$, and write
$g_s,g_\eta$ for the two pullbacks to the geometric generic point of
the coordinate line.  Restriction to the geometric generic point of the
coordinate line is compatible with internal Hom, and
Lemma [lemma-restriction-geometric-generic-fibre] and
Lemma [lemma-double-dual-geometric-generic-fibre], applied on each
geometric fibre, give, locally on $X$, isomorphisms

$$
g_\eta^*\mathbb D_{X_{\bar\eta}}M\simeq \mathbb D_{X'_{\bar\eta'}}M'\otimes A(1)[2],
\qquad
g_s^*\mathbb D_{X_s}L\simeq \mathbb D_{X'_{s'}}(g_s^*L)\otimes A(1)[2]
\tag{E.16}
$$

for $L\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_s,A)$. The twist comes from the
dualizing complexes. For a closed embedding over $\mathbf A^1$
into $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1}$, smooth purity gives $A(r+1)[2r+2]$
before generic restriction and $A(r)[2r]$ after it. Moreover, the comparison of the complexes with closed support for the embedding preserves
evaluation. Thus on $\mathbf A^r_{\mathbf A^1_S}$ the identifications of
the dualizing complexes before and after slicing differ by $A(1)[2]$ on
both fibres. Finally, the group $P$ acts trivially on $A(1)[2]$, because roots of
unity of order prime to the residue characteristic lift over a strictly
henselian trait. So the twist commutes with taking $P$-invariants.

In a continuous family of maps of a compact manifold, the Lefschetz
number does not change. The algebraic counterpart is the following
proposition: the trace class of the specialized correspondence $u_s$ is the
specialization $\operatorname{sp}_F$ of the trace class of $u$. Here
$\operatorname{sp}_F$ is a map of sections of dualizing complexes on the
fixed scheme. A trace class is
built from three pieces: the cohomological correspondence $u$, the
external product $K\boxtimes\mathbb DK$ in which $u$ becomes a section,
and the evaluation map along the diagonal to the dualizing complex.
Nearby cycles commute with each piece. They commute with external products
by Proposition [proposition-external-kunneth-formula-nearby-cycles], with Verdier duality
by Proposition [proposition-nearby-cycles-commute-verdier-duality], and with the four
operations through the base change maps of Section [sec-Base-change-for-nearby-cycles].
We prove the proposition by putting these compatibilities together.
Theorem [theorem-contracting-correspondences-local-terms] uses it to
transfer the computation to the normal cone. For this it also needs
Corollary [corollary-specialization-when-fixed-point-scheme]:
$\operatorname{sp}_F$ is the identity when the fixed scheme is, up to
nilpotents, a constant family $Y\times S$.

Neither properness of the legs $c_1,c_2$ nor smoothness of $F$ is
assumed. This matters, because we apply the proposition to the
deformation of a correspondence to the normal cone. Its generic fibre is
the original correspondence, but its fixed scheme, which we describe in
Lemma [lemma-fixed-point-scheme-deformation] of
Section [sec-Contracting-correspondences], may be singular and nonreduced.

A trace class has two ingredients besides $u$: the external duality
isomorphism, which turns $u$ into a section of
$c^!(K\boxtimes\mathbb DK)$, and the evaluation along the diagonal. In
the proof we compare both once and for all on $X\times_SX$, for the
universal kernel $K\boxtimes\mathbb DK$, and then pull the comparison
back along $c$. After taking adjoints, each comparison reduces to the
pairing (E.12) that defines $\delta_K$.

We fix the maps. In the setting of
Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class], let
$P_X=K\boxtimes\mathbb DK$ be the external product of
Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism].  The comparison map for
external products is

$$
\Pi_{M,N}=\mu(\alpha_{p_1}\otimes\alpha_{p_2}):
\Psi_XM\boxtimes \Psi_XN\longrightarrow \Psi_{X\times_SX}(M\boxtimes N),
$$

and it is invertible by
Proposition [proposition-external-kunneth-formula-nearby-cycles].
Using it and the isomorphism $\delta_K=\delta_{X,K}$ of
Proposition [proposition-nearby-cycles-commute-verdier-duality],
we define the isomorphism

$$
\rho:\Psi_{X\times_SX}P_X\xrightarrow{\Pi_{K,\mathbb DK}^{-1}}
K'\boxtimes \Psi_X\mathbb DK\xrightarrow{1\boxtimes\delta_K}K'\boxtimes\mathbb DK'.
$$

Write $\lambda_K:P_X\xrightarrow\sim
\cHom_A(p_2^*K,p_1^!K)$ for the external duality isomorphism of
Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism], and
$e_K:P_X\to R\Delta_*\omega_X$ for the evaluation along the diagonal
(Definition [definition-trace-morphism]). Let

$$
\mathfrak h:\Psi_{X\times_SX}\cHom_A(p_2^*K,p_1^!K)\longrightarrow
\cHom_A(p_{2s}^*K',p_{1s}^!K')
$$

be the comparison obtained from the tensor–Hom mate of
$\Psi(\operatorname{ev})\mu$ by precomposing with $\alpha_{p_2}$
and postcomposing with $\beta_{p_1}$. For the correspondence $c$, let
$\lambda_{c,K}:c^!P_X\xrightarrow\sim\cHom_A(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$ be the
external duality isomorphism on $C$, and define $\mathfrak h_c$ as
$\mathfrak h$, with $\alpha_{c_2}$ and $\beta_{c_1}$ in place of
$\alpha_{p_2}$ and $\beta_{p_1}$.

By pulling the first identity back along $c$, we compute the section of
$c_s^!P_{X_s}$ that corresponds to $u_s$.

The proposition is useful only if $\operatorname{sp}_F$ loses no
information. In the situation of the contracting argument the fixed
scheme does not move in the family, and then specialization is the
identity.

Let $c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$ be a correspondence, and let
$Z\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed subscheme. Suppose that the leg $c_2$,
along which we take ordinary pullback, contracts towards $Z$ faster
than $c_1$, as measured by powers of ideals. Then the trace class near
a connected component of the fixed point scheme meeting $Z$ can be
computed by restricting the correspondence to $Z$. With our convention
$u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ for the legs, the leg that contracts is $c_2$; in
[varshavsky05] it is the first leg.

The contraction becomes geometric on the deformation to the normal cone
(Lemma [lemma-normal-cones-contracting-ideals] below). Let $I$ be the ideal
of $Z$ and $I_i=c_i^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_C$. Under the hypothesis
$I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$, the special fibre of $c_2$ maps into the zero
section, while the inverse image of the zero section under $c_1$ is the
zero section. On the special fibre the trace class therefore only sees $Z$.

As in Proposition [proposition-specialization-trace-class], write $F=\Fix(c)$ for
the fixed scheme, and let $d=c_1|_F=c_2|_F:F\to X$ be the common map.
We will show that a connected component of $F$ that meets $Z$ lies in
$Z$ set-theoretically, and that the deformed fixed scheme is constant up
to nilpotents. Both follow from the hypothesis $I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}$,
because the two legs agree on $F$.

The deformation of $F$ to the normal cone of $d^{-1}(Z)$ embeds in the
fixed scheme of the deformed correspondence. Put $I_F=d^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_F$, so
that $d^{-1}(Z)=V(I_F)$. Since $d=c_1|_F$, the ideal $I_F^r$ is the
image of $I_1^r$ in $\mathcal O_F$ for every $r$. Hence the closed
immersion $F\hookrightarrow C$ induces a surjection of deformation
algebras

$$
\mathcal O_{C_T}[I_1/t]\twoheadrightarrow
\mathcal O_{F_T}[I_F/t],
$$

that is, a closed immersion
$\mathcal D_{d^{-1}(Z)}F\hookrightarrow\mathcal D_{Z'}C$. Its two
composites with $\widetilde c_1$ and $\widetilde c_2$ are the maps
induced by $c_1|_F$ and $c_2|_F$, which are equal. So it factors through
the fixed scheme $\widetilde F=\Fix(\widetilde c)$ of
$\widetilde c=(\widetilde c_1,\widetilde c_2)$. We write

$$
\iota_F:\mathcal D_{d^{-1}(Z)}F\longrightarrow\widetilde F
\tag{E.20}
$$

for the resulting closed immersion.

Up to nilpotents, then, the fixed scheme of the deformed
correspondence is the constant family $F_T$. This is why the
specialization of trace classes can be inverted in the proof of
Theorem [theorem-contracting-correspondences-local-terms].
The hypothesis that $F$ is connected and meets $Z$ is needed. For instance, in
Example [example-contracting-squaring], the component $F=\{0\}$
gives the constant family $x'=0$, but the fixed point $x=1$ does not meet
$Z$, and there the deformation gives only the generic-fibre point
$x'=1/t$, not the constant family $\{1\}_T$.

The proof of the main theorem combines the two lemmas on the
deformation with Verdier's theorem and with the specialization of trace
classes. The statement of the main theorem involves the restriction of a correspondence to
$Z$, which we construct first.

Let $c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$ be a correspondence, let
$Z\hookrightarrow X$ have ideal $I$, and suppose that
$c_2^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_C\subset c_1^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_C$. Then
$c_1^{-1}(Z)\subset c_2^{-1}(Z)$. As before
Lemma [lemma-lift-correspondence-invariant-decomposition], we put

$$
C_Z=(c_1^{-1}Z)_{\mathrm{red}},\qquad
c_Z=(c_{Z,1},c_{Z,2}):C_Z\longrightarrow Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times Z_{\mathrm{red}},
$$

with $i:Z_{\mathrm{red}}\hookrightarrow X$ and
$i':C_Z\hookrightarrow C$. For $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ put $K_Z=i^*K$. The
square formed by $i'$, $i$, $c_1$ and $c_{Z,1}$ is cartesian up to
reduction. Hence invariance under nilpotent thickenings and base
change for direct image with compact support give
$i^*Rc_{1!}\simeq Rc_{Z,1!}i'^*$. Since the second leg maps $C_Z$ into
$Z_{\mathrm{red}}$, we also have $i'^*c_2^*K\simeq c_{Z,2}^*K_Z$. For a
cohomological correspondence $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ with adjoint
$\widehat u:Rc_{1!}c_2^*K\to K$ under $Rc_{1!}\dashv c_1^!$, the
*restriction* $u_Z:c_{Z,2}^*K_Z\to c_{Z,1}^!K_Z$ of $u$ to $Z$ is the
adjoint under $Rc_{Z,1!}\dashv c_{Z,1}^!$ of

$$
Rc_{Z,1!}c_{Z,2}^*K_Z
\simeq i^*Rc_{1!}c_2^*K
\xrightarrow{i^*\widehat u}K_Z.
\tag{E.21}
$$

Equivalently, $u_Z$ is $i'^*u$ followed by the base change map
$i'^*c_1^!K\to c_{Z,1}^!K_Z$, which in general is not an
isomorphism. This is the restriction to $Z$ that occurs in
Lemma [lemma-closed-piece-pushforward]. If $F_0$ is an open and
closed subscheme of $\Fix(c)$, put $F_{0,Z}=\Fix(c_Z)\times_{\Fix(c)}F_0$,
and let $h_{F_0}:F_{0,Z}\to F_0$ be the projection.

For $Z$ a point, the theorem specializes to
Corollary [corollary-contracting-local-terms-point]. Under its
hypotheses the local term at $F_0$ is the categorical trace of $u_Z$.
For $c=(\mathrm{id}_X,h)$ this is
$\operatorname{tr}(u_{\bar y}\mid K_{\bar y})$.

If $Z$ is a point, the restricted correspondence is a correspondence of
the point, and the theorem computes the local term as a trace on a
stalk.
Here $X$ may be singular.

Rankin's argument (Chapter [chap-Purity-of-real-sheaves]) bounds the
eigenvalues of a real sheaf by the largest determinant weight of its
constituents, that is, the weight of the determinant divided by the rank.
For this it needs the determinant weights of the factors of tensor and
exterior powers of a lisse sheaf
(Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations]),
before anyone knows how these powers decompose. The tool is an element
of the arithmetic monodromy group, of positive degree, that acts by a
scalar on each simple factor of every tensor construction. This scalar
then gives the determinant weight.

In a simple example Frobenius itself does this. Take
$V=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\oplus\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)$ on a curve over $\mathbf F_q$, on which a Frobenius
element $s$ of degree one acts by $\operatorname{diag}(1,q)$. Here the
geometric monodromy is trivial, so the arithmetic monodromy group $G$ is
the torus $\{\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\}$, and $\rho(s)$ is central in
it. Hence on every tensor construction $\rho(s)$ acts by a scalar on each
simple factor. For instance, it acts by $1$ and $q$ on the factors of
$V$, of weights $0$ and $2$, and by $q$ on $\bigwedge^2V$.

In general $\rho(s)$ is not central, and we must correct a power of it
by an element of the geometric monodromy group $H$. An element of $H$
alone would not do, since its determinants on these factors are roots of
unity. What we want instead is a central element of the form $h\rho(s)^N$ with
$h\in H$ and $N>0$.

Such an element exists by Lemma [lemma-identity-component]. For a
semisimple Weil representation $V$, the identity component $G^\circ$ is
generated by $Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ and the identity component $H^\circ$.
So a power of Frobenius lying in $G^\circ$ is an element of
$Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ times an element of $H^\circ$. Averaging over the
components of $G$ then makes it central in $G$. This is the algebraic
form of a familiar fact about compact Lie groups: a connected compact
group is the product of the identity component of its center and its
derived group.

For algebraic groups over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ we argue with the Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$ of $G^\circ$. Since $\mathfrak g$ acts faithfully and
semisimply on $V$, it is reductive, that is,

$$
\mathfrak g=Z(\mathfrak g)+[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]
$$

(Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation]).
The derived algebra lies in the Lie algebra of $H$, because commutators
of $G$ lie in $H$. It remains to use that a closed connected subgroup of
$G^\circ$ with the full Lie algebra is all of $G^\circ$.

The tools behind this argument need characteristic zero. Cartier's
theorem that algebraic groups are smooth
(Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem]) lets us recognize a
closed subgroup by its Lie algebra; this fails for
$\mu_p\subset\mathbf G_m$ in characteristic $p$. Similarly, the decomposition of $\mathfrak g$ rests on Cartan's criterion, which fails there too. Since
the monodromy groups are defined over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, this does not restrict
us. For the theorems of Lie, Engel and Cartan we refer to
Humphreys [humphreys72].

Throughout, $\Omega$ is an algebraically closed
field of characteristic zero, and all Lie algebras and representations
are finite-dimensional. By an algebraic group we mean a group scheme of finite
type over $\Omega$. In particular, stabilizers and centralizers are taken as subgroup
schemes, and by Cartier's theorem below they are smooth. The Lie algebra
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ of an algebraic group $G$ is its tangent space
at the identity; for a closed subgroup of $\GL(V)$ we describe it by
dual numbers in Section [sec-Lie-algebras].

To pass from Lie algebras back to groups we use the following
principle: a closed subgroup of a connected group $G$ with the same Lie
algebra is all of $G$ (Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms]). For reduced groups this
is a dimension count: the dimension of a smooth group equals that
of its tangent space at $1$, and a closed subset of the irreducible
variety $G$ of the same dimension is all of $G$. The difficulty is that
stabilizers and centralizers are defined by equations and need not be
reduced. For example, in characteristic $p$, the subgroup $\mu_p\subset\mathbf G_m$
defined by $x^p=1$ is a single nonreduced point with tangent space
$\operatorname{Lie}(\mathbf G_m)$, and the principle fails. However, Cartier's
theorem (Proposition [proposition-cartier-s-theorem]) shows that this cannot
happen in characteristic zero: every algebraic group is smooth. In the
proof we apply the comultiplication to a nilpotent function at the
identity and divide by an integer, and this division is where we use
characteristic zero. The facts about connected components and images of
homomorphisms in Lemma [lemma-connected-components-images-homomorphisms] are standard
consequences of smoothness and of Chevalley's theorem.

Since algebraic groups over $\Omega$ are smooth, their topology is as
simple as that of a Lie group: irreducible and connected components
coincide, and the dimension of a closed subgroup can be computed from
its Lie algebra.

Let $G$ be a connected algebraic group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.
We need two facts (Lemma [lemma-stable-subspaces-center]). First, in a
representation, $G$ and $\mathfrak g$ have the same stable subspaces.
Second, the Lie algebra of the identity component of the center of $G$ is
the center of $\mathfrak g$. In the proof of
Lemma [lemma-identity-component] we compare the monodromy groups
through their Lie algebras, and both facts are used there. By the
first, a representation that is semisimple for $G^\circ$ is semisimple
for its Lie algebra. This is what lets
Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation]
apply to the Weil representation. With the second we translate the
decomposition of the Lie algebra into the identity
$G^\circ=Z(G^\circ)^\circ H^\circ$.

We prove both facts by the principle of the previous section, applied
to a stabilizer and to the kernel of the adjoint representation. Their
Lie algebras are computed with dual numbers. The first fact needs $G$ to
be connected. For example, the finite group $\{\pm1\}\subset\GL_1$ has
zero Lie algebra, so every subspace of a representation is stable under
its Lie algebra. But if $-1$ acts on $M=\Omega^2$ by
$\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, then it does not stabilize the line spanned
by $(1,1)$.

For a closed subgroup $G\subseteq\GL(V)$, the tangent space
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ is described by
dual-number points at $1$:

$$
X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
1+\varepsilon X\in G(\Omega[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2).
$$

The bracket is $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. To see that $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is
closed under the bracket, note that over
$\Omega[\varepsilon,\eta]/(\varepsilon^2,\eta^2)$ the commutator of
$1+\varepsilon X$ and $1+\eta Y$ is $1+\varepsilon\eta[X,Y]$. Its entries
lie in the subring $\Omega[\varepsilon\eta]$, which is a ring of dual numbers.
The equations of $G$ hold for this matrix in the larger ring, hence in
this subring. Therefore $[X,Y]\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. The
differential of a representation $r:G\to\GL(M)$ is characterized
by

$$
r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X).
$$

Applying $r$ to the commutator of $1+\varepsilon X$ and $1+\eta Y$, we see
that $dr[X,Y]=[dr(X),dr(Y)]$, so $dr$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism.

The decomposition $\mathfrak l=Z(\mathfrak l)+[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak l]$
fails for Lie algebras in general. Consider the algebra $\mathfrak b$ of
upper triangular $2\times2$ matrices. Its center consists of the scalars,
and $[\mathfrak b,\mathfrak b]$ consists of the strictly upper triangular
matrices. So their sum has dimension two and misses
$\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$. Here $\mathfrak b$ is solvable and is its own
radical, much larger than its center. Its standard representation on
$\Omega^2$ is faithful but not semisimple, since the line $\Omega e_1$
has no stable complement. In general the obstruction is the radical,
that is, the largest solvable ideal. In
Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation] we show that a faithful
semisimple representation forces the radical to be central. This
gives the decomposition.

The derived series of a Lie algebra is
$D^0\mathfrak l=\mathfrak l$,
$D^{n+1}\mathfrak l=[D^n\mathfrak l,D^n\mathfrak l]$, and
$\mathfrak l$ is solvable if this series reaches zero.
The radical $\operatorname{rad}\mathfrak l$ is the sum of all solvable
ideals of $\mathfrak l$. To see that it is itself solvable, note that an extension of solvable Lie algebras is
solvable. Indeed, if the quotient of $\mathfrak l$ by a solvable ideal is
solvable, the derived series of $\mathfrak l$ lies in that ideal after
finitely many steps, and then reaches zero. Hence the sum of two
solvable ideals is solvable, and $\operatorname{rad}\mathfrak l$ is the
largest solvable ideal of $\mathfrak l$ [humphreys72, §3.1]. From the same book we use
three classical theorems, and we only sketch their
proofs.

See [humphreys72, §4.1]. By induction one finds a common
eigenvector for an ideal of codimension one, and then shows by a trace
computation, which we redo in the proof of
Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation], that the corresponding
eigenspace is stable under the remaining direction.

This is Engel's theorem in its matrix form [humphreys72, §3.3]. The
first assertion is proved by induction on $\dim\mathfrak n$, using that
a maximal proper subalgebra is an ideal of codimension one. The
triangular basis then follows by induction on $\dim M$.

See [humphreys72, §4.3]. It suffices to show that every element $X$
of $[\mathfrak a,\mathfrak a]$ is nilpotent. Then
$[\mathfrak a,\mathfrak a]$ is solvable by
Lemma [lemma-engel-s-theorem], and hence so is $\mathfrak a$.
To see that $X$ is nilpotent, one pairs $X$ with operators that are
polynomials in its semisimple part. Let $\lambda_i$ be the eigenvalues
of the semisimple part, and let $f$ be a $\mathbf Q$-linear functional
on their $\mathbf Q$-span with values in $\mathbf Q$. The hypothesis
gives $\sum_i\lambda_i f(\lambda_i)=0$. Applying $f$ to this identity
gives $\sum_i f(\lambda_i)^2=0$. This is a vanishing sum of squares of
rational numbers, so $f$ vanishes on all $\lambda_i$, and $f=0$. As
$f$ was arbitrary, all $\lambda_i$ are zero. This step is where we
use characteristic zero.

For $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ the decomposition into scalars and trace-zero
matrices, $\mathfrak{gl}_n=\Omega\cdot1\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_n$, has the form
$\mathfrak l=Z(\mathfrak l)+[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak l]$. We prove this
decomposition for every Lie algebra with a faithful semisimple representation
(Proposition [proposition-lie-algebras-faithful-semisimple-representation]),
as Lemma [lemma-identity-component] requires. The proof has two
steps. First, the radical acts by scalars on each simple summand. To see
this, we take a common eigenvector given by Lie's theorem. A trace
computation, in which we divide by the dimension of a subspace, shows
that its eigenspace is stable under all of $\mathfrak l$. Since the
representation is faithful, the radical is then central.
Second, the quotient by the center has zero radical. For such a Lie
algebra the Killing form is nondegenerate by Cartan's criterion. This
forces the algebra to equal its derived algebra
(Lemma [lemma-killing]). The upper triangular
algebra $\mathfrak b$ of the previous section shows that the
hypothesis of semisimplicity cannot be dropped.

This is the semisimplicity criterion of [humphreys72, §§5.1–5.2]; we
include the short deduction from Cartan's criterion.

For $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, with basis $e,h,f$, the brackets $[h,e]=2e$,
$[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$ already show that $[\mathfrak{sl}_2,\mathfrak{sl}_2]=\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
The lemma gives the second half of the next proposition, once we know
that the quotient by the center has zero radical.

On the étale site the constant sheaf $\mathbf Z_\ell$ on
$\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q$ has $H^1=0$, although
$\varprojlim_nH^1(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q,\mathbf Z/\ell^n)=\mathbf Z_\ell$
(Section [sec-Weil-cohomology]). Moreover, Frobenius eigenvalues live in
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, but SGA 4 constructs $Rf_!$ and $f^!$ and proves the finiteness
theorems only for $\mathbf Z/\ell^n$ [sga4], [sga4-5]. So the theory we need is not the one SGA 4 provides. This part has to
overcome two difficulties. The first concerns the coefficients: we must pass
to the limit over $n$ without losing cohomology.
Classically one does this with systems $(F_n)$ and makes every derived
construction by hand [ekedahl90]. We work instead on the pro-étale site
of Bhatt and Scholze (Chapter [chap-The-pro-etale-site]). There $\mathbf Z_\ell$ is a sheaf
of rings with the expected cohomology, and one definition serves all the
coefficient rings

$$
A,\ \mathbf Z_\ell,\ \mathcal O_E,\ \mathbf Q_\ell,\ E,\ \overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell,
$$

compatibly with every change of coefficients between them
(Section [sec-Change-of-coefficients]).

What the rest of the notes needs from this part is the table of
Section [sec-The-function-sheaf-dictionary]: for every morphism $f$ of schemes of finite
type over $k$, the operations $f^*$, $Rf_*$, $Rf_!$, $f^!$,
$\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ and $\cHom$, with their adjunctions, base change and
projection formulas, and the finiteness statement that each carries
constructible complexes to constructible complexes
(Theorem [theorem-exceptional-inverse-image] and
Proposition [proposition-six-operations-dctf]). The later parts use these
operations as their basic tools. For example, the trace formula of
Part II sums trace functions over the fibres of $f$ by
applying $Rf_!$, and Poincaré duality comes from the computation of
$f^!\Lambda$ for the structure morphism $f$ of a smooth variety. Similarly,
the Fourier transform of Part III is built from $f^*$,
$\otimes^{\mathbf L}$ and $Rf_!$.

The second difficulty is to show that $f^!$ preserves constructible
complexes, and it would be there even with finite coefficients. It arises
because $f^!$ is given only by its universal property, and already for a
closed immersion $i$ with open complement $j$ its value is not obvious: we know only that $i^!K$
sits in a triangle $i^!K\to i^*K\to i^*Rj_*j^*K$. To see that it is
constructible we need to know that $Rj_*$ preserves constructibility, and this
is Deligne's generic base change theorem. Accordingly, we construct $f^!$ in
Chapter [chap-Construction-of-f] and prove that it preserves
constructible complexes in Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f], as
sketched in Section [sec-The-six-operations].

The two difficulties are handled separately, so that each geometric
argument is made only once. The geometric inputs, namely proper base change
(Chapter [chap-Proper-base-change]) and the computation of $f^!$ on
charts (Chapter [chap-Constructibility-of-f]), are proved with
torsion coefficients on the étale site, where SGA 4 applies. They are then
transferred to $\ell$-adic coefficients without being proved again. Two
facts make this transfer possible
(Chapters [chap-Constructible-complexes]
and [chap-The-six-operations-on-Dbctf]). First, a constructible complex over
$\mathcal O_E$ is determined by its reductions modulo $\pi_E^n$
(Proposition [proposition-integral-constructibility-criterion]), so its
properties can be read off from torsion complexes. Second, whether a natural
map between two such constructions is an isomorphism can be checked with
finite coefficients
(Proposition [proposition-isomorphisms-reduce-finite-coefficients]). For
example, smooth base change for $\mathbf Z_\ell$, $E$ and $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ follows from smooth
base change for finite rings in this way (Section [sec-ell-adic-coefficients-3]).

At the end of Part I we have, for every separated
$X_0$ of finite type over $\mathbf F_q$, cohomology groups $H^i_c$ with an
action of Frobenius, and they are finite because $Rf_!$ preserves $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$.
Nothing yet connects them with the numbers $\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ of which
the zeta function is made. This part supplies the connection: Weil's axioms
(b) and (c), the trace formula and Poincaré duality, and with them
rationality and the functional equation (Section [sec-Rationality-and-the-functional-equation]).

For the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbf F_3$ these two axioms,
together with the single count $N_1=4$, determine the zeta function and
every $N_m$ (Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula],
Example [example-running-example-trace-formula]).

Both axioms are statements about the diagonal. For example, on a compact
oriented manifold $M$, the Künneth components of the class of the diagonal
in $H^*(M\times M)$ form the copairing inverse to the cup product pairing,
and the Lefschetz number of a map $\varphi$ is the intersection number of
its graph with the diagonal. A scheme, however, comes with no orientation
and no class of the diagonal, and smooth purity is what provides them. It
says that
$f^!\simeq f^*(d)[2d]$ for $f$ smooth of relative dimension $d$
(Theorem [theorem-smooth-purity-all-admissible-coefficients]), and this
isomorphism gives the trace map.

Verdier duality (Theorems [theorem-verdier-biduality]
and [theorem-global-verdier-duality]) says that $\mathbb D=\cHom(-,\omega)$
is an involution of $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}$ exchanging $Rf_!$ with $Rf_*$. For smooth proper
$X$ it turns the trace map into a perfect pairing between $H^i$ and
$H^{2d-i}(d)$ (Corollary [corollary-cup-product-pairing]), and this
pairing is compatible with Frobenius
(Theorem [theorem-poincare-duality-frobenius]). Verdier duality also
gives the vanishing in (a) for such $X$
(Theorem [theorem-trace-isomorphism-top-degree]).

For the trace formula we use the Künneth formula for Verdier duals
(Lemma [lemma-external-duality-trace-morphism]), which turns a
correspondence $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ into a class on $C$; for an
endomorphism, $C$ is the graph. Restricting this class to the diagonal
gives the Lefschetz–Verdier formula
(Theorem [theorem-proper-pushforward-lefschetz-verdier]), which says that
on a proper scheme the trace of $u$ on cohomology is a sum of local terms
over the fixed locus.

This does not yet count points, for two reasons. A local term is computed
from $\cHom(c_2^*K,c_1^!K)$ near a fixed point, and the stalk of $K$ does
not determine it (Remark [remark-locality-warning]). Moreover $X$ need
not be proper. Both problems are settled by one computation on a curve: the
local term of Frobenius at a rational point is the trace on the stalk
(Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve]). The computation
works because Frobenius has zero differential, so that its graph meets
the diagonal with multiplicity one and is tangent to a coordinate axis. The
result is the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula
(Theorem [theorem-grothendieck-lefschetz-trace-formula]): for every Weil
complex $K$, $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Frob}^m\mid R\Gamma_c(X,K))$ is the
sum over $X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$ of the traces of Frobenius on the stalks.

Smooth purity and Verdier duality hold over any finite or algebraically
closed field, and their compatibility with Frobenius follows from their
construction (Section [sec-Weil-complexes]).

After Parts I and II we can write
the number of points of a smooth proper variety as an alternating sum of
powers of Frobenius eigenvalues. But we know nothing about the size of these
eigenvalues, so the formula alone estimates nothing. For a curve of genus $g$
the formula reads $N_m=1+q^m-\sum_j\alpha_j^m$. It gives Weil's bound
$|N_m-1-q^m|\le2gq^{m/2}$ only once we know that $|\alpha_j|=q^{1/2}$. This Part
proves the analogous statement in every dimension, Weil's axiom (d)
(Corollary [corollary-purity-cohomology-smooth-proper-variety]): for smooth
proper $X_0$ of pure dimension $d$, every eigenvalue $\alpha$ of Frobenius on
$H^i(X,\mathbf Q_\ell)$ satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|=q^{i/2}$ for every
complex embedding $\iota$.
Theorem [theorem-weil-conjectures-smooth-proper-schemes] deduces from it
the Riemann hypothesis, the integrality of the factors $P_i$ and their
independence of $\ell$.

For curves Weil proved this with the Jacobian. There the eigenvalues on $H^1$ are those of Frobenius on a Tate module, and the positivity of the Rosati
involution forces $|\alpha|=q^{1/2}$. In higher dimension, however, no such structure is available. Instead, Deligne's first proof [deligne74] fibred $X_0$ by a
Lefschetz pencil and used the monodromy of the pencil. In his second paper [deligne80], by contrast, he proved a theorem about all sheaves:

> if $K$ has weights at most $w$, then so does $Rf_!K$

(Theorem [theorem-weights-rf-shriek]; weights are defined in
Definition [definition-weights]). In particular, for the constant sheaf on a smooth proper $X_0$, the theorem gives the upper bound
$|\iota(\alpha)|\le q^{i/2}$ on $H^i$. Since Poincaré duality pairs $\alpha$ with $q^d/\alpha$ on $H^{2d-i}$, the upper bound on $H^{2d-i}$ gives the lower bound on $H^i$. Here we follow Laumon's proof [laumon87] of the Deligne–Laumon theorem, which replaces the Lefschetz pencil
by the $\ell$-adic Fourier transform.

The theorem has to be about sheaves because the proof fibres the variety,
locally, in curves over a variety of smaller dimension, and along such a fibration the direct image of the constant sheaf is no longer constant.
Everything therefore comes down to a pure lisse sheaf $F$ of weight $w$ on a
curve $C$. There we must show that $H^r_c(C,F)$ has weights at most $w+r$
(Theorem [theorem-weight-bound-curve]), and only $H^1_c$ is hard.

On a curve the one tool is the trace formula. It writes the $L$-function, a
product of local factors over the closed points, as the ratio of the
characteristic polynomials on $H^1_c$ and $H^2_c$. The difficulty is cancellation: a large local eigenvalue gives a local factor with a pole near the origin, but the other factors might cancel it. Rankin's trick from the theory of modular forms rules this out when the traces are real, because then
the even tensor powers have Euler factors with nonnegative coefficients. By
Lemma [lemma-positivity-convergence], no factor of such a product can have a
pole closer to the origin than the product itself. On an affine curve, moreover, only $H^2_c$ contributes poles, and their position is controlled by the
determinants. These determinants are pure because a lisse sheaf of rank one has
finite geometric monodromy (Section [sec-Sheaves-of-rank-one]). The outcome is the bound $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_x^\beta$, where $\beta$ is the largest determinant weight
(Proposition [proposition-bound-largest-determinant-weight]). Applied to exterior powers, this bound shows that every irreducible constituent of a real sheaf is
pure (Theorem [theorem-purity-real-sheaves-curves],
Chapter [chap-Purity-of-real-sheaves]).

This bounds eigenvalues at points of a curve. What we must bound, however, is
a cohomology group $H^1_c(\mathbf A^1,j_*M)$, for a pure lisse sheaf $M$ on a
dense open $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$. The Fourier transform (Chapter [chap-The-Fourier-transform]) turns this group into the stalk of a sheaf on
the dual line, and a twist of that sheaf is a quotient of a real sheaf. The
Plancherel formula, together with two facts about pure sheaves on curves
(Chapter [chap-Pure-sheaves-on-curves]), shows that the sheaf has weight $w+1$.

In higher dimension the same positivity shows that real sheaves on any
base are mixed (Theorem [theorem-real-constructible-sheaves-are-mixed]).
This lets us apply the curve case along a fibration
(Chapter [chap-The-Deligne-Laumon-theorem-in-general]). The Weil conjectures are then a
short deduction (Chapter [chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures]).

To define $Rf_!$ in
Part I we must compactify every separated
morphism of finite type, and to prove proper base change we must
dominate every proper morphism by a projective one. These are Nagata's
theorem and Chow's lemma (Appendix [chap-Nagata-compactification-and-Chows-lemma]). Nagata's
theorem, followed by normalization, also gives the smooth
compactification of a curve used in Part III
(Lemma [lemma-proper-smooth-model]).

Proper base change ends with a change of separably closed
ground field. There we need the cohomology of curves for all torsion
coefficients, including torsion divisible by the characteristic
(Theorem [theorem-cohomology-curves]). Purity starts from
sheaves of rank one. Their geometric monodromy is finite because
Frobenius fixes no class in $H^1$ of a curve
(Proposition [proposition-no-fixed-class-degree-one]). For
coefficients prime to the characteristic, both facts come from the
Jacobian. Indeed, $H^1(C,\mu_n)$ is the $n$-torsion of the Jacobian, and
a fixed class would give $\ell$-power torsion points of unbounded order
among its finitely many rational points.
Appendices [chap-Abelian-varieties], [chap-The-Picard-scheme-of-a-curve]
and [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves] prove both facts.

Rankin's argument in Chapter [chap-Purity-of-real-sheaves] rests on
the determinant weights of tensor and exterior powers
(Proposition [proposition-determinant-weights-tensor-operations]).
These come from the structure of the monodromy group
(Lemma [lemma-identity-component]), and
Appendix [chap-Algebraic-groups-in-characteristic-zero] proves the facts about algebraic
groups over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ behind it.

Appendix [chap-Specialization-and-contracting-correspondences] is of a different kind. Following
Varshavsky [varshavsky05], it computes the local terms of contracting
correspondences in a second way; Chapter [chap-The-trace-formula]
does not depend on it.

1. For Noetherian $X$, every locally closed subset is constructible,
   so in Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves](2) any finite stratification
   by locally closed subschemes may be used.
2. For finite $A$ and qcqs $X$, $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ is the pullback of the
   usual étale category $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X_{\acute{e}t},A)$ by
   Corollary [corollary-finite-tor-amplitude-under-comparison].
3. If $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, the ring $\Lambda(*)$ is a field,
   so each $P_i$ is a finite-dimensional vector space, and
   a lisse module is locally free of
   finite rank. In other words, a constructible $E$- or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaf is
   one that is lisse on the strata of a finite stratification
   [bhatt-scholze15, Definition 6.8.6].
4. If $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E$, locally on a stratum a constructible
   $\mathcal O_{E,X}$-module is $P\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_{E,X}$
   for a finitely generated $\mathcal O_E$-module $P$. For example,
   $\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E$ is constructible.
5. For the admissible coefficients, the constructible sheaves form an
   abelian category. For finite $A$ this is the classical theory of
   sheaves with finite stalks, and the other cases are
   Lemma [lemma-constructible-sheaves],
   Corollary [corollary-coefficient-heart-b] and
   Lemma [lemma-structure-integral-constructible-complexes], which we
   prove in Subsection [subsec-Integral-coefficients].
6. For finite $A$, a lisse $A_X$-module is the same as a locally
   constant sheaf with finite stalks. For $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E$ a lisse
   module may have torsion, such as $\mathcal O_{E,X}/\pi_E$; the lisse
   $\mathcal O_{E,X}$-modules without torsion are the locally free ones of
   finite rank, since a finitely generated torsion free $\mathcal O_E$-module
   is free.

Let $\mathcal V$ be a nonzero lisse Weil sheaf of rank $r$ on a smooth
geometrically connected curve. If the irreducible constituents
$\mathcal V_1,\dots,\mathcal V_n$ of $\mathcal V$ are pure of weights
$w_1,\dots,w_n$, then
$\operatorname{dw}_\iota(\mathcal V)=\sum_a\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal V_a)w_a/r$.
In particular a sheaf pure of weight $w$ has determinant weight $w$.

identity of rational functions, not of power series at $T=0$, since
$1/(q^dT)$ is not a power series in $T$.

What duality does not give is the absolute value of the eigenvalues
$\alpha$. In Chapters [chap-Weights]–[chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures] we prove

read them off from $Z(X_0,T)$ alone. In Chapter [chap-Proof-of-the-Weil-conjectures] we use
this to show that they are polynomials with integer coefficients that do
not depend on $\ell$.

Over $\mathcal O_E$, derived duality gives only the natural
universal coefficient exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow
\Ext^1_{\mathcal O_E}(H_c^{i+1}(X,K),\mathcal O_E)
\longrightarrow H^{2d-i}(X,K^\vee(d))
\longrightarrow
\Hom_{\mathcal O_E}(H_c^i(X,K),\mathcal O_E)
\longrightarrow0.
$$

It comes from applying derived Hom to a bounded finite free model of
$R\Gamma_c(X,K)$, since $\mathcal O_E$ has global dimension one.
The sequence need not split canonically, and because of its $\Ext^1$ term
the pairings on individual cohomology modules need not be perfect. For
example, on a point the perfect
complex $[\mathcal O_E\xrightarrow{\pi_E}\mathcal O_E]$ in degrees
$-1,0$ has $H^0=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$, whereas its dual has
$H^0=0$ and $H^1=\mathcal O_E/\pi_E$. Derived evaluation
is an isomorphism, but the degree-zero pairing is not perfect.

Over a finite ring $A$ that is not injective as a module over
itself, derived Hom out of a
bounded complex of finite projective modules records all the
groups $\Ext^i_A(-,A)$ of the cohomology modules, and this information
may be lost in their ordinary duals. Moreover, the cohomology modules of a
complex in $D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$ need not have finite Tor dimension, so the
derived pairing cannot be reduced to pairings of cohomology sheaves.

In Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences], $K_0$ need not be a lattice in a
lisse sheaf, and $\theta$ need not be invertible even when $\psi_E$ is.
The factor $\pi_E^{-N}$ is needed because $\psi_E$ itself need not be
integral: on a point, the automorphism $\ell^{-1}$ of $E$ preserves no lattice.
Even with this factor, $\theta$ cannot always be chosen invertible, already on
a point. On $E^2$, the two eigenvalues of $\operatorname{diag}(1,\ell)$
cannot both become units after multiplying the operator by a single
scalar. So Lemma [lemma-integral-models-rational-frobenius-correspondences]
only makes $\pi_E^N\psi_E$ integral, and the reductions of $\theta$ may fail to
be invertible. For this reason Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-frobenius-correspondence]
is stated for arbitrary Frobenius correspondences.

Let $X_0$ be a smooth curve and $y\in X_0(\mathbf F_{q^m})$. The
trace formula on $\mathbf P^1$ needs Proposition [proposition-frobenius-local-term-curve]
below, which says that the local term at $y$ of any morphism
$\psi:(\Phi_X^m)^*K\to K$ is the naive trace
$\operatorname{tr}_A(\psi_{\bar y}\mid K_{\bar y})$, also when $K$ is not
lisse at $y$. To prove it, we filter $K$ by the open complement of $y$ and the point $y$. By additivity of traces this reduces the proposition to two cases:
the point itself, where Lemma [lemma-local-terms-point] applies, and the case
$K_{\bar y}=0$, where we must show that the local term vanishes.

The second case needs a geometric argument. Indeed, the local term is defined on a neighbourhood of $(y,y)$ in $X\times X$, where the Frobenius graph
meets the diagonal, and the vanishing of the stalk at $y$ does not
by itself control it. For this we follow [sga5, III B, §§2–4]. In this approach the local term is a restriction map from the graph to the diagonal, and blowing up $(y,y)$ separates the two curves. After the blowup the local term becomes a restriction to punctured curves
near the point where two transverse divisors meet. There it vanishes when the monodromy is an $\ell$-group. In general we reduce to that case by passing to finite covers of degree prime to $\ell$
(Appendix [chap-Cohomology-of-torsion-sheaves-on-curves]); for such a cover the trace map
splits the pullback.

reason the vanishing holds for every $\psi$, for every finite $\ell$-primary
ring $A$, and for every $K$ with $K_{\bar y}=0$. In particular it holds for
$j_!K$ on $\mathbf P^1$, which is not lisse at infinity. We forget the
$A$-action only in Lemma [lemma-cohomology-near-two-transverse-divisors],
to detect a zero object.

In (8.1), smooth base change assumes that $g$ is smooth and
allows any $f$ of finite type, whereas proper base change assumes that $f$
is proper and allows any $g$. Smooth purity
(Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity]) gives a
third base change isomorphism $g'^*f^!\simeq f'^!g^*$, for the exceptional
inverse image, when $f$ is smooth and $g$ is arbitrary. By contrast, neither

In (8.1), smooth base change assumes that $g$ is smooth and
allows any $f$ of finite type. Proper base change assumes that $f$ is
proper and allows any $g$. Smooth purity
(Chapter [chap-Smooth-purity]) gives a
third base change isomorphism $g'^*f^!\simeq f'^!g^*$, for the exceptional
inverse image, when $f$ is smooth and $g$ is arbitrary. Neither smooth nor
proper base change applies to the open immersion
$j:\mathbf G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ of the beginning of this chapter,
where base change along the immersion of the origin fails.
Theorem [theorem-smooth-base-change-all-admissible] does not apply
because the immersion of the origin is not smooth. Proper base change does
not apply because $j$ is not proper.

objects.body:
**Convention.** For proper base change, schemes are arbitrary unless an additional
hypothesis is stated. The theorem concerns the classical part of
$D^+(T_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, for a discrete commutative ring $\Lambda$,
but the intermediate calculations (acyclicity, curves, Chow's lemma) are made on
$T_{\acute{e}t}$, with abelian sheaves or modules over its discrete constant
ring. There we write $D^+(T_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ for the bounded below derived
category. Inverse image of étale sheaves along $u:S\to T$ is written
$u^*:\Sh(T_{\acute{e}t})\to\Sh(S_{\acute{e}t})$, as for module sheaves; it is exact,
and so is its extension to $D^+(T_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D^+(S_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$. The derived direct image is written $Ru_*$. Torsion always
means torsion of the underlying abelian sheaves.

Proper base change holds for torsion coefficients of every
characteristic. Accordingly, until Section [sec-Finite-coefficients], $\ell$
denotes an arbitrary prime, which may equal a residue
characteristic. From that section on, we return to the standing
finite-type hypotheses and the standing condition on $\ell$.

**Convention.** Put $k_0=\mathbf F_q$, $k=\overline{\mathbf F}_q$, and fix a prime
$\ell\nmid q$ and a field embedding $\iota:\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$.
For $X_0/k_0$ separated of finite type, we write $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$,
and for a closed point $x$ of $X_0$ write $\deg(x)=[\kappa(x):k_0]$ for
its degree and $q_x=q^{\deg(x)}=\#\kappa(x)$. Moreover, geometric Frobenius, Weil complexes and their Frobenius operators are those of
Section [sec-Weil-complexes]. As there, a Weil sheaf is a Weil complex concentrated in degree zero, and the six operations carry Weil structures to Weil
structures. In this Part Weil sheaves and complexes have coefficients in
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$; a Weil complex $K$ with coefficients in a finite extension
$E\subset\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ is called pure, mixed, or of weights at most $w$ if
$K\otimes_E\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ is (see Lemma [lemma-weil-sheaves-point-mixed] and the
remark after it for why scalars must be extended).

On a connected normal scheme of finite type over a field, we identify a
lisse $E$-sheaf with the corresponding continuous representation of the
profinite fundamental group, by
Proposition [proposition-lattices-representations-normal-scheme], proved in
Section [sec-Lisse-sheaves-as-representations] below. This covers all arguments with representations below, since they take place on smooth schemes. Moreover, a lisse Weil $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-sheaf has a lisse Weil model over some finite extension
$E/\mathbf Q_\ell$, and two models become identified after a finite extension of
scalars. This model includes the Weil isomorphism, which need not
preserve a geometric $\mathcal O_E$-lattice.

For a geometrically connected smooth curve $U_0$, put $U=U_0\times_{k_0}k$
and choose a geometric point $\bar\eta$ of $U$. We then write $\pi_1(U)$ and $\pi_1(U_0)$ for $\pi_1(U,\bar\eta)$ and $\pi_1(U_0,\bar\eta)$.  The inverse image
of the integer powers of geometric Frobenius in $\pi_1(U_0)$ is its Weil
group $W(U_0)$.  It contains the geometric fundamental group, with an
exact sequence

$$
1\longrightarrow \pi_1(U)\longrightarrow W(U_0)
\xrightarrow{\deg}\mathbf Z\longrightarrow1.
$$

A degree-one lift $s$ splits this sequence as a group extension.
In these terms, lisse Weil sheaves are the same as representations $\rho$ of $W(U_0)$,
defined over a finite extension of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, whose restriction to
$\pi_1(U)$ is continuous. For
$x\in|U_0|$, the local Frobenius $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ at $x$
(Theorem [theorem-trace-formula-euler-product]) is a conjugacy class of degree $\deg(x)$.

For $K\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ the unit of the adjunction between
$\nu_X^*:D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and
$R\nu_{X,*}$ is an isomorphism

$$
K\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*K.
\tag{2.7}
$$

Consequently $\nu_X^*:D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is fully faithful,
and there is a canonical isomorphism

$$
R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\nu_X^*K)
\simeq R\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},K).
$$

Let $X$ be a scheme and $\mathcal A$ a Grothendieck abelian category.
For a bounded below object $K\in D(X_{\acute{e}t},\mathcal A)$, the unit of the
derived adjunction $\nu_X^*\dashv R\nu_{X,*}$ is an isomorphism

$$
K\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*K.
\tag{2.7}
$$

Here $\nu_X^*$ on derived categories is induced by the exact inverse image
on sheaves. In particular, taking $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Mod}(\Lambda)$ for a
discrete commutative ring $\Lambda$ gives the comparison on
$D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$.

For every $K\in D(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and every $M\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$,
the map

$$
\Hom_{D(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)}(K,M)\longrightarrow
\Hom_{D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)}(\nu_X^*K,\nu_X^*M),\qquad
f\longmapsto\nu_X^*f,
$$

is bijective. Here $\nu_X^*$ is applied termwise to complexes, and no
boundedness assumption on $K$ is needed. Consequently
$\nu_X^*:D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ is fully faithful.

Let $X$ be a scheme and $\mathcal A$ a Grothendieck abelian category.
For every $L\in D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\mathcal A)$ there is a canonical
isomorphism, natural in $L$,

$$
R\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},R\nu_{X,*}L)
\simeq R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},L).
$$

No boundedness assumption on $L$ is needed. In particular, for a discrete
commutative ring $\Lambda$ and $K\in D^+(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$, there is
a canonical isomorphism

$$
R\Gamma(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\nu_X^*K)
\simeq R\Gamma(X_{\acute{e}t},K).
$$

Let $f:X\to S$ be proper with $S$ qcqs. There are a proper
surjection $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and a closed immersion
$i_S:\widetilde X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^n_S$ such that
$f\pi=q_Si_S$, where $q_S:\mathbf P^n_S\to S$ is the projection. Moreover,

$$
i_X=(\pi,i_S):\widetilde X\hookrightarrow
X\times_S\mathbf P^n_S=\mathbf P^n_X
$$

is a closed immersion. Both $\pi$ and $f\pi$ are projective.

Let $f:X\to S$ be proper with $S$ qcqs. There are a proper
surjection $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and a closed immersion
$i_S:\widetilde X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^n_S$ such that
$f\pi=q_Si_S$, where $q_S:\mathbf P^n_S\to S$ is the projection.

Moreover,

$$
i_X=(\pi,i_S):\widetilde X\hookrightarrow
X\times_S\mathbf P^n_S=\mathbf P^n_X
$$

is a closed immersion. Both $\pi$ and $f\pi$ are projective.

Let $f:X\to S$ be separated and of finite type with $S$ qcqs.
There are an integer $n\geq 0$, a scheme $\widetilde X$, a proper
surjection $\pi:\widetilde X\to X$ and an immersion
$i_S:\widetilde X\to\mathbf P^n_S$ such that $f\pi=q_Si_S$, where
$q_S:\mathbf P^n_S\to S$ is the projection.

attrs.title: Classical sheaves as the essential image

objects.body:
Let $X$ be a scheme and $A$ a Grothendieck abelian category. The comparison
functor

$$
\nu_X^*:\Sh(X_{\acute{e}t},A)\longrightarrow
\Sh(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},A)
$$

is fully faithful.

For sheaves of sets, the unit $F\to\nu_{X,*}\nu_X^*F$ is an isomorphism.
For a sheaf of sets $G$ on $X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, the following
conditions are equivalent:

1. There is an étale sheaf $F$ and an isomorphism $G\simeq\nu_X^*F$.
2. $G$ is classical in the sense of Definition
   [definition-classical-pro-etale-sheaves].
3. The counit $\nu_X^*\nu_{X,*}G\to G$ is an isomorphism.

Let $\Lambda$ be a discrete commutative ring and $G$ a sheaf of
$\Lambda_X$-modules. If $G$ is classical, that is, if for every affine
étale presentation $U=\varprojlim_iU_i$ the restriction maps induce an
isomorphism

$$
\varinjlim_i G(U_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }G(U)
$$

of $\Lambda$-modules, then there is an étale $\Lambda$-module sheaf $F$
and an isomorphism $\nu_X^*F\simeq G$. Consequently, $\nu_X^*$ is an
exact equivalence between $\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)$ and
the full subcategory of classical $\Lambda_X$-module sheaves on
$X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.

objects.body:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C$ be a separated scheme of finite
type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, and let $F$ be a classical torsion
abelian sheaf on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. With cohomology taken on
$C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, the following assertions hold:

- $(C_{1})$ $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>2$.
- $(C_{2})$ If $C$ is affine, $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>1$.
- $(C_{3})$ If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ and $F$ is $p$-primary,
  $H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>1$.
- $(C_{4})$ If $F$ is constructible with finite stalks and prime to
  $\operatorname{char}k$, all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite.
- $(C_{5})$ If $C$ is proper and $F$ is constructible with finite stalks,
  all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite.
- $(C_{6})$ If $k'/k$ is an extension of algebraically closed fields and $F$
  is prime to $\operatorname{char}k$, the pullback maps
  $H^q(C,F)\to H^q(C_{k'},F|)$ are isomorphisms.
- $(C_{7})$ If $C$ is proper, the maps in $(C_6)$ are isomorphisms for every
  torsion $F$.
- $(C_{8})$ For any open $U\subseteq C$, restriction
  $H^2(C,F)\to H^2(U,F|_U)$ is surjective.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C$ be a separated scheme of finite
type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, and let $F$ be a torsion abelian sheaf
on $C_{\acute{e}t}$. Then

$$
H^q(C,F)=0\qquad(q>2).
$$

By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], the same vanishing holds for the classical sheaf
$\nu_C^*F$ with cohomology taken on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$; every classical
torsion abelian sheaf on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is of this form.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C$ be an affine scheme of finite
type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, and let $F$ be a torsion abelian sheaf
on $C_{\acute{e}t}$. Then

$$
H^q(C,F)=0\qquad(q>1).
$$

By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], the same vanishing holds for the classical sheaf
$\nu_C^*F$ with cohomology taken on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$; every classical
torsion abelian sheaf on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ is of this form.

If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ and $F$ is $p$-primary,
$H^q(C,F)=0$ for $q>1$.

If $F$ is constructible with finite stalks and prime to
$\operatorname{char}k$, all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite.

If $C$ is proper and $F$ is constructible with finite stalks,
all $H^q(C,F)$ are finite.

If $k'/k$ is an extension of algebraically closed fields and $F$
is prime to $\operatorname{char}k$, the pullback maps
$H^q(C,F)\to H^q(C_{k'},F|)$ are isomorphisms.

Let $k'/k$ be an extension of algebraically closed fields, let $C$ be a
proper scheme of finite type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, let $\Lambda$
be a commutative ring, and let $F$ be a sheaf of $\Lambda$-modules on
$C_{\acute{e}t}$ whose geometric stalks are torsion abelian groups.
The pullback maps

$$
H^q(C,F)\longrightarrow H^q(C_{k'},F|_{C_{k'}})
$$

are isomorphisms for all $q\geq0$, with cohomology taken on the
underlying abelian sheaves. The statement applies to any cartesian
square presenting the base change $C_{k'}$.

By Theorem [theorem-bounded-below-cohomology-comparison], the same holds for the classical sheaf $\nu_C^*F$,
with cohomology taken on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$ and
$(C_{k'})_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$.

For any open $U\subseteq C$, restriction
$H^2(C,F)\to H^2(U,F|_U)$ is surjective.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, let $C$ be a separated scheme of finite
type over $k$ with $\dim C\leq1$, and let $F$ be a classical torsion
abelian sheaf on $C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$. With cohomology taken on
$C_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t}$, the following assertions hold:

For $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, every object of $\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ is compact in $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$.
More precisely, for $C\in\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ and every family $(K_\lambda)$
of objects of $\Dic(X,\Lambda)$, the natural map

$$
\bigoplus_\lambda\Hom(C,K_\lambda)
\longrightarrow\Hom\Bigl(C,\bigoplus_\lambda K_\lambda\Bigr)
$$

is an isomorphism.

For $\Lambda=E$ or $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, every object of $\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ is compact in $\Loc(\Dbc(X,\Lambda))$.
More precisely, for $C\in\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ and every family $(K_\lambda)$
of objects of $\Dic(X,\Lambda)$, the natural map

$$
\bigoplus_\lambda\Hom(C,K_\lambda)
\longrightarrow\Hom\Bigl(C,\bigoplus_\lambda K_\lambda\Bigr)
$$

is an isomorphism.

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated. For a discrete
Noetherian $\Lambda$, every constructible
pro-étale $\Lambda_X$-module sheaf is classical. The functor
$\nu_X^*$ gives an equivalence from constructible étale sheaves of
$\Lambda$-modules to $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$, and an equivalence
$D^b_c(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\to\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ of bounded constructible
derived categories.

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let $\Lambda$ be a
discrete commutative Noetherian ring. Every constructible pro-étale
$\Lambda_X$-module sheaf $F$ is classical: for every pro-étale affine
presentation $U=\varprojlim_i U_i$ with affine étale stages, the
restriction maps induce an isomorphism of $\Lambda$-modules

$$
\varinjlim_i F(U_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }F(U).
$$

Here constructibility is the affine-local finite-presentation condition
of Definition [definition-constructible-sheaves].

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let $\Lambda$ be a
discrete commutative Noetherian ring. There is an equivalence from the
full subcategory of constructible étale sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules
to $\Cons(X,\Lambda)$ whose forward functor, after inclusion into all
pro-étale $\Lambda_X$-module sheaves, is naturally isomorphic to the
restriction of the canonical inverse image $\nu_X^*$.

Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let $\Lambda$ be a
discrete commutative Noetherian ring. Let

$$
\nu_X^*:D(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\longrightarrow
D(X_{\mathrm{pro}\acute{e}t},\Lambda)
$$

be the functor obtained by applying the exact inverse image termwise to
complexes, so that $H^q(\nu_X^*K)\simeq\nu_X^*H^q(K)$ for every
$q\in\mathbf Z$. Then $\nu_X^*$ restricts to an equivalence
$D^b_c(X_{\acute{e}t},\Lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Dbc(X,\Lambda)$ of the
full bounded constructible subcategories.
*Shared context.* Let $X$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let $\Lambda$ be discrete Noetherian.

If $g$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the canonical natural

$$
\nu_Y^*Rg_{\acute{e}t,*}K\longrightarrow

\tag{2.9}

Let $(R,J)$ be a henselian pair, let $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be
proper, and let $i:Z_0=Z\times_R\operatorname{Spec}(R/J)\hookrightarrow Z$.

Let $c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$ be a correspondence, and let
$Z\hookrightarrow X$ have ideal $I$. Let $F_0$ be a connected component
of $\Fix(c)$ that is open and closed and whose image meets $Z$. Choose

$$
I_2=c_2^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_W\subset
I_1=c_1^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_W,
\qquad I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}\quad\text{for some }n\geq1.

Let $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$, let $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ be a cohomological
correspondence, and let $u_Z$ be the restriction
(E.21) to $Z$ of $u|_W$, for the
correspondence $c|_W$, with $c_Z:C_Z=(W\cap c_1^{-1}Z)_{\mathrm{red}}\to
Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times Z_{\mathrm{red}}$. Then $h_{F_0}$ is an
isomorphism after reduction, and

$$
\operatorname{Tr}_c(u)|_{F_0}
=(h_{F_0})_*\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{c_Z}(u_Z)|_{F_{0,Z}}\bigr),
$$

where $(h_{F_0})_*:H^0(F_{0,Z},\omega_{F_{0,Z}})\to H^0(F_0,\omega_{F_0})$
is the induced isomorphism. In particular, if $F_0$ is proper, then
$\operatorname{LT}_{F_0}(u)=\operatorname{LT}_{F_{0,Z}}(u_Z)$.

Let $c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times X$ be a correspondence, and let
$Z\hookrightarrow X$ have ideal $I$. Let $F_0$ be a connected component
of $\Fix(c)$ that is open and closed and whose image meets $Z$. Choose
an open neighbourhood $W\subset C$ of $F_0$ on which

$$
I_2=c_2^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_W\subset
I_1=c_1^{-1}(I)\mathcal O_W,
\qquad I_2^n\subset I_1^{n+1}\quad\text{for some }n\geq1.

Let $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{ctf}}(X,A)$, let $u:c_2^*K\to c_1^!K$ be a cohomological
correspondence, and let $u_Z$ be the restriction
(E.21) to $Z$ of $u|_W$, for the
correspondence $c|_W$, with $c_Z:C_Z=(W\cap c_1^{-1}Z)_{\mathrm{red}}\to
Z_{\mathrm{red}}\times Z_{\mathrm{red}}$. Then $h_{F_0}$ is an

$$

In particular, if $F_0$ is proper, then

of weights at most $w$. Then $R^if_!F$ is mixed of weights at most

Let $T$ be qcqs, let $U\subseteq T$ be a quasi-compact open, and let
$q:W\to T$ be separated and of finite type, with $W_U\to U$ an
isomorphism. Then there is a $U$-admissible blow-up

$$
b:T'=\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal K}(T)\longrightarrow T
$$

whose centre satisfies $V(\mathcal K)=T\setminus U$, such that the
strict transform $W'\to T'$ of $q$ is an open immersion. In particular,
$b^{-1}(U)$ is schematically dense in $T'$.
